Initially created: 2025-12-05T09:40:38.731+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Later School Tiāntái
The Qí Xuāndé Empress Dowager issued an edict to Xiāo Yǎn, promoting him from Duke of Jiàn'ān Commandery to Duke of Liáng.
Yǎn accepted the ambition.
Soon after, he was promoted to King.
Soon after, he accepted the abdication of Qí.
The state was thus named Liáng.
Gāozǔ Wǔdì,
whose taboo name was Yǎn,
courtesy name Shúdá,
and pet name Liàn'ér,
was a native of Zhōngdū Lǐ in Nánlánlíng,
with the surname Xiāo.
He was of the same lineage as Qí, descending from Huáin Yīn Lìng Zhěng.
Three generations later came Shùnzhī.
Shùnzhī was a collateral cousin to Qí Gāodì.
The Emperor
was Shùnzhī's son.
According to the "Record of Emperor Wǔ" in the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, there are eighteen scrolls in total.
Numbered one and two in order.
This scroll,
under "Emperor Wǔ,"
should have the character
(one).
Tiānjiān first year (Rénwǔ, 502 CE).
From this year, before the third month,
it was still the second year of Zhōngxīng under Qí Hédì.
1 Spring,
first month.
Qí Hédì dispatched Acting Shìzhōng Xí Chǎnwén and others to express sympathy and solace in Jiànkāng.
2 The Grand Marshal Yǎn issued an order:
"All wasteful expenditures from the time of Dōnghūn,
except for those that serve to practice rites and music,
or to maintain military preparedness,
are to be entirely prohibited."
3 On the day Wùxū,
the Xuāndé Empress Dowager was welcomed into the palace to hold court and issue decrees.
Yǎn relinquished his authority to issue decrees.
Yǎn's exercise of authority to issue decrees is seen in the previous scroll, last year.
He temporarily relinquished it to observe the popular sentiment.
Cháo
is pronounced as "yáo" in straight-through tone.
4 On the day Jǐhài,
Xiāo Bǐng, the General who Pacifies the North, was made Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nányǎn Zhōu.
Bǐng
was Yǎn's paternal cousin.
5 On the day Rén'yín,

Grand Marshal Yǎn was promoted to Grand Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, permitted to wear his sword and shoes into the palace hall, and to be addressed without his personal name during ceremonies.
6 On the day Jǐyǒu,
Wáng Liàng, the Chief Clerk to the Grand Marshal, was appointed Central Secretariat Director and Director of the Department of State Affairs.
7 Initially,

the Grand Marshal, together with the Palace Attendant Fàn Yún, the Grand Administrator of Nánqīnghé Shěn Yuē, and the Chief Clerk of the Right to the Minister of Education Rèn Fǎng, were all residing in the Western Residence of the Prince of Jìnglíng.
This event is recorded in scroll 136, during Qí Wǔdì's Yǒngmíng second year.
Shǒu
is pronounced as "yòu" in "shì yòu" tone.
Rèn
is pronounced as "rén."
Fǎng
is pronounced as "fēn liǎng" tone.
Dūn
means "thick" or "generous."
Hǎo
is pronounced as "hū dào" tone.
He appointed Yún as Consultative Adjutant to the Grand Marshal and concurrently Chief Recorder.
Yǎn was a Recorder of the Department of State Affairs.
He made Yún responsible for recording affairs of the office.
He was made Military Adjutant of Yǎn's Grand General of Agile Cavalry office.
Piào
is pronounced as "pǐ miào" tone.
Qí
is pronounced as "qí jì" tone.
He participated in planning and deliberation.
Former Grand Administrator of Wúxīng Xiè Fěi and Libationer of the Directorate of Education Hé Yìn had both previously resigned their offices and returned home.
At the beginning of Qí Míngdì's Jiànwǔ era,
Fěi and Yìn both resigned their offices and left.
Fěi
is pronounced as "fū wěi" tone.
Xiān
is pronounced as "xī jiàn" tone.
Neither Fěi nor Yìn came.
The Grand Marshal secretly harbored the ambition to accept the abdication.
Shěn Yuē subtly broached the subject,
but the Grand Marshal did not respond.
On another day,
he further said:
"The present differs from antiquity.
One cannot expect pure customs in this age.
Pure customs
refer to the simple customs of antiquity.
Everyone hopes to achieve even a small功.
Now even children and herdsmen know that the Qí dynasty's mandate is exhausted,
and that Your Excellency should succeed to its destiny.
Astrological portents and prophecies are also clearly manifest.
The will of Heaven cannot be defied,
and popular sentiment cannot be lost.
If the Mandate of Heaven rests with you,
even if you wish to be humble and modest,
it cannot be helped."
The Yì Jīng says: "Modesty, when honored, shines forth."
"I am still thinking about it."
Yuē said:
"When Your Excellency first established your command at Fán and Miǎn,
that was the time to think.
Now the royal enterprise is accomplished,
what more is there to think about?
If you do not quickly settle this great undertaking,
should even one person raise an objection,
it would damage your prestige and virtue.
Moreover, people are not metal or stone;
the times are difficult to guarantee.
How can you bequeath the fief of Jiàn'ān to your descendants?
If the Son of Heaven returns to the capital,
and the high officials are in their positions,
then the distinction between ruler and minister will be settled,
and there will be no more divergent hearts.
With a sagacious ruler above
and loyal ministers below,
how could anyone dare to join Your Excellency in rebellion again?"
The Grand Marshal assented.
When Yuē left,
the Grand Marshal summoned Fàn Yún and told him.
Yún's reply was roughly in agreement with Yuē's intent.
The Grand Marshal said:
"The wise are indeed so in agreement without prior consultation.
Bring Xiūwén back with you early tomorrow!"
Jiāng
means "to carry,"
"to hold,"
"to lead."
Xiūwén
was Shěn Yuē's courtesy name.
He spoke to Yuē.
Yuē said:
"You must wait for me!"
Yún agreed,
but Yuē entered earlier than planned.
The Grand Marshal ordered the drafting of the relevant documents.
Yuē then produced imperial edicts and various appointments from his bosom.
The Grand Marshal did not change anything.
Shortly after, Yún arrived from outside.
He reached the palace gate
but could not enter.
He paced outside the Shòuguāng Pavilion,
only exclaiming,
"Duōduō!"
There was a Shòuguāng Bureau within the southern imperial forbidden palace.
Duō
is pronounced as "dāng mò" tone.
Máo Huǎng said: "Duōduō"
is an exclamation of sighing.
He asked:
"How am I to be placed?"
Yuē raised his hand to the left,
meaning he would be placed as the Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs.
Chǔ
is pronounced as "chāng lǚ" tone.
"It does not fall short of my expectations."
After a moment,
the Grand Marshal summoned Yún in.
He praised Yuē's outstanding talent and wisdom,
and also said:
"I raised troops three years ago.
In the eleventh month of Yǒngyuán second year of Dōnghūn Hóu,
Yǎn raised troops.
From then until now is exactly three years.
However, it is you two who have accomplished this imperial enterprise."
On the day Jiǎyín,
an imperial edict promoted the Grand Marshal to Prime Minister,
overseeing all governmental affairs, and Governor of Yáng Zhōu.
He was enfeoffed with ten commanderies as Duke of Liáng.
At that time, the ten commanderies of Liáng Jùn in Yù Zhōu, Lìyáng, Yìxīng in Nánxú Zhōu, Huáinán, Xuānchéng, Wúxīng, Kuàijī, Xīn'ān, and Dōngyáng in Yáng Zhōu, were made the Duchy of Liáng.
Xiāng
is pronounced as "xī liàng" tone.
The Hundred Offices of Liáng were established.
The title of Recorder of the Department of State Affairs was removed,
and the position of Grand General of Agile Cavalry remained as before.
Second month,
on the day Xīnyǒu,
the Duke of Liáng formally accepted the mandate.
Qí Xiāngdōng Wáng Bǎojì
was the son of Ānlù Zhāowáng Miǎn.
Miǎn
was the younger brother of Qí Míngdì.
Miǎn,
read as "Mǐ Yǎn".
When Dōnghūn Hóu died,
Bǎojì expected the popular sentiment to turn to him,
and sat waiting for the imperial carriage.
Subsequently, Wáng Zhēnguó and others presented the head to Liáng Gōng.
Liáng Gōng appointed Bǎojì as Tàicháng,
but Bǎojì felt uneasy in his heart.
On the day Rénxū,
Liáng Gōng accused Bǎojì of rebellion,
and killed him along with his younger brothers, Jiānglíng Gōng Bǎolǎn and Rǔnán Gōng Bǎohóng.
8 On the day Bǐngyín,
an edict was issued for Liáng Guó to select all important officials,
all to conform to the system of the celestial court.
Thereupon, Shěn Yuē was made Lìbù Shàngshū and concurrent Yòu Púshè,
and Fàn Yún was made Shìzhōng.
Liáng Gōng kept Dōnghūn Hóu's leftover women,
which somewhat interfered with governmental affairs.
Fàn Yún spoke about this,
but Liáng Gōng did not heed him.
Yún entered to see him together with Shìzhōng and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Mào.
From Shěn Yuē to Wáng Mào,
all were officials of Liáng Guó.
Jiàn,
read as "Xián Biàn".
"In the past, when Pèi Gōng entered Guān,
he did not favor any women.
This is why Fàn Zēng feared his great ambition.
The story is found in Volume 9, Hàn Gāodì, Year 1.
People across the land are looking forward to your reputation;
why follow in the footsteps of a chaotic and fallen regime,
and be burdened by female virtue?"
The Zuǒzhuàn says: Fù Chén said: Female virtue has no limit.
Dù Yù's commentary says: The ambition of women,
if approached, knows no bounds or contentment.
Lěi,
read as "Lì Ruì".
"Fàn Yún's words are correct.
If Your Grace truly has the world at heart,
there is no reason to keep these."
Liáng Gōng remained silent.
Yún immediately requested to bestow the remaining women upon Wáng Mào.
Liáng Gōng admired his intention and granted it.
The next day,
Yún and Mào were each gifted a million coins.
On the day Bǐngxū,
an edict was issued to Liáng Gōng to increase his fief by ten commanderies
and advance his peerage to king.
At this time, Nánqiáo and Lújiāng of Yùzhōu,
Xúnyáng of Jiāngzhōu,
Wǔchāng and Xīyáng of Yǐngzhōu,
Nánlángyé, Nándōnghǎi, and Jìnlíng of Nánsúzhōu,
and Línhǎi and Yǒngjiā of Yángzhōu—these ten commanderies were added to Liáng Guó.
On the day Guǐsì,
he received the mandate,
and a general amnesty was granted within his state and the prefectures and commanderies
for all crimes below death.
From the advancement of his peerage to king onwards,
all edicts were issued in the name of Xuāndé Tàihòu exercising imperial authority.
9 On the day Xīnchǒu,
Qí Shàolíng Wáng Bǎoyōu, Jìnxī Wáng Bǎosōng, and Guìyáng Wáng Bǎozhēn were killed.
The Nánshǐ Qí Jì records
"Bǎoyōu",
while his biography records
"Bǎoxiū".
All three kings were sons of Míngdì.
When Liáng Wáng was about to kill the Qí princes,
the guards were not yet strict.
The eunuch Yán Wénzhì, from Púyáng Wáng Bǎoyín's household, conspired with his attendants Má Gǒng and others to secretly dig a hole in the wall to let Bǎoyín escape at night.
A small boat was prepared at the riverbank,
and Bǎoyín wore a black cloth robe,
with over a thousand coins tied around his waist.
He secretly went to the riverside,
treading barefoot,
his feet having no intact skin.
The guards pursued him until dawn.
Bǎoyín pretended to be a fisherman,
floating up and down the river for over ten lǐ,
and the pursuers did not suspect him.
After they dispersed,
he crossed to the west bank and took refuge in the home of a commoner, Huà Wénróng.
"Wait for dispersal" means
waiting for the pursuers to disperse.
Huà,
read as "Hù Huà".
He hired a donkey and rode it,
hiding by day and traveling by night,
arriving at the east city of Shòuyáng.
The Wèi garrison commander Dù Yuánlún rushed to inform the governor of Yángzhōu, Rènchéng Wáng Chéng,
who sent carriages and cavalry to escort him.
Bǎoyín was sixteen years old at the time,
emaciated from walking,
and those who saw him thought he was a captive being sold.
Chéng treated him with the rites due to a guest.
Bǎoyín requested to wear mourning clothes for his deceased lord (the emperor), the most severe form of mourning.
Chéng sent someone to explain the circumstances and rites,
and provided him with the less severe mourning clothes for a deceased elder brother.
Chéng led his officials to offer condolences.
Bǎoyín behaved courteously in his residence,
maintaining the demeanor of extreme sorrow.
According to the rites,
one should show extreme sorrow during the mourning for one's lord or father.
Shuài,
read as "lǜ".
Chǔ,
read as "Chāng Lǚ".
Thus, all offered condolences and comfort;
only the Xiàhóu clan did not appear.
The Xiàhóu clan was originally from Qiáojùn, Qiáo County,
residing in Shòuyáng.
Xià,
read as "Hù Yǎ".
Chéng deeply esteemed him.
This sets the stage for Xiāo Bǎoyín's later eminence in Wèi but his ultimate failure.
10 Qí Hédì returned east,
meaning he was returning east to Jiànkāng.
After the military campaigns in Jīngzhōu,
both public and private resources were depleted.
Dànbō diligently governed,
greatly expanding military farms,
reducing corvée labor,
and visiting the families of soldiers who died in battle,
supplying their needs.
Feeling that he held a heavy responsibility at a young age,
he said to his subordinate officials:
"If governance is not good,
it is something that gentlemen should collectively regret.
I am now open-minded;
you should hide nothing!"
Consequently, everyone was able to express their thoughts fully.
When people had lawsuits, they would stand before him awaiting instructions,
and decisions were made in an instant,
with no backlog of cases in the offices.
The people of Jīng were greatly pleased.
11 Qí Hédì arrived at Gūshú.
On the day Bǐngchén,
an edict was issued to abdicate the throne to Liáng.
12 On the day Dīngsì,
Lúlíng Wáng Bǎoyuán died.
It was not from illness.
Bǎoyuán
was the fifth son of Qí Míngdì.
13 The Lǔyáng Mán, led by Lǔ Běiyàn and others, raised an army and attacked Wèi Yǐngzhōu.
Wèi established Yǐngzhōu at Rǔyīn.
Also,
Yǐngchuān Prefecture formerly had Yǐngzhōu established there.
14 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Xīnyǒu,
Xuāndé Tàihòu issued an order saying:
"The Western Edict has arrived."
Although Qí Hédì had already arrived at Gūshú,
his territory was still west of Jiànkāng,
hence "Western Edict".
"To follow the precedents of previous dynasties" means
taking previous dynasties as standards.
"Tomorrow, I can appear before the imperial carriage."
"Míng" means
the next morning.
"This humble widow will retire to a separate palace."
In ancient times, when a ruler died,
his surviving wife would refer to herself as "humble widow".
Shǐ,
read as "Shū Lì".
Xǐ,
read as "Sī Shì".
Fú,
pronounced "fú".
On the day Rénxū,
an imperial proclamation was issued,
dispatching concurrent Tàibǎo and Shàngshūlìng Liàng and others to present the imperial seal and sash to Liáng Gōng's palace.
Liàng refers to Wáng Liàng.
On the day Bǐngyín,
Liáng Wáng ascended the imperial throne in the southern suburbs,
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the reign title.
He began to change the reign title to Tiānjiān.
He posthumously bestowed the title of Chéngxiàng upon his elder brother Yì,
enfeoffed him as Chángshā Wáng,
and gave him the posthumous title Xuānwǔ.
His funeral rites were to follow the precedent of Jìn Ānpíng Xiàn Wáng.
Yì was killed by Dōnghūn Hóu,
and his funeral was not conducted according to rites.
Now, he was to be buried according to the rites for Jìn Ānpíng Wáng Fú.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Shùn Hè Dì 奉和帝 was enfeoffed as the King of Bālíng,
and was housed in Gūshú.
The ceremonies of honor and distinction
all emulated those of the early Qí dynasty.
This imitated the rites for revering the King of Rǔyīn of the Qí dynasty.
The Empress Wáng 王 was made the Queen of Bālíng.
In the Qí era, the enfeoffments of kings and marquises
were all downgraded and abridged.
"Downgraded" means
a king was downgraded to a duke,
and a duke to a marquis.
"Abridged" means
their feudal states were abolished.
*Shěng* 省
is pronounced *suǒgěng*.
This was to prepare for the three distinguished guests (sān kè).
The deceased imperial father was posthumously honored as Emperor Wén,
with the temple name Tàizǔ;
the deceased imperial mother was honored as Empress Xiàn.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: "The *Nán Shǐ* says the posthumous honors were conferred in the fifth month."
We follow the *Liáng Shū* here.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán of the Marquis of Dōnghūn,
Xī Shì 郗氏 died in Xiāngyáng.
*Xī* 郗
is pronounced *chǒuzhī*.
The imperial younger brother, Grand Protector Hóng 宏, was established as the King of Línchuān;
the Inspector of Nánxú Prefecture, Xiù 秀, as the King of Ānchéng;
the Inspector of Yōng Prefecture, Wěi 偉, as the King of Jiàn'ān;
the General of the Left Guard, Huī 恢, as the King of Póyáng;
and the Inspector of Jīng Prefecture, Dàn 憺, as the King of Shǐxīng.
Hóng was appointed Inspector of Yáng Prefecture.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Wáng Liàng 王亮, the Director of the Central Secretariat, was appointed Minister of Personnel;
Wáng Yíng 王瑩, the Chief Clerk of the Chancellor, was appointed Director of the Central Secretariat;
Shěn Yuē 沈約, the Minister of Personnel, was appointed Deputy Minister of Personnel;
and Fàn Yún 范雲, the concurrently serving Attendant-in-ordinary, was appointed Cavalry Regular Attendant and Minister of Personnel.
A decree was issued that all women from the imperial harem, the music bureau, Xījiě, and the *Bàoshì* were to be released.
On the *wùchén* day,
the King of Bālíng died.
At that time, the Emperor wished to make Nánhǎi Commandery the state of Bālíng,
and relocate the king there.
Shěn Yuē said:
"Ancient and modern affairs are different. What Wèi Wǔ said was, 'One should not covet an empty name and suffer actual calamity.'"
Shěn Yuē dreamt that the sword of Qí Hè Dì 齊和帝 cut off his tongue,
and Heaven's retribution was indeed not amiss.
So, he sent his confidant Zhèng Bóqín 鄭伯禽 to Gūshú
to present the king with pure gold.
The king said:
"I don't need gold when I die;
good wine is enough."
So he drank himself into a stupor.
Bóqín then murdered him.
He was fifteen years old at the time.
*Zhē* 摺
is pronounced *luòhé*.
When the king was stationed in Jīng Prefecture,
Yán Jiàn Yuǎn 顏見遠 of Lángxié served as the Recorder.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Yán Jiàn Yuǎn became Censor for Writing and concurrently Vice-Censor-in-chief.
After the abdication,
Jiàn Yuǎn abstained from food for several days and died.
The histories state that among the Qí officials who died for Hè Dì, there was only one Yán Jiàn Yuǎn.
"I myself answered to Heaven and followed the people."
"Following the people"
was to avoid using the taboo personal name of the imperial father, Shùnzhī 順之.
"And Yán Jiàn Yuǎn even went to this extent!"
This statement is not fit for instruction.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
an edict stated:
"The relevant authorities shall, in accordance with the precedents of Zhōu and Hàn,
deliberate on regulations for commutation of penalties."
The *Shùn Diǎn* says: "Gold can be used to commute penalties."
The commentary says: "If one is mistakenly sentenced,
one can pay gold to redeem the crime."
King Mù of Zhōu instructed on the commutation of penalties in the Xià dynasty,
also allowing those suspected of the five punishments
to pay a redemption fine.
Emperor Wén of Hàn ordered the people to pay grain to redeem crimes;
Emperor Wǔ ordered those facing capital punishment to pay redemption,
fifty million cash to reduce the sentence by one degree.
From Yú to Zhōu, those suspected of errors could redeem themselves;
in Hàn, all criminals could enter into redemption.
"All redemptions stop punishments;
officials, scribes, and soldiers of the ministries and provinces who wish to redeem themselves are permitted to do so."
Xiè Shù Xiàn Gōng 謝沭縣公 Bǎo Yì 寶義 was appointed King of Bālíng,
to maintain the sacrifices to the Qí dynasty.
When the Emperor received the abdication,
Bǎo Yì, as the King of Jìn'ān, was demoted to Duke of Xiè Shù County.
The *Jìn Zhì* states that Xiè Shù County belonged to Lín Hè Commandery.
*Shù* 沭
is pronounced *shíyù*.
He could not speak,
and therefore alone was spared.
Zǐkè 子恪, the Marquis of Nánkāng of Qí, and his younger brother Zǐfàn 子範, the Marquis of Qíyáng, once came for an audience due to a certain matter.
Zǐkè and Zǐfàn
were sons of Yí 嶷, the King of Yùzhāng of Qí.
Qíyáng County
was established by Wú,
and in Sòng belonged to Línglíng Commandery.
*Jiàn* 見
is pronounced *xiánbiàn*.
"The realm is a public instrument;
it cannot be taken by force.
If there is no destined fate, even Xiàng Jí's 項籍 strength will ultimately fail.
Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng was suspicious,
and poisoned all his brothers who had even a slight reputation.
This refers to Shuò 鑠, King of Nánpíng.
*Cū* 粗
is pronounced *zuòwǔ*.
This refers to Yán Jùn 顏竣, Wáng Sēngdá 王僧達, Zhōu Lǎng 周朗, Shěn Huáiwén 沈懷文, and others.
*Cháo* 朝
is pronounced *zhíyáo*.
Or, one who was not suspected ultimately became a calamity,
like your ancestor who was suspected for his talent and strategy,
but there was nothing that could be done.
This specifically refers to those who were suspected but could not be eliminated,
meaning Emperor Gāo of Qí.
*Zú* 卒
is pronounced *zǐxù*.
And his descendants all died by his hand.
This specifically refers to those who were not suspected but ultimately became a calamity,
meaning Emperor Míng killed all the descendants of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
How could they have known that I would have this day!
Therefore, it is known that those with the Mandate of Heaven are not harmed by men.
When I first pacified Jiànkāng,
everyone advised me to eliminate your kind to unify the people's hearts.
If I had acted on that advice at the time,
who could have said no!
It is precisely because, since the east of the River,
during times of dynastic change, there has always been mutual slaughter,
which grieves the harmonious *qì*,
and thus the national fortune does not last long.
Moreover,
although Qí and Liáng are said to be a revolution,
the circumstances are different from previous generations.
Although my brothers and I are no longer in mourning for you,
kin within the five degrees of mourning,
up to *tǎnbù* and *miǎnbù*, wear no mourning clothes.
*Qù* 去
is pronounced *qiānglǚ*.
*Fù* 復
is pronounced *fúyòu*;
below, "kěfù" and "wúfù" are the same.
At the beginning of the Qí enterprise, we also shared hardship.
During the abdication between Qí and Sòng,
my imperial father Shùnzhī participated in supporting the founding.
How can we suddenly treat each other like strangers on the road!
If your brothers truly have the Mandate of Heaven,
I cannot kill you;
if you do not have the Mandate of Heaven,
why would you do this!
It would only show my lack of measure.
Moreover, Jiànwǔ brought calamity upon your family.
This refers to Emperor Míng of Qí exterminating the descendants of Emperor Gāo and Emperor Wǔ during the Jiànwǔ reign.
Not only did I clear my family's shame,
but I also avenged your brothers.
If you could, during the Jiànwǔ and Yǒngyuán eras,
Yǒngyuán
was the reign title of the Marquis of Dōnghūn of Qí.
This implies that Emperor Míng of Qí and his son caused chaos,
and the descendants of Emperor Gāo and Emperor Wǔ were legitimate.

General Zhāng Xiāo zhī invaded Wèi's Huáinán,
and captured Mùlíng garrison.
Wèi's Rènchéng Wáng Chéng sent Auxiliary General Chéng Xìng to attack him.
Xiāo zhī was defeated and fled.
Wèi recaptured Mùlíng.
The commentary to the Shǔi Jīng says,
Mùlíng Shān is southwest of Huáng Shuǐ,
and has Mùlíng Guān.
Huáng Shuǐ flows east past the south of Jìn's Xīyáng City,
then east past the south of Nánguāng City,
then east past the east of Yìyáng Jùn,
then northeast into the Huái,
where it is called Huángkǒu.
The Táng Zhì says,
Mùlíng Guān is south of Guāngzhōu's Guāngshān Xiàn, and northeast of Huángzhōu's Máchéng Xiàn.
Fù,
pronounced Hú Yòu.
37 Liú Jìlián sent his generals Lǐ Fèngbó and others to resist Dèng Yuánqǐ.
Yuánqǐ fought them,
with alternating victories and defeats.
After a long time,
Fèngbó and the others were defeated,
and returned to Chéngdū.
Yuánqǐ advanced and garrisoned Xīpíng.
Emperor Ān of Jìn established Huáiníng Jùn for refugees from Qín and Yōng.
In the sixteenth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng, it was temporarily administered in Chéngdū.
Its subordinate county was Xīpíng,
probably also temporarily administered outside Chéngdū city,
thus becoming de facto territory.
The city gates were closed and they defended staunchly.
Yuánqǐ advanced and garrisoned Jiǎngqiáo,
twenty *lǐ* from Chéngdū,
leaving his baggage train at Pín.
Fèngbó and the others took a shortcut to attack Pín,
captured it,
and all the military supplies were lost.
Yuánqǐ abandoned Pín,
and directly besieged the prefectural city.
The city official Jiāng Xī zhī planned to surrender the city,
but failed and died.
Sòng had eighteen staff officers (*cānjūn*) for various bureaus;
the city bureau was one of them.
Jiàng,
pronounced Hù Jiāng.
38 Wèi's Chénliú Gōngzhǔ was widowed.
The Minister of Personnel Gāo Zhào and the Governor of Qínzhōu Zhāng Yí both wished to marry her.
The Princess assented to Yí but not to Zhào.
Zhào was angered,
and slandered Yí to the Wèi emperor,
who consequently was dismissed for several years.
39 In this year,
there was a great drought east of the Jiāng.
Rice cost five thousand per *dòu*,
and many people starved to death.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *Yǐmǎo* day,
the Minister of Personnel Shěn Yuē was made Left Minister of Personnel,
the Minister of Personnel Fàn Yún was made Right Minister of Personnel,
and the Minister of the Secretariat Wáng Liàng was made Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Left.
On the *Bǐngchén* day,
Liàng was dismissed from his title
and demoted to commoner
for feigning illness and not ascending the hall on New Year's Day.
2 On the *Yǐhài* day,
the Wèi emperor ploughed the sacrificial field.
3 The Dī people of Wèi's Liángzhōu, Yáng Huì, rebelled.
Yáng Chún and others, acting as administrators of Liángzhōu, suppressed them.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán of Qí's Dōnghūn, a letter from Wèi's Governor of Liángzhōu Yáng Chún invited the Dī king Yáng Jíshǐ to surrender.
Now he is acting as administrator of Liángzhōu;
this should be investigated.
4 Food ran out in Chéngdū city.
A *shēng* of rice cost three thousand,
and people resorted to cannibalism.
Liú Jìlián ate porridge for several months,
with no way out.
The Emperor sent Chief Scribe Zhào Jǐngyuè to convey the imperial edict accepting Jìlián's surrender.
Jìlián, stripped to the waist, pleaded guilty.
Dèng Yuánqǐ moved Jìlián outside the city,
and shortly thereafter visited him,
treating him with courtesy.
Jìlián thanked him, saying:
"If I had known this earlier,
why would there have been the events of the past!"
He meant that the reason he had previously resisted with arms and refused orders
was truly because Zhū Dáochēn had caused discord.
Yuánqǐ executed Lǐ Fèngbó and the others,
and sent Jìlián to Jiànkāng.
Initially,
when Yuánqǐ was on the way,
fearing that the mission would not succeed,
and having no means of reward,
he promised all who came to him official appointments.
Thus, those who accepted commissions as Aide-de-camp or Administrator numbered nearly two thousand.
When Jìlián arrived at Jiànkāng,
he entered the Dōngyèmén,
bowing his head to the ground every few steps
until he reached the Emperor.
The Emperor smiled and said:
"You wished to emulate Liú Bèi,
but you didn't even measure up to Gōngsūn Shù."
This refers to Gōngsūn Shù's refusal to surrender to Hàn.
Wòlóng [Crouching Dragon]
refers to Zhūgě Kǒngmíng.
5 In the third month,
on the *Jǐsì* day,
the Wèi Empress tended silkworms in the northern suburbs.
6 On the *Gēngchén* day,
Wèi's Governor of Yángzhōu, Rènchéng Wáng Chéng, sent the commandant of Chángfēng City, Qí Dáoxiǎn, to invade.
The Xìngpǔ says
that the Qí surname
descends from Bóqí.
According to the commentary to the Shǔi Jīng,
Yīnshān Guān is southwest of Yìyáng Xiàn.
The Táng Zhì says,
northeast of Huángzhōu's Máchéng Xiàn there is Yīnshān Guān.
7 Xiāo Bǎoyín lay prostrate beneath the Wèi palace gates.
This refers to the palace gates of the Wèi court.
*Què* is the ancient *xiàngwèi*.
Even with strong winds and heavy rain,
he never moved even for a moment. Just then, Chén Bózhī surrendered to Wèi,
and also requested troops to prove his worth.
The Wèi emperor then summoned the Eight Seated Officials and the Secretariat to deliberate.
The Eight Seated Officials
refer to the Ministers and Vice Ministers and the various Department Heads.
The Secretariat
refers to officials such as the Palace Attendant and the Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
Zhàn,
same as *zàn*.
Jiàng,
pronounced Hù Jiāng.
Zuò,
pronounced Cú Wò.
In the fourth month,
on the *Guǐwèi* new moon day,
Bǎoyín was appointed Area Commander-in-chief of three prefectures including Dōngyáng, General Who Guards the East, Governor of Yángzhōu, Duke of Dānyáng, and King of Qí.
He was given very generous gifts,
allotted ten thousand soldiers,
and ordered to garrison Dōngchéng.
This was probably the territory of Dōngchéng Xiàn of the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
as it was east of Shòuyáng,
hence Dōngyángzhōu was established there.
He garrisoned Yángshí,
which is Yángshí Chéng,
located northwest of Lújiāng and
southeast of Huòqiū.
Bǎoyín was to be officially appointed the next day.
*Míng* refers to the next morning.
The Wèi people also allowed Bǎoyín to recruit brave and strong men from all directions,
obtaining several thousand.
Yán Wénzhì, Huá Wénróng, and six others were all made generals and military commanders.
Yán Wénzhì led Bǎoyín to defect to Huá Wénróng,
and Wénróng and others led Bǎoyín to defect to the North.
Huá,
pronounced Hù Huā.
Even after the appointed time, he still abstained from alcohol and meat.
*Lǐ*
means observing a one-year mourning period for brothers.
He ate coarse vegetables and wore plain clothes,
never laughing.
8 On the *Guǐmǎo* day,
Cài Fǎdù presented twenty scrolls of the Liáng Code,
thirty scrolls of regulations,
and forty scrolls of statutes.
An imperial edict ordered their promulgation.
9 In the fifth month,
on the *Dīngsì* day,
Fàn Yún, Marquis of Xiāochéng, died.
He was Marquis of Xiāochéng County.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Miǎnyáng Jùn's Jìnglíng Xiàn
was formerly called Xiāochéng.
Zú,
pronounced Zǐ Xù;
same below.
Fàn Yún’s
diligence in handling affairs was such that he left nothing undone.
When faced with complicated and difficult situations,
his energy surpassed that of others.
After his death,
the public believed that Shěn Yuē should take charge of the *shūguǎn* (pivotal administration).
*Shūguǎn*
refers to managing the central mechanisms of government.
Modern people still refer to the Privy Council as the *Shūguǎn*.
Viewing it this way,
although Shěn Yuē’s position was to the right of Fàn Yún,
his trusted appointment was far inferior to Yún’s.
[Emperor Wǔ] did not appoint Shěn Yuē; instead,
he appointed Xú Miǎn, the Left Aide to the Department of State Affairs, and Zhōu Shě, the Right General of the Guards,
to jointly participate in state administration.
Shě’s generosity was not equal to Miǎn’s,
but his integrity and simplicity surpassed Miǎn’s.
Both were praised as worthy chancellors,
often remaining in the provincial office,
rarely getting time off.
*Xiūxià*
means to rest and go off duty.
[Their dogs were startled and barked;]
Whenever there was a memorial or a report,
they would burn the draft.
Shě was involved in confidential matters for over twenty years,
never leaving the emperor’s side.
He oversaw national history, imperial edicts, rituals, laws, and military strategies.
He would talk and joke with people,
ceaselessly throughout the day.
*Xuè*
(pronounced *qì què*),
means joking words.
Everyone especially admired him.
The historians generally described their entire lives.
On the 10th day of *rénshēn*,
all prefectures and counties were forbidden from presenting tribute to the two palaces,
except that all provinces and Kuàijī were permitted to offer local products.
If it was not a local product,
it was also not allowed to be offered as tribute.
On the 11th day of *jiǎxū*,
Yáng Chūn and others of Wèi greatly defeated the rebellious Dī,
beheading several thousand.
In the spring of that year,
Yáng Huì of the Dī tribe rebelled.
In the 6th month,
on the 12th day, *rénwǔ* (the 1st day of the month),
Wèi enfeoffed Imperial Younger Brother Yuè as the Prince of Rǔnán.
Rènchéng Wáng Chéng, the Inspector of Yángzhōu for Wèi, memorialized, stating:
“Xiāo Yǎn has repeatedly cut off the eastern pass,
wishing to make Lake Cháohú overflow and flood the Wèi garrisons south of the Huái River.
As Wú and Chǔ are accustomed to water,
they will flood and plunder,
and the land south of the Huái River will likely cease to be part of our territory.
Shòuyáng is over five hundred *lǐ* from the Jiāng River,
and the populace is greatly alarmed,
all fearing water damage.
If we were to seize the people’s desire [for peace],
attack the enemy’s weakness,
pre-order the various provinces,
assemble soldiers and horses,
and gather a large force
in the autumn,
making strategic plans as opportunities arise,
even if unification cannot be certainly achieved,
the area west of the Jiāng River will certainly be free from trouble.”
On the 13th day of *bǐngxū*,
Wèi dispatched 20,000 men from the six provinces of Jì, Dìng, Yíng, Xiāng, Bìng, and Jì,
and 1,500 horses,
ordering them to assemble in Huáinán by mid-autumn,
combining with the 30,000 vanguard troops already at Shòuyáng.
*Xiānbīng*
refers to the troops already stationed at Shòuyáng.
Xiāo Bǎoyín and Chén Bózhī were both placed under Chéng’s command.
Xiè Fěi traveled by light boat to the palace,
and an edict appointed him as Attendant-in-Chief, Grand Chancellor, and Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Fěi declined, citing a leg ailment that made it impossible for him to bow.
He wore a commoner’s cap and was carried in a sedan chair to the Yúnlóng Gate to express his thanks.
An edict granted him an audience in the Huálín Park,
where he rode in a small cart to his seat.
The next morning,
the Emperor visited Fěi’s residence.
Xiè Fěi had served the Sòng and Qí dynasties and
had a residence in Jiànkāng.
Fěi earnestly reiterated his original intention [to retire],
but it was not granted.
He then requested to return to the east to welcome his mother,
which was permitted.
Before his departure,
the Emperor again paid a visit,
composing a poem to bid him farewell.
Imperial envoys escorting and welcoming him
were seen continuously on the road.
All those who conveyed imperial orders were called *wángrén*.
An edict ordered the establishment of his office in his old residence,
treating him with exceptional courtesy.
Fěi had always disliked troublesome matters
and did not attend to his official duties,
which greatly disappointed the public.
Xiè Fěi was also far inferior to Fán Yīng.
*Shěng*
(pronounced *xī jǐng*), means to attend to.
On the 15th day of *jiǎwǔ*,
Wáng Yíng, the Palace Secretariat Director, was appointed Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
In the autumn,
in the 7th month,
on the 16th day of *yǐmǎo*,
Wèi’s Prince Píngyáng Píng died.
After Wèi had abolished the salt marsh prohibition,
at the beginning of the Wèi emperor’s reign, Chief Secretary Zhēn Chēn memorialized to abolish the salt prohibition.
Péngchéng Wáng Xié and Xíng Luán believed it was not permissible.
The Wèi emperor issued an edict granting Zhēn Chēn’s request.
The *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* catalog had already mentioned its essence.
This matter should have been recorded in Volume 143, under the 2nd year of Yǒngyuán of the Qí Dōnghūn Emperor,
but the main text of the *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* omitted it,
mistakenly placing it in Volume 146, under the 5th year of Tiānjiān.
On the 17th day of *gēngwǔ*,
the profits from the salt marshes were again collected for the public treasury.
On the 18th day of *xīnwèi*,
Wèi appointed Péngchéng Wáng Xié as Grand Preceptor,
but Xié firmly declined.
The Wèi emperor issued an edict urging him to accept,
and also wrote a family letter,
making earnest requests.
Writing a family letter
means using the etiquette of family uncles and nephews.
He accepted the appointment.
In the 8th month,
on the 19th day of *gēngzǐ*,
Wèi appointed Yuán Yīng, the General Who Guards the South, to oversee all military affairs for the expedition against Yìyáng.
Cài Dàogōng, the Inspector of Sīzhōu, hearing that the Wèi army was approaching,
dispatched Yang You, the General of Valiant Cavalry, to lead over 3,000 households from outside the city to secure Xiánshǒushān,
where three stockades were built.
In the winter,
in the 10th month,
Yuán Yīng led his armies to besiege the Xiánshǒu stockades.
Rèn Mǎjū, a resident of the stockade, beheaded Yáng Yóu and surrendered to Wèi.

Rènchéng Wáng Chéng (任城王澄) ordered the military commanders Dǎng Fǎzōng (党法宗), Fù Shùyǎn (傅豎眼), Tàiyuán Wáng Shénniàn (太原王神念) and others to divide their forces and attack Dōngguān (東關), Dàxiàn (大峴), Huáilíng (淮陵), and Jiǔshān (九山).
"Huáilíng" (淮陵)
should probably be
"Suīlíng" (睢陵).
Qí (齊) established Xúzhōu (徐州) in Zhōnglí (鍾離),
and also temporarily established the county of Suīlíng (睢陵) in Jìyīn Jùn (濟陰郡) within its borders.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Zhōnglí Jùn (鍾離郡) has Huàmíng Xiàn (化明縣),
formerly known as Suīlíng (睢陵),
where Jìyīn Jùn (濟陰郡) was established.
Huàmíng (化明)
was Zhāoyì Xiàn (招義縣) of Táng Háo Zhōu (唐濠州).
Some say: According to the Sòng Zhì (宋志),
Nán Xúzhōu (南徐州) administered Huáilíng Jùn (淮陵郡).
Suīlíng (睢陵) and Huáilíng (淮陵) both belonged to the Hàn Xú Bù (漢徐部).
At that time, since Xúzhōu (徐州) was established in Zhōnglí (鍾離),
it is possible that Huáilíng (淮陵) was also established within the borders of Zhōnglí (鍾離).
This is not certain.
Wèi Shōu Zhì (魏收志) states that
Chénliú (陳留) and Zhōnglí (鍾離) two commanderies had Cháogē Xiàn (朝歌縣),
and the county had Jiǔshān Chéng (九山城) and Huángxī Shuǐ (黃溪水).
According to the Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註),
the Yellow River originates from Huángwǔ Shān (黃武山),
flows northeast,
passing through Nánguāng Chéng (南光城) and Yìyáng (弋陽) commanderies.
It is now known that southwest of Xūyí Xiàn (盱眙縣) in Zhāoxìn Jūn (招信軍), at a distance of fifteen *li*, there are three cities.
Another fifteen *li* to the west leads to Huáilíng (淮陵),
a city by the Chíhé (池河).
The Chíhé (池河) flows west of Huáilíng Chéng (淮陵城) and then north,
entering the Huái (淮),
and is called Chíhé Kǒu (池河口).
Jiǔshān Diàn (九山店) is north of the Huái (淮),
directly south of Huáilíng (淮陵).
East of Jiǔshān Diàn (九山店) is Xiàn'gāng Hú (陷堈湖),
and south is Mǎchéng (馬城).
When the Huái (淮) River reaches this point,
it is called Jiǔshān Wān (九山灣).
To its east is Fènghuáng Zhōu (鳳凰州),
in the middle of the Huái (淮) River,
approximately ten *li* long.
Today, locals also call Jiǔshān Wān (九山灣) Shīzi Dù (獅子渡),
a vital crossing point for northern troops crossing the Huái (淮).
Xiàn (峴),
pronounced like *hù diǎn*.
Chéng (澄) followed with the main army.
Shùyǎn (豎眼)
was the son of Língyuè (靈越).
Fù Língyuè (傅靈越) rose in rebellion with Xuē Āndū (薛安都),
attacking Zhāng Yǒng (張永) in support of Yìjiā (義嘉),
but his army was routed and he died.
Shù (豎),
pronounced like *ér zhǔ*.
Wèi Shōu Zhì (魏收志) states that
Huòzhōu (霍州) had Běiyǐngchuān Jùn (北潁川郡),
which administered Yǐngchuān (潁川) and two other counties.
Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) states that
Liáng (梁) established Huòzhōu (霍州),
with its seat in Qián Xiàn (灊縣) at Tiānzhù Shān (天柱山).
Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史) Sīmǎ Míngsù (司馬明素) led three thousand troops to rescue Jiǔshān (九山),
and Xúzhōu Zhǎngshǐ (徐州長史) Pān Bólín (潘伯鄰) rescued Huáilíng (淮陵).
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) Wáng Xiè (王燮) defended Jiāochéng (焦城).
Dǎng Fǎzōng (党法宗) and others advanced and captured Jiāochéng (焦城),
and defeated Huáilíng (淮陵).
In the eleventh month,
on the *rénwǔ* (壬午) day,
Míngsù (明素) was captured,
and Bólín (伯鄰) was executed.
Previously,
the Nánliáng Tàishǒu (南梁太守) Féng Dàogēn (馮道根) was garrisoned at Fùlíng (阜陵).
The Féng Dàogēn Zhuàn (馮道根傳) states that
he held the post of Nánliáng Tàishǒu (南梁太守) while leading the Fùlíng (阜陵) garrison.
Xiān (先),
pronounced like *xī jiàn*.
He repaired the city walls and moats,
and sent out scouts far.
As if an enemy was about to arrive,
many ridiculed him.
Dàogēn (道根) said:
"Prudent defense and courageous battle,
this is what it means."
His precautions were as if he was timid,
but when facing battle, he was courageous.
Dǎng Fǎzōng (党法宗) and his two hundred thousand troops suddenly arrived at the city,
and everyone was panic-stricken.
Dàogēn (道根) ordered the main gate to be opened wide,
leisurely ascended the city wall,
selected two hundred elite soldiers to sally forth and fight the Wèi (魏) troops,
and defeated them.
The Wèi (魏) people saw his composed demeanor
and that the battle was not going well,
so they withdrew.
Dàogēn (道根) led a hundred cavalry to attack Gāozǔ Zhēn (高祖珍),
and defeated them.
The Wèi (魏) armies' provisions and transport were cut off,
and they retreated.
Dàogēn (道根) was appointed Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史).
At this time, Liáng Yùzhōu (梁豫州) was governed from Jìnxī (晉熙).
Dàogēn (道根) was probably still garrisoned at Fùlíng (阜陵),
merely holding the title of Cìshǐ (刺史).
Yáng Jíshǐ (楊集始), King Ān (安) of Wǔxìng (武興), died.
On the *jǐwèi* (己未) day,
Wèi (魏) appointed his heir Shàoxiān (紹先) as King of Wǔxìng (武興).
Shàoxiān (紹先) was young,
and the affairs of the state were decided by his two paternal uncles Jíqǐ (集起) and Jíyì (集義).
On the *yǐhài* (乙亥) day,
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射) Shěn Yuē (沈約) resigned due to his mother's mourning.
After Wèi (魏) moved to Luòyáng (洛陽),
the northern frontier became desolate and remote,
leading to famine,
and the common people suffered greatly.
The Wèi (魏) ruler appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射) Yuán Huái (源懷) as Shìzhōng (侍中) and Xíngtái (行臺).
Wèi Dàowǔ (魏道武) established the office of Xíngtái (行臺) in Yè (鄴) and Zhōngshān (中山);
now it was established on the northern frontier.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: At the end of Wèi (魏), Sīmǎ Shī (司馬師) attacked Zhūgě Dàn (諸葛誕).
Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) Péi Xiù (裴秀), Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射) Chén Tài (陳泰), and Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎) Zhōng Huì (鍾會) followed as Xíngtái (行臺).
In Běiqí (北齊), the Xíngtái (行臺) began to concurrently manage civilian affairs starting with Xīn Shù (辛術).
In Suí (隋), it was called Xíngtái Shěng (行臺省).
Six garrisons
were set up along the borders of the three prefectures.
Shǐ (使),
pronounced like *shū lì*;
same below.
Xíng (行),
pronounced like *xià mèng*.
Héng (恆),
pronounced like *hù dēng*.
Yān (燕),
pronounced like *yīn jiān*.
He was to evaluate and grade officials,
and was tasked with both providing relief to the poor
and inspecting officials.
Diàn (殿),
pronounced like *dīng liàn*.
Huái (懷) facilitated the exchange of goods to meet needs,
and the starving people relied on him.
Yōuyě Zhènjiàng (沃野鎮將) Yú Zuò (于祚).
Yōuyě (沃野) was a subordinate county of Hàn Shuòfāng Jùn (漢朔方郡).
Wèi (魏) pacified Hèlián (赫連),
and established a garrison there along with Tǒngwàn (統萬),
which was not among the six garrisons.
Jiàng (將),
pronounced like *jí liàng*;
same below.
Shìfù (世父),
the paternal uncle who inherited the main lineage.
At the time, Yú Jìng (于勁) was powerful,
his influence swaying the court and the countryside.
Zuò (祚) was known to accept bribes.
When Huái (懷) was about to enter the garrison,
Zuò (祚) met him at the roadside,
but Huái (懷) did not speak to him,
and immediately impeached and dismissed him from office.
Huáisuò Zhènjiàng (懷朔鎮將) Yuán Nísū (元尼須) was an old acquaintance of Huái (懷),
and was notoriously corrupt.
Sū È Yǎnyì (蘇鶚演義) says: *lángjí* (狼籍) describes
the appearance of things being chaotic and messy;

He said to Huái (懷):
"The length of my life
depends on your words,
how can you not be lenient with me!"
Huái (懷) said:
"Today, Yuán Huái (源懷) is at a drinking party with an old friend,
not a place for judicial inquiry.
Tomorrow,
the public court will be the place for the envoy to investigate the crimes of the garrison commander."
Nísū (尼須) wept silently, unable to respond,
and was eventually impeached and punished.
Huái (懷) also reported:
"The border garrisons have few matters but too many officials.
In the Yōuyě (沃野) garrison alone, there are over eight hundred people from the commander down."
Jiàng (將)
refers to the garrison commander.
Jiàng (將),
pronounced like *jí liàng*.
The Wèi (魏) ruler agreed.
On the *yǐyǒu* (乙酉) day,
General Wú Ziyáng (吳子陽) fought Yuán Yīng (元英) of Wèi (魏) at Báishā (白沙),
and Ziyáng (子陽) was defeated.
Báishā (白沙) is within the borders of Qí'ān Jùn (齊安郡).
Wèi Shōu Zhì (魏收志) states that
there was Shāzhōu (沙州),
governed from Báishā Guān Chéng (白沙關城),

Huángzhōu Huángpí Xiàn (黃州黃陂縣) has Báishā Guān (白沙關).
Fán Sù'ān (樊素安), a barbarian of Wèi Dōngjīngzhōu (魏東荊州), rebelled.
On the *yǐyǒu* (乙酉) day,
Lǐ Chóng (李崇), Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍), was appointed Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (鎮南將軍) and Dūdū Zhēngmán Zhūjūn Shì (都督征蠻諸軍事),

25 Fényì’s Jí Fēn's father was the Magistrate of Yuánxiāng.
He was falsely accused by corrupt officials
and arrested, brought to the Tíngwèi.
His crime was punishable by death.
Fēn was fifteen years old.
He struck the Dēngwéngǔ (Petition Drum)
to beg to die in his father's place.
The Emperor, seeing his youth,
suspected someone had instructed him.
He ordered the Tíngwèi Qīng, Cài Fǎdù, to induce and threaten him severely
to ascertain the truth of his statement.
"Induce"
means to open a path to life for him;
"threaten"
means to intimidate him with ropes, shackles, and manacles,
indicating an impending interrogation.
"Kuǎn"
means sincerity.
"Yòu"
is pronounced *yǒu*.
Fēn was questioned,
"You seek to die for your father.
An imperial edict has already granted permission.
Are you truly able to die?"
This is what is meant by "threatening him."
"Kǎo"
is pronounced *kǎo*.
"Jí"
is pronounced *jí*.
"Bù"
is read as *fǒu*.
"If you were taught by someone,
you may still recant."
Fēn said,
"Though this prisoner is foolish and young,
how can I not know that death is something to be feared!
But I cannot bear to see my father suffer the ultimate penalty,
so I seek to die in his place.
This is no minor matter;
how could I be instructed by others?
The clear edict allowing me to take his place
is no different from ascending to heaven.
How could I have second thoughts?"
To reverse a previous statement is "huí";
to differ from a previous statement is "èr."
"The Emperor knows your esteemed father is innocent
and will soon be released.
He views you as a promising youth.
If you were to change your statement now,
fortunately, both father and son could be saved."
Fēn said,
"My father is entangled in a grave impeachment,
and will surely face the prescribed punishment.
This prisoner closes his eyes and strains his neck,
only awaiting the great execution.
I have no further words to say."
At that time, Fēn was fully shackled.
Fǎdù pitied him
and ordered him to be given smaller ones.
Fēn refused,
saying,
"A prisoner guilty of a capital crime
should only have more restraints,
how can they be reduced!"
He ultimately did not remove them.
Fǎdù reported the entire matter.
The Emperor then pardoned his father's crime.
Dānyáng Yǐn Wáng Zhì inquired about his case at the Tíngwèi
and also questioned his hometown,
wishing to nominate him at the beginning of the year as a paragon of filial piety.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, all nominations for officials came from the prefectures and villages,
hence the inquiry into his hometown.
Fēn said, "How strange is Magistrate Wáng!
How lightly does he regard Fēn!
A father disgraced, a son dying – this is the proper course of conduct.
If Fēn were to accept this nomination, it would be exploiting his father's misfortune for fame.
What greater disgrace could there be!"
He firmly refused and stopped the matter.
26 The Wèi ruler took the daughter of Gāo Zhào's elder brother, Yǎn, as his Guìpín.
27 The Wèi Sànqí Chángshì Zhào Xiū,
who rose from humble origins to sudden wealth,
relied on imperial favor to act arrogantly and wantonly,
oppressing princes and dukes,
and was detested by all.
The Wèi ruler built residences for Xiū,
comparable to those of the various princes,
and neighbors who donated land were sometimes promoted to major commanderies.
Xiū requested leave to return home to bury his father.
All expenses and labor required
were provided by the government.
Xiū indulged in debauchery on the journey.
Xiū, on his return from Luòyáng to Zhàojùn, indulged in debauchery on the road.
His crimes and misdeeds were somewhat exposed;
upon his return,
his former favor slightly waned.
Gāo Zhào secretly compiled his crimes.
Shìzhōng, Lǐng Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi Zhēn Chēn, Huángmén Láng Lǐ Píng, and Tíngwèi Qīng Yángpíng Wáng Xiǎn
had all previously flattered and attached themselves to Xiū.
At this point, they feared being implicated,
fearing being implicated and suffering disaster due to their association.
"Zhēn"
is pronounced *zhēn*.
"Chēn"
is pronounced *chén*.
The Emperor ordered Shàngshū Yuán Shào to investigate.
An imperial edict exposed Xiū's transgressions.
He was spared death,
flogged one hundred times,
and exiled to Dūnhuáng to serve as a soldier.
However, Xiū was foolish and ignorant,
initially unaware of this.
He was then playing backgammon at Lǐngjūn Yú Jìng's residence.
Several Yǔlín soldiers, proclaiming an imperial edict, called him
and sent him to the Lǐngjūn Fǔ.
Zhēn Chēn and Wáng Xiǎn supervised the punishment.
They first interrogated five strong men who had been involved in the matter
and made them take turns whipping him,
intending to kill him.
Xiū was naturally robust
and able to endure severe torture;
secretly, the whipping reached three hundred strokes, but he did not die.
They immediately summoned post horses
and urged him to get on the road.
Upon leaving the city, he could not support himself.
He was lifted and tied onto the saddle.
"Jǔ"
means to lift.
Xiū was so exhausted he could not ride by himself,
so two people lifted him and placed him on the horse,
tying him to the saddle.
After traveling eighty *lǐ*,
he died.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he blamed Yuán Shào for not reporting it sooner.
Shào said,
"Xiū's flattery and favoritism
made him a deep pestilence for the nation.
I did not take advantage of this opportunity to eliminate him..."
"Xìn"
means crack.
"Xìn"
is pronounced *xìn*.
The Emperor, deeming his words righteous,
did not punish him.
When Shào exited,
Guǎngpíng Wáng Huái bowed to him, saying,
"Your rectitude surpasses that of Jí Àn."
Shào said,
"I only regret that his execution was somewhat late,
which is my shame."
Shào was the grandson of Sù.
Chángshān Wáng Sù can be found in Volume 122, Yuánjiā 11th year of Sòng Wéndì.
Guǎngpíng Wáng Huái,
son of Xiàowén,
called Shào "Wēng" due to the order of seniority in their clan.
Zhēn Chēn and Lǐ Píng were both dismissed from office for being Xiū's associates.
More than twenty people from his entourage who were implicated with Xiū died or were dismissed.
Sànqí Chángshì Gāo Cōng had been close to Xiū,
but also ingratiated himself with Gāo Zhào as a kinsman,
and thus was uniquely spared.
1 In the spring,
first month,
on the *gēngxū* day,
Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Zhào Zǔyuè fought against the Wèi Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Chén Bózhī at Dōngguān.

2 On the *guǐchǒu* day,

the Wèi greatly pardoned,

5 Xiāo Bǎoyín’s army reached Rǔyīn.
Dōngchéng had already been captured by Liáng,
so he camped at Qīxián Temple in Shòuyáng.
In the second month,
on the day of Wùzǐ,
General Jiāng Qìngzhēn took advantage of Wèi’s Rènchéng Wáng Chéng being away.
Last year, Wèi sent Chéng to invade,
and his army was stationed outside.
He occupied their outer wall.
Chief Clerk Wéi Zuǎn was caught off guard and lost his plan.
Rènchéng Tàimèngshì led soldiers to ascend the battlements,
first defending key positions.
A "key position" (yào) is one that the enemy must attack
and we must defend.
A "convenient position" (biàn)
is one with a strategic advantage that can be held

"Pí" (battlements),
pronounced pín mí.
She comforted both new and old.
"New" refers to
the soldiers and people of Shòuyáng;
"old" refers to
the officers and soldiers who came from the north.
Some say: "new" refers to
recent adherents;
"old" refers to
existing citizens.
The soldiers were all inspired to fight.
Tàimèngshì personally inspected the city defenses,

Xiāo Bǎoyín led his troops to arrive,
and together with the provincial army, they attacked.

The time before sunset
is called xiàpū.
Wéi Zuǎn was dismissed from office for this.
Rènchéng Wáng Chéng attacked Zhōnglí.
The Emperor sent Champion General Zhāng Huìshào and others, leading five thousand soldiers, to deliver grain to Zhōnglí.
Chéng sent Pacifying General Liú Sīzǔ and others to intercept them.
On the day of Dīngyǒu,
they battled at Shàoyáng.
This is Shàoyáng Prefecture.
They captured Huìshào and ten other generals,
and almost completely annihilated the enemy soldiers.
Sīzǔ
was a paternal cousin of Fāng.
Liú Fāng was highly esteemed for his Confucian scholarship during the Tàihé era.
"Bài" (defeated),
pronounced bǔ mài.
"Jiàng" (general),
pronounced jí liàng.
"Cóng" (from),
pronounced cái yòng.
He should have been enfeoffed as a Marquis of a Thousand Households.

When he didn't get them,
the matter was dropped.
The historians remarked that Wèi's rewards and punishments were inappropriate.
Yuán Huī was the grandson of Sù.
The Emperor dispatched Pacifying General Cáo Jǐngzōng and Rear Army General Wáng Sēngbǐng and others, leading thirty thousand infantry and cavalry, to relieve Yìyáng.
"Rear Army" refers to
the Rear Army General.
"Shuài" (to lead)
is read as lǜ.
Zuòxiàn is south of Guān.
Now, thirty-five lǐ south of Xìnyáng Commandery, there is Cáo Diàn,
which was built when Jǐngzōng garrisoned at the mouth of Zuòxiàn.
"Xiàn" (mountain pass),
pronounced hù diǎn.
Yuán Yīng sent Champion General Yuán Chěng and others to occupy Fánchéng to resist them.
In the third month,
on the day of Réngshēn,
they severely defeated Sēngbǐng at Fánchéng,
capturing and beheading over four thousand people.
Sēngbǐng was defeated at Fánchéng
and did not manage to reach Zuòxiàn.
Otherwise, this Fánchéng would not be the one in Xiāngyáng,
but a different place.
Wèi issued an edict to Rènchéng Wáng Chéng,
stating:
"In the fourth month, the Huái River will rise,
allowing unimpeded boat travel.
The southern army will seize this opportunity.
Do not be blinded by profit and regret it later."
Coincidentally, there was heavy rain,
and the Huái River rose sharply.
Chéng led his troops back to Shòuyáng.
The Wèi army's retreat was indeed in disarray,

The Middle Secretariat Attendant from Qíjùn, Jiǎ Sībó, served as Chéng's army supervisor.

Chéng, knowing him to be a scholar,
thought he would surely die.
When he arrived,
Chéng was overjoyed and said:
" 'The benevolent are sure to be brave!' "
This is a saying of Confucius from the Analects.
Sībó attributed his survival to being lost,

The Emperor requested an exchange of the captured Wèi generals and soldiers for Zhāng Huìshào from Wèi,
and the Wèi people returned him.
Kǎoyì says: Huìshào's biography does not mention being captured or returned.
We follow the Wèi Shū here.
6 Wèi's Grand Tutor, concurrently serving as Grand Minister of Works and Supervisor of the Grand Secretariat, Běihǎi Wáng Xiáng,
was arrogant, extravagant, fond of music and women,
and insatiably greedy.
He extensively built mansions,
seizing people's residences.
He favored those around him,
and there were solicitations everywhere.
Both inside and outside the court, there was widespread resentment.
The Wèi Emperor, considering him a respected relative,
maintained his kindness and courtesy without fail.
All major military and state affairs were referred to him for decision,
and his requests were always granted.
When the Wèi Emperor first took personal control of the government,
he summoned his paternal uncles with soldiers.
This event is recorded in the previous volume, Qí Hédì Zhōngxīng Yuánnián.
The defenses were strict and firm.
Gāo Tàimǔ was terrified, riding in a carriage after him and crying.
After he was spared,
she said to Xiáng:
"From now on, I do not desire wealth and honor.
I only wish that mother and son can protect each other,
and we will make a living by sweeping the streets."
When Xiáng again took power,
in the first month of Qí Hédì Zhōngxīng Yuánnián,
the Wèi Emperor took personal control of the government.
In the eleventh month,
Xiáng became Grand Minister of Works.
He exclusively assisted Xiáng in his greed and cruelty.
Champion General Rú Hào,
with his cleverness and ingenuity, was favored by the Emperor.
He was always by the Emperor's side,
transmitting imperial commands and presenting memorials from the palace gate.
He abused his power and accepted bribes,
causing the court and public to fear him.
Xiáng also associated with him.
Hào married the paternal cousin of Shàngshū Lìng Gāo Zhào.
Hào's wife's elder sister was married to Xiáng's paternal cousin, Āndìng Wáng Xiè.
Xiáng committed incest with Xiè's wife,
and because of this, he and Hào became even more intimate.
General of the Imperial Guard Liú Zhòu,
originally recommended by Xiáng;
Palace General Cháng Jìxián, known for his skill in horse rearing;
and Chén Sǎojìng, who was in charge of combs and hairpins;
all gained the Emperor's favor
and conspired with Hào,
selling their power and influence.
Gāo Zhào originally came from Gāolì,
and people at the time looked down on him.
After the Emperor dismissed the Six Regents,
Emperor Gāozǔ of Wèi died,
entrusting six men to assist the young emperor.
This event is recorded in volume 142, Qí Dōnghūn Hóu Yǒngyuán Yuánnián.
This event is recorded in the previous volume, Qí Hédì Zhōngxīng Yuánnián.
Because Zhào had very few close relatives at court,
he formed alliances and gathered supporters.
Those who attached themselves to him were promoted extraordinarily within ten days to a month,
while those who did not were framed with grave offenses.
He was particularly wary of the various princes.
Since Xiáng's position was above his,
he wanted to remove him
and solely control the court.
Therefore, he slandered him to the Emperor,
saying
that "Xiáng, along with Hào, Zhòu, Jìxián, and Sǎojìng, were plotting rebellion."
In summer,
the fourth month,
the Emperor secretly summoned the Commandant of Justice, Cuī Liàng, into the Forbidden City at night.
He ordered him to impeach Xiáng for his greed, depravity, and extravagance,
and Hào and the other four for their arrogance, power, and avarice.
Hào and the others were arrested and imprisoned in the Southern Terrace.
A hundred tiger guards were sent to surround Xiáng's residence.
Fearing that Xiáng might be alarmed and escape,
he sent his close attendant Guō Yì to open the Jīnyǒng Gate and gallop out to convey the imperial decree,
showing him the Commandant of Justice's impeachment memorial.
Xiáng said:
"If it is indeed as the Commandant of Justice has reported,
what is there to worry about?
I only fear that some greater crime will be falsely brought against me.
If people gave me things,
I certainly received them."
The next morning,
the relevant authorities memorialized to punish Hào and the others.
All were granted death.
The Emperor brought Gāoyáng Wáng Yōng and four other princes to deliberate and thoroughly investigate the charges against Xiáng.
Xiáng was guarded by a single carriage,
sent to Huálín Yuán,
his mother and wife followed him in,
given a few young male and female servants,
and heavily surrounded and guarded.
Communication in and out was cut off.
In the fifth month,
on the day Dīngwèi, the first day of the month,
an imperial edict was issued to pardon Xiáng from death,
reducing him to a commoner.
After a short while,
Xiáng was moved to Tàifǔ Sì,
where the restrictions and confinement became even stricter.
His mother and wife were both returned to their southern residence,
and were allowed to visit him once every five days.
Originally,
Xiáng had married the daughter of Sòng Wáng Liú Chǎng,
but treated her distantly and coolly.
After Xiáng was confined,
Gāo Tàitài then learned about the matter of Āndìng Gāo,
and angrily said:
"You have so many wives and concubines,
why did you need that Gāolì slave girl, leading to such a crime!"
She beat him over a hundred times with a staff,
causing wounds that festered,
and it was more than ten days before he could stand again.
She also beat Liú several tens of times,
saying:
"All women are jealous,
why are you alone not jealous!"
Liú smiled and accepted the punishment,
and did not say anything in the end.
A few of Xiáng's household servants secretly formed a group,
wanting to abduct Xiáng and get him out.
They secretly wrote down their names,
and entrusted a maidservant to pass them to Xiáng.
As Xiáng was about to read it,
the officer in charge of the gate guards saw him from a distance,
rushed in, snatched it from Xiáng's hand,
and reported it.
Xiáng cried out in anguish several times,
and died suddenly.
An imperial edict ordered the relevant officials to bury him with due rites.
"Gate guard officer" refers to
the soldiers guarding the gate to prevent Xiáng from escaping.
Previously,
Yuán Xiǎn, a clerk of the Board of Works, presented a chicken chick
with four wings and four legs.
"Clerk of the Board of Works"
is similar to the present-day directors of the Six Boards of the Secretariat,
an official position.
In Jiāngnán, the Supervisor of the Manufacturing Bureau had a Clerk of the Board of Works.
Previously,
the character "xiān" (先) was pronounced "xī jiàn fān."
Guāng submitted a memorial saying:
"In the early Yuánpíng reign of Emperor Yuán of Hàn,
a female chicken in the household of the Chancellor's clerk incubated chicks,
gradually transforming into a male.
Shīgǔ said:
'Initially, it incubated chicks,
then gradually transformed into a male.'
'Fú' (伏)
is pronounced 'fáng fù fān.'
Shīgǔ said: 'Spurs'
are the bone attached to a chicken's leg,
used for stabbing during fights.
'Jiāng' (將)
means to lead its flock.
There was a presentation of a rooster with horns.
Liú Xiàng considered it a sign that
'the chicken is a small domestic animal, symbolizing the minor officials who are in charge of people's daily lives
and small ministers who hold power in government.
This event is recorded in the 'Wǔxíng Zhì' of the 'Xī Hàn Shū.'
Shí Xiǎn's execution was
its manifestation.'
In the first year of Guānghé of Emperor Líng,
a female chicken in Nángōng Sì was about to transform into a male,
but its head crest had not yet changed.
An edict was issued to ask the Cài Yōng, a Counselor of the Palace,
who replied: 'The head is the head of state,
symbolizing the ruler.
Now the chicken's body has changed,
but not yet its head,
and the emperor knows of it.
This signifies that something will occur but not be fully accomplished.
If the response is not precise,
and the government makes no reforms,
the head crest might form,
and the disaster will become greater.'
This event is recorded in the 'Cài Yōng Zhuàn' of the 'Hòu Hàn Shū.'
The empire subsequently fell into great chaos.
Although the condition of the chicken today is different from that in Hàn,
its implications are quite similar,
which is indeed frightening.
I, your subject, interpret this based on the words of Xiàng and Yōng:
The numerous wings and feet
also symbolize the lower ranks inciting and assisting each other;
being a chick and not yet fully grown,
with relatively small feet and feathers,
also indicates that its power is still weak and
easy to control.
I, your subject, have heard that the appearance of calamities and anomalies
are all meant to show good or ill fortune.
A wise ruler, seeing them, fears,
and is thus able to bring forth blessings.
A foolish ruler, seeing them, is arrogant,
and thus brings forth disaster.
Perhaps there are now those who rise from humble origins to positions of honor,
involving themselves in governance,
similar to Shí Xiǎn of previous generations!
I beg Your Majesty to advance the worthy and dismiss the wicked,
then the omens will be quelled and blessings will gather."
A few days later,
Hào and others were executed,
and the Emperor esteemed Guāng even more.
The Wèi ruler considered the execution of Rú Hào and others as proof of Guāng's words,
wondering if Gāo Zhào alone was not someone who rose from humble origins to a position of honor,
involving himself in governance!
Gāo Zhào persuaded the Emperor
to have the commanders of the palace guards and the imperial guards guard the residences of the various princes.
This was almost equivalent to house arrest.
Péngchéng Wáng Xié strongly remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
Xié's aspirations were lofty,
and he disliked glory and power.
He avoided official duties and stayed at home,
but going out offered no pleasure of mountains and rivers,
and staying in brought no company of kindred spirits.
He was alone with his wife and children,
often feeling depressed and unhappy.
7 The Wèi people besieged Yìyáng.
The city had fewer than five thousand soldiers,
and food supplies for only half a year.
The Wèi army attacked relentlessly day and night.
The Inspector Cài Dàogōng resisted them in every direction,
repelling every assault.
They held out for over a hundred days,
killing and capturing countless enemies.
Wèi had besieged Yìyáng since the tenth month of last year,
and Cài Dàogōng died in the fifth month of this year.
From this point onward,
it refers to the period before Dàogōng's illness became severe.
"Shèng" (勝)
is pronounced "shēng."
[The Wèi army] was about to retreat.
It happened that Dàogōng's illness became critical,
so he called his younger cousin, the General of Cavalry, Líng'ēn,
his nephew, the Director of the Department of State Affairs, Sēngxié, and all his generals and advisors,
and said:
"I have received great kindness from the state,
but cannot eliminate the bandits.
My suffering is now increasingly severe,
and I cannot hold out much longer.
You all must uphold your integrity to the death,
so that I will have no regrets after I die!"
Everyone wept.
After Dàogōng died,
Líng'ēn provisionally took charge of the provincial affairs,
and took his place in defending the city.
8 In the sixth month,
on the day Guǐwèi,
there was a general amnesty.
9 Wèi experienced a severe drought.
Xíng Luán, the Palace Attendant and concurrently Minister, reported:
"In ancient times, enlightened kings valued grain and silk,
and held gold and jade lightly.
Why?
Because grain and silk sustained the people and secured the nation,
while gold and jade were useless and corrupted morality.
The late emperor deeply reflected on extravagance,
striving to promote frugality,
even using paper and silk for screens and hangings,
and copper and iron for bridles.
The gold in the treasury
was merely enough for current needs,
and was not accumulated by purchasing more at the expense of national resources.
By the beginning of the Jǐngmíng era,
inheriting an era of peace and prosperity,
the four borders were clear and tranquil,
and distant and near peoples came together.
Consequently, tribute baskets followed one after another.
The two words 'tribute baskets' originate from the 'Yǔ Gòng,'
referring to precious and fine objects
brought as tribute in baskets.
All the presented tributes
were many times more than usual.

and Xīchāng Hóu Yuānzǎo replaced him.
Yuānzǎo
was the son of Yì.
Yì had died at the hands of Dōnghūn.
Yǐn Tiānbǎo sent a speedy messenger to inform Yuánqǐ.
When the Wèi bandits invaded Jìnshòu,
Wáng Jǐngyìn and others all sent urgent appeals.
The multitude urged Yuánqǐ to rush to their rescue.
Yuánqǐ said:
"The imperial court is ten thousand *lǐ* away,
and the army cannot arrive quickly.
If the bandits spread their infestation,
‘infestation’ (qīnyín)
is compared to a carbuncle,
where the poison invades good flesh, becoming ‘infected flesh’ (yínròu).
The responsibility of supervision
is none other than mine.
Why rush to their rescue?"
The historian says that Dèng Yuánqǐ's request to return home was not from the heart.
扑 (pū),
read as pǔ-mù.
When he went to rescue Hánzhōng,
Jìnshòu had already fallen.
As Xiāo Yuānzǎo was about to arrive,
Yuánqǐ prepared to return,
taking all the grain, supplies, and equipment
without leaving anything behind.
When Yuānzǎo entered the city,
he resented this;
he also requested his fine horses.
Yuánqǐ said:
"Young gentleman,
what need do you have for a horse?"
Yuānzǎo was enraged,
and in his drunkenness,
killed him.
Yuánqǐ had nourished the bandits for his own gain,
but ultimately did not escape death.
Although Yuānzǎo killed him out of personal anger,
he was not without fault.
少 (shǎo),
read as shī-zhào.
恚 (huì),
read as yú-bì.
Crying,
and asking the reason,
Yuānzǎo said:
"The Son of Heaven has issued an edict."
The crowd then dispersed.
He then falsely accused him of rebellion,
and the Emperor suspected it.
A former subordinate of Yuánqǐ, Luó Yán from Guǎnghàn, went to the palace to argue his case.
The Emperor said:
"It is indeed as I had judged."
He sent an envoy to rebuke Yuānzǎo, saying:
"Yuánqǐ avenged your enemy,"
meaning he cooperated to execute Dōnghūn,
avenging his father's enemy.
量 (liáng),
sound liáng.
為 (wéi),
read as yú-wěi;
same below.
"How is that for loyalty and filial piety!"
Thereupon, Yuānzǎo was demoted in title to Guànjūn Jiāngjūn,
and Yuánqǐ was posthumously granted Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
with the posthumous title Zhōng Hóu.
Lǐ Yánshòu commented: Yuánqǐ diligently fostered loyalty,
Máo Cháng said: To please those above by serving those below is called *xūfù*.
Referring to opening up the lands of Liáng and Yì.
but the seeds of disaster were already planted.
The demotion of Guànjūn
was too light a punishment.
The governance and justice of Liáng
was a failure in this regard.
The beginning of private resentment
started from this,
and that the dynasty was not long-lived,
was it not fitting!
11The people of Yìzhōu, Jiāo Sēnghù, gathered a crowd and started a
rebellion.
Xiāo Yuānzǎo was not yet twenty years old;
A person is called *ruòguàn* at twenty.
冠 (guàn),
read as gǔ-wán.
some objected,
Yuānzǎo was furious,
and had them executed by the steps.
Then, he rode in a *píngjiānyú* to patrol the bandit encampments.
*Píngjiānyú*
means people carry it at shoulder height,
hence *píngjiān*.
行 (xíng),
read as xià-mèng.
Arrows fell like rain.
His attendants raised shields to block the arrows,
but Yuānzǎo ordered them to remove them.
Because of this, the morale of the people greatly increased,
and he attacked Sēnghù and others,

12In the sixth month,
on the *gēngxū* day,
the temple of Kǒngzǐ was first established.
13Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Chāozōng,
judging from the *Wǔdài Zhì*,
at this time Liáng established Yùzhōu in Jìnxī,
now the area of Huáiníng Xiàn in Ānqìng Fǔ.
on the *dīngmǎo* day,
Xūe Zhēndù, the Wèi Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, sent his acting commander Lǐ Shūrrén and others to attack him.
Chāozōng's troops were greatly defeated.
14Guànjūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Jǐngyìn, Lǐ Quǎn, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Lǔ Fāngdá and others fought against Wèi Wáng Zú,
and were repeatedly defeated.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Zú advanced and pressed upon Fúchéng.
15In the eighth month,
on the *rényín* day,
Wèi Zhōngshān Wáng Yīng invaded Yōngzhōu.
16On the *gēngxū* day,
Qín and Liáng two *zhōu* Cìshǐ Lǔ Fāngdá fought against Wèi Wáng Zú's commanders Jì Hóngyǎ and Lú Zǔqiān.
They were defeated,
and Fāngdá and fifteen other generals all died.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Wáng Jǐngyìn and others again fought against Zǔqiān,
and were defeated.
Jǐngyìn and twenty-four other generals all died.
17Yáng Gōngzé arrived at Luòkǒu
and fought against Wèi Yùzhōu Zhǎngshǐ Shí Róng,
beheading him.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Jiāngjūn Jiāng Qìngzhēn fought against Wèi at Yángshí,
but was unsuccessful.
Yángshí
is likely the same as Yángshí, where Chén Bózhī was stationed.
18The *man* of Yōngzhōu, Miǎndōng Tàishǒu Tián Qīngxǐ, rebelled and surrendered to Wèi.
According to *Běishǐ*,
the territory Qīngxǐ occupied was probably east of Xiāngyáng
and west of Jìnglíng.
沔 (miǎn),
read as mí-yǎn.
19In Wèi, a *zhī* fungus grew in the west corridor of the Tàijí Diàn.
The corridors of a palace are called *xù*.
Guāng submitted a memorial,
believing
that "This is what Zhuāngzǐ called 'vapor rising to form fungi.'
Soft and fragile things
grow in desolate, damp places,
and should not grow in the high and splendid locations of a palace hall;
now, it suddenly appears,
and its appearance is lush and spreading,
truly peculiar.
Wild trees growing in the court,
wild birds entering the temple,
ancients all considered these signs of decline and ruin.
Thus, Tàiwù and Zhōngzōng, fearing disaster, cultivated virtue,
and the Yin dynasty prospered.
During the time of Shāng Wáng Tàiwù,
in Bó, an auspicious mulberry and a grain plant grew together in the court,
growing to a great circumference overnight.
Tàiwù, fearing this, cultivated virtue,
and the auspicious mulberry withered and died,
and the Yin dynasty revived.
When Gāozōng sacrificed to Chéng Tāng,
a flying pheasant landed on the ear of the tripod and crowed.
Zǔ Jǐ said:
'Only if the former kings rectify their affairs,
and hold court with the feudal lords,
possessing all under Heaven,
it is like moving it in one's palm.'
'Zhōngzōng'
should be
'Gāozōng'.
朝 (cháo),
read as zhí-yáo.
'A nation prospers while omens of misfortune are ignored.'
This is
what he meant.
Currently, in the southwest,
military conflicts have not ceased,
and within the imperial domains,
a great drought has lasted for a long time.
The people are toiling, and things are withering,
nothing is more severe than this.
Those who receive Heaven's mandate and nurture the people should show compassion;
I humbly pray Your Majesty will reflect deeply and reform the sacred Way,
curb the pleasures of nocturnal banquets,
and nurture your prosperous years,
then the Wèi dynasty can eternally flourish,
and Your Imperial Majesty's lifespan will equal the mountains."
At this time, the Wèi ruler was fond of banquets,
thus Guāng mentioned it.
On the 20th of the 9th month,
on the jǐsì day,
Yáng Gōngzè and others fought against Yuán Sōng, the Governor of Yángzhōu of Wèi;
Gōngzè was defeated.
In the winter of the 21st year,
in the 10th month,
on the bǐngwǔ day,
the Emperor launched a large-scale expedition against Wèi.
He appointed Xiāo Hóng, Prince of Línchuān and Governor of Yángzhōu, as the Dūdū Běitǎo Zhū Jūnshì,
and Liǔ Dàn, the Shàngshū Yòupúshè, as his deputy.
Princes, dukes, and officials below them each offered national rents and field grains to assist the army.
"National rents" refers to
the rents collected by their enfeoffed territories.
"Field grains" refers to
the grains collected from their official lands.
On the 22nd, Yáng Jíqǐ and Yáng Jíyì enthroned Yáng Shàoxiān as Emperor,
and they themselves both claimed the title of King.
In the 11th month,
on the wùchén day, the first day of the month,
Wèi dispatched Yáng Chūn, the Guānglù Dàfū, to lead troops to suppress them.
23 Wèi Wángzú besieged Fúchéng,
and the Shǔ people were terrified.
Two or three tenths of the garrisons in Yìzhōu cities surrendered to Wèi,
and over fifty thousand households registered themselves.
Xíng Luán submitted a memorial to the Wèi emperor,
requesting to advance and conquer Shǔ while still victorious,
arguing
that "Jiànkāng and Chéngdū
are ten thousand *lǐ* apart.
Land travel is already cut off;
though one can reach Shǔ by going west from Xiāngyáng and following the land route,
since Liángzhōu has fallen to Wèi,
the land route is severed.
A naval force sailing west
would not arrive within a year.
Yìzhōu has no external military support,
which is the first opportunity.
Recently, during Liú Jìlián's rebellion
and Dèng Yuánqǐ's siege,
(as seen in the first and second years of the previous volume),
the officials and common people lost the will to hold firm,
which is the second opportunity.
Xiāo Yuānzǎo is a young man wearing skirts and clogs,
not yet familiar with governing affairs.
Many renowned generals of old
have been imprisoned or executed.
Those now entrusted with power
are all young men from his close circle,
which is the third opportunity.
Shǔ's sole reliance
is on Jiàngé.
Now that Nán'ān has been captured,
its strategic pass has been taken.
By occupying their territory,
one-third is already ours.
From Nán'ān to Fú,
the path is wide and unimpeded.
and the morale of the rear troops is broken,
which is the fourth opportunity.
Yuānzǎo is a close blood relative of Xiāo Yǎn;
he will certainly not fight to the death.
If Fúchéng is captured,
how could Yuānzǎo sit in the city and be trapped?
He will surely flee at the first sign of trouble.
If he comes out to fight,
the soldiers of Yōng and Shǔ are cowardly and weak,
their bows and arrows few and feeble,
which is the fifth opportunity.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
the eight states of Yōng and Shǔ all followed.
Yōng
refers to the land of Shàngyōng.
Shǔ
refers to the land of Shǔjùn.
They are not accustomed to military life.
We have relied on the utmost efforts of our generals and soldiers,
frequently achieving minor victories.
Having overcome critical obstructions,
the hearts of the people are subdued.
Looking towards Fú and Yì,
(at that time, the administrator of Zǐtóng governed Fúchéng,
and the regional inspector of Yìzhōu governed Chéngdū),
it is only because of too few troops and a lack of provisions
that it is not suitable to advance now.
If we do not seize it now,
it will be difficult to plan for later.
Moreover, Yìzhōu is prosperous,
with a population of one hundred thousand households.
Compared to Shòuchūn and Yìyáng,
its benefits are threefold."
(Wèi had already obtained Shòuchūn and Yìyáng before this,
hence the statement.)
"The opportune moment must not be missed.
If you wish to merely secure the borders and pacify the people,
then your subject is idle here;
I request to return to serve my parents."
The Wèi emperor decreed,
"The campaign to pacify Shǔ
shall await further imperial edicts.
The enemy has not yet been subdued;
how can you use serving your parents as an excuse!"
Luán further memorialized, stating,
"Formerly, Dèng Ài and Zhōng Huì led an army of one hundred and eighty thousand,
exhausting the resources of Zhōngguó,
and barely managed to pacify Shǔ.
(The details can be found in Volume 78, fourth year of Jǐngyuán of Emperor Yuán of Wèi.)
*Nán*
is pronounced *dàn*.
*Shuài*
is read as *lǜ*.
This is a true display of strength.
Moreover, my talent is not that of the ancients;

The reason I dare

To go there now is easy,

Acting on our strength,
it is logically conquerable.
Now Wángzú is already pressing on Fúchéng.
If Fú is captured,
then Yìzhōu will be a captive possession,

Furthermore, Zǐtóng has already annexed tens of thousands of households,"

"Moreover,
Jiàngé is a natural stronghold;

(Zhūgě Kǒngmíng, when he was chancellor of Shǔ,

Because the plank road was thirty *lǐ* long and extremely perilous,

Jiāng Wéi resisted Zhōng Huì there.
Jìn incorporated that area into Zǐtóng Commandery.
Huán Wēn entered Shǔ

"It is not an easy task.
Since the army crossed Jiàngé,

Furthermore, my intention

*Duàn*
is pronounced *dīngguǎn*.
"A lone city defending itself,

I now wish to have units follow one another,

If we succeed, it will be a great advantage;
if not, we will be safe.
Moreover,
Bāxī and Nánzhèng are
fourteen hundred *lǐ* apart,

*Láo*

"It was then memorialized to be abolished.
The people of that land,

Although they mostly reside in mountain valleys,

"However, because they are far from the provincial capital,

is pronounced *shī zhǎo*.
Many harbor different intentions.
During Dàoqiān's initial righteous uprising,

(The land of Bāxī
