*Mào*
is pronounced *mào*.
*Tiē*
means calm,
peaceful,
submissive.
"It would become a part of the state
without the need for military expeditions."
Lǐ Xióng and Qiáo Zòng took Shu;
to the east, they could not pass Diànjiāng.
Given the might of Fú Qín's military,
taking Liáng and Yì was like turning one's hand over;
east of Diànjiāng,
Fú Qín could not possess it.
Xíng Luán's plan for Shu
also only aimed at west of Diànjiāng,
for the strategic advantage of the terrain was indeed reliable.
Our dynasty, since losing Shu in the Shàodìng era,
Péng Dàyǎ then made Yú his administrative seat as a military governor,
maintaining control over the Four Shu for nearly forty years.
Yú
was the ancient land of Diànjiāng.
Diàn
is pronounced like "dié."
Previously,
the Wèi ruler appointed Wáng Zú as the Inspector of Yìzhōu.
The Emperor sent the Grand Administrator of Tiānmén, Zhāng Qí, to lead troops to rescue Yìzhōu.
Before his arrival,
the Wèi ruler instead appointed Yáng Zhǐ of Tàishān, military commander of Liángzhōu, as the Inspector of Yìzhōu.
Wáng Zú, hearing of this,
was displeased,
and immediately withdrew his troops,

After a long time,
Zú defected from Wèi.
Xíng Luán, in Liángzhōu,
treated the powerful families with respect,
and cared for the common people with kindness;
the people of the province were pleased with him.
When Luán conquered Bāxī,
he ordered military commander Lǐ Zhòngqiān to guard it.
Zhòngqiān indulged in wine and women,
squandering military supplies;
when state affairs were consulted,
no one could see him.
Luán was furious, gnashing his teeth;
Zhòngqiān was afraid,
and plotted rebellion.
The city's inhabitants cut off his head,
and surrendered the city.
History states why Wèi could not pacify Shu.
Jiàng
is pronounced as "hù jiāng fān."
24th day of the twelfth month,
gēngshēn,
Wèi dispatched Piyáoqí Dàjiàngjūn Yuán Huái to attack the Dī of Wǔxīng;
Xíng Luán and others were all subject to his command.
25th day, Sītú, Shàngshūlìng Xiè Fěi resigned due to his mother's mourning.
26th day, this year,
there was a great harvest;
ráng
means abundant.
Poetry: "A bumper year, abundant, abundant."
1st day of spring,
first month,
dīngmǎo shuò,
Wèi's Empress gave birth to Zǐ Chāng;
a general amnesty was declared.
2nd day, Yáng Jíyì besieged Wèi's Guānchéng;
this is Yángpíng Guānchéng.
Jíyì engaged in a counter-attack,
attacking and defeating them with upright eyes;
taking advantage of the victory, he pursued the fleeing enemy.
On the rénshēn day,
he captured Wǔxīng,
seized Yáng Shàoxiān,
and sent him to Luòyáng.
Yáng Jíqǐ and Yáng Jíyì fled,
and thus their state was extinguished.
In the sixth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
the Dī King Yáng Máosōu first occupied the hundred qǐng of Chóuchí;
thereafter, it gradually flourished,
possessing all the land of the Hàn commandery of Wǔdū,
invading Lǒngxī and Tiānshuǐ to the north,
and Hànzhōng to the south.
When Tuòbá rose to power,
they took the lands of Wǔdū and Chóuchí,
and the Yáng clan merely held Wǔxīng.
Now that Wèi had taken Hànzhōng,
they then eliminated the Yáng clan.
It was also renamed Dōngyìzhōu.
Dōngyìzhōu governed the commanderies of Wǔxīng, Chóuchí, Pántóu, Guǎngcháng, Guǎngyè, Zǐtóng, and Luòcóng.
3rd day, yǐhài,
former Sītú Xiè Fěi was appointed Zhōngshūjiān and Sītú.
4th day, Inspector of Jìzhōu Huán Hé attacked Wèi's Nánqīngzhōu,
but failed.
Liáng's Qīng and Jì provinces were administered from Yùzhōu.
Wèi Xiǎnzǔ took the Three Qí,
and established Dōngxúzhōu at Hùnchéng,
governing the commanderies of Dōng'ān and Dōngguǎn.
In the twenty-second year of Tàihé of Gāozǔ,
it was renamed Nánqīngzhōu.
In the Five Dynasties Gazetteer,
Yíshuǐ County of Yízhōu
previously had Nánqīngzhōu established there.
5th day, the Túcă gé Wáng Fǎzhì of Wèi's Qínzhōu gathered two thousand people,
and elected the Qínzhōu Clerk Lǚ Gǒu'ér as their leader,
changing the era name to Jiànmíng,
establishing officials,
and attacking and pressuring commanderies and counties.
Chén Zhān, a commoner from Jìngzhōu, also gathered a crowd and proclaimed himself king,
changing the era name to Shèngmíng.
Wèi established Jìngzhōu,
administered from Línjìngchéng,
governing the commanderies of Āndìng, Lǒngdōng, Xīnpíng, Zhàopíng, Píngliáng, and Píngyuán.
6th day, jǐmǎo,
Yáng Jíqǐ and his brothers led their followers to surrender to Jiàn
[Wèi].
7th day, jiǎshēn,
the imperial son Gāng was enfeoffed as the King of Jìn'ān.
8th day of the second month,
bǐngchén,
the Wèi ruler issued an edict to kings, dukes, and below, to speak frankly and offer loyal remonstrance.
Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ Yáng Gù submitted a memorial,
stating
that "the current priority
should be to strengthen ties with the imperial clan,
diligently attend to governmental affairs,
value agriculture and sericulture,
disdain artisans and merchants,
cease discussions of empty subtleties and recondite theories,
and reduce unnecessary expenditures on Buddhist monks,
to alleviate the suffering of hunger and cold."
At this time, the Wèi ruler entrusted power to Gāo Zhào,
neglected the imperial clan,
favored Buddhist practices,
and did not attend to governance,
which is why Gù mentioned these points.
9th day, wǔwǔ,
Wèi dispatched Yòuwèi Jiàngjūn Yuán Lì to lead all armies to suppress Lǚ Gǒu'ér.
Lì
was the son of Xiǎoxīnchéng.
Xiǎoxīnchéng is mentioned in volume 129, in the fifth year of Dàmíng of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng.
10th day, yǐchǒu,
Inspector of Xúzhōu, Lìyáng Chāng Yìzhī, fought against Wèi's Píngnán Jiàngjūn Chén Bózhī at Liángchéng.
During the Tàiyuán era of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn,
Liáng Commandery was provisionally established in the area of Shòuchūn south of the Huái River,
hence there was Liángchéng,
its location being northeast of Shòuyáng
and southwest of Zhōnglí.
11th day, General Xiāo Bǐng led troops to attack Wèi's Xúzhōu,
and besieged Huáiyáng.
Jiǎochéng was on the south bank of the Huái River,
and Huáiyáng was eighteen lǐ north of Jiǎochéng,
administered from Sùyù.
Later, Liáng established Huáiyáng Commandery at Jiǎochéng.
Bǐng
is pronounced as "bǐng."
12th day of the third month,
bǐngyín shuò,
there was a solar eclipse.
13th day, jǐmǎo,
Wèi's Inspector of Jīngzhōu Zhào Yí and Píngnán Jiàngjūn Xī Kāngshēng rescued Huáiyáng.
14th day, Yì, son of Wèi's Xiányáng Wáng Xǐ,
sought permission to bury his father after an amnesty (Xǐ's execution is mentioned in volume 144, first year of Zhōngxīng of Emperor Hédì of Qí).
The Wèi ruler did not permit it.
On the guǐwèi day,
Yì, along with his brothers Chāng and Yè, defected.
The Emperor appointed Yì as the King of Xiányáng;
Yì, being the son of Li, his legitimate mother by Yè,
requested to yield the title to him,
but the Emperor did not allow it.
15th day, Fúguó Jiàngjūn Liú Sīxiào defeated Wèi's Inspector of Qīngzhōu Yuán Xì at Jiāoshuǐ.
According to Wèi Shōu's Records,
Jiāoshuǐ is in Jìmò County, Guǎngcháng Commandery, Guāngzhōu.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states that
Jiāoshuǐ originates from Jiāoshān in Qiánzōu County,
flows north past the east of Yí'ān County,
then northeast past the north of Jiāodōng County city for a hundred lǐ,
and flows into the sea.
Bài
is pronounced as "bǔ mài fān."
16 Línchuān Wáng Hóng (臨川王宏) had his secretary (記室) Wúxīng Qiū Chí (吳興丘遲) write a letter to Chén Bózhī (陳伯之), saying:
"At the time of your departure,
there was no other reason,
it was simply that you could not examine yourself inwardly
and were swayed by external rumors,
becoming deluded and reckless,
which led to this situation.
The Emperor bent the law and extended his grace,
letting a boat-swallowing fish escape.
The Hàn (漢) dynasty, chastising the harshness of Qín (秦) law,
made its net sparse and wide,
which at the time was called 'letting a boat-swallowing fish escape.'
Your relatives are living peacefully,
your high towers have not fallen,
and your beloved concubine is still there.
'Pine and cypress are not cut' means that their ancestral graves would not be destroyed or leveled.
'Relatives are living peacefully' means that his relatives in Jiāngnán (江南) were not implicated in the rebellion
and lived undisturbed as before.
'High towers have not fallen' means that his residence had not been submerged or filled with water,
and his ponds and towers were as they were.
'Beloved concubine is still there' means that his maids and concubines still guarded his home,
not being confiscated by the government or scattered to other households.
Formerly, Yōngmén Zǐ (雍門子) saw Mèngcháng Jūn (孟嘗君)
and chanted:
'The high towers have already fallen,
the winding ponds have already been leveled,
thorns and thistles grow on the tombs,
and shepherd boys play upon them.
Will Mèngcháng Jūn also come to this?'
Mèngcháng Jūn sighed deeply at this.
'A swallow nesting on a flying curtain,'
'a fish swimming in a cooking pot'—
the ancients often used these sayings
to indicate an imminent burning to a crisp.
In the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (左傳),
Wú Jìzhá (吳季札) said to Sūn Línfù (孫林父):
'Your dwelling here
is like a swallow nesting on a curtain.'
Dù Yù (杜預) annotated: 'This means extreme danger.'
I hope you will soon strive for a good plan
and seek abundant blessings for yourself."
On *gēngyín* (庚寅),
Bózhī (伯之) came from Shòuyáng Liángchéng (壽陽梁城) with eight thousand troops to surrender.
Bózhī (伯之) had defected to Wèi (魏) in the first year of the reign period (元年),
and now he returned.
*Jiàng* (降) is pronounced *xiàjiāng* (下江).
An edict reinstated Bózhī (伯zhī) as Governor (刺史) of Xīyù Zhōu (西豫州);
before he could take office,
he was again appointed as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍).
He was not allowed to be stationed at a border town,
fearing he might rebel again.
*Fù* (復) is pronounced *fúyòu* (扶又).
He died at home.
17 In the beginning,
the Wèi (魏) Imperial Censor (御史中尉) Zhēn Chēn (甄琛)
memorialized, stating:
"In the *Zhōu Lǐ* (周禮),
there were officials for mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes, such as the *Yú* (虞) and *Héng* (衡) officials,
who established strict prohibitions for them.
This was to take from them in due season,
not to cause harm or destruction,
so although these officials were appointed,
they actually guarded these resources for the people.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* (周禮) says: The Mountain Yú (山虞) was in charge of the regulations for mountains and forests,
making prohibitions for things and guarding them.
He ordered the myriad people to cut timber in season,
with specified dates,
and those who stole wood were punished.
The Forest Héng (林衡) was in charge of the prohibitions for forests and woodlands and regulated their management,
timing the forests and woodlands and administering rewards and punishments.
The River Héng (川衡) was in charge of inspecting the prohibitions for rivers and marshes and regulating their management,
dismissing their guardians in due season,
and arresting and punishing those who violated the prohibitions.
The Marsh Yú (澤虞) was in charge of the regulations for the state marshes,
establishing strict prohibitions for them,
making the people of that land guard their resources,
bringing them into the royal treasury in due season,
and distributing the remainder to the myriad people.
*Wéi* (為) is pronounced *yúwèi* (于偽);
the following *wéi* (為) has the same pronunciation.
Just as one must generously care for one's children and grandchildren,
the rulers of the world
must generously care for the multitude of people.
There has never been a parent who begrudged their children vinegar or sauces,
or one who, being rich with all living things, monopolized a single item.
Now the county government monopolizes and guards the Hédōng (河東) salt ponds and collects their profits,
which is to solely provide for the mouth and belly, neglecting the four limbs.
The Son of Heaven is rich with the four seas,
why should he worry about poverty!
I beg that the salt prohibition be lifted
and shared with the people!"
Lù Shàngshū Shì Xié (錄尚書事勰) and Shàngshū Xíng Luán (尚書邢巒) memorialized,
believing
that "Chēn's (琛) proposal,
if discussed in theory, is lofty in principle,
but if put into practice, will be deficient in execution.
We privately believe that those in ancient times who were skilled at governing the people
always adapted to the times, whether prosperous or difficult,
and adjusted to circumstances, whether abundant or frugal,
using labor and sustenance, growth and rest, to complete their natures and lives.
If one were to let them grow naturally
and follow their own eating and drinking,
this would be treating all things as 'straw dogs.'
Lǎozi (老子) said: 'Heaven and Earth are not benevolent;
they treat the myriad things as straw dogs.'
The commentary says: Heaven bestows and Earth transforms,
not out of benevolence or grace.
Heaven and Earth give birth to all things,
regarding them as straw, grass, dogs, and livestock,
allowing them to be natural.
Therefore, the sages collected goods from mountains and marshes to lighten the taxes on fields,
and collected taxes from passes and markets to aid the tenth-part reserves.
This means that the tenth-part tax on fields was insufficient to meet national expenses,
so goods from mountains and marshes were collected and taxes from passes and markets were levied to supplement it.
None of this was for personal gain;
it was to utilize the productions of Heaven and Earth
and benefit the people of Heaven and Earth.
Now the prohibition on salt ponds
has been in place for a long time.
Accumulating and then distributing it
serves to assist the military and the state,
not solely to supply delicacies for the Imperial Kitchen (太官)
or ornaments for the Rear Palace.
Since the profit is not for oneself,
then 'their interests' and 'our interests' are one.
However, since the salt prohibition was implemented,
officials have often been negligent,
and in the process of receipt and disbursement,
things have sometimes not followed the law.
This causes the common people to sigh and complain,
and peddlers to speak lightly of it.
This is due to the users lacking proper methods,
not the creators being at fault.
To abolish it suddenly
would, we fear, deviate from the original intent.
To change things with every action
makes the law like a game of *yìqí* (弈棋).
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (左傳) says: 'One who plays *yì* (弈) and cannot decide where to place a piece will not defeat his opponent.'
This is used here to illustrate that changing things with every action means there is no fixed law.
It is proper to follow the old system."
From this point onward,
the combined record is in Volume 143, Qí Dōnghūn (齊東昏), Yǒngmíng (永明) second year.
Chēn's (琛) proposal was implemented at the beginning of Jǐngmíng (景明) era,
then suspended in Jǐngmíng (景明) fourth year.
Now the salt prohibition is again abolished,
which means his proposal is finally adopted.
*Zú* (卒) is pronounced *zǐxù* (子恤).
In the fourth month,
on *yǐwèi* (乙未),
the salt pond prohibition was abolished.
The recovery of salt profits can be seen in the upper volume, second year.
18 On *gēngxū* (庚戌),
Wèi (魏) appointed Zhōngshān Wáng Yīng (中山王英) as General Who Conquers the South (征南將軍), Grand Coordinator (都督) of the military affairs of Yáng (揚) and Xú (徐) two prefectures,
leading a force of over ten myriad to resist the Liáng (梁) army,
giving instructions to all section commanders,
and acting at his discretion wherever he went.
The Governor (刺史) of Jiāng Zhōu (江州), Wáng Mào (王茂), led tens of thousands of soldiers to invade Wèi (魏)'s Jīng Zhōu (荊州),
enticing Wèi (魏)'s border people and various tribal groups to establish Wǎn Zhōu (宛州),
and sent Léi Bàoláng (雷豹狼) and others, appointed by him as Governor (刺史) of Wǎn Zhōu (宛州), to attack and capture Wèi (魏)'s Hénán Chéng (河南城).
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's (蕭子顯) *Qí Zhì* (齊志) says,
Yōng Zhōu (雍州) had Hénán Jùn (河南郡),
which administered five counties,
but only Jíyáng (棘陽) was actual territory.
Thus, Hénán Jùn (河南郡) must have been within the borders of Nányáng (南陽)'s Jíyáng (棘陽) county.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志) says,
Xīnyě (新野) county in Dèng Zhōu (鄧州) was formerly called Jíyáng (棘陽).
On *xīnyǒu* (辛酉),
Mào (茂) was defeated in battle,
losing over two thousand men.
*Kǎo Yì* (考異) says: The biography of Dàyǎn (大眼) states,
"captured and beheaded over seven thousand,"
but here we follow the *Wèi Dì Jì* (魏帝紀).
Mào (茂) fled back;
Dàyǎn (大眼) pursued him to the Hàn Shuǐ (漢水)
and captured five cities.
Wèi (魏)'s General Who Attacks the Captives (征虜將軍) Yǔwén Fú (宇文福) raided Sī Zhōu (司州),
captured over a thousand people, and departed.
In the fifth month,
on *xīnwèi* (辛未),
the Crown Prince's Right Guard Commander (太子右衞率) Zhāng Huìshào (張惠紹) and others invaded Wèi (魏)'s Xú Zhōu (徐州),
captured Sùyù (宿預),
and seized the city lord Mǎ Chénglóng (馬成龍).
Emperor Ān (安帝) of Jìn (晉) established Sùyù (宿預) county,
belonging to Huáiyáng Jùn (淮陽郡).
Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) of Wèi (魏) made it the seat of Nán Xú Zhōu (南徐州).
On *yǐhài* (乙亥)
the Governor (刺史) of Běi Xú Zhōu (北徐州), Chāng Yìzhī (昌義之), captured Liáng Chéng (梁城).
Nán Xú (南徐) was governed from Jīngkǒu (京口), hence Zhōnglí (鍾離) was made Běi Xú (北徐).
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Wéi Ruì sent his Eldest Scribe, Wáng Chāo, and others to attack Xiǎoxiàn,
but they failed to take it.
Ruì personally supervised the construction of the siege works.
The Wèi troops sent out several hundred men to array themselves outside the gate.
Ruì wanted to attack them,
but all the generals said:
“They came lightly before,
without battle preparations.
They will slowly return, don their armor,
and then we can advance.”
Ruì said:
“Not so.
The Wèi have over two thousand men in the city,
enough to hold it securely.
Now, for no reason, they sent men outside;
these must be their bravest and most skilled.
If we can defeat them,
the city will fall of its own accord.”
The assembled officers still hesitated.
Ruì pointed to his staff of authority and said:
“The court conferred this upon me
not for decoration.
Wéi Ruì’s orders must not be defied!”
He then advanced to attack them.
The soldiers all fought to the death,
and the Wèi army was defeated and fled.
Taking advantage of this, they pressed the attack,
capturing the city by midnight.
They then proceeded to Héféi.
Earlier,
the Right Army Sīmǎ, Hú Jǐnglüè, and others had attacked Héféi,
but after a long time, it had not fallen.
Ruì surveyed the terrain.
At night,
he led his troops to dam the Féishuǐ.
Soon,
the dam was complete, and the water flowed through,
with boats and ships arriving in succession.
The Wèi had built small eastern and western cities flanking Héféi.
Ruì first attacked these two cities.
The Wèi general, Yáng Língyìn, suddenly arrived with fifty thousand troops.
The troops were afraid they were no match
and requested to send a memorial asking for reinforcements.
Ruì laughed and said:
“When the enemy has reached the city walls,
to then ask for reinforcements,
what good would that do!
Moreover, if I ask for reinforcements,
they too will get reinforcements.
The value of troops lies in using unusual tactics,
not in their numbers!”
He then attacked Língyìn
and defeated him.
Ruì ordered his military commander, Wáng Huáijìng, to build a city on the bank to guard the dam.
The Wèi attacked and captured it,
and over a thousand men in the city were all lost.
The Wèi, emboldened by their victory, advanced to the foot of the dike.
Their military might was very strong.
The generals wanted to retreat to Cháohú,
or some wanted to defend Sānchā.
The 'Kǎoyì' states: 'Nánshǐ' records "Sānzhàng."
We now follow 'Liángshū.'
The waters of Cháohú here divide into three channels,
hence the name.
Retreating to defend here
would be advantageous for ships to enter,
which is why the troops desired it.
“How could this be!”
He ordered umbrellas, fans, banners, and flags to be taken out
and planted at the foot of the dike,
showing no intention of moving.
The Wèi troops came to dig at the dike.
Ruì personally contended with them.
The Wèi soldiers retreated,
and he then built a stronghold on the dike to secure himself.
Ruì constructed a fighting ship
as tall as the city of Héféi.
It overlooked the city on all four sides,
and the people in the city all wept.
The defending general, Dù Yuánlún, ascended the city wall to supervise the battle,
was hit by a crossbow bolt, and died.
On the day Xīnsì,
the city fell.
Over ten thousand heads were captured and cut off,
and cattle and sheep were seized in the tens of thousands.
Ruì was naturally frail
and had never ridden a horse.
In every battle,
he always rode in a sedan chair, encouraging his officers and soldiers,
his courage unmatched.
During the day, he received guests and travelers.
At midnight, he would get up
to calculate military dispatches,
lighting lamps until dawn.
He managed his troops
as if he could never do enough,
so aspiring volunteers vied to join him.
Wherever he stopped, the lodgings and buildings,
and the surrounding walls, all conformed to regulations.
When the various armies advanced to Dōnglíng,
The 'Shuǐjīngzhù' states: "In the northwest of Jīnlán Xiàn, Lújiāng, there is Dàsū Shān in Dōnglíng Xiāng,
the source of the Guànshuǐ."
Examining various gazetteers, there is no Jīnlán Xiàn;
it is unknown in what era it was established.
The imperial edict to withdraw the troops
must have been after the army's defeat at Luòkǒu.
The historian records it here at the end of Ruì's affairs.
According to Yáo Sīlián's 'Liángshū,'
at that time, Wèi defended Pìchéng,
twenty *lǐ* from Dōnglíng.
Ruì sent all the baggage trains ahead,
personally riding in a small sedan chair to guard the rear.
The Wèi troops respected Ruì’s prestige and reputation,
and, seeing him, dared not approach,
so the entire army returned safely.
Thereupon, the seat of Yùzhōu was moved to Héféi.
Yùzhōu moved from Jìnxī to Héféi.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Wèi sent Shàngshū Yuán Yáo south to resist the Liáng troops.
On the day Guǐwèi,
Wèi sent Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Yú Jìng to command the various armies of Qín and Lǒng.
On the day Dīnghài,
Lújiāng Tàishǒu Wénxǐ Péi Suì captured Wèi’s Yángshí Chéng.
On the day Gēngyín,
he also captured Huòqiū Chéng.
The 'Shuǐjīngzhù' states: "Cáo Wèi's Ānfēng Dūwèi governed south of Ānfēng Jīn.
Later, its former city was established as Huòqiū Shù.
The Suí established Huòqiū Xiàn,
now about a hundred *lǐ* east of Shòuchūn."
Dù Yòu said: "Huòqiū
was the land of Hàn's Sōngzī Xiàn."
The 'Kǎoyì' states: "Péi Suì's biography in 'Liángshū' says:
'In the fifth year,
he campaigned at Shàoyáng Zhōu.
The Wèi people built a long bridge to cross.
Suì built a rampart to press against the bridge,
secretly building concealed assault ships.
As the Huái River suddenly swelled,
Suì rode his ships directly to the side of the bridge.
The Wèi forces were startled and scattered.
Suì, taking advantage of the victory, pursued and attacked,
thoroughly defeating them,
then advanced to capture Yángshí and Huòqiū Chéng,
pacified Xiǎoxiàn,
and attacked Héféi.' "
The 'Wèi Dìjì' records:
"On the day Xīnsì,
Yǎn (referring to Wéi Ruì, whose courtesy name was Yǎn) was about to take Héféi.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Yángshí and Huòqiū also fell."
According to Wéi Ruì's biography,
when Ruì attacked Shàoyáng Zhōu,
he ordered Suì to burn the bridge with ships.
This event was after the capture of Héféi.
Also, the 'Liáng Dìjì' states:
On the day Xīnsì,
Ruì captured Héféi.
On the day Dīnghài,
Suì captured Yángshí.
On the day Gēngyín,
he captured Huòqiū.
We follow this account.
The 'Suìzhuàn' recording the capture of the two cities after the defeat at Shàoyáng Zhōu
is an error.
In the sixth month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Qīng and Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ Héng Hé captured Qúshān Chéng.
On the day Yǐsì,
Wèi Ānxī Jiāngjūn Yuán Lì attacked Wáng Fǎzhì,
defeated him,
and cut off six thousand heads.
Zhāng Huìshào and the Acting Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Sòng Hēi advanced by both land and water,
heading towards Péngchéng,
and besieged Gāozhǒng Shù.
The 'Shuǐjīngzhù' states: "South of Xiàoshān in Péngchéng, there is the tomb of Chǔ Yuán Wáng,
about ten *zhàng* high and a hundred *bù* wide."
It is probably here that Wèi established a stronghold!
Qù, pronounced "qī yù fān" (an archaic way to indicate pronunciation).
On the day Dīngwèi,
Huìshào's troops suffered a disadvantage,
and Hēi died in battle.
Crown Prince Tǒng, at five years old,
could recite all five classics.
On the day Gēngxū,
he first moved out from the forbidden palace to reside in the Eastern Palace.
On the day Dīngsì,
The Grand General of Agile Cavalry (Piaòqí Dàjiāngjūn) of Wèi, Yuán Huái, Duke Huì of Féngyì, died.
Huái was by nature broad-minded and simple,
disliking trivialities.
He often said:
"As a nobleman, one should grasp the main principles;
why bother with every detail?
It is like building a house:
as long as its exterior looks tall and prominent,
its pillars and beams are level and straight,
and its foundation and walls are firm and strong,
that is enough.
If the ax cuts unevenly,
or the carvings are not precise,
these are not flaws of the house."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Bǐngyín,
Huán Hé attacked Wèi's Yǎnzhōu
and captured Gùchéng.
Gùchéng
is presumably the same as Bàodú Gùchéng.
Bàodú Gùchéng is located within Lánlíng Commandery.
Lǚ Gǒugér led a host of over 100,000 men and encamped at Gūshān,
besieging Qínzhōu.
This Gūshān should be around Shàngguī.
Wèi's Qínzhōu was governed from Shàngguī,
which oversaw Tiānshuǐ, Lüèyáng, and Hànyáng Commanderies.
They were severely defeated.
Lǐ Sháo, acting Qínzhōu Inspector, launched a surprise attack on Gūshān,
capturing Gǒugér's parents, wife, and children.
On the day Gēngchén,
Gǒugér, with his followers, surrendered to Lì.
Yáng Chūn, acting Minister of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Qīng), separately campaigned against Chén Zhān.
Zhān held a strategic stronghold and resisted.
Some generals suggested laying ambushes in mountain paths
to cut off his access,
waiting for his supplies to run out before attacking.
Others wanted to cut down trees and burn the mountains
before advancing.
Chūn said:
"Neither of these is a good plan.
Since the imperial army arrived,
it has conquered everywhere it went.
The reason the rebels are hiding deeply
is simply to avoid death.
Now, if we restrain all the armies
from further raiding,
the rebels will surely think we are deterred by the danger and will not advance.
When they are unprepared,
we will strike decisively,
and they can be pacified in one fell swoop."
So, he halted his troops and did not advance.
The rebels indeed came out to raid.
Chūn again used horses and livestock to lure them,
not pursuing or attacking them.
After a long time,
he secretly selected elite soldiers,
muzzled them, and launched a night raid,
beheading Zhān
and sending his head.
Qín and Jīng provinces were both pacified.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Wáng Bó'áo, Inspector of Xúzhōu, fought with Wèi's King Zhōngshān Yīng at Yīnlíng.
Yīnlíng County
belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty, and to Huáinán Commandery during the Jìn dynasty.
Liáng's Běiqiáo Commandery was governed from Yīnlíng City.
The Suí dynasty changed Běiqiáo Commandery to Quánjiāo County,
which belonged to Jiāngdū Commandery.
During the Táng dynasty, Quánjiāo County belonged to Chúzhōu.
Over five thousand men were lost.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Wèi mobilized 100,000 men from Dìng, Jì, Yíng, Xiāng, Bīng, and Sì provinces to reinforce the southern expeditionary force.
The Emperor dispatched General Jué Niàn with 10,000 men to garrison Méngshān
and recruit the people of Yǎnzhōu.
Many surrendered.
Wèi Shōu's records state
that there is a Méngshān southeast of Xīntài County, Dōng'ān Commandery, Nánqīngzhōu.
It is probably that Méngshān is what was anciently called Dōngméng.
It, along with Gùchéng and Gūshān, are all near the eastern border of Wèi's Yǎnzhōu.
Therefore, Liáng's forces linked up and occupied it
to recruit the people of Yǎnzhōu.
The "Biography of Xíng Luán" in the History of the Northern Dynasties (Běishǐ Xíng Luán zhuàn)
mentions that at this time, Liáng people were invading Xú and Yǎn,
which is correct.
Jué
is a surname.
The "Surname Compendium" (Xìngyuàn) states
that there was Jué Shànshū in the Hàn dynasty.
將 (jiàng)
is pronounced liàng.
降 (jiàng)
is pronounced jiàng.
General Xiāo Jí garrisoned Gùchéng,
and Huán Hé garrisoned Gūshān.
Wèi Shōu's records state
that Lánlíng County, Lánlíng Commandery, has Shígūshān,
and Chānglǜ County also has Gūshān.
Separate General Yuán Hé attacked Jí,
and Commander Bì Zǔxiǔ attacked Niàn.
On the day Rén'yín,
Lǔ severely defeated Hé at Gūshān.
Héng captured Gùchéng,
and Zǔxiǔ attacked Niàn,
putting him to flight.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Wèi issued an imperial edict for the General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn), King Ānlè Quán, to oversee the newly mobilized armies proceeding to Huáinán.
Quán was the son of Chánglè.
King Ānlè Chánglè is mentioned in volume 133, third year of Sòng Cāngwú Wáng Yuánhuī.
樂 (lè)
is pronounced luò.
詮 (quán)
is pronounced quán.
General Lán Huáigōng fought with Wèi's Xíng Luán at Suīkǒu.
Huáigōng was defeated,
and Luán advanced to besiege Sùyù.
Huáigōng then built a city south of the Qīng River (Qīngnán).
Qīngnán means south of the Qīng River.
復 (fù)
is pronounced fù.
In the ninth month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
it was captured,
and Huáigōng was beheaded.
Tens of thousands were killed or captured.
Zhāng Huìshào abandoned Sùyù.
This and the later mention that Zhāng Huìshào retreated with his troops upon hearing of the defeat at Luòkǒu
is actually the same incident.
See later explanation.
And fled back.
Línchuān Wáng Hóng (臨川王宏), as the emperor's younger brother, led an army.
Their weapons and equipment were excellent and new,
and the military appearance was very grand.
Northerners considered it unprecedented for hundreds of years.
The army camped at Luòkǒu (洛口).
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù (水經註) states: Luòjiàn (洛澗) is north of Xīqǔyáng (西曲陽) County,
where Liú Láozhī (劉牢之) slew the Qín (秦) general Liáng Chéng (梁成).
It flows north through Qín Xū (秦墟),
and then empties into the Huái (淮),
hence it is called Luòkǒu (洛口).
This refers to Chāng Yìzhī's (昌義之) victory over Liáng Chéng (梁城).
Hóng (宏) was timid and cowardly by nature,
and his dispositions were disorderly.
Wèi (魏) issued an edict for Xíng Luán (邢巒) to lead his troops across the Huái (淮),

Hóng (宏), hearing this,
was afraid,

Lǚ Sēngzhēn (呂僧珍) said:
"To know difficulty and retreat,

Hóng (宏) said:
"I also think so."
Liǔ Dàn (柳惔) said:
"Since our great army has arrived,

Péi Suì (裴邃) said:

Mǎ Xiānpín (馬仙琕) said:

We must advance a foot to our death,

Chāng Yìzhī (昌義之) was enraged,

"Lǚ Sēngzhēn (呂僧珍) should be executed!

Zhū Sēngyǒng (朱僧勇) and Hú Xīnshēng (胡辛生) drew their swords and withdrew (tùi).
"退" (tuì, withdraw),

"If you wish to retreat, retreat on your own.

The debaters withdrew.
Sēngzhēn (僧珍) apologized to the generals, saying:

meaning Hóng's (宏) heart disease (xīnfēng) had flared up.
"I was deeply afraid that it would lead to great discouragement,

Hóng (宏) dared not immediately disregard the public opinion,

The Wèi (魏) people, knowing his lack of martial spirit,
sent him women's headwear (jīn guó),

"Do not fear Xiāo Niáng (蕭娘) or Lǚ Lǎo (呂姥)."
This means he was timid and cowardly,
like women and girls.
Lǎo (姥),
pronounced mò bǔ.
Hǔ (虎, tiger),
refers to Wéi Ruì (韋叡).
Sēngzhēn (僧珍) sighed and said:

Shǐxīng Wáng Dàn (始興王憺) and Wúpíng Hóu Bǐng (吳平侯昺).
Shuài (帥, commander),
pronounced suǒ lèi.
The main army remained at Luòkǒu (洛口).
Hóng (宏) stubbornly refused to listen,

Consequently, the officers and soldiers were all filled with indignation.
Wèi Xī Kāngshēng (魏奚康生) sent Yáng Dàyǎn (楊大眼) galloping to Zhōngshān Wáng Yīng (中山王英), saying:

Yīng (英) said:

Zhāng Huìshào (張惠紹)'s orders were strict and clear;

He encamped at Xiàpī (下邳).
It has been previously mentioned that Zhāng Huìshào (張惠紹) abandoned Sùyù (宿預) and fled back.
Sùyù (宿預) is more than a hundred *lǐ* southeast of Xiàpī (下邳).
This mention of camping at Xiàpī (下邳)

Lǐ Yánshòu (李延壽) included this event in the biography of Línchuān Wáng Hóng (臨川王宏),

Huìshào (惠紹) admonished them, saying:

Guórén (國人),

Jiàng (降, surrender),

On the *jǐchǒu* day, that night,

The Kǎo Yì (考異) states: The biography of Hóng (宏) in the Liáng Shū (梁書) says,

This is completely untrue.
We now follow the Nán Shǐ (南史).
The land and water routes were filled (with retreating soldiers),

Nearly fifty thousand people died.
Hóng (宏) crossed the river in a small boat,

Hóng (宏) had no reply,

Yuānyóu (淵猷) was Yuānzǎo's (淵藻) younger brother.

Wèi (魏) Emperor decreed Zhōngshān Wáng Yīng (中山王英) to take advantage of the victory to pacify the southeast.
Pursuing the fleeing army to Mǎtóu (馬頭),

In winter,

Luán (巒) again submitted a memorial,

If one were to consider a strategy of gain or loss,

Yīng (英) planned to take Zhōnglí (鍾離) with eighty days' provisions,

Without engaging in battle with the enemy,

I would rather bear the responsibility for cowardice and not advancing,

Zhōnglí (鍾離) has natural defenses,
known to the court nobles,
meaning known to the esteemed ministers of the court.
朝 (cháo)

if they do not know;

Shìzhōng (侍中) Lú Chǎng (盧昶) had always disliked Luán (巒).

彈 (tán)

Huī (暉) and Lú Chǎng (盧昶) were both favored by the Wèi (魏) ruler but were greedy and indulgent.

All official appointments had fixed prices:

選 (xuǎn)

The Wèi 魏 people used carts to carry earth to fill the moat,

If anyone failed to turn back in time,

Soon, the moat was filled.
Wherever the battering rams struck,

The Wèi 魏 people attacked fiercely day and night,

In one day, there were dozens of battles,

I beg for a little more leeway!"
The Wèi 魏 sovereign again issued an edict saying:

Yīng 英 still insisted in his memorial that he would surely capture it.

The Art of War says: "It is difficult to plan against an enemy with those who have a history of constant victories,"

Jiào 校,

Yīnlíng 陰陵 must have been to the southwest of Zhōnglí 鍾離,

The soldiers feared the strength of the Wèi 魏 army

*Fù*

*Jǐ*

*Gōng*

Dù Yòu's *Tōngdiǎn* states: For building a city wall,
the width at the bottom should be double its height,
and the width at the top should be half of the width at the bottom.
If the city wall is five *zhàng* high,
the width at the bottom is two *zhàng* five *chǐ*,
and the width at the top is one *zhàng* two *chǐ* five *cùn*.
The height, width, and narrowness should be based on this standard.
Calculating the work: The top width plus the bottom width equals three *zhàng* seven *chǐ* five *cùn*.
Half of that is one *zhàng* eight *chǐ* seven *cùn* five *fēn*.
Multiply this by the height of five *zhàng*,
and the volume of one *chǐ* of city wall is ninety-three *zhàng* seven *chǐ* five *cùn*.
For each *gōng*,
two *chǐ* of earth are built daily.
This requires approximately forty-seven men.
For a city wall of five *chǐ* per pace, two hundred and thirty-five men are needed.
For one hundred paces, twenty-three thousand five hundred men are needed.
If you know one *lǐ*, you can know ten *lǐ*.
The excavation and carrying of baskets are all calculated within this great *gōng*.
The moat's surface width is two *zhàng*,
its depth is one *zhàng*,
and its bottom width is one *zhàng*.
Add the surface width to the bottom width and take a majority of it;
you get one *zhàng* five *chǐ*.
Multiply this by the depth of one *zhàng*,
and digging one *chǐ* of moat yields a volume of fifteen *zhàng*.
Each person is calculated to excavate three *zhàng* per day,
so five men are needed.
For five *chǐ* per pace, twenty-five men are needed.
For ten paces, two hundred and fifty men are needed.
For one *lǐ*, seventy thousand five hundred men are needed.
With this as the calculation,
one hundred *lǐ* can be known.
*Bǐ*

Wéi Ruì refused.
The army panicked,
but Wéi Ruì shouted loudly from atop the city wall,

This was a resolute battle.
When two armies' camps are close,

Wéi Ruì in this situation

In recent years, if the defense of Xiāngyáng

Alas,
how painful!
All were overrun by Yáng Dàyǎn.
Cáo Jǐngzōng recruited over a thousand brave warriors

When Yáng Dàyǎn came to attack,

Any raiders

The Emperor ordered Jǐngzōng and others to prepare large warships in advance,

The two histories of Liáng and Wèi likely recorded the dates as reported;

Shěn Yuē said: Emperor Wǔ of Jìn divided Fúfēng to create Qín Guó.
When the Central Plains fell into chaos,

Dàogēn and others personally engaged in battle.

Ruì sent a message to Chāng Yìzhī.

Wèi Shōu's Zhì states:

Tiānjiān, seventh year (Wùzǐ, 508 CE)
1st. Spring,
First month.
