3 An imperial edict commanded Xú Miǎn (徐勉), Shàngshū (尚書) of the Lìbù (吏部), to establish a system of nine ranks and eighteen classes for all civil officials.
Those with more classes were considered nobler.
In the second month,
on the day Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
the ranks of Zhèn (鎮) and Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍) and below were increased to ten ranks,
totaling twenty-four classes;
those not reaching the tenth rank
had an additional eight classes.
Also, twenty-four classes of generals for foreign relations were established,
totaling one hundred and nine titles.
Chéngxiàng (丞相), Tàizǎi (太宰), Tàifù (太傅), Tàibǎo (太保), Dà Sīmǎ (大司馬), Dà Jiāngjūn (大將軍), Tàiwèi (太尉), Sītú (司徒), and Sīkōng (司空) were in the eighteenth class.
All Jiāngjūn (將軍) who established their own administration and received the honorific Yídóng Sānsī (儀同三司), and Zuǒ-Yòu Guānglù Kāifǔ Yídóng Sānsī (左‧右光祿開府儀同三司) were in the seventeenth class.
Shàngshūlìng (尚書令), Tàizǐ Tàifù (太子太傅), and Zuǒ-Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (左‧右光祿大夫) were in the sixteenth class.
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè (尚書左僕射), Tàizǐ Shǎofù (太子少傅), Shàngshū Púshè (尚書僕射), Yòu Púshè (右僕射), Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監), Tèjìn (特進), and Lǐng-Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (領‧護軍將軍) were in the fifteenth class.
Zhōng Lǐng-Hùjūn (中領‧護軍), Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書), Tàizǐ Zhānshì (太子詹事), Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫), and Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿) were in the fourteenth class.
Zhōngshūlìng (中書令), Liècáo Shàngshū (列曹尚書), Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (國子祭酒), Zōngzhèng-Tàifǔ Qīng (宗正‧太府卿), and Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫) were in the thirteenth class.
Shìzhōng (侍中), Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Zuǒ-Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn (左‧右衞將軍), Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ (司徒左長史), and Wèiwèi Qīng (衞尉卿) were in the twelfth class.

Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞), Shàngshū Lìbù Láng (尚書吏部郎), Mìshū Jiān (秘書監), Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍), Tàizǐ Zuǒ-Yòu Èrwèi Shuài (太子左‧右二衞率), Zuǒ-Yòu Xiāo-Yóu (左‧右驍‧游), Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Shī (皇弟‧皇子師), Sīnóng-Shǎofǔ-Tíngwèi Qīng (司農‧少府‧廷尉卿), Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子), and Guānglù Qīng (光祿卿) were in the eleventh class.

Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng (給事黃門侍郎), Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Fǔ Chángshǐ (皇弟‧皇子府長史), Tàipú-Dàjiàng Qīng (太僕‧大匠卿), Tàizǐ Jiālìng-Shuàigēnglìng-Pú (太子家令‧率更令‧僕), Yángzhōu Biéjià (揚州別駕), Zhōngsàn Dàfū (中散大夫), Sītú Yòu Chángshǐ (司徒右長史), Yúnqí (雲騎), Yóuqí (游騎), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Fǔ Sīmǎ (皇弟‧皇子府司馬), and Zhūyī Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (朱衣直閤將軍) were in the tenth class.

Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞), Hónglú Qīng (鴻臚卿), Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎), Guózǐ Bóshì (國子博士), Tàizǐ Shùzǐ (太子庶子), Yángzhōu Zhōngcóngshì (揚州中從事), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Gōngfǔ Cóngshì Zhōngláng (皇弟‧皇子公府從事中郎), Tàizhōu Qīng (太舟卿), Dàchángqiū (大長秋), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Fǔ Zīyì (皇弟‧皇子府諮議), Sìwángfǔ Chángshǐ (嗣王府長史), Qián-Zuǒ-Yòu-Hòu Sìjūn (前‧左‧右‧後四軍), Sìwángfǔ Sīmǎ (嗣王府司馬), and Shùxìng Gōngfǔ Chángshǐ-Sīmǎ (庶姓公府長史‧司馬) were in the ninth class.

Mìshū Chéng (秘書丞), Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人), Sītú Zuǒ Xīyuàn (司徒左西掾), Sītú Shǔ (司徒屬), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Yǒu (皇弟‧皇子友), Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎), Shàngshū Yòuchéng (尚書右丞), Nánxúzhōu Biéjià (南徐州別駕), and Huángdì-Huángzǐ-Gōngfǔ Yuànshǔ (皇弟‧皇子‧公府掾屬),

Huángdì-Huángzǐ Dānwèi Èrwèi Sīmǎ (皇弟‧皇子單為二衞司馬), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Gōngfǔ Cóngshì Zhōngláng (嗣王‧庶姓公府從事中郎), Zuǒ-Yòu Zhōnglángjiāng (左‧右中郎將), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Gōngfǔ Zīyì (嗣王‧庶姓公府諮議), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Zhī Shùzǐfǔ Chángshǐ-Sīmǎ (皇弟‧皇子之庶子府長史‧司馬), Fānwángfǔ Chángshǐ-Sīmǎ (蕃王府長史‧司馬), and Shùxìng Chíjié Fǔ Chángshǐ-Sīmǎ (庶姓持節府長史‧司馬) were in the eighth class.

Wǔxiào (五校), Dōnggōng Sānxiào (東宮三校), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Zhī Shùzǐfǔ Zhōng Lùshì-Zhōng Jìshì-Zhōng Zhíbīng Cānjūn (皇弟‧皇子之庶子府中錄事‧中記室‧中直兵參軍), Nánxúzhōu Zhōngcóngshì (南徐州中從事), and Huángdì-Huángzǐ Zhī Shùzǐfǔ-Fānwángfǔ Zīyì (皇弟‧皇子之庶子府‧蕃王府諮議) were in the seventh class.

Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (太子洗馬), Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (通直散騎侍郎), Sītú Zhǔbù (司徒主簿), Shàngshū Shìláng (尚書侍郎), Zhùzuò Láng (著作郎), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Fǔ Gōngcáoshǐ (皇弟‧皇子府功曹史), Wǔjīng Bóshì (五經博士), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Fǔ Lùshì-Jìshì-Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (皇弟‧皇子府錄事‧記室‧中兵參軍), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Jīng-Jiāng-Yōng-Yǐng-Nánxú Wǔzhōu Biéjià (皇弟‧皇子荊‧江‧雍‧郢‧南徐五州別駕), Lǐng-Hùjūn Chángshǐ-Sīmǎ (領‧護軍長史‧司馬), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Gōngfǔ Yuànshǔ (嗣王‧庶姓公府掾屬), Nántái Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ (南臺治書侍御史), Tíngwèi Sānguān (廷尉三官), Yèzhě Púshè (謁者僕射), Tàizǐ Mén Dàfū (太子門大夫), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Gōngfǔ Zhōng Lùshì-Zhōng Jìshì-Zhōng Zhíbīng Cānjūn (嗣王‧庶姓公府中錄事‧中記室‧中直兵參軍), and Shùxìng Fǔ Zīyì (庶姓府諮議) were in the sixth class.

Shàngshū Lángzhōng (尚書郎中), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Wénxué jí Fǔ Zhǔbù (皇弟‧皇子文學及府主簿), Tàizǐ Tàifù-Shǎofù Chéng (太子太傅‧少傅丞), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Xiāng-Yù-Sī-Yì-Guǎng-Qīng-Héng Qīzhōu Biéjià (皇弟‧皇子湘‧豫‧司‧益‧廣‧青‧衡七州別駕), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Jīng-Jiāng-Yōng-Yǐng-Nányǎn Wǔzhōu Zhōngcóngshì (皇弟‧皇子荊‧江‧雍‧郢‧南兗五州中從事), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Jīng-Jiāng děng Wǔzhōu Biéjià (嗣王‧庶姓荊‧江等五州別駕), Tàicháng Chéng (太常丞), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Guólángzhōnglìng (皇弟‧皇子國郎中令), Sānjiàng (三將), Dōnggōng Èrjiàng (東宮二將), Sìwángfǔ Gōngcáoshǐ (嗣王府功曹史), Shùxìng Gōngfǔ Lùshì-Jìshì-Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (庶姓公府錄事‧記室‧中兵參軍), and Huángdì-Huángzǐ Zhī Shùzǐfǔ-Fānwángfǔ Zhōng Lùshì-Zhōng Jìshì-Zhōng Zhíbīng Cānjūn (皇弟‧皇子之庶子府‧蕃王府中錄事‧中記室‧中直兵參軍) were in the fifth class.

Jǐshìzhōng (給事中), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Fǔ Zhèngcānjūn (皇弟‧皇子府正參軍), Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人), Jiànkāng Sānguān (建康三官), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Běixú-Běiyǎn-Liáng-Jiāo-Nánliáng Wǔzhōu Biéjià (皇弟‧皇子北徐‧北兗‧梁‧交‧南梁五州別駕), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Xiāng-Yù-Sī-Yì-Guǎng-Qīng-Héng Qīzhōu Biéjià-Zhōngcóngshì (皇弟‧皇子湘‧豫‧司‧益‧廣‧青‧衡七州別駕‧中從事), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Xiāng-Yù děng Qīzhōu Biéjià (嗣王‧庶姓湘‧豫等七州別駕), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Jīng-Jiāng děng Wǔzhōu Zhōngcóngshì (嗣王‧庶姓荊‧江等五州中從事), Zōngzhèng-Tàifǔ-Wèiwèi-Sīnóng-Shǎofǔ-Tíngwèi-Tàizǐ Zhānshì děng Chéng (宗正‧太府‧衞尉‧司農‧少府‧廷尉‧太子詹事等丞), Jīshè-Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn (積射‧強弩將軍), Tàizǐ Zuǒ-Yòu Jīnnǔ Jiāngjūn (太子左‧右積弩將軍), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Guódànóng (皇弟‧皇子國大農), Sìwáng Guólángzhōnglìng (嗣王國郎中令), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Gōngfǔ Zhǔbù (嗣王‧庶姓公府主簿), and Huángdì-Huángzǐ Zhī Shùzǐfǔ-Fānwángfǔ Gōngcáoshǐ-Lùshì-Jìshì-Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (皇弟‧皇子之庶子府‧蕃王府功曹史‧錄事‧記室‧中兵參軍) were in the fourth class.

Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人), Sītú Jìjiǔ (司徒祭酒), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Gōngfǔ Jìjiǔ (皇弟‧皇子公府祭酒), Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Fǔ Xíngcānjūn (皇弟‧皇子府行參軍), Tàizǐ Tàifù-Shǎofù Wǔguān-Gōngcáo-Zhǔbù (太子太傅‧少傅五官‧功曹‧主簿), Èrwèi Sīmǎ (二衞司馬), Gōngchēlìng (公車令), Zhòuzǐ-Lǜ Bóshì (冑子‧律博士), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Yuè-Guì-Níng-Huò Sìzhōu Biéjià (皇弟‧皇子越‧桂‧寧‧霍四州別駕), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Běixú-Běiyǎn-Liáng-Jiāo-Nánliáng Wǔzhōu Zhōngcóngshì (皇弟‧皇子北徐‧北兗‧梁‧交‧南梁五州中從事), Shùxìng Běixú děng Wǔzhōu Biéjià (庶姓北徐等五州別駕), Xiāng-Yù-Sī-Yì-Guǎng-Qīng-Héng Qīzhōu Zhōngcóngshì (湘‧豫‧司‧益‧廣‧青‧衡七州中從事), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Gōngfǔ Zhèngcānjūn (嗣王‧庶姓公府正參軍), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Zhī Shùzǐfǔ-Fānwángfǔ Cáozhǔbù (皇弟‧皇子之庶子府‧蕃王府曹主簿), Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (武衞將軍), Guānglù Chéng (光祿丞), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Guózhōngwèi-Tàipú-Dàjiàng Chéng (皇弟‧皇子國中尉‧太僕‧大匠丞), Sìwáng Guódànóng (嗣王國大農), Fānwáng Guólángzhōnglìng (蕃王國郎中令), Shùxìng Chíjié Fǔ Zhōng Lùshì-Zhōng Jìshì-Zhōng Zhíbīng Cānjūn (庶姓持節府中錄事‧中記室‧中直兵參軍), and Běiguǎnlìng (北館令) were in the third class.

Mìshū Láng (秘書郎), Zhùzuò Zuǒláng (著作佐郎), Yáng-Nánxúzhōu Zhǔbù (揚、南徐州主簿), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Gōngfǔ Jìjiǔ (嗣王‧庶姓公府祭酒), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Dānwèi Lǐng-Hù-Zhānshì (皇弟‧皇子單為領‧護‧詹事), Èrwèi děng Gōngcáo-Wǔguān-Zhǔbù (二衞等功曹‧五官‧主簿), Tàixué Bóshì (太學博士), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Guóchángshì (皇弟‧皇子國常侍), Fèngcháoqǐng (奉朝請), Guózǐ Zhùjiào (國子助教), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Yuè-Guì-Níng-Huò Sìzhōu Zhōngcóngshì (皇弟‧皇子越‧桂‧寧‧霍四州中從事), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Jīng-Jiāng děng Wǔzhōu Zhǔbù (皇弟皇子荊‧江等五州主簿), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Yuè-Guì děng Sìzhōu Biéjià (嗣王‧庶姓越‧桂等四州別駕), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Běixú děng Wǔzhōu Zhōngcóngshì (嗣王‧庶姓北徐等五州中從事), Hónglú Chéng (鴻臚丞), Shàngshū Wǔdōulìshǐ (尚書五都令史), Wǔqí Chángshì (武騎常侍), Cáiguān Jiāngjūn (材官將軍), Míngtáng-Èrmiào-Dìlínglìng (明堂‧二廟‧帝陵令), Sìwáng-Shùxìng Gōngfǔ Xíngcānjūn (嗣王‧庶姓公府行參軍), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Zhī Shùzǐfǔ Zhèngcānjūn (皇弟‧皇子之庶子府正參軍), Fānwáng Guódànóng (蕃王國大農), Shùxìng Chíjié Fǔ Lùshì-Jìshì-Zhōngzhíbīng Cānjūn (庶姓持節府錄事‧記室‧中直兵參軍), and Shùxìng Chíjié Fǔ Gōngcáoshǐ (庶姓持節府功曹史) were in the second class.

Yáng-Nánxúzhōu Xīcáo-Jìjiǔ-Cóngshì (揚、南徐州西曹‧祭酒‧從事), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Guóshìláng (皇弟‧皇子國侍郎), Sìwáng Guóchángshì (嗣王國常侍), Nánxúzhōu Yìcáo Cóngshì (南徐州議曹從事), Dōnggōng Tōngshì Shèrén (東宮通事舍人), Nántái Shìyùshǐ (南臺侍御史), Dàzhōu Chéng (大舟丞), Èrwèi-Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn-Huángdì-Huángzǐ Zhī Shùzǐfǔ-Fānwángfǔ Xíngcānjūn (二衞‧殿中將軍‧皇弟‧皇子之庶子府‧蕃王府行參軍), Fānwáng Guózhōngwèi (蕃王國中尉), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Xiāng-Yù děng Qīzhōu Zhǔbù (皇弟‧皇子湘‧豫等七州主簿), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Jīng-Yōng děng Zhōu Xīcáojìjiǔ-Yìcáo Cóngshì (皇弟‧皇子荊‧雍等州西曹祭酒‧議曹從事), Huángdì-Huángzǐ Xīcáo-Cóngshì Jìjiǔ-Yìcáo Jìjiǔ-Bùchuán Cóngshì (皇弟‧皇子西曹‧從事祭酒‧議曹祭酒‧部傳從事), Sìwáng Shùxìng Yuè-Guì děng Sìzhōu Zhōngcóngshì (嗣王庶姓越‧桂等四州中從事), Sìwáng Shùxìng Jīng-Jiāng děng Wǔzhōu Zhǔbù (嗣王庶姓荊‧江等五州主簿), Shùxìng Chíjié Fǔ Zhǔbù (庶姓持節府主簿), Rǔyīn-Bālíng Èrguó Lángzhōnglìng (汝陰‧巴陵二國郎中令), Tàiguān-Tàilè-Tàishì-Tàishǐ-Tàiyī-Tàizhù-Dōngxīyě-Zuǒyòushàngfāng-Nánběiwǔkù-Chēfǔ děng Lìng (太官‧太樂‧太市‧太史‧太醫‧太祝‧東西冶‧左右尚方‧南北武庫‧車府等令) were in the first class.
An edict also stated that
"the names of generals,
both high and low, were mixed and disordered,
requiring further clarification and regularization."
Thereupon, the relevant authorities proposed the establishment of one hundred and twenty-five general titles.
Zhèn (鎮), Wèi (衞), Piàojí (驃騎), and Chējí (車騎) were in the twenty-fourth class,
for both internal and external use;
Zhēngdōng (征東),
Zhēngxī (征西), Zhēngnán (征南), Zhēngběi (征北) were for external use,
Zhōngjūn (中軍), Zhōngwèi (中衞), Zhōngfǔ (中撫), Zhōnghù (中護) were for internal use,
these were in the twenty-third class;
Zhèndōng (鎮東), Zhènxī (鎮西), Zhènnán (鎮南), Zhènběi (鎮北) were for external use,
Zhènzuǒ (鎮左), Zhènyòu (鎮右), Zhènqián (鎮前), Zhènhòu (鎮後) were for internal use,
these were in the twenty-second class;
Āndōng (安東), Ānxī (安西), Ānnán (安南), Ānběi (安北) were for external use,
Ānzuǒ (安左), Ānyòu (安右), Ānqián (安前), Ānhòu (安後) were for internal use,
these were in the twenty-first class;
Píngdōng (平東), Píngxī (平xī), Píngnán (平南), Píngběi (平北) were for external use,
Yìzuǒ (翊左), Yìyòu (翊右), Yìqián (翊前), Yìhòu (翊後) were for internal use,
these were in the twentieth class: these were the "heavy-titled generals."
Zhōngwǔ (忠武) and Jūnshī (軍師) were in the nineteenth class;
Wǔchén (武臣), Zhǎoyá (爪牙), Lóngqí (龍騎), and Yúnhuī (雲麾) were in the eighteenth class,
replacing the old Qián-Hòu-Zuǒ-Yòu Sìjiāngjūn (前、後、左、右四將軍);
Zhènbīng (鎮兵), Yìshī (翊師), Xuānhuì (宣惠), and Xuānyì (宣毅) were in the seventeenth class,
replacing the old Sì Zhōnglángjiāng (四中郎將): ten titles made one rank.
Zhìwēi (智威), Rénwēi (仁威), Yǒngwēi (勇威), Xìnwēi (信威), and Yánwēi (嚴威) were in the sixteenth class,
replacing the old Zhēnglǔ (征虜);
Zhìwǔ (智武), Rénwǔ (仁武), Yǒngwǔ (勇武), Xìnwǔ (信武), and Yánwǔ (嚴武) were in the fifteenth class,
replacing the old Guānjūn (冠軍): ten titles made one rank,
these were called the "Five Virtues Generals."
Qīngchē (輕車), Zhēngyuǎn (征遠), Zhènshuò (鎮朔), Wǔlǚ (武旅), and Zhēnyì (貞毅) were in the fourteenth class,
replacing the old Fǔguó (輔國).
Generally, for generals who received an additional title,
it only went up to Zhēnyì (貞毅),
promoting them one step further,
and the most capable could then be compared in position to the dukes.
Níngyuǎn (寧遠), Míngwēi (明威), Zhènyuǎn (振遠), Diànyào (電耀), and Wēiyào (威耀) were in the thirteenth class,
replacing the old Níngshuò (寧朔): ten titles made one rank.
Wǔwēi (武威), Wǔqí (武騎), Wǔměng (武猛), Zhuàngwǔ (壯武), and Biāowǔ (飆武) were in the twelfth class;
Diànwēi (電威), Chíruì (馳銳), Zhuīfēng (追鋒), Yǔqí (羽騎), and Túqí (突騎) were in the eleventh class: ten titles made one rank.
Zhéchōng (折衝), Guānwǔ (冠武), Héróng (和戎), Ānlěi (安壘), and Měngliè (猛烈) were in the tenth class;
Sǎodí (掃狄), Xióngxìn (雄信), Sǎolǔ (掃虜), Wǔruì (武銳), and Chuífēng (椎鋒) were in the ninth class: ten titles made one rank.
Lüèyuǎn (略遠), Zhēnwēi (貞威), Juéshèng (決勝), Kāiyuǎn (開遠), and Guāngyě (光野) were in the eighth class;
Lìfēng (厲鋒), Qīngruì (輕銳), Tǎodí (討狄), Dànglǔ (蕩虜), and Dàngyí (蕩夷) were in the seventh class: ten titles made one rank.
Wǔyì (武毅), Tiěqí (鐵騎), Lóuchuán (樓船), Xuānměng (宣猛), and Shùgōng (樹功) were in the sixth class;
Kèdí (克狄), Pínglǔ (平虜), Tǎoyí (討夷), Píngdí (平狄), and Wēiróng (威戎) were in the fifth class: ten titles made one rank.
Fúbō (伏波), Xióngjí (雄戟), Chángjiàn (長劍), Chōngguān (衝冠), and Diāoqí (雕騎) were in the fourth class;
Cìfēi (佽飛), Ānyí (安夷), Kèrúng (克戎), Suídí (綏狄), and Wēilǔ (威虜) were in the third class: ten titles made one rank.
Qiánfēng (前鋒), Wǔyì (武義), Kāibiān (開邊), Zhāoyuǎn (招遠), and Quánwēi (全威) were in the second class;
Suílǔ (綏虜), Dàngkòu (蕩寇), Héngyě (橫野), and Chíshè (馳射) were in the first class: ten titles made one rank.
In total, there were ten ranks,
and twenty-four classes,
with more classes indicating higher status.
The system stipulated that
the ten ranks
used the full number,
corresponding to the ten heavenly stems;
the twenty-four classes corresponded to the twenty-four solar terms.
In the official register, all major titles were placed last,
indicating that promotion in the selection system proceeded from lower to higher.
For those who did not reach the tenth rank but required military titles,
there were Yámén (牙門) replacing the old Jiànwēi (建威),
Qímén (期門) replacing the old Jiànwǔ (建武),
these were in the eighth class;
Hòuqí (候騎) replacing the old Zhènwēi (振威),
Xióngqú (熊渠) replacing the old Zhènwǔ (振武),
these were in the seventh class;
Zhōngjiān (中堅) replacing the old Fènwēi (奮威),
Diǎnrong (典戎) replacing the old Fènwǔ (奮武),
these were in the sixth class;
Gēchuán (戈船) replacing the old Yángwēi (揚威),
Xiùyī (繡衣) replacing the old Yángwǔ (揚武),
these were in the fifth class;
Zhíxùn (執訊) replacing the old Guǎngwēi (廣威),
Xíngzhèn (行陣) replacing the old Guǎngwǔ (廣武),
these were in the fourth class;
Yīngyáng (鷹揚) was in the third class;
Língjiāng (陵江) was in the second class;
Piānjiāngjūn (偏將軍) and Bíjiāngjūn (裨將軍) were in the first class: totaling fourteen titles,
separately forming eight classes,
symbolizing the eight winds,
and their application was very light.
There were also Wǔ'ān (武安), Zhènyuǎn (鎮遠), Xióngyì (雄義) analogous to Chējí (車騎) in the twenty-fourth class;
Fǔdōng (撫東), Fǔxī (撫西), Fǔnán (撫南), Fǔběi (撫北) analogous to the Four Zhēng (四征) in the twenty-third class;
Níngdōng (寧東), Níngxī (寧西), Níngnán (寧南), Níngběi (寧北) analogous to the Four Zhèn (四鎮) in the twenty-second class;
Wēidōng (威東), Wēixī (威西), Wēinán (威南), Wēiběi (威北) analogous to the Four Ān (四安) in the twenty-first class;
Suídōng (綏東), Suíxī (綏西), Suínán (綏南), Suíběi (綏北) analogous to the Four Píng (四平) in the twentieth class: totaling nineteen titles for one rank.
Ānyuǎn (安遠), Ānbiān (安邊) analogous to Zhōngwǔ (忠武), Jūnshī (軍師) in the nineteenth class;
Fǔyì (輔義), Ānshā (安沙), Wèihǎi (衛海), Fǔhé (撫河) analogous to Wǔchén (武臣) and the other four titles in the eighteenth class;
Píngyuǎn (平遠),
Fǔshuò (撫朔), Níngshā (寧沙), Hánghǎi (航海) analogous to Zhènbīng (鎮兵) and the other four titles in the seventeenth class: totaling ten titles for one rank.
Yìhǎi (翊海), Shuòyě (朔野), Tuòyuǎn (拓遠), Wēihé (威河), Lóngmù (龍幕) analogous to Zhìwēi (智威) and the other five titles in the sixteenth class;
Wēilǒng (威隴), Ānmò (安漠), Suíbiān (綏邊), Níngkòu (寧寇), Tīshān (梯山) analogous to Zhìwǔ (智武) and the other five titles in the fifteenth class: totaling ten titles for one rank.
Níngjìng (寧境), Suíhé (綏河), Míngxìn (明信), Míngyì (明義), Wēimò (威漠) analogous to Qīngchē (輕車) and the other five titles in the fourteenth class;
Ānlǒng (安隴), Xiàngyì (向義), Xuānjié (宣節), Zhènshuò (振朔), Hòulǜ (候律) analogous to Níngyuǎn (寧遠) and the other five titles in the thirteenth class: totaling ten titles for one rank.
Píngkòu (平寇), Dìngyuǎn (定遠), Nínglǒng (寧隴), Línghǎi (陵海), Zhènmò (振漠) analogous to Wǔwēi (武威) and the other five titles in the twelfth class;
Chíyì (馳義), Héngshuò (橫朔), Míngjié (明節), Zhíxìn (執信), Huáidé (懷德) analogous to Diànwēi (電威) and the other five titles in the eleventh class: totaling ten titles for one rank.
Fǔbiān (撫邊), Dìnglǒng (定隴), Suíguān (綏關), Lìxìn (立信), Fèngyì (奉義) analogous to Zhéchōng (折衝) and the other five titles in the tenth class;
Suílǒng (綏隴), Níngbiān (寧邊), Dìngshuò (定朔), Lìjié (立節), Huáiwēi (懷威) analogous to Sǎodí (掃狄) and the other five titles in the ninth class: totaling ten titles for one rank.
Huáiguān (懷關), Jìngshuò (靜朔), Sǎokòu (掃寇), Nínghé (寧河), Ānshuò (安朔) analogous to Lüèyuǎn (略遠) and the other five titles in the eighth class;
Yánghuà (揚化), Chāolǒng (超隴), Zhíyì (執義), Láihuà (來化), Dùzhàng (度嶂) analogous to Lìfēng (厲鋒) and the other five titles in the seventh class: totaling ten titles for one rank.
Pínghé (平河), Zhènlǒng (振隴), Xióngbiān (雄邊), Héngshā (橫沙), Níngguān (寧關) analogous to Wǔyì (武毅) and the other five titles in the sixth class;
Huáixìn (懷信), Xuānyì (宣義), Hóngjié (弘節), Fúliáo (浮遼), Záokōng (鑿空) analogous to Kèdí (克狄) and the other five titles in the fifth class: totaling ten titles for one rank.
Hǎnhǎi (扞海), Kuǎnsāi (款塞), Guīyì (歸義), Línghé (陵河), Míngxìn (明信) analogous to Fúbō (伏波) and the other five titles in the fourth class;
Fèngzhōng (奉忠), Shǒuyì (守義), Hóngxìn (弘信), Yìhuà (抑化), Lìyì (立義) analogous to Cìfēi (佽飛) and the other five titles in the third class: totaling ten titles for one rank.
Suífāng (綏方), Fèngzhèng (奉正), Chénghuà (承化), Fúhǎi (浮海), Dùhé (渡河) analogous to Xiānfēng (先鋒) and the other five titles in the second class;
Huáiyì (懷義), Fèngxìn (奉信), Guīchéng (歸誠), Huáizé (懷澤), Fúyì (伏義) analogous to Suílǔ (綏虜) and the other five titles in the first class: totaling ten titles for one rank.
In all, there were one hundred and nine titles,
also forming twenty-four classes,
for application to foreign countries.
3 On the day Gēngwǔ (庚午),
an edict commanded the establishment of one Zhōuwàng (州望), one Jùnzōng (郡宗), and one Xiāngháo (鄉豪) each,
to be exclusively in charge of searching and recommending.
"Sōu" (搜) means to seek;
it meant to seek out talent and recommend them to the emperor.
4 On the day Yǐhài (乙亥),
Lǚ Sēngzhēn (呂僧珍), Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Nányǎnzhōu (南兗州), was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍).
The Lǐngjūn (領軍) managed internal and external military affairs;
since the Xiàojiàn (孝建) era of Sòng (宋),
the Zhìjú (制局) held power,
sharing military authority with the Lǐngjūn (領軍),
and all officials from Diǎnshì (典事) upwards could present memorials,
while the Lǐngjūn (領軍) merely folded his hands.
When Wú Pínghóu Bǐng (吳平侯昺) held the office, he was strict and resolute,
and the government offices were solemn.
The Zhìjú Jiān (制局監) were all imperial favorites,
and many could not endure his commands,
which is why he could not remain long in the capital.
On the day Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
he was sent out as Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Yōngzhōu (雍州).
Sēngzhēn (僧珍) was appointed first,
and Bǐng (昺) was sent out the next day.
Bǐng (昺) is pronounced "bǐng."
Yōng (雍) is pronounced "yōng" (於用翻).
5 In the third month,
on the day Wùzǐ (戊子),
Wèi (魏) Imperial Prince Chāng (昌) died;
Shìyùshī (侍御師) Wáng Xiǎn (王顯) failed in his treatment.
Yīshī (醫師) refers to attendants and imperial physicians,
and thus became the name of an official.
In the Later Wèi (魏) system,
the Tàiyīlìng (太醫令) belonged to the Tàicháng (太常),
in charge of medicine;
but the Ménxiàshěng (門下省) separately had a Shàngyàojú Shìyùshī (尚藥局侍御師),
which is probably today's imperial physician.
This Wáng Xiǎn (王顯) is another person,
not the Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi (御史中尉) Wáng Xiǎn (王顯).
Zhì (治) is pronounced "zhì" (直之翻).
6 In the summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo (乙卯),
the Crown Prince took a consort,
and a general amnesty was declared.
7 In the fifth month,
on the day Jǐhài (己亥),
an edict commanded the re-establishment of Zōngzhèng (宗正), Tàipú (太僕), Dàjiàng (大匠), and Hónglú (鴻臚),
and also increased Tàifǔ (太府) and Tàizhōu (太舟),
still making a total of twelve Qīng (卿).
8 On the day Guǐmǎo,
Ānchéngwáng Xiù was appointed Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Previously,
the Mǎyíng barbarians of Bālíng had been raiding along the river,
and the provincial and commandery authorities were unable to suppress them.
Xiù dispatched his Fánggé, Wén Chì, to lead a force to burn their forests.
According to the Liáng regulations,
Zhíhé were appointed in the Shànggōng and Dōnggōng,
and Fánggé were appointed for kings and dukes.
Wén
is a surname.
Shuài
is read as "suài".
The provincial border was cleared of raiders.
The barbarians had nowhere to rely on for refuge,
hence they dared not raid.
9 In the autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Wèi emperor established Noble Consort Gāo as empress.
Shàngshūlìng Gāo Zhào became increasingly valued, important, and influential.
Zhào often altered old regulations from previous reigns,
reduced and cut down on enfeoffments and official ranks,
and demoted and dismissed meritorious individuals,
which led to widespread complaints.
All ministers and imperial kinsmen demeaned themselves before him,
except for Dùzhī Shàngshū Yuán Kuāng, who openly contended with Zhào.
He had a coffin made and placed in his office,
intending to carry the coffin to the imperial court to denounce Zhào's crimes,
and then commit suicide as a strong remonstrance.
Zhào heard of this and disliked him.
It happened that Kuāng was discussing matters of weights and measures with Tàicháng Liú Fāng.
The Wèi, while discussing music,
also discussed and settled weights and measures.
Liàng
is read "lìràng".
Kuāng then had a heated argument with Zhào,
Jìng
means "to dispute".
comparing Zhào to Zhào Gāo.
The judicial authorities sentenced Kuāng to death;
an imperial edict pardoned his death sentence,
demoting him to Guānglù Dàfū.
10 In the eighth month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
Jìngláng Zhuànggōng Cáo Jǐngzōng passed away.
11 Initially,
the Wèi emperor had arranged for Jīngzhàowáng Yú to marry Empress Yú's sister,
but Yú did not love her.
He loved his concubine, Lady Lǐ,
who bore him a son, Bǎoyuè.
Empress Yú summoned Lady Lǐ into the palace
and flogged her.
Yú was arrogant, extravagant, greedy, and dissolute,
and many of his actions were unlawful.
The emperor summoned Yú into the forbidden palace for investigation and interrogation,
caned Yú fifty strokes,
and sent him out as Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Yú considered himself older,
but his power and position were inferior to his two younger brothers.
The two younger brothers were
Qīnghéwáng Yì
and Guǎngpíngwáng Huái.
Moreover,
he and his concubine had repeatedly suffered humiliation.
Gāo Zhào frequently slandered Yú and his brothers,
and Yú could not bear his resentment.
On the day Guǐhài,
he killed his Chángshǐ Yáng Língyǐn and Sīmǎ Lǐ Zūn,
falsely claiming to have received a secret memorial from Qīnghéwáng Yì,
stating,
"Gāo Zhào has committed regicide."
He then set up an altar south of Xìndū.
The Wèi Inspector of Jìzhōu governed Xìndū.
He declared a general amnesty,
changed the era name to Jiànpíng,
and established Lady Lǐ as empress.
Fǎcáo Cānjūn Cuī Bójì refused to comply,
and Yú killed him.
All the northern provincial and garrison commanders suspected a change in the Wèi court.
This refers to the provincial and garrison commanders north of Jìzhōu.
Cháo
is read "zhíyáo".
The provincial and garrison commanders then settled.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
the Wèi appointed Shàngshū Lǐ Píng as Dūdū of the northern expeditionary forces and acting Jìzhōu affairs to suppress Yú.
Píng
was Chóngzhī's paternal cousin.
12 On the day Dīngmǎo,
the Wèi declared a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Yǒngpíng.
13 Wèi Jīngzhàowáng Yú sent an envoy to persuade the Administrator of Píngyuán, Qīnghé Fáng Liàng.
Liàng beheaded his envoy.
Yú dispatched his general Zhāng Línghé to attack him,
but he was defeated by Liàng.
Lǐ Píng's army reached Jīngxiàn.
Jīngxiàn
belonged to Ānpíng Guó in the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
and Wèi Shōu's records place it in Jùlù Jùn.
That night,
several thousand barbarian soldiers attacked Píng's camp,
and arrows reached Píng's tent.
Píng lay still without moving,
and soon the situation settled by itself.
The barbarian soldiers were probably also under Lǐ Píng's command,
intending to cause an internal disturbance,
but Píng did not move,
so they settled down on their own.
On the first day of the month Xīnsì,
Yú confronted them in battle at Cǎloqiáo south of the city.
Píng vigorously attacked,
heavily defeating him.
Yú escaped and fled into the city.
Píng advanced and besieged him.
On the day Rénchén,
Ānlèwáng Quán defeated Yú's forces north of the city.
14 On the day Guǐsì,
imperial prince Jì was established as Nánkāngwáng.
When Empress Gāo was enthroned in the
Wèi dynasty, Wǔxuān Wáng Xié of Péngchéng
earnestly remonstrated, but the Wèi ruler did not listen.
Gāo Zhào consequently resented him,
and repeatedly slandered Xié to the Wèi ruler,
but the Wèi ruler did not believe it.
Xié recommended his maternal uncle Pān Sēnggù as the Grand Administrator of Chánglè.
When Jīngzhào Wáng Yú rebelled,
he coerced Sēnggù into joining him.
Jìzhōu and Chánglè Commandery were both governed from Xìndū,
hence Sēnggù was coerced by Yú.
Lè
is pronounced Luò.
[They] drew barbarian bandits from the south.
South of Yīquè,
bordering the Huái, Rǔ, Jiāng, and Miǎnjiāng rivers,
there were all barbarian groups.
Gāozǔ Zhēn had previously served as Xié’s guard;
at this time, he had already left office,
hence he is called "former guard".
[They] fabricated the matter.
Zhào ordered the侍zhōng Yuán Huī to report it,
but Huī did not comply.
He then ordered the Zuǒwèi Yuán Zhēn to speak of it.
The Emperor questioned Huī,
and Huī made it clear that Xié was not so.
He then questioned Zhào,
and Zhào cited Wèi Yǎn and Gāozǔ Zhēn as witnesses.
The Emperor then believed it.
On the day of Wùxū,
Xié, along with Gāoyáng Wáng Yōng, Guǎngyáng Wáng Jiā, Qīnghé Wáng Yì, Guǎngpíng Wáng Huái, and Gāo Zhào were all summoned to a banquet.
Xié’s wife, of the Lǐ clan, was about to give birth,
so he firmly declined to attend.
Messengers from the palace followed one after another to summon him.
Having no choice,
he bade farewell and boarded his carriage.
Entering the Dōngyèmén,
and crossing a small bridge,
the ox refused to move forward.
They struck it for a long time.
"A long time"
means "a bit long,"
or some say "very long."
Then they removed the ox,
and men pulled it forward.
The banquet was held within the Forbidden City.
By night,
everyone was drunk,
and each went to a separate place to rest.
They were ordered to go to a convenient and comfortable place
to relieve the effects of alcohol and restore their vital energy.
Xié said,
"I am innocent.
I wish to see His Majesty once;
then I will die without regret!"
Yuán Zhēn said,
"How can His Majesty be seen again!"
Xié said,
"His Majesty is sagacious and enlightened,
and should not kill me without cause.
I beg to confront my accuser to clarify right and wrong!"
A warrior struck him with the pommel of his sword.
Xié cried out loudly,
"Injustice!
O August Heaven!
Loyal, yet I am slain."
The warrior struck him again.
Xié then drank poisoned wine,
and the warrior killed him.
Towards dawn,
his body was wrapped in a blanket and carried back to his residence.
It was announced that the Prince had died from intoxication.
Lady Lǐ wailed loudly, saying,
"Gāo Zhào has wrongly murdered someone!
If the Way of Heaven has spiritual power,
how can you die a good death!"
The Wèi ruler mourned in the East Hall,
and his posthumous official titles and funeral rites were all exceptionally generous.
Among the noble and humble in court,
none were not disheartened.
Men and women on the roads all wept, saying,
"Duke Gāo Líng has wrongly killed a worthy prince."
Zhào was Shàngshū Lìng,
hence he was called Línggōng.
This laid the groundwork for Gāo Zhào’s punishment.
È
is pronounced as "wū lù".
Jīngzhào Wáng Yú could not defend Xìndū.
On the day of Guǐmǎo,
he burned the gate,
and fled with Lady Lǐ and his four sons, accompanied by over a hundred riders.
Lǐ Píng entered Xìndū,
beheaded Wéi Chāo and others appointed by Yú as Jìzhōu Pastors,
and dispatched Commander Shūsūn Tóu to pursue and capture Yú.
He placed him in Xìndū
and reported it.
His ministers requested Yú’s execution,
but the Wèi ruler did not permit it.
He ordered him to be sent in chains to Luòyáng,
to be disciplined with family instruction.
Yú was the Wèi ruler’s younger brother,
hence he wished to instruct and reprimand him.
Gāo Zhào secretly sent someone to kill him.
The Kǎoyì states: The biographies of Yú in the Wèishū and Běishǐ both say:
"Every time Yú stayed overnight at a post station,
he would hold Lǐ’s hand,
expressing his private feelings to the fullest.
Even when in shackles,
he drank and enjoyed himself as usual,
showing no sign of shame or fear.
When he reached Yěwáng,
Yú told people:
‘Although the sovereign’s benevolence is profound,
and he cannot bear to kill me,
what face do I have to see His Majesty!’
Thereupon, he sighed and wept,
and died of a broken heart.
Some say Gāo Zhào had someone kill him."
According to our assessment, since Yú was defeated and captured,
he still showed no shame or fear.
How could he be ashamed to see the Wèi ruler,
and then suddenly die from a surge of emotion?
It must be that Zhào secretly had someone kill Yú,
and then used these words to deceive the Wèi ruler.
The Wèi ruler pardoned them all.
The Wèi ruler was about to slaughter the Lǐ clan.
Zhōngshū Lìng Cuī Guāng remonstrated, saying,
"Lady Lǐ is pregnant.
To inflict punishment that includes disemboweling a fetus
is the act of Jié and Zhòu.
King Wǔ enumerated Zhòu’s crimes, saying, 'He disemboweled pregnant women.'
I request that we wait until she has given birth
before carrying out the execution."
He agreed.
Lǐ Píng captured over a thousand of Yú’s remaining followers,
and was about to kill them all.
Lùshì Cānjūn Gāo Hào said,
"These were all coerced followers.
Since they were previously promised pardon and exemption,
it is fitting to submit a memorial."
Píng agreed,
and they all escaped death.
Hào
was Yòu’s grandson.
Gāo Yòu,
a cousin of Yǔn,
served Wèi Xiàowén with his literary talent.
Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Gāo Zhí led his provincial army to attack Yú,
achieving merits that should have been rewarded with enfeoffment.
Zhí refused it,
saying,
"Our family is laden with great kindness [from the emperor],
and we exert our efforts for the state.
'Exert our efforts'
means to devote oneself and die for the cause.
Hè
is pronounced as 'xià kě'.
How dare we seek reward!"
Zhí
was Zhào’s son.
Lǐ Píng was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
Gāo Zhào and Zhōngwèi Wáng Xiǎn had long resented Píng.
Xiǎn impeached Píng for secretly confiscating official "mouths" (personnel) in Jìzhōu.
This refers to rebel men and women who were confiscated and became official "mouths" (indentured servants).
È
is pronounced as "wū lù".
Dàn
is pronounced as "tú dān".
[He was] dismissed from office,
and forbidden from entering the palace gates with his official credentials.
Initially,
during Xiǎn Zǔ's reign,
over ten thousand Rouran households
surrendered to Wèi.
They were settled in the two garrisons of Gāo Píng and Bó Gǔ Lǜ.
Wèi Shì Zǔ established the Gāo Píng Garrison in Tàiyán 2nd year (436 CE);
later, Sù Zōng changed it to Yuán Zhōu in Zhèngguāng 5th year (524 CE).
Also, the Bó Gǔ Lǜ Garrison was established in Tàiyán 2nd year (436 CE);
Sù Zōng changed it to Líng Zhōu during the Xiàochāng period (525-528 CE).
Sòng Bái said: In Tàihé 10th year (486 CE), the Bó Gǔ Lǜ Garrison was renamed Wò Yě Garrison.
When they surrendered,
Hù Jiāng Fān.
Almost all of them rebelled and fled,
with only over a thousand households remaining.
Tàizhōng Dàfū Wáng Tōng requested that they be moved north of the Huái River to cut off their rebellions.
An imperial edict commanded Tàipú Qīng Yáng Chūn, holding a staff of authority, to move them.
Chūn submitted a memorial, stating:
"The former court placed them in the border regions,
in order to attract and pacify foreign peoples,
and also to distinguish between the Huá and the Róng.
Now, the newly surrendered households are very numerous;
if the old ones are moved,
the new ones will certainly not feel secure,
which would be to drive them to rebellion.
Moreover, these people wear fur and eat meat,
they enjoy winter and are accustomed to cold;
the southern lands are humid and hot,
and if they go there, they will certainly all perish.
In advancing, we will lose their loyalty and submission;
in retreating, we will gain no benefit of border defense.
Settling them in the middle of the summer lands
might lead to future troubles;
this is not a good strategy."
The emperor did not heed him,
and so they were moved to Jì Zhōu,
settled along the river.
When the rebellion of Jīngzhào Wáng Yú occurred,
they all floated down the river to join Yú,
plundering everywhere they went,
just as Chūn had predicted.
16 Gēngzǐ ,
Wèi Yǐngzhōu Sīmǎ Péng Zhēn and others rebelled against Wèi,
secretly leading Liáng troops to advance towards Yìyáng.
The garrison commanders of the Three Passes, Hóu Dēng and others, surrendered with their cities.
Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ Lóu Yuè fortified the city and defended himself.
Wèi appointed Zhōngshān Wáng Yīng as the Supreme Commander of all southern expeditionary forces,
leading thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to depart from Rǔnán to relieve him.
17 In winter,
10th month,
Wèi Xuánhù Garrison Commander Bái Zǎoshēng killed Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Sīmǎ Yuè,
styling himself Píngběi Jiāngjūn,
and sought aid from Sī Zhōu's
Mǎ Xiánpǐn.
At that time, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Ānchéng Wáng Xiù was the Supreme Commander.
Xiù, as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, supervised various zhou,
and Sī Zhōu was under his jurisdiction.
The previous note described the request for a response,
with a note in scroll 120 under Sòng Wéndì Yuánjiā 1st year.
It was deemed appropriate to report to Tiāntái and await a reply.
In the Jiang Zuo region, the court was generally referred to as Tái,
and also as Tiāntái.
"They rely on me for their survival,"
"They"
refers to Bái Zǎoshēng.
"Waiting for an imperial edict, though customary,"
means the old system required waiting for a Tái imperial edict.
So, he immediately dispatched troops to go there.
The Emperor also issued an edict to Xiánpǐn to rescue Zǎoshēng.
Xiánpǐn advanced and stationed at Chǔwáng Chéng.
Chǔwáng Chéng was formerly Chǔwáng Shù.
He sent two thousand troops to assist in defending Xuánhù.
An edict appointed Zǎoshēng as Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
The "Kǎo Yì" states: In the Liáng Dì Jì,
10th month, Bǐngzǐ,
"Wèi Yángguān commander Xǔ Jìngzhēn surrendered with his city.
An edict ordered a major northern expedition,
with Shǐxīng Wáng Dàn leading troops into Qīng,
and Wáng Mào leading troops towards Sùyù.
Dīngchǒu,
Bái Zǎoshēng and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Hú Xùn submitted with their cities.
Zǎoshēng was appointed Sīzhōu, and Hú Xùn was appointed Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the 1st month of the following year, Rénchén,
Wèi Zhèndōng Cānjūn Chéng Jǐngjùn beheaded Sùyù Garrison Commander Yán Zhòngbǎo,
and surrendered with the city.
In the 2nd month, Dīngmǎo,
Wèi Chǔwáng Chéng commander Lǐ Guóxīng surrendered with his city."
The names, dates, and events differ from the Wèi Shū,
and a thorough check of all biographies also found no mention of these events.
Therefore, we follow the Wèi Shū.
18 Bǐngyín,
Zhāng Jì, the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng, was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
19 Wèi appointed Shàngshū Xíng Luán to manage the affairs of Yù Zhōu,
leading troops to attack Bái Zǎoshēng.
The Wèi sovereign asked him:
"Do you say
Zǎoshēng will flee
or hold out?
When can it be pacified?"
He replied:
"Zǎoshēng does not possess deep strategies or great wisdom.
It is merely that Sīmǎ Yuè was tyrannical and cruel,
and he seized upon the public's anger to incite rebellion.
The people, pressed by his vicious might,
had no choice but to follow him.
Even if Liáng troops enter the city,
with waterways blocked and
grain supplies cut off,
he will still be captured like a bird.
Zǎoshēng, having received aid from Liáng,
is drowned in desire for profit,
and will surely defend rather than flee.
If the imperial army approaches,
the officers and people will surely turn and submit.
It will not be beyond this year
before his head is sent to the capital."
The Wèi sovereign was pleased,
ordering Luán to depart first,
and then Zhōngshān Wáng Yīng to follow.
Luán led eight hundred cavalry,
marching day and night at double speed,
reaching Bào Kǒu in five days.
Bǐngzǐ,
Zǎoshēng dispatched his major general Hú Xiàozhì with seven thousand troops,
to meet him in battle two hundred *li* from the city.
Luán fought fiercely,
utterly defeating them,
and advanced victoriously straight to Xuánhù.
Zǎoshēng came out of the city to meet him in battle,
and was again defeated.
Consequently, Luán crossed the Rǔ River
and besieged his city.
An edict conferred upon Luán the title of Supreme Commander of all southern expeditionary forces.
Dīngchǒu,
Wèi Zhèndōng Cānjūn Chéng Jǐngjùn killed Sùyù Garrison Commander Yán Zhòngxián,
and surrendered with the city.
At that time, Wèi's Yǐng Zhōu and Yù Zhōu,
from Xuánhù south to all cities in Ānlù, had all been lost.
Only the city of Yìyáng was firmly held by Wèi.
The barbarian chieftain Tián Yìzōng led the Mán barbarians to attach themselves to Wèi.
Wèi appointed him as Dōng Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wèi's Dōng Yùzhōu governed from Xīnxī Guǎnglíng City,
administering the prefectures of Rǔnán, Dōng Xīncài, Xīncài, Yìyáng, and Chánglíng.
Yìzōng did not comply.
11th month,
Gēngyín,
Wèi dispatched Āndōng Jiāngjūn Yáng Chūn with forty thousand troops to attack Sùyù.
The Wèi sovereign heard of Xíng Luán's repeated victories,
and ordered Zhōngshān Wáng Yīng to proceed to Yìyáng.
Yīng, having few troops,
repeatedly memorialized requesting more soldiers,
but was not granted them.
Yīng reached Xuánhù,
and immediately joined Luán in attacking it.
12th month,
Jǐwèi,
Qí Gǒu'ér and others opened the gates and surrendered,
beheading Bái Zǎoshēng and dozens of his followers.
Yīng then led his troops forward towards Yìyáng.
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Zhāng Dàoníng had previously garrisoned at Chǔwáng Chéng.
Guǐhài,
he abandoned the city and fled.
Yīng pursued him,
and beheaded him.
Wèi Yìyáng Tàishǒu Dí Dào Xīn Xiáng and Lóu Yuè jointly defended Yìyáng.
Generals Hú Wǔchéng and Táo Pínglǔ attacked them.
Xiáng launched a night raid on their camp,
captured Pínglǔ,
and beheaded Wǔchéng.
Because of this, the provincial territory was preserved.
When merits were to be rewarded,
Lóu Yuè was ashamed that his own achievements were inferior,
and sowed discord with the powerful officials,
so the rewards were not granted.
20 Rénshēn,
Wèi Dōngjīngzhōu memorialized,
"Huán Huī's younger brother Shúxìng has successively pacified the Tàiyáng Mán barbarians,
with over ten thousand households submitting.
We request the establishment of sixteen commanderies
and fifty counties."
From this time onward,
the barbarian commanderies and counties of the left could not be counted.
Dào Yuán was
Fàn's son.
Lì Fàn is mentioned in scroll 132 under Sòng Míngdì Tàishǐ 3rd year.
21 In this year,
Rouran Tāhàn Kèhán again sent Hēxī Wùliùbá to present sable furs to Wèi.
The Wèi sovereign did not accept them,
replying to him as before.
The previous event is in the previous scroll, year 5.
Initially,
Gāochē Hóubèi Qióngqí was killed by the Yēdá.
The Yēdá state,
a branch of the Dàyuèzhī,
is also said to be a separate branch of the Gāochē.
Their origin is north of Sāiběi.
From Mount Jīnshān southwards,
it is west of Yútián.
It is 10,100 *lǐ* from Cháng'ān.
Its royal capital, Bádǐ Chéng,
is likely Rājagṛha.
嚈,
pronounced *yì shè*.
噠,
pronounced *dāng gē*,
also *tuó gé*,
also *zhái yà*.
Their multitudes dispersed,
some fleeing to Wèi,
some to Rourán.
The Wèi ruler sent Yǔlínjiān Hénán Mèng Wēi to pacify and accept the surrendered households,
settling them at Gāopíng Zhèn.
Gāochē King Āfúzhìluó was cruel and violent,
so the people of the state killed him
and enthroned his kinsman Bálìyán.
The Yēdá supported Mí'étū to attack Gāochē.
The people of the state killed Bálìyán
and welcomed Mí'étū to enthrone him.
Mí'étū battled Tuóhàn Kèhán at Púlèihǎi,
was defeated,
and fled west over three hundred *lǐ*.
Tuóhàn encamped at Yīwú Běishān.
At that time, Gāochāng King Qū Jiā requested to relocate into Wèi territory.
Mèng Wēi was then Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn.
The Wèi ruler sent Wēi to mobilize three thousand soldiers from Liángzhōu to welcome him.
Upon reaching Yīwú,
Tuóhàn saw Wēi's army,
was afraid, and fled.
Mí'étū heard of their disarray and panic,
pursued and attacked them,
greatly defeating them.
He killed Tuóhàn north of Púlèihǎi,
cut off his hair and sent it to Wēi,
and also dispatched an envoy to pay tribute to Wèi.
The Wèi ruler sent Dōngchéng Zǐyú Liàng to respond to him,
bestowing very generous gifts.
Gāochāng King Jiā missed the appointed time and did not arrive,
so Wēi withdrew his troops and returned.
Tuóhàn Kèhán's son Chǒunú was enthroned,
and styled Dòuluófúbádòufá Kèhán.
Wèi Shōu said: In Wèi speech, it means
"Zhāngzhì."
The old rituals of Sòng and Qí prescribed that all sacrifices to Heaven be performed in *gǔnmiǎn*.
Jiān Zhùzuòláng Gāoyáng Xǔ Mào requested to make the *dàqiú*,
and this was granted.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* "Tiānguān" states: The *Sīqiú* is in charge of making the *dàqiú* to provide the king's attire for sacrificing to Heaven.
Zhèng Zhòng's commentary says: The *dàqiú*
is a black lambskin robe,
worn for sacrificing to Heaven,
to show plainness.
At that time, the officials searched for the regulations of the *dàqiú*,
but only Zhèng Xuán's commentary on *Sīfú* said: The *dàqiú*
is a lambskin robe.
Since there was no other source,
it could not be used as a basis.
Based on the *liùmiǎn* attire, all were black above and crimson below.
Now it should be made of black silk,
its style like a fur robe,
its skirt crimson,
all without patterns or embroidery.
The *miǎn* should have no tassels.
The decree said: Granted.
The Emperor was about to perform rites at the Tàimiào.
He decreed that
"during fast days, music is not played.
From now on, when the imperial carriage first departs,
the drum and wind instruments shall follow but not play.
Upon returning to the palace,
the normal ceremony shall be observed."
Upon returning to the palace, the drum and wind instruments would play.
吹,
pronounced *chāng ruì*.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the xīn-sì day,
the Emperor performed sacrifices in the southern suburbs
and issued a general amnesty.
At that time, there were requests to perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices at Kuàijī and Guóshān.
Guóshān is in Guóshān County, Yìxīng.
The Suí dynasty abolished Yìxīng Commandery, making it Yìxīng County,
and incorporated Guóshān into it.
In the first year of Tàipíng Xīngguó of our dynasty,
due to the taboo personal name of Tàizōng’s former princely residence,
Yìxīng was changed to Yíxīng.
Kuài,
read like ‘guài’ (工外翻).
The Emperor intended to proceed with it.
Xǔ Mào advised,
believing that
"Shùn performed the chái sacrifice on Dài Zōng;
this was part of his巡狩 (xúnshòu) tours.
Yet Zhèng Xuán quotes the *Xiàojīng Gōumìng Jué* which says: 'Fēng on Tàishān,
where merits are assessed and a chái sacrifice offered;
shàn on Liángfǔ,
where a stone is carved to record the reign name.'
This is a distorted interpretation from an apocryphal text,
not the standard meaning of the orthodox classics.
Shùn conducted a xúnshòu every five years,
making a complete tour of the Four Peaks throughout spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
The *Shùn Diǎn* states:
'In the second month of the year,
he made an eastern xúnshòu to Dài Zōng,
performing chái and望秩 (wàngzhì) sacrifices to the mountains and rivers.
In the fifth month,
he made a southern xúnshòu to the Southern Peak.
In the eighth month,
he made a western xúnshòu to the Western Peak.
In the eleventh month,
he made a northern xúnshòu to the Northern Peak.'
Zài,
read like ‘zǐhài’ (子亥翻).
How frequent these tours were!
Furthermore, regarding the seventy-two rulers mentioned by Guǎn Yíwú,
before Suì Rén,
the world was simple and the people pure.
How could there have been the use of gold seals and jade tablets?
When governance was by tying knots,
how could there have been engraved texts to announce completion?
Yíwú also said: 'Only a ruler who has received the Mandate of Heaven is entitled to perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices.'
King Chéng of Zhōu was not a ruler who had received the Mandate of Heaven;
why then was he able to perform fēng on Tàishān and shàn at Shèshǒu?
Shénnóng is the same as Yándì,
yet Yíwú separates them into two people—
his delusion is extreme.
If a ruler is sagely,
there is no need for fēng and shàn;
if a ruler is ordinary,
they should not perform fēng and shàn.
Lord Huán of Qí once desired to undertake this matter,
and Yíwú, knowing it was impossible,
therefore brought up strange omens to dissuade him.
The *Bān Zhì* says: After Lord Huán of Qí established his hegemony,
he assembled the feudal lords at Kuíqiū,
and desired to perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"In antiquity, seventy-two families performed fēng on Tàishān and shàn on Liángfù.
Yíwú only recorded twelve of them.
Formerly, Wúhuái Shì performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Yúnyún;
Fúxī performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Yúnyún;
Shénnóng Shì performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Yúnyún;
Yándì performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Yúnyún;
Huángdì performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Tíngtíng;
Zhuānxù performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Yúnyún;
Dì Kù performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Yúnyún;
Yáo performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Yúnyún;
Shùn performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Yúnyún;
Yǔ performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Kuàijī;
Tāng performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn on Yúnyún;
King Chéng performed fēng on Tàishān,
and shàn at Shèshǒu: all received the Mandate before being able to perform fēng and shàn."
Lord Huán said:
"I have gathered the feudal lords nine times,
and unified the world.
How was this different from the Three Dynasties receiving the Mandate of Heaven?"
Guǎn Zhòng, seeing that Lord Huán could not be persuaded by words,
then presented matters to him, saying:
"For the ancient fēng and shàn,
the millet from Háo Shàng
and the grain from Běilǐ
were used for the offerings;
one three-ridged stalk of cogongrass from the Jiāng and Huái rivers
was used for the mat;
flounder from the East Sea
and 'bi-yì' birds from the West Sea
were brought. Only then would fifteen kinds of creatures arrive without being summoned.
Now, phoenixes and qílín do not appear,
auspicious grain does not grow,
while mugwort and weeds flourish,
and owls fly about wildly.
To then wish to perform fēng and shàn,
is it not improper?"
Lord Huán then stopped.
Sūn Hào once sent the concurrent Minister of Works Dǒng Cháo to Yángxiàn to perform fēng and shàn at Guóshān.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* says: Yìxīng
was formerly called Yángxiàn.
This is not worthy of being followed as a precedent.
Therefore, the rites of fēng and shàn
are all things heard by hearsay,
having lost their original meaning,
due to the ruler’s desire for fame above,
and the ministers’ flattering approval below.
In ancient times, sacrifices to Heaven and Earth
followed established rites.
The way of sincerity and reverence
was fulfilled and complete by these.
As for fēng and shàn,
they are not things I would dare to hear about."
The Emperor praised and accepted his advice,
then further expounded on Mào’s argument,
using the imperial decree to respond to those who had made the request.
Because of this, the matter was dropped.
2 Wèi Prince Yīng of Zhōngshān arrived at Yìyáng,
intending to take the Three Passes.
He first strategized, saying:
"The Three Passes rely on each other like left and right hands.
If one pass is captured,
the other two will fall without needing to be attacked.
Attacking the difficult is not as good as attacking the easy.
We should first attack the Eastern Pass."
The Eastern Pass is Wǔyáng Pass.
Yì,
read like ‘yǐshǐ’ (以豉翻);
the following 'shìyì' is similar.
He then sent his Chief Clerk Lǐ Huá to lead five units towards the Western Pass.
Wǔ Tǒng,
refers to the troops of the five commanders.
The Western Pass is Píngjìng Pass.
Shuài,
read as ‘lǜ’.
He himself supervised the various armies heading towards the Eastern Pass.
Previously,
Mǎ Xiánpǐn had dispatched the Cavalier General Mǎ Guǎng to garrison Chángbó,
and Army Commander Hú Wénchāo to garrison Sōngxiàn.
On the bǐng-shēn day,
Yīng arrived at Chángbó.
On the wù-xū day,
Chángbó fell,
and Mǎ Guǎng fled into Wǔyáng.
Yīng advanced and besieged it.
The Emperor sent Champion General Péng Wèngshēng and Cavalry General Xú Yuánjì with troops to relieve Wǔyáng.
Yīng deliberately let them enter the city,
saying:
"I see the strategic position of this city is easy to capture."
After Wèngshēng and others had entered,
Yīng pressed his troops to attack it,
and captured it in six days,
taking captive three generals and over seven thousand soldiers.
He then attacked Guǎngxiàn.
Guǎngxiàn
is probably Huángxiàn Pass.
He also attacked the Western Pass,
and Mǎ Xiánpǐn also abandoned the city and fled.
The Emperor sent Administrator Wéi Ruì of Nánjùn to lead troops to rescue Xiánpǐn.
After the victory at Shàoyáng,
Ruì was promoted to Left Guard General,
and soon after became Anxi Chief Clerk and Administrator of Nánjùn.
He increased the height of the city walls by over two zhàng,
dug a larger moat,
and erected high towers.
Many ridiculed him for showing timidity,
but Ruì said:
"Not so.
A general must have moments of caution;
one cannot always be brave."
Prince Yīng of Zhōngshān urgently pursued Mǎ Xiánpǐn,
intending to avenge the shame of Shàoyáng.
Upon hearing of Ruì's arrival,
he retreated.
The Emperor also issued an edict to withdraw the troops.
Initially,
the Wèi ruler sent Dǒng Shào of Zhòuhóng, a Zhōngshū Shèlùn, to comfort the rebellious city.
Zhòuhóng County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Rǔnán Commandery;
during the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Rǔyīn Commandery;
during the Wèi dynasty, it belonged to Xīncài Commandery.
Mèng Kāng said: 鮦
is pronounced zhòu-hóng.
The Suí dynasty abolished Xīncài Commandery and made it a county,
belonging to Yùzhōu.
The territory of Zhòuhóng was within the borders of Xīncài County.
勞
is pronounced lì-dào.
He was sent to Jiànkāng.
After the Wèi ruler conquered Xuánhù,
he ordered two of the four generals including Qí Gǒng'ér to be dispatched,
and issued an edict to Yángzhōu for their transfer.
Wèi Yángzhōu was governed from Shòuyáng.
移
refers to a formal communication.
Kǎoyì says: Shào's biography states
"returned to Gǒng'ér and ten others,"
but we follow Sīmǎ Yuè's biography here.
Língjūn Jiāngjūn Lǚ Sēngzhēn spoke with Shào,
admiring his literary style and meaning.
He reported this to the emperor,
who then sent Zhǔshū Huò Língchāo to tell Shào:
"Today I allow you to return,
so that you may establish good relations between our two houses,
and bring peace to both peoples.
Would this not be excellent!"
He then summoned him for an audience,
bestowed clothes and other articles,
and had Shèlùn Zhōu Shě comfort him.
Shèlùn
refers to Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèlùn.
勞
is pronounced lì-dào.
"Wars have raged for many years,
and the people and their possessions have been utterly devastated.
It is for this reason that I am not ashamed to speak first and seek good relations with the Wèi court.
Previously, there were also letters for which no reply was ever received.
You should thoroughly convey this intention.
Now I send Chuánzhào Huò
Língxiù to escort you to your country,
hoping for good news soon."
He further said to Shào:
"Do you know why you did not die?
Your capture today
is by heaven's will.
Indeed, rulers are established for the sake of the people,
and all who are above the people
cannot but consider this!
If you wish to establish good relations,
I will now return Sùyù to them,
and they should return Hànzhōng to us."
Shào returned to Wèi and reported this,
but the Wèi ruler did not agree.
3 In the third month,
Yuán Zhì, the Wèi Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, led an army of seventy thousand to attack Chángōu.
Chángōu is north of the Hàn River.
According to the biography of Wú Pínghóu Bǐng in the Liángshū,
"Zhì was defeated at Chángōu,
and floating corpses covered the Hàn River,"
which means the waters of Chángōu flowed south into the Hàn.
潺
is pronounced shì-shān.
The Mán barbarians all crossed the Hàn River and surrendered,
and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Wú Pínghóu Bǐng accepted them.
All the gāngjì believed that the Mán barbarians were a constant border threat,
and it would be better to eliminate them now.
Zhōujùn Shàngzuǒ
refers to gāngjì,
meaning they managed the affairs of the prefectures and commanderies.
Bǐng said, "When they are in dire straits and surrender,
it is inauspicious for me to execute them.
Moreover, when the Wèi people invade,
it is not good that we have the Mán barbarians as a shield!"
No, it is good!
He then opened Fánchéng to receive their surrender,
and ordered Sīmǎ Zhū Sīyuǎn and others to attack Zhì at Chángōu.
They heavily defeated him,
beheading over ten thousand.
Zhì
was Qí's grandson.
The matter of Tuòbá Qí can be found in volume 120, Yuánjiā fourth year of Emperor Wén of Sòng.
4 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Línchuān Wáng Hóng was made Sīkōng,
and Chēqí Jiāngjūn Wáng Mào was additionally granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
5 On the day Dīngmǎo,
Lǐ Guóxīng, the lord of Wèi Chǔwáng Chéng, surrendered with his city.
6 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Guǐsì,
Bālíng Wáng Xiāo Bǎoyì died.
7 In the ninth month,
on the day Xīnsì,
Wèi enfeoffed Hào, the son of the late Běihǎi Wáng Xiáng, as Běihǎi Wáng.
The matter of Xiáng's disgrace and death can be found in volume 145, Tiānjiān first year.
8 Gōngsūn Chóng of Wèi created a musical ruler,
taking twelve *shǔ* (millet grains) as one *cùn*;
Liú Fāng disagreed,
instead taking ten *shǔ* as one *cùn*.
Shàngshū Lìng Gāo Zhào and others memorialized:
"The eight musical instruments created by Chóng and his measurements are all inconsistent with the classics and commentaries.
When questioned why this was so,
he said, 'If one strictly follows the classic texts,
the sounds will not be harmonious.'
We request that Fāng be ordered to create musical instruments according to the Zhōulǐ again,
and once completed, let them be discussed collectively and presented,
adopting the better ones."
An imperial edict agreed to this.
Indeed, those who create music first establish the *lǜ* (pitch standards).
The *lǜ* originates from the Huángzhōng (yellow bell),
the length of the Huángzhōng is determined by *shǔ*,
and the capacity of the Huángzhōng's *yuè* (tube) is determined by *shǔ*.
Although the Zhōulǐ Diǎntóng is said to be in charge of harmonizing the six *lǜ* and six *tóng*,
to distinguish the sounds of heaven, earth, the four directions, yin, and yang,
and to make musical instruments,
it never specifies the exact lengths of measures
or quantities of capacities.
Since the Dōngguān Kǎogōng emerged during the Hàn dynasty,
and the Fúshì, when making bells, only spoke of their width, length, circular diameter, depth, and thickness,
the method of accumulating *shǔ* was not mentioned.
Zhào's request to have Fāng create musical instruments according to the Zhōulǐ,
we do not know what he would base it on.
Wèi Shōu said: During the Tàihé period,
an edict ordered Zhōngshū Jiān Gāo Lǘ to correct the musical scales,
but it could not be settled for a long time.
Lǘ memorialized that Tàiyuè Jìjiǔ Gōngsūn Chóng participate in the matters of *lǜlǚ* (pitch standards), bells, and lithophones.
In the fourth year of Jǐngmíng,
an ancient bronze weight was found in Bìngzhōu,
and an edict assigned it to Chóng to be the standard for bells and pitches.
During the Yǒngpíng period,
Chóng created a new ruler,
using the length of one *shǔ* to accumulate the *cùn* measurement.
Later, Tàicháng Qīng Liú Fāng received an edict to revise the music,
taking the width of one middle-sized *jùshǔ* (black millet grain) as one *fēn*,

The three parties were in dispute

In the nineteenth year of Tàihé,
Gāozǔ decreed that the width of one *shǔ* be used to divide the *fēn* unit,
and ninety *shǔ*'s length to set the bronze ruler.
The responsible officials memorialized to follow the previous edict,
and Fāng's ruler was consistent with what Gāozǔ had established,
so he was then put in charge of revising the bells and lithophones.

in the tenth month,

Fēng Liàng of Nányáng, a recluse, was skilled in ingenious craftsmanship.

From then on, people from far and near were influenced by this trend,

Dídào county in Jīnchéng Commandery;
Later Wèi established Wǔshǐ Commandery.
Her peers, following custom, congratulated her, saying,

Previously,

The old system stipulated that the five Dū Lìshǐ (Chief Clerks) of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) should all be from humble backgrounds.

This was a clerk in the Ministry of War for the General of Illustrious Might.

They were the first to be selected for these positions.
In the sixth month,

(Wú Chéngbó's forces) attacked and captured Yī and Shè counties.

remote and on the seacoast,

It is not urgent for us,
but it is advantageous for the enemy.
Because it is advantageous,
they will fight to the death to contest it;
because it is not urgent,
we are forced to fight.
To use an unwilling army to attack a determined-to-die army,

and the cost will be immense.
Even if we gain Qújūshān,
it will only lead to further conflict,
and it will be difficult to hold it permanently.
It is what is called a 'useless field.'

holding this useless land,

'Cóng' [從],

18th day of the *jiǎyín* year (day 51 of the sexagenary cycle).

When the Wèi emperor was enthroned,
Yuán Zhāo (元昭) was also in the Ménxià department,
hence he kept petitioning against it.
*Fù* (復) is pronounced *fú yòu* (扶又).
*Shàng* (上) is pronounced *shí zhǎng* (時掌).
Tàifù (太傅) Yì (懌) and others submitted a memorial, stating:

*Jiǎ* (假) is pronounced the same as *xiá* (遐).
Attending to the imperial chambers

and implemented through imperial decrees.
*Shàng* (上) is pronounced *shí zhǎng* (時掌).
*Hé* (劾) is pronounced *hù gài* (戶概),
also *hù dé* (戶得).

'Resist him' means to insist it was unacceptable and refuse Zhōng (忠).
Although he had the intention, it was not carried out,

I have disgraced my office and enjoyed emoluments,

I request to return to my private residence,

Sībài (司敗) is Sīkòu (司寇).

23. On the *jǐyǒu* day (day 46 of the sexagenary cycle),
