Although Dàjiàn (Dàjiàn) is known as a natural stronghold,
with defiles that can be defended,
the path between its towering walls is quite flat.
Xiǎojiàn (Xiǎojiàn), however, was carved into the rock and built with suspended walkways,
allowing no passage,
which is what Lǐ Bái (Lǐ Bái) referred to as
"One man holding the pass,
ten thousand cannot open it."
12 In the eighth month,
on the yìsì (乙巳) day,

Wèi appointed Hú Guózhēn (Hú Guózhēn) as General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), Commissioner with the Authority of the Three Excellencies (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Governor of Yōngzhōu (Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Guózhēn (Guózhēn) was old,
and the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) in fact did not want him to go out,
wishing only to show him the honor of a frontier post;
he ultimately did not go.
13 After Kāng Xuàn (Kāng Xuàn) returned,
Zhāng Bàozǐ (Zhāng Bàozǐ) no longer repaired the Huái weir.
In the ninth month,
on the dīngchǒu (丁丑) day,
the Huái River (Huái Shuǐ) suddenly rose dramatically.
The weir collapsed,
its sound like thunder,
heard three hundred lǐ (里) away.
Along the Huái (Huái), cities, garrisons, and villages, over a hundred thousand people, were all swept into the sea.
Originally,
the Wèi people were troubled by the Huái weir.
They appointed Rènchéng Prince Chéng (Rènchéng Wáng Chéng) as Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) and Grand Commander of all Southern Expeditionary Forces (Dà Dūdū Nántǎo Zhū Jūnshì),
gathering an army of one hundred thousand,
intending to depart from Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu) to attack the weir.
Shàngshū Yòu Púshè (尚書右僕射) Lǐ Píng (Lǐ Píng) believed
that "without recourse to military force,
it will eventually collapse on its own."
When news of its destruction arrived,
the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) was greatly pleased
and richly rewarded Píng (Píng).
Chéng (Chéng) thus did not proceed.
14 On the rénchén (壬辰) day,
a general amnesty was declared.
15 The Empress Dowager Hú (Hú Tàihòu) of Wèi (Wèi) frequently visited the homes of imperial relatives, distinguished officials, and nobles.
Shìzhōng (Shìzhōng) Cuī Guāng (Cuī Guāng) submitted a memorial advising against this, saying:
"According to the Rites (Lǐ),
if a feudal lord enters the home of a minister not for the purpose of inquiring about illness or offering condolences for a death,
it is called 'the lord and minister engaging in jest' (jūnchén wéi xuè).
This is from the Lǐyùn (Lǐyùn) chapter of the Lǐjì (Lǐjì).
The commentary says: If one visits without cause,
it is a jest or game.
Duke Líng (Líng Gōng) of Chén (Chén) and Kǒng Níng (Kǒng Níng) and Yí Xíngfù (Yí Xíngfù) frequently went to the Xià (Xià) family home,
which led to their assassination.
This clearly illustrates the principle of not going to a minister's home unnecessarily.
For a lady,
while her parents are alive, she may return home to inquire after them (guīníng);
after their death, she sends a minister to do so (shǐ qīng níng).
In the Zǔozhuàn (Zǔozhuàn), Duke Zhuāng (Zhuāng) twenty-seventh year, winter,
Bó Jī (Bó Jī) came,
which was a guīníng.
Dù Yù (Dù Yù)'s commentary states: Níng (Níng)
means to inquire about the parents' well-being.
In the twelfth year of Duke Xiāng (Xiāng),
Zǐ Gēng (Zǐ Gēng), the Sīmǎ (Sīmǎ) of Chǔ (Chǔ), visited Qín (Qín),
doing so for the lady's níng (níng);
this was a ritual (lǐ).
The commentary says: For a feudal lord's lady,
after her parents have passed away,
she sends a minister for guīníng,
hence it is called a ritual.
Huò Guāng (Huò Guāng),
an maternal uncle,
personally served as chief minister (zǎifǔ);
yet the empress still received common ministers behind a military curtain (wǔzhàng).
This event is recorded in volume twenty-four, first year of Yuánpíng (Yuánpíng) reign of Emperor Zhāo (Zhāo) of Hàn (Hàn).
Currently, the imperial clan is flourishing,
distinguished officials and nobles are being promoted,
and the requests for such visits are numerous,
which will become an established practice.
'Flourishing' (fāng yǎn)
means having many descendants.
'Promoted' (zēng qiān)
means increasing their rank and moving up in office.
'Zhī' (Zhī)
means respectful.
This refers to the families of imperial relatives, distinguished officials, and nobles,
who, whenever there is a auspicious event,
all request the Empress Dowager to honor them with her presence.
Then the entire land will depend on this,
and all living beings will look up to her with joy."
Rènchéng Wáng Chéng (Rènchéng Wáng Chéng) believed that the selection of frontier generals in the north was becoming too lax,
fearing that the bandits and barbarians might spy on the border,
and that the imperial mausoleums (shānlíng) would be endangered.
From Emperor Xiǎnzǔ (Xiǎnzǔ) of Wèi (Wèi) upwards,
all the imperial mausoleums were in Yúnzhōng (Yúnzhōng).
He proposed strengthening the military preparations, and an edict was issued for the dukes and ministers to discuss this.
Yuán Fān (Yuán Fān), the Shàokīng (Shàokīng) of Tíngwèi (Tíngwèi), argued that
since Qín (Qín) and Hàn (Hàn), there was only one of each of the Nine Ministers (Jiǔqīng);
in the fifteenth year of Tàihé (Tàihé) reign of Wèi (Wèi), a Shàokīng (Shàokīng) was established for each of the Nine Ministers,

likely following the legacy system of the Zhōu Guān (Zhōu Guān) where the Six Ministers (Liùqīng) had a Xiǎozǎi (Xiǎozǎi), Xiǎosītú (Xiǎosītú), Xiǎozōngbó (Xiǎozōngbó), Xiǎosīmǎ (Xiǎosīmǎ), Xiǎosīkòu (Xiǎosīkòu), and Xiǎosīkōng (Xiǎosīkōng).
"Currently, in the border prefectures and commanderies,
officials are not selected based on merit,
but only on their rank and seniority.
Some are corrupt individuals
who extensively establish garrisons and patrols,
appoint many commanders,
using their own associates or relatives by marriage,
or accepting bribes and favors.
They have no intention of defending against bandits,
only of amassing wealth.
Their brave and strong soldiers
are driven to plunder.
If they encounter a strong enemy,
they immediately become slaves.
If they capture anyone,
they seize their wealth for themselves.
The weak, old, and young,
who have a slight understanding of metal and iron work,
or a little skill in carpentry,
are all relentlessly exploited in fortified camps,
forced into countless arduous tasks.
Others fell timber in deep mountains,
or weeded grass on open plains,
trading back and forth,
their presence lining the roads.
These people's salaries are meager,
and their resources are limited.
All their actual silk is collected,
while they are given imaginary grain.
Their strength is exhausted,
their clothing is thin,
their labor is used,
their food is rationed.
Throughout winter and summer,
afflicted by illness and suffering,
seven or eight out of ten die in ditches.
From ancient times to the present,
border soldiers have all suffered from this.
Màou (Màou)
pronounced mào.
The disturbance of our borders
is all due to the wrong people being in charge of the frontier.
I suggest that from now on,
in all the northern and southern border vassal states and the commanderies and counties under their jurisdiction,
from the staff officers and military commanders down to the garrison masters,
all should be recommended by court officials, princes, and dukes and below, selecting those they know.
It is imperative to choose talented individuals,
without being restricted by rank or grade.
If they perform their duties well or fail in office,
both they and their recommenders shall be rewarded or punished accordingly."
The Empress Dowager was unable to adopt this advice.
By the end of Zhèngguāng (Zhèngguāng) reign,
bandits and rebels rose en masse in the north,
subsequently threatening the old capital
and desecrating the imperial mausoleums (shānlíng),
just as Chéng (Chéng) had worried.
In the fourth year of Zhèngguāng (Zhèngguāng),
Pòliùhán Bálíng (Pòliùhán Bálíng) and Wèi Kěgū (Wèi Kěgū) rebelled,
and in the early years of Xiàochāng (Xiàochāng),
Yúnzhōng (Yúnzhōng) was lost.
16 In winter,
the eleventh month,
Lǐ Cè (Lǐ Cè), the Cìshǐ (Cìshǐ) of Jiāozhōu (Jiāozhōu), beheaded Ruǎn Zōngxiào (Ruǎn Zōngxiào), a rebel in Jiāozhōu (Jiāozhōu),
and sent his head to Jiànkāng (Jiànkāng).
17. Previously,
Wèi Shìzōng had begun building the Yáoguāng Temple,
but it was not completed.
This year,
Empress Dowager Hú again built the Yǒngníng Temple.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: "The Gǔ Canal flows south,
emerging between the Taìwèi and Sītú wards.
To the west of the water is the Yǒngníng Temple."
She also built the Shíkū Temple at the entrance to Yīquè,
all exemplifying the utmost beauty of civil engineering.
The Yǒngníng Temple was especially grand,
with one golden statue eighteen feet tall,
ten statues the size of an average person,
and two jade statues.
It had a nine-story stupa,
the foundation of which was dug so deep
it reached the Yellow Springs.
Dù Yù said: "The springs beneath the earth
are therefore called the Yellow Springs."
The top finial was another ten *zhàng* high,
and every quiet night,
the sound of its bells could be heard ten *lǐ* away.
The Buddha hall was like the Tàijí Hall,
and the south gate was like the Duānmén.
There were a thousand monastic cells,
adorned with pearls, jade, brocade, and embroidery,
astounding the hearts and eyes of all.
Since Buddhism entered China,
no stupa or temple
had been built with such magnificence.
In the Yǒngmíng era of Hàn,
Buddhism entered China.
Buddhist disciples collected and revered relics,
constructing palaces
called "towers" (*tǎ*),
which is also a foreign term,
akin to ancestral temples.
Hence, the world refers to them as "towers and temples" (*tǎmiào*).
Lǐ Chóng, the Inspector of Yángzhōu, submitted a memorial,
stating
"It has been nearly thirty years since Gāozǔ moved the capital.
The relocation of the capital is mentioned in volume 138, in the 11th year of Qí Shìzōng's Yǒngmíng era.
The Imperial Academy lies in ruin,
and the city gates, government offices, and temples are also quite dilapidated.
This is not how one carries on and exalts the legacy of one's predecessors.
The 'Great Announcement' says: 'If a father builds a house and lays its foundation,
and his son is unwilling to undertake the main hall,
how much less will he be willing to undertake the framework!'
Although the Guózǐ (Imperial College) now has the name of a school official,
it has no actual teaching.
How is this different from *tùsī* and *yànmài*,
or the Southern箕 and Northern斗!
The Èryǎ states: Táng, Méng, Nǚluó,
and Tùsī are all names for the same plant.
The Shìmíng states: Táng,
Méng,
Nǚluó,
and Tùsī
are four names for one thing.
Máo's Commentary on the Odes states: Nǚluó
is Tùsī;
Tùsī
is Sōngluó.
Lù Jī's Commentary on Grasses and Trees states: Tùsī
is a vine that grows on other plants,
yellow-red like gold.
The medicinal ingredient *tùsīzǐ* comes from this.
Sōngluó
grows on pines,
its branches are distinctly green,
and it is quite different from Tùsī.
The Běncǎo states: Tùsī grows in rivers, marshes, fields, and wilderness,
spreading over grasses and trees.
Qúmài
is also called Yànmài,
or Quèmài.
Its sprouts are like those of wheat,
but its spikelets are slender and sparse.
This means Tùsī has the name 'silk' but cannot be woven,
and Yànmài has the name 'wheat' but cannot be eaten.
An ancient song says: 'The *tùsī* in the field,
how can it be reeled into thread?
The *yànmài* by the roadside,
when can it ever be harvested?'
The Odes say: 'There is a箕 in the south,
but it cannot be used for winnowing.
There is a斗 in the north,
but it cannot be used for scooping wine.'
All these refer to having a name but no reality.
There should be some progress and retreat.
It is advisable to halt the extravagant decorative works of the Shàngfāng,
reduce the civil engineering efforts for Yǒngníng,
lessen the material and tile work for Yáoguāng,
and decrease the carving labor for the Shíkū Temple,
as well as other non-urgent public works.
During the farmers' slack seasons, these few repairs should be carried out,
so that the nation's appearance becomes solemn and distinguished,
and ritual and moral transformation flourish.
Would this not be splendid! "
The Empress Dowager replied with a gracious decree,
but did not adopt his suggestions.
The Empress Dowager was fond of Buddhism.
Many common people gave up their households to become *shāmén* (monks).
If a family had only one son,
and he became a *shāmén*,
that household would be cut off.
*Hǎo*,
pronounced as *dào* (tone marks omitted for this phonetic annotation).
"Of the three thousand sins, none is greater than unfilial conduct.
Of the great unfilial conduct, none surpasses cutting off the ancestral line.
Confucius said:
'Among the three thousand categories of punishments,
no crime is greater than unfilial conduct.'"
Mencius said:
"There are three forms of unfilial conduct,
and having no heir is the greatest."
*Yáng*,
pronounced as *zhànggěng* (tone marks omitted for this phonetic annotation),
also *chàng*.
They freely pursue their inclination towards the Dharma,
abandoning their elderly parents,
forsaking their homes and neglecting their support,
thereby failing in present-day rites while seeking future benefits!
Buddhist doctrine holds that cultivation in this life sows seeds for future karmic results.
*Bèi*,
pronounced as *púmèi* (tone marks omitted for this phonetic annotation).
*Yǎng*,
pronounced as *yúliàng* (tone marks omitted for this phonetic annotation).
'How can one know about death?'
The Analects records Confucius's reply to Zǐlù.
*Yān*,
pronounced as *yúqián* (tone marks omitted for this phonetic annotation).
Furthermore,
the southern territories are not yet pacified,
and public works remain burdensome.
The common people,
in fact, often evade service.
If this were further permitted,
I fear that filial piety and compassion would be abandoned,
and every household would become *shāmén*."
The Dūtǒng Sēng Xiān and others were furious that Yáng called it
"ghost teaching,"
considering it a slander against the Buddha.
The Wèi dynasty had a Shāmén Tǒng,
called Dūtǒng,
similar to today's Dū Sēnglù.
The Empress Dowager reproached him,
and Yáng said:
"Heaven is called *shén* (spirit),
earth is called *qí* (earth spirit),
and humans are called *guǐ* (ghost).
The commentaries say: 'When manifest, there are rites and music;
when hidden, there are *guǐshén*.'
Therefore, what is manifest is grand and splendid,
and what is hidden is a *guǐjiào* (ghost teaching).
The Buddha originated from humans;
to call it *guǐ* (ghost)
is, in my foolish opinion, not slander."
Although the Empress Dowager knew Yáng's words were reasonable,
it was difficult to go against the wishes of Xiān and others,
so she fined Yáng one *liǎng* of gold.
18. Tián Yìzōng, the Grand General who Conquers the South of Wèi, requested to be the Inspector of Dōngyùzhōu,
in order to attract his two sons.
The Empress Dowager did not permit it,
and he eventually died in Luòyáng.
Tián Yìzōng's two sons rebelled;
see volume above, 13th year.
*Zú*,
pronounced as *zǐxù* (tone marks omitted for this phonetic annotation).
19. Fúbá Kèhán of Rouran,
who was robust and skilled in warfare,
*Kè*,
pronounced as *cóngkān* (tone marks omitted for this phonetic annotation) in the entering tone.
*Hán*,
pronounced as *hán*.
attacked Gāochē to the west,
severely defeating them,
capturing their king Mí'étú.
He tied Mí'étú's feet to a worn-out horse
and dragged him to death,
then lacquered his head to make a drinking vessel.
Mí'étú killed Rouran's Tuó Hán; see volume above, 7th year.
Fúbá vanquished and destroyed them all,
and his kingdom became strong again.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
on the *xīnwèi* day,
the Emperor sacrificed at the Southern Suburb.
2. The remaining bandits of Wèi Dàchéng again gathered.
They were remnants of the *shāmén* Fǎqìng's party.
Yǔwén Fú's son, Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng Yán, led his servants and retainers to resist them.
The bandits set fire to the monastic hall.
Yán rushed into the fire, carrying Fú out,
his skin and hair all scorched.
He rallied his troops to fight fiercely,
and the bandits subsequently scattered and fled.
They were pursued and suppressed,
bringing peace.
3 On the jiǎxū day,
Wèi granted a general amnesty.
4 In the early days of Wèi,
the common people generally did not use money.
In the nineteenth year of Tàihé of Gāozǔ,
they first minted Tàihé Wǔzhū coins,
sending money artisans to various locations to cast them.
If commoners wished to mint money,
they were allowed to use government furnaces,
but the copper had to be refined and pure,
without any impurities.
In the third year of Yǒngpíng of Shìzōng,
Wǔzhū coins were again minted,
and it was forbidden throughout the realm to use money that did not conform to the standard style.
Subsequently, the coins used in Luòyáng and various prefectures and garrisons differed,
hindering commercial trade.
Shàngshū Lìng Rènchéng Wáng Chéng submitted a memorial,
stating:
"For unusable coins,
the law has clear regulations,
referring to 'chicken-eye' and 'ring-chisel' coins.
'Chicken-eye' coins
refer to coins that are thin and small,
with eyes like a chicken's eye.
'Ring-chisel' coins
mean that the hole is chiseled to extract copper,
leaving only a mere sliver of its substance.
'Huan' (鐶) is pronounced 'hù guān fān'.
Calculated, the coins currently circulating in the various prefectures of Hénán
all fall outside the restrictions.
The past prohibitions
have perplexed me.
Furthermore, Héběi has no new coins,
and the old ones are also prohibited.
They rely solely on plain silk-gauze and coarsely woven cloth,
with narrow widths and short lengths,
not conforming to the usual standards.
They tear a bolt into a chi
to make up for what is lacking,
merely creating the labor of shuttle and loom,
yet unable to escape the suffering of hunger and cold.
This is surely not the intention
of providing relief to the frozen and starving, and nurturing the common people.
The use of coins,
strung together and carried,
does not require measurement;
it is balanced and simple,
suitable for aiding the world,
and can be called profoundly appropriate.
I beg that all various prefectures and garrisons be instructed that
the Tàihé coins, the newly minted Wǔzhū coins, and other ancient coins that are convenient for local use,
as long as they are completely sound both inside and out,
even if there are differences in size,
should all be permitted to circulate.
Differences in value
will naturally follow local prices.
Thus, goods will circulate throughout the realm,
and there will be no obstruction for public or private affairs.
As for 'chicken-eye' and 'ring-chisel' coins, as well as those illicitly cast, or large ones damaged to become small, or new, cleverly forged, and non-standard ones,
they shall be punished according to the law."
The emperor approved.
However, there was little money in Héběi,
and the people still used goods for exchange,
so money did not enter the markets.
5 Many Wèi people secretly claimed military merits.
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Lú Tóng reviewed the merit records of the Lìbù
and thereupon conducted an inspection,
discovering over three hundred people who had illicitly gained ranks.
He then memorialized:
"I beg that the merit registers of the Lìbù and Zhōngbīng two bureaus be gathered,
compared entry by entry with the memorialized cases,
and two new copies made,
one for the Lìbù,
and one to be kept by the Bīngjú.
Also,
for those who have beheaded an enemy in battle and achieved one rank or more,
the Xíngtái Jūnsī should immediately issue a voucher,
which is to be vertically split down the middle.
One half is given to the person with merit,
and the other half is sent to the Ménxià.
This is what Hán Yù referred to in his poem 'Jì Cuī Lì Zhī Shī'
as 'should be like dividing a branch'.
Nowadays, people also call a document for dividing property a 'branch account'.
'Shù' (豎) is pronounced 'ér yǔ fān'.
The Empress Dowager approved.
Lú Tóng
was a descendant of Lú Xuán.
(Lú Xuán is mentioned in scroll 122, Yuánjiā eighth year of Sòng Wéndì.)
The Empress Dowager desired to use the internal and external examination registers, the Lìbù's appointment documents, the Zhōngbīng's merit files, and all the best reports from the various halls
to investigate and verify those who had illicitly gained ranks and official positions.
The Empress Dowager granted permission.
Shàngshū Lìng Rènchéng Wáng Chéng presented a memorial, stating:
"The law dislikes complexity,
and governance values clarity and simplicity.
The role of the Yùshǐ
is to supervise based on hearsay.
If there is news of someone illicitly claiming merit or falsely gaining a rank,
they should only be required to produce one register,
meticulously investigate the truth,
and punish according to the statutes.
How can one transfer the files of one department
(taking the files of the Shàngshū Shěng to the Yùshǐ Tái is what is meant by 'transferring')
from the first year of Jǐngmíng until this year, a total of eighteen years?
Now, to speak of matters spanning two 'jì' (periods of twelve years)
(presumably the ranks and merits conferred at the beginning of Jǐngmíng were the lists of meritorious individuals submitted during the campaigns on the Huái and Hàn rivers at the end of Tàihé),
who can bear such a crime!
This is truly something that the sagely court should regard with gravity and caution."
The Empress Dowager then ceased the action.
Also, because Kuāng's many suggestions were not followed,
fearing he might resign
('cháo' (朝) is pronounced 'zhí yáo fān';
'shù' (數) is pronounced 'suǒ jiǎo fān';
'cí jiě' (辭解) means to resign from office),
she added him to the position of Zhèn Dōng Jiāngjūn.
In the second month,
on the dīngwèi day,
Kuāng was appointed Dōngpíng Wáng.
(This was to prepare a coffin for Kuāng, and a pretext to attack Chéng.)
6 In the third month,
on the bǐngzǐ day,
an edict was issued to the weaving officials,
stating that brocades should not depict images of immortals, birds, or beasts.
('Zhīguān' (織官) is like the 'zhīshì lìng' and 'chéng' of the Hàn dynasty.)
This was deemed contrary to benevolence and clemency.
7 On the dīnghài day,
Wèi Guǎngpíng Wénmù Wáng Huái died.
8 Summer,
fourth month,
on the wùshēn day,
Wèi appointed Zhōngshū Jiān Hú Guózhēn as Sītú.
9 An imperial edict stated that using sacrificial animals in ancestral temples
accumulated obstacles in the netherworld.
('Míng' (冥) means 'yōu' (幽).
'Yōu' implies ghosts and spirits;
'míngdào' (冥道) is the way of ghosts and spirits.
'Lěi' (累) is pronounced 'lì ruì fān'.
'Kǎo Yì' states: In the 'Liáng Dì Jì', this edict was on the jiǎzǐ day of the fourth month.
'Nán Shǐ' says it was in the second month,
stating:
"Prayers and announcements to Heaven, Earth, and the ancestral temples,
with the principle of reducing killing, wished to be extended to all sentient beings.
Sacrificial animals at suburban altars and temples were all replaced with flour figures,
but not for mountain and river sacrifices."
According to the 'Cháng Lì', the xīnmǎo day was the first day of this month,
and there was no jiǎzǐ day.
The 'Suí Zhì' only says fourth month,
and does not mention removing sacrificial animals from suburban rites.
We follow this.
The edict proposed removing sacrificial animals from ancestral temples,
meaning no more blood sacrifices,
but the emperor ultimately did not comply.
The 'bāzuò' then deliberated on replacing "yī yuán dà wǔ" with large dried meat.
('Jì Qǔ Lǐ' states: a bull is called 'yī yuán dà wǔ'.
Zhèng Xuán says: 'yuán' (元) means head,
'wǔ' (武) means tracks.
'Zuò' (坐) is pronounced 'zǔ wò fān'.)
10 Autumn,
eighth month,
on the dīngwèi day,
an edict instructed Wèi Tàishī Gāoyáng Wáng Yōng to move into the Ménxià,
to participate in deciding matters memorialized to the Shàngshū.
(The character "Wèi"
should be placed
before
"zhào".)
11 Winter,
tenth month,
an edict noted that ancestral temples still used dried and cured meats.
(Zhèng Xuán says: 'pú' (脯) is dried meat.
'xiū' (脩) is pounded and cured meat.
Thin slices are called 'pú',
while pounded meat flavored with ginger and cinnamon is called 'duànxiū'.)
Therefore, large cakes were used to replace large dried meats,
and all other offerings consisted of vegetables and fruits.
Additionally, the Zhìjìng Diàn and Jǐngyáng Tái were built,
seating for the Seven Ancestral Temples was arranged,
and clean offerings were made twice each month.
12 On the yǐmǎo day,
Wèi issued an edict:
Northern Capital scholars and commoners who had not yet relocated
were all permitted to remain as permanent residents.
(Wèi referred to its capital as the Northern Capital.)
13 In the eleventh month,
on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Móu Hànchǒng (牟漢寵), the Inspector of Bázhōu, rebelled
and surrendered to the Wèi.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志) states: In Bāxī Commandery,
the Liáng (梁) established Nánliángzhōu and Běibāzhōu.
Jiàng (降) means
*hùjiāngfān* (戶江翻).
14 In the twelfth month,
Fúbá Kèhán (伏跋可汗) of Rouran (柔然) sent the *sìjīn* (俟斤) Wèibǐjiàn (尉比建) and others to request peace from the Wèi.
*Sìjīn* (俟斤)
was the title of a Rouran minister.
*Sì* (俟) means
*qúxīfān* (渠希翻).
*Wèi* (尉) means
*yūwùfān* (紆勿翻).
15 In this year,
Féng Dàogēn (馮道根), the General of the Right Guard, was appointed Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Dàogēn was cautious, honest, and taciturn.
In military campaigns, he was able to restrain his officers and soldiers.
When other generals vied for credit,
Dàogēn alone remained silent.
His governance was clean and simple,
and the officials and people cherished him.
The Emperor once sighed, saying,
"Wherever Dàogēn is,
the court no longer needs to remember there is such a province."
16 Cuī Liàng (崔亮), the Wèi Minister, memorialized to request permission to mine copper and cast coins in the Wángwū (王屋) Mountains and other locations.
This was granted.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* states: In the Wángwū (王屋) County of Hénèi Commandery, there are the Wángwū Mountains.
The coins became slightly thinner and smaller,
and their value decreased with use.
At this time, coins were light,
which was the case in both the North and the South.
Could this have been a matter of fate?
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the Wèi appointed Yáng Dìng (楊定), a Dī (氐) chieftain, as the Prince of Yīnpíng.
2 The Qiāng (羌) in Qínzhōu (秦州) of Wèi rebelled.
3 In the second month,
on the *guǐsì* day,
Xiù (秀), the Prince Kāng of Ānchéng, passed away.
Although Xiù (秀) and the Emperor were commoner brothers,
once they became ruler and subject, his caution, reverence, and respect surpassed that of those of humble status.
The Emperor increasingly esteemed him for this.
Xiù (秀) and his younger brother, Dàn (憺), the Prince of Shǐxīng, were especially close and affectionate.
Dàn (憺) had long been in Jīngzhōu (荊州)
and often
divided his emolument in half to provide for Xiù (秀).
Xiù (秀) and Dàn (憺) were both sons of Wú Tài (吳太).
In the first year of Zhōngxīng (中興) of Emperor Hé (和) of Qí (齊),
Dàn (憺) oversaw Yōngzhōu (雍州).
In the first year of Tiānjiān (天監),
he was promoted to oversee Jīngzhōu (荊州).
In the fifth year,
he was summoned to the capital.
Jīngzhōu (荊州) was crucial for the western frontier,
and its salary and income were generous.
Dàn (憺) means
*túdǎmfān* (徒敢翻),
also *túlǎmfān* (徒覽翻).
Nor did he refuse much.
4 On the *jiǎchén* day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
5 On the *jǐyǒu* day,
the Wèi proclaimed a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Shénguī.
6 The Dī (氐) in Dōngyìzhōu (東益州) of Wèi rebelled.
7 The Wèi ruler received the Rouran (柔然) envoys
and reprimanded them for the incompleteness of their vassal rites.
It was debated whether to follow the precedent of the Hàn (漢) in dealing with the Xiongnu (匈奴)
and send an envoy in return.
Emperor Xuān (宣) of Hàn (漢) treated Hūhánxié (呼韓邪) as superior to other vassal kings,
as he acknowledged allegiance.
According to Zhāng Lún's (張倫) memorial, he advised being sworn brothers,
following the precedent of Emperors Wén (文) and Jǐng (景) of Hàn (漢).
He believed:
"Tàizǔ (太祖) laid the foundation for the imperial enterprise,
and was busy with daily affairs,
thus allowing the scoundrels to roam freely in one direction,
meaning that Dàowǔ (道武) advanced south,
and Shèlún (社崙) was able to dominate the northern desert.
This was to be urgent with the Chinese and lenient with the barbarians.
Gāozǔ (高祖) was preoccupied with affairs in the south
and had no time for a northern expedition.
Meaning that Xiàowén (孝文) moved the capital south to Luòyáng
and waged war on the Huái (淮) and Hàn (漢) rivers,
and did not have time to attack the Rouran (柔然).
When barbarian envoys came,
they were received but not answered.
See Volume 146, sixth year.
If the state is rich and the army strong,
why fear to adopt a ritual of parity with an enemy,
and what is sought by doing so?
Although the barbarians now come seeking virtue,
they also wish to observe our strength and weakness.
If we send a royal envoy to their court
and become sworn brothers,
I fear this is not the intention of our ancestors.
If the situation is unavoidable,
an imperial edict should be issued,
demonstrating the protocol of superior and subordinate,
and ministers should be commanded to deliver a letter,
explaining the way of submission.
Observe whether they comply or refuse,
then gradually advance or retreat with grace and might,
then the dignity of the ruler will be correctly established.
How can it be because the barbarians have expanded their territory,
meaning Fúbá (伏跋) had recently defeated Gāochē (高車) and extinguished rebellious neighboring states?"
His advice was not followed.
Lún (倫) was the son of Báizé (白澤).
Zhāng Báizé (張白澤) is mentioned in Volume 134, first year of Shēngmíng (昇明) of Emperor Shùn (順) of Sòng (宋).
8 In the third month,
on the *xīnwèi* day,
Yú Zhōng (于忠), Duke Wǔjìng of Língshòu (靈壽) of Wèi, passed away.
9 The Dī (氐) in Nánqínzhōu (南秦州) of Wèi rebelled.
Cuī Xí (崔襲), General of Dragon's Might, was dispatched with a credential to persuade them.
10 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day,
Hú Guózhēn (胡國珍), Duke Wénxuān of Qín (秦) of Wèi, passed away.
He was posthumously granted the *jiǎhuángyuè* (假黃鉞), Chancellor, Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside, Grand Tutor,
titled Grand Preeminent Duke of Qín,
and buried with extraordinary rites.
He was given posthumous gifts, funerary clothes, and ceremonial guards,
with utmost generosity.
Furthermore, the coffin of Empress Dowager's mother, Lady Huángfǔ, was welcomed
and buried together with Guózhēn (國珍),
called the Grand Preeminent Consort Xiàomù of Qín.
Zhāng Pǔhuì (張普惠) of Chángshān (常山), the Grand Master Remonstrant, believed that no imperial father-in-law in previous generations had been called
"Grand Preeminent,"
and that the title "Grand Preeminent" should not be applied to a minister.
He went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial explaining this,
but no one among the attendants dared to convey it.
It happened that when the Hú (胡) family was digging the tomb,
a large rock was encountered below.
Pǔhuì (普惠) then secretly submitted a memorial,
believing:
"There cannot be two suns in the sky,
nor two kings on earth.
'Grand Preeminent' (太上)
is a name derived from 'Supreme' (上).
The Empress Dowager calls her 'Order' (令) to follow the 'Edict' (敕) below,
which is to adopt the principle of 'three obediences,'
and distantly align with Mother Wén (文母) who was among the 'Ten Worthies.'
King Wǔ (武王) said:
'I have ten capable ministers.'
Confucius said:
'Talent is scarce; there was a woman among them,
so there were only nine men.'

Earlier scholars believed the 'Ten Worthies' were Tàigōng Wàng (太公望), Zhōugōng Dàn (周公旦), Shàogōng Shì (召公奭), Bìgōng Gāo (畢公高), Rónggōng (榮公), Tàidiān (太顛), Hóngyāo (閎夭), Sǎnyíshēng (散宜生), Nángōng Kuò (南宮括), and Mother Wén.
I fear this deviates from the meaning of following edicts.
Confucius said, 'Surely, the rectification of names is essential!'
The *Analects* records Confucius's words in response to Zǐlù.
And to lightly alter the divination,
this may also be how Heaven, Earth, and the spirits issue a supreme warning and awaken sagely sentiments.
I humbly wish that the title that presses upon the Supreme be halted,
to invite the blessing of humility."
The Empress Dowager then personally went to Guózhēn's (國珍) residence,
summoned officials of the fifth rank and above for extensive discussion.
The princes and dukes all catered to the Empress Dowager's wishes,
competing to challenge and question Pǔhuì (普惠);
Pǔhuì (普惠) responded with quick wit and discernment,
and none could defeat him.
The Empress Dowager had Yuán Chā (元叉) convey an order to Pǔhuì (普惠), saying:
"What I do is the aspiration of a filial child.
What you present is the way of a loyal minister.
All the dukes have already reached a consensus,
and you should not stubbornly insist on changing my mind.
If you have any further insights,
do not hesitate to speak."
The Empress Dowager built a temple for the Grand Preeminent Consort,
its magnificence matching Yǒngníng (永寧).
The Grand Secretary (尚書, Shàngshū) memorialized, proposing to restore the tax on cotton and hemp from the people.
Zhāng Pǔhuì (張普惠) submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Gāozǔ (高祖) abolished the large dou (斗),
removed the long chi (尺),
and changed the heavy steelyard,
to show love for the people and lighten their burdens.
Knowing that the army and the state required cotton and hemp,
he therefore increased the tax on silk by eight liǎng (兩) of cotton,
and on cloth by fifteen jīn (斤) of hemp.
The people, seeing what was reduced by the scales and rulers,
gained more than just cotton and hemp,
and thus willingly supplied the tribute.
Since then,
the silk and cloth levied,
have gradually become longer and wider again,
causing the common people to lament,
a sentiment heard throughout the court and countryside.
The Grand Secretaries (宰輔, Zǎifǔ) did not investigate the root cause, which lay in the increasing width and length of the fabric,
and hastily abolished the cotton and hemp tax.
Yú Zhōng (于忠) abolished the cotton and hemp tax
fourteen years ago.
Now there is a desire to collect it again.
This is to abandon the great trust of all under heaven,
to discard an established imperial decree that has already been implemented,
to pursue past errors,
and to invite future mistakes.
They do not consider that there is a large quantity of cotton and hemp in the imperial stores,
but corrupt officials are conspiring to steal it.
Why is this?
The goods submitted,
sometimes exceed the weight by a hundred zhū (銖),
yet we have not heard of officials punishing the zhōu (州) and jùn (郡) in accordance with the law;
but if there is even a small instance of excessive or poor quality,
then the household head is implicated,
along with the three elders (三長, Sāncháng).
The household head (戶主, Hùzhǔ)
is the head of a family,
and thus the master of a household.
The three elders are mentioned in volume 136, during the fourth year of Yǒngmíng (永明) of Qí Shìzǔ (齊世祖).
Many transgress the regulations,
corrupt officials receive salaries,
and people demand longer, wider, thicker, and heavier goods,
without any standard or limit.
We have never heard of anyone returning surplus of a correct duān (端) when submitting to the government.
Six zhàng (丈) of cloth is a duān.
The Ěryǎ (爾雅) states: twice a zhàng is called a duān,
twice a duān is called a liǎng (兩),
and twice a liǎng is called a pǐ (匹).
Dù Yù (杜預) said: two zhàng is a duān,
two duān is a liǎng,
which is what is called a pǐ.
The Shuōwén (說文) says: fú (幅),
is the width of cloth.
Fèng (俸),
pronounced fú yòng fān.
We should first rectify the weights and measures,
clearly establish strict prohibitions,
and not allow any excess or overflow.
This will let all under heaven know that the hearts of the two Sages (二聖, Èrshèng) cherish the people and uphold the law to this extent,
and then the governance of Tàihé (太和) will be seen again in the sacred turtle (神龜, Shénguī)."
Pǔhuì (普惠) also observed that the Wèi (魏) ruler delighted in excursions to royal parks and gardens,
did not personally attend to court,
excessively revered Buddhist law,
and largely entrusted affairs of the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples to officials.
He submitted a memorial sharply remonstrating,
stating:
"Cultivating a thoughtless, dark karma,
incurring huge expenses upon the living people,
reducing stipends and diminishing labor,
to supply idle monks nearby,
adorning cloud temples,
and inviting uncertain rewards in the distant future—
while officials who serve from dawn (昧爽之臣, Mèishuǎng zhī chén) prostrate themselves outside,
refers to corrupt officials entering the court.
Kǒng Ānguó (孔安國) said: mèishǔang (昧爽),
dark.
Shuǎng (爽),
bright,
early morning.
Jī (稽),
pronounced qǐ.
Transgressing rituals and going against the times,
neither human nor spiritual harmony is achieved.
I foolishly believe that cultivating morning and evening causes
to seek kalpa (祇劫, Qíjié) fruits,
is not as good as gaining the joyful hearts of all nations to serve one's parents,
making all under heaven peaceful,
and preventing disasters from arising.
This uses the meaning from the Xiàojīng (孝經).
Shū (淑),
good.
Personally performing the reverence of suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples,
personally observing the rituals of the first and fifteenth of the month.
Yū (紆),
to wind,
to bend.
The schools of the Five Emperors (五帝, Wǔdì) were called Chéngjūn (成均).
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said: Shìcài (釋菜) and Diànbì (奠幣) are rituals to honor the former teachers.
He also said: Shìdiàn (釋奠) is merely setting out offerings and pouring libations.
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) said: Shìdiàn includes livestock and silk;
Shìcài (釋菜) only offers duckweed.
Qiānmǔ (千畝),
refers to the ceremonial plowing field (藉田, Jiètián).
Restore the long-withheld ranks of all officials,
ensure that what has already been started is completed simply and quickly,
and entirely cease any new construction.
Then filial piety and brotherly love can communicate with the gods,
and moral instruction can illuminate the four seas.
By being frugal and loving the people,
both law and custom will benefit."
Soon an imperial edict ordered an external discussion of the Shìdiàn (釋奠) ceremony.
Also, from then on, officials were granted an audience (陛見, Bìjiàn) monthly.
All these followed Pǔhuì's (普惠) words.
Pǔhuì (普惠) again submitted a memorial discussing the gains and losses of current governance.
The Empress Dowager (太后, Tàihòu) and the Emperor (帝, Dì) summoned Pǔhuì (普ǔhuì) to Xuānguāng Diàn (宣光殿),
and questioned him on various matters.
The concubine's younger brother of Línchuān Wáng Hóng (臨川王宏), Wú Fǎshòu (吳法壽), committed murder and hid in Hóng's (宏) residence.
The Emperor (上, Shàng) ordered Hóng (宏) to hand him over,
and he was executed that very day.
The Southern Censorate (南司, Nánsī) memorialized to dismiss Hóng (宏) from office.
The Censorate (御史臺, Yùshǐtái) was also called Nántái (南臺)
and Nánsī (南司).
"Loving Hóng (宏) is the private affection of brothers,
dismissing Hóng (宏) is the righteous law of the ruler;
the memorial is acceptable."
In the fifth month,
on the day of wùyín (戊寅),
Sītú (司徒), Piàojì Dàjiàngjūn (驃騎大將軍), Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史) Línchuān Wáng Hóng (臨川王宏) was dismissed.
Since Hóng's (宏) defeat at Luòkǒu (洛口),
mentioned in volume 146, year five,
every time there was a theft in the capital,
Hóng (宏) was always named,
and he was repeatedly impeached by officials,
but the Emperor (上, Shàng) always pardoned him.
The Emperor (上, Shàng) visited Guāngzhái Sì (光宅寺).
The Emperor (帝, Dì) made the old residence of Sānqiáo (三橋) into Guāngzhái Sì (光zhái Sì).
Sānqiáo (三橋) was in Tóngxià Lǐ (同夏里), Mòlíng Xiàn (秣陵縣).
Hóng's (宏) residence faced the Qínhuái (秦淮) River,
and a floating bridge was built in front of his residence;
it was called Piàojì Háng (驃騎航),
named after Hóng's (宏) official title.
When the Emperor (上, Shàng) was about to depart,
his heart was moved,
so he crossed at Zhūquè Háng (朱雀航).
When the incident occurred,
it was said to be instigated by Hóng (宏).
The Emperor (上, Shàng) wept and said to Hóng (宏):
"My talent surpasses yours a hundredfold,
yet even I fear I might not be capable of handling such matters.
What are you doing?
It is not that I cannot be Hàn Wéndì (漢文帝),
referring to the execution of Huáinán Lìwáng Cháng (淮南厲王長).
Hóng (宏) prostrated himself, claiming innocence,
thus, due to harboring Fǎshòu (法壽), Hóng (宏) was dismissed from office.
Hóng 奢 was excessively extravagant and
insatiably accumulated wealth.
His storehouses amounted to nearly a hundred rooms.
垂 (chuí)
means almost reaching (jǐ jí).
The locks and keys were very strict.
籥 (yuè)
is the same as 鑰 (yào),
referring to the bolt of a lock (guān mǔ).
This was secretly reported.
The Emperor, who had deep affection for his siblings,
was greatly displeased.
On another day,
he sent a lavish meal to Hóng’s beloved concubine, Lady Jiāng, saying:
“I will come to feast with you.”
He went alone, taking his old acquaintance, Shèshēng Xiàowèi Qiū Tuōqīng,
and had a great drink with Hóng and Lady Jiāng.
After becoming half-drunk,
he said:
“I now wish to tour your private chambers.”
He immediately called for a sedan chair and went straight to the back of the hall.
Hóng feared the Emperor would see his hoard of treasures,
and his face showed terror.
The Emperor grew even more suspicious.
Thereupon, he inspected every room.
Every million cash was formed into one pile,
marked with a yellow banner.
Ten million formed one storehouse,
from which hung a purple banner.
There were over thirty such rooms.
The Emperor and Tuōqīng counted on their fingers,
seeing over three hundred million cash.
The remaining rooms stored various goods such as cloth, silk, floss, lacquer, honey, ramie, and wax,
which were simply seen to fill the storehouses,
their quantity unknown.
The Emperor then realized that these were not for military expenses,
and was greatly pleased.
He said:
“Āliù,
your household management is superb!”
Hóng was the sixth among his brothers.
阿 (ā)
is pronounced with the 'ān' entering tone.
He raised a torch and returned.
From then on, the brothers became even more harmonious.
Hóng owned dozens of pawnshops in the capital.
He issued loans with interest-bearing tickets.
He always used fields, residences, and shops as collateral for these contracts.
When the term expired,
he would drive out the certificate holders and seize their homes.
In the capital,
the common people in the east
lost their livelihoods, not just one.
The Emperor later learned of this,
and decreed that interest-bearing tickets could no longer be used to drive people out and seize their property.
This began from that time.
The Shìzhōng and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn, Wú Pínghóu Bǐng,
was elegant and forceful in character,
and highly esteemed by the Emperor.
All major military and state affairs were discussed and decided with him.
He was appointed Ānyòu Jiāngjūn,
and Administrator of Yángzhōu.
Ānyòu Jiāngjūn
was one of the hundred general titles established by the Emperor.
Bǐng
is pronounced bǐng.
監 (jiān)
is pronounced gōng xián fān.
Bǐng
was the Emperor's paternal cousin.
Yángzhōu was the capital region.
Bǐng considered that he was surpassing the intimacy of a blood relative by holding this position,
so he earnestly declined.
The Emperor did not permit it.
While in the province, he was especially praised for his clear judgment.
His decrees and instructions were strict and orderly.
On the day Xīnsì,
Hóng was appointed Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn and Zhōngshū Jiān.
In the sixth month,
on the day Yǐyǒu,
he was again made acting Sītú with his original title.
Original title
refers to the title of Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Your servant Guāng says: Hóng, as a general, caused the defeat of three armies;
as a minister, he was involved in great treason.
Gāozǔ pardoned his capital offense, which was acceptable.
But within a few tens of days, he was restored to the position of a Sāngōng.
The kindness shown to his brother was indeed profound,
but where then was the law of the monarch?
Previously, in Luòyáng, there was a three-character stone classic erected by Hàn.
The matter of the stone classics can be found in volume 47, during the fourth year of Xīpíng of Hàn Língdì.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Cài Yōng rectified and set the texts of the Five Classics,
carving them on stone and erecting them outside the Imperial Academy gate.
During the Zhèngshǐ reign of Wèi, another three-character stone classic (ancient script, seal script, clerical script) was erected.
By the time of Wèi,
Féng Xī and Cháng Bófū successively served as Luòzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wèi's capital was Píngchéng,
designating Luòyáng as Luòzhōu.
After moving the capital to Luòyáng,
it was then changed to Sīzhōu.
Subsequently, it fell into great disrepair.
What remained was abandoned in the overgrown wilderness.
Both officials and common people took pieces at will.
Shìzhōng and Lǐng Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Cuī Guāng requested to send officials to guard them,
and ordered Guózǐ Bóshì Lǐ Yù and others to mend their imperfections.
Empress Hú Tàihòu granted permission.
However, Yuán Chā and Liú Téng then rebelled,
and the matter was consequently shelved.
The rebellion of Chā and Téng
is mentioned in the next volume, second year of Pǔtōng.
In autumn,
seventh month,
the Qiāng chief Tiěhū of Wèi's Hézhōu
rebelled, styling himself King of Shuǐchí.
Hézhōu governed Páohǎn,
and administered the commanderies of Jīnchéng, Wǔshǐ, Hónghé, and Líntáo.
Shuǐchí County was established as a commandery in the fourth year of Zhēnjūn of Wèi,
later changed to a county,
subordinate to Hónghé Commandery.
During the Suí dynasty, Hónghé Commandery was merged into Dāngyí County.
Its territory was within the borders of Líntán County, Táo Zhōu, during the Táng dynasty.
Cáo Wèi established the Shàngshū Zhǔkè Láng.
He strictly ordered the prefectures, commanderies, and all armies
not to infringe upon the common people's belongings,
and also not to lightly engage in battle with the bandits.
Then he demonstrated both might and grace to them,
making them realize regret and fear.
In the eighth month,
Tiěhū and others led their followers to Yuán Zǐgōng and surrendered.
The whole affair lasted less than two *xún* (twenty days).
This states that from Zǐgōng's arrival at Hézhōu until the bandits surrendered,
the whole affair lasted less than two *xún*.
帥 (shuài)
is read as shuài.
降 (jiàng)
is pronounced with the hù jiāng fān.
He was the son of Huái.
Yuán Huái
was the son of Yuán Hè,
who served successively under Wénchéng, Xiànwén, Xiàowén, and Xuānwǔ.
The Wèi eunuch Liú Téng
could not write,
but was full of wicked schemes
and skilled at discerning people's intentions.
Empress Hú Tàihòu, for his service in protecting her,
which is mentioned in the fourteenth year of the previous entry,
then meddled in political affairs.
He accepted bribes to seek official positions for people,
and none were unsuccessful.
Héjiān Wáng Chēn
was the son of Jiǎn.
Qíjùn Wáng Jiǎn is mentioned in volume 137, ninth year of Yǒngmíng of Qí Wǔdì.
琛 (chēn)
is pronounced chǒu lín fān.

measuring ten *chǐ* (丈) long with thirteen strings.
The hidden interval is nine *chǐ* (尺) to correspond to the nine *cùn* (寸) of the Huángzhōng (黃鍾) *lǜ* (律).
Under the central string, there are marks dividing *cùn* (寸) to indicate the clear and turbid sections of the sixty *lǜ* (律).'
Fáng's (房) discussion of *lǜ* (律) is more detailed than what Liú Xīn (劉歆) presented;
his method was practiced by official historians
and used by the celestial observation department.
The *lǜ* (律) method says: Yang (陽) takes a circle as its form,
and its nature is movement;
Yin (陰) takes a square as its measure,
and its nature is stillness.
Moving ones number three,
still ones number two.
When Yang (陽) generates Yin (陰), it doubles;
when Yin (陰) generates Yang (陽), it quadruples;
all are 'three and one'.
Yang (陽) generating Yin (陰) is called 'downward generation';
Yin (陰) generating Yang (陽) is called 'upward generation'.
Upward generation must not exceed the clarity or turbidity of Huángzhōng (黃鍾);
downward generation must not reach the numerical value of Huángzhōng (黃鍾).
All follow the principle of 'three for Heaven and two for Earth, round cover and square base, six pairs supporting odd numbers.'
Huángzhōng (黃鍾) is
the head of the *lǜlǚ* (律呂),
and it generates the eleven *lǜ* (律).
In their mutual generation,
all are divided into three and then augmented or diminished.
Therefore, the value of the twelve *lǜ* (律) is one hundred seventy-seven thousand one hundred forty-seven,
which is the actual value of Huángzhōng (黃鍾).
Multiply by two and divide by three,
this is the actual value of the downward-generated Línzhōng (林鍾);
multiply by four and divide by three,
this is the actual value of the upward-generated Tàicù (太簇).
Extending this upwards and downwards determines the actual values of the sixty *lǜ* (律).
Using the number nine-three, nineteen thousand six hundred eighty-three, as the divisor,
the *lǜ* (律) are in *cùn* (寸),
and on the *zhǔn* (準) they are in *chǐ* (尺).
What is less than a whole unit, when multiplied by ten, becomes *fēn* (分);
what is again less than ten, when multiplied by ten, becomes *xiǎofēn* (小分).
The remainder is used to correct their strength or weakness.

the Jiāng, Huái, and the sea all overflowed.

Yuán Yīng served Wèi Xiàowén and Xuānwǔ,

Xiàng,

Xī was fond of literature,

Before his death,

"My brother and I both received the trust and favor of the Empress Dowager.
My brother held a large prefecture,
while I entered to serve,
with earnest words and expressions,
her grace was like that of a kind mother.
Now the Empress Dowager is deposed in the Northern Palace,
Grand Tutor, Prince Qīnghé, Héng, has suffered cruel execution,
and the Young Emperor,
is alone in the front hall.
With ruler and parent in such a state,
I could not feel at ease.
Therefore, I led soldiers and commoners, wishing to establish a great righteous cause in the world.
However, my wisdom and strength are shallow and limited,
and I was immediately captured.
Xuán,
means 'to return'.
Below, I am ashamed before those who knew me.
It was for the sake of honor and righteousness that I acted,
and I could not do otherwise.
My intestines flow and my head is smashed,
what more can I say!
All you gentlemen,
each uphold your integrity,
for the country and for yourselves,
strive to protect your honor! "
Those who heard this pitied him.
Xī's head arrived in Luòyáng,
and his relatives and old friends dared not look.
Only the former Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn, Diāo Zhěng, collected his corpse and buried it.
Zhěng

Diāo Yōng left Jìn and entered Wèi,

Jìyīn Commandery,

Jì,
pronounced *zǐ lǐ fān*.
He was then allowed to return to his post.
Chā appointed Tóng as Huángmén Shìláng.
Yuán Luè fled and took refuge with his old friend, Sīmǎ Shǐbīn of Hénèi.
Shǐbīn and Luè tied together bundles of reeds and crossed Mèngjīn by night,

Túnliú County, since the Hàn and Jìn dynasties, belonged to Shàngdǎng Commandery.

Shuāng said:
"There will always be one death.

Please do not worry about it."
Luè firmly requested to flee south.
Shuāng then sent his nephew Chāng to escort Luè across the river.
He then came to defect,
and the Emperor enfeoffed Luè as Prince Zhōngshān.
This sets the stage for Luè's later return to Wèi.
He was a descendant of Yōng's clan.
Chā falsely accused Diāo Zhěng of sending Luè away,

Yùshǐ Wáng Jī and others strongly defended and exonerated him,

10 On the day *Jiǎzǐ*,

The *Wǔdài Zhì* states: Línglíng Commandery, Línglíng County, formerly had Yǒngchāng County established.

Qí,
pronounced *qí jì fān*.

His conduct was almost as it had been on ordinary days.
The historian states that Wéi Ruì, in a court that worshiped Buddha,
corrected it with righteousness,
almost like one who served his ruler with the Dao.
11 In the ninth month,
on the day *Wùxū*,
Wèi appointed Prince Gāoyáng Yōng as Chéngxiàng,
to comprehensively manage internal and external affairs,
and to jointly decide on all matters with Yuán Chā.
12 Initially,
Róurán's Tuóhàn Kèhán had taken Hòulǘlíng Shì, the wife of Fúmíngdūn,
and fathered Fúbá Kèhán and Ānàhuái, among six sons.
Kè,
from *kān rù shēng*.
Hán,
pronounced *hán*.
Ānàhuái,
pronounced *gǔ huí fān*.
Suddenly, his youngest son, Zǔhuì, disappeared.
Despite searching, he could not be found.
A shamaness, Dìwàn, claimed that Zǔhuì was now in heaven,
and that she could summon him.
She then erected a tent in a great marsh,
and sacrificed to the heavenly gods.
Zǔhuì suddenly appeared inside the tent,
claiming he had always been in heaven.
Fúbá was greatly pleased,
and named Dìwàn "Saintly Woman,"
taking her as Kèhèdūn.
The ruler of Róurán was called Kèhán,
and his principal wife was called Kèhèdūn.
She also had a beautiful and alluring appearance.
Fúbá respected and loved her,
trusting her words and
interfering with national politics.
This continued for years.
As Zǔhuì gradually grew up,
he told his mother:
"I was always at Dìwàn's house.
I never went to heaven;
Dìwàn taught me that I went to heaven."
His mother fully reported the situation to Fúbá.
Fúbá said:
"Dìwàn can foreknow the future;
do not slander her."
Later, Dìwàn, feeling afraid,
slandered Zǔhuì to Fúbá and had him killed.
Hòulǘlíng Shì sent her grand minister, Jùliè and others, to strangle Dìwàn.
Fúbá was enraged
and wished to execute Jùliè and others.
At that time, Āzhìluó invaded.
Āzhìluó was a separate barbarian tribe,
dwelling east of the Northern River,
and had always been allied with Wèi.
One account says: Āzhìluó
was of the Gāochē tribe.
Their army was defeated and returned.
Hòulǘlíng Shì and the ministers jointly killed Fúbá,
and enthroned his younger brother Ānàhuái as Kèhán.
Ten days after Ānàhuái's ascension,
his clan cousin Shìfā led tens of thousands of people and attacked him.
Ānàhuái was defeated in battle
and, with his younger brother Yǐjūfá, fled to Wèi on light cavalry.
Shìfā killed Hòulǘlíng Shì and Ānàhuái's two younger brothers.
The history states that Róurán was in chaos.
13In Wèi, Qīnghé Wáng Yì died.
Rǔnán Wáng Yuè had no intention of hating Yuán Chā.
He awaited him with Sāngluò Jiǔ.
*Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: Hédōng Jùn had many relocated people.
Among the people was one named Liú Duò.
He was skilled at brewing.
He drew water from the river
and brewed a fragrant strong wine.
It was aged for a year of withered branches
and served at the time when mulberry leaves fall.
Hence, the wine got its name.
The color of the fragrant wine
was clear white like rice-washing water.
Its unique aroma permeated the air,
unlike any other.
With the fragrance of orchids and the richness of musk,
it created its own refined aroma.
Among the tributes from various regions,
it was the finest drink.
From kings and dukes to ordinary friends, all invited each other to drink it,
always saying "Suǒláng."
"Suǒláng" was a reversed pronunciation of Sāngluò.
It also became the subject of excellent poems
and brilliant discussions among the Central Secretariat officials.
Yuán Chā was greatly pleased.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *Yǐmǎo* day,
Yuè was appointed Shìzhōng and Tàiwèi.
Yuè demanded Yì's clothes and playthings from Yì's son Dǎn.
Dǎn did not comply with the request in a timely manner.
Moreover, he procrastinated and did not deliver them in time,
and what he did deliver did not satisfy Yuè's wishes.
稱,
尺證翻.
(Dǎn) almost died.
14The Róurán Kèhán Ānàguī was about to arrive in Wèi.
The Wèizhǔ sent Sīkōng Jīngzhào Wáng Jì, Shìzhōng Cuī Guāng, and others to welcome him successively.
They were granted very generous rewards.
The Wèizhǔ received Ānàguī in Xiǎnyáng Diàn

Ānàguī was seated below the imperial princes.
As the banquet was about to end,
Ānàguī stood behind his seat, holding a petition.
An imperial edict summoned him to stand before the emperor's seat.
Ānàguī bowed twice and said:
"Your servant, due to family difficulties,
has come lightly to the imperial court.
The subjects of my native country
have all fled and scattered.
Your Majesty's benevolence is as vast as heaven and earth.
I beg for troops to escort me back to my native country,
to execute the rebels
and gather the scattered refugees.
Your servant will then command the remaining people
and serve Your Majesty.
I cannot express everything verbally.
There is a separate petition to present."
He then handed the petition to Zhōngshū Shèrén Cháng Jǐng to be reported.
Jǐng
was the grandson of Shuǎng.
Cháng Shuǎng is mentioned in Volume 123, during the 6th year of Yuánjiā of Sòng Wéndì.
In the eleventh month,
on the *Jǐhài* day,
Wèi established Ānàguī as Shuòfāng Gōng and Rúrú Wáng,
granting him clothes and light chariots,
stipend, welfare, and ceremonial guards,
all as befitted an imperial prince.
At that time, Wèi was strong and prosperous.
To the east of the imperial road, south of the Luò Shuǐ Bridge, four lodges were built.
To the west of the road, four residential quarters were established: those who surrendered from Jiāngnán were housed in Jīnlíng Guǎn.
After three years, they were granted residences in Guīzhèng Lǐ.
Those who surrendered from the northern barbarians were housed in Yānrán Guǎn
and granted residences in Guīdé Lǐ.
Those who surrendered from the eastern barbarians were housed in Fúsāng Guǎn
and granted residences in Mùhuà Lǐ.
Those who surrendered from the western barbarians were housed in Yānzī Guǎn
and granted residences in Mùyì Lǐ.
The four lodges were all named after the four cardinal directions: Jīnlíng is in Jiāngnán (south of the Yangtze River).
Yānrán is north of the desert.
Fúsāng is in the east,
where the sun rises.
Yānzī is in the west,
where the sun sets.
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* says: In the Great Wilderness,
above Yánggǔ there is Fúsāng,
where the sun rises.
On Mount Huīyě there is a tree
with green leaves and red flowers,
named Ruòmù,
where the sun sets.
It grows west of Kūnlún,
southwest of Niǎoshǔ Shān,
and is called Yānzī.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says: West of Xìliǔ
is Yānzī, where the sun sets.
The *Shízhōu Jì* says: Fúsāng is in the Bìhǎi,
thousands of *zhàng* tall
and over a thousand *wéi* in circumference.
It has two trunks from the same root,
leaning on each other.
Hence it is named Fúsāng.

Ānàguī repeatedly requested to return to his country.

on the *Rénzǐ* day,

means *jièshǒu* (border).

15On the *Xīnyǒu* day,
Wèi appointed Jīngzhào Wáng Jì as Sītú.
16Wèi sent envoy Liú Shànmíng to pay a visit,

1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the *Xīnsì* day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the southern suburb.
2 An Orphanage Garden was established in Jiànkāng
to take in and care for the poor.
In ancient times, widowers, widows, orphans, childless elders, and the disabled were cared for.
The Emperor was not truly following ancient practice,
but rather emulating the actions of the Buddhist elder Xūdáduō.
3 On the *Wùzǐ* day,
a general amnesty was declared.

5 The Wèi 發d 15,000 soldiers from nearby commanderies
—nearby commanderies
meaning those surrounding the capital.
They were to escort the Ròurán Qíhán Ānànchuái (阿那⿰王褱) back to his country.
The Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, Zhāng Pǔhuì (張普惠), submitted a memorial,
arguing:
“The Rúurúu (蠕蠕) have long been a frontier menace.
This year, Heaven has sent them calamity and chaos,
tormenting their hearts.
This is probably to make them realize the joy of a righteous path,
so they may change their ways, prostrate themselves, and serve the Great Wèi.
Your Majesty should tranquilize the people and govern with humility to win over their hearts.
Ānànchuái (阿那⿰王褱) has submitted himself and surrendered his life;
it is appropriate to pacify him.
However, to instead trouble ourselves first,
raise an army within the capital region,
and send it to the desolate frontiers
to rescue a generations-old formidable enemy
and aid a villainous foe whom Heaven seeks to destroy,
your humble servant does not see the wisdom in this.
This is merely a frontier general’s greed for temporary merit,
without considering that weapons are instruments of ill omen,
which kings use only when absolutely necessary.”
(This draws on the meaning of Lǎozi’s words.)
“Your sagely benevolence has provided provisions,
and you have sent 15,000 men with Yáng Jūn (楊鈞) as their general.
To wish to settle the Rúurúu (蠕蠕)
by acting at an inopportune moment—
how can this succeed?
Should there be a calamitous defeat,
would Yáng Jūn’s (楊鈞) flesh
be sufficient to eat?”
(This uses the meaning of Sūn Shū’áo’s (孫叔敖) rejection of Wǔ Cān (伍參) in the Zǔozhuàn (左傳).)
“Not to consider the great plan for security and danger—
this is what makes your humble servant’s heart chill.
Moreover, regarding Ānànchuái’s (阿那⿰王褱) return,
what trust and righteousness has he betrayed?
As a lowly subject, I am not qualified to deliberate on this.
” (In the Hàn dynasty, all officials from the rank of Counselor (議郎) upwards could participate in major court deliberations.
The two Assistants of the Department of State Affairs (尚書二丞) at that time were not considered low in rank,
yet Zhāng Pǔhuì (張普惠) considered himself ‘lowly and not qualified to deliberate.’
This is probably because after the Cáo Wèi (曹魏) dynasty,
major court deliberations were restricted to officials of the ‘Eight Thrones’ (八坐) rank and above.
All documents still passed through the hands of the two Assistants of the Department of State Affairs (尚書二丞).)
“When Ānànchuái (阿那⿰王褱) took leave at the Western Hall,
an imperial edict bestowed upon him military equipment, clothing and blankets, various silks, grain, and livestock—
every item was generously provided.”
(Cǎi (采)
is the same as Cǎi (綵).
Chù (畜)
is pronounced xù.)
“When Ānànchuái (阿那⿰王褱) fled south,

Shìfà (示發) fled to Dìdòugān (地豆干).”
(The Wèishū (魏書) states: The kingdom of Dìdòugān (地豆干) is located over a thousand *lǐ* west of Shìwéi (室韋).)

“Since the Rúurúu (柔然) have already established a new ruler,

To go lightly and return empty-handed

Unless a large number of troops is added,
there will be no way to escort him back north.”
In the second month,
the Wèi (魏) sent Diéchūn Jùrén (牒云具仁),

As their conversations became more and more assertive,

Xī Kāngshēng (奚康shēng) also felt a subtle fear and unease.

2. In the third month,

Summer,
fourth month,

Wèi Kěgū attacked Huáishuò Garrison for a year,

Yáng Jūn sent Hèbá Shèng to Lín huáiwáng Yù to report the emergency.

"I am Hèbá Pòhú!"

Shèng met Yù in Yúnzhōng.
Kǎoyì says: Shèng's biography states:

According to the Hòuwèi Dìlǐ Zhì,
Yúnzhōng
was formerly called Shuòzhōu;

According to Wèi's initial capital at Píngchéng,

After Xiàochāng, the garrisons were changed to prefectures (zhōu),

Dù Yòu believed that Wèi's capital was Píngchéng,

He also said: After the move to Luò,
Shuòzhōu was established over three hundred lǐ north of the commandery.
He also said: In the early Hòuwèi,

north of the old city of Dìngxiāng.
If they are all said to be over three hundred lǐ north of the commandery,

Sòng Bái said: Shuòzhōu, Mǎyì Commandery,

In the Hòuwèi, it was within the imperial domain,

Shuòzhōu was established at the old city of Dìngxiāng, three hundred eighty lǐ north of the prefecture.
He also said: In the early Hòuwèi,
Yúnzhōng was the old city of Dìngxiāng.
Thus, Shuòzhōu and the early Hòuwèi's Yúnzhōng were one place.
This history (Tōngjiàn) later records that Huáishuò Garrison was renamed Shuòzhōu,
and Shuòzhōu was further renamed Yúnzhōu.
This is evidence of what the Wèi Zhì calls Yúnzhōng being formerly named Shuòzhōu.
If so, Huáishuò Garrison and Yúnzhōng are two different places.
Later,
Lǐ Chóng, after the defeat of Cuī Xiān at Báidào,
withdrew to Yúnzhōng,
and later withdrew from Yúnzhōng to Píngchéng.
The sequence of his retreats and distances can be seen,

Upon detailed examination,
the establishment of prefectures and commanderies throughout history
had confusing names,

"Huáishuò is besieged,

Jìn,

The Emperor said:

"This
indeed meets everyone's expectations."
Chóng said:
"I considered the six garrisons (liùzhèn) remote and desolate,

However, I am seventy years old,
and moreover, I am tired and ill.
I am unfit for military service,

The Emperor did not permit it.
Xiūyì
was the son of Tiāncì.
Tiāncì is mentioned in volume 133 under the 7th year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng of Sòng.
Your subject, Guāng, says: Lǐ Chóng's memorial

and to achieve victory without visible action.
Since Wèi Sùzōng could not utilize it,

he expressed no words of shame or apology,

How could such an unenlightened ruler
be consulted!
The Shī Jīng says:
"When hearing words, you respond;
When reciting words, you are as if drunk.
Not employing what is good,
You instead cause me to act perversely."
This is from the ode Sāngróu.
The commentary says: When hearing words from the street, he responds;
When seeing words from poems or books recited, he is profoundly asleep as if drunk,
unable to employ what is good,
but instead makes me perform rebellious acts.
