cí-qiū fān).
長 (zhǎng,
zhī-liǎng fān).
Once, during a hunt,
a tribesman shot a tiger
but accidentally hit his thigh.
Dàiqín pulled out the arrow,
and did not investigate further.
All his subordinates were touched and pleased.
He rose to the office of Sìzhōu Cìshǐ,
was granted the title of Liángjùn Gōng,
and died at over ninety years of age.
His son Xīnxīng succeeded him.
In Xīnxīng's time,
his livestock especially multiplied.
Cattle, sheep, camels, and horses,
separated by color into herds,
spread across the valleys,
innumerable.
Whenever Wèi launched an expedition,
Xīnxīng would always offer horses and provisions to assist the army.
Gāozǔ commended him.
When Xīnxīng grew old,
he requested to pass his title to his son Róng,
which the Wèi court permitted.
Róng was divinely astute and decisive,
and governed his troops with strict order.
At that time, armies were rising in all directions,
and Róng secretly harbored great ambitions.
He dispersed his livestock and assets,
recruited brave and fierce men,
and formed alliances with powerful heroes.
The matter of Ěrzhū Róng began here.
驍 (xiāo,
jiān-yáo fān).
At that time, Wèi established Shuòzhōu in Huáisuò Zhèn,
and also established Tàian Jùn.
Xiǎndù
was the elder brother of Xiǎnzhì.
15 On the day Wùxū,
Mòzhé Niànshēng dispatched his Dūdū Dòu Shuāng to attack Wèi's Pántóu Jùn.
Pántóu Jùn belonged to Dōngyìzhōu.
Wǔdài Zhì:
Xīngzhōu Chángjǔ Xiàn.
Wèi established Pántóu Jùn.
16 In the ninth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Chéng Jǐngjùn captured Wèi's Suīlíng.
On the day Wǔwǔ,
Zhào Jǐngyuè, the Cìshǐ of Běiyǎnzhōu, besieged Jīngshān.
Liáng's Běiyǎnzhōu was administered at Huáin.
Shuǐjīng Zhù says: Dìlǐ Zhì,
Píng'ā Xiàn has Dāngtú Shān.
The Huái River flows out to the left of Jīngshān,
and to the right of Dāngtú.
Wèi Shōu's Zhì states: Liáng's Běixúzhōu Pèijùn Yǐwú Xiàn has Dāngtú Shān and Jīngshān.
Today's Huáiyuǎn Jūn is squarely located at Jīngshān.
According to Shěn Yuē's Zhì,
all belong to the Mǎtóu Jùn area.
Wǔdài Zhì: Zhōnglí Jùn Túshān Xiàn,
the ancient Dāngtú.
Later Qí established Jīngshān Jùn.
On the night of Rénxū,
he broke through the gate and entered,
capturing its outer wall.
Chángsūn Zhì, the Wèi Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu, resisted him,
fighting nine battles in one day.
Cài Xiùchéng, of the rear army, lost his way and did not arrive,
so he withdrew his troops.
A separate commander attacked Wèi's Huáiyáng.
This was a separate commander sent by Liáng,
not part of Péi Suì's forces.
將 (jiàng,
jí-liàng fān);
same below.
Ānlè Wáng Jiàn rescued Huáiyáng.
Jiàn
was Quán's son.
17 Wèi's Xīdào Hángtái Yuán Xiūyì contracted a wind illness
and could not command the army.
On the day Rénshēn,
Wèi appointed Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè Qí Wáng Xiāo Bǎoyín as Xīdào Hángtái Dàdūdū,
to lead the various generals to suppress Mòzhé Niànshēng.
This laid the groundwork for Xiāo Bǎoyín's rebellion against Wèi in Guānzhōng.
Sòng Yǐng secretly sought aid from Tǔyùhún Wáng Fúliánchóu.
吐 (tǔ,
from tūn, entering tone).
谷 (gǔ,
sound yù).
Yú Pútí abandoned the city and fled;
he was pursued and beheaded.
The city residents Zhào Tiān'ān and others again nominated Sòng Yǐng as Cìshǐ.
18 Héjiān Wáng Chēn's army arrived at Xīxiáshí,
lifted the siege of Wōyáng,
and restored the Jīngshān garrison.
Wáng Shénniàn, Cìshǐ of Qīng and Jì zhōu, fought him
but was defeated by Chēn.
In winter,
tenth month,
on the day Wùyín,
Péi Suì and Yuán Shù attacked Wèi's Jiànlíng Chéng
and captured it.
On the day Xīnsì,
they captured Qūmù.
"Qūmù"
should be
"Qūshù."
Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Shù River passes east of the old city of Jiànlíng Xiàn,
and then south, west of Língshān.
Wèi built a great weir to block the water from flowing west.
At the confluence of two canals,
a city was established for defense,
called Qūshù Shù.
沭 (shù,
shí-yù fān).
19 Wèi's Yíngzhōu city residents Liú Āndìng and Jiù Déxīng
Wèishū Guānshì Zhì: The Túlài Shì changed to Jiù Shì,
one of the western clans.
seized the city and rebelled.
City resident Wáng È'ér beheaded Āndìng and surrendered.
Déxīng fled east
and proclaimed himself King of Yān.
Hú Chēn (胡琛) sent his general Sùqín Míngdá (宿勤明達) to raid Bīn (豳), Xià (夏), and Běihuá (北華) prefectures.
In the fifteenth year of Tài-hé (太和) of Emperor Gāo-zǔ (高祖) of the Wèi (魏) dynasty,
Dōng-Qín-zhōu (東秦州) was established in Xìngchéng (杏城),
later renamed Běihuá-zhōu (北華州).
It governed Zhōngbù (中部) and Fúchéng (敷城),
a total of two commanderies.
Sùqín (宿勤)
is a Hú (胡) compound surname.
Xià (夏)
is pronounced "hù yǎ fān".
Huá (華)
is pronounced "hù huà fān".
(The Wèi court) dispatched Dūdū (都督) Běihǎi-wáng Hào (北海王顥) to lead the generals to suppress them.
Hào (顥)
was the son of Xiáng (詳).
Xiáng (詳) incurred displeasure and is mentioned in volume 145, Tiān-jiān (天監) third year.
Shuài (帥)
is read as "lǜ".
On the day Jiǎ-shēn (甲申),
Péng Bǎosūn (彭寶孫) captured Tánqiū (檀丘).
On the day Xīn-mǎo (辛卯),
Péi Suì (裴邃) captured Díchéng (狄城);
the Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) states: the Fěi (肥) River flows from Díqiū (荻丘), past the old city of Chéngdé (成德) county in Hàn (漢)'s Jiǔjiāng (九江) commandery to its west.
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) renamed it Píng’ā (平阿);
it then flows north into Sháopí (芍陂).
On the day Bǐng-shēn (丙申)
(Péi Suì) again captured Pìchéng (甓城),
and advanced to camp at Líjiāng (黎漿).
On the day Rén-yín (壬寅),
Wèi (魏)'s Dōnghǎi (東海) administrator Wéi Jìngxīn (韋敬欣) surrendered with Sìwú (司吾) city.
This was the old city of Sìwú (司吾) county in Hàn (漢)'s Dōnghǎi (東海) commandery.
On the day Jiǎ-chén (甲辰),
(Péi Suì) also captured Qínxū (秦墟),
and many Wèi (魏) defending generals abandoned their cities and fled.
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) states: the Luò (洛) River flows past the old city of Qǔyáng (曲陽) county in Hàn (漢)'s Huáinán (淮南) commandery to its east.
Yìng Shào (應劭) said: the county is on the sunny side of the bend in the Huái (淮) River.
The Luò (洛) River then passes north through Qínxū (秦墟),
flows down into the Huái (淮),
and is called Luòkǒu (洛口).
The Wèi Shōu Zhì (魏收志) states: Qǔyáng (曲陽) county belonged to Běipèi (北沛) commandery of Huòzhōu (霍州).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: Qǔyáng (曲陽) county was later abolished and merged into Zhōnglí (鍾離) and Dìngyuǎn (定遠) counties.
Wèi (魏) sent Huángmén-shìláng (黃門侍郎) Lú Tóng (盧同) with a staff of authority to Yíngzhōu (營州) to express comfort,
where Jiù Déxīng (就德興) had surrendered but then revolted again.
An edict appointed Lú Tóng (盧同) as Yōuzhōu (幽州) Cìshǐ (刺史) and concurrently Shàngshū-xíngtái (尚書行臺).
Lú Tóng (盧同) was repeatedly defeated by Jiù Déxīng (就德興) and returned.
The Hú (胡) of Shuòfāng (朔方) in Wèi (魏) revolted,
besieging Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Xiàzhōu (夏州).
Food in the city was exhausted, and they boiled horse hides to eat,
but the populace showed no disloyalty.
Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍) wanted to go out himself to seek provisions,
leaving his son Yánbó (延伯) to guard Tǒngwàn (統萬).
His generals and subordinates all said:
"Now the four directions are in revolt,
provisions are exhausted, and aid is cut off.
It would be better for father and son to leave together."
Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍) wept and said:
"Our family has for generations been indebted to the national grace.
I ought to dedicate my life to this city.
But there is no food to sustain the defense,
so I wish to go to Dōngzhōu (東州)
to procure several months' worth of food for you gentlemen.
If by good fortune I obtain it,
our preservation is assured."
So he led the weak to Dōng-xiàzhōu (東夏州) to transport grain.
Yánbó (延伯) and the generals and subordinates wept as they sent him off.
After Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍) had traveled for several days,
the Hú (胡) leader Cáo Āgèbá (曹阿各拔) ambushed and captured him.
Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍) secretly sent someone with a letter,
instructing those in the city to exert themselves and hold fast.
The entire city was anxious and afraid.
Yánbó (延伯) exhorted them, saying:
"My father's fate is uncertain,
and my heart is consumed with anxiety.
However,
I am obeying orders to defend the city, and the task is weighty,
so I dare not sacrifice public duty for private feelings.
I hope you gentlemen understand this sentiment."
Thereupon, the multitude was moved by his righteousness,
and all became greatly spirited.
Although Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍) was captured,
the Hú (胡) people always treated him with the respect due to an elder.
Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍) explained the advantages and disadvantages,
urging Cáo Āgèbá (曹阿各拔) to surrender.
Coincidentally, Cáo Āgèbá (曹阿各拔) died,
and his younger brother Sāngshēng (桑生) eventually led his followers to surrender with Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍).
Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍) met Xíngtái (行臺) Běihǎi-wáng Hào (北海王顥),
and fully explained the feasibility of destroying the various rebels.
Hào (顥) supplied Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍) with troops,
ordering him to be the vanguard.
At this time, the entire territory of Dōng-xiàzhōu (東夏州) had revolted,
with strongholds established everywhere.
Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍) fought his way forward,
in ninety days,
engaging in dozens of battles.
He then pacified Dōng-xiàzhōu (東夏州),
collected taxes in grain to supply Tǒngwàn (統萬),
and thus the two Xià (夏) prefectures were preserved.
Yuán Zǐyōng (源子雍)
was the son of Huái (懷).
History states that all the sons of the Yuán (源) clan had talent,
but Heaven sent chaos and disorder,
and ultimately they could not save the Wèi (魏) dynasty from its decline.
Wèi (魏)'s Guǎngyáng-wáng Shēn (廣陽王深) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Now the six garrisons have all revolted,
and the two tribes of Gāochē (高車) have also joined them.
The Gāochē (高車), from Āfúzhìluó (阿伏至羅) to Qióngqí (窮奇), are divided into two tribes,
namely the Eastern and Western Dìlè (敕勒).
There is certainly no chance of victory.
It would be better to select and train elite soldiers to guard the various key points of Héngzhōu (恆州).
'Various key points'
refers to strategic locations.
Héng (恆)
is pronounced "hù dēng fān".
So (Guǎngyáng-wáng Shēn) and Lǐ Chóng (李崇) led their troops back to Píngchéng (平城).
Lǐ Chóng (李崇) said to his generals:
"Yúnzhōng (雲中)
is a crucial pass on the Bái (白) Road.
From this perspective,
Wèi (魏)'s Yúnzhōng (雲中),
Hàn (漢)'s Shèngyuè (盛樂) county,
and Táng (唐)'s Zhènwǔ-jūn Jiédùshǐ (振武軍節度使) headquarters
were all on the sunny side of Yúnshān (雲山).
If this place is not secure,
then Bìng (幷) and Sì (肆) will be in danger.
One person should be left to guard it.
Who is suitable?"
The multitude nominated Fèi Mù (費穆),
so Lǐ Chóng (李崇) requested that Fèi Mù (費穆) be made Shuòzhōu (朔州) Cìshǐ (刺史).
'Requested'
means to submit a memorial.
At that time, Yúnzhōng (雲中) had already been changed to Yúnzhōu (雲州).
"Shuò" (朔)
should be
"Yún" (雲).
Hèbá Dùbá (賀拔度拔) and his son, and Wǔchuān (武川)'s Yǔwén Gōng (宇文肱) gathered local heroes and eminent figures,
together attacked Wèi Kěgū (衞可孤),
and killed him. Hèbá Dùbá (賀拔度拔) soon died in battle with the Tiělè (鐵勒).
Yǔwén Gōng (宇文肱)
was the great-great-grandson of Yìdòuguī (逸豆歸).
Yǔwén Gōng (宇文肱)
was the father of Yǔwén Tài (宇文泰).
Yìdòuguī (逸豆歸)
was defeated by Mùróng Huàng (慕容皝) in the second year of Jiàn-yuán (建元) of Emperor Kāng (康) of Jìn (晉).
Lǐ Chóng (李崇) appointed Guózǐ-bóshì (國子博士) Zǔ Yíng (祖瑩) as Chángshǐ (長史).
Guǎngyáng-wáng Shēn (廣陽王深) memorialized that Zǔ Yíng (祖瑩) had fraudulently inflated the number of enemy heads taken
and embezzled military funds. Zǔ Yíng (祖瑩) was consequently dismissed from office.
Lǐ Chóng (李崇) was also stripped of his office and title and recalled.
Guǎngyáng-wáng Shēn (廣陽王深) then solely controlled military and political affairs.
This sets the stage for Guǎngyáng-wáng Shēn (廣陽王深) to be later troubled internally by slander and externally by rebels.
Mòzhé Tiānshēng (莫折天生) advanced to attack Wèi (魏)'s Qízhōu (岐州).
In the eleventh month, on the day Wù-shēn (戊申),
(he) captured it,
seizing Dūdū (都督) Yuán Zhì (元志) and Cìshǐ (刺史) Péi Fēnzhī (裴芬之),
and sending them to Mòzhé Niànshēng (莫折念生), who killed them.
Mòzhé Niànshēng (莫折念生) then sent Bǔ Hú (卜胡) and others to raid Jīngzhōu (涇州),
defeating Guānglù-dàfū (光祿大夫) Xuē Luán (薛巒) east of Píngliáng (平涼).
Wèi (魏) established Píngliáng (平涼) commandery,
with its seat in Qúnyīn (鶉陰) county,
where Píngliáng (平涼) city was located.
'Defeated' (敗)
is pronounced "bǔ mài fān".
(Xuē Luán) was the grandson of Āndū (安都).
In the early years of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Sòng (宋),
Xuē Āndū (薛安都) surrendered to Wèi (魏).
On the day Bǐng-chén (丙辰), Péng Bǎosūn (彭寶孫) captured Wèi (魏)'s Dōngguǎn (東莞).
On the day Rén-xū (壬戌),
Péi Suì (裴邃) attacked Ānchéng (安城) in Shòuyáng (壽陽).
The Wèi Shōu Zhì (魏收志) states:
Liáng (梁) established Xīnxīng (新興) commandery,
with its seat in Ānchéng (安城) county.
On the day Bǐng-yín (丙寅)
Mǎtóu (馬頭) and Ānchéng (安城) both surrendered.
The people of Gāopíng (高平) attacked and killed Bǔ Hú (卜胡),
and together welcomed Hú Chēn (胡琛).
29 The Wèi appointed Yáng Yù, Huangmén Shìláng, to concurrently serve as Shìzhōng,
holding the jié to supervise Běihǎi Wáng Yuán Hào’s army,
to rescue Bīnzhoū.
The siege of Bīnzhoū was lifted.
The Shǔ bandits Zhāng Yìnglóng and Jiāng Shéndá attacked Yōngzhoū.
These Shǔ bandits
were Shǔ people who had been relocated to Guānzhōng,
and who took advantage of the Wèi’s chaos to rise up as brigands,
hence they were called Shǔ bandits.
Later, when Ěrzhū Tiānguāng campaigned westward,
the Shǔ bandits blocked the roads;
they were all his partisans.
Yōng,
read like ‘yòng’.
In one day and one night,
nine dispatches were exchanged.
Dūdū Lǐ Shūréng hesitated and did not go.
Yù said:
“Cháng’ān
is the fundamental base of Guānzhōng.
If Cháng’ān cannot be defended,
the main army will naturally scatter like瓦,
what good is it to remain here?”
So he and Shūréng advanced and attacked them,
decapitating Shéndá,
and the remaining bandits scattered.
30 In the twelfth month,
on the day wùyín,
Jīngshān of Wèi surrendered.
31 On the day rénchén,
the Wèi appointed Jīngzhào Wáng Jì as Tàishī and Dàjiāngjūn,
to supervise all the western armies to suppress Mòzhé Niànsheng.
32 On the day yǐsì,
Wǔyǒng Jiāngjūn Lǐ Guóxìng attacked Píngjìng Guān of Wèi.
On the day xīncǎo,
Xìnwēi Zhǎngshǐ Yáng Gān attacked Wǔyáng Guān.
On the day rényín,
Xiàn Guān was attacked.
These were the three passes of Yìyáng.
Xiàn,
read like ‘diǎn’.
Guóxìng advanced to besiege Yǐngzhoū.
Péi Xún, the Wèi Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhoū, and the tribal chief Tián Pǔtè, the Xīyǐngzhoū Cìshǐ, cooperated to resist them.
The Wèi Yǐngzhoū was administered from Yìyáng,
and Xīyǐngzhoū must have been west of Yìyáng,
in barbarian territory.
Qíu,
read like ‘qiū’.
Wèi reinforcements arrived,
and Guóxìng withdrew.
Xún
was Jùn’s grandson.
See Péi Jùn in Volume 124, Yuánjiā 22nd year of Sòng Wéndì.
33 The various Hú tribes of Fénzhoū of Wèi rebelled.
Wèi Xiàowén Dì established Fénzhoū in Tàihé 12th year,
administering from Púzǐ,
overseeing Xīhé, Tǔjīng, Wǔchéng, and Dìngyáng,
a total of four commanderies.
Troops were dispatched to suppress them.
34 Wèi Wèi Zǐjiàn recruited and persuaded the various Dī tribes of Nánqín,
who gradually surrendered and submitted.
He then recovered six commanderies and twelve garrisons,
and decapitated
Hán Zǔxiāng.
The Wèi appointed Zǐjiàn to concurrently serve as Shàngshū,
as Xíngtái,
with his Cìshǐ position unchanged.
Cìshǐ
refers to Zǐjiàn’s original position as Dōngyìzhoū Cìshǐ.
The Wèi established Liángzhoū in Nánzhèng,
Bāzhoū in Hán Bāxī Jùn,
Yìzhoū in Jìnshòu Jùn,
Dōngyìzhoū in Wǔxīng Jùn,
Qínzhoū in Shàngguī,
and Nánqínzhoū in Chóuchí.
35 Mòzhé Niànsheng sent troops to attack Liángzhoū.
The city residents, led by Zhào Tiān’ān, again seized the Cìshǐ to respond to him.
36 That year,
Shìzhōng and Tàizǐ Zhānshì Zhōu Shě was dismissed for an offense.
Sànqí Chángshì Zhū Yì of Qiántáng replaced him in managing confidential matters.
He oversaw military planning,
changes in regional governors,
and imperial ceremonies and edicts.
Zhū Yì was skilled in literature and classical studies,
possessed many talents,
and was energetic and eloquent.
The emperor relied on him for these qualities.
He set the stage for Zhū Yì’s disruption of Liáng.
Sàn,
read like ‘dàn’.
Qí,
read like ‘jì’.
Yì,
read like ‘yì’.
Hào,
read like ‘hào’.
Cháo,
read like ‘zhāo’.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day bǐngwǔ,
Yōngzhoū Cìshǐ Jìn’ān Wáng Gāng sent Ānběi Zhǎngshǐ Liǔ Hún to defeat Wèi Nánxiāng Jùn.
Sīmǎ Dǒng Dāngmén defeated Wèi Jìn Chéng.
On the day gēngxū,
he further defeated the two cities of Mǎquān and Diāoyáng.
2 On the day xīnhài,
the emperor performed sacrifices at the southern suburb,
and granted a general amnesty.
3 Wèi Xúzhoū Cìshǐ Yuán Fǎsēng,
who had always been close to Yuán Chā,
seeing Chā’s arrogance and indulgence,
feared that disaster would befall him,
and thus plotted rebellion.
The Wèi sent Zhōngshū Shèláng Zhāng Wénbó to Péngchéng.
Fǎsēng said to him:
“I wish to leave danger and seek safety with you.
Can you follow me?”
Wénbó replied:
“I would rather die and see the pines and cypresses of Wénlíng.”
Wénlíng
refers to the tomb of Xiàowén Dì.
Fǎsēng killed him.
On the day gēngshēn,
Fǎsēng killed Xíngtái Gāo Liàng,
and proclaimed himself emperor.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Fǎsēng’s biography writes
“Gāo Mó.”
Now we follow the *Wèi Dì Jì*.
Also, the *Wèi Jì* says
“proclaimed himself King of Sòng,”
Fǎsēng’s biography and the *Běi Shǐ* both say
“proclaimed the imperial title,”
and the *Liáng Shū* Fǎsēng’s biography says
“proclaimed himself emperor.”
Upon examination, Fǎsēng installed his sons as kings,
so he must have proclaimed himself emperor.
Now we follow the *Liáng Shū*.
He installed his sons as kings.
The Wèi dispatched troops to attack him,
so Fǎsēng sent his son Jǐngzhòng to surrender.
Āndōng Zhǎngshǐ Yuán Xiǎnhé
was Lì’s son.
See Yuán Lì in Volume 146, Tiānjiān 5th year.
Fǎsēng captured him,
held his hand,
and ordered him to sit together.
Xiǎnhé refused,
saying:
“Both you and I come from the imperial family.
Yuán Fǎsēng was the great-grandson of Yángpíng Wáng Xī.
Xī

The Wèi dynasty appointed Cuī Yánbó, the Inspector of Qízhōu, as General Who Conquers the West and Grand Military Governor of the Western Route,

By day, he conversed and jested as usual;

He was so deeply suspicious that he was not his father's son,

From then on, he always harbored dissenting ambitions,

Zōng had great courage and strength,

and his princely title was advanced to Dùnqīu Wáng.
Chángsūn Zhì, Inspector of Yǒngzhōu, was made General of Agile Cavalry and Grand Minister with Ceremonial Privileges Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers,
and granted the title of Féngyì Wáng.
Yuán Chén, Palace Minister of Works, was made Shàngshū Yòu Púshè,
and granted the title of Wèijùn Wáng.
Gōng, Prince of Guǎnglíng and Grand Master of Bright Radiance with Gold and Purple, was granted additional ceremonial privileges equal to the Three Ducal Ministers.
The number of others who rose from humble origins to sudden wealth
was countless.
Yánshí
was Chōng's son.
Lǐ Chōng was influential during the times of Wénmíng and Xiàowén.
Shèng
is pronounced shēng.
He gained a super-promotion.
Xú Hè's younger brother Xiàn Bó was the Administrator of Běihǎi,
and Jì Chǎn was the Chief Clerk of Qīngzhōu.
Hè sent someone to inform them,
and they all fled with their families,
joining Hè in escaping to Tàishān.
Tàishān Commandery belonged to Yǎnzhōu,
hence it is called "fleeing east to Yǎnzhōu."
He was killed by his subordinates.
On the Dīngwèi day,
an edict ordered the lifting of martial law both inside and outside the capital.
10 Yuán Xiǎndá, Inspector of Wèi's Yǐngzhōu, requested to surrender.
An edict ordered Yuán Shù, Inspector of Yǐngzhōu, to welcome him.
Wèi conquered Yìyáng,
and made Liáng's Sīzhōu into Yǐngzhōu.
Liáng's Yǐngzhōu was governed from Jiāngxià Commandery.
He then remained to garrison it.
Wèi's Yǐngzhōu was renamed Běisīzhōu,
with Kuí as its Inspector,
concurrently overseeing Sīzhōu.
In the early Liáng dynasty,
after Yìyáng fell,
Sīzhōu was provisionally established south of the passes,
in the area of present-day Huángpí County, Huángzhōu.
After Yìyáng was recovered,
it was then designated Běisīzhōu.
They pressed upon Xīncài;
Xiàhóu Dǎn, Inspector of Yùzhōu, besieged Nándùn,
and attacked Chén and Xiàng.
Yuán Zǐgōng, Wèi's Xíngtái, resisted them.
11 On the Gēngxū day,
Wèi granted Ěrzhū Róng's son Chāluó the title of Prince of Liángjùn.
12 Ròurán's Dòubīng Kèhán frequently paid tribute to Wèi,
Kè
follows the *kān* entering tone.
Hán
is pronounced Hán.
Shù
is pronounced suǒ jiǎo fān.
His memorial did not refer to himself as a subject.
13 When Wèi Rǔnánwáng Yuè and Dōngdào Xíngtái Línhuáiwáng Yù heard of the chaos at Húyīn,
they both came to defect.
Earlier,
all Wèi defectors had referred to Wèi officials as "false"
. Yù alone, in his memorial, referred to himself as "Wèi Línhuáiwáng";
the Emperor, appreciating his sincerity and simplicity,
did not blame him.
Wèi Běihǎiwáng Hào was on his way to Xiāngzhōu,
and when he reached Jíqùn,
he heard of Gě Róng's southern invasion and Ěrzhū Róng's tyrannical behavior.
Secretly, he devised a plan for his own safety,
delaying his advance;
he appointed his maternal uncle, Yīnzhōu Cìshǐ Fàn Zūn, to act as the governor of Xiāngzhōu,
replacing the former governor Lǐ Shén, and to defend Yè Xíngtái.
Zhēn Mì knew that Hào had other intentions,
so he led his followers to depose Zūn,
and again appointed Lǐ Shén to manage the affairs of the province,
sending troops to welcome Hào,
and at the same time observe his movements.
When Hào heard of this,
he led his attendants and came to defect.
This prepares the ground for Hào's return north later.
"Shuài"
is read as "shuài."
He was Zhēn Chēn's paternal cousin.
Zhēn Chēn served Wèi Xuānwǔdì.
"Cóng"
is pronounced "cái yòng."
The seat of Wèi Běiqīngzhōu was Dōngyáng,
very far from the Liáng border.
The "Wǔdài Zhì" records: Dōnghǎijùn,
Liáng established Nán and Běi Èrqīngzhōujùn,
administering Huáirén Xiàn.
It also notes: Liáng established Nán and Běi Èrqīngzhōu.
The implication is that Yuán Shìjùn defected with the territory of Huáirén.
The "Zhì" also says: Chūnlíngjùn,
the Later Wèi established Nánjīngzhōu.
"Jiàng"
is pronounced "hù jiāng."
14 In the fifth month,
on the Dīngsì day, the first day of the month,
Wèi bestowed upon Ěrzhū Róng the title of Běidào Dàxíngtái.
Shàngshū Yòupúshè Yuán Luó was appointed Dōngdào Dàshǐ,
with Guānglùxūn Yuán Xīn as his deputy,
to tour the regions, dismiss and promote officials,
with prior action and subsequent report.
Xīn
was Yǔ's son.
Yǔ
was Emperor Xiàowén's younger brother,
enfeoffed as Guǎnglíngwáng.
15 Ěrzhū Róng entered to meet the Wèi Emperor in the Míngguāng Diàn,
deeply apologizing for the events at Héqiáo,
swearing that he would never again harbor disloyal intentions.
The Emperor rose to stop him,
and in turn swore an oath to Róng,
saying that he harbored no doubts.
Róng was pleased,
then requested wine and drank it,
becoming thoroughly drunk;
the Emperor wanted to execute him,
but his attendants earnestly remonstrated,
so he stopped,
and immediately went by sedan chair to the residence of the Zhōngchángshì.
Róng did not awaken until midnight,
and consequently remained sleepless until dawn;
from then on, he no longer lodged within the Forbidden Palace.
Róng's daughter had previously been Sùzōng's concubine.
Róng wanted Jìngzōng to establish her as Empress,
but the Emperor hesitated, undecided.
Huángmén Shìláng Zǔ Yíng said:
"In the past, when Wéngōng was in Qín,
Huái Yíng entered to serve;
there are instances where things go against custom but align with righteousness.
The Zuǒzhuàn states: Jìn Crown Prince Yǔ was held hostage in Qín,
and the Count of Qín gave him his daughter in marriage.
Prince Yǔ escaped back home,
and Gōngzǐ Chóng'ěr entered Qín,
where the Count of Qín gave him five daughters,
with Huái Yíng among them.
Qín belonged to the Yíng clan;
Yǔ's posthumous title was Huáigōng,
hence Huái Yíng.
Hàn Confucians considered acting against principle but in accord with reason to be 'expediency,'
and Zǔ Yíng based his argument on this.
'Pín'
is pronounced 'pí bīn.'
The Emperor then followed his advice,
and Róng was very pleased.
Ěrzhū Róng's demeanor was light and frivolous,
and he enjoyed galloping and archery.
Whenever he entered court,
he did nothing else but play at mounting and dismounting his horse.
At banquets and archery contests in the Xīlín Yuán,
he always requested the Empress to come out and watch,
and also summoned the kings, dukes, and princesses to be in the same hall.
Whenever the Emperor hit the target,
he would spontaneously rise, dance, and shout,
and all the generals, ministers, and high officials would circle around,
even the princesses could not avoid following suit and raising their sleeves.
When the wine ran high and their ears were hot,
he would certainly sit cross-legged and sing barbarian songs;
"Kuāngzuò"
means to sit properly.
"Lǔgē"
means Hu songs.
He would join hands with his attendants, stamp their feet, and sing the Huíbō Yuè as they exited.
This is what is called "tàgē."
Huíbō Yuè
is the name of a tune.
"Yuè"
is pronounced "luò."
His moods were unstable;
swords, spears, bows, and arrows
were never out of his hand.
Whenever he felt anger or dislike,
he would strike or shoot,
and his attendants were constantly in fear of death.
Once, he saw a shāmí riding a horse double,
A "shāmí"
is one who has renounced worldly life to become a monk,
received ordination but not yet the full precepts.
"Riding double"
means two people riding one horse together.
"Zhòng"
is pronounced "zhí lóng."
When the horse became exhausted and could no longer move,
he made the bystanders strike each other's heads,
and did not stop until they were dead.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
Róng returned to Jìnyáng,
and the Emperor saw him off at Mángyīn.
Mángyīn
is the north side of Mount Máng.
Tiānmù was appointed Shìzhōng, Lù Shàngshūshì, Jīngqí Dàdūdū, and concurrently Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Sānggān Zhū Ruì, Xíngtái Lángzhōng, was appointed Huángmén Shìláng and concurrently Zhōngshū Shèrén.
All crucial court positions
were filled by his trusted confidants.
16 On the Bǐngyín day,
the Wèi Emperor decreed:
"Since Xiàochāng,
all those who have been wronged or suppressed and have no one to complain to,
shall gather at the east gate of Huálín,
and I will personally address their cases."
At that time, after the chaos of war,
the granaries were empty.
An edict was issued:
"Those who contribute eight thousand *shí* of grain shall be granted the rank of Sǎnhóu.
This is a reward for officials who contribute grain.
According to the Wèi system,
Sǎnhóu is one rank below Kāiguóhóu.
'Sǎn'
is pronounced 'xī dàn.'
Shāmí are to be granted the position of Tǒng in their prefecture and Wéinà in their commandery or county."
Wéinà
each managed the monks in their respective commanderies and counties.
When Ěrzhū Róng hastened to Luòyáng,
he sent his Dūdū Fán Zǐhú to take Tángzhōu.
Tángzhōu Cìshǐ Cuī Yuánzhēn and Xíngtái Lì Yùn resisted the attack
and did not yield.
On the Yǐhài day,
Zǐhú captured Píngyáng,
executing Yuánzhēn and Yùn.
Yuánzhēn
was Tǐng's paternal cousin.
17 General Cáo Yìzōng besieged Wèi Jīngzhōu,
damming the water to flood the city,
but it did not submerge by several planks.
At that time, Wèi was beset by many difficulties
and could not send aid.
Supplies within the city were exhausted,
so Cìshǐ Wáng Pí cooked porridge and distributed it equally among the officers and soldiers for food.
Whenever he went out to battle,
he did not wear armor,
but looked up to the sky and shouted loudly:
"Jīngzhōu city
was established by Emperor Xiàowén.
Wèi Xiàowéndì established Jīngzhōu in Rángchéng during the Tàihé period.
Let an arrow strike Wáng Pí's forehead;
otherwise,
Wáng Pí will surely defeat the rebels!"
This lasted for three years,
with many battles fought before and after,
yet he was not wounded.
On the Guǐwèi day,
Wèi appointed Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Fèi Mù as Dūdū Nánzhēng Zhūjūnshì,
leading troops to relieve the city.
18 When Wèi Línhuáiwáng Yù heard that the Wèi Emperor had stabilized his position,
he requested to return, citing his elderly mother,
his plea being earnest and sincere.
The Emperor regretted losing his talent but could not refuse.
In the sixth month,
on the Dīnghài day,
he sent Yù back.
Wèi appointed Yù as Shìzhōng, Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn,
and bestowed upon him the title Yídóng Sānsī.
19 Wèi yuánwài sànqí chángshì Gāo Gān,
was the paternal cousin's son of Yòuzhī.
Gāo Yòu
was Yǔnzhī's paternal grand-cousin.
"Cóng"
is pronounced "cái yòng" (cái yòng fān).
Gāo Gān had a long-standing relationship with the Wèi emperor.
When Ěrzhū Róng was advancing towards Luòyáng,

Hearing of the chaos at Héyīn,

and repeatedly defeated the provincial armies.

Áo Cáo resumed looting and plundering.
Ěrzhū Róng enticed and captured him,
and he was detained with Xuē Xiūyì in Jìnyáng.
Xuē Xiūyì, as the Longmén Zhènjiāng,
had sided with Xiāo Bǎoyín.
After surrendering, he became duplicitous,
and was thus also detained.
"Yòu"
is pronounced "yǒu" (yīn yǒu).
The character was used for names.
Áo Cáo's father, seeing his son's imposing and arrogant manner (ángzáng áocáo),
therefore made it his courtesy name.
20 Gě Róng's army was short of food,
so he dispatched his pùyè Rèn Bāo to lead troops south to plunder as far as Qìnshuǐ.
Qìnshuǐ County,
since the Hàn dynasty, had belonged to Hénèi Commandery.
"Rèn"
is pronounced "rén" (yīn rén).
"Qìn"
is pronounced "qiān jìn" (qiān jìn fān).
Zōngzhèng Zhēnsūn and others were ordered to attack him.
Previously, Xíng Gǎo of Hékān, former zhǔbù of the Yōuzhōu Píngběi Fǔ, led over 100,000 displaced households from north of the Yellow River in rebellion in Běihǎi, Qīngzhōu.
He declared himself Hán Wáng
and changed the reign title to Tiāntǒǒng.
On the day Wùshēn,
Wèi appointed Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn Lǐ Shūrén as Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī,
leading troops to suppress him.
On the day Xīnhài,
the Wèi emperor decreed:
"I shall personally command the six armies (liù róng).
"Róng"
means "military."
"Liù róng"
is synonymous with "liù jūn."
Dàjiāngjūn Ěrzhū Róng shall be the Left Army,
Shàngdǎng Wáng Tiānmù the Front Army,
Sītú Yáng Chūn the Right Army,
and Sīkōng Mù Shào the Rear Army."

21 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Yǐchǒu,
Wèi added the title Zhùguó Dàjiāngjūn and Lù Shàngshūshì to Ěrzhū Róng.
Wèi first established the title Zhùguó Dàjiāngjūn,
and Zhǎngsūn Sōng was given this title as a founding meritorious official.
22 On the day Rénzǐ,
Wèi subjects from Guāngzhōu led by Liú Jǔ gathered a multitude and rebelled in Púyáng,
proclaiming himself Huángwǔ Dàjiāngjūn.
23 In this month,
Wànqí Chǒunú declared himself Tiānzǐ
and established various officials.
At this time, the kingdom of Bōsī presented a shīzi (lion) to Wèi.
The capital of Bōsī was Sùlì Chéng,
west of Niǔmì,
and it was the ancient Tiáozhī Guó;
it was 24,228 lǐ from the capital of Dài.
He changed the reign title to Shénshòu.
24 Wèi Tàishān Tàishǒu Yáng Kǎn,

constantly harbored the aspiration to return south.
Xú Hé went to seek refuge with him,
and consequently persuaded Kǎn to raise an army;
Kǎn agreed.
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Dūn,
Kǎn's paternal cousin,
secretly learned of this
and held the prefecture to resist Kǎn.
In the eighth month,
Kǎn led his troops to attack Dūn,
but failed.
The Wèi Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ administered Xiáqiū,
and the Tàishān Tàishǒu administered Bó.
[Yáng Kǎn] then sent an envoy to surrender.
An imperial edict ordered Guǎngjìn Xiànhóu Tàishān Yáng Yārén and others to lead troops to receive him.
According to Shěn Yuē's Zhì: Póyáng Commandery had Guǎngjìn County,
originally established by Wú as Guǎngchāng County;
in the first year of Tàikāng during the reign of Jìn Wǔdì,
its name was changed to Guǎngjìn.
Kǎn executed the envoy and refused to accept the surrender.
Jiāngjūn Wáng Biàn invaded Wèi Xúzhōu.
The people of Fān Commandery, led by Xù Língzhēn, gathered 10,000 men and attacked Fān Commandery in response to Liáng.
Wèi Xúzhōu was administered in Péngchéng,
and governed Péngchéng, Nányángpíng, Fān, Pèi, Lánlíng, Běijìyīn, and Dàng Commanderies.
Fān County,
in the Hàn and Jìn dynasties, belonged to Lǔ Guó.
In the third year of Xiàochāng during the Wèi dynasty, Fān Commandery was established,
administered in Fānchéng.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì: Téng County, Xúzhōu,
was formerly called Fān,
and Fān Commandery was established there;
in the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng during the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Téng Commandery,
and shortly thereafter the commandery was abolished and became a county.
"Fān"
is pronounced "pí" (yīn pí),
and also "fān" (yòu yīn fān).
[Xù Língzhēn] was beheaded,
and Wáng Biàn withdrew.
25 On the day Jiǎchén,
Wèi Dàdūdū Zōngzhèng Zhēnsūn attacked Liú Jǔ in Púyáng
and annihilated him.
26 Gě Róng 葛榮 led his troops to besiege Yè 鄴.
His multitude numbered a million,
and his roving forces had already crossed Jí Jùn 汲郡.
Jí Jùn 汲郡
was Wèi Zhōu 衞州 in the Suí 隋 and Táng 唐 dynasties.
Ěrzhū Róng 爾朱榮 memorialized, requesting to attack him.
In the ninth month,
Ěrzhū Róng 爾朱榮 summoned his nephew, the governor of Sì Zhōu 肆州, Tiānguāng 天光, to remain and garrison Jìnyáng 晉陽,
saying:
"Where I cannot personally reach,
no one but you can satisfy my wishes."
He personally led seven thousand elite cavalry,
each horse having a spare.
Wèi Shōu's 魏收 *Wèi Shū* 魏書 says: he led seventy thousand cavalry.
帥 *shuài*
is read *lǜ* 率.
騎 *jì*
is read *qí jì fān* 奇寄翻.
He marched east out of Fúkǒu 滏口,
with Hóu Jǐng 侯景 as his vanguard.
Gě Róng 葛榮 had been a bandit for a long time.
In the seventh year of Liáng Pǔtōng 梁普通 [526 CE],
Gě Róng 葛róng acquired the forces of Xiānyú Xiūlǐ 鮮于脩禮,
and plundered Héběi 河北.
Ěrzhū Róng's 爾朱榮 forces were no match in number,
and commentators believed there was no chance of victory.
When Gě Róng 葛榮 heard this,
joy showed on his face.
He ordered his troops, saying:
"This one is easy to deal with!
All of you prepare long ropes;
when he arrives, just tie him up."
From Yè 鄴 northward,
his formations stretched for dozens of *lǐ* 里,
advancing like an open winnowing basket.
It was like the opening of a winnowing basket.
陳 *chén*
is read *zhèn* 陣.
Ěrzhū Róng 爾朱榮 deployed a surprise force,
dividing three or more supervising generals into one group.
Each group had several hundred cavalry.
He ordered them to raise dust and beat drums wherever they were,
to make the bandits unable to gauge their numbers.
Moreover, when men and horses fought in close quarters,
swords were inferior to clubs.
He ordered his soldiers to carry one sleeve-club,
placed at the side of their horses.
When it came to battle, considering the hindrance to pursuit,
he did not allow beheading for merit.
"Beheading for merit"
means beheading to count military achievements.
He divided and commanded the brave and strong to charge in all directions.
His commands were strict and clear,
and the warriors fought with unified spirit.
Ěrzhū Róng 爾朱榮 personally plunged into the enemy formation,
emerging from behind the bandits.
They attacked from both front and rear,
thoroughly defeating them.
Gě Róng 葛榮 was captured in the formation,
and the rest of his forces all surrendered.
As the bandit multitude was vast,
if they were immediately divided,
he feared they would be suspicious and afraid,
or might re-gather.
So he issued an order that everyone could follow their own preferences,
relatives could stay together,
and they could reside wherever they pleased.
Thereupon, everyone was greatly pleased,
and immediately dispersed.
"Immediately"
means "at that very moment."
After they had traveled a hundred *lǐ* 里 or more,
he then began to divide the routes for escort and leadership,
settling them appropriately,
so that all found their proper place.
He promoted their chieftains,
assigning them offices according to their talents.
All those newly attached were pacified.
People at the time admired his swift and decisive arrangements.
Gě Róng 葛榮 was sent to Luò 洛 in a cage cart,
and the five prefectures of Jì 冀, Dìng 定, Cāng 滄, Yíng 瀛, and Yīn 殷 were all pacified.
At that time, Shàngdǎng Wáng ěrzhū Tiānmù 上黨王爾朱天穆 was encamped south of Cháogē 朝歌,
and Mù Shào 穆紹 and Yáng Chūn 楊椿 had not yet set out,
when Gě Róng 葛榮 was already destroyed.
So all the troops were dismissed.
In the summer of that year,
the Wèi 魏 emperor was about to campaign in the north,
appointing Ěrzhū Róng 爾朱榮 as the commander of the left army,
Yáng Chūn 楊椿 as the commander of the right army,
and Mù Shào 穆紹 as the commander of the rear army.
Initially,
Yǔwén Gōng 宇文肱 followed Xiānyú Xiūlǐ 鮮于脩禮 to attack Dìng Zhōu 定州,
and died in battle at the Táng Hé 唐河.
Wèi Shōu's 魏收 *Zhì* 志 states: In Dìng Zhōu's 定州 Zhōngshān Jùn 中山郡 Táng Xiàn 唐縣 there is the Táng Shuǐ 唐水.
The *Shuǐ Jīng* 水經 says: Táng Shuǐ 唐水 originates northwest of Lúnú Xiàn 盧奴縣,
flows east to the northwest corner of Tángchéng 唐城,
is dammed to form a lake,
its waters flow south into a small ditch,
and then empty into the Qǐ Shuǐ 滱水.
After Xiūlǐ 脩禮 died,
Yǔwén Gōng 宇文肱 followed Gě Róng 葛榮;
when Gě Róng 葛榮 was defeated,
Ěrzhū Róng 爾朱榮 admired Yǔwén Tàī's 宇文泰 talent,
and made him Commander-in-Chief.
Yǔwén Tàī's 宇文泰 career began here.
On the *yǐhài* 乙亥 day,
Wèi 魏 granted a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Yǒng'ān 永安.
On the *xīnsì* 辛巳 day,
Ěrzhū Róng 爾朱榮 was appointed Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng 大丞相) and Supervisor of All Military Affairs Outside the Capital in Héběi 河北 (Dūdū Héběi Jīwài Zhū Jūshì 都督河北畿外諸軍事).
Róng's 榮 sons, Píngchāng Gōng ěrzhū Wénshū 平昌公爾朱文殊 and Chānglè Gōng ěrzhū Wénchàng 昌樂公爾朱文暢, were both promoted to prince.
Yáng Chūn 楊椿 was appointed Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo 太保),
and Chéngyáng Wáng Huī 城陽王徽 was appointed Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒).
In winter,
tenth month,
on the *dīnghài* 丁亥 day,
Gě Róng 葛榮 arrived in Luò 洛.
The Wèi 魏 emperor held court at the Chānghé Mén 閶闔門.
On the west side of Luòchéng 洛城 were the three gates: Guǎngyáng 廣陽, Xīmíng 西明, and Chānghé 閶闔.
Also, the gate to the Luòyáng Gōngchéng 洛陽宮城 was called Chānghé 閶闔,
a note for which has already been seen in volume eighty-four under Jìn Huìdì Tàipíng Yuánnián 晉惠帝太安元年.
He was executed in the marketplace.
27 The emperor appointed Wèi Běihǎi Wáng Hào 魏北海王顥 as Wèi Wáng 魏王,
and sent Chén Qìngzhī 陳慶之, General of the Eastern Palace Rectification Chamber, with troops to escort him back north.
28 On the *bǐngshēn* 丙申 day,
Wèi 魏 appointed Tàiyuán Wáng Shìzǐ Ěrzhū Pútí 太原王世子爾朱菩提 as General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojí Dà Jiāngjūn 驃騎大將軍) and Erudite for Administration (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 開府儀同三司).
On the *dīngyǒu* 丁酉 day,
Chánglè 長樂 and seven other commanderies, each with ten thousand households,
making a total of one hundred thousand households including previous grants,
were made the state of Tàiyuán Wáng Róng 太原王榮.
On the *wùxū* 戊戌 day,
Róng 榮 was further elevated to Grand Preceptor (Tàishī 太師).
These were all rewards for the merit of capturing Gě Róng 葛榮.
29 On the *rénzǐ* 壬子 day,
Wèi Jiāngyáng Wǔliè Wáng Jì 魏江陽武烈王繼 passed away.
30 Wèi 魏 sent General Zheng Lǔ Hán Zǐxī 征虜將軍韓子熙 to persuade Xíng Gǎo 邢杲 to surrender.
Gǎo 杲 feigned surrender and then rebelled again.
Lǐ Shūrén 李叔仁 attacked Gǎo 杲 at the Wéi Shuǐ 惟水.
"Wéi Shuǐ" 惟水
should be
"Wéi Shuǐ" 濰水.
[Chapter: Yǐ Shíyī Háng Běn 乙十一行本 correctly writes
"Wéi" 濰;
Tuì Zhāi 退齋校 also agrees.]
The *Shuǐ Jīng* 水經 says: Wéi Shuǐ 濰水 emerges from Lángyé Jī Xiàn 琅邪箕縣,
flows northeast past the west of Dōngwǔchéng Xiàn 東武城縣,
then north past the east of Píngchāng Xiàn 平昌縣,
then north past the west of Gāomì Xiàn 高密縣,
then north past the east of Chúnyú Xiàn 淳于縣,
then northeast past the west of the old city of Xiàmì Xiàn 下密縣,
then northeast past the east of Dūchāng Xiàn 都昌縣,
and then northeast into the sea.
The *Wǔ Dài Zhì* 五代志 says: In the Later Wèi's 後魏 Běihǎi Jùn 北海郡, Jiāodōng Xiàn 膠東縣
was changed to Wéi Shuǐ Xiàn 濰水縣 by Suí 隋,
and later again changed to Xiàmì Xiàn 下密縣.
濰 *wéi*,
has the sound *wéi* 惟.
31 Wèi Fèi Mù 魏費穆 arrived at Jīng Zhōu 荊州 suddenly.
Cáo Yìzōng's 曹義宗 army was defeated
and captured by Wèi 魏,
and the siege of Jīng Zhōu 荊州 was finally lifted.
Jīng Zhōu 荊州 had been under siege for three years before it was lifted.
32 Yuán Hào 元顥 attacked and seized Zhì Chéng 銍城 from Wèi 魏.
Zhì Xiàn 銍縣,
in Hàn 漢 belonged to Pèi Jùn 沛郡,
in Wèi 魏 and Jìn 晉 belonged to Qiáo Jùn 譙郡.
Sòng Bái 宋白 says: Sù Zhōu's 宿州 Línhuàn Xiàn 臨渙縣
is the land of Hàn's 漢 Zhì Xiàn 銍縣.
銍 *zhì*,
read *zhúyǐ fān* 竹乙翻.
33 Wèi’s Acting Director of the Department of State Affairs, Senior Deputy Director of the Left, Yú Huī, and others, with several hundred thousand troops,
attacked Yáng Kǎn at Xiáqiū.
Liú Xù said: Xiáqiū
was the territory of Xiá in the State of Lǔ during the Spring and Autumn period.
The Sòng dynasty made it the seat of Yǎnzhōu.
The Suí dynasty first established Xiáqiū County.
(It is said that) Kǎn asked for military aid from Liáng.
Kǎn believed him,
and Hè then came to defect.
Huī and others surrounded Kǎn in more than ten layers.
Arrows in the palisades were exhausted,
and the southern army did not advance.
In the eleventh month,
on the guǐhài night,
Kǎn broke through the encirclement and escaped.
Fighting and marching,
they left Wèi territory after one day and one night,
reaching Zhākǒu.
The Commentary on the Water Classic quotes the Records of Commanderies and States, saying: Bìyáng has the Zhā River,
which flows south into the Yí,
and then empties into the Shù.
It is called Zhākǒu.
The meeting of the feudal lords with Wú at Zhā in the Spring and Autumn period refers to this place.
Zhā,
pronounced cè jiā.
(They had) two thousand horses.
All the soldiers sang mournful songs throughout the night.
Kǎn then apologized, saying:
“You all yearn for your homes.
It is unreasonable for me to ask you to follow me.
You are free to stay or go.”
This means one may leave or stay,
each according to their will.
They all bowed and left.
Wèi recaptured Tàishān.
Huī
was the son of Jìng.
Yú Jìng served Emperor Xiàowén of Wèi.
34 On the wùyín day,
Wèi appointed the Prince of Shàngdǎng, Tiānmù, as Grand General, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and hereditary Inspector of Bīngzhōu.
35 In the twelfth month,
on the gēngzǐ day,
Wèi decreed Yú Huī to return his army to campaign against Xíng Gǎo.
36 Hán Lóu, a remnant of Gě Róng’s faction, again occupied Yōuzhōu and rebelled.
This sets the stage for Ěrzhū Róng sending a general to pacify Hán Lóu.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu.
Ěrzhū Róng appointed the General of the Guard, Hèbá Shèng, as Grand Commander,
garrisoning Zhōngshān.
Lóu feared Shèng’s reputation
and dared not move south.

Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì 9
Zhōngdàtōng First Year (jǐyǒu, 529)
The reign title was changed in the tenth month of this year.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the jiǎyín day,
Wèi’s Military Governor Péng Lè, a subordinate of Yú Huī, led over two thousand cavalry to defect to Hán Lóu.
Huī withdrew his forces.
He dared not advance again to campaign against Xíng Gǎo.
Shuài
is read as lǜ.
Qí
is pronounced qī jì.
2 On the xīnyǒu day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices to the southern suburbs
and declared a general amnesty.
3 On the jiǎzǐ day,
Wèi’s Prince of Rǔnán, Yuè, requested to return to his state,
which was granted.
Yuè came to defect and meet the Emperor in the previous year of the previous volume.
4 On the xīnsì day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices in the Míngtáng.
5 Second month,
on the jiǎwǔ day,
the Wèi ruler posthumously honored the Prince Wǔxuān of Péngchéng as Emperor Wénmù,
with the temple name Sùzǔ;
his mother, Lǐ, as Empress Wénmù.
When the spirit tablets were to be moved to the imperial ancestral temple,
considering Gāozǔ as his paternal uncle,
the Grand Marshal and concurrently Director of the Department of State Affairs, Prince of Línhuái, Yù, submitted a memorial of remonstrance,
arguing that
“Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn established the temple for the Taishang Huang in Xiāngjiē.
Xiāngjiē
was within the old Hàn capital of Cháng’ān,
northeast of the Left Fēngyì Prefecture.
The matter is recorded in Volume 43, Jiànwǔ 19th year.
The mourning period had already ceased.
Mourning extending to merely baring one’s arm and wearing a headband, or no mourning at all, is called cessation of mourning.
He was admitted to inherit the main lineage.
Emperor Yuán of Hàn, in the main lineage, was five generations removed from Emperor Jǐng.
Counting by generations of ancestors and descendants, he was seven generations removed from Emperor Jǐng.
Guāngwǔ was also seven generations removed from Emperor Jǐng.
In the order of the five degrees of mourning,
when kinship ceased, there was no mourning.
However, Emperor Guāngwǔ restored the dynasty,
using the omen of the Red Liú’s nine-nine,
succeeding Emperor Yuán as the ninth generation,
and separately establishing four ancestral temples for Marquis Jié of Chōnglíng and his descendants in Chōnglíng.
(Sùzǔ’s) merit, though surpassing all limits,
and though his achievements reached the heavens,
still, he faced north as a minister.
Moreover,
both empresses will be honored with sacrifices together,
which would mean sovereign and minister sharing the same banquet,
and sister-in-law and brother-in-law sharing the same room.
I humbly believe this is unacceptable.”
The Minister of Personnel, Lǐ Shénjùn, also remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
Yù further requested to change
“dì”
to
“huáng.”
He requested to change
“dì”
to
“huáng,”
also citing Emperor Dào and Emperor Gòng of Hàn as precedents.
Qù
is pronounced qiāng lǚ.
Zhuó
is pronounced zé lüè.
6 An imperial edict revised the two hundred forty general titles into forty-four ranks.
In Tiānjiān seventh year,
the general titles were set to twenty-four ranks.
This year,
officials proposed moving the Níngyuǎn General from its rank into the Míngwēi General rank, and promoting it to the Qīngchē rank.
The Zhēngyuǎn and Dù Generals from the Qīngchē rank were moved into the Níngyuǎn rank.
Furthermore, the Ānyuǎn General was established to replace Zhēnwǔ,
and Xuānyuǎn to replace Míngliè.
Titles for barbarian chieftains were also appended by analogy.
Selection and promotion were to follow this new system,
thus it became the established rule.
A promotion advanced one rank,
and a demotion retreated one rank.
Bān (rank) is the same as jiē (grade).
Within the same rank, superiority or inferiority determined precedence.
Zhèn, Wèi, Piàojì, Chējì Generals were in the same rank.
The Four Zhōng and Four Zhēng Generals were in the same rank.
The Eight Ān Generals were in the same rank.
The Four Píng and Four Yì Generals were in the same rank.
Zhōngwǔ and Jūnshī Generals were in the same rank.
Wǔchén, Zhuǎyá, Lóngqí, Yúnhuī, Guànjūn Generals were in the same rank.
Zhènbīng, Yìshī, Xuānyì, Xuānhuì Four Generals,
and the Eastern, Western, Southern, Northern Four Zhōngláng Generals were in the same rank.
Zhìwēi, Rénwēi, Yǒngwēi, Xìnwēi, Yánwēi Generals were in the same rank.
Zhìwǔ, Rénwǔ, Yǒngwǔ, Xìnwǔ, Yánwǔ Generals were in the same rank,
known as the Five Virtues Generals.
Qīngchē, Zhènshuò, Wǔlǚ, Zhēnyì, Míngwēi Generals were in the same rank.
Níngyuǎn, Ānyuǎn, Zhēngyuǎn, Zhènyuǎn, Xuānyuǎn Generals were in the same rank.
Wēixióng, Wēiměng, Wēiliè, Wēizhèn, Wēixìn, Wēishèng, Wēilüè, Wēifēng, Wēilì, Wēiguāng Generals were in the same rank.
Wǔměng, Wǔlüè, Wǔshèng, Wǔlì, Wǔyì, Wǔjiàn, Wǔliè, Wǔwēi, Wǔruì, Wǔyǒng Generals were in the same rank.
Měngyì, Měngliè, Měngwēi, Měngruì, Měngzhèn, Měngjìn, Měngzhì, Měnglüè, Měngshèng, Měngjùn Generals were in the same rank.
Zhuàngwǔ, Zhuàngyǒng, Zhuàngliè, Zhuàngměng, Zhuàngruì, Zhuàngshèng, Zhuàngyì, Zhuàngzhì, Zhuàngyì, Zhuànglì Generals were in the same rank.
Xiāoxióng,
Xiāojié, Xiāoměng, Xiāoliè, Xiāowǔ, Xiāoyǒng, Xiāoruì, Xiāomíng, Xiāoshèng, Xiāoxùn Generals were in the same rank.
Xióngměng, Xióngwēi, Xióngmíng, Xióngliè, Xióngxìn, Xióngwǔ, Xióngyǒng, Xióngyì, Xióngzhuàng, Xióngjiàn Generals were in the same rank.
Zhōngyǒng, Zhōngliè, Zhōngměng, Zhōngruì, Zhōngzhuàng, Zhōngyì, Zhōnghàn, Zhōngxìn, Zhōngyì, Zhōngshèng Generals were in the same rank.
Míngzhì, Mínglüè, Míngyuǎn, Míngyǒng, Míngliè, Míngwēi, Míngshèng, Míngjìn, Míngruì, Míngyì Generals were in the same rank.
Guāngliè, Guāngmíng, Guāngyīng, Guāngyuǎn, Guāngshèng, Guāngruì, Guāngmìng, Guāngyǒng, Guāngróng, Guāngyě Generals were in the same rank.
Biāoyǒng, Biāoměng, Biāoliè, Biāoruì, Biāoqí, Biāojuè, Biāoqǐ, Biāolüè, Biāoshèng, Biāochū Generals were in the same rank.
Lóngxiáng, Hǔshì, Yúnqí, Fēngliè, Diànwēi, Léiyīn, Chíruì, Zhuīruì, Yǔqí, Túqí Generals were in the same rank.
Kāiyuǎn, Lüèyuǎn, Zhēnwēi, Juéshèng, Qīngyě, Jiānruì, Qīngruì, Báshān, Yúnyǒng, Zhènlǚ Generals were in the same rank.
Chāowǔ, Tiěqí, Lóuchuán, Xuānměng, Shùgōng, Kèdí, Pínglǔ, Léngwēi, Zhāowēi, Wēiróng Generals were in the same rank.
Fúbō, Xióngjǐ, Chángjiàn, Chōngguān, Diāoqí, Cìfēi, Yǒngqí, Pòdí, Kèdí, Wēilǔ Generals were in the same rank.
Qiánfēng, Wǔyì, Kāibiān, Zhāoyuǎn, Quánwēi, Pòzhèn, Dàngkòu, Tiǎnlǔ, Héngyě, Chíshè Generals were in the same rank.
Yámén and Qímén Generals were in the same rank.
Hòuqí and Xióngqú Generals were in the same rank.
Zhōngjiān and Diǎnrong Generals were in the same rank.
Zhíxùn and Xíngzhèn Generals were in the same rank.
Fúwǔ and Huáiqí Generals were in the same rank.
Piān and Bí Generals were in the same rank: a total of two hundred forty titles,
divided into forty-four ranks.
7 On the rényín day,
Wèi decreed the Prince of Jìyīn, Huīyè, concurrently to be Acting Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and to supervise Qiū Dàqiān and others in garrisoning Liángguó.
Huīyè
was the great-grandson of Xiǎoxīnchéng.
Xiǎoxīnchéng is mentioned in Volume 129, Sòng Emperor Xiàowǔ, Dàmíng fifth year.
8 Third month,
on the rénxū day,
Wèi decreed the Prince of Shàngdǎng, Tiānmù, to campaign against Xíng Gǎo,
with Fèi Mù as the Grand Commander of the vanguard.
9 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Guǐwèi day,
Wèi moved the spirit tablets of Sùzǔ and Empress Wénmù to the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
They also posthumously honored Péngchéng Wáng Shào as Xiàoxuān Huángdì.
Línhuái Wáng Yù remonstrated, saying:
“This matter is unprecedented in ancient times.”
The statement means that there has never been a case of an emperor posthumously honoring his elder brother as an emperor.
Now, according to records from after Táng Gāozōng,
it was common to posthumously title their younger relatives as emperors.
The originator of this was Wèi Jìngzōng.
“What will later generations think?!”
This uses the sense of Cáo Guì’s words in the Zuǒzhuàn.
10Wèi Yuán Tiānmù was about to attack Xíng Gǎo.
As Běihǎi Wáng Hào was then invading,
he gathered civil and military officials to discuss it.
The multitude all said:
“Gǎo’s forces are strong and prosperous;
he should be dealt with first.”
Xíngtái Shàngshū Xuē Shú said:
“Although Xíng Gǎo’s army is numerous,
they are merely petty thieves and dog-like prowlers,
without grand ambitions.
Hào is a close relative of the imperial house.
Hào
was the son of Běihǎi Wáng Xiáng,
a cousin of the Wèi ruler.
His situation is unpredictable;
it is advisable to eliminate him first.”
Tiānmù, seeing that most of the generals wanted to attack Gǎo,
and as the Wèi court also considered Hào isolated and weak and not a cause for concern,
ordered Tiānmù and others to first pacify Qí territory,
then return their forces to attack Hào.
So he led his troops eastward.
Hào, with Chén Qìngzhī, took advantage of the emptiness from Zhìchéng, advanced and captured Yíngchéng,
then reached Liángguó.
The Shuǐjīngzhù
states that this was the land of Shāsuí in the Spring and Autumn period.
Dù Yù’s commentary considers it to be Shāyángtíng, north of Nínglíng Xiàn in Liángguó,
popularly called Tángchéng.
The characters “Yíng”
and “Táng”
are similar in form,
implying it is this place but the character is mistaken.
Zhì,
read as Zhì Lì fān.
They divided their forces to construct nine fortresses to resist him.
Qìngzhī attacked them;
from dawn to shēn,
he captured three of their strongholds.
Dàqiān requested to surrender.
Hào ascended the altar and offered burnt sacrifices,
taking the imperial throne south of Suīyángchéng,
and changed the era name to Xiàojī.
Jìyīn Wáng Huīyè led 20,000 Yǔlín troops and garrisoned Kǎochéng.
In the Former Hàn, Liángguó had Zī Xiàn.
In the Latter Hàn, Emperor Zhāng renamed it Kǎochéng,
subordinate to Chénliú Jùn.
It was abolished in Jìn.
In Sòng, it belonged to Jìyáng Jùn.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Kǎochéng Xiàn of Liáng Jùn.
The Later Wèi called it Kǎoyáng,
and established Běiliáng Jùn.
Suí restored it as Kǎochéng Xiàn,
subordinate to Sòng Zhōu.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Huīyè was captured.
Kǎoyì states: In the Wèi Shū Dìjì, the capture of Kǎochéng was after Xīnchǒu.
Now we follow the Liáng Dìjì.
11On the Xīnchǒu day,
Wèi Shàngdǎng Wáng Tiānmù and Ěrzhū Zhào defeated Xíng Gǎo in Jìnán.
Gǎo surrendered
and was sent to Luòyáng
where he was executed.
Zhào
was Róng’s cousin.
12In the fifth month,
on the Dīngsì day,
Wèi appointed Dōngnán Dào Dàdūdū Yáng Yù to guard Yíngyáng,
Shàngshū Púyè Ěrzhū Shìlóng to guard Hǔláo,
and Shìzhōng Ěrzhū Shìchéng to guard Èbàn.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
a state of emergency was declared both inside and outside the capital.
On the Wùchén day,
Běihǎi Wáng Hào captured Liángguó.
Hào appointed Chén Qìngzhī as Wèi Jiāngjūn and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
and led his troops westward.
Leading his troops westward,
he aimed directly for Luòyáng.
They occupied Yíngyáng.
Qìngzhī attacked it,
but had not yet captured it.
Hào sent someone to persuade Yù to surrender,
but Yù refused.
Tiānmù and Piàojì Jiāngjūn Ěrzhū Tǔmò'ér arrived successively with a large army.
All the Liáng soldiers were terrified.
Qìngzhī dismounted and fed his horses,
then addressed his officers and men, saying:
“Since we arrived here,
the cities we have slaughtered and the lands we have plundered
are indeed not few;
you gentlemen have killed people’s fathers and brothers, and plundered people’s sons and daughters,
also countless times.
Tiānmù’s forces
are all our mortal enemies.
Our troops number only seven thousand,
while the barbarians number over three hundred thousand.
Today’s matter
is such that only by being resolved to die can we hope to live.
The barbarian cavalry are numerous;
we cannot engage them in open battle.
We must, before they are fully assembled,
swiftly attack and capture their city and hold it.
Let none of you hesitate,
lest you invite slaughter upon yourselves.”
Then he beat the drums,
ordering them to ascend the walls.
The officers and men immediately led each other, swarming like ants, and entered.
On the Guǐyǒu day,
they captured Yíngyáng,
and seized Yáng Yù.
Yáng Yù underestimated Qìngzhī’s small army
and did not anticipate their close-quarters, fierce attack,
hence the city fell.
The commentary says:
“Do not despise a small enemy.”
It also says:
“Without preparedness and caution,
one cannot lead an army.”
“Your Majesty crossed the Jiāng three thousand lǐ,
without expending a single arrow.
Yesterday, beneath the city of Yíngyáng, over five hundred people were killed or wounded in one morning.
We beg for Yáng Yù’s execution to satisfy the desires of the multitude!”
Hào said:
“While I was in Jiāngdōng, I heard the Liáng ruler say
that when he first raised his army to advance on the capital,
Yuán Áng, as the administrator of Wú Jùn, did not surrender,
and he always praised his loyalty and integrity.”
The matter is found in Volume 144, Qí Hédì Zhōngxīng Yuánnián.
Jiàng,
read as hù jiāng fān.
“How can I kill him?!”
“Apart from this, you gentlemen may take what you wish.”
Thereupon, thirty-seven commanders of Yù’s subordinate units were beheaded,
and all their hearts were gouged out and eaten.
Soon after, Tiānmù and others led their forces to besiege the city.
Qìngzhī led three thousand cavalry to fight fiercely with their backs to the city walls,
and utterly routed them.
Tiānmù and Tǔmò'ér both fled.
Qìngzhī then attacked Hǔláo.
Ěrzhū Shìlóng abandoned the city and fled,
and Wèi Dōngzhōnglángjiāng Xīn Zuǎn was captured.
The Wèi Dōngzhōngláng Fǔ was in Hǔláo.
The Wèi ruler was about to flee from Hào,
but did not know where to go.
Some advised him to go to Cháng'ān.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Gāo Dàomù said:
“Guānzhōng is desolate and ruined;
how can we go there again?!
Hào’s troops are not many;
he advanced deeply by taking advantage of the emptiness,
because the commanders were not the right people,
which is why he could reach this point.
If Your Majesty
personally leads the Imperial Guards,
recruits with generous rewards,
and fights one battle with our backs to the city,
we, your servants, will exert our utmost strength,
and we will certainly defeat Hào’s isolated army.
Should there be an uncertainty in the outcome,
then the imperial carriage should cross the Hé,
and summon Dà Jiāngjūn Tiānmù and Dà Chéngxiàng Róng to each lead their armies to converge.
Attacking in a pincer movement,
success will surely be seen within ten days to a month.
This is a foolproof strategy.”
The Wèi ruler followed his advice.
On the Jiǎxū day,
the Wèi ruler traveled north.
At night,
he reached the north of Hénèi Jùn.
The seat of Hénèi Jùn was Yěwáng.
The Wèi ruler went north from Luò to Hénèi.
He should have reached the south of the commandery city that night,
not the north.
This might be an error.
Proclaiming this far and wide,
the four directions then first knew the Wèi ruler’s whereabouts.
On the Yǐhài day,
the Wèi ruler entered Hénèi.
Lín Huái Wáng Yù,
Ān Fēng Wáng Yánmíng,
led all the officials,
sealed the armories and treasuries,

He led his forces west into Qiāntún Shān.
The Bān Zhì says: Jiāntóu Shān is west of Jīngyáng Xiàn in Āndìng Jùn,
where the Jīng River originates.
Shīgǔ’s note says: ‘Jiān’
is pronounced *qiān*.
This mountain is southeast of today’s Língzhōu,
and is popularly corrupted to Jiāntún Shān.
Dù Yòu said: [AS-FBED] Qiāntún Shān is in today’s Yuánzhōu Gāopíng Xiàn.
Ěrzhū Róng, because Tiānguāng had lost Xiélì
and failed to capture Dàoluò,
again sent an envoy to flog him one hundred times.
An imperial edict demoted Tiānguāng to Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and reduced his noble rank to marquis. Tiānguāng pursued Dàoluò to Qiāntún.
Dàoluò was defeated and fled
into Lǒng.
Lǒng
is Lǒng Shān.
Jìn Wǔdì divided Tiānshuǐ to establish Luèyáng Jùn.
During the Suí dynasty, it was abolished and became Lǒngchéng Xiàn,
subordinate to Qínzhōu.
The Kǎoyì says: The Wèi Dì Jì records
“the Hú King Qìngyún of Báimǎ Lónghè.”
Now we follow the Ěrzhū Tiānguāng Zhuàn.
‘Shuài’,
read *suǒ lèi fān*.
Qìngyún captured him,
and was very pleased,
thinking that great things could be achieved.
So he declared himself emperor at Shuǐluò Chéng.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù says: The Shuǐluò River originates from Lǒng Shān,
flows west past the west of Shuǐluò Tíng,
and flows south into Luèyáng Chuān.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: Shuǐluò Chéng is one hundred *lǐ* southwest of Déshùn Jūn.
Fàn Zhòngyān said: West of Cháonà,
east of Qín Tíng,
there is Shuǐluò Chéng.
He appointed Dàoluò as Dàjiāngjūn. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Tiānguāng led his armies into Lǒng,
reaching Shuǐluò Chéng.
Qìngyún and Dàoluò came out to fight.
Tiānguāng shot Dàoluò in the arm,
who dropped his bow and fled back,
and captured their east city.
The rebels combined their forces and moved towards the west city.
There was no water in the city,
and the troops were parched.
A defector reported that Qìngyún and Dàoluò intended to break out and flee.
Fearing to lose them,
Tiānguāng sent someone to persuade Qìngyún to surrender early,
saying:
“If you cannot decide for yourselves,
you should listen to your people.
Discuss it tonight,
and report back early tomorrow morning.”
Qìngyún and others hoped for a slight delay,
intending to break out that night,
so they replied:
“Please wait until tomorrow.”
Tiānguāng then sent a message to them, saying:
“I know you need water.
‘Xū’
means ‘what one desires.’
You may drink water from the stream.”
The rebel troops were pleased
and no longer had any thought of escaping.
Tiānguāng secretly ordered his soldiers to make many wooden spears,
each seven *chǐ* long.
These were *jùmǎ qiāng*.
Dù Yòu said: *Jùmǎ qiāng* are made of wood, two *chǐ* in diameter,
and of varying lengths as needed.
Holes are drilled in a cross shape,
and bars are inserted horizontally and vertically,
ten *chǐ* long,
sharpened at the ends to block critical roads.
He arranged them around the city,
making them denser at vital points.
He also hid men among the spears
to guard against a breakout,
and secretly ordered long ladders to be bound at the north of the city.
That night,
Qìngyún and Dàoluò indeed galloped out,
encountered the spears,
and their horses were wounded and fell.
The hidden troops rose up
and captured them immediately.
Soldiers climbed the ladders into the city,
and the remaining rebels all exited the south of the city,
stopped by the spears,
and in desperation, begged to surrender.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Tiānguāng seized all their weapons and buried them alive.
Seventeen thousand people died,
and their families were distributed.
Thereupon, Sān Qín, Hé, Wèi, Guā, Liáng, and Shàn Zhōu all surrendered.
Sān Qín
refers to Qín, Dōng Qín, and Nán Qín.
Hézhōu
was the land of Qǐfú.
In the sixth year of Wèi Tàiwǔ Zhēnjūn,
Bāohǎn Zhèn was established.
Later it was renamed Hézhōu,
administering Jīnchéng, Wǔshǐ, Hónghé, and Líntáo Commanderies.
Wèizhōu administered Lǒngxī, Nán’ān, Nán’ānyáng, and Guǎngníng Commanderies.
Guāzhōu
is the ancient land of Dūnhuáng.
Shànzhōu
was the land of the Tūfà clan,
governed by the Hàn Jīnchéng Xībù Dūwèi.
Shīgǔ said: Guāzhōu
is what the Zuǒ Zhuàn refers to as where the Yǔnxìng Zhī Róng resided in Guāzhōu.
Even today,
large melons are produced in that area,
so long that a fox can enter a melon to eat it,
with its head and tail not protruding.
Tiān Guāng (天光) attacked Jūnlüèyáng (軍略陽).
An imperial edict reinstated Tiān Guāng's (天光) official titles and ranks.
Soon after, he was granted the titles of Shìzhōng (侍中) and Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司).
Hèbá Yuè (賀拔岳) was appointed governor of Jīngzhōu (涇州),
and Hóumòchén Yuè (侯莫陳悅) was appointed governor of Wèizhōu (渭州).
The citizens of Qínzhōu (秦州) plotted to assassinate their governor, Luò Chāo (駱超).
The citizens of Nán Qínzhōu (南秦州) plotted to assassinate their governor, Xīn Xiǎn (辛顯).
Both Chāo (超) and Xiǎn (顯) became aware of the plots.
They fled to Tiān Guāng (天光),
who dispatched troops to suppress the uprisings.
Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉) Yǔwén Tài (宇文泰) followed Hèbá Yuè (賀拔岳) into Guān (關),
and for his merits, was promoted to Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍)
and acting governor of Yuánzhōu (原州).
At that time, Guān (關) and Lǒng (隴) were devastated.
Tài (泰) governed them with kindness and trust,
and the people were all moved and pleased,
saying:
"If we had met Administrator Yǔwén (宇文) earlier,
how could we have followed the rebellion!"
This laid the foundation for Yǔwén Tài (宇文泰) to acquire Hèbá Yuè's (賀拔岳) troops and establish his great enterprise west of Guān (關).
In the eighth month,
on the Gēngxū (庚戌) day,
the Emperor bid farewell to the Prince of Wèi (魏王) Yuè (悅) at Déyáng Táng (德陽堂),
and sent troops to escort him to the border.
A textual criticism states: Yuè's (悅) biography says:
"He was enthroned as the Lord of Wèi (魏主),
and his reign was named Gēngxīng (更興)."
Yǎn (衍) sent his general Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) to escort him to the border,
hoping to invade and pressure him.
However, Wáng Sēngbiàn's (王僧辯) biography does not mention escorting Yuè (悅).
It was probably Wáng Biàn (王弁).
Although Érzhū Róng (爾朱榮) of Wèi (魏) resided in a frontier region,
he remotely controlled the imperial government,
appointed his relatives and partisans,
placed them around the Lord of Wèi (魏主),
and monitored his every move,
knowing everything, great or small.
Although the Lord of Wèi (魏主) was controlled by Róng (榮),
he was by nature diligent in governance,
never weary morning or night.
He personally reviewed petitions and lawsuits many times,
and rectified unjust cases.
When Róng (榮) heard of this,
he was displeased.
Historians say that the Lord of Wèi (魏主) was unable to conceal his abilities.
Róng (榮) once recommended someone for the post of Qǔyáng (曲陽) county magistrate.
According to Róng's (榮) biography,
this was the Shàng Qǔyáng (上曲陽) county,
which belonged to Chángshān Jùn (常山郡) in the Hàn (漢) and Jìn (晉) dynasties,
and to Zhōngshān Jùn (中山郡) in the Later Wèi (後魏).
"Guānbǔ" (關補) means
to first appoint someone and then report it to the Ministry of Personnel.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) says: Gǔchéng Xiàn (鼓城縣) of Zhàozhōu (趙州)
was formerly called Qǔyáng (曲陽).
Liú Xù (劉昫) says: Hàn's (漢) Shàng Qǔyáng Xiàn (上曲陽縣)
was renamed Héngyáng (恆陽) in the Suí (隋) dynasty.
In the fifteenth year of Yuánhé (元和) of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
it was renamed Qǔyáng (曲陽).
The Qǔyáng (曲陽) of Zhàozhōu (趙州)
is Xià Qǔyáng (下曲陽).
Not submitting (the appointment) meant
that the ranks were too far apart,
and the person should not have been appointed county magistrate.
Róng (榮) was furious,
and immediately sent the appointee to seize the position.
Shénjùn (神儁) was afraid and resigned his post.
Róng (榮) made Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射) Érzhū Shìlóng (爾朱世隆) take charge of selections.
Róng (榮) proposed appointing northern people as governors of various Hénán (河南) prefectures,
but the Emperor did not consent.
Tàizǎi (太宰) Tiānmù (天穆) had an audience and argued for it,
but the Emperor still did not consent.
Tiānmù (天穆) said:
"Since Tiānzhù (天柱) has rendered great service,
and is the Prime Minister of the nation,
if he asks to replace all officials in the empire,
I fear Your Majesty would not be able to refuse him.
How can you refuse to appoint a few people as governors?"
The Emperor sternly replied:
"If Tiānzhù (天柱) ceases to be a subject,
I would indeed have to comply;
but if he still maintains the etiquette of a subject,
there is no reason to replace all officials in the empire."
When Róng (榮) heard this,
he was greatly enraged and resentful,
saying:
"By whom did the Son of Heaven come to be established?
Now he does not heed my words!"
Empress Érzhū (爾朱皇后) was jealous,
and often became angry.
The Emperor sent Érzhū Shìlóng (爾朱世隆) to speak to her about the great principle.
The Empress said:
"The Son of Heaven was established by my family.
Now it is like this;
my father originally decided things himself,
and now he will also decide again."
Jué (決)
means "to judge" or "to decide,"
referring to the judgment of all matters under heaven.
Fù (復)
is pronounced "fú yòu fān."
"It's just that I didn't do it myself."
"Zhǐ" (止)
should be
"zhèng" (正).
"Your servant is now also a prince."
The Emperor was externally pressured by Róng (榮)
and internally pressured by the Empress.
He was always disgruntled and did not find joy in being the Son of Heaven.
He only hoped that the bandits would not cease,
wishing for them to hold Róng (榮) in check.
When Guān (關) and Lǒng (隴) were pacified,
on the day the victory was reported,
he was not particularly happy.
He said to Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Prince Lín Huái (臨淮王) Yù (彧):
"Now there are no more bandits in the empire."
Yù (彧) saw the Emperor's displeasure
and said:
"I fear that after the bandits are pacified,
Your Majesty's concerns will only increase."
The Emperor feared others would find this strange,
so he changed the subject and confused it, saying:
"Indeed.
Pacifying the devastated remnants..."
"Huāngyú" (荒餘)
refers to the people remaining after the devastation of war.
When Róng (榮) saw that everything was peaceful in all directions,
he submitted a memorial stating:
"My staff officer Xǔ Zhōu (許周) urged me to accept the Nine Imperial Honors.
I disliked his words and have already dismissed him."
Róng (榮) at that time hoped to receive special honors,
so he hinted his intentions to the court.
The Emperor did not actually want to grant them to him,
but praised his loyalty instead.
Yuán Róng
loved hunting and did not stop for cold or heat.
He would arrange encirclements and advance,
commanding his soldiers to be absolutely uniform,
and even if they encountered dangers or obstacles,
they were not allowed to evade them.
If a single deer escaped,
several people would surely be executed.
One soldier saw a tiger and ran away.
Yuán Róng said to him:
"Are you afraid of death?"
He immediately beheaded him.
From then on, whenever he hunted,
the soldiers were like entering a battlefield.
Once he saw a tiger in a deep valley,
Yuán Róng ordered more than ten men to wrestle it with their bare hands,
without causing it injury.
Several men died,
but eventually, they captured it.
He took pleasure in this,
which his subordinates found extremely distressing.
Tàizǎi Tiānmù gently said to Yuán Róng:
"Your Highness's achievements and enterprises are already magnificent,
and there is no trouble in the four directions.
You should only cultivate governance and nurture the people,
conducting hunts according to the seasons.
According to the rites,
there is a spring hunt (sōu), summer field hunt (tián), autumn hunt (mǐn), and winter hunt (shòu).
Dù Yù says: Sōu
means to seek out and select infertile animals.
Miáo
means to eliminate pests for the crops.
Mǐn
means to kill;
it is named 'killing'
to accord with the autumn atmosphere.
Shòu
means to encircle and guard;
by winter, all things are fully grown,
and one takes whatever is caught,
without needing to select.
Why injure the harmonious qi?"
Yuán Róng pushed up his sleeves and said:
"The Empress Líng, a female ruler,
could not rectify herself.
To support the Son of Heaven is the constant principle for human subjects.
Followers of Gě Róng,
were originally all slaves,
who took advantage of the times to rebel.
It's like a runaway slave;
once caught, that's it.
Recently, I have received great favor from the state,
but I have not yet unified the realm.
How can I speak of achievements so prematurely?
I hear that the court officials are still lax and indulgent.
This autumn, I want to lead the soldiers and horses with you, brother,
to conduct a grand hunt on Sōnggāo Mountain,
ordering corrupt court nobles
to enter the enclosure and wrestle tigers.
Then, we will exit Lǔyáng,
traverse the three Jīng prefectures,
seize all the 'raw barbarians',
and resettle them in the Six Garrisons.
Dù Yòu says: The Northern Jīng Prefecture
is now Yīyáng County;
the Eastern Jīng Prefecture
was later renamed Huáizhōu,
now Huái'ān Commandery;
Jīng Prefecture
is now Nányáng Commandery.
I further note that Yuán Róng's words 'exit Lǔyáng'
imply he has already passed Yīyáng and gone south.
The Wǔdài Zhì records: Chōnglíng Commandery
was where the Latter Wèi established Nánjīng Prefecture.
This should complete the number of three Jīng prefectures.
'Raw barbarians'
refers to all the barbarian households
who had not yet submitted to the Wèi.
The Six Garrisons rebelled,
and their garrison households were desolate and ruined,
hence the desire to resettle them.
We will pacify the Fén Hú.
The Jī Hú all resided in the Fénzhōu area,
hence they were called Fén Hú.
We will select and train elite cavalry,
divide them, and send them to the Jiāng and Huái regions.
If Xiāo Yǎn surrenders,
I will beg for a marquisate of ten thousand households;
if he does not surrender,
I will cross with several thousand cavalry directly and capture him.
Only then, with you brother, will I support the Son of Heaven
and tour the four directions,
and only then can it be called an achievement!
If I don't hunt frequently now,
the soldiers will become lazy.
How can they be used again?"
Chéngyáng Wáng Huīzhī
was the emperor's maternal cousin;
Shìzhōng Lǐ Yù
was Yán Shí's son
and the emperor's brother-in-law.
Huī and Yù desired power and favor,
and feared Yuán Róng as a threat to themselves.
They daily slandered Yuán Róng to the emperor,
advising the emperor to eliminate him.
The emperor, having learned from the calamity of Héyīn,

Yuán Luó
was the younger brother of Chā.
It happened that Yuán Róng requested an audience,
wishing to see the empress's childbirth (jiéwǎn rǔ),

They also wanted to kill his faction and

The emperor was hesitant and undecided,

Zhōngshū Shìláng Xíng Zǐcái and his like had already evacuated eastward.
(Xíng Shào,
courtesy name Zǐcái.

(His biography states: as a youth, he avoided it,

They took it upon themselves to leave or stay.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Wēn Zǐshēng presented a letter to the emperor.
The emperor had always hoped Yuán Róng would not come.
When he saw the letter,
realizing Yuán Róng would definitely come,
his expression became very displeased.
(Zǐcái's given name was Shào,
and he went by his courtesy name.
He was a clan-junior-cousin of Luán.)
(Xíng Luán served Emperor Xuānwǔ of Wèi,
frequently commanded troops,

(The Kǎo Yì states: The Běi Shǐ, Xíng Luán's chapter's heading says

Yòu's cousin Qíu,
Qíu's sons Zāng, Shào.")
(The Wèi Shū also says

(Thus, Zāng and Shào were Luán's clan-junior-cousins,
not clan-grandsons.)
(Previous histories all followed this.)
Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn Xī Yì,
who had exchanged messages in the early days of Jiànyì (the incident is recorded in volume 252, Dàtōng 2nd year),
still kept silent about his feelings
because he was considered a trusted confidant of Yuán Róng.
Xī Yì said:
"If there must be a change,
I would rather die for Your Majesty
than serve the Qìhú."
(The Èrzhū clan
were of Qìhú stock.)
(Qì,
Qīqì fan.)
"I assure you, Tiānzhù has no ulterior motives,
and I will not forget your loyalty and sincerity."
(Kuǎn,
means sincerity.)
Èrzhū Shìlóng suspected the emperor intended to initiate a coup,
so he anonymously posted a letter on his own gate, saying:
"The Son of Heaven, with Yáng Kǎn, Gāo Dàomù, and others, is plotting
to kill the Heavenly Pillar."
He took it and presented it to Róng.
Róng, confident in his strength,
did not take it seriously.
He tore up the letter with his own hand,
spat on the ground, and said:
"Shìlóng has no guts.
Who dares to harbor such intentions!"
Róng's wife, Běixiāng Chánggōngzhǔ, also advised Róng not to go.
Róng's wife was not of the Yuán clan;

but we follow the *Wèi Dìjì* (Annals of Emperor Wèi) here."
According to the *Kǎoyì*,
"Xiāngjùn Chánggōngzhǔ"
is correct.
The *Tōngjiàn* (Comprehensive Mirror) has
"Běixiāng Chánggōngzhǔ,"

The *Wǔdài Zhì* (Treatise on the Five Dynasties) states: "Xiāng County of Shàngdǎng Commandery.

Later, Wèi removed the
character 'Wǔ'
to make it Xiāng Commandery."
Confirmed by the fact that Wèi Shōu's *Zhì* (Treatise) contains no Běixiāng Commandery,
it is therefore correct to follow Xiāng Commandery.
唾 (tuò),
pronounced tuò.
長 (cháng),
pronounced zhǎng.
That month,
Róng, with four or five thousand cavalry, departed from Bīngzhōu.
People at the time all said,
"Róng is rebelling,"
and also said,
"The Son of Heaven will surely plot against Róng."
In the ninth month,
Róng arrived in Luòyáng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: "The *Wèi Dìjì* states:
'On *xīnmǎo* day,
Róng and Tiānmù came from Jìnyáng to pay respects at court.'

Róng arrived in the capital in early ninth month,

The first day of that month was *jiǎxū*,
so *xīnmǎo* would be the eighteenth,
which is incorrect."
As Grand Preceptor Tiānmù was in Bīngzhōu,
fearing future trouble,
the emperor restrained himself from acting yet,
and also summoned Tiānmù.
Someone informed Róng, saying:
"The emperor intends to plot against you."
Róng immediately presented a full memorial,
and the emperor said:
"Outsiders also say that the King wishes to harm me,
how can one believe such things!"
Thereupon, Róng no longer harbored suspicions.
Whenever he entered to see the emperor,
his retinue never exceeded several dozen,
and they all went unarmored, carrying no weapons.
The emperor wanted to stop him.
Chéngyáng Wáng Huī said:
"Even if he doesn't rebel,
how can this be tolerated?"
耐 (nài),
means 'endure'.
Previously,
a long comet appeared in the Central Terrace,
sweeping across Dàjiǎo (Arcturus).
Gāo Róngzǔ from Héngzhōu was somewhat knowledgeable in astronomy.
Róng asked him,
and he replied:
"It is an omen of abolishing the old and establishing the new."
Sāntái (Three Terraces):
the upper star of the Central Terrace represents the three ducal ministers (sāngōng) of the feudal lords.
Dàjiǎo (Arcturus)
is the seat of the Heavenly King.
Tradition says: "Comets are for abolishing the old and establishing the new."
先 (xiān),
pronounced xiān.
先 (xiān),

恆 (héng),
pronounced héng.
Lǐ Xiǎnhé, a Langzhong (Gentleman of the Palace) of the Traveling Chancellery, said:
"When the Heavenly Pillar arrives,
why wouldn't there be nine bestowals (jiǔxī)?
Why must the King demand them himself!"
Lǐ Xiǎnhé was probably a Langzhong of the Traveling Chancellery for Bīng and Sì provinces.
He was following Róng to Luòyáng at the time.
索 (suǒ),
pronounced suǒ.
Grand Supervisor Guō Luóyè said:
"This year is truly suitable for drafting the abdication text."
During the Disaster of Héyīn, Róng had already recruited court officials to draft the abdication text,

Guō Luóyè
is also known as Guō Luóshā.
Assistant Administrator Chǔ Guāng said:
"People say there is a purple aura above the city of Bīngzhōu,
why worry that the Heavenly Pillar will not respond to it!"
Róng's subordinates all slighted and insulted the emperor's attendants,
without any restraint.
Therefore, all these matters were reported to the emperor.
Xī Yì again saw the emperor,
requesting a private audience.
求間 (qiú jiàn),
means 'to request a private audience'.
Knowing his sincerity,
the emperor then summoned Chéngyáng Wáng Huī, as well as Yáng Kǎn and Lǐ Yù, and told them Xī Yì's words.
Róng's youngest daughter was married to Chénliú Wáng Kuān, the emperor's nephew.
Róng once pointed to him and said:
"I will eventually gain strength from this son-in-law."
Huī reported this to the emperor,
saying:
