and granted the title Prince Chángshān (常山王).
Shìlóng's (世隆) elder brother, Tiānzhù Chángshǐ (天柱長史) Yànbó (彥伯), was made Shìzhōng (侍中).
Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史) Zhòngyuǎn (仲遠) was made Chēqí Dàjiàngjūn (車騎大將軍),
concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射) and Sān Xúzhōu Dàxíngtái (三徐州大行臺).
Zhòngyuǎn (仲遠) also raised troops and marched towards Luòyáng (洛陽).
The three Xúzhōu (徐州) were: Xúzhōu (徐州) with its seat at Péngchéng (彭城);
Běi Xúzhōu (北徐州) with its seat at Lángyé (琅邪),
established in the second year of Yǒng'ān (永安),
administering the two commanderies of Dōngtàishān (東泰山) and Lángyé (琅邪);
and Dōng Xúzhōu (東徐州) with its seat at Xiàpī (下邳).
All these appointments were made by Prince Chángguǎng (長廣王).
When Ěrzhū Tiānguāng (爾朱天光) captured Píngliáng (平涼),
Sùqín Míngdá (宿勤明達) requested to surrender.
Sùqín Míngdá (宿勤明達) and Wànqí Chǒunú (万俟醜奴)
were both generals of Hú Chēn (胡琛).
Having surrendered,
Hù Jiāng Fān (戶江翻).
He fled north.
Tiānguāng (天光) dispatched Hèbá Yuè (賀拔岳) to attack him.
Míngdá (明達) fled to Dōngxià (東夏).
Dōngxià (東夏)
was Táng's (唐) Yánzhōu (延州).
Xià (夏),
Hù Yǎ Fān (戶雅翻).
He did not pursue them further,
but returned to Jīngzhōu (涇州) to await Tiānguāng (天光).
Tiānguāng (天光) and Hóumòchén Yuè (侯莫陳悅) also descended into Lǒng (隴),
and plotted with Yuè (岳) to lead their troops towards Luò (洛).
Emperor Jìngzōng (敬宗) of Wèi (魏) sent Zhū Ruì (朱瑞) to console and persuade Tiānguāng (天光).
Tiānguāng (天光) plotted with Yuè (岳),
intending to make the Emperor flee outside the capital and then establish another member of the imperial clan.
So he repeatedly memorialized, saying:
"This subject truly has no disloyal intentions;
I merely wish to honor the Emperor and atone for the crimes of the imperial clan."
He also ordered his subordinates to memorialize, saying:
"Tiānguāng (天光) secretly harbors treacherous designs;
we hope you will devise a good strategy to guard against him."
Tiānguāng (天光) created two opposing stances to confuse the Wèi (魏) court.
Lú Wénwěi (盧文偉), the Tàishǒu (太守) of Fányáng (范陽), lured Hóu Yuān (侯淵), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Píngzhōu (平州), out hunting,
then closed the city gates and refused him entry.
Yuān (淵) originally held Píngzhōu (平州)
and garrisoned Fányáng (范陽).
Fányáng (范陽)
was originally Zhuōjùn (涿郡),
renamed by Emperor Zhāng (章帝) of the Later Hàn (後漢).
Yòu (誘),
sounds like Yǒu (酉).
He mourned Róng (榮)
and ordered his troops to march south.
Advancing,
he reached Zhōngshān (中山).
Wèi Lángēn (魏蘭根), the Xíngtái Púyè (行臺僕射), intercepted him,
but was defeated by Yuān (淵).
Jìngzōng (敬宗) appointed Prince Chéngyáng (城陽王) Huī (徽) as concurrent Dàsīmǎ (大司馬) and Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事),
to oversee internal and external affairs.
Huī (徽) believed that since Róng (榮) was dead,
his followers would naturally disperse.
However, as Ěrzhū Shìlóng (爾朱世隆) and others raised troops in four directions,
their factions grew daily.
Huī (徽) was anxious and fearful,
not knowing what to do.
He was naturally jealous
and did not wish anyone to surpass him.
Whenever he discussed matters with the Emperor alone,
if any official offered a plan,
Huī (徽) would immediately persuade the Emperor not to accept it,
and would say:
"What is there to worry about with these petty rebels! They will surely be pacified!"
He also hoarded wealth and goods,
and rewards were generally meager,
or if many, they would be reduced in the middle,
or given and then reclaimed.
Thus, there was only wasted expenditure, and no gratitude was inspired.
Historians say Huī (徽) misled the Wèi (魏) emperor.
Fù (復),
Fú Yòu Fān (扶又翻).
In the eleventh month,
on the day Guǐyǒu (癸酉), the first day of the month,
Jìngzōng (敬宗) appointed Zhèng Xiānhù (鄭先護), the Chēqí Jiàngjūn (車騎將軍), as Dàdūdū (大都督),
to jointly attack Ěrzhū Zhòngyuǎn (爾朱仲遠) with Xíngtái (行臺) Yáng Yù (楊昱).
On the day Yǐhài (乙亥),
Chángsūn Zhì (長孫稚), the Sītú (司徒), was made Tàiwèi (太尉),
and Yù (彧), Prince Línchuái (臨淮王), was made Sītú (司徒).
On the day Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
Ěrzhū Tiānguāng (爾朱天光), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yōngzhōu (雍州) and Duke Guǎngzōng (廣宗公), was promoted to the rank of prince.
From this point back to the official titles of Zhèng Xiānhù (鄭先護),
all were granted by Jìngzōng (敬宗).
Ěrzhū Zhòngyuǎn (爾朱仲遠) attacked Xīyǎnzhoū (西兗州).
During the Tàihé (太和) period of Wèi (魏), Xīyǎnzhoū (西兗州) was established at Huátái (滑臺);
during the Xiàochāng (孝昌) period, Xīyǎnzhoū (西兗州) was established at Dìngtáo (定陶).
The text below states that Zhòngyuǎn (仲遠) fought Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝) east of Huátái (滑臺),
which means that at that time, Huátái (滑臺) was still Xīyǎnzhoū (西兗州).
On the day Dīngchǒu (丁丑)
he captured it,
and seized Cìshǐ (刺史) Wáng Yǎn (王衍).
Yǎn (衍)
was Sù's (肅) nephew.
Wáng Sù (王肅) left Qí (齊) and entered Wèi (魏), becoming prominent.
On the day Guǐwèi (癸未),
Jìngzōng (敬宗) appointed Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝), the Yòuwèi Jiàngjūn (右衞將軍), as Dōngzhēng Dūdū (東征都督).
On the day Rénchén (壬辰),
he further appointed Zhèng Xiānhù (鄭先護) as concurrent Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射) and Xíngtái (行臺),
to jointly attack Zhòngyuǎn (仲遠) with Shèng (勝).
On the day Wùxū (戊戌),
an imperial edict disbanded Wèi Lángēn's (魏蘭根) Xíngtái (行臺),
and appointed Xuē Tánshàng (薛曇尚), the Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ (定州刺史), as concurrent Shàngshū (尚書),
to serve as Běidào Xíngtái (北道行臺).
Zhèng Xiānhù (鄭先護) suspected Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝)
and kept him outside the camp.
On the day Gēngzǐ (庚子),
Shèng (勝) fought Zhòngyuǎn (仲遠) east of Huátái (滑臺),
his army was defeated,
and he surrendered to Zhòngyuǎn (仲遠).
Previously,
Ěrzhū Róng (爾朱榮) once casually asked his attendants:
"If I were gone one day,
who could lead the army?"
All named Ěrzhū Zhào (爾朱兆).
Róng (榮) said:
"Though Zhào (兆) is brave in battle,
he can command no more than three thousand cavalry;
with more, there would be chaos.
The only one capable of replacing me
is Hèliùhún (賀六渾)."
He then warned Zhào (兆), saying:
"You are not his equal;
eventually, you will have your nose pierced by him."
He used the analogy of an ox;
once an ox's nose is pierced,
it is controlled by humans.
When Zhào (兆) led his troops towards Luò (洛),
he sent an envoy to summon Huān (歡).
Huān (歡) sent his Chángshǐ (長史) Sūn Téng (孫騰) to Zhào (兆),
excusing himself by saying
that "the mountain Shǔ (蜀) people have not yet been pacified.
The Shǔ (蜀) people who migrated to Fén (汾) and Jìn (晉) and live in the mountains
are called mountain Shǔ (蜀).
I cannot abandon them
and cause future trouble.
When Shǔ (蜀) is settled,
I will form a pincer movement across the river."
Zhào (兆) was displeased,
saying:
"Go back and tell Gāo Jìnzhōu (高晉州),
I had a propitious dream.
I dreamed of ascending a high mound with my ancestors.
The land beside the mound
was already well-cultivated,
except for the *mǎlìn* (馬藺) grass,
The *Běncǎo* (本草) says: *líshí* (蠡實) is *mǎlìnzǐ* (馬藺子),
found in Jìzhōu (冀州).
The *Tújīng* (圖經) says: *Mǎlìnzǐ* (馬藺子)
grows in the valleys of Hédōng (河東),
its leaves resemble scallions but are long and thick.
The *Yǎnyì* (衍義) says: Cattle and horses
do not eat *mǎlìn* (馬藺) leaves,
because their leaves are already hard as soon as they emerge from the soil.
It disappeared as I touched it.
Seeing this,
I shall succeed in everything I undertake."
Téng (騰) returned and reported this.
Huān (歡) said:
"Zhào (兆) is so foolish,
yet dares to commit such perverse rebellion.
My situation means I cannot long serve the Ěrzhū (爾朱) clan."
This laid the groundwork for Huān (歡) to raise an army against the Ěrzhū (爾朱).
Bèi (悖),
Pú Nèi Fān (蒲內翻),
also Pú Mò Fān (蒲沒翻).
In the twelfth month,
on the *rén yín* day,
Ěrzhū Zhào attacked Dāngǔ.
Commander Cuī Bófèng was killed in battle.
Commander Shǐ Wǔlóng opened the defenses and offered to surrender.
Yuán Zǐgōng retreated.
Zhào, with light troops, doubled his pace and marched continuously,
crossing the Hébriáoxī.
A *Kǎoyì* (Textual Research) says: The *Gālán Jì* states,
"crossed at Léibō."
We now follow the *Wèi Shū*'s biography of Zhào.
Jìngzōng, believing the Great River to be deep and wide,
thought Zhào could not cross suddenly.
On that day,
the water did not reach the horses' bellies.
On the *jiǎ chén* day,
a violent wind blew,
and yellow dust filled the sky.
Zhào's cavalry knocked on the palace gates.
The palace guards then realized,
bent their bows to shoot,
but their arrows could not be fired,
and they scattered in an instant.
Huàshān Wáng Zhì,
a great-grandson of Jīn.
Jīn's involvement in the turmoil is detailed in Volume 104, Jìn Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán First Year.
The Wèi began with this,
and also ended with this.
Is it Heaven's will,
or human doing?
The Emperor, upon first hearing of Zhào's southward advance,
wished to personally lead his armies to suppress him.
Zhì persuaded the Emperor, saying:
"The Yellow River is ten thousand *rèn* deep,
how could Zhào cross it!"
The Emperor thus felt at ease.
When Zhào entered the palace,
Zhì again ordered the guards not to fight.
The Emperor walked out beyond the Yúnlóng Gate,
and encountered Chéngyáng Wáng Huī riding away on horseback.
The Emperor repeatedly called to him,
but Huī ignored him and left.
Huī had participated in the great affairs of the state;
if he failed and did not immediately die,
where was he going?
He was locked up in a tower of the Yǒngníng Temple.
The Emperor was very cold,
and asked Zhào for a headscarf.
A headscarf
is what is called a *pàtóu*.
Zhào set up camp in the Shàngshū Province,
using the Son of Heaven's golden drums,
and placed a water clock in the courtyard.
He clubbed the imperial princes to death.
The imperial princes
were born of Empress Ěrzhū.
*Pū*
is pronounced "bǐjiǎo".
He let his soldiers plunder extensively,
killing Sīkōng Lín huáiwáng Yù, Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Fànyángwáng Huì, Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Yánshí, and others.
Chéngyáng Wáng Huī fled to Shānnán.
Shānnán
is south of the southern mountains of Yī and Yǐng.
A *Kǎoyì* says: The *Wèi Shū* writes
"Kòu Mí."
According to the surnames of Kòu Zàn's grandchildren, all contain the character
"zǔ".
Perhaps his given name was Mí, courtesy name Zǔrén.
We now follow the *Gālán Jì*.
All were promoted by Huī,
and because of their former kindness,
he turned to them.
Huī carried one hundred *jīn* of gold and fifty horses.
Zǔrén coveted his wealth.
Though he outwardly accepted him,
he privately told his family:
"I hear that Ěrzhū Zhào is offering a reward for Chéngyáng Wáng.
Whoever captures him will be enfeoffed as a marquis of a thousand households.
Today, wealth and honor have arrived!"
So he scared Huī, saying that government arrests were imminent,
and told him to flee elsewhere.
He sent men to waylay and kill him on the road,
and sent his head to Zhào.
Huī betrayed Jìngzōng,
and Zǔrén also betrayed Huī.
How swift was the retribution for their evil deeds!
Heaven is not to be deceived, so it is.
Zhào dreamt that Huī said to him:
"I have two hundred *jīn* of gold and one hundred horses at Zǔrén's house;
you can take them."
When Zhào awoke,
he believed his dream to be true,
and immediately arrested Zǔrén,
demanding his gold and horses.
Zǔrén thought someone had secretly informed,
and immediately confessed.
He said,
"I did indeed get one hundred *jīn* of gold and fifty horses."
*Kuǎn*
means sincerity and truth.
The confession of a prisoner is called *kuǎn*,
meaning the truth has been obtained.
According to the dream, Zhào demanded them.
Zǔrén's family originally had thirty *jīn* of gold and thirty horses,
which they all handed over to Zhào.
Zhào still did not believe him,
became angry,
seized Zǔrén,
hung him upside down from a tall tree,
weighted his feet with large stones,
and flogged him to death.
Ěrzhū Shìlóng arrived in Luòyáng.
He arrived in Luòyáng from Chángzǐ.
He reproached Shìlóng, saying:
"Uncle has been at court for a long time.
Shìlóng was a cousin of Róng.
Zhào was a nephew of Róng.
Hence, he called Shìlóng 'Uncle'.
When Empress Líng was regent,
Shìlóng was already at court,
hence 'for a long time'.
*Cháo*
is pronounced 'zhí yáo'.
How could you let the pillar of the state suffer misfortune!"
He gripped his sword and glared,
his tone and expression very severe.
Shìlóng spoke humbly and bowed in apology,
and only then was he spared.
From this, he deeply resented Zhào.
This laid the groundwork for the mutual suspicion and eventual destruction of the Ěrzhū brothers and uncle-nephew.
On the *wù shēn* day,
Wèi Chángguǎngwáng granted a general amnesty.
When Ěrzhū Róng died,
Jìngzōng ordered Héxī rebel leader Hédòulíng Bùfán to attack Xiùróng.
Bùfán resided west of the Northern River.
Hédòulíng is a three-character barbarian surname.
The *Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì* lists Hédòulíng among the southern surnames.
*Shuài*
is pronounced "suǒlèi".
*Hè*
is pronounced "xiàmò".
Bùfán advanced southward,
his military strength very formidable. Thus, Zhào did not have time to linger,
and quickly returned to Jìnyáng to resist him.
He left Ěrzhū Shìlóng, Dùlǜ, Yànbó, and others to guard Luòyáng.
On the *jiǎ yín* day,
Zhào relocated Jìngzōng to Jìnyáng.
Zhào himself supervised the inspection of resources at Héliáng.
Héliáng
is Hébriáo.
*Jiān*
is pronounced "gōngxián".
He led his cavalry on an eastern patrol,
intending to intercept him,
but failed.
He then wrote to Zhào,
explaining the consequences and benefits,
saying it was improper to harm the Son of Heaven
and earn a bad reputation.
Zhào was angered
and did not accept it.
Ěrzhū Tiānguāng, with light cavalry, entered Luò,
met Shìlóng and others,
and then returned to Yōngzhōu.
Previously,
Jìngzōng feared that the northern army would be at a disadvantage.
The northern army
refers to Yuán Zǐgōng's army stationed at Dāngǔ.
He claimed it was for an expedition against the barbarians,
appointing Gāo Dàomù as the Southern Route Grand Executive.
Before he could depart, Zhào entered Luò.
Dàomù feigned illness and left.
Shìlóng killed him.
The officials requested posthumous honors for Lǐ Miáo.
Shìlóng said:
"At that time, public opinion
was that in one or two more days, they would unleash the troops to plunder extensively
and burn down the capital and surrounding areas.
Thanks to Miáo,
the capital was preserved.
This was a good deed for the whole world,
and should not be revoked."
When Ěrzhū Róng died,
Shìlóng and others levied troops from Fáng Mú, a native of Dài and the Grand Administrator of Dàníng.
Wèi Shōu's records state: During the Xiàochāng reign of Wèi, Tàiníng Commandery was established,
subordinate to Jiànzhōu.
Its territory should be within the present-day Qìnshuǐ County of Zézhōu in the Táng Dynasty.
"Dà"
should be
"Tài."
Previously, Fáng Mú had executed three of their envoys,
and dispatched his younger brother Yù to Luòyáng.
When Zhào gained his ambition,
his partisan, Shìlán Āndìng, the Prefect of Jiànzhōu—
Shìlán
is the surname;
Āndìng
is his given name—
the people of Shǔ in the commandery heard of it
and all rebelled.
This refers to the people of Shǔ residing in Tàiníng,
similar to the Fén-Shǔ and Jiàng-Shǔ people.
Fáng Mú was ordered to comfort and reassure them at the front.
When the various bandits saw Mú,
there was none who did not bow from afar.
The horse Mú had previously ridden,
Āndìng had given to his generals and soldiers.
After a defeat in battle,
the people of Shǔ obtained it
and, thinking Mú had been killed,
all wept sorrowfully.
They cared for his horse well,
not allowing anyone to ride it.
Children and women competed to offer grass and grain,
all saying, "This is Lord Fáng's horse!"
Ěrzhū Shìlóng heard of this,
pardoned his offense,
and made him Chief Clerk of his administration.
Yáng Jìn, the Grand Imperial Censor of the Northern Route,
finding his forces few,
remained in Yè to recruit more,
intending to enter Bìngzhōu from Fúkǒu.
Coincidentally, Ěrzhū Zhào entered Luò,
so Jìn dispersed his troops
and returned to court with light cavalry.
Ěrzhū Shìlóng and his brothers secretly plotted,
fearing that Wèi Shì, the mother of the Prince of Chángguǎng, would interfere in court politics.
They waited for her to go out,
and sent dozens of cavalry, disguised as robbers, to kill her in a capital lane.
A straight road is called "jiē" (street),
a winding one is called "xiàng" (lane).
Jīngxiàng
refers to the winding lanes of Luòjīng.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
Sī,
pronounced xiāng lì fān.
On the day of Jiǎzǐ,
Ěrzhū Zhào strangled Jìngzōng in the Sānjí Buddhist Temple in Jìnyáng.
He was twenty-four years old.
The deposed emperor posthumously bestowed on him the title of Wǔhuái Emperor.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ was enthroned,
due to a temple taboo,
the posthumous title was changed to Xiàozhuāng Emperor,
and the temple name was Jìngzōng.
Yì,
pronounced yú cì fān,
also yú jì fān.
In this month,
Hédòulíng Bùfān greatly defeated Ěrzhū Zhào at Xiùróng,
pressing southwards towards Jìnyáng.
Zhào, in fear,
sent someone to summon Gāo Huān to combine forces.
The "Kǎo Yì" states: In Mùróng Shàozōng's biography in the "Běiqí Shǐ":
"Zhào summoned Gāozǔ.
Shàozōng advised, 'Today, the world is in turmoil,
and people harbor ambitious designs.
This is precisely the time for wise men to employ their strategies.
Gāo Jìnzhōu is mighty in talent and fierce in spirit,
with extraordinary strategic brilliance that covers the age,
like a qiónglóng (horned dragon).
How can one lend him clouds and rain?'
Zhào angrily said, 'I and Jìnzhōu treat each other with sincerity.
How can you suddenly sow discord between us!'
He imprisoned Shàozōng.
After several days,
he released him."
The "Běi Shǐ"
states Shàozōng's words were uttered when Shénwǔ requested to lead the surrendered households to settle in Shāndōng.
However, Zhào first summoned Huān to save himself,
which was not a time for suspicion and resentment.
We now follow the "Běi Shǐ."
Huān said,
"Zhào is in dire straits now,
so there is no need to fear any other concerns."
Thereupon, he set out.
Hèbá Yān Guòér, one of Huān's confidants, requested to proceed slowly to wear down Zhào.
Huān often delayed,
citing that there were no bridges across the river
and thus he could not cross.
This river is probably the Fén Hé.
Zhào was repeatedly defeated and
sent urgent pleas to Huān.
Huān then went to join him.
Zhào at that time moved south to avoid Bùfān.
When Bùfān reached Pínglè Commandery—
"Pínglè Commandery,"
according to Ěrzhū Zhào's biography, should be
"Lèpíng Commandery."
During the Latter Hàn Dynasty, Emperor Xiàndì divided Tàiyuán to establish Lèpíng Commandery,
with its seat at Zhānchéng.
Líaozhōu of the Táng Dynasty was its territory—
he greatly defeated him and
executed Bùfān at Shígǔ Shān.
Wèi Shōu's records state: Shígǔ Shān is in Xiùróng County, Xiùróng Commandery.
Zhào was grateful to Huān and
swore brotherhood with him.
He went to Huān with dozens of cavalry
and feasted and drank all night.
Initially,
over two hundred thousand of Gě Róng's troops migrated into Bìng and Sì,
and were oppressed by the Qìhú.
Qìhú
refers to the people of Ěrzhū's tribe.
Qì,
pronounced qī qì fān.
They rebelled twenty-six times, both large and small,
and half were executed,
yet they still ceaselessly plotted rebellion.
Zhào was troubled by this and
asked Huān for advice.
Huān said,
"The rebels from the Six Garrisons
cannot all be killed.
Since the defeats of Pòliùhán Bálíng and Dù Luòzhōu,
their forces all joined Gě Róng,
and they are all people from the Six Garrisons.
If only their commanders are punished for their offenses,
then those to be punished will be few."
Zhào said,
"Excellent!
Who can be made their envoy?"
Hèbá Yǔn was present at the time
and requested that Huān be appointed to lead them.
Huān punched him in the mouth,
breaking a tooth,
and said,
"In the past, when I was Tiānzhù,

This event is found in volume 150, Pǔtōng 5th year.
You did not come with Shìlóng and the others,
but marched east to attack Zhòngyuǎn,
this is a second crime.
This event is found in the previous volume, previous year.
What more do you have to say now?"
Shèng replied:
"Kěgū was a great scourge to the state.
My father and I executed him,
our merit was not small.
Do you instead consider this a crime?
When Tiānzhù was killed,
it was a ruler executing a minister.
I would rather fail the king
than fail the imperial court.
As for today's matter,
my life and death are in the king's hands.
But bandits are close at hand,
and kin are at odds.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been a state like this that did not perish.
I do not fear death,
but I fear the king will make a miscalculation."
Zhào then spared him.
Gāo Huān (高歡) was about to engage in battle with Zhào (兆),
but feared the strength of Zhào's (兆) forces.
He consulted with his trusted Dūdū (都督) Duàn Sháo (段韶).
The title "Qīnxìn Dūdū (親信都督)"
was first established at the end of the Wèi (魏) dynasty by various generals who had personal troops,
to oversee these personal troops.
Sháo (韶) said:
"What is meant by 'multitudes'
is gaining the allegiance unto death of the people."
This means gaining the utmost effort unto death from the people.
"It is about gaining the hearts of all under heaven.
The Ěrzhū (爾朱) clan first assassinated the Son of Heaven,
then slaughtered high officials,
and finally oppressed the common people.
Your Highness (王) is attacking the rebellious with righteousness;
it is like hot water melting snow.
How can their forces be strong!"
Huān (歡) said:
"Even so,
I am facing a large enemy with a small force.
I fear that without the Mandate of Heaven, I cannot succeed."
Sháo (韶) said:
"I have heard that 'the small can defeat the great,
a small Way can overcome great depravity.'
And 'Heaven shows no partiality,
but aids only the virtuous.'
'The small can defeat the great,
a small Way can overcome great depravity,'
is a saying of Jì Liáng (季梁), a grandee of Suí (隨), recorded in the *Zuǒzhuàn* (左傳).
'Heaven shows no partiality,
but aids only the virtuous,'
is from the words of Cài Zhòng zhī Mìng (蔡仲之命) in the *Shū* (書).
Duàn Sháo's (段韶) father and son rose from the northern frontier,
skilled in horsemanship and archery.
How could they utter words from the *Shū* (書)?
Wèi Shōu (魏收) recorded it thus because Sháo (韶) was an honored relative in the Northern Qí (齊),
and his clan was powerful,
so he simply put those words into his mouth.
Mencius (孟子) said:
'It is better to have no books
than to believe implicitly in all of them.'
How true!
If the hearts of heroes are lost within,
the wise will not strategize,
and the brave will not fight.
Once the hearts of the people are gone,
how can Heaven's will not follow suit!"
Sháo (韶) was the son of Róng (榮).
Duàn Róng (段榮) and Gāo Huān (高歡) were close.
On the *Xīnhài* day,
Huān (歡) severely defeated Zhào (兆) at Guǎng'ā (廣阿),

In the eleventh month,

On the *Gēngchén* day,
Gāo Huān (高歡) of Wèi (魏) led his troops to attack Yè (鄴).
Liú Dàn (劉誕), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Xiāngzhōu (相州), fortified the city and held firm.
In this year,
Wáng Qǐdé (王乞得), a citizen of Nányánzhōu (南兗州) in Wèi (魏), robbed the Cìshǐ (刺史) Liú Shìmíng (劉世明),
and the entire prefecture surrendered.
Nányánzhōu (南兗州) was established during the Zhèngguāng (正光) era of Wèi (魏),
with its seat in Qiáochéng (譙城),
administering Chenlíu (陳留), Liáng (梁), Qiáo (譙), Pèi (沛), Xiàcài (下蔡), Běiliáng (北梁), Mǎtóu (馬頭), and other commanderies.

when the households crossed the river.

Shìmíng (世明) was appointed Grand General Pacifying the West (Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn 征西大將jūn) and Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yǐngzhōu (郢州),

Shìmíng (世明) refused the appointment

Shìmíng (世明) arrived in Luòyáng (洛陽),

"One exerts their ability and takes office;

in the first month,

After the Emperor (上) had enfeoffed Zhāomíng's (昭明) sons,

He meant that the Emperor (帝) had once adopted Zhèngdé (正德) as a son,

Yángzhì (颺摯),

He dug tunnels,
set up pillars, and then burned them,

Tunnels were dug under the city wall but were not yet completed.
Fearing that the earth would collapse and prevent the completion of the work,

the pillars were burned,

Líng (㥄)
was the fifth-generation descendant of Chěng (逞).
Yuán Fǎsēng (元法僧), the Tàiwèi (太尉), was appointed Prince of Eastern Wèi (Dōngwèi Wáng 東魏王).
The Emperor (上) had already appointed Yuán Yuè (元悅) as Prince of Wèi (魏)
and sent him to enter from the western route;
he also sent Yuán Fǎsēng (元法僧) to enter from the eastern route,

Yáng Kǎn (羊侃), Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yǎnzhōu (兗州), was appointed Jūnsīmǎ (軍司馬),
and traveled with Fǎsēng (法僧).
The shopkeepers all closed their establishments and did not come out.
Hé Zhìtōng (何智通), the Shàofǔ Chéng (少府丞), reported the matter as it happened.
Lún (綸) was reprimanded and sent back to his residence.
He then dispatched his retainer Dài Zǐgāo (戴子高) and others to stab Zhìtōng (智通) with a spear in the Dūxiàng (都巷).
Dūxiàng (都巷)
is the same as the earlier mentioned Jīngxiàng (京巷).
*Shuò* (槊)
pronounced 'sè jiǎo fān' (色角翻).
*Cì* (刺)
pronounced 'qī yì fān' (七亦翻).
Zhìtōng (智通) recognized Zǐgāo (子高).
He took his blood and used his finger to write the character

on the carriage wall,
then he died.

On the *Gēngxū* day,
Lún (綸) was dismissed as a commoner,
and locked in his residence.
After two *xún* (旬) (twenty days),
his lock was removed,
and after a while, his title was restored.
the Prince of Āndìng (安定王) posthumously honored Jìngzōng (敬宗) as Emperor Wǔhuái (武懷皇帝).
After Lǎng (朗) had abdicated,
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武帝) enfeoffed him as Prince of Āndìng (安定王).
On the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
Gāo Huān (高歡) was appointed Chéngxiàng (丞相), Zhùguó Dàjiāngjūn (柱國大將軍), and Tàishī (太師).
In the third month,
on the *Bǐngyín* day,
Gāo Chéng (高澄) was appointed Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍).
On the *Dīngchǒu* day,
the Prince of Āndìng (安定王) led the hundred officials to reside in Yè (鄴).
Ěrzhū Zhào (爾朱兆) and Ěrzhū Shìlóng (爾朱世隆) and others were mutually suspicious and obstructed each other.
Shìlóng (世隆) used humble words and generous gifts to persuade Zhào (兆),
wanting him to go to Luò (洛) and granting him whatever he desired.
He also requested that Emperor Jiémiǎn (節閔帝) take Zhào's (兆) daughter as empress.
Zhào (兆) was then pleased,
and he, along with Tiānguāng (天光) and Dùlǜ (度律), renewed their vows,
and became close again.
Húsi Chūn (斛斯椿) secretly told Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝):
“Everyone hates and resents the Érzhū (爾朱) clan,
yet we serve them.
Our demise is imminent.
It would be better to plot against them.”
Shèng (勝) said:
“Tiānguāng (天光) and Zhào (兆) each hold a region.
It will be very difficult to eliminate them all.
If we don't eliminate them completely,
it will certainly lead to future trouble.
What should we do?”
Chūn (椿) said:
“This is easily achieved.”
Then he persuaded Shìlóng (世隆) to summon Tiānguāng (天光) and others to Luòyáng (洛陽)
to jointly attack Gāo Huān (高歡).
Shìlóng (世隆) repeatedly summoned Tiānguāng (天光),
but Tiānguāng (天光) did not come.
He sent Chūn (椿) himself to invite him,
saying:
“Gāo Huān (高歡) is stirring up rebellion.
Only you, the King, can settle it.
How can you sit idly by and watch your clan be annihilated?!”
Tiānguāng (天光), having no choice,
was about to set out east.
He consulted Hèbá Yuè (賀拔岳), the Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州), for advice.
Hèbá Yuè (賀拔岳) had moved from Qízhōu (岐州) to become Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州).
Yōng (雍),
read as ‘yòng’.
“Our royal house spans three regions.
Zhào (兆) holds the north of Bīng (幷) and Fén (汾),
Tiānguāng (天光) controls Guān (關) and Lǒng (隴) in the west,
Zhòngyuǎn (仲遠) commands Xú (徐) and Yǎn (兗).
Thus, we span three regions.
Gāo Huān’s (高歡) rabble
cannot possibly be our match!
As long as we are united in spirit and effort,
there is no venture that will not succeed.
But if there is suspicion among kin,
then we won't even have time to ensure our own survival,
how can we control others?
In my humble opinion,
it would be best to first secure Guānzhōng (關中) to solidify our foundation.
Send out elite troops to join forces with the main army.
Advancing, we can conquer the enemy;
retreating, we can protect ourselves.”
Tiānguāng (天光) did not follow this advice.
In the intercalary month,
on the day Rén Yín (壬寅),
Tiānguāng (天光) from Cháng’ān (長安),
Zhào (兆) from Jìnyáng (晉陽),
Dùlǜ (度律) from Luòyáng (洛陽),
and Zhòngyuǎn (仲遠) from Dōngjùn (東郡) all met at Yè (鄴).
Their forces numbered two hundred thousand,
camping along both sides of the Huán Shuǐ (洹水).
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù (水經註) states: The Huán Shuǐ (洹水) flows past the south of Yè (鄴) city.
Huán (洹),
read as ‘yuán’.
They commanded the combined forces.
Gāo Huān (高歡) ordered the Minister of Personnel, Fēng Lóngzhī (封隆之), to defend Yè (鄴).
On the day Guǐ Chǒu (癸丑),
he moved out to encamp at Zǐmò (紫陌).
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù (水經註) states: The Zhāng Shuǐ (漳水) flows east out of the mountains past Yè (鄴),
then north past the west of Jìmò (祭陌).
During the Warring States period,
folk witches would arrange marriages for the River God,
making offerings on this path.
Tián Róng (田融) believed it to be Zǐmò (紫陌).
In the eleventh year of Jiànwǔ (建武) of Zhào (趙),
a floating bridge was built over the water at Zǐmò (紫陌).
Huān (歡) said: “The troops under Gāo Dūdū (高都督) are all Hàn (漢) soldiers.
I fear they may not be sufficient for the task.
I wish to allot over a thousand Xiānbēi (鮮卑) soldiers to be mixed in and used.
What do you think?”
Áocáo (敖曹) said:
“The troops I lead
have been well-trained for a long time.
In previous battles,
they were no less capable than the Xiānbēi (鮮卑).
If we mix them now,
their dispositions will not be compatible.
If victorious, they will contend for credit; if they retreat, they will shift blame.
There is no need to reassign them.”
On the day Gēng Shēn (庚申),
Érzhū Zhào (爾朱兆), leading three thousand light cavalry, attacked Yè (鄴) city by night.
They knocked on the west gate,
but failed to breach it and retreated.
On the day Rén Xū (壬戌),
Huān (歡) had fewer than two thousand warhorses and fewer than thirty thousand infantry.
His numbers were no match for the enemy.
So, he formed a circular array at Hánlíng (韓陵).
The Wǔ Dài Zhì (五代志) states: There is Hánlíng Shān (韓陵山) in Yè (鄴) county.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: It is northeast of Ānyáng (安陽) county in Xiāngzhōu (相州).
Chén (陳),
read as ‘zhèn’.
At this, all the officers and soldiers were determined to fight to the death.
Zhào (兆), seeing Huān (歡),
accused Huān (歡) from afar of betraying him.
Huān (歡) said:
“The original reason we exerted our efforts together
was to jointly assist the imperial house.
Where is the Son of Heaven now?”
Zhào (兆) said:
“Yǒng’ān (永安) wrongfully harmed Tiānzhù (天柱),
I am merely seeking revenge.”
Jìngzōng’s (敬宗) reign title was Yǒng’ān (永安),
hence he is referred to by it.
“I heard Tiānzhù’s (天柱) plan in the past.
You were standing in front of the door.
How can you say you did not rebel?!”
“Let us expose his conspiracy before both armies
to justify the crimes of the Érzhū (爾朱) clan.

“Today, our righteousness is severed.”
Then they fought.
Huān (歡) commanded the central army,
Gāo Áocáo (高敖曹) commanded the left army,
and Huān’s (歡) paternal younger brother Yuè (岳) commanded the right army.
Huān (歡) was losing the battle.
Zhào (兆) and others pressed their advantage.
Yuè (岳) charged their front with five hundred cavalry.
The detached general Húfú Dūn (斛律敦) gathered the scattered soldiers and pursued their rear.
Áocáo (敖曹) sallied out from Lìyuán (栗園) with a thousand cavalry and struck them from the flank.
Zhào (兆) and others were utterly defeated.
Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝) and the Inspector of Xúzhōu (徐州), Dù Dé (杜德), surrendered to Huān (歡) on the battlefield.
Zhào (兆) clutched his chest before Mùróng Shàozōng (慕容紹宗) and said:
“Not listening to your words
has brought me to this!”
This refers to Shàozōng (紹宗) advising Zhào (兆) to let Huān (歡) command the provincial and garrison troops, but Zhào (兆) did not follow it.
He fled west from Yè (鄴) back to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Xú Guǎng's (徐廣) Chēfú Yízhì (車服儀制) states: The horn (角)
is not recorded in earlier historical documents.

used to startle Chinese horses.

Zhào (兆) returned to Jìnyáng (晉陽),

Qín (秦) established Dōngjùn (東郡).

He wanted to personally lead troops to defend Héquiáo (河橋),

The Grand Commander Húsi Chūn (斛斯椿) said to Commanders Jiǎ Xiǎndù (賈顯度) and Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì (賈顯智):
“If we don’t first capture the Érzhū (爾朱) clan,

Shìlóng (世隆) sent his external military assistant, Yáng Shūyuān (陽叔淵),

Běizhōng (北中)
was the city of the Běizhōng Lángfǔ (北中郎府),

He ordered him to admit them in sequence.
When Chūn (椿) arrived,

So, he cunningly told Shūyuān (叔淵):
“Tiānguāng’s (天光) subordinates are all Westerners.
I hear they intend to extensively loot Luòyì (洛邑)

Shūyuān (叔淵) believed him.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Jiǎ Zǐ (甲子),
Chūn (椿) and others entered and seized Héquiáo (河橋),
killing all partisans of the Érzhū (爾朱) clan.
Dùlǜ (度律) and Tiānguāng (天光) wanted to attack them,

The soldiers and horses were exhausted,

So, they fled west.
Upon reaching Léibēi Jīn (灅陂津),
they were captured by someone
and sent to Chūn’s (椿) location.
Léibēi Jīn (灅陂津) was west of Héquiáo (河橋),
also called Léibō (雷波),
the very place where Érzhū Zhào (爾朱兆) assaulted Luò (洛) by leading cavalry to wade across the shallow waters.
Lěi (灅),
read as ‘shuǐ’.
Separately, Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì (賈顯智) and Zhāng Huān (張歡) were dispatched to lead cavalry to ambush Shìlóng (世隆)
and captured him.
Yànbó (彥伯) was on duty in the palace guard at the time.
Chángsūn Zhì (長孫稚) at the Shénhǔ Mén (神虎門) announced:
“Gāo Huān’s (高歡) righteous merit has already risen.
We request the execution of the Érzhū (爾朱) clan.”
Emperor Jiémǐn (節閔) sent his chamberlain Guō Chóng (郭崇) to inform Yànbó (彥伯).
Yànbó (彥伯) fled in a panic,
was captured by someone,

Their heads, along with those of Dùlǜ (度律) and Tiānguāng (天光), were sent to Gāo Huān (高歡).
Jí Mǐn Dì sent the Censor-in-Chief Lú Biàn to extend condolences to Huān at Yè.
Huān had him meet with the Prince of Āndìng.
Biàn resisted the order and refused to comply.
Huān could not force him,
so he let him go.
Biàn
was the nephew of Tóng.
Lú Tóng first attached himself to Yuán Chā to advance his career.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Hóu Jǐng, the General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry and acting governor of Jìzhōu, surrendered to the Prince of Āndìng.
Jǐng was appointed Minister of Personnel, Grand Administrator of the Southern Route, and Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Ěrzhū Zhòngyuǎn came over to surrender.
Qióng Níng and Zhāng Zǐqī, commandants under Zhòngyuǎn, came from Huátái to surrender to Huān.
Huān reproached them, saying:
"You served Zhòngyuǎn,
benefited from his glory and profit,
made numerous oaths and covenants,
promising to share life and death.
Qì means
'oath'.
Chóng means
'many'.
You were the ringleaders
(this refers to the previous year when Zhòngyuǎn raised troops to march on Luòyáng);
now you have betrayed him again.
Serving the Son of Heaven, you were disloyal;
serving Zhòngyuǎn, you were faithless.
Even dogs and horses recognize those who feed them;
you are not even as good as dogs and horses!"
Thereupon, he had them executed.
When Ěrzhū Tiānguāng moved east,
he left his younger brother Xiǎnshòu to guard Cháng'ān,
and summoned Hóu Mòchén Yuè, the Inspector of Qínzhōu, intending to go east with him.
Hèbá Yuè knew Tiānguāng would surely fail,
and wanted to keep Yuè to plot against Xiǎnshòu in response to Gāo Huān,
but had not yet come up with a plan.
Yǔwén Tài said to Yuè:
"Today, Tiānguāng is still close,
and Yuè may not have a change of heart.
If we tell him this,
I fear he will be alarmed and frightened.
However, although Yuè is the commanding general,
he cannot control his subordinates.
If we first persuade his troops,
everyone will certainly consider staying.
Yuè, missing Ěrzhū's deadline to advance,
and fearing a change in popular sentiment if he retreats,
if we persuade him under these circumstances,
there is nothing that will not succeed."
Yuè was greatly pleased,
and immediately ordered Tài to enter Yuè's army and persuade him.
Yuè then joined Yuè in attacking Cháng'ān.
Yuè was the Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
originally governing Cháng'ān;
when Tiānguāng went east,
he was sent to defend the northwest.
Xiǎnshòu abandoned the city and fled;
they pursued him to Huáyīn
and captured him.
Huān appointed Yuè as the Grand Administrator of Guānxī.
The "Kǎo Yì" states: "The 'Běi Shǐ' says:
'Xuē Xiàotōng was the Director of the Department of the Secretariat,
and said: "Guānzhōng is strategically important and the old capital of Qín and Hàn.
We must plan in advance to guard it as a fallback.
Even if we suffer losses north of the Yellow River,

Jí Mǐn Dì deeply agreed,

Hú Sīchūn had a little talent

Huān bowed twice,
and Xiū also bowed.
Huān left to prepare imperial robes and carriages,

Yán (嚴) here means to be on alert.

He said:

The Book of Documents says: "The position of Heaven is difficult indeed."

The King of Píngyáng looked at the memorial urging him to ascend the throne and made this statement;

From Emperor Xiàowén, the Wèi dynasty adopted the customs of the Xià (Han) to transform the barbarians.

Màiyì Commandery's Shànyáng County,

courtesy name Tǔwàn Rén.

Zú (卒),

Ōu (毆),

The Ruler of Wèi, avoiding the taboo of Guǎngpíng Wǔmùwáng's name,

The rules for posthumous titles state: "Wǔ (martial) without accomplishment is Zhuāng (solemn)";

In autumn,
the seventh month,

Wèi reinstated Nányángwáng Bǎojù as Tàiwèi.

Huān's army camped in Wǔxiāng.
The Jìn established Wǔxiāng County,

Bìng Zhōu was pacified.
Huān considered Jìnyáng to be a place of strategic importance with its four natural barriers.
The area of Tàiyuán Commandery,

On the 12th day, Wèi resettled people from Xià Zhōu, and Guō Qiān, one of them, revolted in Qīng Zhōu.
Guō Qiān, having moved from Xià Zhōu to Qīng Zhōu,

Yáng Kǎn traveled to Guānzhú.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Suī River flows southeast from Suīyáng,

Lush green bamboo by the water shades the banks,
a verdant sight as far as the eye can see.

In the ninth month,

On Yǐ-sì,

In winter,
in the eleventh month,
on Dīng-yǒu,
the sun reached its southernmost point.
On the summer solstice, the sun reaches its northernmost point.
On the winter solstice, the sun reaches its southernmost point.

Bān Zhì states: The sun travels on the path of light,
reaching Dōngjǐng at the summer solstice,

Sīmǎ Biāo's Zhì states: The sun's path begins in the south,

When it is furthest and longest,

The sun's path converges in the north,
the closer it is to the pole,
the shorter its shadow.
When it is closest and shortest,
it is the summer solstice.
In ancient times, people served Heaven according to celestial phenomena,

Zhōngdàtōng Fifth Year (Guǐ-chǒu, 533)
1 Spring,
first month,
on Xīn-mǎo,
the Emperor performed the southern suburban sacrifice

Gāo Huān defeated Ěrzhū Zhào at Chìhóng Lǐng,

Hōng (谼)
is pronounced like "hù gōng".

We now follow the Qí Shū.
Zhào fled to the desolate mountains,

treated them very generously.
Yìgù (義故)
is equivalent to Yìjiù (義舊, 'old acquaintance through righteousness').
All of Zhào's attendants secretly communicated with Huān,
but only Zhāng Liàng did not send any messages.
Huān admired this
and appointed him as a Staff Officer in the Chéngxiàng's office.

Wèi appointed Lǐ Píng as Xíngtái,
giving him command over all armies attacking Xiáshí.
This was a revival of the system established in the early Wèi.
At the end of Zhèngguāng, when banditry arose,

his grandmother, Fèng Shì, as Wǔmù Hòu,
and his mother, Lǐ Shì, as Huáng Tàihòu.
6 Cáo Fèng, the Inspector of Láozhōu, and Léi Néngshèng, the Inspector of Dōngjīngzhōu, and others surrendered their cities to Wèi.
Cáo Fèng and Léi Néngshèng
were both southern barbarians,
and they were given the positions of Zìshǐ (Inspector) in their respective territories.
Jiàng (降)
is pronounced like "hù jiāng".
7 Hú Sīchūn, the Grandee Secretary of Wèi, heard of the deaths of Qiáo Níng and Zhāng Zǐqī.
The deaths of Níng and Zǐqī
are recorded in the previous year of the preceding volume.
He secretly advised the Wèi ruler, along with Nányáng Wáng Bǎojù, General of the Palace Guard Yuán Pí, and Wáng Sīzhèng, to plot against Chancellor Huān.
Chūn had always harbored the intention to plot against Huān,
and due to the deaths of Qiáo and Zhāng, fearing that disaster would soon reach him,
he resolved to act.
He was a great-grandson of Zūn.
At the beginning of Dàowǔ's reign, Chángshān Wáng Zūn had assisted in the founding of the dynasty.
The Emperor was displeased by this.
Chūn advised the Emperor to establish a department of *bùqǔ* (privately-raised soldiers) within the inner palace,
and also to increase the number of Wǔzhí (imperial guardsmen).
From the Zhíhé (Palace Guards) downwards,
there were several hundred personnel in each category.
Wǔzhí (武直)
refers to the armed guardsmen who were on duty in the palace chambers.
According to the records of the Five Dynasties, in the system of the Northern Qí,
the generals of the Lǐngjūn Fǔ (Headquarters of the Commander of the Guards)
were in charge of guarding the palace from the Forbidden Chambers to the Zhūhuá Gé (Red Flower Pavilion) and outwards,
and all imperial guard officials were under their command.
Additionally, the Zuǒyòu Wèi Fǔ (Left and Right Guard Headquarters)
each had one general
in charge of the left and right wings,
encompassing areas outside the Zhūhuá Gé,
each assisted by two Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (Generals of the Martial Guard).

Among the officials subordinate to the Yùzhàng (Imperial Standard) were the Yùzhàng Zhèngfù Dūdū (Chief and Deputy Commanders of the Imperial Standard), the Yùzhàng Wǔzhí (Five Ranks of the Imperial Standard), and other personnel.

Subordinate to the Zhídàng (Direct Charge) were the Zhídàng Zhèngfù Dūdū (Chief and Deputy Commanders of the Direct Charge), the Zhírù Zhèngfù Dūdū (Chief and Deputy Commanders of the Direct Entry), the Xūnwǔ Qiánfēng Zhèngfù Dūdū (Chief and Deputy Commanders of the Vanguard of Meritorious Martiality), the Xūnwǔ Qiánfēng Wǔzhí (Five Ranks of the Vanguard of Meritorious Martiality), and other personnel.

Subordinate to the Zhíwèi (Direct Guard) were the Zhíwèi Zhèngfù Dūdū (Chief and Deputy Commanders of the Direct Guard), the Yìwèi Zhèngfù Dūdū (Chief and Deputy Commanders of the Wing Guard), and other personnel.
Subordinate to the Zhítū (Direct Assault) were the Zhítū Dūdū (Commander of the Direct Assault), the Qiánfēng Sǎndūdū (Dispersed Commander of the Vanguard), and other personnel.

Subordinate to the Zhíhé (Palace Guards) were the Zhūyī Zhíhé (Crimson-Robed Palace Guards), Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (Palace Guard Generals), Zhíqǐn (Palace Attendants), Zhízhāi (Palace Chamber Attendants), Zhíhòu (Palace Waiters), and their subordinates.
There were also Yúnqí (Cloud Riders), Wǔqí (Martial Riders), Xiāoqí (Valiant Riders), Yóují (Skirmishers), and generals of the Front, Left, Right, and Rear;
Zuǒyòu Hǔbēn (Left and Right Tiger Swift) Zhonglangjiāng (Commanders of the Gentleman-of-the-Household);
and colonels of the Bùbīng (Infantry), Yuèqí (Elite Cavalry), Shèshēng (Archer-Sound), Túnqí (Encamped Cavalry), Chángshuǐ (Long Water), etc.;
Fèngchē and Qí Èrdūdūwèi (Commanders of the Chariot and Cavalry Escort);

Yǔlín Jiān (Superintendent of the Feathered Forest), Cóng Púshè (Minister of the Attendant Retinue), Jīnǔ (Massed Crossbows), Jīshè (Massed Archers), Qiángnǔ (Strong Crossbows), Diànzhōng (Within the Palace) generals, as well as Yuánwài Jiāngjūn (Generals without Portfolio), Wǔqí Chángshì (Martial Rider Regular Attendants), Diànzhōng Sīmǎ Dū (Superintendent of the Palace Cavalry), Yuánwài Sīmǎ Dū (Superintendent of Cavalry without Portfolio), and others.
This system likely originated in the Jìn dynasty,
with additions and deletions in successive generations.
Observing the Northern Qí system,
one can generally see the increases made at that time.
The Emperor frequently went on excursions,
and Chūn personally organized
them into separate formations.
Consequently, the Emperor exclusively decided on court affairs and military strategies with Chūn.
The Emperor, knowing that Hèbá Yuè, Grand Xíngtái of Guānzhōng, commanded a large army,
secretly allied with him.
He also appointed Grandee Secretary Hèbá Shèng as Dūdū of the armies of the seven prefectures including the three Jīng prefectures,
intending to rely on the Shèng brothers to counter Huān.
This means relying on Shèng and Yuè.
While Gāo Gān, Grandee Secretary and Minister of Works, was in Xìndū,
he suffered the loss of his father
and did not have time to complete the mourning period.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ ascended the throne,
Gān submitted a memorial requesting to resign from his position to observe mourning.
An imperial edict permitted him to resign as Grandee Secretary.
(This sentence is complete.)
Although Gān had sought to retire,
he did not expect to be granted permission so quickly.
Once he had left the inner court,
he was no longer involved in many court affairs,
and he was often discontent.
Since the Emperor had become estranged from Huān,
he hoped to use Gān for his own purposes.
Once, after a banquet in the Huálín Yuán (Flower Forest Garden),
he kept Gān alone
and said to him:
"Minister of Works, your family has been loyal for generations,
meaning from Gāo Yǔn onwards.
Although our relationship is that of ruler and minister,
in righteousness we are like brothers.
We should swear an oath together
to strengthen our bond."
He pressed him earnestly.
Gān replied:
"I have pledged my life to the state;
how dare I be disloyal?"
At the time, events were sudden,
and he did not expect the Emperor to have other plans,
so he did not firmly refuse,
nor did he inform Huān.
However, when the Emperor established his *bùqǔ*,
Gān privately told his trusted confidants:
"The Emperor does not rely on meritorious elders but instead gathers petty individuals,
and frequently sends Yuán Shìbì and Wáng Sīzhèng to go back and forth to Guānxī to consult with Hèbá Yuè.
He also sent Hèbá Shèng to Jīngzhōu,
outwardly showing distance and suspicion,
but inwardly establishing a faction,
allowing their brothers to be close,
hoping to seize control of the west.
Disaster is about to strike,
and it will surely involve us."
He then secretly informed Huān.
Huān summoned Gān to Bìngzhōu,
where they discussed current affairs face-to-face.
Gān then advised Huān to accept the abdication of Wèi.
Huān covered his mouth with his sleeve and said:
"Do not speak such nonsense!
I will now appoint you, Minister of Works, as Grandee Secretary again,
and all affairs of the Ménxià (Chancellery) will be entrusted to you."
Huān repeatedly requested this,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Gān knew that trouble was about to arise,
and secretly requested Huān to make him Inspector of Xúzhōu.
In the second month,
on the *xīnyǒu* day,
Gān was appointed General of Agile Cavalry, Initiator of a Household with Three Sī, and Inspector of Xúzhōu.
Xiányáng Wáng Tǎn was appointed Minister of Works.
This was to lay the groundwork for the Wèi ruler to kill Gāo Gān and attack Gāo Huān.
8 On the *guǐwèi* day,
the Emperor visited Tóngtài Sì,
where he lectured on the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
It lasted for seven days,
and tens of thousands of people attended.
9 Before Zhèngguāng of Wèi,
Āzhìluó had always been allied with Wèi.
Āzhìluó
refers to the Gāochē people.
The Wèi Shū states: "In the third year of Xīnghé during Emperor Xiàojìng's reign,
Fùfúluó Yuèjūnzǐ, the ruler of Āzhìluó, came to surrender,
and was enfeoffed as King of Gāochē."
Āzhìluó also rebelled,
but Chancellor Huān appeased them,
and Āzhìluó surrendered again,
a total of 100,000 households.
In the third month,
on the *xīnmǎo* day,
an edict again appointed Huān as Grand Xíngtái.
Wèi had just abolished the various Xíngtái,
but now again appointed Huān to this position
to win over Āzhìluó.
Huān gave them grain and silk.
Some advised that this was a wasteful and useless expense,
but Huān did not heed them.
Later, when he managed the affairs of Héxī,
it proved to be very useful.
This refers to the time when he rescued Cáo Ní and conquered Wànqí Shòuluògān.
Gāo Gàn (高乾) was sent to Xúzhōu (徐州).
The Wèi (魏) lord, hearing that he had leaked state secrets,
then issued an edict to Chancellor Huān (歡), saying:
"Gàn Yōng (乾邕) and I had a private alliance.
Now he has become fickle and two-faced."
Huān (歡), hearing of his alliance with the emperor,
also disliked him.
He immediately took Gàn's (乾) previous memorials discussing current affairs and sent an envoy to seal and deliver them to the emperor.
The emperor summoned Gàn (乾)
and, in the presence of Huān's (歡) envoy, reprimanded him.
Gàn (乾) said:
"Your Majesty has established a different plan,
and yet you call me two-faced.
When the ruler adds guilt,
how can one decline?"
He was then granted death.
The emperor also secretly ordered Pān Shàoyè (潘紹業), the Inspector of Dōng Xúzhōu (東徐州), to kill his brother Áo Cáo (敖曹).
According to Lǐ Yánshòu's (李延壽) Qí Jì (齊紀),
the Wèi (魏) lord sent Pān Shàoyè (潘紹業), the Inspector of Dōng Xúzhōu (東徐州), with a secret edict to Páng Cāngyīng (龐蒼鷹), the Administrator of Chánglè (長樂), to kill Áo Cáo (敖曹).
This would mean that Gāo Áo Cáo (高敖曹) was in Xìndū (信都) at this time.
Strongmen were ambushed on the road,
seizing Shàoyè (紹業)
and finding the imperial edict in his robe collar.
He then, with more than ten horsemen, fled to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Huān (歡) embraced his head and wept, saying:
"The Son of Heaven has wrongly harmed Sīkōng (司空)."
Áo Cáo's (敖曹) elder brother Zhòngmì (仲密) was the Inspector of Guāngzhōu (光州).
The emperor ordered Qīngzhōu (青州) to block his return path.
Zhòngmì (仲密) also secretly traveled to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Zhòngmì's (仲密) given name was Shèn (慎),
but he was known by his courtesy name.
11. Wèi (魏) Grand Tutor, Prince of Lǔjùn (魯郡), Wáng Sù (王肅) passed away.
12. On the day Bǐngchén (丙辰),
the Prince Yuán Xiāng (元襄) of Nánpíng (南平), Wěi (偉), passed away.
13. On the day Dīngsì (丁巳),
Wèi (魏) appointed Zhào Jùnwáng Chén (趙郡王諶) as Grand Commandant
and Nányángwáng Bǎo Jù (南陽王寶炬) as Grand Guardian.
14. When Wèi (魏) Ěrzhū Zhào (爾朱兆) entered Luò (洛),
(Zhào (兆) entered Luò (洛), see year two, volume one hundred fifty-four.)
all the bells and chimes were destroyed.
Emperor Jiémǐn (節閔) ordered Chángsūn Zhì (長孫稚), Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Zǔ Yíng (祖瑩), Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, among others, to re-cast them.
By this time, they were completed
and named Dàchéng Yuè (大成樂, Grand Perfection Music).
15. In Wèi (魏) Qīngzhōu (青州), the commoner Gěng Xiáng (耿翔) gathered a multitude and plundered Sān Qí (三齊).
Sān Qí (三齊)
is referred to by the old names from the Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢) dynasties.
He focused solely on high-flown talk
and made no preparations for defense.
In summer,
fourth month,
Xiáng (翔) suddenly attacked the prefecture city.
In the second year of Wèi Yǒng'ān (永安),
Jiāozhōu (膠州) was established,
with its seat in Dōngwǔchéng (東武城),
administering Dōngwǔ (東武), Gāomì (高密), and Píngchāng (平昌) commanderies.
Dōngwǔchéng (東武城)
is today's Zhūchéng (諸城) County in Mìzhōu (密州).
Càn (粲) said:
"How can this be?!"
Those around him then said that they had already entered the city gate.
Càn (粲) then slowly said:
"When King Gěng (耿) arrives,
he can be led to the administrative office.
The rest of his forces
should be entrusted to the city residents."
Xiáng (翔) beheaded him
and sent his head to surrender.
16. In the fifth month,
Wèi (魏) commoners Wáng Zǎo (王早) and others from Dōng Xúzhōu (東徐州) killed Inspector Cuī Xiáng (崔庠)
and surrendered from Xiàpī (下邳).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異, Examination of Differences) states: The *Liáng Dìjì* (梁帝紀, Annals of Emperor Liáng) states:
"In the sixth month,
on the day Jǐmǎo (己卯),
Lán Bǎo (蘭寶), lord of Wèi Jiànyìchéng (魏建義城), surrendered from Xiàpī (下邳) city."
We now follow the *Wèishū* (魏書).
17. In the sixth month,
on the day Rénshēn (壬申),
Wèi (魏) appointed Fán Zihú (樊子鵠), the General of Agile Cavalry, as the Grand Envoy for Qīng (青) and Jiāo (膠)
to oversee Cài Jùn (蔡儁), the Inspector of Jìzhōu (濟州), and others in suppressing Gěng Xiáng (耿翔).
In autumn,
seventh month,
the Wèi (魏) army arrived at Qīngzhōu (青州).
Xiáng (翔) abandoned the city and fled to surrender,
and an edict appointed him Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
18. On the day Rénchén (壬辰),
Wèi (魏) appointed Guǎnglínwáng Xīn (廣陵王欣) as Grand Marshal,
and Zhào Jùnwáng Chén (趙郡王諶) as Grand Tutor.
On the day Gēngxū (庚戌),
the former Minister of Works, Hèbá Yǔn (賀拔允), was appointed Grand Commandant.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Wèi Dìjì* (魏帝紀) writes
"Hèbá Wò (賀拔渥)".
According to Yǔn's (允) courtesy name Ājúní (阿鞠埿),
the character
"ní" (埿)
was likely mistaken for
In the beginning,
Hèbá Yuè (賀拔岳) sent Féng Jǐng (馮景), a *Xíngtái Láng* (行臺郎), to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Chancellor Huān (歡), hearing of Yuè's (岳) envoy,
was greatly pleased and said:
"Does Hèbá Gōng (賀拔公) remember me?!"
He swore a blood oath with Jǐng (景),
pledging brotherhood with Yuè (岳).
Upon returning, Jǐng (景) said to Yuè (岳):
"Huān (歡) is excessively cunning and deceitful;
he cannot be trusted."
The *Fǔ Sīmǎ* (府司馬) Yǔwén Tài (宇文泰) volunteered to go to Jìnyáng (晉陽)
to observe Huān's (歡) character.
Huān (歡) was struck by his appearance and said:
"This child has an extraordinary look."
He intended to keep him,
but Tài (泰) insisted on returning to report.
Huān (歡), having sent him off, regretted it
and dispatched couriers to pursue him urgently,
but he did not catch him at the pass and returned.
Xiàng Yǔ (項羽) not killing Pèigōng (沛公),
Cáo Cāo (曹操) dismissing Liú Bèi (劉備),
Huán Xuán (桓玄) tolerating Liú Yù (劉裕) –
these are similar cases.
Those with the Mandate of Heaven
are indeed beyond human plotting.
Tài (泰) arrived in Cháng'ān (長安)
and said to Yuè (岳):
"The reason Gāo Huān (高歡) has not yet usurped the throne
is precisely that he fears your brothers;
people like Hóumòchén Yuè (侯莫陳悅) are not to be feared.
You only need to secretly make preparations,
and plotting against Huān (歡) will not be difficult.
Now, Fèiyětóu (費也頭) has no fewer than ten thousand mounted archers,
Húbá Mí'étū (斛拔彌俄突), the Inspector of Xiàzhōu (夏州), has over three thousand elite soldiers,
Cáo Ní (曹泥), the Inspector of Língzhōu (靈州), and Hédòulíng Yìlì (紇豆陵伊利) and others, leaders of the refugee communities in Héxī (河西),
each command their own forces and are of uncertain allegiance.
If you lead your army close to Lǒng (隴),
seizing its strategic points,
awe them with your might,
and win them over with your benevolence,
you can gather their soldiers and horses to augment our army.
Pacify the Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) to the west,
and soothe the Shāsài (沙塞) to the north.
(Líng (靈) and Xià (夏) are outside the *sài* (塞),
bordering the desert to the north.)
To assist the Wèi (魏) imperial house
this is an accomplishment (jǔ (舉)) like Huán (桓) and Wén (文)."
is also written as
"gōng" (功).)
He again sent Tài (泰) to Luòyáng (洛陽) to request matters
and secretly laid out the situation.
The Wèi (魏) lord was pleased
and promoted Tài (泰) to General of the Imperial Guard,
sending him back to report.
In the eighth month,
the emperor appointed Yuè (岳) as Grand Inspector of all military affairs in twenty prefectures including Yōng (雍) and Huá (華), and Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州).
(In the eleventh year of Wèi Tàihé (太和),
Huázhōu (華州) was separated from Yōngzhōu (雍州)
and administered Huáshān (華山), Chéngchéng (澄城), and Báishuǐ (白水) commanderies.)

The twenty prefectures were: Yōng (雍), Huá (華), Dōnghuá (東華), Qí (岐), Nánqí (南岐), Bīn (豳), Yuán (原), Hé (河), Wèi (渭), Jīng (涇), Xià (夏), Dōngxià (東夏), Qín (秦), Nánqín (南秦), Liáng (梁), Nánliáng (南梁), Dōngliáng (東梁), Bā (巴), Yì (益), and Dōngyì (東益).
(Yōng (雍) pronounced: "yòng".
Huá (華) pronounced: "huà".)
An envoy was sent to bestow this upon him.
Yuè (岳) then led his troops westward to garrison Píngliáng (平涼),
using the pretext of grazing horses.
This was the "close to Lǒng (隴)" mentioned earlier.
Only Cáo Ní (曹泥) sided with Huān (歡).
The Inspectors of Qín (秦), Nánqín (南秦), Hé (河), and Wèi (渭) prefectures all met in Píngliáng (平涼)
and received Yuè's (岳) command.
Yuè (岳), considering Xiàzhōu (夏州) to be a critical border stronghold,
desired to find a capable Inspector to govern it.
The assembly nominated Yǔwén Tài (宇文泰).
Yuè (岳) said:
"Yǔwén (宇文) Assistant Minister is my right and left hand;
how can he be dispensed with?"
After deliberating for several days,
he finally memorialized to appoint him.
19. In the ninth month,
on the day Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
Wèi (魏) Chancellor Huān (歡) memorialized to decline his princely title,
which was not permitted.
He requested to divide his ten thousand households of fiefdoms to be distributed to meritorious and righteous individuals.
(Meritorious and righteous individuals
refers to those who rose up from Xìndū (信都)
and rendered meritorious service in suppressing Ěrzhū (爾朱).)
20. In winter,
tenth month,
on the day Gēngshēn (庚申),
Hè Jìngrōng (何敬容), the Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and Xiè Jǔ (謝舉), the Minister of Personnel, was appointed Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
In the eleventh month of the 21st year,
on the *guǐ-sì* day,
the Wèi appointed Dí Zhēn (邸珍) of Zhōngshān, Inspector of Yīnzhōu, as Grand Commander of Xúzhōu, Traveling Vice-Director of the Eastern Department, and *Púshè*,
to suppress Xiàpī.
Dí
is a surname.
*Fēngsú Tōng* says: "In the Hàn dynasty, there was Dí Dù (邸杜), Administrator of Shàngjùn."
He was attacking Wáng Zǎo (王早).
In the twelfth month of the 22nd year,
on the *dīng-sì* day,
the Wèi ruler hunted at Sōnggāo;
on the *jǐ-sì* day,
he visited Wēntāng.
Passing by Sōnggāo to the south,
only Liángxiàn (梁縣) in Rǔzhōu has hot springs.
On the *dīng-chǒu* day,
he returned to the palace.
Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝), Inspector of Jīngzhōu for Wèi, raided Yōngzhōu.
This refers to the Yōngzhōu of the Liáng dynasty,
with its seat at Xiāngyáng.
He incited various barbarians.
Lúlíng Wáng Xù (廬陵王續), Inspector of Yōngzhōu, dispatched troops to attack him,
but was repeatedly defeated.
The region south of the Hàn River was shaken.
Shèng then sent troops to attack Féngyì, Āndìng, Miǎnyáng, and Zànchéng,
capturing them all.
*Wǔdài Zhì* says: "The prefecture of Féngyì was provisionally established in Lánshuǐ Xiàn (藍水縣) of Jìnglíng Jùn (竟陵郡)."
Miǎnyáng Jùn (沔陽郡) later became Fùzhōu.
In Yīnchéng Xiàn (陰城縣) of Xiāngyáng Jùn,
Zànchéng Jùn (酇城郡) was previously established.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's (蕭子顯) *Qí Zhì* says: "Among the prefectures under the Níngmán Fǔ (寧蠻府) was Āndìng Jùn (安定郡),
which administered Xīn'ān (新安) and other counties."
*Wǔdài Zhì* states
that Xīn'ān Xiàn (新安縣) was merged into Nánzhāng Xiàn (南漳縣) of Xiāngyáng Jùn.
Thus, the provisional Āndìng Jùn was likely established within the Nánzhāng area.
Lánshuǐ
was merged into Chángshòu Xiàn (長壽縣) of Yǐngzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
Yīnchéng
was merged into Gǔchéng Xiàn (穀城縣).
Shěn Yuè's (沈約) *Zhì* says: "Féngyì Jùn had its seat in Ruò Xiàn (鄀縣) of Xiāngyáng Jùn."
Miǎn
is pronounced *mǐ-yǎn*.
Zàn
is pronounced *zàn*.
*Wǔdài Zhì* says: "Gǔchéng Xiàn (穀城縣)
belonged to Xiāngyáng Jùn.
It was formerly called Yìchéng (義城),
and Yìchéng Jùn (義城郡) was established there."
They failed to take it,
and so returned.
Thereupon, the region north of the Miǎn River was utterly devastated.
Zhònglǐ (仲禮) was the grandson of Qìngyuǎn (慶遠).
See Liǔ Qìngyuǎn (柳慶遠) in volume 143, second year of Yǒngyuán of Qí Dōnghūn Hóu (齊東昏侯).
Huān (歡), Chancellor of Wèi, was troubled by the strength of Hèbá Yuè (賀拔岳) and Hóumòchén Yuè (侯莫陳悅).
Zuǒchéng Zhái Sōng (翟嵩) said:
"I can sow discord between them
and make them destroy each other."
Huān sent him.
