he encouraged him to welcome the Son of Heaven and achieve the great undertaking of a rising monarch.
This indicates that he knew Yǔwén Tài's talent was sufficient for great deeds,
which is called 'acting after careful assessment'.
Zǎi,
pronounced like "zǐ hài".
Chancellor Huān, hearing that Tài had pacified Qín and Lǒng,
sent envoys with sweet words and generous gifts to ally with him.
Tài refused,
sealed his letter,
and ordered Dūdū Jìběi Zhāng Guǐ to present it to the Wei sovereign.
Hú-sī Chūn asked Guǐ:
"Gāo Huān's rebellious plot
is known to everyone on the road.
The hope of the people
rests solely on the west.
We do not know how Yǔwén compares to Hèbá?"
Meaning, how does Tài's talent compare to Hèbá Yuè?
"Yǔwén Gōng is capable of governing the state with his civil abilities,
and suppressing chaos with his military prowess."
Chūn said:
"If it is truly as you say,
he is indeed reliable."
The Wei sovereign ordered Tài to dispatch two thousand cavalry to garrison Dōngyōngzhōu,
to serve as a reinforcing force.
At that time, Dōngyōngzhōu was established at Zhèngxiàn in Huázhōu.
Tài appointed Grand Dūdū Wǔchuān Liáng Yù as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and had him lead five thousand infantry and cavalry as the vanguard.
Earlier,
Chancellor Huān had dispatched his Dūdū Tàiyán Hán Guǐ to lead ten thousand troops to hold Púfǎn to rescue Hóumòchén Yuè.
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Jiǎ Xiǎndù welcomed him by boat.
Liáng Yù met Xiǎndù
and persuaded him to follow Tài.
Xiǎndù immediately went out to welcome Yù,
and Yù entered and occupied Cháng'ān.
The Wei sovereign appointed Tài as Shìzhōng, Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Guānxī Dàdūdū, and Earl of Luèyáng County,
with the authority to confer titles and appointments by imperial decree.
Tài then appointed Kòu Luò as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Lǐ Bì as Qínzhōu Cìshǐ,
and former Luèyáng Tàishǒu Zhāng Xiàn as Nánqízhōu Cìshǐ.
Nánqízhōu Cìshǐ Lú Dàibó refused to be replaced.
Tài sent light cavalry to raid and capture him.
The historian attributes Yǔwén Tài's ability to establish hegemony to this.
Shìzhōng Fēng Lóngzhī said to Chancellor Huān:
"Hú-sī Chūn and others are now in the capital,
and will surely instigate trouble."
Lóngzhī and Púyè Sūn Téng competed to marry the Wei sovereign's sister, Princess Píngyuán.
The princess went to Lóngzhī,
and Téng leaked his words to Chūn,
who reported it to the Emperor.
Lóngzhī, fearing,
fled back to his hometown.
Huān summoned Lóngzhī to Jìnyáng.
At this time, Téng, carrying a weapon, entered the secretariat,
killed an Imperial Censor,
and fearing punishment,
also fled to Huān.
Lǐngjūn Lóu Zhāo resigned due to illness and returned to Jìnyáng.
None of Gāo Huān's confidants remained in Luò.
He reassigned Dūdū and the Cìshǐ of Hénán and Guānxī.
Huáshān Wáng Zhì was in Xúzhōu.
Huān ordered Grand Dūdū Dǐ Zhēn to seize his keys of office.
Last year,
Huān had ordered Dǐ Zhēn to oversee Xúzhōu and attack Xiàpéi,
thereby seizing its city.
Huá,
pronounced like "hù huà".
Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Cài Jùn,
all were members of Huān's faction.
The Emperor abolished Jiànzhōu to remove worthy officials.
Jiànzhōu was located on the Tàiháng route,
a vital pass for entering Luò from Jìnyáng.
Abolishing the prefecture and removing worthy officials
not only eliminated Huān's faction members
but also removed Huān's host for the southern route.
Qù,
pronounced like "qiāng lǚ".
He replaced him with Rǔyángwáng Shūzhāo.
Huān submitted a memorial:
"Jùn has great merits and cannot be dismissed;
Rǔyáng has admirable virtue and should receive a great fief;
my younger brother Yǒngbǎo
holds the humble post of Dìngzhōu."
(The *Běi Shǐ* says: Huān's brother Chēn,
courtesy name Yuánbǎo.
"Yǒng"
should probably be
"Yuán".)
The Emperor did not listen.
In the fifth month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Wei sovereign increased the number of officials in the meritorious prefectures'庶子 (shùzǐ),
with six hundred in each wing;
he also increased the cavalry officers,
with two hundred in each wing.
The meritorious prefectures'庶子 and cavalry officers
were all palace guards.
Qí,
pronounced like "qí jì".
The Wei lord (Wèi zhǔ) wanted to attack Jìnyáng (Jìnyáng).
Gāo Huān (Gāo Huān) was then residing in Jìnyáng.
On a xīnmǎo day,
an edict was issued to prepare for war,
stating,
“We ourselves wish to lead an attack on Liáng (Liáng).”
He dispatched troops from various prefectures in Hénán (Hénán),
and conducted a grand review in Luòyáng (Luòyáng),
facing the Luòshuǐ (Luòshuǐ) to the south,
and bordering Mángshān (Mángshān) to the north.
The emperor, in military attire, watched the review with Húsi Chūn (Húsi Chūn).
In the sixth month,
on a dīngsì day,
the Wei lord secretly issued an edict to Chancellor Huān,
stating,
“Yǔwén Hēidá (Yǔwén Hēidá) and Hèbá Shèng (Hèbá Shèng) harbor disloyal intentions.
Yǔwén Tài (Yǔwén Tài)’s
courtesy name is Hēidá.
Secretly prepare for this;
you, the king, should also provide support.
Burn this after reading.”
Huān presented a memorial, believing
“Jīng (Jīng) and Yōng (Yōng) are about to rebel.
Jīng
refers to Hèbá Shèng;
Yōng
refers to Yǔwén Tài.
Yōng,
read as yōng.
(My forces will) cross from Hédōng (Hédōng),
and I have also dispatched Kùdí Gān (Kùdí Gān) and others, the Cìshǐ (Cìshǐ) of Héngzhōu (Héngzhōu), to lead forty thousand troops to cross at Láiwéijīn (Láiwéijīn).
Lóu Zhāo (Lóu Zhāo) and others, the Língjūn Jiāngjūn (Língjūn Jiāngjūn), will lead fifty thousand troops to attack Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu).
Wèi Jǐng (Wèi Jǐng) and others, the Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu), will lead seventy thousand troops from Shāndōng (Shāndōng) and fifty thousand cavalry to attack Jiāngzuǒ (Jiāngzuǒ).
All are ordered to rally their respective divisions,
awaiting further instructions.”
The emperor knew Huān had detected his intentions,
so he produced Huān’s memorial,
had his officials discuss it,
and wished to halt Huān’s army.
Huān also gathered his subordinate officials in Bìngzhōu (Bìngzhōu) to discuss it.
Gāo Huān established the Grand Chancellor’s office in Bìngzhōu,
and his subordinate officials all resided there.
He then said:
“I have been slandered by favored sycophants,
and Your Majesty has suddenly become suspicious.
If I dared to betray Your Majesty,
may I be struck by divine calamity,
and my descendants be exterminated.
If Your Majesty trusts my loyal heart,
may weapons remain sheathed,
and I wish for one or two sycophants to be considered for dismissal.”
Zhēn (斟)
means to deliberate.
Liàng (量)
means to measure.
Zhēnliàng (斟量)
is what people today call zhuóliàng (酌量) (to consider).
Liàng,
pronounced liáng.
“Chū (出)”
should be
“chù (黜).”
On a dīngmǎo day,
the emperor sent Grand Commander Yuán Zǐgōng (Yuán Zǐgōng) to guard Yánghú (Yánghú).
Yánghú
is Yanghu City,
in Báishuǐ (Báishuǐ) County, Shàojùn (Shàojùn).
Báishuǐ was Yuán (Yuán) County of Hédōng (Hédōng) in the Hàn (Hàn) Dynasty.
The Shuǐjīngzhù (Shuǐjīngzhù) says: The Báishuǐ flows past the north of the old Yuán County city,
and then southeast past the east of Yánghú City.
The city was the Húqiū (Húqiū) Pavilion of Yuán County.
The Báishuǐ then flows southeast to join the Yellow River.
According to this, Yánghú is on the north bank of Xiáogǔ (Xiáogǔ).
The Wei lord wanted to enter the pass,
so he first sent Zǐgōng to guard it,
to prevent Huān from intercepting him.
He also appointed Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì (Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì), the Yítóng Sānsī (Yítóng Sānsī), as Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu),
and ordered him to lead Húsi Yuánshòu (Húsi Yuánshòu), the Cìshǐ of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu), east to Jìzhōu.
Yuánshòu
was Chūn’s younger brother.
Cài Jùn (Cài Jùn) refused to be replaced,
and the emperor grew even angrier.
On a xīnwèi day,
the emperor again compiled the opinions of the civil and military officials in Luòyáng to reply to Huān,
and also had Shèrén (Shèrén) Wēn Zǐshēng (Wēn Zǐshēng) compose an imperial edict for Huān, saying:
“We, without wielding a single blade,
became emperor by sitting still.
It is said that our parents gave us life,
but High King Gāo (Gāo Wáng) bestowed our nobility.
Now, if we were to betray the king for no reason,
and scheme to attack each other,
then may we and our descendants suffer the same fate as the king’s oath.
Recently, we feared that Yǔwén (Yǔwén) would cause trouble,
and Hèbá (Hèbá) would respond to it,
so we prepared for war,
intending to provide mutual support with the king.
Now, observing their actions,
there are no further unusual signs.
The Southeast has not submitted
for a long time;
today, the population of the empire has been halved,
and it is not advisable to exhaust our military might.
We are ignorant and dim-witted;
we do not know who the sycophants are.
The death of Gāo Gān (Gāo Gān) recently,
was it solely our intention?
It means that Huān also disliked Gān,
and sealed and presented his discussion of current affairs,
thus causing him to be killed.
How easily can people’s ears and eyes be deceived!
It is said that Kùdí Gān told the king:
‘We originally wanted to enthrone a weakling ruler;
there was no need to establish this mature lord,
making him ungovernable.
Now, if we simply march for fifteen days,
we can depose him
and enthrone another.’
Such discussions
must come from the king’s trusted retainers,
not from the mouths of sycophants!
Last year Fēng Lóngzhī (Fēng Lóngzhī) rebelled,
and this year Sūn Téng (Sūn Téng) fled.
You neither punished them nor sent them (to us);
who would not blame the king?
It means Huān neither punished the two men
nor sent them in chains to Luòyáng.
Why did you not behead and send their heads?
Although the king has reported ‘going west,’
‘going west’ means intending to attack Yǔwén Tài in the west.
(You) might want to cross south to Luòyáng,
or east to Jiāngzuǒ (Jiāngzuǒ).
The four routes advancing simultaneously
refer to the troops from Hédōng, Láiwéijīn,
and Lóu Zhāo and Wèi Jǐng.
Lóu Zhāo attacking Jīngzhōu
and Wèi Jǐng approaching Jiāngzuǒ
both point south towards Luòyáng;
the troops from Hédōng and Láiwéijīn
would restrain Yǔwén Tài, preventing him from moving east.
Gāo Huān’s strategy was indeed this,
and the Wei lord had seen through his intentions and spoke of it.
How can those who hear this not be suspicious?
If the king remains peacefully in the north,
even if we have a million troops here,
we will never harbor intentions against him;
if the king raises his banner and points south,
even if we have no horses or wheels,
we will still fight to the death with bare fists.
We were originally of little virtue,
and the king established us.
The common people are ignorant
and might think it is actually permissible.
If we are plotted against by others,
it will highlight our shortcomings;
even if we are killed by the king,
humiliated and ground to powder,
we will have no regrets!
We originally hoped that ruler and minister would be of one body,
like a tally fitting together,
but we did not expect such a complete estrangement today!”
People today still call detailed explanation fēnshū (分疏).
Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Sīzhèng spoke to the Wei Emperor, saying:
"Gāo Huān's intentions
are clear for all to see.
Luòyáng is not a place for military endeavors.
Yǔwén Tài is devoted to the imperial house;
if we go and join him now,
we can restore the old capital.
How can we fear not succeeding?"
The Emperor deeply agreed with this.
He dispatched Sànqí Shìláng Hédōng Liǔ Qìng to meet Tài at Gāopíng
to discuss current affairs.
Tài requested to welcome the imperial carriage.
Qìng returned with the report.
The Emperor then privately said to Qìng,
"What do you think if I were to head towards Jīngzhōu?"
Qìng replied,
"Guānzhōng has strategic advantages,
and Yǔwén Tài's talent and strategy are reliable.
Jīngzhōu is not a vital strategic location,
and it is vulnerable to attacks from Liáng in the south.
Your humble servant does not see it as advisable."
The Emperor then asked Gěnéi Dūdū Yǔwén Xiǎnhé.
At the time, both the Southern and Northern Dynasties had Zhíhé Jiāngjūn,
and Wei also established Gěnéi Dūdū,
following Húxī Chūn's suggestion.
At that time, the Emperor extensively summoned troops from various prefectures and commanderies.
Dōngjùn Tàishǒu Hédōng Péi Xiá led his部部 [bù] to Luòyáng.
Wáng Sīzhèng asked,
"Now that the powerful minister [Gāo Huān] wields authority,
and the imperial house is daily diminishing,
what should be done?"
Xiá replied,
"Yǔwén Tài is supported by the entire army [sān jūn],
and occupies the 'hundred-two' land.
The Book of Han states: Tián Kěn said,
'Qín
is a strategically advantageous state.
Bordered by rivers and blocked by mountains,
separated by a thousand li,
with a million soldiers bearing halberds,
Qín gained the "hundred-two."'
Sū Lín's note says: 'Hundred-two'
means two hundredths of a million people.
Qín's land is dangerous and strong;
twenty thousand people are enough to contend with a million from other feudal lords.
How could he willingly surrender power to others?
Even if we wished to throw ourselves upon him,
I fear it would be no different from avoiding boiling water by entering fire."
Sīzhèng asked,
"If that is the case, what should be done?"
Xiá replied,
"Plotting against Huān brings immediate danger,
and a western tour [to Yǔwén Tài] carries future concerns.
For now, it is best to go to Guān Yòu and then slowly consider what is appropriate."
Sīzhèng agreed with this.
He then introduced Xiá to the Emperor,
who appointed him Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng.
Initially,
Chancellor Huān, considering that Luòyáng had long suffered from war and chaos,
wished to move the capital to Yè.
The Emperor said,
"Gāozǔ established the capital at Hé and Luò,
making it a foundation for ten thousand generations;
since the King has rendered meritorious service to the state,
he should follow the old practices of Tàihé."
Huān then stopped.
By this time, he again contemplated moving the capital.
He dispatched three thousand cavalry to garrison Jiànxīng.
Mùróng Yǒng had divided Shàngdǎng to establish Jiànxīng Commandery.
Wèi considered it Jiànzhōu.
Qí (騎),
read Qí Jì fān.
He gathered grain from all the prefectures [through state purchase]
and transported it all into Yèchéng.
The state purchase of grain to supplement army provisions [hé dí yǐ chōng jūn shí]
seems to have started here.
Throughout the Táng to Sòng dynasties, the people eventually could not bear its burden.
Jì (濟),
read Zǐ Lǐ fān.
"If the King truly wishes to appease popular sentiment [rén qíng]
and quell public opinion,
there is only one way: recall the troops from Hédōng,
dismiss the garrison at Jiànxīng,
and send the grain from Xiāngzhōu.
Xiāngzhōu's seat of government is Yèchéng.
Xiāng (相),
read Xī Liàng fān.
Allow Cài Jùn to be relieved,
and Dí Zhēn to leave Xú.
Lay down weapons and disperse horses,
so that each attends to their own household affairs.
Should provisions be needed,
dispatch separate transport.
Then slanderers will be silenced,
doubts and regrets will not arise.
The King can rest easy in Tàiyuán,
and I will rule with folded hands in Jīngluò.
If the King turns his horse's head southward,
'inquiring about the weight of the tripods,'
though I am not warlike,
for the sake of the altars of soil and grain and the imperial ancestral temples,
I would wish to stop but could not.
The decision rests with the King;
it is not something I can determine.
To build a mountain, stopping at the last basketful,
I feel regret for the King's sake."
The 'Lǚ Áo' chapter of the Book of Documents says: "Building a mountain of nine fathoms,
success is forfeited at the last basketful."
Kǒng Ānguó commented: "This illustrates something nearly accomplished,
but if it lacks one basketful,
it is still not a mountain."
The Analects states: Kǒngzǐ said, "It is like building a mountain;
if it lacks one basketful,
and one stops,
that is one's own stopping."
Xiāng wéi (相為),
read Yú Wěi fān.
The Emperor appointed Guǎngníng Tàishǒu Guǎngníng Rèn Xiáng as concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè, with the added title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Xiáng abandoned his post and fled.
He crossed the Hé,
occupied his commandery, and waited for Huān.
The History of Wei by Wèi Shōu states: Guǎngníng Commandery belonged to Shuòzhōu,
administering Shímén and Zhōngchuān counties.
The History of the Five Dynasties states: Mǎyì Commandery's Shànyáng County,
later Qí established Guǎngníng Commandery.
Since Xiàochāng, it was provisionally administered within Bìngzhōu's borders.
At that time, Huān was in Bìngzhōu.
Xiáng should have gone directly to Huān;
there was no need to occupy a commandery and wait for Huān to come south.
Furthermore, according to the History of the Five Dynasties,
Jiànzhōu's Qìnshuǐ County
had formerly established Guǎngníng Commandery.
The Guǎngníng that Xiáng occupied was likely that of Qìnshuǐ;
if it was his hometown, then it would be the Guǎngníng of Shuòzhōu.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, enumerating Huān's faults and misdeeds,
and summoning Hèbá Shèng to the traveling imperial residence.
Shèng asked his Tàibǎo Yuàn Fànyáng Lú Róu about this.
Róu said,
"Gāo Huān is rebellious and perverse.
If you sweep your forces and head to the capital,
to fight a decisive battle,
living or dying by it,
that is the best plan.
To block at Lǔyáng in the north,
and annex the old Chǔ in the south—
Jiānglíng,
the capital of the old Chǔ, is within its borders—
and draw in Guānzhōng from the west,
with a million armed men,
observing the opportune moment to act,
that is the middle plan.
To offer the three Jīng territories [Sānjīng zhī dì]
and seek refuge with Liáng,
sacrificing both achievement and reputation,
that is the worst plan."
Shèng smiled and did not respond.
Hèbá Shèng was neither able to assist the emperor [qín wáng]
nor secure his territory.
He fled by himself to Liáng,
and indeed, it turned out as Lú Róu had predicted.
Shèng's original intention
was to dismiss Róu's words as those of a mere scholar,
thus taking them lightly.
Little did he know that by broadly observing past events [bó guān wǎng jì]
and silently discerning the changes of the times [mò chá shí biàn] to discuss victory and defeat while seated,
a scholar's insight
is indeed beyond what a warrior or brave general can achieve.
The Emperor appointed Yǔwén Tài as concurrently Shàngshū Púyè,
and made him Guānxī Dàxíngtái.
He promised to marry him to Fēngyì Chánggōngzhǔ.
He said to Tài's Zhàngnèi Dūdū Qínjùn Yáng Jiàn,
"According to Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì,
Wei had no Qínjùn.
The History of the Five Dynasties says: Fúfēng Yōngxiàn,
Later Wei established Qínpíng Commandery.
Also Yōngzhōu Lǐquán County,
Later Wei called it Níngyí,
Western Wei established Níngyí Commandery,
Later Zhōu renamed it Qínjùn.
"You return and tell the Xíngtái [Yǔwén Tài]
to send cavalry to welcome me!"
He appointed Jiàn as Zhíhé Jiāngjūn.
Tài appointed former Qínzhōu Cìshǐ Luò Chāo as Dàdūdū,
who led a thousand light cavalry to Luòyáng.
He also sent Jiàn and Chángshǐ Yǔwén Cè
to go out from the pass to meet and receive.
"To meet and receive" refers to the Wei Emperor.
Chéngxiàng Gāo Huān summoned his brother, Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ Gāo Chēn, and ordered him to guard Jìnyáng.
He commanded Chángshǐ Cuī Xiān to assist him.
Cuī Xiān
was the son of Cuī Tǐng.
The *Tōngjiàn* considers this a different Cuī Xiān, the one defeated by Pòliùhán Bálíng.
Gāo Huān addressed his troops, saying:
"I, following Èrzhū Tiāndàn's mandate,
established a great righteous cause throughout the land,
and supported the Emperor,
as recorded in the fourth year of the previous volume.
Hu Hétú Sīchūn's slanderous schemes have unjustly
made loyalty seem like rebellion.
Now, as we march south,
it is only to execute Sīchūn."
He appointed Gāo Áo Cáo as vanguard.
Yǔwén Tài also issued a manifesto to the prefectures and commanderies,
enumerating Gāo Huān's crimes,
and personally led a large army from Gāopíng,
with his vanguard encamped at Hóngnóng.
Hébá Shèng's army was stationed at the Rǔshuǐ.
Hébá Shèng probably set out from Lǔyáng,
encamped within the bounds of Xiāngchéng,
and merely stopped after crossing the border.
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
the Wèi emperor personally led an army of over 100,000 to encamp at Héqiáo,
with Hú Sīchūn as the vanguard,
arrayed north of Mángshān.
Sīchūn requested to lead two thousand elite cavalry to cross the river by night and ambush the exhausted enemy.
The Emperor initially assented;
but Huángmén Shìláng Yáng Kuān advised the Emperor:
"Gāo Huān, a subject attacking his sovereign,
will stop at nothing!
If we lend troops to others now,
I fear other complications may arise.
If Sīchūn crosses the river,
and by some chance achieves success,
it would be to eliminate one Gāo Huān
and create another Gāo Huān."
The Emperor then ordered Sīchūn to stop his movement.
Sīchūn sighed, saying:
"A short while ago, Yínghuò entered the Nándǒu.
The *Jìn Tiānwén Zhì* states: The six stars of Nándǒu
are the Heavenly Temple.
Matters concerning the Son of Heaven
are divined from Dǒu.
Yínghuò,
the Star of Punishment,
entering it,
means the Son of Heaven is not secure in his position.
This is what was later referred to as
'the Son of Heaven running down from his hall.'
Not using my plan,
is this not fate?"
Yǔwén Tài heard of this
and said to his attendants:
"Gāo Huān has traveled eight or nine hundred *lǐ* in a few days.
This is something military strategists avoid.
We should take advantage of this to attack him.
But the Emperor, with the heavy burden of the myriad chariots,
cannot cross the river to engage in decisive battle,
but is instead guarding the ford.
Moreover, the long river stretches for ten thousand *lǐ*,
making defense difficult.
If they manage to cross at one point,
the great enterprise will be lost."
He immediately appointed Dàdūdū Zhào Guì as a separate circuit *Xíngtái*,
to cross from Púfǎn
and proceed towards Bìngzhōu,
advancing by a separate route,
showing an intention to threaten Gāo Huān's rear.
Qù (趣)
is pronounced as "qī yù."
This was to welcome the Wèi emperor.
Jiāng (將)
is pronounced as "jí liàng."
The Emperor sent Hú Sīchūn, together with *Xíngtái* Zhǎngsūn Zhì and Dàdūdū Yǐngchuān Wáng Bīnzhī, to garrison Hǔláo;
*Xíngtái* Zhǎngsūn Zǐyàn to garrison Shǎn;
and Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì and Hú Sī Yuánshòu to garrison Huátái.
Bīnzhī
was the younger brother of Yuán Jiànzhī;
Ānlè Wáng Yuán Jiànzhī is mentioned in volume 150, Pǔtōng fourth year.
He was the son of Zhǎngsūn Zhì.
Gāo Huān sent Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Dòu Tài to advance towards Huátái,
and Jiànzhōu Cìshǐ Hán Xián to advance towards Shíjì.

Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì (高祖武皇帝) 13
Dàtóng (大同) First Year (Yǐmǎo, 535)
1 Spring,
First month,
Wùshēn (戊申) day,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign title was changed.
2 On this day,
Emperor Wén of Wèi (魏文帝) ascended the throne west of the city.
"West of the city"
means west of Cháng'ān (長安) city.
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven ascended the throne in the front hall.
From the time Gāo Huān (高歡) established Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武帝), Wèi (魏) reverted to barbarian rites,
offering sacrifices to Heaven in the suburbs before ascending the throne.
The reign title was changed to Dàtǒng (大統),
and his father, the Prince of Jīngzhào (京兆王), was posthumously honored as Emperor Wénjǐng (文景皇帝),
and his mother, Lady Yáng (楊氏), as Empress.
3 Kězhūhún Dàoyuán (可朱渾道元), the Wèi (魏) Inspector of Wèizhōu (渭州), had previously submitted to Hóumòchén Yuè (侯莫陳悅).
When Yuè (悅) died,
Yuè (悅) died,
see the previous volume, Dàtōng (大通) sixth year.
(Yǔwén Tái) could not conquer him,
made an alliance, and withdrew.
Dàoyuán (道元) had lived in Huáishuò (懷朔) for generations,
and was friendly with Gāo Huān (高歡), the Eastern Wèi (東魏) Chancellor.
Also, his mother and elder brother were both in Yè (鄴),
because of this he often communicated with Huān (歡).
Tái (泰) wanted to attack him.
Dàoyuán (道元) led his department of three thousand households northwest across Wūlánjīn (烏蘭津) to Língzhōu (靈州).
Wūlánjīn (烏蘭津) was northwest of Píngliáng (平涼).
Táng (唐) divided Guìníng Garrison (會寧鎮) of Píngliáng (平涼) to establish Huìzhōu (會州),
and also established Wūlán (烏蘭) County under its jurisdiction.
Southwest of the county was Wūlán Pass (烏蘭關).
Shuài (帥)
is read shuài.
When Huān (歡) heard of it,
he sent provisions to welcome him,
and appointed him Grand General of Cavalry (車騎大將軍).
Qí (騎)
is read qí jì.
Dàoyuán (道元) arrived at Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Huān (歡) first learned of the death of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武帝).
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武) of Wèi (魏) died in the twelfth month of the previous year.
The Eastern Wèi (東魏) ruler ordered his ministers to deliberate on it.
Pān Chónghé (潘崇和), a Grand Academician of the Imperial Academy (太學博士), believed:
"If a ruler treats a minister without propriety, then there is no mourning attire.
The Tán Gōng (檀弓) records: Rǔ Mùgōng (魯繆公) asked Zǐsī (子思):
'Wearing mourning attire for a former ruler,
is this ancient?'
Zǐsī (子思) replied:
'The gentlemen of antiquity,
advanced people with propriety,
and dismissed people with propriety,
therefore there was the rite of wearing mourning attire for a former ruler.
The gentlemen of today,
advance people as if they would place them on their knees,
and dismiss people as if they would cast them into an abyss.
Is it not good if they do not become the leaders of conflict?
How then
can there be the rite of wearing mourning attire?'
Mencius: Qí Xuānwáng (齊宣王) said:
'The rites prescribe mourning attire for a former ruler,
under what circumstances should one wear it?'
Mencius said:
'If advice is followed and words are heeded,
and beneficent kindness reaches the people;
if one leaves due to a reason,
then the ruler sends someone to escort them beyond the border,
and also precedes them to their destination;
if after three years they do not return,
then their fields and villages are taken back;
this is called having the three proprieties.
In such a case, one wears mourning attire for them.
But now as a minister,
if advice is not followed,
if words are not heeded,
and beneficent kindness does not reach the people;
if one leaves due to a reason,
then the ruler seizes and arrests them,
and also pushes them to extremes in their destination;
and on the day they leave, their fields and villages are immediately taken back;
this is called treating them as an enemy.
What mourning attire is there for an enemy!'
The people of Zhōu Wǔ (周武) did not submit to Zhòu (紂)."
Wèi Jìlóng (衞既隆) and Lǐ Tóngguǐ (李同軌), Doctors of the National University (國子博士), argued:
"Gāo Hòu (高后) and Yǒngxī (永熙) were not yet explicitly separated,
so mourning attire should be worn for him."
Eastern Wèi (東魏) agreed.
When Huān (歡) first established Xiàowǔ (孝武),
he took his eldest daughter as Empress.
When the Emperor fled west,
the Empress remained and did not follow.
4 Lǐ Hǔ (李虎), Grand General of Agile Cavalry (驍騎大將軍) and Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) of Wèi (魏), and others, persuaded the Fèiyětóu (費也頭) people,
and together attacked Língzhōu (靈州).
After forty days,
Cáo Ní (曹泥) requested to surrender.
5 On the day *jǐyǒu*,
Wèi promoted Chancellor Lüèyáng Gōng Tàizhōng to Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn, Lù Shàngshū Shì, and Dàxíngtái,
and enfeoffed him as King of Āndìng;
Tàizhōng firmly declined the royal title and the position of Lù Shàngshū,
so he was enfeoffed as Duke of Āndìng.
Shàngshū Lìng Húxī Chūn was made Tàibǎo,
and Guǎngpíng Wáng Zàn was made Sītú.
6 On the day *yǐmǎo*,
the Wèi ruler established Lady Yǐfú as empress.
The Yǐfú family's ancestors were leaders of the Tǔyùhún,
residing in Qīnghǎi,
which was the place conquered by Tūfà Nǔchén.
When Wèi pacified Liángzhōu,
the empress's great-great-grandfather Mòhuái led his tribe to submit,
and later, following Xiàowén to relocate to Luò,
they settled there.
The empress was benevolent, forgiving, and frugal,
not prone to jealousy,
and the emperor greatly esteemed her.
Given the esteem in which Wèi Wéndì held Empress Yǐfú,
and yet she ultimately succumbed to the pressure of a powerful enemy,
which led to her tragic death,
it is truly lamentable.
7 Liú Lìshēng of the Jīhú,
since Xiàochāng,
had proclaimed himself Son of Heaven,
changed the era name to Shénjiā,
and resided in Yúnyáng Gǔ.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: The Jīhú,
also called Bùluòjī,
are a separate branch of the Xiōngnú,
descendants of Liú Yuánhǎi's Five Tribes.
Some say they are descendants of the Shānrong and Chìdí.
From Líshí westward,
and Āndìng eastward,
an area of seven or eight hundred *lǐ* square,
they inhabit the mountain valleys,
and their clans are numerous and flourishing.
This area was called
"Húhuāng."
It means that they were originally of Hú ethnicity,
who harassed the Hàn people,
as if they were beyond the *huāngfú* (wild territories).
*Bèi*,
read *píyì fān*.
On the day *rénxū*,
Dōng Wèi Chancellor Huān launched a surprise attack
and utterly defeated them.
8 Bóhǎi Shìzǐ Chéng had an affair with Huān's concubine, Lady Zhèng.
Huān had enfeoffed him as King of Bóhǎi,
making Chéng his heir apparent.
Returning from attacking the Jīhú,
two maids served as witnesses;
Huān whipped Chéng a hundred times and confined him,
and Lóu was also isolated and not allowed to see him.
Huān took the empress of Wèi Jìngzōng, Lady Ěrzhū, as his concubine,
and she was favored,
giving birth to a son, Yóu.
Huān wished to make him the heir.
Chéng sought help from Sīmǎ Zǐrú.
Zǐrú went to see Huān,
feigning ignorance,
and asked to see Lóu;
Huān told him what had happened.
Zǐrú said:
"Xiāonàn also had an affair with Zǐrú's concubine;
such matters can simply be covered up.
She is the king's first wife,
and she has always used her family's wealth to serve the king;
Chéng Zhèngshū said: The ancients said
'to *jiéfà* as husband and wife,'
just as they said
'to *jiéfà* serve the lord,'
'to *jiéfà* fight the Xiōngnú';
it only refers to the initial coming-of-age hairstyle,
how could it mean a shared topknot!
According to Lóu's original biography: As a youth, she saw Huān working on the city wall,
admired him,
and sent a maid to convey her feelings.
She also repeatedly offered private wealth,
asking him to use it to marry her,
and her parents had no choice but to agree.
Her back has no intact skin,
and she attends to him day and night;
later, to avoid the Gé rebels,
the Gé rebels

Despite poverty,
she would burn horse dung
*Rán*,

*Suí Zhì*: *Xuē* (boots)
are Hú footwear.
They are convenient for use
and worn with military attire.
The couple were well-matched,
and her two daughters married into the imperial family,
the elder married Emperor Xiàowǔ,
and the younger married Emperor Xiàojìng.
He refers to Chéng as the heir apparent.
How can this be shaken!
His brother Zhāo was then the Língjūn Jiāngjūn.
Moreover, the maids' words are not necessarily credible!"
Huān then ordered Zǐrú to re-investigate.
Zǐrú saw Chéng
and rebuked him, saying:
"Why would a man fear authority and falsely accuse himself!"
He then taught the two maids to retract their statements,
and threatened the accuser into hanging herself,

"It was indeed false testimony."
Huān was greatly pleased,
and summoned Lóu and Chéng.
Seeing Huān from a distance,
Lóu kowtowed at every step.
Chéng bowed as he advanced.
Father and son, husband and wife wept together,
and relations were restored to their former state.
Huān hosted a banquet and said:
"The one who saved my son and me
is Sīmǎ Zǐrú!"
He bestowed upon him one hundred and thirty *jīn* of gold.
9 On the day *jiǎzǐ*,
Wèi appointed Guǎnglíng Wáng Xīn as Tàifù,
and Yítóng Sānsī Mòqí Shòuluògān as Sīkōng.
10 On the day *jǐsì*,
Dōng Wèi appointed Chancellor Huān as Xiàngguó,
granted him *jiǎhuángyuè*,
and special honors;
he firmly declined.
11 Dōng Wèi Dàxíngtái Shàngshū Sīmǎ Zǐrú, leading Dàdūdū Dòu Tàizhōng, Tàizhōu Cìshǐ Hán Guǐ, and others, attacked Tóngguān.
According to Hán Guǐ's biography,
he was Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
Also, checking Wèi Shōu's records,
Dōng Wèi established Qínzhōu in Hédōng,

and Xī Wèi changed it to Huázhōu.
*Huá*,
read *hùhuà fān*.
Ladders leaned against the city wall,
and by dawn,
Dōng Wèi soldiers climbed the ladders and entered.
Cìshǐ Wáng Pí was still lying down and had not yet risen.
Hearing a clamor outside his chamber,
he stripped to his waist, baring his topknot, and barefoot,
he grabbed a white cudgel and shouted as he went out.
The Dōng Wèi soldiers were startled and retreated upon seeing him.
Pí chased them to the east gate.
His attendants gradually gathered,
engaged in battle,
and defeated them.
Zǐrú and the others then withdrew.
Military operations rely on spirit and momentum;
the courage or cowardice of soldiers
depends on their commander for spirit and momentum.
Wáng Pí was brave in facing the enemy, and his attendants were also brave in battle.
This is why they were able to repel the enemy even when unprepared and unexpected.
12 In the second month,

Dōng Wèi appointed Xiányáng Wáng Tǎn as Tàifù,

and transport their timber to Yè.
15〠On the day *dīnghài*,
the emperor plowed the *jiètián*.
16 Lóu Zhāo (婁昭) and others, Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) of the Eastern Wèi, attacked Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
Fán Zǐhú (樊子鵠) ordered Yán Sīdá (嚴思達), the former Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jiāozhōu (膠州), to guard Dōngpíng (東平).
Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) Zhì (志) states: Dōngpíng (東平) commandery was established during the Tàicháng (泰常) era,
abolished at the end of Tàihé (太和),
and re-established during the Jiànyì (建義) era.
Its seat was Qínchéng (秦城),
and it belonged to Jìzhōu (濟州).
Qínchéng (秦城) was within the borders of Fànxiàn (范縣).
Zǐhú then led his troops to besiege Xiáqiū (瑕丘).
After a long time, it did not fall.
Zhāo flooded the city.
On the day Jǐchǒu (己丑),
Dàyě Bá (大野拔) met Zǐhú (子鵠) to discuss matters,
and then beheaded him and surrendered.
Initially,
Zǐhú, with few troops,
had driven all the old and weak to serve as soldiers.
When Zǐhú died,
they all scattered and fled.
The generals advised Lóu Zhāo (婁昭) to capture and execute them all.
Zhāo said:
“This province is unfortunate,
having been ravaged by bandits.
They look eagerly to the imperial army to save them from misery.
If we execute them again now,

He spared them all.
17 On the day Wùxū (戊戌),
Chén Qìngzhī (陳慶之), Cìshǐ of Sīzhōu (司州), campaigned against the Eastern Wèi.

The seat of the Eastern Wèi Yùzhōu (豫州) was Rǔnán (汝南).
Yáo (堯)
is the surname;
Xióng (雄)
is the given name.

the Eastern Wèi appointed Gāo Shèng (高盛) as Tàiwèi (太尉),
Gāo Áocáo (高敖曹) as Sītú (司徒),

19 Gāo Huān (高歡), Chancellor of the Eastern Wèi, falsely made peace with Liú Líshēng (劉蠡升),
promising to give his daughter in marriage to Líshēng’s (蠡升)太子 (tàizǐ, crown prince).
Líshēng (蠡升) did not prepare.
Huān (歡) raised troops and attacked him.
On the day Xīnyǒu (辛酉),
Líshēng’s (蠡升) Northern King beheaded Líshēng (蠡升) and surrendered.
The remaining followers again enthroned his son, the Prince of Nánhǎi (南海王).
Huān (歡) advanced and attacked,
capturing him,
and taking captive his empress, various princes, dukes, ministers, and over four hundred others,
along with over fifty thousand households, both Huá (華) and Yí (夷).
On the day Rénshēn (壬申),
Huān (歡) held court in Yè (鄴).
He married Empress Xiàowǔdì (孝武帝后) to Péngchéng Wáng Sháo (彭城王韶).
Empress Xiàowǔdì (孝武帝后)
was Huān’s (歡) eldest daughter.
20 Yuán Tàì (元泰), Chancellor of the Wèi, seeing that military campaigns had not ceased
and that officials and commoners were weary and distressed,
ordered the relevant departments to deliberate on what in ancient and modern times could be convenient for the current era and suitable for governance,
and created twenty-four new regulations,
which he presented and implemented.
Tàì (泰) employed Sū Chuò (蘇綽) of Wǔgōng (武功) as a Xíngtái Lángzhōng (行臺郎中).
Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) Zhì (志) states: In the eleventh year of Tàihé (太和),
Wǔgōng (武功) commandery was established by dividing Fúfēng (扶風),
and it belonged to Qízhōu (岐州).
It was the land of the Wǔgōng (武功) county of the Hàn and Wèi.
Tàì (泰) had not yet known him,
but everyone in the department praised his ability,
and whenever there was a doubtful matter, they would go to him to resolve it.
They went to Sū Chuò (蘇綽) to resolve doubts.
This ‘go to’ (就, jiù)
is the same as in Mencius’s (孟子)
“if you wish to make a plan, then go to him” (欲有謀焉則就之).
Huìdá (惠達) could not answer,
and asked to go out to discuss it.
Going out,
he reported it to Chuò (綽).
Chuò (綽) made arrangements for him.
Huìdá (惠達) returned and reported it,
and Tàì (泰) praised it,
saying:
“Who discussed this with you?”
Huìdá (惠達) answered with Chuò’s (綽) name,
and also praised Chuò (綽) as having the talent of a king’s assistant.
Tàì (泰) then promoted Chuò (綽) to Zhùzuò Láng (著作郎).
Tàì (泰) and his ministers went to Kūnmíng Chí (昆明池) to watch fishing.
They traveled to the old Cāngchí (倉池) of the Hàn dynasty.
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) states: A branch canal of the Juéshuǐ (泬水) reaches west of Zhāngmén (章門),
and a flying canal draws water into the city,
forming Cāngchí (倉池) to the east.
The pond was west of Wèiyānggōng (未央宮).
The pond had a Jiàntái (漸臺).
When the Hàn army rose,
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) died on this terrace.
Sū Chuò’s (蘇綽) biography also says: they traveled to the old Cāngchí (倉池) of the Hàn dynasty west of Cháng'ān (長安) city.
No one knew about it.
Tàì (泰) summoned Chuò (綽) and asked him,
and he fully explained the situation.
Tàì (泰) was pleased,
and then asked about the origin of heaven and earth and creation,
and the traces of rise and fall of successive dynasties.
Chuò (綽) answered fluently.
Tàì (泰) and Chuò (綽) rode side by side at a slow pace,
and when they reached the pond,
they returned without setting up nets.
The intention was to ask Chuò (綽),
not to watch fishing.
Huán (還)
is read xuán (旋) in the first instance,
and also as its original character.
Tàì (泰) questioned him about government affairs,
listening while reclining.
Chuò (綽) pointed out the essentials of governance.
Tàì (泰) rose,
adjusted his clothes, and sat upright respectfully,
unconsciously moving his knees forward to the mat.
First, he listened while reclining,
then rose and adjusted his clothes to sit upright respectfully,
and then unconsciously moved his knees forward to the mat.
This shows that Chuò’s (綽) words deeply resonated with Tàì’s (泰) heart,
and he grew more respectful over time.
Tiānxiǎo (天曉) means dawn.
Tàì (泰) said to Zhōu Huìdá (周惠達):
“Sū Chuò (蘇綽) is truly an extraordinary scholar.
I will entrust him with governance.”
He immediately appointed him Dàxíngtái Zuǒchéng (大行臺左丞),
to participate in handling confidential matters.
From then on, his favor and treatment grew daily.
Chuò (綽) first established the official document procedures of ‘red out, black in’ (朱出、墨入) and the methods for accounting ledgers and household registers.
Accounting ledgers
are to fully record the general number of taxes and corvée for the coming year,
to report to the Dùzhī (度支).
Household registers
are records of households and populations.
Whenever there is a capable ruler in the world,
there will always be competent individuals who emerge to serve him.
If one says there are no talents in the world,
I do not believe it.
21 The Eastern Wèi appointed Fēng Yánzhī (封延之) as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Qīngzhōu (青州),
replacing Hóu Yuān (侯淵).
Yuān (淵), having lost his provincial post, felt fearful.

At night,
Yuān (淵) attacked the southern suburb of Qīngzhōu (青州),

In summer,
in the fourth month,
Chancellor Huān (歡) ordered Cài Jùn (蔡儁), Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jìzhōu (濟州), to suppress him.
Many of Yuān’s (淵) subordinates rebelled.
Yuān (淵) wanted to flee south,

22 Yuán Qìnghé (元慶和) attacked Chéngfù (城父) of the Eastern Wèi.
Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) Zhì (志) states:
Jùnyí (浚儀) county of Chénliú (陳留) commandery has Chéngfù (城父) city.

During the Sòng,
Jùnyí (浚儀) county was established.
Also, examining Shěn Yuè’s (沈約) Zhì (志),
Chénliú (陳留) Jùnyí (浚儀) county was relocated and governed within the borders of Chángyuán (長垣) county of Qiáojùn (譙郡).
Thus, it is known that what various Zhì (志) refer to as Jùnyí (浚儀)
is not the Jùnyí (浚儀) of our dynasty’s Kāifēng Fǔ (開封府).
Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) Zhì (志) of Jùnyí (浚儀) county of Chénliú (陳留) commandery of Liángzhōu (梁州)
is the Jùnyí (浚儀) of our dynasty’s Kāifēng (開封).
Zhēnzōng (真宗) changed Jùnyí (浚儀) to Xiángfú (祥符).
What is called Chéngfù (城父)
is today’s Chéngfù (城父) county of Bózhōu (亳州).
Fù (父)
is pronounced fǔ.
Dòu Tàì (竇泰) led thirty thousand men towards Chéngfù (城父).
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) led thirty thousand men towards Péngchéng (彭城).
Rèn Xiáng (任祥) was appointed Xíngtái Púshè (行臺僕射) of the Southeast Route,
to command all armies.
23 In the fifth month,
the Wèi bestowed the title Zhùguó (柱國) upon Chancellor Tàì (泰).
This was the official title of Zhùguó Dàjiāngjūn (柱國大將軍).
24 Yuán Qìnghé (元慶和) led his troops to press against Nányǎnzhōu (南兗州) of the Eastern Wèi.
Hán Xián (韓賢), Cìshǐ (刺史) of Luòzhōu (洛州) of the Eastern Wèi, resisted him.
After the Eastern Wèi moved to Yè (鄴),
Luòyáng (洛陽) was made Luòzhōu (洛州),
administering Luòyáng (洛陽), Héyīn (河陰), Xīn'ān (新安), Zhōngchuān (中川), Hénán (河南), and Yángchéng (陽城) commanderies.
Qìnghé (慶和) attacked Nándùn (南頓).
Yáo Xióng (堯雄), Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yùzhōu (豫州), defeated him.
In the 25th autumn,
seventh month,
on the *Jiǎxū* day,
Wèi appointed Niànxián, Grand Master of Cavalry, concurrently performing the duties of the Three Dukes, as Grand Commandant.
Wànqí Shòuluògān was appointed Minister of Works.
Yuèlè Gōng, Grand Master of Cavalry, concurrently performing the duties of the Three Dukes, was appointed Grand Guardian.
Yuèlè came from the Yuèlè tribe,
and thus adopted it as his surname.
Yìzhōu Inspector Pōyáng Wáng Fàn, Nánliángzhōu Inspector Fán Wénchì,
according to the *Wǔdàizhì*: Pǔ'ān Commandery.
Liáng established Nánliángzhōu,
later renamed Ānzhōu.
Western Wèi renamed it Shǐzhōu.
During the Táng dynasty, Shǐzhōu was renamed Jiànzhōu.
and Wèi Dōngyìzhōu Inspector Fù Jìnghé surrendered.
Fàn
was the son of Huī.
Pōyáng Wáng Huī
was the son of Fèi,
and the younger brother of Shàng.
He was also the son of Shùyǎn.
Wèi issued an edict enumerating twenty crimes of Gāo Huān,
and declared:
"We shall personally command the six armies
and, with the Chancellor, sweep away the wicked. "
Huān also issued a manifesto to Wèi,
calling Yǔwén Hēidá and Húxī Chūn rebellious traitors,
and stating,
"Now, I dispatch my various generals
with an army of a million men
to set a date for a western expedition. "
Dōng Wèi dispatched Acting Director of the Secretariat Yuán Yàn to attack Yuán Qìnghé.
Someone accused Dōng Wèi Minister of Works Jìyīn Wáng Huīyè and Seven Divisions Minister Xuē Shú of being disloyal to Wèi.
Cáo Wèi established Five Divisions Ministers,
referring to the Central Division, Outer Division, Cavalry Division, Auxiliary Division, and Capital Division.
By the Jìn dynasty,
the Central Division and Outer Division were divided into Left and Right,
forming seven offices with the original five divisions.
However, the Minister position was only for Five Divisions,
there was no title of Seven Divisions Minister.
It was not until the Latter Wèi that the Seven Divisions Minister first appeared.
Northern Qí reverted to Five Divisions.
Shú,
pronounced like "chāng liù fān."
Jì,
pronounced like "zǐ lǐ fān."
On the *Xīnmǎo* day,
they were apprehended and sent to Jìnyáng,
and all were dismissed from office.
At that time, Dōng Wèi Chancellor Huān resided in Jìnyáng,
so the two were apprehended and sent there
for his judgment.
In the Spring and Autumn period,
Jìn acted as the regional hegemon,
apprehending rebellious rulers and officials from various states and sending them to the capital.
Even the *Jīng* (Confucian Classics) criticized this.
How much more egregious is it to apprehend them from the capital and send them to Jìnyáng!
On the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
Dōng Wèi conscripted 76,000 people to construct a new palace in Yè,
and ordered Palace Assistant Commander Gāo Lóngzhī and Minister of Works Armory Officer Cān Jūn Xīn Shù
to oversee its construction.
In the ducal government of Yuán Wèi, there were offices such as Law, Ink, Field, Water, Armor, Armory, Collection, and Scholar,
all held by Military Counselors.
Shù
was the son of Chēn.
Xīn Chēn is mentioned in Volume 147, Tiānjiān sixth year.
Chēn,
pronounced like "chǒu lín fān."
Zhào Gāng traveled from among the barbarians to meet Dōng Wèi Dōngjīngzhōu Inspector Zhàojùn Lǐ Mǐn,
and persuaded him to join Wèi.
Mǐn agreed,
and Gāng was thus able to reach Cháng'ān.
Chancellor Tài appointed Gāng as Left Grand Master of Guanglu.
Gāng advised Tài to summon Hèbá Shèng and Dúgū Xìn, et al., from Liáng.
Gāng was lost among the barbarians.
Shèng and Xìn fled to Liáng,
both mentioned in the previous volume, previous year.
Shuì,
pronounced like "shì ruì fān."
In the ninth month,
on the *Dīngsì* day,
Dōng Wèi appointed Xiāngchéng Wáng Xù, Grand Master of Cavalry, concurrently performing the duties of the Three Dukes, as Grand Guardian.
In winter,
tenth month,
Wèi Grand Preceptor, Shàngdǎng Wénxuān Wáng Zhǎngsūn Zhì passed away.
Wèi Qínzhōu Inspector Wáng Chāoshì
was the older brother of Chancellor Tài's wife.
According to the maternal relatives' seniority,
he was called 'nèi xióng' (wife's elder brother) or 'nèi dì' (wife's younger brother).
Tài memorialized to increase his punishment,
and an imperial edict ordered him to commit suicide.
In the eleventh month,
on the *Dīngwèi* day,
Court Attendant, Central Guard General Xú Miǎn passed away.
Although Miǎn's integrity was not equal to Fàn Yún's,
he also did not flatter or merely conform.
Therefore, in the Liáng era, when speaking of virtuous chancellors, Fàn and Xú were mentioned.
After Fàn and Xú passed away,
Zhūyì was solely entrusted with power,
and Liáng was almost doomed.
On the *Guǐchǒu* day,
the Dōng Wèi emperor sacrificed at the Altar of Heaven.
On the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
the Dōng Wèi Chānghé Gate suffered a fire.
When the gate was first completed,
Gāo Lóngzhī, riding on horseback, observed it from afar
and said to its builder:
"The southwest is one inch higher."
Measuring it proved him correct.
Taifu Minister Rèn Xīnjí, priding himself on his skill,
refused to make the correction.
Lóngzhī resented him.
At this time, he slandered him to Chancellor Huān, saying:
"Xīnjí secretly communicated with Western Wèi
and had someone deliberately set the fire."
Huān executed him.
Běiliángzhōu Inspector Lán Qīn led troops to attack Nánzhèng.
Liáng had made Nánzhèng Běiliángzhōu.
It was probably because Qīn was appointed inspector
to make him plan for Nánzhèng.
Dōng Wèi appointed Huān's son, Yáng, as Grand General of Agile Cavalry, Grand Master of Cavalry, concurrently performing the duties of the Three Dukes,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Tàiyuán.
Yáng was internally shrewd and decisive but outwardly appeared unintelligent.
His brothers and the public all mocked and despised him;
only Huān regarded him as extraordinary,
saying to his Chief Clerk Xuē Shú:
"This child's insight surpasses mine."
When he was young,
Huān once wanted to test his sons' awareness,
and made each of them untangle tangled silk.
Only Yáng drew his knife and cut it,
saying:
"The tangled must be cut!"
Then, he assigned each a troop of soldiers and sent them out.
He had Commander Péng Lè lead armored cavalry to feign an attack on them.
His elder brother Chéng and others were all terrified and faltered,
but Yáng alone commanded his troops to fight Lè.
When Lè removed his helmet and revealed himself,
Yáng still captured him and presented him.
Originally,
Grand Director of the Secretariat Right Assistant Yáng Yīn's cousin, Qízhōu Inspector Yòuqīng,
was killed by Emperor Xiàowǔ for his blunt speech.
Yīn's colleague Guō Xiù, jealous of his ability,
frightened him by saying:
"King Gāo wants to send you to the Emperor."
Yīn was afraid,
changed his name, and fled to Tiánhéng Island.
According to the *Wǔdàizhì*,
Jiànjí County in Dōnglái Commandery has Tiánhéng Island.
Huān heard he was still alive
and summoned him to be Tàiyuán Gōng Kāifǔ Sīmǎ,
which prepared for Yáng Yīn to be intimately trusted by Yáng.
He later became Grand Director of the Secretariat Right Assistant again.
In the twelfth month,
on the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
Dōng Wèi civil and military officials were given salaries according to their duties.
The difference in salaries was based on the lightness or heaviness of their assigned duties.
Liàng,
pronounced "liáng."
Wèi appointed Niànxián as Grand Preceptor,
and Hézhōu Inspector Liáng Jǐngruì as Grand Commandant.
That year,
the rebel leader Xiānyú Chēn from Pōyáng proclaimed the era name Shàngyuàn,
and had an army of over ten thousand men.
Pōyáng Grand Administrator Wú Jùn Lù Xiāng attacked and captured him,
and investigated his accomplices,
with no one dying unjustly.
The people sang of him:
"After Xiānyú was pacified, good and evil were distinguished.
No one died unjustly, thanks to Lord Lù."
Róurán Head Qīng Kèhán sought a marriage alliance with Dōng Wèi.
Chancellor Huān made his sister, Princess of Chángshān, Princess Lánlíng,
and married her to him.
Róurán frequently invaded Wèi.
Wèi sent Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat Kùdí Zhì as an envoy to Róurán
to arrange a peace and marriage alliance.
From then on, Róurán no longer posed a threat.
1. In spring,
first month,
on the *Xīnhài* day,
Wèi sacrificed at the southern suburb,
now using Divine Progenitor Emperor as the co-sacrificer.
In the sixteenth year of Tàihé of Wèi Gāozǔ,
Grand Progenitor Emperor Dàowǔ was made the co-sacrificer at the southern suburb.
Divine Progenitor Emperor was Tuòbá Lìwēi, the ancestor of Wèi;
seen in the biography of Jìn Wǔdì.
2. On the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
Dōng Wèi Chancellor Huān personally led ten thousand cavalry to raid Wèi Xiàzhōu.
Without cooking for himself,
he arrived in four days.
Using tied spears as ladders,
he entered the city at night,
captured Inspector Húbá Émítū,
and then employed him.
He left Commander Zhāng Qióng to guard the city with troops
and relocated five thousand households of its population back to his territory.
3 Wèi's (Western Wèi) Língzhōu (靈州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Cáo Ní (曹泥) and his son-in-law, Liángzhōu (涼州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Pǔlè Liú Fēng (普樂劉豐), rebelled again and surrendered to Dōng Wèi (東魏).
Wèi (Western Wèi) established Pǔlè Jùn (普樂郡),
subordinate to Língzhōu (靈州).
According to the *Wǔdài Shǐ Zhì* (五代史志), Huíluò Xiàn (迴樂縣) of Língwǔ Jùn (靈武郡)
was established in the Hòu Zhōu (後周) period
and included Pǔlè Jùn (普樂郡).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: From Língzhōu (靈州) southwest to Liángzhōu (涼州) is nine hundred *lǐ* (里).
Last year, Cáo Ní (曹泥) surrendered to Wèi (Western Wèi),
but now he has rebelled again.
The character "樂" (lè),
is pronounced *luò*.
The character "復" (fù),
is pronounced *fú yòu fān*.
The character "降" (jiàng),
is pronounced *hù jiāng fān*.
The *Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: Both *Běi Qí Shū* (北齊書) and *Diǎnlüè* (典略) say
“Zhōu Wén (周文) besieged Ní (泥),”
but the *Zhōu Shū* (周書) does not mention it,
so it merely says "Wèi (Western Wèi) people."
Four *chǐ* (尺) were not submerged.
Dōng Wèi (東魏) Chéngxiàng (丞相) Huān (歡) led thirty thousand cavalry of the Āzhìluó (阿至羅) directly through Língzhōu (靈州),
and circled to appear behind the Wèi (Western Wèi) army,
whereupon the Wèi (Western Wèi) army retreated.
Huān (歡) led his cavalry to welcome Ní (泥) and Fēng (豐),
and brought back five thousand of their remaining households,
would Gāo Huān (高歡) not have wanted to contend with Yǔwén (宇文) for Língzhōu (靈州)?
Though the whip is long,
it cannot reach the horse's belly.
Dōng Wèi (東魏) established Nánfénzhōu (南汾州) in Dìngyáng (定陽).
Suí (隋) changed Dìngyáng Xiàn (定陽縣) to Jíchāng Xiàn (吉昌縣).
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it was the administrative seat of Cízhōu (慈州).
4 Dōng Wèi (東魏) added the nine bestowment articles to Chéngxiàng (丞相) Huān (歡);
he steadfastly declined, and it was stopped.
5 The Emperor (Liáng Wǔdì) built the Huángjī Sì (皇基寺) for Wéndì (文帝) to accumulate merit for him posthumously.
The Emperor posthumously honored his father, Shùnzhī (順之), as Wén Huángdì (文皇帝).
The character "為" (wèi),
is pronounced *yú wěi fān*.
Hóng Shì (弘氏) of Qǔ'ā (曲阿) bought large timber from Xiāngzhōu (湘州) and transported it eastward.
Nánjīn Xiàowèi (南津校尉) Mèng Shàopíng (孟少卿) wanted to curry favor with the Emperor,
according to *Liáng Jì* (梁紀),
in the sixth year of Pǔtōng (普通) [525 AD],
Nánzhōu Jīn (南州津) was reorganized with the establishment of *Xiàowèi* (校尉),
and their stipends were increased.
Nánzhōu (南州) is now Cǎishí (採石).
The character "校" (jiào),
is pronounced *hù jiào fān*.
The character "少" (shào),
is pronounced *shī zhào fān*.
He confiscated the timber to build the temple.
Killing innocent people
and taking their materials to build a temple,
where then are the benefits of the field of merit!
6 In the second month,
on the *yǐhài* (乙亥) day,
the Emperor performed the ritual plowing of the sacrificial field.
7 Dōng Wèi (東魏) Bóhǎi (勃海) Shìzǐ (世子) Chéng (澄),
at the age of fifteen,
was appointed Dà Xíngtái (大行臺) and Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ (幷州刺史).
In the fifth year of Zhōngdàtōng (中大通) [533 AD],
Wèi (Western Wèi) appointed Huān (歡) as Dà Xíngtái (大行臺).
Huān (歡) then bestowed it upon his son Chéng (澄).
Huān (歡) resided in Jìnyáng (晉陽),
and the position of Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ (幷州刺史) was critically important,
so he also appointed Chéng (澄) to it.
Chéngxiàng (丞相) Huān (歡) did not permit it;
but Chéngxiàng Zhǔbù (丞相主簿) Yuè'ān (樂安) Sūn Qiān (孫搴) pleaded for him,
and only then did he permit it.
On the *dīngyǒu* (丁酉) day,
Chéng (澄) was appointed Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令),
and additionally titled Lǐngjūn (領軍) and Jīngjī Dà Dūdū (京畿大都督).
The *Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: The *Wèi Dì Jì* (魏帝紀) says:
“He was Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令), Dà Xíngtái (大行臺), and Dà Dūdū (大都督).”
The *Běi Qí Wénxiāng Jì* (北齊文襄紀) says:
“In the first year of Tiānpíng (天平) [534 AD],
he was Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令), Dà Xíngtái (大行臺), and Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ (幷州刺史);
he entered the court to assist in governance, and was additionally titled Lǐngjūn (領軍) and Zuǒyòu Jīngjī Dà Dūdū (左右京畿大都督).”
Based on this, Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) is not an external post,
and Dà Xíngtái (大行臺) is not an internal post.
Now both are omitted.
He was still regarded as young;
but upon arrival,
he enforced laws strictly,
affairs were not stagnant,
and both the court and the provinces were awe-struck.
He appointed Bìngzhōu Biéjià (幷州別駕) Cuī Xiān (崔暹) as Zuǒ Chéng (左丞) and Lìbù Láng (吏部郎),
and entrusted him personally.
8 Sīmǎ Zǐrú (司馬子如) and Gāo Jìshì (高季式) invited Sūn Qiān (孫搴) to a heavy drinking session,
and he died from extreme intoxication.
Chéngxiàng (丞相) Huān (歡) personally attended his funeral.
Zǐrú (子如) kowtowed and pleaded guilty,
Huān (歡) said:
“You have broken my right arm,
find me a replacement!”
Zǐrú (子如) recommended Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎) Wèi Shōu (魏收),
and Huān (歡) appointed Shōu (收) as Zhǔbù (主簿).
Shōu (收) was the son of Zǐjiàn (子建).
See Wèi Zǐjiàn (魏子建) in Volume 150, fifth year of Pǔtōng (普通) [524 AD].
Huān (歡) said to Jìshì (季式):
“You drank my Zhǔbù (主簿) Sūn (孫) to death,
and Wèi Shōu (魏收)'s handling of documents is not to my liking;
who was the person the Sītú (司徒) once praised as diligent and discreet?”
At that time, Dōng Wèi (東魏) had Gāo Áocáo (高敖曹) as Sītú (司徒).
He replied:
“He is an efficient official who can write clearly in the dark at night.”
He was summoned,
and upon meeting him,
Huān (歡) immediately appointed him Dà Chéngxiàng Gōngcáo (大丞相功曹),
in charge of confidential matters.
The *Kǎo Yì* (考異) states: *Diǎnlüè* (典略) says that
Sūn Qiān (孫搴) died in the fourth month of the tenth year of Dàtóng (大同) [544 AD].
Based on this, Chén Yuánkāng (陳元康) became Gōngcáo (功曹) after Qiān (搴) died.
When Gāo Shèn (高慎) rebelled,
Gāo Chéng (高澄) had already ordered Yuánkāng (元康) to rescue Cuī Xiān (崔暹).
During the Battle of Mángshān (邙山),
Yuánkāng (元康) also advised Gāo Huān (高歡) to pursue Yǔwén Tài (宇文泰).
These events all took place in the ninth year [543 AD].
The *Běi Shǐ Yuánkāng Zhuàn* (北史元康傳) also states,
“He drafted military dispatches for Liú Lǐshēng (劉蠡升).”
Based on this, Lǐshēng (蠡升) was destroyed in the first year [535 AD],
and Sūn Qiān (孫搴) was still alive in the second year [536 AD].
This is not adopted now.
Thus, Qiān (搴)'s death should be placed after Chéng (澄) entered court to assist.
At that time, the state had many military and governmental affairs,
and Yuánkāng (元康) knew everything when asked.
Sometimes when Huān (歡) went out,
before leaving,
he would leave Yuánkāng (元康) behind,
and issue over ninety orders from horseback.
Yuánkāng (元康) counted them on his fingers
and could remember all of them.
Together with Gōngcáo (功曹) Píngyuán (平原) Zhào Yànshēn (趙彥深), he managed confidential matters,
and people at the time called them Chén (陳) and Zhào (趙).
Yuánkāng (元康)'s influence surpassed Zhào (趙)'s,
and his nature was also gentle and cautious,
so Huān (歡) was very close to him,
saying:
“Such a person
is truly hard to find;
heaven has bestowed him upon me.”
Yànshēn (彥深)'s given name was Yǐn (隱),
and he was known by his courtesy name.
9 Dōng Wèi (東魏) Chéngxiàng (丞相) Huān (歡) ordered the Āzhìluó (阿至羅) to press Wèi (Western Wèi) Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (秦州刺史) Wànqí Pǔ (万俟普),
and Huān (歡) responded with his troops.
10 In the third month,
on the *wùshēn* (戊申) day,
Dānyáng (丹楊) Táo Hóngjǐng (陶弘景) died.
Hóngjǐng (弘景) was extensively learned and skilled in many arts,
and fond of the art of nourishing life.
He served Qí (南齊) as Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請),
then abandoned his official post
and lived in seclusion on Máoshān (茅山).
Máoshān (茅山) is now fifty *lǐ* (里) south of Jìankāng Fǔ (建康府)'s Jùróng Xiàn (句容縣).
The *Shān Jì* (山記) states: During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, there were three Máojūn (茅君) who
each rode a crane here,
hence the name.
The character "卒" (zú),
is pronounced *zǐ xù fān*.
The character "好" (hào),
is pronounced *hū dào fān*.
The character "朝" (cháo),
is pronounced *zhí yáo fān*.
The Emperor (Liáng Wǔdì)'s gracious treatment was very sincere;
whenever he received Hóngjǐng (弘景)'s letters,
he would burn incense and reverently accept them.
He repeatedly sent handwritten imperial edicts to invite him,
but Hóngjǐng (弘景) did not emerge.
Whenever the state had important matters of fortune or misfortune, or military campaigns,
he would always consult him first,
often sending several messages within a month.
"月中" (*yuè zhōng*),
means "within one month."
refers to a messenger or message.
He was called the "Prime Minister in the Mountains."
Before his death,
he wrote a poem:
“Yífǔ (夷甫) indulged in unrestraint,
Píngshū (平叔) sat discussing emptiness.
How could they know that the Zhāoyáng Diàn (昭陽殿)
would become the palace of the Chányú (單于)!”
Hóngjǐng (弘景)'s biography states: Later, when Hóu Jǐng (侯景) usurped power,
it indeed happened in the Zhāoyáng Diàn (昭陽殿).
The historians say that those who cultivate the Dao (道) can perceive the times and know fate.
He was not skilled in military affairs,
hence Hóngjǐng (弘景)'s poem alludes to it.
11 On the *jiǎyín* (甲寅) day,
Dōng Wèi (東魏) appointed Huàshān Wáng (華山王) Zhì (鷙) as Dà Sīmǎ (大司馬).
12 The Wèi (魏) appointed Lǐ Shūrén (李叔仁), the Prefect of Liángzhōu (涼州), as Sītú (司徒),
and Wànqí Luò (万俟洛) as Tàizǎi (太宰).
Luò (洛)'s
courtesy name was Shòuluògān (受洛干),
also known as Shòulèqgān (壽樂干).
Shòu (受) and Shòu (壽) are homophones,
and Luò (洛) and Lè (樂) are also homophones.
According to records, the Northern Qí (北齊) had the office of Tàizǎi (太宰),
which continued the Jìn (晉) system;
the Western Wèi (西魏) used the Zhōu (周) system,
establishing a Dàzhǒngzǎi (大冢宰),
but no Tàizǎi (太宰).
13 Summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Yǐwèi (乙未),
Yuán Fǎsēng (儀元法僧), the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, 驃騎大將軍) and Kǎifǔ Tóngsānsī (開府同三司) of ceremonies, was appointed Tàiwèi (太尉).
Below the Liáng (梁) office of Kǎifǔ Yítóngsānsī (開府儀同三司),
there was also the Kǎifǔ Tóngsānsī (開府同三司) of ceremonies.
14 Jiāng Zǐsì (江子四) of Kǎochéng (考城), the Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòuchéng, 尚書右丞), submitted four memorials,
thoroughly discussing the successes and failures of governance.
In the fifth month,
on the day Guǐmǎo (癸卯),
an imperial edict stated:
"The ancients said,
'When the roof leaks above,
those below are aware.'
I have faults,
but I am unable to perceive them myself.
The matters stated in the memorials by Jiāng Zǐsì (江子四) and others
should be promptly investigated by the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū, 尚書),
and if there are harmful grievances to the people,
they should be quickly reported in detail!"
The memorials submitted by Jiāng Zǐsì (江子四)
certainly did not dare to mention that the Emperor excessively trusted Buddhism,
and that exhausting the military and expanding territory only served to harm the people,
or that laws were lenient towards the powerful and noble but harsh towards ordinary people, and similar matters.
Rather, he merely focused on minor details to discuss successes and failures.
15 On the day Wùchén (戊辰),
Gāo Shèng (高盛) of the Eastern Wèi (東魏) passed away.
Gāo Shèng (高盛)
was the Tàiwèi (太尉) of the Eastern Wèi (東魏).
16 Yuèbō Gōng (越勒肱) of the Wèi (魏) passed away.
Yuèbō Gōng (越勒肱)
was the Sīkōng (司空) of the Wèi (魏).

17 Wànqí Pǔ (万俟普), the Prefect of Qínzhōu (秦州) of the Wèi (魏), along with his son Tàizǎi (太宰) Luò (洛), Chìgān Bǎolè (叱干寶樂), the Prefect of Bīnzhōu (豳州), Pòliùhán Cháng (破六韓常), the Right General of the Imperial Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn, 右衞將軍), and three hundred commanding officers, defected to the Eastern Wèi (東魏).
As the troops of Āzhìluó (阿至羅) were nearby,
Pǔ (普) and others took advantage of this to flee east.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The defection of Pǔ (普) to the Eastern Wèi (東魏) is recorded in the Dìjì (帝紀) of the Běiqí Shū (北齊書) in the third month on the day Jiǎwǔ (甲午),
and in the Diǎnlüè (典略) in the sixth month.
The Qíjì (齊紀) of the Běishǐ (北史) places it in the sixth month on the day Jiǎwǔ (甲午);
the Dìjì (帝紀) of the Zhōushū (周書), the Wèijì (魏紀) of the Běishǐ (北史), and the Qíjì (齊紀) place it in the fifth month,
which is followed here.

It should be noted that since the Kǎoyì (考異) previously cited the Dìjì (帝紀) of the Běiqí Shū (北齊書), and then the Qíjì (齊紀) of the Běishǐ (北史), it is incorrect to have the Qíjì (齊紀) appear again after the Wèijì (魏紀) of the Běishǐ (北史);
there must be an error.
They traveled over a thousand *lǐ* to Hébĕi (河北),
but failed to reach it and returned.
Hébĕi (河北)
refers to the north of the Xīhé (西河) at Lóngmén (龍門).
Huán (還)
is pronounced *cóng xuān*,
and also as written;
the same applies below.
18 Autumn, in the seventh month,
on the day Gēngzǐ (庚子),
the Eastern Wèi (東魏) granted a general amnesty.
19 The Emperor treated the Wèi (魏) surrendered general Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝) and others very generously.
Shèng (勝) requested to attack Gāo Huān (高歡),
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Shèng (勝) and the others wished to return home.
Shǐ Níng (史寧), the former Grand Commander of Jīngzhōu (荊州) and Governor of Fǔníng (撫寧), said to Shèng (勝):
According to Níng (寧)'s biography,
Níng (寧) resided in Fǔníng Zhèn (撫寧鎮).
An examination shows no Fǔníng (撫寧) among the Northern Garrisons (Běizhèn, 北鎮) of Wèi (魏),
so it is likely Fǔmíng (撫冥).
Furthermore, according to the Wǔdài Zhì (五代志), in Jiāngxiàn (開疆縣) of Diāoyīn Jùn (雕陰郡), there was a Fǔníng Jùn (撫寧郡) in the Later Wèi (後魏),
and also a Fǔníng Xiàn (撫寧縣),
also belonging to Diāoyīn Jùn (雕陰郡).
"Zhū [AS-82FA] always had his words heeded by the Liáng (梁) ruler;
please form a strong bond with him."
Shèng (勝) followed this advice.
The Emperor permitted Shèng (勝), Níng (寧), and Lú Ròu (盧柔) to all return north.
Lú Ròu (盧柔) had probably accompanied Shèng (勝) when he defected the previous year.
Shèng (勝), mindful of the Emperor's kindness,
thereafter refused to shoot any southward-facing animals.
When they reached Xiāngchéng (襄城),
Huān (歡), the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng, 丞相) of the Eastern Wèi (東魏), sent Hóu Jǐng (侯景) with light cavalry to intercept them.
Shèng (勝) and the others abandoned their boats and fled back via mountain paths.
Shèng (勝) and the others traveled by boat,
probably entering the Yǐng (潁) from the Huái (淮), then the Rǔ (汝) from the Yǐng (潁), going upstream westward,
entering mountain paths,
and taking Wǔguān (武關) from Sānyā (三鵶).
More than half died on the way.
Upon reaching Cháng'ān (長安),
they went to the palace gate to beg forgiveness.
The Wèi (魏) ruler took Shèng (勝)'s hand and sighed, saying:
"The imperial carriage's displacement
is heaven's will,
not your fault."
Tàizǐ (泰), the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng, 丞iàng), appointed Lú Ròu (盧柔) as a Principal Secretary (Cóngshì Zhōngláng, 從事中郎),
and entrusted him with confidential matters alongside Sū Chuò (蘇綽).
20 In the ninth month,
on the day Rén'yín (壬寅),

the Eastern Wèi (東魏) appointed Hóu Jǐng (侯景), the Prefect of Dìngzhōu (定州), concurrently as Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòupúyè, 尚書右僕射) and Southern Circuit Administrator (Nándào Xíngtái, 南道行臺),
to lead his generals in an invasion.
21 The Wèi (魏) appointed Fúfēng Wáng (扶風王) Fú (孚) as Sītú (司徒),
and Húsī Chūn (斛斯椿) as Tàifù (太傅).
22 Winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Yǐhài (乙亥),
an edict ordered a large-scale expedition to attack the Eastern Wèi (東魏).
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) of the Eastern Wèi (東魏) led seventy thousand troops to invade Chǔzhōu (楚州).
Wèi Shōu (魏收)'s record states: The Liáng (梁) established Chǔzhōu (楚州),
with its seat in Chǔchéng (楚城), administering Rǔyáng (汝陽), Wǔchéng (仵城), and Chéngyáng (城陽) Commanderies.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states: In Rǔnán Chéngyáng Xiàn (汝南城陽縣),
the Liáng (梁) established Chǔzhōu (楚州).
When they advanced to the Huái (淮) River,
Chén Qìngzhī (陳慶之), the Prefect of the Southern and Northern Sī (司) Commanderies, defeated them,
and Jǐng (景) abandoned his baggage train and fled.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Jǐhài (己亥),
the northern expeditionary forces were disbanded.
23 The Wèi (魏) again changed the temple name of its progenitor, Shényuán Huángdì (神元皇帝), to Tàizǔ (太祖),
and Dàowǔ Huángdì (道武皇帝) to Lièzǔ (烈祖).
The Wèi (魏)'s change of the temple names of the two ancestors
is recorded in volume 137 under Qí Wǔdì (齊武帝)'s Yǒngmíng (永明) ninth year.
Fù (復)
is pronounced *fú yòu fān*.
24 In the twelfth month,
the Eastern Wèi (東魏) appointed Wèi Jǐng (尉景), the Prefect of Bìngzhōu (幷州), as Tàibǎo (太保).
25 On the day Rénshēn (壬申),
the Eastern Wèi (東魏) sent an envoy to request peace,
and the Emperor permitted it.
26 Gāo Dǎn (高亶), the Prince Wénxuān (文宣王) of Qīnghé (清河) of the Eastern Wèi (東魏), passed away.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Guódiǎn (國典) says,
"Dǎn (亶) was poisoned by Gāo Huān (高歡)."
The Diǎnlüè (典略), when Emperor Tàizǔ (太祖) of Zhōu (周) enumerated Huān (歡)'s crimes,
also stated that Dǎn (亶) was killed.
Neither the Wèishū (魏書) nor the Běishǐ (北史) contain a biography for Dǎn (亶);
however, their Dìjì (帝紀) all state that Dǎn (亶) *hōng* (薨) (died),
which is followed here.
27 On the day Dīngchǒu (丁丑),
Huān (歡), the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng, 丞相) of the Eastern Wèi (東魏), led his armies to attack the Wèi (魏),
sending Sītú (司徒) Gāo Áocáo (高敖曹) to quickly seize Shàngluò (上洛),
and Grand Commander (Dàdūdū, 大都督) Dòu Tài (竇泰) to quickly seize Tóngguān (潼關).
28 On the day Guǐwèi (癸未),
the Eastern Wèi (東魏) appointed Xiányáng Wáng (咸陽王) Tǎn (坦) as Tàishī (太師).
29 In this year,
a great famine struck Guānzhōng (關中) of the Wèi (魏).
People resorted to cannibalism,
and seven or eight out of ten died.
1 Spring,
in the first month,
the Emperor performed sacrifices at the southern suburb,
and granted a general amnesty.
2 Dōng Wèi Chancellor Huān's army was at Pú​bǎn,
and built three pontoon bridges,
intending to cross the river.
Wèi Chancellor Tài's army was at Guǎng​yáng.
Wèi Shōu's Zhì says,
in the first year of Jǐng​míng,
Guǎng​yáng County was established,
subordinate to Fēng​yì Commandery.
"The enemy is attacking us on three sides,
making pontoon bridges to show they are determined to cross.
This is to tie down our army,
so that Dòu Tài can enter from the west.
Ever since Huān raised his army,
Dòu Tài has always been the vanguard.
His troops are mostly elite soldiers,
repeatedly victorious and therefore arrogant.
If we attack them now,
we will surely defeat them.
If we defeat Tài,
then Huān will retreat without a fight."
All the generals said:
"The enemy is close,
abandoning them to attack those far away.
If anything goes wrong,
what regret will be enough!
It is better to divide our forces to resist them."
Chancellor Tài said:
"Huān attacked Tóng​guān twice,
and our army did not go out to Bà​shàng.
In the sixth year of Zhōng​dà​tōng,
Huān attacked Tóng​guān;
in the first year [of this reign],
Huān's troops again attacked Tóng​guān.
He thinks we will also defend ourselves,
and holds us lightly.
Taking advantage of this to attack them,
what is there to worry about not defeating them!
Although the enemy is building pontoon bridges,
they cannot cross immediately.
In no more than five days,
I will surely capture Dòu Tài!"
Xíng​tái Zuǒ​chéng Sū Chuò and Zhōng​bīng Cān​jūn, the Dài man Dá​xī Wǔ, also agreed.
On the day Gēng​xū,
Chancellor Tài returned to Cháng​'ān,
but the generals' opinions still differed.
Chancellor Tài concealed his plan,
and asked his clan nephew, Zhí​shì Láng​zhōng Shēn.
Jìn Wǔ​dì established Zhí​shì Láng,
which was above the various Cáo Láng of the Shàng​shū.
"Dòu Tài is
Huān's fierce general.
If the main army attacks Pú​bǎn,
then Huān will hold his ground and Tài will come to his rescue.
We will be attacked from both front and rear;
this is a dangerous path.
It is better to select light, elite troops to secretly exit through Xiǎo​guān.
Xiǎo​guān is to the left of Tóng​guān.
In the Táng dynasty, it was called Jìn​gǔ.
He will surely come to engage in a decisive battle.
Huān, being cautious, will not immediately come to rescue.
If we swiftly attack Tài,
he can surely be captured.
If Tài is captured, Huān's momentum will naturally be thwarted.
Then, turning back to attack him,
we can decide the victory."
Chancellor Tài said:
"This is exactly what I thought."
So he publicly announced his intention to secure Lǒng​yòu.
On the day Xīn​hài,
he paid homage to the Wèi lord and then secretly moved his army eastward.
At dawn on the day Guǐ​chǒu,
they reached Xiǎo​guān.
Dòu Tài, suddenly hearing of the army's arrival,
from Fēng​líng​dù,
Chancellor Tài went out through Mǎ​mù​zé.
The Shuǐ​jīng Zhù says: The fortress of Táo​lín,
where a lake emerges,
contains many wild horses.
The Sān​qín Jì says,
Táo​lín Sāi is four hundred *lǐ* east of Cháng​'ān.
If military horses pass through,
they are pastured on Huà​shān,
resting under the trees.
Mǎ​mù​zé,
is likely this very place.
He was thoroughly defeated,
all his officers and men were lost,
Dòu Tài committed suicide,
and his head was sent to Cháng​'ān.
Chancellor Huān, because the river ice was thin,
could not come to his rescue,
so he dismantled the pontoon bridges and retreated.
Yí​tóng, the Dài man Xuē​gū Yán, formed the rear guard.
The Tōng​zhì​lüè writes it as Sà​gū,
a compound surname.
Diàn [殿],
pronounced Dīng Liàn.
He sustained fifteen saber wounds,
broke [his weapon],
and only then managed to escape.
Chancellor Tài also led his army back.
This entire section refers to Chancellor Tài [宇文泰],
to distinguish him from Dòu Tài.
A review of earlier and later accounts shows that
Gāo Huān and Yǔ​wén Tài are both referred to as Chancellor,
but here, the distinction is particularly clear.
Gāo Áo​cáo advanced from Shāng​shān, fighting all the way,
Dù Yòu says: Shāng​shān is in Shāng​zhōu's Shàng​luò County.
And then attacked Shàng​luò.
Quán Yuè of the commandery and his younger brother Měng​lüè, together with Dù Zhú of Shùn​yáng, conspired to surrender the city to him.
Luò​zhōu Cì​shǐ Quán Qǐ knew about it.
This is the Luò​zhōu that was changed during Wèi Tài​hé,
governed from Shàng​luò,
and at that time belonged to Xī Wèi.
Qǐ's
courtesy name was Sī​dào;
pronounced Qù Zhì.
Dù Zhú fled and returned to Áo​cáo,
Áo​cáo used him as a local guide to attack the city.
Áo​cáo was struck by a stray arrow,
which pierced his body three times,
and he fainted for a long time,
but then remounted his horse,
removed his helmet, and inspected the city walls.
Qǐ held out for more than ten days,
and his two sons Yuán​lǐ and Zhòng​zūn fought bravely to resist him.
Zhòng​zūn's eye was injured,
making him unable to fight again,
and so the city fell.
Qǐ saw Áo​cáo and said:
"My strength has given out,
but my heart is not subdued."
Áo​cáo appointed Dù Zhú as Luò​zhōu Cì​shǐ.
Áo​cáo's wounds were severe,
and he said:
"I regret not seeing Jì​shì become Cì​shǐ."
Jì​shì was
Áo​cáo's younger brother.
He immediately appointed Jì​shì as Jì​zhōu Cì​shǐ.
Áo​cáo wanted to enter Lán​tián​guān.
The Táng Zhì says: Lán​tián County in Jīng​zhào has Lán​tián​guān,
which was formerly Yáo​guān.
Jì [濟],
pronounced Zǐ Lǐ.
"Dòu Tài's army is destroyed,
people's hearts are fearful and shaken,
we should return quickly.
The road is treacherous and the enemy is strong,
saving ourselves is enough."
Áo​cáo could not bear to abandon his troops,
so he fought hard to preserve his entire army and returned,
taking Quán Qǐ and Quán Yuán​lǐ with him.
Quán Zhòng​zūn, due to severe injuries, did not go.
Qǐ secretly admonished his two sons, saying:
"My remaining life is not long.
Your talents and abilities are sufficient to achieve merit.
Do not, because I am in the east,
violate your duty as subjects."
Yuán​lǐ escaped and returned en route.
Although Quán and Dù were both local magnates,
the locals esteemed Quán more than Dù.
Yuán​lǐ and Zhòng​zūn secretly allied with local gentry,
attacked Zhú,
and killed him.
Wèi appointed Yuán​lǐ as hereditary Luò​zhōu Cì​shǐ.
3 In the second month,
on the day Dīng​hài,
the emperor ploughed the sacrificial field.
4 On the day Jǐ​chǒu,
Shàng​shū Zuǒ Pú​shè Hé Jìng​róng was appointed Zhōng​quán Jiāng​jūn,
Zhōng​quán Jiāng​jūn was
one of the two hundred forty titles.

Huái​lǐ County,
under Hàn belonged to Fú​fēng,
under Jìn belonged to Shǐ​píng Commandery,
later under Wèi it again belonged to Fú​fēng.
Xǐ [璽],
pronounced Sī Shì.
6 In the third month,
on the day Xīn​wèi,
Dōng Wèi moved the spirit tablets of seven emperors into the new temple.
The seven emperors: Dào​wǔ, Míng​yuán, Tài​wǔ, Wén​chéng, Xiàn​wén, Xiào​wén, Xuān​wǔ.
7 Wèi's Hú​sī Chūn died.
At that time, Hú​sī Chūn was Wèi Tài​fù.
According to records, Chūn lived between the time of Ěr​zhū and Gāo Huān,
and with his wisdom and cunning, he sowed discord between their lords and ministers.
The Ěr​zhū clan was subsequently destroyed by him,
and Gāo Huān could not control him either.
However, after entering Guān​zhōng,
he was ranked alongside Yǔ​wén Tài,
as if he had no ability;
power was not in his hands,
so he had no means to wield his wisdom and cunning.
8 In summer,
in the fifth month,
Wèi appointed Guǎng​líng Wáng Xīn as Tài​zǎi,
and Hè​bá Shèng as Tài​shī.
9 In the sixth month,
Wèi appointed Fúfēng Wáng Fú as Tàibǎo,
Liáng Jǐngruì as Tàifù,
Guǎngpíng Wáng Zàn as Tàiwèi,
and the Grand Administrator-Designate Yítóng Sānsī, Wǔchuān Wáng Méng, as Sīkōng.
10 Gāo Huān, the Chancellor of Dōng Wèi, traveled to Tiānchí in Fényáng.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: "North of Fényáng County in Tàiyuán, on Yānjīng Shān, there is a large pool.
The pool is on a mountain plateau,
and people of the world call it Tiānchí.
It is over a square *lǐ*,

An inscription emerged, saying

Huān's courtesy name is Hèlùhún,
hence it refers to him.
He is to rule all under Heaven.
The Hé, Luò, and Yī are the 'three rivers';
the Jīng, Wèi, and Luò can also be the 'three rivers'.
The 'Luò' of
'Jīng, Wèi, and Luò'
refers to the Luò Shuǐ in Guānzhōng,
which now flows through Fū, Fáng, and Tóng prefectures before entering the Wèi."
Dāng wáng (to rule),
pronounced as Yú Kuàng.
"Eventually, you will seize Guān and Luò."
Huān said:
"Ordinary people often say I'm rebellious without reason,
what more will they say if they hear this!

Xiūzhī
was Gù's son.

Gāo Huān's ambition

Jiān (occasionally),

is Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng.
Sàn (leisurely),

Qí (horseman),

Píng's grandson;

Chǎng's son.

Xiàn's great-grandson;

At that time, the South
and North maintained good relations,

Wèi (to act as),

Chān (to spy),
