also Chǒu Yàn.
12 Dúgū Xìn requested to return north,
and the Emperor permitted it.
Xìn's parents were both in Shāndōng.
When Wèi Xiàowǔ moved west,
Xìn abandoned his parents to follow him.
Xìn said:
"One who serves his ruler dares not consider his private kin and harbor disloyal thoughts."
The Emperor considered this righteous
and sent him off with generous rites.
Xìn and Yáng Zhōng both arrived in Cháng'ān
and submitted a memorial to apologize for their offenses.
Wèi, recognizing Xìn's achievement in pacifying the Three Jīngs,
(The pacification of the Three Jīngs is mentioned in the previous volume, Dàtōng 6th year.)
added the titles of Shìzhōng and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
with his other official ranks and titles remaining as before.
Chancellor Tàiyǔ loved Yáng Zhōng's bravery
and kept him under his personal command.
13 Wèi Yǔwén Shēn advised Chancellor Yǔwén Tàiyǔ to capture Héngnóng.
In the eighth month,
on the day Dīngchǒu,
Yǔwén Tàiyǔ led Lǐ Bì and eleven other generals to attack Dōng Wèi.
He appointed Yú Jǐn, the Cǐshǐ of Běi Yōngzhōu, as the vanguard
and attacked Pándòu,
capturing it.
On the day Wùzǐ,
they reached Héngnóng.
On the day Gēngyín,
they captured it
and seized Lǐ Huībó, the Cǐshǐ of Dōng Wèi's Shǎnzhōu.
The Wèi Shōu Zhì states: "In Tàihé 11th year,
Shǎnzhōu was established,
governing Shǎnchéng,
administering Héngnóng Jùn,
and overseeing Xīhéngnóng, Miǎnchí, Shíchéng, and Héběi Jùn."
Shǎn (Shǎn),
pronounced as Shì Rǎn.
At that time, many cities north of the Hé (Yellow River) had sided with Dōng Wèi.
Zuǒ Chéng Yáng Biāo stated that his father, Měng, had once been the Ling of Báishuǐ in Shàojùn.
Zuǒ Chéng refers to Xíngtái Zuǒ Chéng.
The Wèi Shōu Zhì states: "In Huángxīng 4th year,
Shàojùn was established,
governing Báishuǐ Xiàn."
The Wǔdài Zhì states: "Jiàngjùn Yuánxiàn,
Hòu Wèi established Shàojùn and Báishuǐ Xiàn there."
Péi Qìngsūn's biography states: "Shàojùn governed Yánghú Chéng,
over two hundred *lǐ* from Zhǐguān."
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "Yuánxiàn has Shàotíng,
after which the commandery was named."
Sòng Bái said: "Jiàngzhōu Yuánxiàn,
its land is where Zhōu and Shào divided Shǎn.
Today, sixty *lǐ* east of the county, there is Shàoyuán Címiào and an ancient Táng tree."
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, Xiāng 23rd year: "The Marquis of Qí attacked Jìn,
took Cháogē,
entered Mèngmén,
ascended Tàiháng,
arrayed his army at Yíngtíng,
and garrisoned Píshào."
Hòu Wèi Xiànwén 4th year established Shàozhōu.
Biāo (Biāo),
same as Biāo.
He requested to go and persuade them
to capture Shàojùn;
Yǔwén Tàiyǔ permitted it.
Yáng Biāo then, with local strongmen Wáng Fùlián and others, raised troops,
captured the Shàojùn Administrator Chéng Bǎo and four county magistrates,
and beheaded them.
He memorialized to appoint Fùlián as Jùnshǒu
and sent spies to persuade the Dōng Wèi castles and strongholds.
Within a month,
a great many submitted.
Dōng Wèi appointed Sīmǎ Gōng, the Cǐshǐ of Dōng Yōngzhōu, to garrison Zhèngpíng.
Zhèngpíng was originally the land of Hàn and Jìn's Línfén Xiàn;
in Wèi Zhēnjūn 7th year,
Tàipíng Xiàn was established by division;
in Shénquè 1st year,
it was renamed Zhèngpíng;
in Tàihé 18th year,
Zhèngpíng Jùn was established,
administering Wénxǐ Xiàn,
and belonged to Dōng Yōngzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: "Jiàngzhōu
governed Zhèngpíng Xiàn."
Sīmǎ Gōng abandoned the city and fled.
Yǔwén Tàiyǔ appointed Yáng Biāo to act as the administrator of Zhèngpíng Jùn.
14th, the Emperor repaired the Āyùwáng Pagoda at Chánggàn Sì.
Buddha's nail and hair relics were unearthed.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor visited the temple,
and hosted an "unobstructed feast" (wú'ài shí).
Today, Chánggàn Lǐ is located in Shàngyuán Xiàn of Jiànkāng Fǔ,
five lǐ from the county seat.
Lǐ Bái's "Chánggàn Xíng" mentions
"living together in Chánggàn Lǐ,"
which refers to the eastern alleys of Mòlíng Xiàn.
In Jiāngdōng, the area between mountains and ridges is called "gān."
Buddhist monks recorded in national histories: After the Buddha's Nirvāṇa,
celestial beings wrapped the Buddha in new white silk,
and offered fragrant flowers.
After seven full days,
he was placed in a golden coffin,
and sent out of the royal palace for about three lǐ.
Within the palace, each made firewood from sandalwood,
and celestial beings each burned the firewood with fire.
Eight hù and four dòu of relics were collected.
Each king received a small amount,
which they took back to their respective countries
to build Buddhist temples.
Āyùwáng erected a stupa at the site of the Buddha's Nirvāṇa.
Lǐ Yánshòu's "Fúnán Zhuàn" states: As for the pagoda of Chánggàn Sì,
during the Wú period, a nun resided there,
establishing a small monastery.
Sūn Chén had it demolished.
After Wú was pacified,
various Daoist monks re-established it at the old site.
During the Xián'ān period of Jìn Jiǎnwén Dì, a pagoda was built.
In the ninth year of Tàiyuán of Xiàowǔ Dì, a golden finial (xiānglún) and a dew-collecting plate (chénglù) were added.
Later, there was a Hú person named Liú Sàhé from Líshí Xiàn, Xīhé, who fell ill and died suddenly,
but revived after seven days.
Because of this, he became a monk,
named Huìdá.
He traveled to Chánggàn Lǐ in Dānyáng,
where there was an Āyùwáng Pagoda.
He excavated one zhàng deep
and found a golden casket containing three relics and Buddha's nails and hair.
He moved the relics closer to the north,
and built a pagoda to the west, facing the pagoda built by Jiǎnwén Dì.
When the Emperor had it opened,
they first dug four chǐ into the earth,
and found a dragon's cave and various precious items such as gold and silver hairpins, bracelets, rings, and tweezers, abandoned by former people, reaching about nine chǐ deep.
Below the stone foundation,
there was a stone casket.
Inside the casket was an iron jar,
containing a silver crucible.
Inside the crucible was a golden thread jar,
containing three relics,
the size of millet grains,
round, regular, and lustrous.
Inside the casket was a glass bowl.
Within the bowl, they found four relics, hair, and nails.
There were four nails,
all the color of sandalwood.
The hair was greenish-blue.
When the monks stretched it with their hands,
it would lengthen or shorten with the hand.
When released, it would immediately coil into a snail shape.
The Emperor then hosted a grand "unobstructed assembly" (wú'ài dàhuì),
erected two stūpas (chà),
and each time placed the relics and nails and hair, first in a golden jar, then in a jade jar, heavily encased.
These were placed inside a seven-treasure pagoda,
and then the precious pagoda was enclosed in a stone casket.
These were divided and placed under the two stūpas.
15th, in the ninth month,
the Rourán invaded Sānduī, east of Wèi, for Wèi.
Wèi Shōu's "Zhì" states: Píngkòu Xiàn of Sìzhōu Yǒng'ān Jùn,
in the seventh year of Zhēnjūn,
was merged with Sānduī Xiàn and belonged to it;
there was a Sānduī garrison.
The Suí dynasty changed Píngkòu Xiàn to Guō Xiàn,
belonging to Yànmén Jùn.
Sòng Bái said: Jìnglè Xiàn of Lánzhōu,
was originally the land of Hàn Fényáng Xiàn.
Within the city walls, there are three mounds (duīfù),
commonly known as Sānduī Chéng.
"Wéi" (為)
is pronounced yúwěi.
The Rourán retreated and fled.
The Director of the Field Secretariat, Dù Bì, seeing that many civil and military officials were corrupt,
spoke to Chancellor Huān,
requesting to rectify them.
Huān said:
"Bì, come here!
I will tell you!
Corruption in the realm
has been a long-standing custom.
Currently, many of the commanders' families are in Guānxī;
this refers to the troops of Kězhūhún Dàoyuán, Wànsì Pǔ, Liú Fēngshēng, and others.
"Jiàng" (將)
is pronounced jíliàng.
People's loyalties are unsettled;
in Jiāngdōng, there is also the old man of Wú, Xiāo Yǎn,
who exclusively focuses on caps, robes, rites, and music.
The gentry of the Central Plains look to him as the legitimate sovereign.
If I were to strictly enforce discipline
without any leniency,
I fear that all the commanders would defect to Hēidá,
and all the scholars would flee to Xiāo Yǎn.
With people scattered,
how can we build a state!
You should wait a little longer.
I will not forget this."
History states that Gāo Huān adopted expedient measures to consolidate his followers,
overlooking minor faults to achieve major success.
"Shǎo" (少)
is pronounced shīzhǎo.
When Huān was about to send troops to resist Wèi,
Dù Bì requested to first eliminate internal enemies.
Huān asked who the internal enemies were.
Bì replied:
"Those honored nobles who plunder the common people."
Huān did not respond, but ordered all his soldiers to draw their bows and nock their arrows,
raise their swords,
and press their spears,
lining the path.
He commanded Bì to pass through them.
Bì trembled and sweated.
Huān then slowly admonished him, saying:
"Though the arrows are nocked, they do not shoot;
though the swords are raised, they do not strike;
though the spears are pressed, they do not thrust.
Yet you have lost your spirit and courage.
These honored men risked their lives in battle,
facing a hundred deaths for one life.
Though they may be greedy and vulgar,
what they have achieved is great.
How can they be treated like ordinary people!"
Bì then bowed his head and expressed his apologies for his oversight.
Whenever Huān issued orders to his soldiers,
he always had Zhāng Huáyuán from Dàijùn, an assistant to the Chancellor, announce them.
When speaking to the Xiānbēi, he would say:
"The Hàn people are your slaves.
Their men plow for you,
their women weave for you.
They transport grain and silk to you,
ensuring your warmth and satiety.
Why do you oppress them?"
When speaking to the Húarén, he would say:
"The Xiānbēi are your guests.
This means guests who work as laborers.
"Yǔ" (語)
is pronounced niújù.
"Wéi" (為)
is pronounced yúwěi;
the same below.
They fight off bandits for you,
ensuring your peace and tranquility.
Why do you resent them?"
History states that Gāo Huān skillfully utilized both the Yi and Huá peoples,
possessing the art of managing and controlling them.
At that time, the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) people collectively held the Huá (華) people in contempt,
except that they feared Gāo Áocáo (高敖曹).
Huān (歡) issued commands to his generals and soldiers,
usually in Xiānbēi (鮮卑) language.
When Áocáo (敖曹) was present among them,
he would speak in Huá (華) language for his sake.
When Áocáo (敖曹) returned from Shàngluò (上洛),
Huān (歡) reinstated him as Jūnsī (軍司) and Dàdūdū (大都督),
commanding seventy-six Dūdū (都督).
He appointed Sīkōng (司空) Hóu Jǐng (侯景) as Xīdào Dàxíngtái (西道大行臺),
sending Jǐng (景) to manage the affairs of Guānxī (關西).
Áocáo (敖曹) played shuò (槊) with Zhèng Yánzǔ (鄭嚴祖), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Běiyùzhōu (北豫州).
During the Tàicháng (泰常) era of Wèi (魏),
Yùzhōu (豫州) was established,
with its seat at Hǔláo (虎牢).
Later, when Rǔnán (汝南) was acquired,
another Yùzhōu (豫州) was established,
and Hǔláo (虎牢) became Běiyùzhōu (北豫州),
administering the commanderies of Guǎngwǔ (廣武), Xíngyáng (滎陽), and Chénggāo (成皋).
Shuò (槊)
is also a game like Bósài (博塞).
Liú Yǔxī (劉禹錫), in his observations on Bó (博), said:
"Initially,
the host would hold the shuò (槊) implements
and place them beneath the eaves,
saying: 'Those who wish to enter the game, make your wager.'
After bowing and yielding,
they would take turns.
There were Bóchǐ (博齒),
the chǐ (齒) differed from the ancient chǐ (齒);
they were made of bone,
with four equal angular ridges,
carved with red and black ink,
paired to form numbers,
corresponding to the sun and moon.
Observing their rotation and stop,
one would compete for position accordingly.
This system has been practiced for a long time,
its origin is unclear.
Since its use necessarily involves throwing,
it is called Bótóuzhào (博投詔)."
Also,
when Érzhū Shìlóng (爾朱世隆) played shuò (槊) with Yuán Shìjùn (元世儁),
suddenly a clattering sound was heard on the board,
and all the pieces stood on end.
Shìlóng (世隆) was greatly disturbed by this,
and soon after, disaster befell him.
Lǐ Yánshòu (李延壽) said: Shuò (槊)
is probably a Hu (胡) game
that recently entered Zhōngguó (中國).
It is said that a certain Hu (胡) king had a younger brother
who was convicted of a crime
and was about to be executed.
He created this game in prison and presented it,
implying that "being alone makes it easy to die."
Áocáo (敖曹) did not dispatch [the message] in time and
jailed its messenger.
The messenger said:
"It is easy to jail,
but difficult to release."
Áocáo (敖曹) approached the jailed man with a knife and slit his throat,
saying:
"What is so difficult!"
Guì (貴) did not dare to dispute him.
The next day,
Guì (貴) and Áocáo (敖曹) were sitting together.
An attendant reported that many laborers working on river repairs had drowned.
Guì (貴) said:
"Yīqiánhàn (一錢漢)" (a disparaging term for a Han person),
meaning that the Han people are cheap.
Áocáo (敖曹) was enraged,
drew his knife, and slashed at Guì (貴).
Guì (貴) fled back to his camp.
Áocáo (敖曹) beat the drums to assemble his troops,
intending to attack him.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) and Mòqí Luò (万俟洛) jointly tried to persuade him,
and after a long time, he stopped.
Áocáo (敖曹) once went to the prime minister's residence,
but the gatekeepers would not admit him.
Áocáo (敖曹) drew his bow and shot them.
Huān (歡) knew of this but did not blame him.
In the 16th intercalary month,
on the Jiǎzǐ (甲子) day,
Wǔlíng (武陵) King Jǐ (紀) was appointed Dūdū (都督) of the armies of Yì (益), Liáng (梁), and thirteen other prefectures, and Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yìzhōu (益州).
This laid the groundwork for the later struggle between Jǐ (紀) and Xiāngdōng (湘東) for the throne.
In the 17th year, the Chancellor of Eastern Wèi (東魏), Huān (歡), led an army of two hundred thousand from Húkǒu (壺口) towards Pújìn (蒲津).
The Bān Zhì (班志) says: Húkǒu (壺口) mountain is in the southeast of Běiqū (北屈) county, Hédōng (河東) commandery.
Běiqū (北屈) was later renamed Qínchāng (禽昌) county by the Latter Wèi (後魏),
belonging to Píngyáng (平陽) commandery;
during the Suí (隋) dynasty, Qínchāng (禽昌) was renamed Xiānglíng (襄陵) county.
將 (jiàng),
read as liàng (亮) (liàng);
same below.
趣 (qū),
read as qī yù (七喻) (qīyù).
At that time, Guānzhōng (關中) was suffering from famine.
The army led by Wèi (魏) Chancellor TàI (泰) numbered less than ten thousand men.
They were quartered and supplied in Héngnóng (恆農) for over fifty days.
Hearing that Huān (歡) was about to cross the river,
TàI (泰) led his troops into Guān (關),
and Gāo Áocáo (高敖曹) then besieged Héngnóng (恆農).
Xuē Shú (薛琡), the Yòuchángshǐ (右長史) of Huān (歡), said to Huān (歡):
"The western bandits have suffered famine for successive years,
which is why they risked death to enter Shǎnzhōu (陝州)
to seize the grain.
Now Áocáo (敖曹) has already besieged Shǎn (陝) city,
so the grain cannot be brought out.
Just station troops on all routes,
and do not engage in open battle.
By the time of the wheat harvest,
their people will naturally starve to death,
and what worry is there that Bǎojù (寶炬) and Hēità (黑獺) will not surrender!
I beg you not to cross the river."
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) said:
"This military campaign is of immense scale.
If, by any chance, we do not achieve victory,
it will be difficult to recover suddenly.
It would be better to divide the army into two forces,
advancing one after another.
If the vanguard wins,
the rear army can exert its full strength;
if the vanguard is defeated,
the rear army can support it."
Huān (歡) did not follow this advice,
and crossed the river from Pújìn (蒲津).
Kǎo Yì (考異) says: The Běiqí Dìjì (北齊帝紀) states:
"In the eleventh month,
on the Rénchén (壬辰) day,
Shénwǔ (神武) crossed from Pújìn (蒲津)."
The Wèi Dìjì (魏帝紀) states:
"In the tenth month,
on the Rénchén (壬辰) day,
defeated at Shāyuàn (沙苑)."
According to the Chánglì (長曆),
the tenth month began on the Rénchén (壬辰) day.
The Běiqí Jì (北齊紀) is incorrect.
Chancellor TàI (泰) sent an envoy to warn Wáng Pí (王羆), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Huázhōu (華州).
Pí (羆) said to the envoy:
"The old pí (羆) (bear) lies across the road,
how can the háozi (貉子) (badgers) pass!"
When Huān (歡) arrived below Féngyì (馮翊) city,
he said to Pí (羆):
"Why don't you surrender early!"
Pí (羆) shouted loudly:
"This city is Wáng Pí's (王羆) tomb;
life and death are here.
Those who wish to die, come!"
Huān (歡) knew it could not be attacked,
so he crossed the Luò (洛) River
and encamped west of Xǔyuán (許原).
The Hàn Zhì (漢志) says: South of Huáidé (懷德) county in Féngyì (馮翊) there is Jīngshān (荊山);
below the mountain is Qiángliáng (強梁) plain,
and the Luò (洛) River flows southeast into the Wèi (渭) River.
Xǔyuán (許原) was likely south of the Luò (洛) River.
Yuwén Tài arrived at Wèinán.
He summoned soldiers from various prefectures,
but they had not yet assembled.
He wanted to advance and attack Gāo Huān,
but his generals, citing the disparity in numbers,
requested to wait for Gāo Huān to move further west to observe his situation.
Yuwén Tài said:
"If Gāo Huān reaches Cháng'ān,
then popular sentiment will be greatly disturbed.
Now that he has come from afar and just arrived,
he can be attacked."
Immediately, he built a pontoon bridge over the Wèi River,
ordered his soldiers to carry three days' rations,
and led light cavalry across the Wèi River.
His heavy baggage proceeded west along the Wèi River from Wèinán.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Rénchén day,
Yuwén Tài arrived at Shāyuàn.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* states: Shāyuàn is north of the Wèi River.
South of Shāyuàn is the ruins of the Hán Huáidé county seat.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* states: Féngyì County has Shāyuàn.
All the generals were apprehensive,
except for Yǔwén Shēn who alone offered congratulations.
Yuwén Tài asked him why,
and he replied:
"Gāo Huān pacified Héběi
and gained much popular support.
Relying on this to defend himself,
it would not be easy to defeat him.
Now, he has led his army across the river,
which is not what the multitude desires.
Gāo Huān alone, ashamed of losing Dòu Tài,
stubbornly ignored advice and came.
This is what is called an army fighting out of resentment,
which can be captured in a single battle.
The reasoning is clear,
why should I not offer congratulations!
I beg you to grant Shēn a command token
to mobilize Wáng Pí's troops to intercept his retreat,
so that not a single one escapes."
Yuwén Tài dispatched Xūchāng Xiàn Gōng Dáxī Wǔ to scout Gāo Huān's army.
Dáxī Wǔ, with three horsemen,
all dressed in the clothes of Gāo Huān's officers and soldiers.
At dusk,
they dismounted a few hundred paces from the camp,
secretly listened and learned their army's password.
Then they mounted their horses and went through the camps,
acting like night patrols.
If anyone did not follow regulations,
they would often flog them.
They fully understood the enemy's situation and returned.
Gāo Huān heard that Yuwén Tài had arrived.
On the Guǐsì day,
he led his troops to meet him.
Scout cavalry reported that Gāo Huān's army was about to arrive.
Yuwén Tài summoned his generals to deliberate.
Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Lǐ Bì said:
"They are numerous and we are few,
so we cannot array ourselves on flat ground.
Ten *lǐ* to the east there is a bend in the Wèi River,
we can occupy it first and await them."
Yuwén Tài followed his advice.
With their backs to the water, they formed their array east and west.
Lǐ Bì was the right flank,
Zhào Guì was the left flank.
Dù Yù commented: Jù refers to a square formation.
Lù Démíng commented: Jù, pronounced like Jù-fǔ-fān.
They agreed to rise upon hearing the drum signal.
In the late afternoon,
the Eastern Wèi army arrived at the bend in the Wèi River.
Dūdū Tàiníng Húlǜ Qiāngjǔ said:
"The Black Otter has come with his entire nation,
intending to fight to the death.
It means he intends to exert his utmost strength in battle to decide victory or defeat.
He might be able to bite people.
Moreover, the reeds at the bend of the Wèi River are deep and the ground is muddy,
making it difficult to exert strength.
It is better to slowly hold him in check
and secretly divide our elite troops to directly attack Cháng'ān.
Once his stronghold is overthrown,
then the Black Otter will be captured without a fight."
If Húlǜ Qiāngjǔ's plan had been implemented, the Western Wèi would have been in peril.
"Why not set fire to it?"
Hóu Jǐng said:
"We should capture the Black Otter alive to show the common people.
If he is burned to death among the multitude,
who will believe it anymore!"
Hóu Jǐng's words here indeed show a mind that relies on superior numbers and underestimates the enemy.
Fù,
pronounced like Fúyòufān.
Subsequent "fù zhàn" and "kě fù tóng" follow this pronunciation.
He continued:
"Our forces are numerous, the enemy few.
One hundred men can capture one,
what worry is there that we won't succeed!"
Gāo Huān followed his advice.
The Eastern Wèi soldiers, seeing that the Wèi army was small,
rushed forward to attack them,
without any formation.
The historian states that the Eastern Wèi generals and soldiers all relied on their numerical superiority and underestimated the enemy,
hence their defeat.
Shǎo,
pronounced like Shīzhǎofān.
Fù,
pronounced like Fúyòufān.
Háng,
pronounced like Hùgāngfān.
Chancellor Yuwén Tài beat the drums,
and the soldiers all rose up in valor.
Yú Jǐn and the other six armies joined battle with them.
Lǐ Bì led his iron cavalry to strike them from the flank.
At that time, the Eastern Wèi forces were concentrated at the left flank.

Word came that Xióng's (雄) army and others were pressing on Yǐngchuān,

All the generals believed,
"Their forces are many, ours are few,
we cannot contend with them head-on."
Guì (貴) said,
"Xióng (雄) and the others think our troops are few,
and they will certainly not dare to advance.
If they combine forces with Rèn Xiáng (任祥) to attack Yǐngchuān,

If Hèruò Tǒng (賀若統) is captured or killed,

Now, if we advance and occupy Yǐngchuān,
we will have a city to defend,
and by striking unexpectedly,
we are bound to defeat them."
So they swiftly marched
and occupied Yǐngchuān,
forming a battle array with their backs to the city to await the enemy.
When Xióng (雄) and the others arrived,
they engaged in battle

Xióng (雄) fled.

More than ten thousand of their soldiers were captured

When Rèn Xiáng (任祥) heard of Xióng's (雄) defeat,

Guì (貴) and Yí Fēng (怡峯) pressed on him, taking advantage of their victory.

Wǎnlíng County,

At that time, most of the prefectures in Hénán (河南) had been lost,

Xíng Mó'nà (邢磨納) of Héjiān (河間), Lú Zhònglǐ (盧仲禮) of Fányáng (范陽), and Zhònglǐ's (仲禮) cousin Zhòngyù (仲裕) all raised troops along the coast to respond to Wèi.
The Eastern Wèi's Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (濟州刺史) Gāo Jìshì (高季式) had over a thousand retainers
and eight hundred horses,
fully equipped with armor and weapons.
Dù Língchūn (杜靈椿) and others from Púyáng (濮陽) became bandits,
amassing nearly ten thousand people.
They attacked cities and plundered the countryside.
Jìshì (季式) dispatched three hundred cavalry,
captured them in one battle,
and then attacked the Yángpíng (陽平) bandits, Lù Wéntú (路文徒)
and others,
completely pacifying them.
Thus, order was restored far and wide.
Someone said to Jìshì (季式),
"Púyáng (濮陽) and Yángpíng (陽平) are commanderies within the imperial domain.
Both commanderies
were assigned to Sīzhōu (司州) by the Eastern Wèi,
hence the statement.
And they did not invade our territory."
Meaning there was no imperial edict for Jìshì (季式) to suppress the bandits,
and the bandits did not invade Jìzhōu's (濟州) territory.
"If by any chance we suffer a defeat,
would we not incur blame?"
The retainers Jìshì (季shì) had personally maintained
were not clothed or fed by the government,
hence they were called private troops.
"Why do you speak so disloyally?
I share the peace and danger with the state;
how could I see bandits and not suppress them?
Moreover, the bandits know that the court army cannot arrive suddenly,
and they do not suspect that troops from an outer prefecture would attack them.
Taking advantage of their unpreparedness,
we are bound to defeat them.
Even if I incur blame for this,
I will have no regrets."

a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the era name was changed to Yuánxiàng (元象).
3. Second month,
On the jǐhài (己亥) day,
the Emperor personally plowed the ancestral field (Jìtián, 藉田).
4. The Eastern Wèi's Grand Commandant Shànwú Hèbá Rén (善無賀拔仁) attacked Wèi's Nánfénzhōu (南汾州).
Cìshǐ (刺史) Wéi Zǐcàn (韋子粲) surrendered to him,
and Chancellor Tà (泰) exterminated Zǐcàn's (子粲) clan.
The Eastern Wèi's Grand Xíngtái Hóu Jǐng (侯景) and others marshaled troops at Hǔláo (虎牢),
intending to recover the prefectures in Hénán (河南).
Wèi's Liáng Jiǒng (梁迥), Wéi Xiàokuān (韋孝寬), and Zhào Jìzōng (趙繼宗) all abandoned their cities and returned west.
Liáng Jiǒng (梁迥) was in Yǐngchuān (潁川),
Wéi Xiàokuān (韋孝寬) was in Rǔnán (汝南),
it is unknown which city Zhào Jìzōng (趙繼宗) abandoned.
Not yet captured.
Guǎngzhōu (廣州) was governed from Xiāngchéng (襄城).
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) gathered his generals to discuss,
and Lú Yǒng (盧勇), who was acting as Luòzhōu Shì (洛州事), requested to advance and observe the situation.
The Eastern Wèi's Luòzhōu (洛州)
was governed from Luòyáng (洛陽).
Zhūjiàng (諸將),
pronounced like jí liàng (即亮);
the same below.
The Bān Zhì (班志) states: In Mìxiàn (密縣) of Hénán Commandery, there is Dàguīshān (大騩山).
Wèi Shōu Zhì (魏收志) states,
Mìxiàn (密縣) belonged to Xíngyáng Commandery.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) states,
in Xīnzhèng County of Xíngyáng Commandery, there is Dàguīshān (大騩山).
Shuài (帥),
read as lǜ (率).
Qí (騎),
pronounced qí jì (奇寄).
Guī (騩) and Kuí (隗) are interchangeable,
pronounced wǔ huì (五賄),
also pronounced guī (歸).
As dusk fell,
Yǒng (勇) placed many banners on treetops.
At night,
he divided his cavalry into ten squadrons,
sounded their horns, and charged straight forward,
capturing Wèi's Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) Chéng Huá (程華),
and beheading Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) Wáng Zhēngmán (王征蠻) before returning.
The Guǎngzhōu (廣州) defending general Luò Chāo (駱超)
subsequently surrendered the city to the Eastern Wèi.
Chancellor Huān (歡) appointed Yǒng (勇) to act as Guǎngzhōu Shì (廣州事).
Yǒng (勇)
was the cousin of Biàn (辯).
Lú Biàn (盧辯) served the Western Wèi,
while Yǒng (勇) served the Eastern Wèi.
Cóng (從),
pronounced cái yòng (才用).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Diǎnlüè (典略) says
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) captured Guǎngzhōu (廣州) in the eleventh month.
However, according to the Běishǐ Wèi Wéndì Jì (北史魏文帝紀),
"In the second month,
the Eastern Wèi captured the four prefectures of Nánfén (南汾), Yǐng (潁), Yù (豫), and Guǎng (廣)."
We follow this account here.
5 At first,
Rouran (柔然) Tóbīng Kèhán (頭兵可汗) had just returned to his country;
the matter is seen in Volume 149, Pǔtōng (普通) 2nd year.
Kě (可),
from kān (刊) entering tone.
Hán (汗),
pronounced hán (寒).
After Yǒng'ān (永安),
he dominated the north,
and his courtesies gradually became arrogant.
Though envoys continued without interruption,
he no longer called himself a subject.
Tóbīng (頭兵) once came to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and admired Zhōngguó (中國) in his heart,
so he established officials like Shìzhōng (侍中) and Huángmén (黃門);
later he obtained Chúnyú Tán (淳于覃), a diǎnqiān (典籤) of Wèi (魏) Rǔyáng Wáng (汝陽王),
whom he personally favored and entrusted with affairs,
making him Mìshūjiān (祕書監),
and entrusting him with literary matters.
When the two Wèis (魏) split,
Tóbīng (頭兵) became increasingly insolent,
frequently causing border troubles.
Wèi (魏) Prime Minister Tà (泰) had just established the new capital in Guānzhōng (關中),
and was about to deal with matters in Shāndōng (山東).
He wished to establish a marital alliance to placate him,
so he made Yúan Yì's (元翌) daughter Huàzhèng Gōngzhǔ (化政公主),
and married her to Tóbīng's (頭兵) younger brother Tǎhán (塔寒).
He also spoke to the Wèi (魏) ruler,
requesting the dethronement of Empress Yǐfú (乙弗),
and the marriage to Tóbīng's (頭兵) daughter.
On the day of Jiǎchén (甲辰),
Empress Yǐfú (乙弗) was made a nun.
Wèi (魏) enthroned Empress Yǐfú (乙弗),
seen in the previous volume, Dàtóng (大同) 1st year.
Tóbīng (頭兵) then detained the Eastern Wèi (東魏) envoy Yúan Zhěng (元整),
and did not send back his envoy.
6 In the third month,
on the day of Xīnyǒu (辛酉),
Eastern Wèi (東魏) Prime Minister Huān (歡), due to the defeat at Shāyuàn (沙苑) –
the defeat is seen in the previous volume, previous year –
issued an edict permitting it;
after a short while,
he was restored to his former position.
The Kǎyì (考異) says: The Běi Qí Dìjì (北齊帝紀) only mentions the year and month Gāozǔ (高祖) relinquished the prime ministership,
but has no text about his restoration.
According to the discussion of the calendar in Xīnghé (興和) 1st year,
there was a prime minister Tiáncáo Cānjūn (田曹參軍) Xìndū Fāng (信都芳).
It was probably restored due to the victory at Mángshān (邙山).
7 The Rouran (柔然) sent Empress Dào (悼) to Wèi (魏).
Empress Yùjiǔlǘ (郁久閭) was posthumously named Dào (悼).
Ten thousand horses and
two thousand camels.
Upon reaching Hēiyánchí (黑鹽池) –
the Tángzhì (唐志) states: Wǔyuán Xiàn (五原縣) in Yánzhōu (鹽州) has Wūchí (烏池) and Báichí (白池).
Wūchí (烏池)
is probably Hēiyánchí (黑鹽池) –
Chéng (乘),
pronounced shéng zhèng.
The Rouran (柔然) encampment's
tents and mats all faced east.
Fúfēng Wáng (扶風王) Fú (孚) requested to face directly south.
The Empress said:
"I have not yet seen the Wèi (魏) ruler,
so I am still a Rouran (柔然) woman.
Wèi (魏) faces south,
I face east."
On the day of Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
Empress Yùjiǔlǘ (郁久閭) was established.
On the day of Dīngchǒu (丁丑),
a general amnesty was declared.
Wáng Méng (王盟) was made Sītú (司徒).
Prime Minister Tà (泰) held court in Cháng'ān (長安),
then returned to garrison Huázhōu (華州).
8 Summer,
fourth month,
on the day of Gēngyín (庚寅),
Eastern Wèi (東魏) Gāo Huān (高歡) held court in Yè (鄴);
having resigned as prime minister,
his surname was recorded instead of his official title.
The Tōngjiàn (通鑑) records facts,
it is not like the Chūnqiū (春秋) which contains praise and criticism.
On the day of Rénchén (壬辰)
he returned to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
9 Fifth month,
on the day of Jiǎxū (甲戌),
Eastern Wèi (東魏) sent the concurrent Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) Zhèng Bóyóu (鄭伯猷) to visit.
The Kǎyì (考異) says: The Wèi Dìjì (魏帝紀) places it on the day of Bǐngchén (丙辰) in the second month,
which was probably when he first received the commission.
We now follow the Liáng Dìjì (梁帝紀).
10 Autumn,
seventh month,
Eastern Wèi (東魏) Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) Wáng Zé (王則) raided Huáinán (淮南).
This Huáinán (淮南)
refers to the area of Guāngchéng (光城) and Yìyáng (弋陽),
south of the upper reaches of the Huái (淮) River,
not the ancient Huáinán Jùn (淮南郡) whose seat was Shòuchūn (壽春).
11 On the day of Guǐhài (癸亥),
an edict was issued declaring a general amnesty
because the convict Lǐ Yìn (李胤) from Dōngyě (東冶) had obtained the Tathāgata's relics.
Rúlái (如來)
is synonymous with Fó (佛) (Buddha).
12 Eastern Wèi (東魏) Hóu Jǐng (侯景), Gāo Áocáo (高敖曹) and others besieged Wèi (魏) Dúgū Xìn (獨孤信) at Jīnyǒng (金墉).
Grand Master Huān (歡) led a large army to follow up.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) burned all the official temples and civilian residences inside and outside Luòyáng (洛陽),
only two or three tenths remaining.
The Wèi (魏) ruler was about to go to Luòyáng (洛陽) to pay respects at the imperial tombs –
from Emperor Xiàowén (孝文) moving the capital to Luò (洛)
until Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武) moving west,
the imperial tombs were all in Luòzhōu (洛州) –
so he went east with Prime Minister Tà (泰),
ordering Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè (尚書左僕射) Zhōu Huìdá (周惠達) to assist Crown Prince Qīn (欽) in defending Cháng'ān (長安),
and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司) Lǐ Bì (李弼) and Chējì Dàjiàngjūn (車騎大將軍) Dáxī Wǔ (達奚武) to lead a thousand cavalry as the vanguard.
Eighth month,
on the day of Gēngyín (庚寅),
Prime Minister Tà (泰) arrived at Gǔchéng (穀城).
The Hànzhì (漢志) says: Hénán Jùn (河南郡) has Gǔchéng Xiàn (穀成縣).
Shīgǔ (師古) noted: It is today's Xīn'ān (新安).
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) says: Gǔchéng Xiàn (穀城縣) city faces the Gǔ (穀) River on its west.
Qí (騎),
pronounced qí jì;
same below.
Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) Tà'ān (太安) Mòduōlóu Dàiwén (莫多婁貸文) requested to lead his division to attack their vanguard.
Mòduōlóu (莫多婁)
is a three-character barbarian surname.
Dàiwén (貸文) was brave but headstrong,
and did not obey orders.
He advanced with Kězhūhún Dàoyuán (可朱渾道元) with a thousand cavalry.
At night,
they encountered Lǐ Bì (李弼) and Dáxī Wǔ (達奚武) at Xiàoshuǐ (孝水).
The Wǔdàizhì (五代志) says: Xīn'ān Xiàn (新安縣) has Xiàoshuǐ (孝水).
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) says: Xiàoshuǐ (孝水) originates from the northern slope of Guīshān (廆山),
flows north into the Gǔ (穀) River,
and is forty lǐ (里) west of Hénán Chéng (河南城).
Dragging firewood to raise dust,
Dàiwén (貸文) fled.
Lǐ Bì (李弼) pursued and beheaded him.
Dàoyuán (道元) escaped alone on horseback,
and all his troops were captured and sent to Héngnóng (恆農).
Tà (泰) advanced his army to Chándōng (瀍東).
The Chán (瀍) River originates from the northern mountain of Gǔchéng Xiàn (穀城縣), Hénán (河南),
flows east to join the Qiānjīn Qú (千金渠),
then flows east past the south of Luòyáng Xiàn (洛陽縣),
then flows east past Yǎnshī Xiàn (偃師縣),
then flows east into the Luò (洛) River.
On the day of Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
Tà (泰) led light cavalry to pursue Hóu Jǐng (侯景) to the river.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) formed a battle array,
with his north resting on Héquán (河橋)
and his south on Mángshān (邙山),
and engaged Tà (泰) in battle.
Tà's (泰) horse was struck by a stray arrow and bolted,
losing its way.
Tà (泰) fell to the ground,
and Eastern Wèi (東魏) soldiers caught up to him.
All his retinue had dispersed.
Dūdū (都督) Lǐ Mù (李穆) dismounted,
and whipped Tà's (泰) back with his whip, cursing:
"Clumsy soldier!
Where is your lord,
that you alone remain here?"
The pursuers did not suspect he was a person of high rank,
and passed him by.
Lǐ Mù (李穆) gave his horse to Tà (泰),
and they escaped together.
The Wèi troops rallied again,
attacked the Eastern Wèi troops,
and utterly defeated them.
Yǔwén Tài had initially engaged with light cavalry and fared poorly,
but when his main forces arrived,
the army's morale revived,
thus utterly defeating the Eastern Wèi.
Gāo Áocáo, Duke Zhōngwǔ of Jīngzhào,
underestimated Tài,
raising his banners and parasols to arrogantly array his troops.
The Wèi men attacked him with full might,
and his entire army was annihilated.
Áocáo fled alone on horseback to Hèyáng Nánchéng.
Hèyáng Nánchéng
was on the south bank of the Héquiáo,
while the north bank was Běizhōngchéng.
He was a cousin of Huān's (a son of Huān's paternal cousin),
and had a grudge against Áocáo,
so he closed the gates and refused him entry.
Áocáo looked up and called for a rope,
but received none.
He drew his sword and started to cut through the door panel, but before he could finish, the pursuing troops arrived.
Dù Yù said: 'Hé' (闔)
means a door panel.
'Wèichè' (未徹)
means not yet pierced through.
'Chè' (徹)
is pronounced 'chìliè'.
The pursuers saw his attendant carrying a golden belt,
asked where Áocáo was,
and the attendant pointed him out.
Áocáo knew he could not escape,
and thrusting his head forward, said:
"Come!
I will grant you the title of Kāiguó Gōng."
He meant that if they obtained his head,
the Western Wèi generals would reward them with the title of Kāiguó Gōng.
Gāo Huān heard of this
and was as distraught as if he had lost his liver and gallbladder.
He had Gāo Yǒnglè beaten with two hundred strokes of the rod,
and posthumously bestowed upon Áocáo the titles of Tàishī, Dàsīmǎ, and Tàiwèi.
Tài rewarded the killer of Áocáo with ten thousand bolts of cloth and silk,
distributing them gradually year by year.
By the time the Zhōu dynasty fell,
the full reward had still not been given.
The Wèi also killed Sòng Xiǎn, the Eastern Wèi Cìshǐ of Xīyǎanzhōu, and others,
capturing fifteen thousand armored soldiers.
Those who drowned in the river numbered in the tens of thousands.
Earlier,
Huān respected Wànqí Pǔzūn for his age,
meaning his rank was high and his years were old.
'Wàn' (万)
is pronounced 'mòběi'.
'Qí' (俟)
is pronounced 'qúzhī'.
He once personally helped him onto his horse.
His son Luò removed his cap and bowed, saying:
"I vow to exert my utmost to repay your profound kindness."
When the Battle of Mángshān occurred,
the various armies crossed the bridge to the north,
meaning they crossed the Héquiáo to the north.
He said to the Wèi men:
"Wànqí Shòuluògān is here!
If you can come, then come!"
The Wèi men feared him and withdrew.
Huān named the place where he encamped Huíluò.
The Táng Gazetteer states: South of the Hèyáng Pass lies the old city of Huíluò.
On that day,
the Eastern and Western Wèi armies deployed vast formations,
with their front and rear widely separated.
From dawn until mid-afternoon,
they fought dozens of engagements.
The histories describe the two armies fighting with great ferocity.
'Sāi' (塞)
is pronounced 'xīzé'.
Dúgū Xìn and Lǐ Yuǎn of Wèi were on the right,
Zhào Guì and Yí Fēng were on the left,
and they all fared poorly in battle.
Moreover, they did not know the whereabouts of the Wèi Emperor and Chancellor Tài,
so they all abandoned their troops and returned first.
Lǐ Hǔ, Niàn Xián, and others, who held the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, were in the rearguard.
Seeing Xìn and the others retreat,
they immediately left with them.
Tài subsequently burned his camps and returned,
leaving Chángsūn Zǐyàn, also a Yítóng Sānsī, to defend Jīnyōng.
Wáng Sīzhèng dismounted,
wielded his long spear, striking left and right,
and with each strike, several people fell.
He penetrated deeply into the enemy formation,
and all his followers were killed.
Sīzhèng suffered severe wounds
and passed out.
It happened to be dusk,
and the enemy also withdrew their troops.
Sīzhèng always wore worn-out clothes and battered armor in battle,
so the enemy did not recognize him as a general,
and thus he escaped.
Léi Wǔ'ān, a commander under his tent, cried out, searching for Sīzhèng at the battle site.
He found that Sīzhèng had already regained consciousness.
He tore his clothes to bind the wounds,
helped Sīzhèng onto a horse,
and after a long night,
they finally returned to the camp.
Cài Yòu, General Píngdōng, dismounted to fight on foot.
Those around him advised him to ride a horse to prepare for sudden emergencies,
meaning if the troops encountered an unforeseen event, he could quickly flee on horseback.
He said:
"The Chancellor loves me as a son.
How could I cherish my life today?"
Leading more than ten men on his left and right, he shouted loudly
and attacked the Eastern Wèi troops,
killing and wounding many.
The Eastern Wèi surrounded him with more than ten layers.
Yòu drew his bow to full string,
fending them off from all sides.
The Eastern Wèi men recruited heavily armored soldiers with long knives to advance directly and capture him.
When they were about thirty paces from Yòu,
his attendants advised him to shoot them.
Yòu said:
"Our lives
depend on this one arrow.
How can I shoot it in vain?"
When they were about ten paces away,
Yòu then shot,
and the target fell at the sound of the bowstring.
The Eastern Wèi troops slightly recoiled,
and Yòu slowly withdrew.
The Wèi Emperor arrived at Héngnóng.
The defending general had already abandoned the city and fled.
The captured and surrendered soldiers of the Eastern Wèi who were in Héngnóng closed the gates together and resisted.
Chancellor Tài attacked and captured it,
executing several hundred of their leaders.
Cài Yòu caught up with Tài at Héngnóng.
That night,
he saw Tài.
Tài said:
"Chéngxiān (138), Cài Yòu's courtesy name was Chéngxiān.
I have no worries now."
Tài was so agitated he could not sleep.
He used Yòu's thigh as a pillow,
and only then found peace.
The histories say Tài was disheartened and lacked courage.
'Zhěn' (枕)
is pronounced 'zhīrèn'.
He always led his soldiers,
but when they returned from battle,
while the other generals vied for credit,
Yòu never spoke of his achievements.
Tài often sighed and said:
"Chéngxiān does not speak of his merits;
I shall enumerate and commend them on his behalf."
The histories say Cài Yòu was profound, brave, and not boastful.
He was appointed Shìzhōng and Dōngdào Xíngtái.
When Wèi campaigned in the east,
few troops were left behind to guard Guānzhōng.
The previously captured Eastern Wèi soldiers, scattered among the populace,
heard of the Wèi army's defeat
and conspired to rebel.
Lǐ Hǔ and others arrived in Cháng'ān,
unable to devise a plan.
They, along with Tàiwèi Wáng Méng, Púshè Zhōu Huìdá, and others, escorted Crown Prince Qīn to encamp north of the Wèi River.
The common people plundered each other,
and Guānzhōng was in great turmoil.
Consequently, Zhào Qīngquè, an Eastern Wèi Dūdū captured at Shāyuàn, and Yōngzhōu civilian Yú Fúdē, and others, rebelled,
occupying
Cháng'ān's inner city.
Fúdē held Xiányáng,
and he and Mùróng Sīqìng, the Xiányáng Tàishǒu, each gathered surrendered soldiers to resist the returning army.
The 'surrendered soldiers'
refers to the Eastern Wèi soldiers who had surrendered to the Western Wèi
and were scattered among the populace.
The 'returning army'
refers to the Western Wèi army returning from the west of Luò.
'Jiàng' (降)
is pronounced 'hùjiāng'.
They fought daily with them.
Dàdūdū Hóumòchén Shùn attacked the rebels,
repeatedly defeating them,
so the rebels dared not venture out.
Shùn
was Chóng's elder brother.
Wáng Pí, Duke Fúfēng, garrisoned Hédōng.
He opened the city gates wide
and gathered all the soldiers, saying:
"I now hear that the main army has suffered a defeat,
and Qīngquè has rebelled.
None of you have a firm resolve.
Wáng Pí has been entrusted here
and will repay this kindness with my death.
Those who share my resolve can hold fast together;
if you are truly afraid of the city falling,
you are free to leave the city."
The crowd was moved by his words,
and all remained steadfast.
The Wèi zhǔ remained in Ménxiāng.
Chéngxiàng Tàibecause the soldiers and horses were exhausted and depleted,
could not advance quickly.
He also said that Qīngquè and his ilk were a rabble,
and could not cause trouble,
saying:
"When I reach Cháng'ān,
and approach them with light cavalry,
they will surely bind themselves."
Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Lù Tōng of Wú Jùn, remonstrated, saying:
Lù Tōng was originally a Wú person.
His great-grandfather, Zǎi, followed Sòng Wǔdì into the passes.
When Liú Yìzhēn was defeated and perished at Hèlián,
he then settled in Guānzhōng.
"The rebel's treacherous plot has long been settled;
they will surely have no intention of changing for the better.
Hornets and scorpions have venom,
Zāng Wénzhòng's words from the Zuǒzhuàn.
*Chài*,
pronounced chǒu mài.
Moreover, the rebels falsely claim that the Eastern invaders are about to arrive.
Eastern invaders,
refers to the troops of Dōng Wèi.
The common people believe this to be true,
taking the rebels' words as truth.
Although our army is now exhausted,
the elite forces are still many.
With Mínggōng's might,
leading a great army to confront them,
how can we worry about not being victorious!"
Tàifollowed his advice,
and led his troops westward.
When the elders saw Tàiarrive,
none were without grief and joy;
men and women congratulated each other.
Huázhōu Cìshǐ Yǔwén Dǎo led troops into Xiányáng,
beheaded Sīqìng,
captured Fúdé,
crossed the Wèi River southwards,
met with Tài,
attacked Qīngquè,
and defeated him.
Tàibǎo Liáng Jǐngruì, who had remained in Cháng'ān due to illness,
conspired with Qīngquè;
Tàikilled him.
Dōng Wèi Tàishī Huān, with seven thousand cavalry, arrived at Mèngjīn from Jìnyáng.
Before crossing,
he heard that the Wèi army had already retreated,
so he crossed the river,
and sent a separate general to pursue the Wèi army to Xiáo.
Wèi Shōu Zhì: In the eleventh year of Tàihé,
Xiáo County was established,
belonging to Héngnóng Commandery,
named after the Sānxiáo Mountains;
during the Suí dynasty, Xiáo County was merged into Hénán Xióng'ěr County.
Chéng Dàchāng said: The Sānxiáo Mountains
are also called Qīnyín Mountain.
Yuánhé Zhì says: From the Eastern Xiáo to the Western Xiáo is thirty-five *lǐ*.
The Eastern Xiáo has a long slope of several *lǐ*,
with steep mounds and sheer ravines,
where chariots cannot run side-by-side.
The Western Xiáo is entirely a stone slope of twelve *lǐ*,
with dangers no different from the Eastern Xiáo.
Both of these Xiáo are east of the Qín Pass
and west of the Hàn Pass.
Huān attacked Jīnyǒng.

Lú Jǐngyù was originally a Confucian scholar.
Tàishī Huān released him,
summoned him to reside at his home,
and made him teach his sons.
Jǐngyù's lectures and discussions were profound and subtle.
Those who challenged him would sometimes insult and criticize him,
with loud voices and harsh expressions,
even speaking disrespectfully,
yet Jǐngyù's demeanor remained solemn,
his manner unchanging.
He calmly responded back and forth,
leaving no opening to be found.
By nature he was pure and tranquil.
Throughout his official career, he experienced both advancements and setbacks,
but showed no expression of gain or loss;
with worn clothes and coarse food,
he was content and at ease,
maintaining a dignified and solemn posture all day,
as if facing guests.

Lǐ Chángshòu, a prominent local figure from Yīchuān, Wèi, was appointed as the Commandant to guard against the barbarians.

Noble officials of Wèi, such as Guǎnglíng Wáng Xīn and President of the Department of State Affairs Zhǎngsūn Zhì, all brought their families to seek refuge with him.

enabling them to reach Guānzhōng.
Gāo Huān of the Eastern Wèi was troubled by this,
and repeatedly sent troops to attack Lǐ Yánsūn,
but could not defeat him.

Gāo Chéng memorialized to have them re-selected.
Xiān was then favored and trusted by Chéng,
and Zhòngmì suspected him of plotting against him,
increasing his resentment.
Zhòngmì's second wife, Lǐ Shì, was beautiful and intelligent.
After Cuī Xiān's sister left,
Lǐ Shì became his second wife,
hence "second wife."
Lǐ Shì did not consent,
her clothes were all torn.
She reported this to Zhòngmì,
which further deepened Zhòngmì's resentment.
Soon after, he was sent out as Běiyùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Běiyùzhōu's seat was Hǔláo.
Chancellor Huān suspected him
and sent Zhènchéng Xī Shòuxīng to oversee military affairs.
The position of Zhènchéng was similar to a Dūdu (military commander) of city defense.
Zhòngmì hosted a banquet for Shòuxīng,
ambushed him with strongmen,
and seized him.
In the second month,
on the day Rénshēn,
he rebelled at Hǔláo
and surrendered to Wèi.
Wèi appointed Zhòngmì as Shìzhōng and Sītú.
Huān (高歡) believed Zhòngmì’s (元仲密) rebellion was caused by Cuī Xiān (崔暹),
and intended to kill him.
Gāo Chéng (高澄) hid Xiān (崔暹)
and earnestly pleaded for him.
Huān (高歡) said:
“I will spare his life,
but he must suffer the rod.”
This meant he would be severely beaten.
He then said to Chén Yuánkāng (陳元康), the Langzhong (郎中) of the Duguan (都官) department of the Dà Xíngtái (大行臺):
“Let Cuī Xiān (崔暹) be beaten,
and I do not wish to see him again.”
Yuánkāng (陳元康) spoke on his behalf to Huān (高歡), saying:
“Your Royal Highness is about to entrust the empire to the Great General.
If the Great General cannot even spare a Cuī Xiān (崔暹) from the rod,
and this is the case between father and son,
what about others!”
Huān (高歡) then released him.
Gāo Jìshì (高季式) was stationed at Yǒng’ān (永安) garrison.
Yǒng’ān (永安) County
was ancient Zhìyì (彘邑).
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, it belonged to Hédōng Jùn (河東郡).
In the Later Hàn (後漢), Emperor Shùn (順帝) renamed it Yǒng’ān Xiàn (永安縣).
Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) monograph states: In the first year of Jiànyì (建義), Yǒng’ān Jùn (永安郡) was established,
with its seat at Yǒng’ān Chéng (永安城),
belonging to Jìnzhōu (晉州).
At that time, Jìshì (高季式) was dismissed from Jìnzhōu (晉州)
and sent to garrison it.
The Suí (隋) dynasty abolished Yǒng’ān Jùn (永安郡)
and renamed it Huòyì Xiàn (霍邑縣).
Jìshì (高季式) ran to inform Huān (高歡),
who treated him as before.
Wèi (魏) Chancellor Tà (宇文泰) led his armies to respond to Zhòngmì (元仲密).
He appointed Lǐ Yuǎn (李遠), the Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince, as vanguard.
Upon reaching Luòyáng (洛陽),
he dispatched Yú Jǐn (于謹), Kaitai Yitong Sansi (開府儀同三司), to attack Bǎigǔ (柏谷),
which he captured.
In the third month,
on the Rénshēn (壬申) day,
they besieged the southern city of the Héqiáo (河橋) bridge.
The Eastern Wèi (東魏) Chancellor Huān (高歡) led an army of 100,000 to north of the Hé (河) river.
Tà (宇文泰) retreated his troops to Chánshàng (瀍上),
and set fire to boats upstream to burn the Héqiáo (河橋) bridge.
Húlǜ Jīn (斛律金) sent the Xíngtái Langzhong (行臺郎中) Zhāng Liàng (張亮) with over a hundred small boats loaded with long chains.
When the fire boats were about to arrive,
he had them nailed down,
pulling the chains towards the bank,
and thus the bridge was saved.
Huān (高歡) crossed the river,
took position on Mángshān (邙山) for battle,
and did not advance for several days.
Tà (宇文泰) left his baggage train at Chánqǔ (瀍曲),
and at night,
ascended Mángshān (邙山) to raid Huān (高歡).
A scout reported to Huān (高歡):
“The enemy is forty li away,
eating dried rations as they come.”
Huān (高歡) said:
“They will surely die of thirst!”
Then he straightened his formation to await them.
Huān (高歡) wanted to hold a firm line,
waiting for them to be tired and thirsty before engaging in battle,
hence he said that.
Gān (乾),
pronounced gān.
At dawn on Wùshēn (戊申),
Tà’s (宇文泰) army met Huān’s (高歡) army.
Páng Lè (彭樂) of Eastern Wèi (東魏) led several thousand cavalry as the right flank,
charging the northern wing of the Wèi (魏) army.
Wherever they went, the enemy collapsed,
and they rode into the Wèi (魏) camp.
Someone reported that Páng Lè (彭樂) had defected,
and Huān (高歡) was furious.
Soon after, dust rose in the northwest,
and Lè’s (彭樂) envoy arrived to report victory,

having captured Wèi (魏) Shìzhōng (侍中), Kaitai Yitong Sansi (開府儀同三司), Dàdūdū (大都督) Línzhāo Wáng Jiǎn (臨洮王柬), Shǔjùn Wáng Róngzōng (蜀郡王榮宗), Jiāngxià Wáng Shēng (江夏王昇), Jùlù Wáng Chǎn (鉅鹿王闡), Qiáojùn Wáng Liàng (譙郡王亮), Zhànshì Zhào Shàn (詹事趙善), and forty-eight generals and officials.
The generals, pressing their advantage, attacked Wèi (魏),
utterly defeating them,
and beheaded over thirty thousand soldiers.
Huān (高歡) sent Páng Lè (彭樂) to pursue Tà (宇文泰).
Tà (宇文泰), in distress,
said to Lè (彭樂):
“Are you not Páng Lè (彭樂)?
You foolish man!
If I am not here today,
how can you exist tomorrow!
Why don’t you quickly return to camp
and collect your gold and treasures!”
Lè (彭樂) followed his words,
obtained a bag of Tà’s (宇文泰) golden belts, and returned,
saying to Huān (高歡):
“The black otter (referring to Tà) has dropped his blade,
he’s terrified!”
Although Huān (高歡) was pleased with the victory, he was angry at Lè (彭樂) for letting Tà (宇文泰) escape.
He ordered Lè (彭樂) to prostrate himself on the ground,
personally grabbed his head,
repeatedly slammed it,
and recounted his failure at Shāyuàn (沙苑),
which is detailed in the third year of the previous volume.
Shǔ (數),
pronounced suǒjù.
He gnashed his teeth in anger for a long time.
Jìnxiè (噤齘),
to gnash teeth in anger.
Jìn (噤),
pronounced zhíjìn,
also written jìn.
Xiè (齘),
pronounced hújiè.
“[I] beg for five thousand cavalry,
and I will capture him for Your Royal Highness again.”
Huān (高歡) said:
“What was your intention in letting him go, to now say you will capture him again?”
He ordered three thousand bolts of silk to be placed on Lè’s (彭樂) back,
and then bestowed them upon him.
Huān (高歡) instructed his son Chéng (高澄) to be on guard against Páng Lè (彭樂)’s ambitions.
The next day,
they fought again.
Tà (宇文泰) commanded the central army,
Zhào Guì (趙貴), Duke of Zhōngshān (中山公), commanded the left army,
and the Lingjun (領軍) Ruòyú Huì (若干惠) and others commanded the right army.
Línghú Défēn (令狐德棻) said: The Ruòyú (若干) clan’s ancestors rose with Wèi (魏),
taking the state as their surname.
The Wèi Shū (魏書) Official Families Monograph states that among the assimilated surnames is the Ruògān (若干) clan.
“Yú” (于)
is written
“Gān” (干).
Sūn Miǎn (孫愐) said: Ruò (若),
pronounced rénzhě.
They were utterly defeated,
and all their infantry were captured.
Huān (高歡) lost his horse.
Hèlián Yángshùn (赫連陽順) dismounted and gave his horse to Huān (高歡).
Huān (高歡) mounted and fled,
accompanied by seven foot soldiers and cavalrymen.
When the pursuing troops arrived,
his trusted Dūdū (都督) Wèi Xīngqìng (尉興慶) said:
“Your Royal Highness, flee quickly!
Xīngqìng (尉興慶) has a hundred arrows at his waist,
enough to kill a hundred men.”
Huān (高歡) said:
“If this matter succeeds,
I will make you Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Huáizhōu (懷州).
Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) monograph states: In the second year of Tiān'ān (天安), Huáizhōu (懷州) was established in Hénèi (河內).
It was abolished in the eighth year of Tàihé (太和),
and re-established at the beginning of Tiānpíng (天平),
administering Hénèi (河內) and Wǔdé (武德) two commanderies.
[I will] employ your son.”
Xīngqìng (尉興慶) said:
“My son is young.
I wish you would employ my elder brother.”
Huān (高歡) agreed.
Xīngqìng (尉興慶) resisted,
and died after exhausting his arrows.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Diǎnlüè (典略) writes “Wèi Xīngjìng” (尉興敬).
We follow the Běi Qí Shū (北齊書) and Běi Shǐ (北史) here.
Among the Eastern Wèi (東魏) soldiers, there were some who fled to Wèi (魏).
They reported Huān’s (高歡) location.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The biography of Zhōu Hèbá Shèng (周賀拔勝) states:
“Tàizǔ (太祖) saw Qí Shénwǔ’s (齊神武) banners and drums and recognized him.”
We follow the Diǎnlüè (典略) here.
All were armed with short weapons
and assigned to Dàdūdū (大都督) Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝) to attack him.
Shèng (賀拔勝) recognized Huān (高歡) amidst the ranks,
grasped his spear, and with thirteen cavalrymen, pursued him.
After galloping for several li,
the spear blade was almost upon him.
He then called out his courtesy name:
“Hèlùhún (賀六渾)!
Hèbá Pòhú (賀拔破胡) will surely kill you!”
Huān (高歡) was almost out of breath.
Liú Hónghuī (劉洪徽), Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Hézhōu (河州), shot Shèng (賀拔勝) from the side,
hitting two of his cavalrymen
(Hézhōu (河州) at that time belonged to Western Wèi (西魏) territory,
Liú Hónghuī (劉洪徽) of Eastern Wèi (東魏) merely held the title of Cǐshǐ (刺史) remotely).
Shè (射),
pronounced ér yì;
same below.
Zhòng (中),
pronounced zhúzhòng.
He killed them.
By the time a replacement horse arrived,
Huān (高歡) had already escaped.
Shèng (賀拔勝) sighed, saying:
“That I did not hold a bow and arrow today, is fate!”
The Wèi Southern Yǐngzhōu Inspector Gěng Lìngguì
shouted,
and entered the enemy ranks alone.
Wèi Shōu’s record states: Liáng established Nán Yǐngzhōu,
with its seat at Chìshíguān,
governing the commanderies of Dìngchéng, Guāngchéng, and Biānchéng.
The Wǔdài Annals state: Dìngchéng County of Guāngzhōu,
was where the Later Qí established Nán Yǐngzhōu.
This was not Wèi territory,
and Gěng Lìngguì merely held the inspectorship remotely.
Hū,
read as huǒgù.
Everyone thought he was dead,
but then he brandished his saber and returned.
This happened several times.
Those in front of Gěng Lìngguì died or were wounded one after another.
He then said to his左右 (attendants/aides):
“How could I enjoy killing people!
A brave warrior eliminating bandits
cannot but act thus.
If one cannot kill bandits,
and is also not wounded by them,
how is that different from chasing someone who is sitting?”
Chasing someone who is sitting refers to
those at the time who held literary discussions,
but could only follow others, sit and chat, and sit and eat.
The five generals of the left army, Zhào Guì and others, fought unfavorably.
The Eastern Wèi army rallied again.
Tàishǐ fought them,
and was also unsuccessful.
As night fell,
the Wèi army consequently retreated.
The Eastern Wèi army pursued them;
Dúgū Xìn and Yú Jǐn gathered scattered soldiers and attacked from the rear.
The pursuing soldiers were startled and disordered,
and the Wèi armies were thus able to survive.
When Yú Huì withdrew at night,
the Eastern Wèi army pursued him;
Huì slowly dismounted,
instructed the cook to prepare food,
and after eating,
said to his attendants:
“To die in Cháng'ān
or to die here,
is there any difference?”
He then raised flags and sounded horns,
gathered scattered soldiers, and slowly returned.
The pursuing cavalry suspected an ambush
and dared not press close.
Tàishǐ then entered the pass
and garrisoned along the Wèi River.
Huān advanced to Shǎn.
Tàishǐ sent Dáxī Wǔ, who was Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and others to resist him.
Fēng Zǐhuì, a secretary of the Xíngtái, said to Huān:
“Unifying East and West
is exactly for today.
In the past, Wèi Tàizǔ pacified Hànzhōng,
but did not press his advantage to take Bā and Shǔ.
This event is found in volume sixty-seven, Jiàn'ān twentieth year of Emperor Xiàndì of Hàn.
Later, he regretted it, but it was too late.
I wish Your Majesty would not doubt this.”
Huān deeply agreed with him
and gathered his generals to discuss whether to advance or stop.
All believed
“there is no green grass in the fields,
and our men and horses are exhausted and thin,
so we cannot pursue far.”
Chén Yuánkāng said:
“Two great rivals have been contending
for many years.
Now, having luckily achieved a great victory,
Heaven has granted it to us,
and the time must not be lost.
We should pursue them while riding on our victory.”
Huān said:
“If we encounter an ambush,
how shall I manage?”
Yuánkāng said:
“Your Majesty previously suffered a defeat at Shāyuàn,
yet they had no ambush;
now they are fleeing in such disarray,
how could they plan far ahead!
If we abandon the pursuit,
it will certainly become a future trouble.”
Huān did not follow this advice.
This serves as a background for Huān's regret at not using Chén Yuánkāng's words.
I say that in the Battle of Mángshān,
both sides were wounded and both lost.
Although Yǔwén Tàishǐ was forced to retreat due to exhaustion,
Gāo Huān’s spirit was also diminished,
how could he dare to advance deep again!
So he returned east.
Tàishǐ summoned Wáng Sīzhèng to Yùbì,
intending to make him garrison Hǔláo.
Before he arrived, Tàishǐ was defeated,
so he made him guard Héngnóng.
Sīzhèng entered the city,
ordered the gates opened, and lay down undressed,
comforting and encouraging his generals and soldiers,
showing that there was nothing to fear.
A few days later,
Liú Fēngshēng arrived below the city.
He was wary of Sīzhèng,
dared not advance,
and led his army back.
Sīzhèng then repaired the city walls,
erected watchtowers,
established farmland,
and accumulated fodder and grain.
From then on, Héngnóng began to have defensive preparations.
Chancellor Tàishǐ requested to demote himself,
but the Wèi sovereign did not allow it.
In this campaign,
all the Wèi generals were without merit,
except for Gěng Lìngguì and the Crown Prince’s Wǔwèi Commander Wáng Húrén.
Wèi changed the title of Dōnggōng Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn to Wǔwèi Commander.
Tàishǐ wanted to bestow upon them the three prefectures of Yōng, Qí, and Běiyōng.
Since the prefectures had varying quality,
he made them draw lots for them,
and also bestowed upon Húrén the name Yǒng,
upon Lìngguì the name Háo,
and upon Wéndá the name Jié,
to honor their achievements.
Thereupon, he extensively recruited powerful families from Guānzhōng and Lǒngyòu to augment the army.
When Gāo Zhòngmì was about to rebel,
he secretly sent people to incite the heroes of Jìzhōu,
so they would act as an internal response.
Gāo Gān and his brothers originally raised an army in Xìndū,
so Zhòngmì incited their heroes,
to create a response in Héběi.
Thus, he gained security.
Gāo Chéng secretly wrote to Lóngzhī, saying:
“Those among Zhòngmì’s faction who went west with him,
it is fitting to confiscate all their family members
to punish future offenders.”
Lóngzhī believed that since the benevolent decree had already been issued,
it was unreasonable to revoke it.
If they were to be arrested and dealt with again,
it would show a lack of trustworthiness to the people.
Should it cause unrest,
the loss would not be small.
So he reported to Chancellor Huān and had the order dismissed.

Qiú,

He occupied a strategic position and rebelled;

Chancellor Huān, considering Gāo Gān's meritorious service for justice,

He referred to Gān dying in battle at Héyáng.
He referred to Gān first fleeing from Yǒng'ān garrison to inform Huān.
Zhòngmì's wife, Lǐ Shì, was to be executed.
Gāo Chéng, dressed in splendid attire, went to see her
and asked:
"How is it today?"
Lǐ Shì remained silent,
whereupon he took her as his wife.
Gāo Chéng, by indulging in lust,
caused a family member to rebel externally,
and his father nearly died in battle.
He persisted in evil and did not repent,
displaying his attire to seduce and take her.
In later days, the disaster of Yáng Yàn,

How could this be fate?

Shǒu,
