known as Běigù.
Cài Mó built a tower upon it to store military supplies.
The Emperor ascended it and gazed for a long time,
saying:
'This ridge is not necessary for defense,
but at Jīngkǒu, it is indeed a magnificent sight,'
whereupon he changed its name to Běigù."
On the day Gēngxū,
he visited Huíbīn Tíng
and feasted the elders from his hometown and those from nearby counties who had come to greet him,
thousands of people, young and old,
each receiving two thousand coins.
6 On the day Rénzǐ,
the Eastern Wèi appointed Gāo Chéng as Dàjiāngjūn and concurrently Lǐng Zhōngshū Jiān,
Yuán Bì as Lù Shàngshū Shì,
the Left Minister Sīmǎ Zǐrú as Shàngshū Lìng,
and Palace Attendant Gāo Yáng as Left Minister.
Chancellor Huān was mostly in Jìnyáng.
Sūn Téng, Sīmǎ Zǐrú, Gāo Yuè, and Gāo Lóngzhī
were all Huān's relatives and associates,
to whom he entrusted the court administration.
They were called the "Four Nobles" in Yè,
and their power and influence overshadowed both the court and the provinces,
often leading to arbitrariness, arrogance, and greed.
Huān wished to diminish their power,
so he appointed Chéng as Dàjiāngjūn and concurrently Lǐng Zhōngshū Jiān,
transferring all confidential matters of the Ménxià to the Zhōngshū.
All matters of the Ménxià Shěng
were managed by the Shìzhōng, Jǐshìzhōng, and others.
Now Gāo Huān transferred them all to the Zhōngshū
to strengthen Chéng's power.
When Sūn Téng saw Chéng,
he refused to show full respect.
Chéng shouted at his attendants to drag him down from the couch,
struck him with the pommel of a sword,
and made him stand outside the gate.
Tài Tàiyuán Gōng Yáng bowed to Gāo Lóngzhī in front of Chéng
and called him "uncle."
Chéng was enraged
and cursed him.
Lóngzhī was originally from Luòyáng.
Huān ordered him to be treated as a younger brother,
so Yáng called him "uncle."
"My son is growing up;
you, Duke, should avoid him."
Thereafter, none of the high officials and below
saw Chéng without fear and trepidation.
Kùdí Gān,
Chéng's paternal aunt's husband,
Gān married Huān's sister.
stood outside the gate
for three days before he was allowed to see him.
Chéng wanted to place his trusted confidants around the Eastern Wèi ruler,
so he promoted Cuī Jìshū, a staff officer of the central army, to Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Whenever Chéng submitted memorials to the Emperor,
offering advice or requests,
if the text was complicated or disorganized,
Jìshū would always revise and clarify it.
The Emperor often discussed his replies to Chéng and his father with Jìshū,
saying:
"Secretary Cuī
is my wet nurse."
Jìshū
was Tǐngzhī's cousin.
7 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
the Emperor returned from Lánlíng.
8 In the fifth month,
on the first day Jiǎshēn,
Wèi Chancellor Tài held court in Cháng'ān.
9 On the day of Jiǎwǔ,
the Eastern Wèi sent Sànqí Chángshì Wèi Jìjǐng to offer a marriage proposal.
Jìjǐng
was the clan uncle of Shōu.
10 The younger brother of Shàngshūlìng Hé Jìngróng's concubine stole official rice.
Jìngróng wrote to Língjūn Hédōng Wáng Yù about it.
On the day of Dīngyǒu,
Jìngróng was dismissed from office due to this incident.
11 Guǎngyáng Wáng Zhàn of the Eastern Wèi passed away.
12 All the sons of Wèi Lángyá Zhēnxìangōng Hèbá Shèng who were in the East
were killed by Chéngxiàng Huān,
in revenge for the grievances at Mángshān.
Chéngxiàng Tàicáng often said to people:
"When facing an enemy, all generals show signs of fear,
but only Hèbá Gōng is like usual when confronting a battle formation;
he is truly greatly courageous!"
13 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Wèi revised its weights and measures.
Shàngshū Sū Chuò was ordered to adjust the thirty-six articles of the system,
compiling them into five volumes,
and they were promulgated.
The twenty-four articles, combined with the twelve new articles,
totaled thirty-six articles.
The twenty-four articles are found in the upper volume, under Dàtóng First Year.
All were dispatched according to the new system.
Within a few years,
the common people found it convenient.
14 Since Zhèngguāng,
the Eastern Wèi's government and laws had been lax,
and many officials were corrupt.
Chéngxiàng Huān proposed that Sīzhōu Zhōng Cóngshì Sòng Yóudào be appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi.
(Wǔdài Zhì: Later Qí's Sīzhōu had a Mù,
and its subordinate officials included Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ and Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ.)
Yóudào was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
Chéng said to Xiān and Yóudào:
"One of you will be in the Southern Terrace (Yùshǐtái),
and the other in the Northern Province (Shàngshūshěng).
You should make the empire solemn and orderly."
Xiān selected Bì Yìyún and others to be Yùshǐ,
and at the time, it was said that he found the right people.
Yìyún
was the great-grandson of Zhòngjìng.
At the beginning of Sòng Míngdì's reign,
Bì Zhòngjìng defected to Wèi.
Chéng wished to lend Xiān prestige and power.
With all the nobles present,
he had Xiān arrive late,
announce his name,
and enter with a haughty gaze and slow steps, with two attendants holding up his robes.
Chéng greeted him from the center of the hall, bowing respectfully.
Xiān sat down without deferring.
After two rounds of wine,
he excused himself and left.
Chéng tried to keep him for a meal,
but Xiān said:
"I just received an imperial order to inspect the Terrace."
So he left without waiting for the meal,
and Chéng descended the steps to see him off.
Another day,
Chéng and the nobles went out
to the Eastern Mountains.
(At that time, the Eastern Mountains near Yèdū were cultivated
as a place for excursions and banquets.)
His vanguard was struck by red staffs,
and Chéng turned his horse to avoid them.
Shàngshūlìng Sīmǎ Zǐrú, being an old friend of Chéngxiàng Huān,
held an important position,
and was arrogant.
He and Tàishī Xiányáng Wáng Tǎn were insatiably corrupt.
Xiān impeached Zǐrú, Tǎn, and Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ Kězhūhún Dàoyuán, among others, for their crimes,
sparing no detail in his writings.
Sòng Yóudào also impeached Zǐrú, Tǎn, Tàibǎo Sūn Téng, Sītú Gāo Lóngzhī, Sīkōng Hóu Jǐng, and Shàngshū Yuán Xiàn, among others.
Chéng arrested Zǐrú and imprisoned him.
After one night,
Zǐrú's hair turned completely white,
and he pleaded:
"Sīmǎ Zǐrú, with a cane, went from Xiàzhōu to seek refuge with the Prince-Chancellor (Huān).
(In Zhōngdàtōng Fourth Year,
Huān defeated the Ěrzhū clan,
and summoned Zǐrú from Nánqízhōu.
The roads in Yōng and Huá were blocked,
so he took the route through Xiàzhōu to return east.)
(Xià is pronounced Hùyǎfān.)
I had a pregnant cow and a calf,
but the calf died on the way.
Only the cow's horns remained;
everything else I took from other people."
Chéngxiàng Huān wrote an imperial decree to Chéng, saying:
"Sīmǎ Lìng
is an old friend of mine.
You should be lenient with him."
Chéng stopped his horse in the street,
released Zǐrú,
and removed his shackles.
Zǐrú, frightened, said:
"Is this not for an execution?"
(He feared Chéng would kill him.)
On the day of Guǐyǒu,
Zǐrú's official titles and peerage were stripped.
In the ninth month,
on the day of Jiǎshēn,
Jìyīn Wáng Huīyè was made Tàiwèi.
Tàishī Xiányáng Wáng Tǎn returned to his residence as a prince,
having been dismissed as Tàishī.
Many others died or were dismissed.
After a long time,
Huān saw Zǐrú
and, pitying his emaciated state,
rested Zǐrú's head on his knee
and personally picked out lice for him.
He bestowed upon him one hundred bottles of wine,
five hundred sheep,
and five hundred shí of rice.
Chéng disciplined him with public law,
while Huān treated him with old kindness.
This was the method by which the father and son (Huān and Chéng) controlled the meritorious nobility.
Gāo Chéng praised Cuī Xiān greatly to all the nobles,
and also admonished and entrusted them to him.
Chéngxiàng Huān wrote to the nobles in Yè:
"Cuī Xiān resides in the Cén Tái.
Xiányáng Wáng and Sīmǎ Lìng are both old friends from my commoner days.
No two people are more honored or intimate with me,
yet they both incurred punishment at the same time,
and I could not save them.
All of you should be cautious!"
Sòng Yóudào submitted hundreds of rebuttals against errors and omissions by the Shàngshū.
He flogged and reprimanded powerful officials in the province, such as Wáng Rú,
causing all officials below the rank of Lìng and Pú to eye him askance.
Gāo Lóngzhī falsely accused Yóudào of uttering seditious words,
a crime punishable by death.
Jìshì Huángmén Shìláng Yáng Yīn said:
"We keep dogs for their barking.
If we kill them for barking a few times,
I fear there will be no barking dogs in the future."
Yóudào was eventually dismissed from office.
Chéng said to Yóudào:
"You should have followed me to Bīngzhōu earlier;
otherwise, that strategist (Gāo Lóngzhī) would have killed you."
Yóudào followed Chéng to Jìnyáng
and was made Dàxíngtái Lìbù.
(After "Bù"
should be the character
"Láng".)
15 On the day of Jǐchǒu,
a general amnesty was declared.
16 After the chaos of war,
the Eastern Wèi found that household registrations were inaccurate,
and corvée and taxes were unevenly distributed.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day of Dīngsì,
Tàibǎo Sūn Téng and Dàsītú Gāo Lóngzhī
(According to Wèi and Qí official systems,
Sītú was never prefixed with "Dà";
the character "Dà" is superfluous.)
were dispatched to various prefectures.
They discovered over six hundred thousand unregistered households,
and all those residing in temporary locations were ordered to return to their original places of registration.
In the eleventh month,
on the day of Jiǎshēn,
Gāo Lóngzhī was appointed Lù Shàngshūshì,
and former Dàsīmǎ Lóu Zhāo was made Sītú.
17 On the day of Gēngzǐ,
the Eastern Wèi emperor sacrificed at the Yuánqiū.
18 Chéngxiàng Huān of the Eastern Wèi attacked the Shānhú
and defeated them.
(The Shānhú were the Jīhú from the mountains of Fénzhōu.)
They were distributed among the various prefectures.
19 In this year,
the Eastern Wèi appointed Sànqí Chángshì Wèi Shōu concurrently as Zhōngshū Shìláng,
to compile the national history.
Since the establishment of good relations between Liáng and Wèi,
the Wèi letters always stated:
"We hope your territory is peaceful and tranquil,
and that our entire land is secure and harmonious."
The Emperor's reply removed
only the character "bǐ" (your).
Shōu first set the letter to say:
"We hope your territory is clear and tranquil,
and now our ten thousand li are secure and harmonious."
The Emperor also imitated this.
Punctuation by Zhāng Zhènglǎng, reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by imperial decree by
Sīmǎ Guāng.
Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì Fifteenth
In the 11th year of Dàtóng (yǐchǒu, 545):
1 Spring,
the first month.
On the day of bǐngshēn,
the Eastern Wèi dispatched Lǐ Jiǎng, concurrently Grand Master of Remonstrance, to come as an envoy.
2 Ěrzhū Wénchàng, Yítóng of the Eastern Wèi, along with Rèn Zhòu, Sīmǎ to the Chancellor, and Zhèng Zhònglǐ, Dūdū, and others,
conspired to cause a disturbance on the night of the full moon of the first month during the Dǎcù game.
The Běi Shǐ states: "It was an old custom of the Wèi clan
to hold a Dǎcù game on the 15th night of the first month.
Those who hit the target would immediately be rewarded with silk."
According to the Wèi Shū,
in the 4th year of Tiānpíng of Emperor Xiàojìng,
spring,
the first month,
the Dǎcù Xiāngtōu game was prohibited.
Perhaps this prohibition was soon relaxed.
Rèn
is pronounced 'rén'.
They enthroned Wénchàng as their leader;
the plot was exposed,
and they all died.
Wénchàng was
the son of Róng;
his elder sister,
the empress of Jìngzōng,
and Zhònglǐ's elder sister, Dàchē,
were all concubines of Huān
and favored,
so their brothers were not implicated.
Huān submitted a memorial, stating:
"Bìngzhōu,
where military equipment is stored,
constantly requires female labor.
I request to establish a palace to house those confiscated and enslaved;
also, to take a daughter of Tǔyùhùn to win their allegiance."
The kingdom of Tǔyùhùn was to the southwest of the Western Wèi.
Gāo Huān crossed the border to take their daughter to win their allegiance,
likely intending to borrow their strength to invade and harass the Western Wèi.
Tǔ
is pronounced as 'tūn' with entering tone.
Yù
is pronounced 'yù'.
On the day of dīngwèi,
the Jìnyáng Palace was established.
In the second month,
on the day of gēngshēn,
the ruler of the Eastern Wèi took the paternal cousin of the Tǔyùhùn Khán as a Rónghuá.
Rónghuá was
an old title for an inner court official in the former Hàn dynasty.
Kè
is pronounced as 'kān' with entering tone.
Hán
is pronounced 'hán'.
Cóng
is pronounced 'cáiyòng'.
3 Zhōu Tàishī Tái, Chancellor of Wèi, dispatched Hú Ānnuòpántuó from Jiǔquán to initiate diplomatic relations with the Tūjué.
The Tūjué were originally a small state in the west,
with the surname Āshǐnà,
residing for generations on the southern side of Jīnshān,
serving as ironworkers for the Ròurán.
By the time of their chieftain Tǔmén,
they began to grow powerful
and frequently encroached upon the western border of Wèi.
When Ānnuòpántuó arrived,
their countrymen all rejoiced, saying:
Below "their country"
should be another
"country"
character,
belonging to the next sentence.
"An envoy from a great country has arrived;
our country will surely flourish."
4 In the third month,
on the day of yǐwèi,
Gāo Huān, Chancellor of the Eastern Wèi, came to court in Yè,
and all officials welcomed him at Zǐmò.
Huān clasped Cuī Xiān's hand and commended him, saying:
"In the past, did the court lack judicial officials?
Yet none dared to impeach.
The Grand Commandant dedicated himself wholeheartedly to the state,
not fearing powerful figures,
thus bringing order far and wide.
Those who charge the front and break the ranks are numerous;
but those who uphold justice with integrity in office
are only now seen.
I have only heard of ancient people who upheld justice with integrity in office;
today I finally see Cuī Xiān.
Gāo Huān and his sons have nothing to repay you with."
He gifted Xiān a fine horse.
Xiān bowed,
the horse bolted in fright,
and Huān personally embraced it,
handing him the reins.
The ruler of the Eastern Wèi hosted a banquet in Huálín Garden.
The city of Yè imitated the system of Jīngluò,
and also had a Huálín Garden.
Huān descended the steps and knelt, saying:
"Only Xiān alone can be encouraged;
I also request that the thousand pieces of silk I won in the archery contest be bestowed upon him."
At that time, there was an archery banquet in Huálín Garden,
and Huān was awarded a thousand pieces of silk.
Huān requested to bestow them upon Xiān.
He said to Xiān:
"Even I envy you,
how much more so others!"
However, Xiān harbored considerable cunning and deceit in his heart.
Initially,
Gāo Yángwáng Bīn of Wèi had a concubine sister, Yùyí,
who was not acknowledged by her family,
and became a courtesan of Sūn Téng;
Téng then abandoned her.
Gāo Chéng met her on the road,
was pleased and took her in,
and she gained exceptional favor.
Bái Jūyì's poem states: "There is no true beauty in the world;
what pleases the eye is beauty."
This is indeed true.
What Yùyí lacked was not beauty,
but rather a seductive charm and skill in bewitching,
which is why she caused gossip among other women and was not tolerated.
Chéng said to Cuī Jìshū:
"Cuī Xiān will surely offer direct remonstrance."
"Zào"
as is,
meaning 'to make'.
When Xiān consulted him on affairs,
Chéng no longer showed him a pleasant countenance.
After three days,
Xiān held a calling card and let it drop before him.
The Xù Shìshuō states: "In ancient times, there was no paper,
so bamboo or wood was shaved to write names,
which was called 'cì'.
Later, when paper was used,
it was called 'míngzhǐ'.
During the prosperity of Lǐ Déyù of Táng,
people sought to show extra courtesy,
changing the custom to a document stating one's full title and inquiring about the host's health,
which was called 'ménzhuàng'."
"What is this for?"
Xiān said fearfully:
"I have not yet been able to inform the princess."
Chéng was greatly pleased,
took Xiān's arm,
and entered to see her.
Jìshū said to others:
"Cuī Xiān often resented my flattery;
before the Great General,
he often said that my uncle should be killed;
but when he himself acted,
he surpassed me."
5 Summer,
the fifth month.
On the day of jiǎchén,
the Eastern Wèi granted a general amnesty.
6 Wèi Wángméng died.
In the 9th year,
Wèi appointed Wángméng as Grand Tutor.
7 Since the Jìn dynasty,
literary compositions competed in extravagance,
and Zhōu Tàishī Tái, Chancellor of Wèi, wished to reform this abuse.
In the sixth month,
on the day of dīngsì,
the ruler of Wèi offered a feast at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
Tái ordered Sū Chuò, Minister of Finance of the Grand Secretariat and concurrently Director of Historiography,
to compose the Dàgào,
to be proclaimed to all officials,
admonishing them regarding governance;
he also commanded:
"From now on, all literary compositions shall follow this style."
Yǔwén Tái ordered Sū Chuò to compose the Dàgào, imitating the style of the Zhōu Shū;
its text is still extant today.
To make all literary compositions of the time follow this style
was also not the way to promote elegance and eliminate superficiality.
8 The Emperor dispatched Yáng Biāo (楊螵), Inspector of Jiāozhōu, to attack Lǐ Bēn (李賁),
appointing Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先) as his Sīmǎ (司馬).
He ordered Xiāo Bó (蕭勃), Inspector of Dìngzhōu, to rendezvous with Biāo on the Xījiāng River.
*Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志) states: Yùlín Commandery,
Dìngzhōu was established during the Liáng dynasty.
Bó, using a deceptive pretext, detained Biāo.
Biāo gathered his generals and asked for their counsel.
Bàxiān said:
“Jiāozhǐ has rebelled and turned traitor.
The fault lies with the imperial clan.”
This refers to Lǐ Bēn's rebellion
being caused by Wǔlín Hóu Zī (武林侯諮).
The details are found in volume 7 of the previous chapter.
“The punishment has been delayed for several years.
Dìngzhōu wishes to enjoy temporary peace,
disregarding the greater strategy.
Your Excellency, having received the imperial decree to suppress the rebels,
should dedicate yourself to this task, come what may.
How can you hesitate and hold back,
prolonging the enemy's strength and discouraging our troops!”
Thereupon, he led his troops and set off first.
Biāo appointed Bàxiān as his vanguard.
Upon reaching Jiāozhōu,
*Kǎoyì* (考異) says: *Diǎnlüè* (典略) states
“reached Jiāozhōu on the *guǐchǒu* day of the twelfth month.”
Yáo Sīlián’s (姚思廉) imperial annals in the *Chén Shū* (陳書) place it in the sixth month;
we now follow this.
They were defeated at Zhūyuān.
Zhūyuān County,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Jiāozhǐ Commandery.
*Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志) states: Zhūyuān County was formerly established as Wǔpíng Commandery.
YUĀN,
pronounced like Yuán.
Bēn fled to Jiāníng City.
Shěn Yuè's (沈約) *Zhì* (志) states: In the third year of Jiànhéng of Sūn Hào (孫晧) of Wú,
Xīnxīng Commandery was established by dividing Jiāozhǐ,
and Jiāníng County was also established.
In the third year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the commandery was renamed Xīnchāng.
*Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志) states: Jiāníng County of Jiāozhǐ Commandery,
formerly established as Xīngzhōu Xīnchāng Commandery,
was renamed Fēngzhōu by the Suí dynasty.
Bó was
the son of Bǐng (昺).
Wú Pínghóu Bǐng (吳平侯昺)
was the Emperor’s paternal cousin.
Bǐng,
pronounced like Bǐng.
9 Wèi (魏) and Tóubīng Kèhán (頭兵可汗) of Rouran (柔然) conspired to join forces to attack Eastern Wèi.
Prime Minister Huān (歡) was concerned about this,
so he sent Dù Bì (杜弼), a Lángzhōng (郎中) of the Xíngtái, as an envoy to Rouran
to seek a marriage alliance for his heir, Chéng (澄).
Tóubīng said:
“If King Gāo (高王) marries her himself, then it can be done.”
Huān hesitated, undecided.
Lóu (婁) said:
“This is a vital matter for the state;
I hope you will not hesitate.”
Heir apparent Chéng and Wèi Jǐng (尉景) also urged him.
Huān then sent Mùróng Yǎn (慕容儼), General Zhennan, to propose the marriage,
naming her the Rúru Ràng (蠕蠕) Princess.
Emperor Míngyuán of Wèi referred to Rouran as Rúru,
implying their squirming, ignorant nature.
Ānà Kuí (阿那⿰王褱) was enfeoffed as Rúru King.
Although it was said to be their national title,
it was still considered derogatory.
When Gāo Huān married their daughter,
calling her the Rúru Princess,
it was then directly taken as a national title,
no longer considered derogatory.
RÚ,
pronounced *rén yǎn fān*.
In the eighth month,
Huān personally welcomed her at Xiàguǎn.
According to *Běishǐ Péngchéng Tàifu* (北史彭城太傳),
Xiàguǎn
should be north of Mùjǐng.
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: Mùjǐng City
is now governed by Yángqǔ County in Bìngzhōu.
He also says: Dàizhōu is the ancient Yīnguǎn City;
there are Shàngguǎn and Xiàguǎn.
Lóu avoided her position as main wife and allowed the princess to reside there.
Huān knelt and bowed in thanks.
Lóu was Huān’s wife from his humble days,
his main wife.
CHÙ,
pronounced *chāng lǚ fān*.
“They will realize it;
I wish you would give her up and not worry about me.”
The historian states that Lóu, for the sake of the state,
had the same intention as Zhào Jī (趙姬) who had Shū Kuí (叔隗) act as the main wife while she herself occupied a lesser position.
Tóubīng sent his younger brother, Tūtūjiā (禿突佳), to escort his daughter
and return the marriage proposal.
Some say
it was “to make the proposal.”
【Zhāng (章): Hú's (胡) note
“or written as *pìn* (聘).”
The twelve-line edition writes
“娉” (pīn);
the Yǐ (乙) eleven-line edition is the same.
It is suspected that the original engraved edition wrote
and Hú's engraved edition corrected the error.
“I will return only after seeing my grandson.”
The princess was stern and resolute by nature,
never willing to speak frivolous words throughout her life.
Huān once fell ill
and could not visit,
which made Tūtūjiā resentful.
Huān, despite his illness, went to him in a carriage.
10 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the *yǐwèi* day,
an edict was issued that offenders were again allowed to pay a fine.
In the third year of Tiānjiān,
the law allowing fines for crimes was abolished,
as seen in volume 145.
FÙ,
pronounced *fú yòu fān*.
11 Eastern Wèi sent Wèi Jǐn (尉瑾), a Zhōngshū Shèrén, to propose marriage.
12 On the *yǐwèi* day,
Prime Minister Huān of Eastern Wèi requested that the shackles of the captives from Mángshān be released
and that they be paired with widows from the populace.
These were Western Wèi soldiers captured in the victory at Mángshān.
The details of the victory are found in volume 9 of the previous chapter.
ZHÌ,
pronounced *zhī rì fān*.
GÒU,

The Later Zhōu established Jiànzhōng Jùn.
In the eleventh
month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
Gāo Huān, having achieved nothing,
submitted a memorial requesting to be relieved of his duties as Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūn.
The Lord of Dōng Wèi granted his request.
When Huān returned from Yùbì,
a rumor spread among the troops that Wéi Xiàokuān had shot and killed the Prime Minister with a dìnggōng-nǔ (a powerful crossbow);
the Wèi people heard of it
and consequently issued an order saying:
“With one shot from a powerful crossbow,
the nefarious body is self-destroyed.”
Huān heard this,
and with effort sat up to see the various nobles,
and made Húlüù Jīn compose a Chìlè song.
Húlüù Jīn
was a person of the Chìlè tribe,
hence he was made to compose a Chìlè song.
Hóng Mài said: Húlüù Jīn sang a Chìlè song,
originally in Xiānbēi language.
According to ancient yuèfǔ, its lyrics are:
“Chìlè plain,
beneath the Yīnshān mountains,
the sky is like a yóulú (felt tent),
enveloping the four wilds.
The sky is azure,
the wilds are vast,
the wind blows the grass low, revealing cattle and sheep.”
I say this was fabricated by later generations.
Chìlè and Xiānbēi are distinct peoples;
Húlüù Jīn came from Chìlè,
hence he was made to compose a Chìlè song,
whereas Gāo Huān was accustomed to Xiānbēi customs.
He was deeply moved and wept.
16 Sū Chuò, Grand Minister of Revenue for the Dàxíngtái and Sīnóng Qīng of Eastern Wèi,
was loyal and frugal by nature,
and always took the unrest of the realm as his own responsibility.
He managed
the myriad affairs of government.
Prime Minister Tài trusted him wholeheartedly,
and no one could sow discord between them.
Sometimes, when Tài went out on an excursion,
he would always pre-sign blank papers and give them to Chuò;
if there was a need for a decision,
Chuò would act according to the circumstances,
and upon Tài’s return,
he would simply inform him.
Chuò often said,
“The way to govern a state
is to love the people like a kind father,
and to instruct them like a strict teacher.”
Whenever he discussed matters with the dukes and ministers,
from day until night,
whether the matter was big or small,
it was as clear as pointing to his palm.
He became ill from overwork and died.
Tài deeply mourned and regretted his loss,
and said to the dukes and ministers:
“Minister Sū was always incorruptible and modest throughout his life.
I wish to fulfill his original aspiration,
but I fear that the ordinary people may not fully understand;
if I were to bestow rich posthumous titles,
it would also go against the understanding we had of each other in the past;
what should be done?”
Máo Yáo, a Shàngshū Lìshǐ,
Shàngshū Lìshǐ
existed since the Eastern Hàn.
The Táng Liù Diǎn states: Since Wèi and Jìn,
the role of Lìshǐ
used people of low status.
During Qí, Liáng, Hòuwèi, and Běiqí,
although they were included in the official ranks,
their status was even more insignificant.
said, “Frugality
is the way to highlight his virtue.”
Tài followed his advice.
Sū Chuò was buried in Wǔgōng.
Sū Chuò
was from Wǔgōng,
and was buried in his hometown.
Tài and his attendant dukes walked him out beyond the city wall of Tóngzhōu.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Fēngyì Jùn,
Hòuwèi established Huázhōu,
Western Wèi changed it to Tóngzhōu.
Sūn Miǎn said: Fēngyì has Jiǔlóng Quán,
the spring has nine sources,
all converging into one stream,
hence the name of the prefecture.
Tài said:
“All the deeds that Minister Sū performed throughout his life,
which his wife, children, and brothers did not know,
I know them all.
Only you knew my heart,
and I knew your aspirations.
We were just about to conquer the world together,
and now you suddenly abandon me and leave.
What can I do!”
Then he cried out in great sorrow,
unaware that the wine cup had fallen from his hand.
17 Hóu Jǐng, Eastern Wèi Sītú, Hénán Dàjiāngjūn, and Dàxíngtái,
had a slightly shorter right foot,
and was not skilled in archery and horsemanship,
but was rich in stratagems.
Generals Gāo Áo cáo, Péng Lè, and others were all unequaled in bravery for a time,
but Jǐng often made light of them,
saying:
“These fellows are all like wild boars charging heedlessly;
where can their momentum lead them!”
Meaning they were brave but lacked strategy.
“I wish to have thirty thousand soldiers,
to roam freely throughout the land,
and I must cross the Jiāng river to capture the old man Xiāo Yǎn,
and make him the abbot of Tàipíng Sì.”
History states that Hóu Jǐng had long harbored ambitions to take control of Jiāngnán.
Tàipíng Sì was probably in Yè.
He held sole command over Hénán,
and relied on him as if he were half of his own body.
Jǐng had always made light of Gāo Chéng,
and once said to Sīmǎ Zǐrú:
“While King Gāo is alive,
I dare not have any other thoughts;
but when the King is gone,
I cannot serve with a young Xiānbēi boy!”
Zǐrú covered his mouth.
When Huān’s illness became severe,
Chéng forged a letter from Huān to summon Jǐng.
Previously,
Jǐng had agreed with Huān:
“Now that I command troops far away,
it is easy for people to use deception;
please add a small mark to all letters you bestow upon me.”
Huān agreed.
Jǐng received the letter with no mark,
and refused to come;
he also heard that Huān’s illness was critical,
and following the advice of Wáng Wěi of Yǐngchuān, his Xíngtái Láng,
he consequently held onto his troops and entrenched himself.
Huān said to Chéng:
“Although I am ill,
your face still shows lingering worry;
why is that?”
Meaning Chéng should be happy about gaining full command of internal and external powers,
and should not have any lingering worries.
Huān said:
“Is it not worry about Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion?”
Chéng replied:
“It is.”
Huān said:
“Jǐng has solely commanded Hénán
for fourteen years.
In the first year of Tiānpíng of Eastern Wèi,
Huān sent Jǐng to take Jīngzhōu,
and thereafter entrusted him with Hénán.
By this time, it had been thirteen years.
Huān’s words here must have been said in the spring just before his death.
I was able to nurture him,
but you are not able to control him.
Now, the four directions are not yet settled;
do not express sorrow too hastily.
Kùdí Gān, an old Xiānbēi man,
and Húlüù Jīn, an old Chìlè man,
both have straightforward and upright characters,
and will never betray you.
Kězhūhún Dàoyuán and Liú Fēngshēng,
came from afar to join me,
and will certainly have no disloyal intentions.
Kězhūhún Dàoyuán defected to Eastern Wèi, see volume 157, the first year of Dàtóng.
Liú Fēngshēng defected to Eastern Wèi, see the second year.
They are kind and generous;
you brothers will surely benefit from their strength.
Hán Guǐ is somewhat reckless;
you should treat him leniently.
Péng Lè is difficult to fathom;
you should guard against him.
He still holds a grudge about the Mángshān incident,
laying the groundwork for Péng Lè’s later execution.
Only Mùróng Shàozōng,
whom I deliberately did not elevate,
I leave him for you.”
He had Chéng generously bestow official titles
to win Shàozōng’s loyalty.
Yí,
from Jì Fān;
the lower part [of the character] is the same as huàn.
“Duàn Xiàoxiān is loyal, honest, benevolent, and generous.
Duàn Sháo,
courtesy name Xiàoxiān.
Among your relatives,
this son is the only one;
for important military matters,
you should discuss them with him.”
He also said:
“In the Battle of Mángshān,
I did not follow Chén Yuánkāng’s advice.
The event is seen in the previous volume, the ninth year of Dàtóng.
I shall die with my eyes open.”
Xiāng Lè was from Guǎngníng.

Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì Sixteen
In the first year of Tàiqīng (Dīngmǎo, 547)
This year, in the fourth month, the reign title was changed to Tàiqīng.
1 Spring,
on the first day of the first month,
there was a solar eclipse,
not complete, like a hook.
2 On the day Rén Yín,
Lúlíng Wēi Wáng Xù, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, passed away.
According to the rules of posthumous titles: "Fierce and strong-willed" is called Wēi.
Xù was always greedy.
Before his death,
he sent a memorial asking to send the Zhōng Lùshì Cānjūn, Xiè Xuānrǒng, to present over a thousand gold and silver vessels.
Zhōng Lùshì Cānjūn
was an officer responsible for recording matters within the inner court,
those close to the emperor.
Jiàn,
its sound is niǎn.
The Emperor asked Xuānrǒng,
"Is this all of King [Xù]'s gold?"
Xuānrǒng replied,
"This is considered much;
how could more be added?
The great king's transgressions are like the eclipse of the sun;
he wished His Majesty to know of them,
thus he ended without concealing them."
Zhōng [終],
refers to death.
Previously,
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì was the Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
He had a minor transgression,
and Xù replaced him,
reporting the situation.
It is said that while Yì was in Jīngzhōu,
there was a palace maid named Lǐ Táorér,
who gained favor due to her talent and intelligence.
When Yì returned,
he took Ms. Lǐ with him.
At that time, engaging in household management was strictly forbidden.
Xù fully reported the situation.
Yì cried to the messenger,
and appealed to the Crown Prince Gāng.
The Crown Prince tried to mediate,
but failed.
Yì, frightened,
sent Ms. Lǐ back to Jīngzhōu.
When Yì heard of Xù's death,
he entered his chambers and jumped for joy,
breaking his shoes.
3 On the day Bǐng Wǔ,
Bóhǎi Xiànwǔ Wáng Huān of the Eastern Wèi passed away.
He was fifty-two years old.
He remained solemn all day,
and people could not fathom him.
In matters of strategy and power, his transformations were like those of a god.
He controlled his armies,
and his laws and commands were severe.
His judgments were clear and discerning,
and he could not be deceived or offended.
When promoting and entrusting people with responsibility,
"shòu" [受],
should be
"shòu" [授].
If they were capable,
he did not inquire about their humble origins.
Those with empty reputations and no substance
were not employed.
He highly valued frugality and simplicity;
his swords, saddles, and bridles had no gold or jade ornamentation.
When young, he could drink heavily;
after assuming great responsibilities,
he would not exceed three cups.
He was good at discerning people and appreciating scholars,
fully protecting old meritorious officials;
such as Wèi Jǐng, Sīmǎ Zǐrú, and Sūn Téng, among others.
Shào [少],
pronounced shī zhào.
Hào [好],
pronounced hū dào.
Many were not punished for their faults.
Such as Quán Qǐ and Péi Ràngzhī.
His heir, Chéng, secretly kept his death private,
following Huān's dying words.
Hóu Jǐng, thinking that he had a grudge against the Gāo family,
felt uneasy internally.
On the day Xīn Hài,
he revolted in Hénán,
and defected to Wèi.
Sīmǎ Shìyún, the Inspector of Yǐngzhōu, answered him with his city.
Jǐng lured and captured Gāo Yuánchéng, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, Lǐ Mì, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, and Huáishuò Bào Xiǎn, the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu, among others.
He sent two hundred soldiers with weapons to enter Xīyǎnzhōu at dusk, intending to seize it by surprise.
Xíng Zǐcái, the Inspector, detected this,
ambushed and captured them all.
He then distributed proclamations to the various prefectures in the east,
telling each to prepare for defense.
Thus, Jǐng could not take it.
Of Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Xíng Zǐcái was the only one who realized it at the time and exposed his treachery.
Who says a scholar
cannot serve as a bulwark for the state!
All the generals believed that Jǐng's rebellion was due to Cuī Xiān.
Cuī Xiān had impeached powerful officials,
and the generals resented him.
Thus, they attributed Jǐng's rebellion as Xiān's fault.
Jiàng [將],
pronounced jì liàng;
the same below.
They wanted to kill Xiān to apologize to Jǐng.
Chén Yuánkāng remonstrated, saying:
"Although the four seas are not yet peaceful,
the legal system is already established.
If, because of several generals outside,
we merely please them,
wrongfully kill the innocent,
and violate the criminal statutes,
how can we not only betray the heavens above,
but also fail to bring peace to the common people below!
The previous case of Cháo Cuò,
I beg Your Grace to be cautious."
The case of Cháo Cuò can be found in Volume 16, in the third year of Hàn Jǐngdì.
The Emperor dispatched Sīkōng Hán Guǐ to lead the various armies to suppress Jǐng.
4 On the day Xīn Yǒu,
the Emperor offered sacrifices to the Southern Suburbs,
and issued a general amnesty.
On the day Jiǎ Zǐ,
he offered sacrifices at the Míngtáng.
5 In the third
month,
Wèi issued an edict:
"From now on, those who should be subjected to castration
shall instead be confiscated by the government,
without punishment."
6 Wèi appointed Ruògān Huì, who held the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, as Sīkōng.
Hóu Jǐng was appointed Tàifù, Hénán Dào Xíngtái, and Shànggǔ Gōng.
On the day Gēng Chén,
Jǐng again sent his Xíngtái Lángzhōng, Dīng Hé, to come
and submit a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has a grudge against Gāo Chéng.
I request to bring into allegiance the thirteen prefectures east of Hángǔ,
west of Xiáqiū,
namely Yù, Guǎng, Yǐng,
Jīng, Xiāng, Yǎn, Nányǎn, Jǐ, Dōngyù, Luò, Yáng, Běijīng, and Běiyáng.
Luò and Yáng
are the names of two prefectures,
as previously noted.
According to Wèi Shōu's records: In the second year of Wǔdìng, Běijīngzhōu was established,
governing Yīyáng, Xīnchéng, and Rǔběi Commanderies.
The Wǔdài Annals state: Lùhún County in Hénán Commandery had the Eastern Wèi Běijīngzhōu.
Xiàngchéng County in Huáiyáng Commandery,
the Eastern Wèi established Běiyángzhōu, and Dānyáng Commandery, Mòlíng Commandery.
Jǐ [濟],
pronounced zǐ lǐ.
The Kǎoyì states: The Liáng Shū's biography of Jǐng says:

"With Gāo Chéng, Inspector of Yùzhōu, Bào Xiǎn, Inspector of Guǎngzhōu, Sīmǎ Shìyún, Inspector of Yǐngzhōu, Láng Chūn, Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Lǐ Mì, Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, Xíng Zǐcái, Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Shí Chángxuān, Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu, Xǔ Jìliáng, Inspector of Jǐzhōu, Qiū Yuánzhēng, Inspector of Dōngyùzhōu, Ěrzhūhún Yuàn, Inspector of Luòzhōu, Lè Xún, Inspector of Yángzhōu, Méi Jìchāng, Inspector of Běijīngzhōu, and Yuán Shénhé, Inspector of Běiyángzhōu,
they secretly conspired
and planned to meet."
Xiāo Sháo's Tàiqīng Jì also lists Hú Yán, Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Fù Shìzhé, Inspector of Yùzhōu, and Kězúhún Luò, Inspector of Yángzhōu,
but no Xíng Zǐcái.
The Diǎn Lüè lists Kùdí Chàng, Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
but no Gāo Chéng, Bào Xiǎn, Xǔ Jìliáng, Ěrzhūhún Yuàn, Lè Xún, or Méi Jìchāng.
Now we follow the Liáng Shū.
However, the Tàiqīng Jì lists two Yùzhōu,
which likely refers to a former official.
Only a brief note is needed.
Moreover, south of the Yellow River,
all is under your servant's control,
as easy as turning one's hand.
If Qí and Sòng are pacified,
Qí [齊]
refers to Qīngzhōu;
Sòng [宋]
refers to Xúzhōu.
Yān and Zhào [燕、趙],
refer to the Hébĕi region.
Shàngshū Púyè Xiè Jǔ and others all said:
"In recent years, we have maintained peace with Wèi.
In the second year of Dàtóng,
the Eastern Wèi sought peace,
and since then, diplomatic exchanges have been uninterrupted.
Now to accept their rebellious minister,
your servant considers it inappropriate."
The Emperor said:
"Although that is true,
if we gain Jǐng, the region north of the frontier can be pacified.
Such opportunities are hard to come by;
how can we be inflexible?"
Meaning, unable to adapt,
like gluing the frets of a zither.
That year,
in the first month,
on the *yǐmǎo* day,
the Emperor dreamed that all the regional governors of the Central Plains came to surrender their territories,
and the entire court celebrated.
In the morning,
he met with *Zhōngshū Shèrén* Zhū [AS-82FA] ,
and told him about it,
adding:
"I rarely dream;
if I dream, it must be true."
Zhū [AS-82FA] said:
"This is an omen of the universe's
unification."
When Dīng Hé arrived,
he reported that Jǐng Dì had made a plan on the *yǐmǎo* day of the first month,
and the Emperor was even more convinced.
The Emperor could not govern his own country,
yet he followed an ominous dream;
his downfall was inevitable.
He once spoke to himself, saying:
"My state is like a golden cup,
without any damage or defect.
Now we suddenly receive Jǐng Dì's territory;
is this appropriate?
If it leads to chaos,
what will regret avail?"
He spoke to himself
during leisure moments;
it was not in response to questions from his attendants,
but he spoke of the matter himself.
This was because the Emperor desired to receive Jǐng Dì's territory,
and he thought of it constantly,
unable to stop himself from speaking.
Someone replied:
"With the sagely and brilliant Emperor governing the world,
both North and South look up to you.
It is only that there has been no opportunity
to fulfill their aspirations.
Now Hóu Jǐng has ceded half of Wèi's land and come.
If it were not heaven that induced his heart —
Dù Yù said: *zhōng*
means 'middle.'
*chuǎi*,
read *chūwěifān*.
*yòu*,
pronounced *yǒu*.
How could he have come to this!
If we refuse to take him in,
I fear it will cut off the hopes of future comers.
This is truly easy to see;
I pray Your Majesty harbors no doubt."
The Emperor then decided to accept Hóu Jǐng.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Hóu Jǐng was appointed *Dà Jiāngjūn*,
enfeoffed as King of Hénán,
appointed *Dūdū Hénán Běi Zhū Jūnshì* and *Dà Xíngtái*,
with the authority to issue decrees like Dèng Yǔ of old.
Zhōu Hóngzhèng, *Píngxī Zīyì Cānjūn*,
who was skilled in divination,
had previously told people:
"The state will have an uprising of troops a few years from now."
When he heard of the acceptance of Hóu Jǐng,
he said:
"The source of chaos is here!"
This was the origin of Hóu Jǐng's rebellion against Liáng.
On the 7th, *dīnghài* day,
the Emperor plowed the ceremonial field.
In the 8th, third month,
on the *gēngzǐ* day,
the Emperor visited Tóngtài Temple,
renouncing his body as in the *Dàtōng* precedent.
The first year of *Dàtōng* was
the beginning of the Emperor's renunciation of his body;
the account can be found in Volume 151.
On the 9th, *jiǎchén* day,
*Sīzhōu Cìshǐ* Yáng Yārén and *Dūdū Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ* Huán Hé were dispatched.
The *Liáng Jì* writes
"Tǔzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Hé."
The *Wǔdài Zhì*: Hǎndōng Commandery had Tǔshān County;
Liáng called it Lóngcháo,
and established Tǔzhōu and the three commanderies of East and West Yǒngníng and Zhēnyáng.
The *Wèi Shōu Zhì*: Liáng established Rénzhōu,
governing Chìkǎn City,
which encompassed Línhuái Commandery,
and administered Jǐwú and Yìchéng Counties.
Below Jǐwú,
a note says
"seat of the *zhōu* and commandery."
The *Wǔdài Zhì*: Péngchéng's Gǔyáng County had Jǐwú and Yìchéng Counties;
Later Qí merged them into Línhuái County.
They were to transport provisions to receive Hóu Jǐng.
On the 10th, Wèi issued a great amnesty.
On the 11th, Gāo Chéng of Eastern Wèi feared that the various *zhōu* might rebel,
so he personally went on a tour of inspection and pacification.
He left Duàn Sháo to guard Jìnyáng,
entrusting him with military affairs;
he appointed *Chéngxiàng Gōngcáo* Zhào Yànshēn as *Dà Xíngtái Dūguān Lángzhōng*.
He had Chén Yuánkāng pre-write dozens of pages of *Chéngxiàng* Huān's instructions and give them to Duàn Sháo and Zhào Yànshēn,
to be implemented sequentially later.
As he was about to depart,
he clasped Zhào Yànshēn's hand and wept, saying:
"I entrust my mother and brothers to you;
I hope you understand my heart!"
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *rénshēn* day,
Gāo Chéng entered the court at Yè.
The Emperor of Eastern Wèi held a banquet for him,
and Gāo Chéng performed a dance;
those who understood knew he would not last.
In the past, King Jǐng of Zhōu, after losing his heir apparent and empress,
held a banquet for guests after the mourning.
Shú Xiàng of Jìn said:
"Will the King not last?
I have heard that
what one delights in will eventually lead to one's end.
Now the King delights in sorrow;
if he ends in sorrow,
he cannot be said to have lasted."
King Jǐng's mourning
was for his consort and eldest son.
To feast after the burial
was criticized by the wise.
Gāo Chéng, however, had lost his father,
kept the mourning a secret,
and while the body was still warm,
forgot the grief of *jīsī* and being barefoot,
indulging in wanton and wild revelry.
Did he still possess a human heart?
Therefore, the disaster of Róng Qí was still light,
while the disaster of Bó Táng was more tragic;
the retribution of Heaven is indeed unfailing.
*Jīsī*
is read *jīlì*.
On the 12th, *bǐngzǐ* day,
his officials offered a ransom.
From the *gēngzǐ* day of renouncing his body to the *bǐngzǐ* day of offering ransom,
it was a total of thirty-seven days.
The affairs of state
cannot be neglected for a single day,
yet he was so lost in Buddhism;
the Emperor forgot the world.
During those thirty-seven days,
the world did not know it was without a ruler,
and the world also forgot its ruler.
On the *dīnghài* day,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
"Dīnghài"
should be
"Dīngchǒu".
The reign title was changed,
as in the *Dàtōng* precedent.
On the 13th, *jiǎwǔ* day,
Eastern Wèi dispatched *Jiān Sànqí Chángshì* Lǐ Xì to make a formal visit.
Lǐ Xì
was the younger brother of Lǐ Huì.
Lǐ Huì is mentioned in Volume 158, Dàtōng 8th year.
The *Kǎo Yì* states: The *Wèi Dì Jì* writes
"Lǐ Wěi".
We follow the main biography here.
In the 14th, fifth month,
on the *dīngyǒu* day, the first day of the month,
Eastern Wèi issued a great amnesty.
On the 15th, *wùxū* day,
Eastern Wèi appointed Xiāngchéng King Xù as *Tàiwèi*.
Gāo Chéng dispatched *Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn* Yuán Zhù and others, leading tens of thousands of troops, to march day and night to surprise Hóu Jǐng.
They met Hóu Jǐng north of Yǐngchuān,
and Yuán Zhù's forces were greatly defeated.
Hóu Jǐng, seeing that Yáng Yārén's army had not yet arrived,
retreated to defend Yǐngchuān.
Hóu Jǐng did not dare to press his victory northward
because, although Gāo Huān was dead,
Gāo Chéng was still able to command his troops.
On the 16th, *jiǎchén* day,

'I could not advance Qú Bóyù
nor dismiss Mí Zǐxiá;
this means I could not correct my lord.
If I cannot correct my lord while alive,
I have no way to fulfill the rites in death.
When I die,
place my body under the window;
that will suffice for me.'
His son followed this.
Duke Líng came to mourn,
was puzzled and asked about it,
and his son informed him.
The Duke said:
'This is my fault.'
He ordered him to be coffined in the guest's position,
advanced Qú Bóyù,
and dismissed Mí Zǐxiá.
Confucius heard of this and said:
'Among the resolute remonstrators of old,
when they died, that was the end.
But none was like Shǐ Yú, who died and remonstrated with his corpse,
whose loyalty moved his lord.'
How dare I forget the heart of Liú Xiàng!"
The account of Liú Xiàng is found in Volume 30, second year of Hàn Emperor Chéng's Yángshuò era.
However, his advice was not adopted.
Jiè
was the grandson of Sīhuà.
During the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
Xiāo Sīhuà successively held regional posts.
According to the *Xīn Tángshū Zǎixiàng Shìxì Biǎo*,
Jiè and the Emperor were descendants of the same thirteenth-generation ancestor, Bāo, the Zhongshan Prime Minister of Later Hàn.
5. On the *jǐwèi* day,
Dōng Wèi's Grand General Chéng held court at Yè.
6. Wèi appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Zhào Guì as Sīkōng.
7. The Wèi imperial grandson was born,
and a great amnesty was declared.
8. In the second month,
Dōng Wèi executed Shí Chángxuān, its Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu;
this was to suppress Hóu Jǐng's faction.
The scribe for Shí Chángxuān wrote that he had attached Nányǎnzhōu to Hóu Jǐng,
which should not be interpreted according to the *Chūnqiū* style of writing.
All were pardoned.
9. Dōng Wèi, having obtained Xuánhù and Xiàngchéng,
completely restored its old territory.
Grand General Chéng repeatedly sent letters and dispatches.
*Yí*
refers to sending a manifesto.
*Shuò*
is pronounced *suǒ jué fān*.
The imperial court had not yet assented.
Chéng said to Zhēnyáng Hóu Yuānmíng:
"The former king and the Lord of Liáng were on good terms
for over ten years.
I heard his Buddhist prayer text said:
'We pray for the Lord of Wèi,
and also for the former king.'
This shows the profound goodwill of the Lord of Liáng;
it is not to be thought that he would suddenly break faith
and cause such turmoil.
I know this is not the original intention of the Lord of Liáng,
but rather stirred up by Hóu Jǐng.
An envoy should be sent to consult.
If the Lord of Liáng does not forget our old friendship,
I also dare not go against the intention of the former king.
All these people shall be immediately sent back,
and Hóu Jǐng's family should also be sent with them."
Yuānmíng then sent Shěngshì Xiàhóu Sēngbiàn to present a memorial to the Emperor,
stating,
"Bóhǎi Wáng Hóng is generous and virtuous.
If relations are renewed,
Yuānmíng will be permitted to return."
When the Emperor received the memorial, he shed tears.
This is what is called the 'benevolence of a woman.'
The Emperor thus fell into Gāo Chéng's trap.
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Zhū Yì and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Zhāng Wǎn and others all said:
"To pacify the bandits and bring peace to the people,
harmony is indeed convenient."
Sīnóng Qīng Fù Qí alone said:
"Why does Gāo Chéng need harmony?
He must be setting a trap,
and therefore commanded Zhēnyáng to send an envoy,
wishing to make Hóu Jǐng suspicious.
If Jǐng feels insecure,
he will certainly plan rebellion.
If we agree to restore relations,
we will just fall into his scheme."
Hóu Jǐng's treachery
was known to Hé Jìngrōng and Xiāo Jiè;
Gāo Chéng's cunning and deceit
were known to Fù Qí.
It was not that the Liáng court truly lacked capable people,
but Emperor Wǔ could not make a decisive choice and employ them.
The Emperor also grew weary of warfare,
and so he followed Yì's suggestion,
bestowing a letter upon Yuānmíng which read:
"I know that Grand General Gāo treats you not poorly.
Receiving your memorial
greatly comforted my heart.
I shall send another envoy
to further strengthen our neighborly friendship."
Sēngbiàn returned,
passing through Shòuyáng.
Hóu Jǐng secretly sought him out and learned of it,
then interrogated him,
and he fully confessed.
"Interrogated" means
arresting and questioning the person.
Chén Qǐ reported to the emperor, saying:
"The Gāo clan harbored a poisonous heart;
their resentment filled the northern land.
What the people wished for, Heaven granted,
causing the joyous destruction of their bodies."
This means that what the people wished for,
Heaven granted and killed him.
"To annihilate them awaits the right time."
"Therefore, he overlooked this victory"
refers to the victory at Wōyáng.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says: When King Wǔ of Chǔ was about to die,
he told his wife Dèng Màn,
"My heart is unsettled."
Dèng Màn said,
"Has the king's fortune reached its limit?
To be full and then unsettled
is the way of Heaven."
Dù Yù's commentary says: "Unsettled"
means "moving and scattered."
"If your core is not ill,
why the urgency to offer a jade disk and seek peace?
Is it not because Qín soldiers block your throat?"
"Qín soldiers"
refers to the soldiers of Xī Wèi.
Xī Wèi occupied Guānzhōng,
hence they were called Qín soldiers.
"Hú cavalry"
refers to the Ròurán soldiers.
"to seek peace with a great nation."
Your servant has heard, '
To let an enemy go for a day [will be] the sorrow of generations.' "
This is a saying of Jìn Xiān Zhěn.
"thus abandoning the hearts of the myriad people!
I secretly believe that when Běi Wèi was strong
(none surpassed the beginning of Tiānjiān era),
in the battle of Zhōnglí,
not a single horse returned."
For the battle of Zhōnglí,
see volume 146, Tiānjiān year 6.
"Your Majesty still attacked and took it;
but now that it is weak,
you instead worry and seek peace.
Abandoning an accomplished feat,
letting a dying captive go,
allowing him to prolong his life and grow strong,
thus leaving trouble for later generations—
this is not merely a cause for foolish officials to wring their wrists,
but truly makes brave men heartbroken.
In the past, when Wǔ Xiàng fled to Wú,
the state of Chǔ was eventually destroyed;"
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says: Chǔ killed Wǔ Shē,
and his son fled to Wú.
King Hélǘ of Wú employed him,
defeated Chǔ, and entered Yǐng.
"Wàn" is pronounced
"wū guàn fān."
"Xiàng" is pronounced
"xī liàng fān."
"Zú" is pronounced
"zǐ xù fān."
"the Liú clan rose to power;"
See the *Hàn Gāo Dì Jì*.
"My heart is aligned with past events.
We truly know that Gāo Chéng resents Jiǎ [Jì]'s presence in Dí,
and detests Suí Huì's dwelling in Qín."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says: In the early days of Duke Líng of Jìn,
Jiǎ Jì fled to Dí,
and Suí Huì fled to Qín.
The Qín people used their counsel,
which troubled the Jìn people.
The six qǐng met at Zhūfú.
Zhào Xuānzǐ said:
"Suí Huì is in Qín,
Jiǎ Jì is in Dí,
disaster is imminent.
What shall we do?"
"Dí"
is the same as "Dí."
"Wù" is pronounced
"wū lù fān."
"I hope to remove their trouble.
If my death would be beneficial,
I would die ten thousand times without demur;
I only fear that a thousand years hence,
it would stain the good historians."
Observing Hóu Jǐng's words here,
his temper was outrageous.
(He) offered three hundred liǎng of gold;
Zhū Yì accepted the gold but did not pass on his memorial.
The history states that Zhū Yì was blinded by profit and disregarded the danger.
On the day *jǐmǎo*
in the third month, the emperor sent an envoy to mourn Chéng.
Hóu Jǐng again reported, saying:
"Between your servant and the Gāo clan,
the animosity is already deep.
Relying on your majestic power,
I intend to avenge this humiliation;
now Your Majesty has again allied with the Gāo clan,
where can your servant place himself!"
This is Hóu Jǐng's heartfelt speech.
"Shǐ" is pronounced
"shū lì fān."
"Xìn" is pronounced
"xǔ jìn fān."
"Fù" is pronounced
"fú yòu fān."
"Chǔ" is pronounced
"chāng lǚ fān."
"to extend the imperial majesty!"
The emperor replied to him, saying:
"Our great principle with you is already settled.
How can we accept when you succeed,
and abandon when you fail!
Now the Gāo clan has sent an envoy to seek peace,
and We also intend to cease military action.
The propriety of advancing or retreating
is governed by the state's constant regulations.
You need only remain calm and at ease,
do not trouble yourself with worries!"
Hóu Jǐng again reported, saying:
"Your servant is now storing grain and gathering troops,
feeding horses and sharpening weapons.
The day and time are set
to conquer Zhào and Wèi.
My army cannot march without a name,
therefore I wish to take Your Majesty as my leader.
Looking at Hóu Jǐng's words here,
it truly cannot be endured.
If the north and south communicate again,
I fear your humble servant's life
will not escape the hands of the Gāo clan."
The emperor again replied:
"We are the lord of ten thousand chariots,
how can We lose faith in one creature!
We presume you deeply understand this,
and need not send another report."
Once his memorials were cut off,
Hóu Jǐng again harbored ill intentions.
"Chéng" is pronounced
"shéng zhèng fān."
Hóu Jǐng then fraudulently wrote a letter from Yè,
requesting to exchange Hóu Jǐng for Zhēnyáng Hóu.
The emperor was about to agree.
Attendant Fù Qí said:
Fù Qí first held the concurrent post of zhōngshū tōngshì shèrén,
and was successively promoted to tàipú, sī nóng qīng,
still concurrently holding the post of shèrén.
"Hóu Jǐng returned to allegiance out of desperation.
To abandon him would be inauspicious;
moreover, after a hundred battles,
how could he willingly allow himself to be bound!"
Xiè Jǔ and Zhū Yì said:
"Hóu Jǐng is a defeated general,
merely the result of a single envoy's effort."
The emperor agreed with them
and replied in a letter:
"Zhēnyáng will arrive in the morning,
Hóu Jǐng will return in the evening."
Hóu Jǐng said to his attendants:
"I knew that old man Wú was heartless!"
The emperor's true feelings were fully revealed here,
yet the emperor himself did not realize it.
Alas!
"Now to sit and wait is also death."
This means to sit and await the actions of the Liáng court
will also inevitably lead to death.
"Shuō" is pronounced
"shì ruì fān."
"Only the king should plan for this!"
Thereupon, he began to plot rebellion:
He summoned all residents of the affiliated cities to be soldiers,
and immediately suspended the collection of market taxes and land rents.
"Market taxes" refers to
assessing the value of goods brought to market by merchants
and collecting taxes on them.
"Land rents" refers to
the regular rent collected based on the acreage.
All were distributed to the generals and soldiers.
Hóu Jǐng's rebellious plot was so conspicuous,
yet the ruler and ministers of Liáng seemed to hear and know nothing;
their downfall was indeed deserved.
In the third month, on the day *guǐsì*,
Dōng Wèi appointed Tàiwèi Xiāngchéng Wáng Xù as Dàsīmǎ,
and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Gāo Yuè as Tàiwèi.
On the day *xīnhài*,
Grand General Chéng advanced south to Líyáng,
crossing the river from Hǔláo to Luòyáng.
Pèi Kuān, the Dàozhǎngshǐ of Wèi Tóngguǐ, fought against Dōng Wèi general Péng Lè and others,
and was captured by Péng Lè.
Chéng treated him with great courtesy,
and Pèi Kuān managed to escape and return.
Chéng returned to Jìnyáng via Tàiháng.
11. Qūliáo Cave killed Lǐ Bēn.
Bēn fled to Qūliáo Cave.
See Volume 159, Dàtóng First Year.
Láo (獠),
read as Lǔ Hào.
Kǎoyì says: The Annals of Chén Gāozǔ states
"Tàiqīng First Year,"
probably referring to the year Bēn was defeated.
Now we follow the Annals of Liáng Dì.
According to the Tōngjiàn, Bēn's defeat was recorded in Dàtóng First Year.
Bēn's elder brother, Tiānbǎo, fled into Jiǔzhēn,
gathered his remaining 20,000 troops, and besieged Àizhōu.
The Wǔdài Zhì says: Jiǔzhēn Commandery,
Liáng established Àizhōu.
An imperial edict appointed Bàxiān as Western Jiāng Supervisor, Gāoyào Administrator, and Overseer of Military Affairs for seven commanderies.
12. Summer,
Fourth month,
Jiǎzǐ.
Zhāng Yǒnghé, a clerk in the Eastern Wèi Ministry of Personnel, and others falsely claimed official positions.
When the matter was discovered,
over 60,000 people were investigated or confessed.
"Investigated" (jiūjiǎn 糾檢)
refers to those exposed by official investigations.
"Confessed" (shǒu 首)
refers to those who surrendered themselves.
The historian says that during a time of chaos and disorder,
officials engaged in misconduct,
and the number of those who improperly sought positions was overwhelmingly large.
Shǒu (首),
also read as shǒu.
13. Jiǎxū.
Eastern Wèi dispatched Grand Commandant Gāo Yuè, Acting Grand Marshal Mùróng Shàozōng, Grand Commander Liú Fēngshēng, and others with 100,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Wáng Sīzhèng at Yǐngchuān.
Wáng Sīzhèng defending Yǐngchuān was first mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
Jiāng (將),
read as jiàng.
Qí (騎),
read as jì.
As if there were no one there.
Yuè, relying on his large numbers,
assailed the city from all sides.
Sīzhèng selected brave and strong warriors to open the gates and sally forth.
Yuè's troops were defeated and fled.
Yuè then built earth mounds
and attacked day and night.
Sīzhèng defended in every direction,
seized their earth mounds,
and placed battlements on them to aid in defense.
14. Fifth month.
Wèi appointed Chancellor Tài as Grand Preceptor,
Guǎnglíng Wáng Xīn as Grand Tutor,
Lǐ Bì as Grand Master of Ancestral Rites,
Zhào Guì as Grand Minister of Justice,
and Yú Jǐn as Grand Minister of Works.
Yǔwén Xiāng Wèi [Xiāng as in prime minister]
imitated the institutions of the Former Zhōu to establish official posts.
Ascended Lǒng,
arrived at Yuánzhōu,
passed the Northern Great Wall.
This was probably the Great Wall built by Qín.
Arrived at Púzhōu.
From Wǔyuán, returned to Púzhōu.
The Wǔdài Zhì says: Hédōng Commandery,
Later Wèi established Qínzhōu,
Later Zhōu changed its name to Púzhōu,
named after Púbǎn.
Qù (趣),
read as qù.
And when he arrived,
it was already healed.
Tài returned to Huázhōu.
15. The Emperor sent Jiànkāng Prefect Xiè Tǐng and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Xú Líng to Eastern Wèi as envoys.
According to the official system of Liáng,
Jiànkāng Prefect ranked 1000 dàn of grain,
Gentleman of the Yellow Gate ranked 2000 dàn.
Xiè Tǐng should not have been above Xú Líng.
Perhaps Xú Líng was the principal envoy,
and Xiè Tǐng merely assisted him.
Sǎn (散),
read as sǎn.
Qí (騎),
read as jì.
Líng (陵)
was the son of Chī.
Xú Chī is mentioned in Volume 155, Dàtōng Third Year.
Chī (摛),
read as chī.
16. Sixth month.
Eastern Wèi Grand General Chéng inspected the northern border.
17. Autumn,
Seventh month,
Gēngyín first day,
there was a solar eclipse.
18. Yǐmǎo.
Eastern Wèi Grand General Chéng paid respects at Yè.
Because many Daoist priests were fraudulent and excessive,
the Southern Suburban Daoist Altar was abolished.
Wèi Tàiwǔ Dì greatly trusted Kòu Qiānzhī,
and established the Southern Suburban Daoist Altar.
Gēngyín.
Chéng returned to Jìnyáng,
and sent Minister Xīn Shù to lead the generals to conquer the area north of the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
In total, they captured twenty-three prefectures.
As Hóu Jǐng had already caused chaos in Liáng,
the following year,
Eastern Wèi finally took full possession of the Huáinán region.
The historian narrates its conclusion by stating it here.
Shuài (帥),
read as shuài.
Jiāng (將),
read as jiàng.
19. Hóu Jǐng, ever since arriving at Shòuyáng,
demanded and sought without end,
but the court never refused.
Jǐng requested to marry into the Wáng or Xiè families.
The Emperor said:
"The Wáng and Xiè families are too high-ranking to be matched with you.
You may seek a match among those of Zhū, Zhāng, and below."
Zhū, Zhāng
refers to the clans of Zhū Yì and Zhāng Wǎn.
(Jǐng) said:
"I will assemble the daughters of the Wú barbarians and marry them to my slaves!"
He also submitted a memorial requesting ten thousand bolts of brocade for soldiers' robes.
The Central Army Commander Zhū Yì suggested giving him blue cloth instead.
Furthermore, he considered the weapons provided by the court to be mostly of poor quality,
and requested blacksmiths from Dōngyě,
intending to produce new ones.
Jǐng appointed Xiàhóu Kuí's son, Fān, as Chief Clerk,
and Xú Sīyù as Administrator.
Fān then removed
"Xià"
and called himself
"Hóu,"
pretending to be a clan nephew.
Xiàhóu Xiáng was a founding meritorious official of the Liáng dynasty;
his sons Dǎn and Kuí both exerted their efforts at the frontiers,
and both achieved renown.
However, Fān was unable to bear the responsibility.
Since the Emperor did not heed Jǐng's words
and made peace with Eastern Wèi,
thereafter Jǐng's memorials became increasingly insolent and disloyal;
upon hearing that Xú Líng and others were sent as envoys to Wèi,
his rebellious intentions grew even stronger.
Yuán Zhēn knew Jǐng had ulterior motives
and repeatedly memorialized requesting to return to court.
Jǐng sought to assist Zhēn, see previous volume, last year.
Cháo (朝),
read as cháo.
"Although the affairs north of the river did not come to fruition,
why worry about losing Jiāngnán?
Why not bear with it a little longer!"
Zhēn was afraid,
fled back to Jiànkāng,
and reported the matter in detail.
The Emperor appointed Zhēn as Shǐxīng Internal Administrator,
but did not question Jǐng.
The Emperor neither questioned Jǐng
nor made preparations for him,
probably because in his dotage he was weary of governance,
and simply resigned himself to helplessness.
Lín Hé Wáng Zhèngdé,
wherever he went, was rapacious, violent, and lawless.
He repeatedly offended the Emperor.
After Zhèngdé had fled to Wèi and then escaped back,
the Emperor restored his original fief.
Zhèngdé's ambition and conduct showed no repentance;
he often openly engaged in robbery and plunder.
When he later followed Yùzhāng Wáng in the northern invasion,
he again abandoned his army and fled.
This was reported by the officials concerned.
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"In the past, when you were in Shǔ,
you associated with petty men,
yet I still considered it a youthful indiscretion.
Later, in Wú Jùn, you massacred the innocent
and plundered wealth.
And when you returned to the capital,
you were dedicated to being a fugitive,
even blocking main roads at Jiāngchéng
and cutting off paths at Hútóu,
seizing people's wives and concubines,
and abducting people's children.
I repeatedly covered for you,
hoping you would reform yourself,
but you showed no change or reform at all.
Your grievances and enmities only grew,
and you fled on a single horse,
harboring thoughts of retaliation.
When you returned,
I again ordered you to command troops as a vanguard with a general's staff.
How could I have known that your wolfish heart had not changed,
and that you desired to ruin the national plan to satisfy your own desires?
Now I pardon you by sending you far away."
Thereupon, he was dismissed from office, stripped of his title,
and exiled to Línhǎi.
Before he reached his place of exile,
a pardon was issued for him;
he was again re-enfeoffed as Lín Hé Wáng due to Zhū Yì's words.
He served as Dānyáng Yǐn.
He was removed from office because of rampant robbery and theft in his jurisdiction.
He was sent out as Nán Yānzhōu.
While in office, he was harsh and demanding,
and the people found his rule unbearable.
From then on, he was dismissed and degraded,
and his resentment grew.
He secretly gathered assassins,
stockpiled rice and goods,
hoping for a national crisis.
Jǐng knew of this.
Zhèngdé had befriended Xú Sīyù in the north,
referring to the time when he fled to Wèi.
"Today the Son of Heaven is old,
and corrupt officials are plunging the country into chaos.
In my view,
disaster and ruin are only a matter of days away.
Your Majesty was once the heir apparent
but was later deposed.
For details, see Volume 149, Pǔtōng Three Years.
Bèi,
pronounced 'pí yì'.
My heart is devoted to Your Majesty.
Though I, Jǐng, am not clever,
I truly wish to serve you.
I hope Your Majesty will live up to the expectations of the common people
and recognize this sincere devotion!"
Zhèngdé was overjoyed and said:
"Lord Hóu's intentions
secretly align with mine.
Heaven has granted this to me!"
He replied:
"The state of the court
is as you, my lord, say.
My intentions
have been long-standing.
Now, I will be the internal force,
and you, my lord, will be the external force.
How could we not succeed!
Affairs of state demand speed.
Now is the time."
Póyáng Wáng Fàn secretly reported Hóu Jǐng's plot of rebellion.
At that time, the Emperor had entrusted border affairs entirely to Zhū Yì,
and all movements and actions concerned him.
Yì believed there could be no such possibility.
The Emperor replied to Fàn, saying:
"Hóu Jǐng is isolated and precarious, depending on others for his life.
He is like an infant relying on milk.
Given this situation,
how could he rebel!"
Fàn reiterated, saying:
"If he is not suppressed early,
disaster will befall the common people."
The Emperor said:
"The court has its own arrangements;
you need not worry so deeply."
This was also the Emperor's reply to Fàn,
not a face-to-face conversation.
Chǔ,
pronounced 'chāng lǚ'.
Fèn,
pronounced 'fú wèn'.
The Emperor did not permit it.
Fàn was not Jǐng's enemy.
If the Emperor had allowed Fàn and sent troops to attack Jǐng,
it would have been like throwing meat to a starving tiger.
Fù,
pronounced 'fú yòu';
'fù' below is not the same.
"Póyáng Wáng really won't allow the court to have a single guest!"
From then on, when Fàn submitted memorials,
Yì no longer forwarded them.
Hóu Jǐng invited Yáng Yārén to rebel together.
Yáng Yārén seized Jǐng's envoy and reported it.
Yáng Yārén returned from Xuánhù,
and his army halted on the Huái River.
"A few hundred rebel captives like Hóu Jǐng,
what can they do!"
An imperial edict ordered the envoy to be handed over to the Jiànkāng prison,
but he was soon released.
Hóu Jǐng became even more fearless,
and memorialized the Emperor, saying:
"If my alleged actions are true,
I should suffer national punishment;
if I am cleared after investigation,
I request that Yáng Yārén be executed!"
The 'Kǎo Yì' states: Both the 'Liáng Shū' and 'Nán Shǐ' say
"both were suppressed and not reported."
The 'Diǎn Lǜe' says,
"Zhū Yì refused it,"
and so on.
This follows the 'Tàiqīng Jì'.
"Gāo Chéng is cunning;
how can he be fully trusted!
Your Majesty accepts his deceitful words
and seeks an alliance with him.
I too secretly laugh at this.
How can I endure breaking my bones
and throwing my life into the enemy's gate?
'Enemy's gate'
refers to the Gāo clan.
Please allow me to command and supervise.
If this is not permitted,
I will lead my armored cavalry
to the riverside,
facing Mǐn and Yuè.
Not only will the court be ashamed,
but the Three Dukes will also eat late."
The Emperor had Zhū Yì convey a message to Hóu Jǐng's envoy, saying:
"For example, a poor family,
keeping ten or five guests,
can still be proud;
I only have one guest,
and yet there are angry words.
This is also my fault."
He increased the rewards of brocade, silk, money, and cloth,
and envoys came and went constantly.
The historian says that the Emperor nurtured Hóu Jǐng's disaster, leading to the ruin of the nation and his own death.
On the day of Wùxū,
Hóu Jǐng rebelled in Shòuyáng,
using the pretext of executing Zhū Yì, the Zhong Lǐngjūn; Xú Lín, the Shǎofù Qīng; Lù Yàn, the Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài; and Zhōu Shízhēn, the Zhìjú Jiān.
Yì and the others were all known for their treacherous flattery, greed,
obscuring the ruler, and manipulating power,
which made them detested by the people of their time.
Hence, Jǐng used this as a pretext for raising an army.
Lín and Yàn
