Hóu Jǐng also burned Chénghuáng, Shìlín Guǎn, and Tàifǔ Sì.
During the Dàtóng period,
Shìlín Guǎn was established west of Táichéng,
and Zhū Yì, Gù Chēn, Kǒng Zǐqū, and others were assigned to lecture there in turn.
Chéng,
pronounced as 'shéng zhèng'.
On the Guǐchǒu day,
Hóu Jǐng made several hundred wooden donkeys to attack the city.
Stones thrown from the city shattered them.
Hóu Jǐng then made pointed-top wooden donkeys,
which stones could not break.
Yáng Kǎn ordered the creation of pheasant-tail torches,
soaked them in grease and wax,
and threw them in bundles to burn the donkeys,
which were quickly consumed.
Dù Yòu said: Swallow-tail torches
are made by binding reeds and grass,
divided into two branches,
shaped like a swallow's tail,
soaked with oil and wax,
set alight,
and dropped from the city wall
to burn those riding the wooden donkeys.
When Kǎn made the pheasant-tail torches,
he attached iron arrowheads,
soaked them in oil,
and threw them onto the donkeys to burn them.
He also constructed high siege towers, over ten *zhàng* tall,
intending to shoot into the city from above.
Kǎn said:
"The carts are high, and the moat is empty.
When they come, they are bound to fall.
We can lie down and watch them."
When the carts moved,
they indeed fell.
Since Hóu Jǐng's attack was unsuccessful,
and many soldiers were killed or wounded,
he then built a long siege wall to cut off inside from outside,
and again sent a message requesting the execution of Zhū Yì and others.
From inside the city, a reward proclamation was also shot out, stating:
"Anyone who can deliver Hóu Jǐng's head
will be granted Hóu Jǐng's position,
and one hundred million cash,
and ten thousand bolts each of cloth and silk."
Zhū Yì and Zhāng Wǎn discussed sending troops to attack them.
They asked Yáng Kǎn,
who said:
"No.
If too few men are sent out now,
they will not be enough to defeat the rebels,
merely blunting our morale;
if too many,
then if we suffer a sudden defeat,
the gates are narrow and the bridges are small,
which will inevitably lead to great losses."
Yì and the others did not listen,
and sent over a thousand men to fight.
Before their forces even engaged,
they retreated,
and more than half of them died by rushing into the water at the bridge.
Kǎn-zǐ Zhuó
was captured by Jǐng,
taken under the city walls,
and shown to Kǎn.
Kǎn said:
"I have sacrificed my whole clan to repay my lord,
and still regret it is not enough.
How can I account for one son?
Please kill him quickly!"
A few days later,
he was brought back again.
Kǎn said to Zhuó:
"I have long thought you were dead.
Are you still alive?!"
He drew his bow and shot him.
Jǐng, admiring his loyalty and righteousness,
did not kill him.
Zhuāng Tiělǜ, fearing that Jǐng would not be victorious,
feigned a desire to welcome his mother,
and with several dozen of his retainers, sped to Lìyáng.
He first sent a letter to trick Tián Yīng and Guō Luò, saying:
"Gǔi"
(wait for multiple interpretations).
"The Marquis-King has already been killed by the imperial army;
the state has ordered me to return to my garrison."
Luò and others were greatly alarmed,
abandoned the city, and fled to Shòuyáng.
Tiělǜ entered the city,
but dared not defend it,
and fled with his mother to Xúnyáng.
In the eleventh month,
on the new moon day of Wùwǔ,
a white horse was sacrificed,
and Chíyóu was worshipped in front of the Tàijí Hall.
Yìng Shào said: "Chíyóu was also an ancient emperor,
fond of the five weapons,
hence we sacrifice to him to seek good fortune."
Xuē Zàn said: "Chíyóu was
a greedy commoner,
not an emperor."
Guǎn Zhòng said: "When Lúshān was cut and its hair-like roots brought forth water,
gold followed it,
Chíyóu received it,
and used it to make swords and halberds."
Lín Hè Wáng Zhèngdé ascended the imperial throne in the Yíxián Hall.
In the sixth year of Tiānjiān,
the Tīngsòng Hall was renamed Yíxián Hall,
located in front of the South Gate.
"Since Pǔtōng,
treachery and wickedness have disturbed the government,
the emperor has long been unwell,
and the state is in danger.
Hénán Wáng Jǐng,
has relinquished his position and come to court."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: Wángzǐ Cháo said:
"The feudal lords relinquished their positions to intervene in the king's government."
"Cháo,"
(Zhí yáo fan).
"I assume this precious position;
a general amnesty should be proclaimed,
and the era name changed to Zhèngpíng."
His heir, Jiànlǐ, was established as Crown Prince,
Jǐng was appointed Chancellor,
given a daughter in marriage,
and all the treasures of the imperial household were used to fund the army.
Thereupon, Jǐng set up camp in front of the palace gates,
and divided 2,000 of his soldiers to attack Dōngfǔ;
Nánpǔ Hóu Tuī resisted them,
and after three days,
they were unsuccessful.
Jǐng personally went to attack it;
arrows and stones rained down.
Xuānchéng Wáng's defense officer, Xǔ Bózhòng, secretly led Jǐng's troops to scale the city wall.
Xuānchéng Wáng Dàqì
was the Crown Prince's eldest son.
Xǔ Bózhòng was his defense officer
in Dōngfǔ,
hence he could act as Jǐng's inside informant.
Yáo Sīlián's Liáng Shū records him as
"Xǔ Yùhuá,"
who was then the commander of the northeast tower of Dōngfǔ.
On Xīnyǒu,
they captured it;
Nánpǔ Hóu Tuī and 3,000 soldiers in the city were killed.
Their bodies were loaded and piled up at Dùmǔ Zhái,
and a distant message was sent to the people in the city:
"If you do not surrender soon,
this is exactly what will happen!"
Jǐng publicly announced that the emperor had already died,
and even those in the city believed it.
On Rénxū,
the Crown Prince requested the emperor to inspect the city.
The emperor proceeded to the Dàsīmǎ Gate;
hearing the sound of the imperial escort from the city wall,
everyone cheered and wept,
and the morale of the masses somewhat stabilized.
When Jiāng Zǐyī returned defeated,
(this refers to the time he returned defeated from downstream Cǎishí).
Zǐyī bowed and said:
"I have pledged my life to the state,
and always feared not meeting a fitting end;
now all my subordinates have abandoned me and left.
How can I, a single man, defeat the bandits?
If the bandits can indeed reach this point,
I swear to break my head to atone for my past crimes,
if not dying before the palace gate,
then I shall die behind it."
On Yǐ
Hài,
Zǐyī requested the Crown Prince,
and with his younger brothers, Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Zǐsì and Dōnggōng Zhǔshuài Zǐwǔ, led over a hundred men to open the Chéngmíng Gate and sally forth to battle.
Zǐyī went straight to the bandit camp;
the bandit ambush remained motionless.
(They did not ascertain his intent,
therefore they did not move.)
"Why do you bandits not come out quickly!"
After a long time,
the bandit cavalry emerged,
attacking them from both sides.
Zǐyī pressed forward,
thrusting his spear at the bandits;
none of his followers dared to continue,
and the bandits cut through his shoulder, and he died.
Zǐsì and Zǐwǔ said to each other:
"Having come out with our brother,
how can we return alone?"
Both removed their helmets and rushed at the bandits.
Zǐsì was struck by a spear,
which pierced his chest, and he died;
Zǐwǔ was wounded in the neck,
and returned to the trench,
where he gave a cry of anguish and collapsed.
The Jiāng Zǐyī brothers died side by side beneath the palace gates,
yet it was not enough to protect the state.
How tragic!
This is why the ancients valued those who could repulse invaders a thousand *lǐ* away.
"Qiàn,"
(Qī yàn fan).
When Jǐng first arrived in Jiànkāng,
he thought the city could be taken within days,
and his orders were strict and orderly;
his soldiers dared not commit violence or plunder.
But after repeated unsuccessful attacks,
morale began to waver.
Jǐng feared that relief forces would gather from all sides,
and his army would collapse overnight;
furthermore, the grain in Shítóu's Chángpíng and other granaries was exhausted,
and the army was short of food.
So he allowed his soldiers to plunder civilian rice, gold, silk, and women.
After this, one *shēng* of rice cost seventy to eighty thousand cash,
people resorted to cannibalism,
and five or six tenths of the population died of starvation.
On Yǐchǒu,
Jǐng erected earthen mounds to the east and west of the city,
forcing civilians and soldiers,
regardless of noble or humble status,
to work, beating them indiscriminately.
The weak and exhausted were killed and used to fill the mounds,
their cries of anguish shaking the earth.
The people dared not hide,
and all came out to join the work.
Within ten days,
the numbers reached tens of thousands.
The city also built earthen mounds to counter them.
The Crown Prince, Xuānchéng Wáng, and others
all personally carried earth,
and wielded shovels and hoes.
On the mounds, they erected Fúróng multi-storied towers,
forty *zhàng* high,
decorated with brocade and felt.
The Fúróng multi-storied towers
had brackets and corbels supporting each layer,
stacked one upon another,
resembling hibiscus flowers.
"Jǐn"
refers to colored silk.
"Jì"
refers to coarse woolen cloth,
woven from animal hair.
"Gāo"
(Jū ào fan).
"Jì"
(sound Jū lì fan).
Thick robes and armor,
called
"sēng téng kè,"
were distributed to the two mounds.
(The two mounds
refer to the East earthen mound and the West earthen mound.)
A heavy rain then fell,
and the city's earthen mound collapsed;
the bandits took advantage of this,
almost entering.
Fierce fighting could not hold them back.
Yáng Kǎn ordered many fires to be thrown,
creating a wall of fire to block their path,
and then slowly built an inner wall,
preventing the bandits from advancing.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) recruited slaves who surrendered,
and all were freed as commoners.
He obtained Zhū Yì's (朱异) slave
and made him a Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司).
Yì's (异) family property was all given to him.
The slave rode a fine horse,
and wore a brocade robe.
From under the city wall, he looked up and insulted Yì (异), saying:
"You served as an official for fifty years,
only then did you become a Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍).
I have only just started serving the Marquis and King,
and am already a Yítóng (儀同)!"
Within three days,
the number of slaves who went out to Hóu Jǐng (侯景) reached into the thousands.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) treated them generously and assigned them to his army.
Everyone was grateful,
and fought to the death for him.
All those who were slaves
were generally malcontents.
Once they were freed as commoners,
they were already overjoyed,
how much more so when they were provided with gold and silk!
How could they not fight to the death for the rebel?
In times of peace, the scholar-officials
tyrannically used their slaves and maidservants.
How could this not only harm themselves,
and harm their families,
but also harm the affairs of the state?
Should one not be warned!
Wéi (為),
Yúwěi (于偽) pronunciation.
The Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州), Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì (湘東王繹), heard that Hóu Jǐng (侯景) was besieging Táichéng (臺城).
On the day Bǐngyín (丙寅),
he ordered a state of emergency.
He issued a dispatch to the governors under his supervision: Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (湘州刺史) Hédōng Wáng Yù (河東王譽), Yǒngzhōu Cìshǐ (雍州刺史) Yuèyáng Wáng Chá (岳陽王詧),
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史) Dāngyáng Gōng Dàxīn (當陽公大心), Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (郢州刺史) Nánpíng Wáng Kè (南平王恪), etc.,
ordering them to dispatch troops for reinforcement.
Dàxīn (大心)
was Dàqì's (大器) younger brother.
Kè (恪)
was Wěi's (偉) son.
Nánpíng Wáng Wěi (南平王偉)
was the Emperor's younger brother.
Zhū Yì (朱异) sent a letter to Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
laying out the advantages and disadvantages.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) replied with a letter,
and also informed the common people and officials in the city,
saying:
"Since recent years, Liáng (梁)
has been dominated by favored officials
who exploit the common people
to satisfy their desires.
If you say this is not so,
you all may observe: today's state ponds and parks,
the mansions of kings and nobles,
the temples and pagodas of monks and nuns;
as well as the officials in office,
with hundreds of concubines,
and thousands of servants,
who neither farm nor weave,
but wear brocade and eat fine food;
if they do not plunder the common people,
from where do they obtain these things!
When Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) letter reached this point,
how could Yì (异) and the others respond!
I aim to punish the powerful and wicked,
not to overthrow the state.
Now the city relies on reinforcements from all directions.
I observe the kings, marquises, and generals,
whose ambition is to preserve themselves.
Who among them can exert their full effort to fight to the death
and contend with me for victory!
The Yangtze River is a natural barrier,
lamented by the two Cáos (曹) —
the matter is recorded in the chronicle of Wèi Wéndì (魏文帝).
The 'Guófēng' (國風) of the Shījīng (詩經) says: 'Who says the river is wide?
A single reed can ferry across it.'
Note: Háng (杭)
means 'to cross.'
Annotation says: 'Who says the river is wide?
One can cross it by adding a single reed.'
Meaning it is narrow.
If it were not for the perfect harmony of heaven and man,
how could it be like this!
I urge each of you to think thrice
and seek supreme good fortune!"
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) also submitted a memorial to the ruler of Eastern Wèi (東魏),
stating:
"Your servant advanced to capture Shòuchūn (壽春),
and intended to rest there temporarily.
However, Xiāo Yǎn (蕭衍) recognized the end of his dynasty
and voluntarily renounced his throne.
Before your servant's army entered his country,
he had already abandoned his body at Tóngtài (同泰) Monastery.
On the twenty-ninth day of last month—
'last month'
refers to the previous month—
the rivers and seas have not yet recovered,
and the weapons of war have temporarily ceased.
I forever recall my homeland,
and both men and horses yearn for it.
I will soon prepare my carriage
to serve your holy countenance.
Your servant's mother and younger siblings,
were long thought to have been slaughtered.
Recently, I received a clear imperial decree,
and only then learned they are still alive.
Chéng (承)
is similar to 'fèng' (奉).
It means, upon receiving the recent decree,
I first learned that my mother and younger siblings were still alive.
The Grand General's (大將軍) grace and concern
for your servant's weakness and inferiority—
how can I ever repay it!
Now I am immediately sending this memorial to welcome my mother, younger siblings, wife, and children.
I humbly wish for your holy compassion
to specially grant their release!"
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) wished to use humble words to bring his family over.
How could Gāo Chéng (高澄) and his brothers fall into his trap!
On the day Jǐsì (己巳),
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì (湘東王繹) dispatched Sīmǎ (司馬) Wú Yè (吳曄) and Tiānmén Tàishǒu (天門太守) Fán Wénjiǎo (樊文皎) and others, leading troops from Jiānglíng (江陵).
Chén Xīn (陳昕) was captured by Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) drank heavily with him,
and wanted Chén Xīn (陳昕) to gather his troops
to use them.
Chén Xīn (陳昕) refused.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) ordered his Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) Fàn Táobàng (范桃棒) to imprison him.
Chén Xīn (陳昕) then persuaded Fàn Táobàng (范桃棒)
to lead his subordinates to ambush and kill Wáng Wěi (王偉) and Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙),
and then surrender to the city.
Fàn Táobàng (范桃棒) agreed
and secretly sent Chén Xīn (陳昕) to climb down the ropes into the city at night.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued an imperial decree engraved on a silver tablet to Fàn Táobàng (范桃棒), saying:
"On the day the matter is settled,
I will enfeoff you as Hénán Wáng (河南王).
You will immediately take Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) followers,
and be given gold, silk, and female musicians."
The Crown Prince, fearing it was a trick,
hesitated and could not decide.
The Emperor angrily said:
"Accepting surrender is normal,
why are you suddenly suspicious!"
The Crown Prince convened a meeting of the grandees.
Zhū Yì (朱异) and Fù Qí (傅岐) said:
"Fàn Táobàng's (范桃棒) surrender is surely not false.
Once Fàn Táobàng (范桃棒) surrenders,
the rebel Hóu Jǐng (侯景) will surely be alarmed.
If we strike him at this moment,
we can achieve a great victory."
The Crown Prince said:
"I will firmly defend the city and wait for external reinforcements.
Once the reinforcements arrive,
will the rebels be difficult to pacify!
This is a foolproof plan.
Now, opening the gate to receive Fàn Táobàng (范桃棒),
how easily can Fàn Táobàng's (范桃棒) true intentions be known!
If, by any chance, he betrays us,
regret will be too late;
the affairs of the state are grave,
we must deliberate further."
Zhū Yì (朱异) said:
"Your Royal Highness, if you consider the urgency of the state,
you should accept Fàn Táobàng (桃棒);
if you still hesitate,
it is beyond my comprehension."
The Crown Prince ultimately could not decide.
Fàn Táobàng (桃棒) again had Chén Xīn (陳昕) report:
"I will only bring my five hundred men.
When we reach the city gate,
we will all take off our armor ourselves.
I beg the imperial court to open the gate and grant us entry.
After the matter is accomplished,
I guarantee the capture of Hóu Jǐng (侯景)."
The 'Kǎoyì' (考異) says: 'Tàiqīng Jì' (太清紀) and 'Nán Shǐ' (南史) both state:
"Fàn Táobàng (桃棒) requested to surrender with two thousand armored soldiers,
and offered Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) head as bounty."
Now, we follow 'Diǎnlüè' (典略).
The doubt intensified.
Zhū Yì (朱异) beat his chest and said:
"If we lose this opportunity,
the affairs of the state are lost!"
Crown Prince Xiāo Gāng (蕭綱) was indeed prone to much doubt and little decisiveness.
That Zhū Yì (朱异) beat his chest at this moment,
how late it was!
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) pulled him out and killed him.
Chén Xīn (陳昕), unaware,
came out as planned.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) intercepted him and captured him,
then forced him to shoot a letter into the city saying:
"Fàn Táobàng (桃棒) will first lightly lead a few tens of men inside."
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) intended to follow in armor,
but Chén Xīn (陳昕) refused,
determined to die.
So Hóu Jǐng (侯景) killed him.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) sent Xiāo Jiànlǐ (蕭見理) and Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) Lú Huīlüè (盧暉略) to garrison Dōngfǔ (東府).
Xiāo Jiànlǐ (蕭見理) was cruel and treacherous.
At night,
he and some bandits plundered at Dàhéng (大桁).
He was struck by a stray arrow and died.
Shàolíng Wáng Lún (邵陵王綸) journeyed to Zhōnglí (鍾離).
He heard that Hóu Jǐng (侯景) had already crossed Cǎishí (采石).
Lún (綸) traveled day and night, covering long distances,
returning his army to provide assistance.
As he crossed the Jiāng (江),
a wind rose in the middle of the river.
One or two tenths of his men and horses drowned.
During Lú Xún's (盧循) rebellion,
Liú Yù (劉裕) braved the wind to cross the Jiāng (江), and the wind then ceased.
During Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) rebellion,
Lún (綸) crossed the Jiāng (江), and the wind rose.
Could it be that Heaven desired to destroy Liáng (梁)?
Therefore, those who are good at observing the affairs of a nation
must observe when Heaven and man provide aid and assistance.
Shěn Yuē's (沈約) account states: Xīfēng Xiàn (西豐縣) belonged to Línchuān Jùn (臨川郡),
established by Wú (吳).
Yǒng'ān Hóu Què (永安侯確) and Ānnán Hóu Jùn (安南侯駿)
were all named after ancient counties for their marquisates.
Wú (吳) divided Wūchéng (烏程) and Yúháng (餘杭) to establish Yǒng'ān Xiàn (永安縣).
Jìn (晉) had already renamed it Wǔkāng (武康).
Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝) divided Jiāng'ān (江安) to establish Ānnán Xiàn (安南縣).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) does not mention it.
Wǔlíng Jùn (武陵郡):
Liáng (梁) established Wǔzhōu (武州).
Dàchéng (大成)
was Dàchūn's (大春) younger brother;
Què (確)
was Lún's (綸) son;
Jùn (駿)
was Yì's (懿) grandson.
Jǐng (景) sent troops to Jiāngchéng (江乘) to resist Lún's (綸) army.
Zhào Bóchāo (趙伯超) said:
"If we take the main road from Huángchéng (黃城),
we will certainly encounter the rebels.
It would be better to head directly to Zhōngshān (鍾山).
Zhōngshān (鍾山)
is Jiǎngshān (蔣山).
Sūn Quán (孫權) of Wú (吳) established the temple of Jiǎng Zǐwén (蔣子文) on this mountain.
Also, because of his ancestor's taboo name, Zhōng (鍾),
it was renamed Jiǎngshān (蔣山).
This would catch the rebels off guard,
and the siege of the city would surely be lifted."
Lún (綸) followed this advice.
Traveling at night, they lost their way
and detoured over twenty *lǐ* (里).
On the morning of Gēngchén (庚辰),
they encamped at Jiǎngshān (蔣山).
Jǐng (景), seeing this, was greatly alarmed.
He sent all the plundered women and treasures to Shítou (石頭),
prepared boats, and intended to flee.
He divided his troops into three routes to attack Lún (綸).
Lún (綸) fought them
and defeated them.
At that time, there was cold snow on the mountain peaks,
so he led his army down to Àijìng Sì (愛敬寺).
The Emperor served Wén Huángdì (文皇帝) and Xiàn Huánghòu (獻皇后) with filial piety at Zhōngshān (鍾山),
establishing Dà'àijìng Sì (大愛敬寺) to accrue blessings.
On Yǐyǒu (乙酉),
Lún (綸) advanced his army to the side of Xuánwǔ Hú (玄武湖).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Tàiqīng Jì (太清紀) records:
"the twenty-ninth day."
The Diǎnlüè (典略) records:
"Rénwǔ (壬午)."
We now follow the Liáng Dìjì (梁帝紀).
There was no battle.
By evening,
Jǐng (景) again proposed a battle for the next day.
Lún (綸) agreed.
Ānnán Hóu Jùn (安南侯駿), seeing Jǐng's (景) army retreat,
thought they were fleeing.
He immediately pursued them with brave warriors.
Jǐng (景) turned his army back to attack them.
Jùn (駿) was defeated and fled,
rushing towards Lún's (綸) army.
Zhào Bóchāo (趙伯超), seeing this,
also led his troops to flee.
Jǐng (景) took advantage of the victory to pursue and attack them.
All the armies collapsed.
Lún (綸) gathered nearly a thousand remaining soldiers
and entered Tiānbǎo Sì (天保寺).
Jǐng (景) pursued them
and set fire to the temple.
Lún (綸) fled to Zhūfāng (朱方),
which was Dāntú (丹徒).
In the Spring and Autumn period, it was the land of Zhūfāng (朱方).
At that time, it was Lánlíng Wǔjìn Xiàn (蘭陵武進縣).
He often fell.
Jǐng (景) seized all of Lún's (綸) baggage,
captured Xīfēng Gōng Dàchūn (西豐公大春), Ānqián Sīmǎ Zhuāngqiū Huì (安前司馬莊丘慧), Commander Huò Jùn (霍俊), and others alive, and returned.
The Emperor established two hundred and forty general titles,
including Ānqián Jiāngjūn (安前將軍), who had a Chángshǐ (長史) and a Sīmǎ (司馬).
Shuài (帥)
is pronounced *suǒ lèi* (所類).
Huán (還)
is pronounced *cóng xuān* (從宣),
or as written (如字).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Diǎnlüè (典略) records
"Guǎnglíng Lìng Cuī Jùn (廣陵令崔俊)."
The Nán Shǐ (南史) records
"Zhíhé Jiāngjūn Hú Zǐyuē (直閤將軍胡子約),
Guǎnglíng Lìng Huò Jùn (廣陵令霍雋)."
We now follow the Tàiqīng Jì (太清紀).
On Bǐngxū (丙戌),
Jǐng (景) displayed the captured heads, prisoners, armor, and weapons of Lún's (綸) army, as well as Dàchūn (大春) and others, below the city.
He made them declare:
"Shàolíng Wáng (邵陵王) has already been killed by mutinous soldiers."
Huò Jùn (霍俊) alone said:
"The King suffered a minor setback,
but his entire army has returned to Jīngkǒu (京口).
Those in the city only need to hold firm,
and reinforcements will arrive soon."
The rebels struck his back with a knife,
but Jùn's (俊) words and expression became even more resolute.
Jǐng (景) admired his integrity and released him.
Línhè Wáng Zhèngdé (臨賀王正德) killed him.
On the evening of that day,
Póyáng Wáng Fàn (鄱陽王範) sent his heir, Sì (嗣), along with Xīyùzhōu Cìshǐ Péi Zhīgāo (西豫州刺史裴之高) and Jiàn'ān Tàishǒu Zhào Fèngjǔ (建安太守趙鳳舉),
Jìn Àndì (晉安帝) divided Lújiāng Jùn (廬江郡) to establish Jìnxī Jùn (晉熙郡) and Huáiníng Xiàn (懷寧縣).
Liáng (梁) established Xīyùzhōu (西豫州).
Suí (隋) made it Tóng'ān Jùn (同安郡).
Táng (唐) made it Shūzhōu (舒州).
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) says: Miǎnyáng Jùn (沔陽郡), Jìnglíng Xiàn (竟陵縣).
Formerly there was Jīngshān Xiàn (京山縣).
Qí (齊) established Jiàn'ān Jùn (建安郡).
But its territory was in Hànyáng (漢陽),
and it was not contiguous with Shūzhōu (舒州).
There was a Jiàn'ān Shù (建安戍) between Shòuyáng (壽陽) and Yìyáng (義陽).
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Zhì (蕭子顯齊志) and the Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) both do not mention a commandery being established here.
The Wǔdài Zhì (五代志) also says: Huángzhōu (黃州), Máchéng Xiàn (麻城縣).
Liáng (梁) established Jiànníng Jùn (建寧郡).
Perhaps the historian mistook Jiànníng (建寧) for Jiàn'ān (建安)?
Further investigation is needed.
They encamped their army at Càizhōu (蔡洲),
to await the armies from upstream.
Fàn (範) appointed Zhīgāo (之高) as superintendent of the right-bank reinforcement armies.
Jǐng (景) drove all the residents from the south bank to the north side of the water.
This refers to the Qínhuái Shuǐ (秦淮水).
West of the main street,
everything was completely cleared.
Běixùzhōu Cìshǐ Fēngshān Hóu Zhèngbiǎo (北徐州刺史封山侯正表) was stationed at Zhōnglí (鍾離).
The Suí Zhì (隋志) mentions Fēngshān Xiàn (封山縣),
belonging to Hépǔ Jùn (合浦郡),
which was probably established by Liáng (梁).
Zhèngbiǎo (正表) made an excuse that ships and provisions were not yet gathered,
and did not advance.
Jǐng (景) appointed Zhèngbiǎo (正表) as Nányànzhōu Cìshǐ (南兗州刺史)
and enfeoffed him as Nánjùn Wáng (南郡王).
Zhèngbiǎo (正表) then erected a stockade at Ōuyáng (歐陽) to cut off the reinforcement armies.
He led a host of ten thousand men,
ostensibly stating they were coming to aid,
but in reality intended to attack Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
He secretly sent a letter to entice Guǎnglíng Lìng Liú Xún (廣陵令劉詢),
instructing him to burn the city as a signal.
Xún (詢) informed Nányànzhōu Cìshǐ Nánkāng Wáng Huìlǐ (南康王會理).
In the twelfth month,
Huìlǐ (會理) ordered Xún (詢) to lead a thousand infantry and cavalry to night-raid Zhèngbiǎo (正表).
They utterly defeated him.
Zhèngbiǎo (正表) fled back to Zhōnglí (鍾離).
Xún (詢) collected his soldiers and provisions
and returned to join Huìlǐ (會理),
entering the city with him to provide aid.
On Guǐsì (癸巳),
Shìzhōng (侍中) and Dūguān Shàngshū Yáng Kǎn (都官尚書羊侃) died.
Fear in the city increased.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) constructed many siege engines,
arraying them before the palace gates.
The great wagons were several *zhàng* (丈) high,
with twenty wheels per wagon.
On Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
he again advanced to attack the city,
using "toad wagons" to transport earth to fill the moats.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì (湘東王繹) sent his heir, Fāngděng (方等), leading ten thousand infantry and cavalry to relieve Jiànkāng (建康).
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
they set out from Gōng'ān (公安).
Yì also dispatched the Administrator of Jìnglíng (竟陵), Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯), leading ten thousand naval troops,
who sailed out from Hànchuān (漢川),
transporting provisions eastward.
The Hàn River (漢水) flowed through Jìnglíng Commandery (竟陵郡) into the [Yangzi] River.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Tàiqīng Jì* (太清紀) states:
"Sēngbiàn led twenty thousand elite soldiers."
We now follow the *Liáng Shū* (梁書).
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
In every battle,
he personally exposed himself to arrows and stones,
taking it upon himself to die for his principles.
As a minister and a son,
one ought to dedicate oneself to the country.
However, preserving one's own life
is how one preserves the country.
When two armies face each other,
with victory or defeat yet undecided,
and the crisis is acute,
personally risking arrows and stones to encourage the officers and soldiers
may be done once,
but how can it be made a regular practice!
Fāngděng took it upon himself to die for his principles,
and made personally risking arrows and stones a regular practice.
This is why he was defeated and died in Xiāngchuān (湘川).
As for someone like Fāngděng,
he may be called a general destined to die;
but when discussing the greater principles of a minister and son,
preserving one's body to preserve the country
can be called loyalty and filial piety.
On the *rényín* day,
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) used fire carts to burn the southeast tower of Táichéng (臺城).
The artisan-official Wú Jǐng (吳景),
who possessed ingenious ideas,
constructed a tower from earth inside the city.
As soon as the fire was extinguished,
the new tower was immediately erected,
which the rebels considered divine.
Jǐng, taking advantage of the fire,
secretly sent men to tunnel under the city wall.
The city wall was about to collapse
before it was discovered.
A careful examination of the context
shows that "Jǐng, taking advantage of the fire"
should be
"the rebels, taking advantage of the fire,"
as it makes the situation and meaning clearer and smoother.
This is likely a confusion between Hóu Jǐng and Wú Jǐng,
making it difficult for readers to distinguish.
[They] formed a crescent shape to confront them,
and also threw fire,
burning their siege equipment,
whereupon the rebels retreated.
The Crown Prince sent the Assistant to the Heir Apparent, Yuán Mènggōng (元孟恭), leading a thousand men to sally forth from the Dàsīmǎ Gate (大司馬門) to fight,
but Mènggōng and his retainers defected to Jǐng.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
Jǐng's earth mounds gradually approached the city towers.
Liǔ Jīn (柳津) ordered the construction of tunnels to remove their earth.
The outer mound collapsed,
crushing almost all the rebels.
Additionally, flying bridges were built inside the city,
suspended over the two earth mounds.
When Jǐng's troops saw the flying bridges rise high,
they scattered and fled in a panic.
The city defenders threw *zhìwěijù* (雉尾炬) (pheasant-tail torches),
burning their eastern mound,
destroying all the towers and palisades.
The rebels lay dead in piles beneath the city wall.
Were those who died beneath the city wall truly rebels?
Hóu Jǐng drove the common people to attack the city,
with his own party pressing them from behind.
Those attacking the city,
if they retreated, died by the rebels' hands;
if they advanced, they died from arrows and stones.
Alas!
Were not those piled dead beneath the city wall
the innocent people of Liáng (梁)?
[They] burned their own siege equipment.
The General of Artisan-Officials, Sòng Nì (宋嶷), surrendered to Jǐng,
and taught him to divert water from Xuánwǔ Hú (玄武湖) to flood Táichéng (臺城).
All areas in front of the palace gates became a vast flood.
The Emperor summoned the Inspector of Héngzhōu (衡州), Wéi Càn (韋粲), to be a Mounted Regular Attendant.
In the second year of Tàipíng (太平) of Sūn Liàng (孫亮) of Wú (吳),
Xiāngdōng Commandery (湘東郡) was established by dividing the eastern part of Chángshā Dūwèi (長沙都尉),
which is today's Héngzhōu.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志),
the Liáng dynasty established Héngzhōu in Hánkúang County (含洭縣) of Nánhǎi Commandery (南海郡);
the Héngzhōu of Xiāngdōng [Commandery]
was first established after the Suí (隋) conquered the Chén (陳).
Càn was the son of Fàng (放).
Wéi Fàng (韋放) is mentioned in Volume 151, Dàtōng (大通) first year.
*Jiān* (監) is pronounced *gōng xián*.
Arriving at Lúlíng (廬陵),
upon hearing of Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Càn reviewed his subordinates,
obtaining five thousand elite soldiers,
and rushed to reinforce by covering double the usual distance.
Arriving at Yùzhāng (豫章),
he heard that Jǐng had already crossed Héngjiāng (橫江).
Càn consulted with the Internal Chief, Liú Xiàoyí (劉孝儀).
Xiàoyí said:
"If this were truly the case,
there would certainly be an imperial edict.
How can we lightly believe rumors
and cause unnecessary alarm!
Perhaps it is not so."
At that time, Xiàoyí was hosting a banquet.
Càn, enraged,
threw his cup to the ground and said:
"The rebels have already crossed the river,
and are threatening the palace.
Both water and land routes are cut off.
How could there be time for a report!
Even if there were no edict,
how can we remain complacent!
How could Wéi Càn (韋粲) feel like drinking wine today!"
He immediately mounted his horse and rode out to organize his troops.
As he was about to depart,
the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州), Dāngyáng Gōng Dàxīn (當陽公大心), sent an envoy to invite Càn.
Càn then rode to meet Dàxīn and said:
"Among the upstream frontier commands,
Jiāngzhōu is the closest to the capital.
According to Shěn Yuē's (沈約) *Zhì* (志), Jiāngzhōu is one thousand four hundred *lǐ* by water from the capital.
However, the middle reaches bear heavy responsibility
and require constant vigilance;
the garrison must not be absent.
For now, it is advisable to create a show of force
and move the garrison to Pénchéng (湓城),
dispatching a general (Pianjiang Cìsuí)
which would suffice for the situation."
Dàxīn agreed
and sent his Central Army Commander, Liǔ Xīn (柳昕), to lead two thousand soldiers with Càn.
When Càn arrived at Nánzhōu (南洲),
his cousin, the Inspector of Sīzhōu (司州), Liǔ Zhònglǐ (柳仲禮), also arrived at Héngjiāng (橫江) with over ten thousand infantry and cavalry.
Càn immediately sent provisions and weapons to supply them,
and also distributed his personal gold and silk to reward the warriors.
The Inspector of Xīyùzhōu (西豫州), Péi Zhīgāo (裴之高), sent boats from Zhānggōngzhōu (張公洲) to ferry Zhònglǐ.
According to Càn's biography,
Zhānggōngzhōu is probably Cáizhōu (蔡洲).
On the *bǐngchén* day,
Càn, Zhònglǐ, and the General of Manifest Bravery, Lǐ Xiàoqīn (李孝欽),
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Liáng Dìjì* (梁帝紀) has "Lǐ Qiānshì" (李遷仕).
We now follow the *Tàiqīng Jì*.
The *Wǔdài Zhì*: Xuānzhōu (宣州), Nánlíng County (南陵縣),
the Liáng dynasty established Nánlíng Commandery (南陵郡).
Càn proposed that Zhònglǐ be made Grand Commander,
and notified the various armies downstream.
The various armies downstream were the troops at Zhānggōngzhōu.
[Zhīgāo] was ashamed to be subordinate to him,
and the discussion remained unresolved for several days.
Càn spoke out among the assembled officers, saying:
"Today, we come together to face the national crisis;
our duty is to eliminate the rebels.
The reason for promoting General Liǔ of Sīzhōu
is precisely because he has long defended the frontiers
and was previously feared by Hóu Jǐng;
moreover, his soldiers and horses are elite and none surpass them.
If we speak of rank,
Liǔ is beneath Càn.
If we speak of age,
he is also younger than Càn.
It is purely for the sake of the country's plans
that we should no longer discuss such matters.
The situation today
values harmony among generals.
If people's minds are not united,
the great enterprise will be lost.
Péi Gōng (裴公) is an old and respected official of the court;
how can he still harbor private feelings to obstruct the grand plan!
Càn asks to resolve this for all the armies."
Thereupon, he went alone in a single boat to Zhīgāo's camp,
and severely rebuked him, saying:
"Now the two palaces are in dire peril,
and the cunning bandit runs rampant.
Ministers and sons should work together with one heart.
How can we contradict each other like spears and shields!
Hán Fēizǐ (韓非子): There was a seller of spears and shields who said:
'My spear is so sharp that nothing cannot be pierced by it.'
He also said:
'My shield is so strong that nothing can pierce it.'
Someone asked him:
'If you use your spear to pierce your shield,
can it be done?'
The seller could not answer.
Later generations' discussions of spears and shields originate from this.
The arrows and blades will then have a target."
Meaning he would attack Zhīgāo.
Consequently, Zhònglǐ was promoted to Grand Commander.
Yáng Báihuá (楊白華), the Administrator of Xuānchéng (宣城), dispatched his son, Yáng Xióng (楊雄), to lead the prefectural troops, arriving subsequently.
The relief forces gathered in great numbers,
exceeding one hundred thousand men.
They erected palisades along the Huái (淮) River.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) also erected palisades on the north bank in response.
Péi Zhīgāo (裴之高) and his younger brother, Péi Zhīhéng (裴之橫), with a naval force of ten thousand, were stationed at Zhānggōng Zhōu (張公洲).
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) imprisoned Zhīgāo's (之高) younger brother, nephew, son, and grandson.
He arrayed his troops by the water,
forming a continuous chain in front of the formation,
with tripods, cauldrons, knives, and saws following behind them.
He said,
"If Lord Péi (裴公) does not surrender,
we will cook them immediately."
Zhīgāo (之高) called for a skilled archer and ordered him to shoot his son.
He fired twice,
but both shots missed.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) led ten thousand infantry and cavalry to challenge them at Hòuzhǔ (後渚).
According to the biography of Wéi Càn (韋粲),
Hòuzhǔ (後渚) was in front of Zhōngxīng Sì (中興寺).
The character 挑 (tiǎo)
is pronounced tú liǎo.
Wéi Càn (韋粲) said,
"It is late in the day and we are weary;
we should not fight yet."
Liǔ Zhònglǐ (柳仲禮) then held his fortifications and did not sally forth.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) also withdrew.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì (湘東王繹) led thirty thousand elite troops, departing from Jiānglíng (江陵).
He left his son, Suíníng Hóu Fāngzhū (綏寧侯方諸), to guard the city.
The Advisory Counselor, Liú Zhīhū (劉之迡), and others submitted three memorials requesting him to stay,
but his directive replied that it was not permitted.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì (湘東王繹) did not genuinely intend to personally lead troops to the rescue;
he merely feigned disallowance.
The character 迡 (hū)
is the same as 遲 (chí),
and also pronounced nǔ jì.
Póyáng Wáng Fàn (鄱陽王範) dispatched his general, Méi Bólóng (梅伯龍), to attack Wáng Xiǎnguì (王顯貴) at Shòuyáng (壽陽).
They captured its outer wall.
They attacked the inner city
but failed to capture it and withdrew.
Fàn (範) increased his forces
and sent them to attack again.
22The Grand General of Eastern Wèi (東魏), Gāo Chéng (高澄), was concerned about the prevalence of debased and poor-quality coins among the populace.
He proposed not prohibiting private minting by the people;
however, a scale would be hung at the market gates,
and coins weighing less than five zhū (五銖)
would not be permitted in the market.
The court deliberated, considering that the year's harvest was poor,
and requested to wait until another year,
whereupon the matter was dropped.
23The Grand Tutor of Wèi (魏), Yǔwén Tài (宇文泰), killed Wáng Mào (王茂), a minister of Āndìng Guó (安定國), though he was not guilty of a crime.
Tài (泰) was enfeoffed as the Duke of Āndìng (安定公), hence he had ministers of the state.
Tài (泰) angrily said,
"You, too, are allied with the criminal,
and shall also be punished!"
He had Qìng (慶) seized before him.
Qìng's (慶) words and demeanor showed no fear.
He said,
"Qìng (慶) has heard that a lord who is clouded by affairs is not clear-sighted,
and a minister who knows this but does not contend is disloyal.
Since Qìng (慶) has exhausted his loyalty,
he dares not spare his life,
but merely fears that the Duke will be unclear-sighted."
Tài (泰) awoke to his error
and immediately ordered Mào (茂) to be pardoned,
but it was too late.
He then bestowed money and silk upon Mào's (茂) family,
saying,
"To acknowledge my mistake."
24On the last day of the month, bǐng chén (丙辰),
Liǔ Zhònglǐ (柳仲禮) entered Wéi Càn's (韋粲) camp at night
and deployed his various armies.
The next morning,
they met in battle.
The generals each held their positions,
and Càn (粲) was ordered to hold Qīngtáng (青塘).
Càn (粲) considered Qīngtáng (青塘) to be a vital route to Shítou (石頭).
Càn's (粲) biography states that Qīngtáng (青塘) was close to Huáizhǔ (淮渚).
According to Chén Bàxiān's (陳霸先) words,
Qīngtáng (青塘) was Qīngxī Táng (青溪塘).
He was somewhat apprehensive about it.
Zhònglǐ (仲禮) said,
"Qīngtáng (青塘) is a vital location;
it cannot be entrusted to anyone but you, elder brother.
If you suspect your troops are too few,
I will dispatch more forces to assist you."
He then sent the Palace Aide-General Liú Shúyìn (劉叔胤) to assist him.
This laid the groundwork for Wéi Càn's (韋粲) defeat and death.
The character 少 (shǎo)
is pronounced shī zhǎo.

Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì (高祖武皇帝) Eighteenth
Tàiqīng (太清) Third Year (jǐ sì, 549 CE)
1 Spring,
First month,
On the dìng sì (丁巳) day, the first of the month,
Liǔ Zhònglǐ (柳仲禮) moved his camp from Xīntíng (新亭) to Dàhéng (大桁).
There was a heavy fog.
Wéi Càn's (韋粲) army lost its way.
By the time they reached Qīngtáng (青塘),
more than half the night had passed.
Their palisades were not yet connected.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) saw them
and immediately led elite troops to attack Càn (粲).
Càn (粲) sent his army commander Zhèng Yì (鄭逸) to counter-attack
and ordered Liú Shúyìn (劉叔胤) to intercept their rear with a naval force,
cutting off their path across the Huái (淮) River.
Yì (逸) was subsequently defeated.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景), taking advantage of his victory, entered Càn's (粲) camp.
His attendants tried to pull Càn (粲) away to avoid the enemy,
but Càn (粲) did not move.
He shouted at his sons and nephews to fight with all their might.
Consequently, he and his son Ní (尼), and three younger brothers Zhù (助), Jǐng (警), and Gòu (構), as well as his cousin Āng (昂), all died in battle.
Several hundred relatives also died.
The histories record Wéi Càn's (韋粲) loyalty and bravery.
He threw down his chopsticks and donned his armor,
then, with a hundred horsemen from his command, galloped to save them.
He fought Hóu Jǐng (侯景) at Qīngtáng (青塘)
and severely defeated him,
beheading several hundred enemies.
More than a thousand men drowned in the Huái (淮) River.
Zhònglǐ's (仲禮) spear was about to reach Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
when the enemy general Zhī Bórén (支伯仁) hacked Zhònglǐ (仲禮) in the shoulder from behind.
His horse became mired in mud.
"Zhī Bórén" (支伯仁)
should be
"Zhī Huàrén" (支化仁).
The character 將 (jiàng)
is pronounced jí liàng;
the same below.
The character 中 (zhòng)
is pronounced zhú zhòng.
The character 淖 (nào)
is pronounced nú jiào,
meaning mud.
The cavalry commander Guō Shānshí (郭山石) rescued him,
and he escaped.
Zhònglǐ (仲禮) suffered a severe wound.
Huì Niàn (惠臶) from Kuàijī (會稽) sucked the wound to stop the bleeding,
thus saving his life.
From then on, Hóu Jǐng (侯景) dared not cross to the south bank again,
and Zhònglǐ (仲禮) also lost his spirit
and no longer spoke of fighting.
Shàolíng Wáng Lún (邵陵王綸) reassembled his scattered troops.
Shàolíng Wáng Lún's (邵陵王綸) defeat and retreat are mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
On the gēng shēn (庚申) day,
he arrayed his camp south of Háng (桁)
and also nominated Liǔ Zhònglǐ (柳仲禮) as Grand Commander.

Yáo Xīng's Buddhist affairs are found in the Jìn Āndì Jì.
笮 (Zé),
read zài gè.
"The palace structures in Jiànkāng are extravagant and luxurious.

Government is achieved through bribes,
eunuchs are powerful and prosperous,
and monks are rich.
The Crown Prince delights in pearls and jade,

his utterances are merely frivolous,
and his poems do not go beyond 'Sāngzhōng'."
'Sāngzhōng'
is found in the 'Wèiguó Fēng' of the Shījīng,
an indecent poem.
"Xiāngdōng is base and greedy.

Nánkāng Wáng Huìlǐ,
the Emperor's son, Xù's son,

Dìngxiāng Hóu Zhī,
Nánpíng Wáng Wěi's son,

沐猴而冠 (mùhóuérguàn) [monkeys in caps],

"Though they hold positions as feudal protectors,

Zuǒzhuàn: Yù Quán strongly remonstrated with Chǔ Zǐ,
Chǔ Zǐ did not follow,
so he confronted him with weapons,

卒 (Zú),
read zǐ xù.
"What further crime could there be?

referring to words from the Yì Dàzhuàn,
the accusations are very strong!
"So that your servant has no worries of a second campaign,

The Emperor read the memorial,
feeling both shame and anger.
The words were all factual, and there was nothing he could do about it,
only shame and anger.
On the first day of Bǐngchén,
an altar was erected in front of the Tàijí Diàn,
and heaven and earth were informed

and had raised beacons and drums in uproar.
Initially,
on the day the city gates were closed,
there were over 100,000 men and women,
and more than 20,000 armored soldiers.
Kǎoyì says: Nánshǐ states
Now following Diǎnluè.
Many people had swollen bodies and shortness of breath.
氣急 (Qìjí)
means shortness of breath and gasping.
被 (Pī),
read pí yì.
Fewer than 4,000 people were manning the walls,
most of whom were emaciated and breathless.
Corpses lay across the roads,
impossible to bury,
and rotting fluids filled the ditches.
Yet the public still hoped for outside aid.
Liǔ Zhònglǐ only gathered courtesans and concubines, and held feasts.
His generals daily requested battle,
but Zhònglǐ refused.
Ānnán Hóu Jùn said to Shàolíng Wáng Lún:
"The city is in such peril,
yet the governor does not rescue it.
If, by any chance, something unforeseen happens,
how will Your Highness face the world?
Now we should divide the army into three routes,
and attack the rebels unexpectedly;
we can then achieve our goal."
Lún did not agree.
Liǔ Jīn ascended the wall and said to Zhònglǐ:
"Your sovereign and father are in distress,
yet you cannot exert your full strength.
A hundred generations from now,
what will they call you?"
Zhònglǐ paid him no mind.
The Emperor asked Jīn for advice,
who replied:
"Your Majesty has Shàolíng,
and your servant has Zhònglǐ;
if they are disloyal and unfilial,
how can the rebels be suppressed?"
Kǎoyì states: Diǎnluè says:
"Liǔ Zhònglǐ's paternal cousin Huī said to Zhònglǐ: 'The situation of the world is like this,
why not seize wealth and honor for yourself?'
Zhònglǐ said: 'Will you now acquire it for me, elder brother?'
Huī said: 'We should simply strengthen our camp and not fight,
let the rebels conquer Táichéng,
imprison the Son of Heaven,
then slowly release our troops.
After they are defeated,
we can again hold the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords.'
Zhònglǐ accepted this."
However, when Jǐng had conquered the city,
the public sentiment all turned away,
and the relief forces dispersed on their own.
How could Zhònglǐ lead them to defeat Jǐng?
Zhònglǐ stayed behind his walls and did not come out,
because he was severely wounded and afraid;
he was not following Huī's plan.
Now following Tàiqīng Jì and Nánshǐ.
Tàiqīng Jì also says:
"Jǐng once ascended the Zhūquè Mén tower
and spoke with him.
He also presented him with gold.
From then on,
he stayed behind his walls and did not fight."
Diǎnluè says:
"Jǐng presented him with a gold ring."
This is also close to slander,
so it is not adopted here.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Xiāo Huìlǐ (南康王) and Yáng Yārén (羊鴉仁), Zhào Bózhāo (趙伯超), and others advanced their camp north of Dōngfǔ (東府) city,
planning to cross the army by night.
However, Yārén and the others had not arrived by dawn,
Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) forces detected them.
Before the camp could be established,
Jǐng sent Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙) to attack them.
Zhào Bózhāo fled at the mere sight of them.
The defeat at Hánshān (寒山),
the defeat by the side of Xuánwǔhú (玄武湖), and this present defeat,
were all caused by Zhào Bózhāo.
Five thousand men were killed in battle or drowned.
Jǐng piled their heads beneath the palace gate,
to display to the people within the city.
Jǐng then sent Yú Zǐyuè (于子悅) to seek peace.
The Emperor (上) sent Shěn Jùn (沈浚), the Censor-in-chief (御史中丞), to Jǐng's location.
Jǐng, in reality, had no intention of leaving.
He said to Jùn:
"The weather is currently hot,
and the army cannot move yet.
I beg to remain in the capital to prove my loyalty."
Jùn, filled with indignation, reprimanded him.
Jǐng did not reply,
but drew his sword and shouted at him,
indicating he would kill Jùn.
"To betray kindness and forget righteousness,
and to violate and abandon sworn oaths,
is indeed unforgivable by heaven and earth!
Shěn Jùn, at the age of fifty,
always feared not dying in his rightful place.
Why should I be intimidated by death!"
He then left directly without looking back.
Jǐng, impressed by his loyalty and uprightness,
spared him.
Thereupon, Jǐng released the water in front of Shíquē (石闕).
The water in front of Shíquē
was water Jǐng had diverted from Xuánwǔhú to flood the city.
It flowed day and night without ceasing.
The Heir Apparent of Shàolíng (邵陵世子), Xiāo Jiān (蕭堅), was stationed at Tàiyángmén (太陽門).
Tàiyángmén
was one of the six gates of Táichéng (臺城).
He did not care for his officers and soldiers.
His clerks, Dǒng Xūn (董勛) and Xióng Tánlǎng (熊曇朗), resented him.
According to verification in the Nán Shǐ (南史),
this Xióng Tánlǎng is not the Xióng Tánlǎng who later became a bandit in Yùzhāng (豫章).
Hóu Jǐng Zhuàn (侯景傳) in the Nán Shǐ (南史) writes
"Bái Tánlǎng" (白曇朗).
"Tán" (曇)
is pronounced "tú hán fān".
On the night of Dīngmǎo,
towards dawn,
Xūn and Tánlǎng at the northwest tower of the city led Jǐng's forces to ascend the wall.
Yǒng'ān Hóu (永安侯) Xiāo Què (蕭確) fought fiercely
but could not repel them.
He then pushed open the door and entered to inform the Emperor, saying:
"The city has fallen."
The Emperor lay calmly and did not move,
saying:
"Can we still fight?"
Què replied:
"No."
The Emperor sighed, saying:
"I obtained it,
and I lost it;
what regret is there!"
He then said to Què:
"You must leave quickly.
Tell your father: do not worry about the two palaces."
He then sent messengers to comfort the various armies outside.
Soon after, Jǐng sent Wáng Wěi (王偉) to the Wéndédéng (文德殿) to pay his respects.
The Emperor ordered the screens to be drawn and the doors opened to let Wěi in.
Wěi bowed and presented Jǐng's memorial,
stating:
"Having been misled by wicked sycophants,
I led my troops to the court,
disturbing your sacred person.
Now I await punishment at the palace gate."
The Emperor asked:
"Where is Jǐng?
He can be summoned."
Jǐng entered and met in the Tàijí Dōngtáng (太極東堂),
protected by five hundred armored soldiers.
Jǐng kowtowed at the foot of the殿 (diàn),
and the Master of Ceremonies (典儀) led him to the couch for the Three Dukes (三公).
The Master of Ceremonies (典儀)
was responsible for court rituals.
The position of Master of Ceremonies still existed until the Táng (唐) Dynasty,
managing the chanting of etiquette in the hall and arranging the order of robes and positions in the court.
"Jiàn" (見)
is pronounced "xián biàn fān".
"Jī" (稽)
is pronounced "qǐ".
The Emperor asked:
"You have been in the army for a long time.
Are you not weary!"
Jǐng dared not look up,
sweat streaming down his face.
The Emperor further asked:
"From what prefecture are you,
that you dare to come to this point?
Are your wife and children still in the north?"
Jǐng could not answer any of these questions.
Rèn Yuē (任約) replied on his behalf from the side, saying:
"Your servant Jǐng's wife and children were all slaughtered by the Gāo (高) clan.
Only I myself have returned to Your Majesty."
Up to this point,
when the Emperor questioned Jǐng, Jǐng was still timid and submissive.
"How many people were there when you first crossed the river?"
Jǐng replied:
"A thousand people."
"How many people besieged Táichéng?"
He replied:
"Ten thousand."
"How many are there now?"
He replied:
"Within all the lands under heaven,
none are not mine."
From this point onwards,
Jǐng's words and demeanor became rebellious.
The Emperor, at a loss for words and in a weakened position,
bowed his head and did not speak.
Alas!
Jǐng then went to Yǒngfú Shěng (永福省) to see the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince also showed no fear.
All the bodyguards dispersed in alarm,
except for Xú Chī (徐摛), the Zhōngshùzǐ (中庶子),
The Crown Prince's Zhōngshùzǐ
had a position similar to that of a Shìzhōng (侍中).
"Chī" (摛)
is pronounced "chǒu zhī fān".
and the Dōnggōng Tōngshì Shèrén (東宮通事舍人),
whose position was similar to that of a Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén (中書通事舍人).
He said: "A marquis or a prince should be seen with proper禮 (lǐ)!
How can this be!"
Jǐng then bowed.
Xúnzǐ (荀子) said: "Those who are good at failing do not perish."
The emperor and his son, though perished here,
did not lose their integrity.
How sad!
He also could not respond.
Jǐng withdrew,
and said to his Xiānggōng (廂公), Wáng Sēngguì (王僧貴):
Jǐng's close and prominent nobles were called Zuǒyòu Xiānggōng (左右廂公).
"I used to ride on horseback facing formations,
with arrows and blades falling all around,
yet my spirits were calm and unhurried,
completely without fear;
but now, seeing Xiāo Gōng (蕭公),
makes one involuntarily tremble.
Is it not because heavenly majesty is not to be offended!
I must not see him again."
Thereupon, he removed all the guards from the two palaces.
The two palaces
refer to the Emperor's palace and the Eastern Palace.
He arrested court officials and princes and sent them to Yǒngfú Shěng (永福省).
He ordered Wáng Wěi (王偉) to guard Wǔdé Diàn (武德殿)
and Yú Zǐyuè (于子悅) to be stationed at Tàijí Dōngtáng (太極東堂).
He issued a false imperial edict, granting a general amnesty,
and unilaterally promoted himself to Grand Chief Controller of all Military Affairs (大都督中外諸軍) and Director of the Department of State Affairs (錄尚書事).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: There was no amnesty recorded in the Liáng Dì Jì (梁帝紀).
Jǐng's promotion was on Gēngwǔ (庚午).
This account follows Tàiqīng Jì (太清紀).
The gentry and common people of Jiànkāng (建康) fled in all directions.
The Crown Prince's Chariot Attendant (太子洗馬), Xiāo Yǔn (蕭允),
arrived at Jīngkǒu (京口),

saying:
"Life and death are determined by fate;

Misfortune comes

On the *jǐsì* day,
Hóu Jǐng dispatched Shíchéng Gōng Dàkuǎn with an imperial edict to disband the external relief forces.

Shàolíng Wáng Lún said:

This means the various armies scattered back to where they came from.
According to Yáo Sīlián's *Liáng Shū*: Dàlián was enfeoffed as Línchéng Xiàn Gōng.

This mistakenly takes Dōngyáng Zhōu for Nányǎn Zhōu,

Zhònglǐ and his brother Jìnglǐ, Yáng Yārén, Wáng Sēngbiàn, and Zhào Bózhāo all opened their camps and surrendered.

Zhònglǐ and the others entered the city,

Zhònglǐ saw his father Jīn,
who wept bitterly and said:

why bother meeting!"

he heard that Táichéng had fallen,

Hóu Jǐng ordered the accumulated corpses within the palace to be burned.
Those critically ill but not yet dead

refers to those who still had a breath remaining.

an edict was issued stating that the military governors and prefects could resume their original posts.
Hóu Jǐng kept Liǔ Jìnglǐ and Yáng Yārén,

and Wáng Sēngbiàn back to Jìnglíng.
Wáng Sēngbiàn was able to return to Jìnglíng,
laying the groundwork for Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì to use him to pacify Hóu Jǐng.
Línhè Wáng Zhèngdé had an agreement with Hóu Jǐng that

When the city gates opened,

Hóu Jǐng instead appointed Zhèngdé as Shìzhōng and Dàsīmǎ,
and all officials were restored to their old posts.
Zhèngdé entered to see the Emperor,
bowing and weeping.
The Emperor said:
"'He gulps down his tears,
what avail is regret now!'"
This is a line from the *Shī* [Odes], "Zhōnggǔ Yǒu Tuī".
*Chuài*,
read *zhāng liè fān*.
*Chuài* means
to weep profusely and without stopping,
read like *chuò*.
Qín Jùn, Yángpíng, and Xūyí, all three commanderies surrendered to Hóu Jǐng.

When the Central Plains fell into chaos,
its people migrated south,
settling in Tángyì.
Tángyì was originally a county,
belonging to Línhuái Jùn in the Western Hàn,
and to Guǎnglíng Guó in the Eastern Hàn.
In the first year of Jìn Huìdì's Yǒngxīng era (304 CE),

Ān Dì changed Tángyì to Qín Jùn.

was formerly called Wèishì,

The *Wǔdài Zhì* says: Dōnghǎi Jùn's Huáirén Xiàn,

Xiàpī Jùn,

] Qīng Zhōu Cìshǐ Míng Shǎoxiá and Shānyáng Tàishǒu Xiāo Lín abandoned their cities and fled.

Jiāngdū Jùn's Shānyáng Xiàn,

Hóu Jǐng appointed Yítóng Sān Sī Xiāo Yōng as Nánxú Zhōu Cìshǐ,
replacing Xīchāng Hóu Yuānzǎo in garrisoning Jīngkǒu.
He also sent his general Xú Xiāng to attack Jìn líng,
and Lù Jīng surrendered the commandery to him.
In the beginning,
the Emperor had appointed Hédōng Wáng Yù as Xiāng Zhōu Cìshǐ,

Zhāng Zuǎn, relying on his talent and reputation,
slighted the young Yù,
and was remiss in his welcome.
When Yù arrived,
he investigated and took custody of the affairs of the prefecture.
"Fù dù" means
the former prefect hands over the various matters and items of the prefecture to the succeeding prefect.
*Yǒng*,
read *yú yòng fān*.
*Shào*,
read *shī zhào fān*.
Hearing of Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he somewhat oppressed Zhāng Zuǎn.
Zhāng Zuǎn, fearing harm,
fled by light boat at night,
intending to go to Yōng bù,
but again feared that Chá would resist him.
Zhāng Zuǎn had an old acquaintance with Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì,
and wanted to use him to kill Yù's brothers,
so he went to Jiānglíng.
When Táichéng fell,
the various princes returned to their respective prefectures and garrisons.
Yù returned from Húkǒu to Xiāng Zhōu.
Dòngtíng and Qīngcǎo together form one lake.
Húkǒu is in Bālíng.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì, as Jīng Zhōu Cìshǐ, was the Area Commander of Jīng, Yōng and other nine prefectures.
Zào, Yù, and Chá were all his subordinates.
He wanted to wait for Yì to arrive and pay his respects,
then returned to Xìn Zhōu.
Zhāng Zuǎn sent a letter to Yì saying:
"Hédōng [Wang Yù] is sailing upriver with masts,

*Qiáng* means
the mast of a boat,
used to hang the sail,
and when the sail catches wind, the boat moves.
From Dòngtíng to Jiānglíng,
one goes upriver against the current,

*Yí*,
read *yú jì fān*.
*Shàng*,
read *shí zhǎng fān*.
"They are plotting mischief together."
The Jiānglíng Yóujūzhǔ Zhū Róng
"Yóujūzhǔ" is
the general commanding a mobile army.
"[Guìyáng] has remained here,
wishing to respond to Yù and Chá."
Yì, alarmed,
scuttled his boats,
sank his rice,
cut his cables,
and rushed back to Jiānglíng on foot through the barbarian territories.
He imprisoned Zào
and killed him.
From this point, a rift grew between Yì, Yù, and Chá.
Hóu Jǐng previously appointed Dǒng Shàoxiān, the former Grand Protector of Línjiāng, as the Xíngtái for Jiāngběi.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Lìyáng Jùn's Wūjiāng Xiàn.
During the Liáng dynasty, Línjiāng Jùn was established.
Dǒng Shàoxiān surrendered to Hóu Jǐng.
See the previous volume, previous year.
He summoned Nán Kāng Wáng Huìlǐ, the Inspector of Nányǎn Zhōu.
On a Rénwǔ day,
Shàoxiān arrived at Guǎnglíng.
His troops numbered less than two hundred,
all of them emaciated and exhausted from days of hunger.
Huìlǐ's soldiers and horses were very numerous.
His subordinates advised Huìlǐ, saying:
"Hóu Jǐng has already captured the capital,
and intends to eliminate all the feudal lords first
before usurping the throne.
If the four directions resist him,
he will soon collapse.
Why abandon the entire territory of the prefecture to the enemy!
It is better to kill Shàoxiān,
raise troops and defend stoutly,
ally with the Wèi,
and await developments."
Huìlǐ was inherently timid,
and immediately handed the city over to him.
Once Shàoxiān entered,
none of the populace dared to move.
Huìlǐ's younger brother, Tōnglǐ, requested to return to Jiànkāng first.
He said to his sister:
"Since things have come to this,
how can our whole family perish!
In the future, I also wish to achieve something,
but I do not know what Heaven's will is."
Shàoxiān confiscated all the civil and military officials, retainers, armor, weapons, gold, and silks in Guǎnglíng.
He sent Huìlǐ back to Jiànkāng alone on horseback.
This laid the groundwork for the failed plot by Huìlǐ's brothers to assassinate Wáng Wěi, which led to their deaths.
The Marquis of Xiāngtán, Tuì, and the Inspector of Běiyǎn Zhōu, the Marquis of Dìngxiāng, Zhī, fled to the Eastern Wèi.
Hóu Jǐng appointed Xiāo Nòngzhāng as the Inspector of Běiyǎn Zhōu,
but the people of the prefecture raised troops to resist him.
Hóu Jǐng sent the Zhíhé Jiāngjūn, Yáng Hǎi, with troops to assist him.
Hǎi surrendered his forces to the Eastern Wèi,
and the Eastern Wèi consequently occupied HuáinYīn.
Zhī
was Wěi's son.
On a Guǐwèi day,
Hóu Jǐng sent Yú Zǐyuè and others with a few hundred weak soldiers to raid Wú Jùn in the east.
Dài Sēngdá, the commander of Xīnchéng garrison, had five thousand elite armored soldiers.
Shěn Yuē states: Southwest of Zhèjiāng,
named Xiàngxī.
Wú established it as Xīnchéng Xiàn,
belonging to Wú Jùn.
Today's Xīnchéng Xiàn in Hángzhōu is that place.
Dá,
pronounced "tā lì."
"The bandits are now lacking food.
What they obtained in the capital
will not last ten days.
If we close the passes and defend,
they can immediately be starved to death."
Local magnate Lù Yìnggōng feared they could not win and their assets would be plundered.
They all advised Jūzhèng to welcome them.
Jūzhèng was inherently timid.
He loaded rice, cattle, and wine, and went to the outskirts to welcome them.
Zǐyuè seized Jūzhèng
and plundered his wealth, children, and women.
The people of the east all erected forts to resist them.
Hóu Jǐng also appointed Rèn Yuē as Nándào Xíngtái,
stationed at Gūshú.
Summer,
fourth month.
Xiāngdōng Shìzǐ Fāngděng arrived at Jiānglíng.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì first learned that Táichéng had fallen.
He ordered trees to be planted for a palisade seven *lǐ* around Jiānglíng,
and three layers of moats to be dug for defense.
Gāo Yuè and others of the Eastern Wèi attacked Yǐngchuān,
but did not succeed.
The Grand General, Chéng, sent more troops to assist them.
The supply routes were continuous.
More than a year passed, yet it still had not fallen.
In the fourth month of the previous year,
Gāo Yuè and others attacked Yǐngchuān.
They dammed the Wěishǔi to flood it.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Shuòfāng Jùn's Chángzé Xiàn.
Later Wèi established Chǎnxī Jùn and Shānlù Xiàn.
The Shuǐjīng states: The Wěishǔi originates from Mǎlǐng Shān, southwest of Mì Xiàn in Hénán.
It flows southeast past the north of Chángshè Xiàn.
Yàn,
pronounced "yú shàn."
Gāo Yuè divided his troops for alternating shifts, advancing in turns.
This means dividing the soldiers into ten or more units;
when unit A rests, unit B advances;
when unit B rests, unit C advances;
when unit C rests, unit D advances;
by the time unit J rests,
unit A advances again.
Thus, the attackers get turns to rest, while the defenders cannot endure the toil.
Wáng Sīzhèng personally faced arrows and stones,
sharing the hardships with his soldiers.
Springs gushed forth in the city,
and they hung pots to cook.
The Grand Tutor, Tàishī Tái, sent the Grand General, Zhào Guì, to command troops from the southeastern prefectures to relieve it.
From Chángshè northward,
all became marshland.
When the troops reached Ráng,
Ráng
was Rángchéng.
The Eastern Wèi sent skilled archers on large ships to shoot at the city from above.
The city was about to fall.
Mùróng Shàozōng, Duke Jǐnghuì of Yàn Jùn, and Liú Fēngshēng went to inspect the dam.
Seeing dust rise from the northeast,
they both went into a ship to take shelter.
Shortly after, a sudden storm arrived,
making everything dim far and near.
The cable broke,
and the boat was blown directly towards the city.
People on the city wall pulled the boat with long hooks,
and arrows and crossbow bolts were fired chaotically.
Shàozōng jumped into the water and drowned.
Fēngshēng swam upwards
towards the earthen hill.
"Yóu" means to float in water and move.
Shàng,
pronounced "shí zhǎng."
On a Jiǎchén day,
the Eastern Wèi promoted Grand General Bóhǎi Wáng Chéng to the rank of Xiāngguó,
ennobled him as Qí Wáng,
and granted him special courtesies.
At that time, Chéng was allowed to perform rituals without announcing his name,
enter court without rushing,
and ascend the hall with sword and shoes.
On a Dīngwèi day,
Chéng entered court in Yè
and firmly declined;
it was not permitted.
Chéng summoned his generals and aides for a secret discussion.
They all advised Chéng to accept the imperial mandate.
Only Sànqí Chángshì Chén Yuánkāng believed it was not yet appropriate.
Chéng consequently resented him.
Cuī Xiān then recommended Lù Yuánguī as Dàxíngtái Láng to diminish Yuánkāng's power.
When Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì went to aid,
he ordered all the prefectures under his command to raise troops.
Yuèyáng Wáng Chá, the Inspector of Yōng Zhōu, sent his Fǔ Sīmǎ Liú Fāngguì with troops to exit Hànkǒu.
Yì summoned Chá to go himself,
but Chá did not comply.
Fāngguì secretly allied with Yì
and plotted to attack Xiāngyáng,
but had not yet acted.
Coincidentally, Chá summoned Fāngguì for another matter.
Fāngguì thought the plot was exposed,
so he occupied Fánchéng and defied the order.
Chá sent troops to attack him.
Yì generously supplied and dispatched Zhāng Zàn to proceed to his post.
When Zàn arrived at Dàdī,
Shěn Yuē Zhì states: Huàshān Jùn's seat was Dàdī.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Xiāngyáng Jùn's Hànnán Xiàn.
During the Sòng, Huàshān Jùn was established.
During the Táng, Hànnán was merged into Yíchéng Xiàn.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Yíchéng is ninety *lǐ* south of Xiāng Zhōu.
Zēng Gǒng said: Sòng Wǔ Dì built the great dike of Yíchéng as a city;
today's county seat is that place.
He beheaded Fāngguì.
When Zàn arrived at Xiāngyáng,
Chá delayed his departure,
only housing him at Báimǎ Sì west of the city.
Chá still managed the military and administrative affairs.
Upon hearing that Táichéng had fallen,
he refused to be relieved.
Dù Àn, who was assisting in defense, deceived Zàn, saying:
"Judging by Yuèyáng's stance, he cannot tolerate your excellency.
It is better to go to Xīshān for now to avoid disaster."
Xīshān refers to the mountains west of Wàn Shān, the various mountains of Zhōnglú Xiàn.
Dài,
pronounced "dài hài."
There were nine brothers,
all famous for their bravery and valor.
The Dù brothers were: Sōng, Cén, Nì, Jí, Yǎn, Àn, Zè, Zǒng, and Yòu'ān,
a total of nine people.
Xiāo,
pronounced "jiān yáo."
Zàn dressed in women's clothes
and rode in a sedan chair with blue cloth,
fleeing into Xīshān.
Chá sent Àn with troops to pursue and capture him.
Zàn begged to become a Buddhist monk,
changing his name to Fǎzàn.
Chá permitted it.
Zhāng Zàn's stirring up discord between the brothers Yù and Chá,
to Xiāngdōng,
was detrimental to his own person
and harmful to his country.
Gēng,
pronounced "gōng héng."
17 Wáng Chōng (王沖), the Chief Clerk of Jīngzhōu (荊州), and others presented a memorial to Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì (湘東王繹),
requesting that he, as Tàiwèi (太尉) and Grand Controller of All Military Affairs, act as the chief convenor of the alliance by imperial authorization;
a chief convenor of the alliance
being one who convenes the alliances of various vassal states.
On the day Bǐngchén (丙辰),
they again requested that he, as Sīkōng (司空), act as the chief convenor of the alliance;

18 Although the Emperor was outwardly controlled by Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
inwardly he was very displeased.
Jǐng (景) wanted to appoint Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙) as Sīkōng (司空);
the Emperor said:
"To harmonize Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽),
what use is this fellow!"
The Three Ducal Ministers regulate Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽),
implying that Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙) was not the right person for the job.
All the imperial halls within the Liáng (梁) palace had chief commanders.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: All instances of "Biàndiàn (便殿)"
refer to places that are not grand and proper.
He also said: Biàndiàn (便殿) are separate halls adjacent to the sleeping quarters.
"Shuài (帥)"
is pronounced suǒ lèi.
Jǐng (景) could not force it,
and was very much in awe of him.
When the Crown Prince entered
and tearfully remonstrated,
the Emperor said:
"Who told you to come!
If the altars of the state have spiritual power,
they should still be able to recover;
if not,
why shed tears!"
Jǐng (景) had his soldiers stationed inside the imperial palace,
some driving donkeys and horses,
carrying bows and swords,
entering and exiting the palace courtyards.
The Emperor, surprised, asked about it,
and Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (直閤將軍) Zhōu Shízhēn (周石zhēn) replied:
"These are the armored soldiers of Vicegerent Hóu (侯丞相)."
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and shouted at Shízhēn (石zhēn):
"It is Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
why call him Vicegerent!"
All those around were terrified.
Thereafter, many of the Emperor's requests were not fulfilled,
and his food and drink were also rationed;
he became ill from worry and indignation.
The Crown Prince entrusted his young son Dàhuán (大圜) to Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì (湘東王繹),
and also sent his nail clippings and hair to him.
In the fifth month,
on the day Bǐngchén (丙辰),
the Emperor lay in the Jìngjūdian (淨居殿),
his mouth bitter,
and could not get honey.
He repeatedly said
"Hè!
Hè!"
and then passed away.
He was eighty-six years old.
Jǐng (景) secretly withheld the news of his death,
and moved the coffin to the Zhāoyángdiàn (昭陽殿).
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) was then residing in Zhāoyángdiàn (昭陽殿).
He made it seem as if the Emperor entered court as usual.
Wáng Wěi (王偉) and Chén Qìng (陳慶) were both attendants of the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince choked back sobs and shed tears,
not daring to utter a sound.
Outside the hall, none of the civil and military officials knew of it.
19 Gāo Yuè (高岳) of the Eastern Wèi (東魏), having lost Mùróng Shàozōng (慕容紹宗) and others,
became disheartened and discouraged,
and dared not again press against Chángshèchéng (長社城).

"Since the King became regent,

Jǐng (景) moved from Zhāoyángdiàn (昭陽殿) to camp in the court hall.

"Cháo (朝)"

Jǐng (景) sometimes even promoted them further,

Towards the end of Gāozǔ's (高祖) reign,
the gentry and commoners of Jiànkāng (建康) competed in lavishness in their clothing, food, and utensils.
They had no more than half a year's supply of grain,
and constantly relied on tribute from all directions.
Máo Huǎng (毛晃) said: The Hàn (漢) had the "Sānfǔ Wěishūguān (三輔委輸官)"
which was in charge of tribute.
Generally, when an object is sent, it is called "shū (輸),"
pronounced in the flat tone;
when referring to the object sent, it is called "shū (輸),"
pronounced in the departing tone.
The "wěi (委)" in "wěishū (委輸)"
is also pronounced in the departing tone.
Roads were cut off,
and within a few months,
people resorted to cannibalism,
yet still could not escape starvation.
Only one or two out of a hundred survived.
The Jīnlíngjì (金陵記) states: During the Liáng (梁) capital,
there were 280,000 households.
From Xī Shítouchéng (西石頭城) in the west,
to Nítáng (倪塘) in the east,
from Shízǐgāng (石子岡) in the south,
to beyond Jiǎngshān (蔣山) in the north,
it was forty lǐ (里) from north to south.
From the chaos of Hóu Jǐng (侯景) until the Chén (陳) dynasty,
the population inside and outside the capital was less than half of what it was during the Sòng (宋) and Qí (齊) dynasties.
Corpses
filled ditches and ravines,
innumerable.
On the day Guǐwèi (癸未),
Jǐng (景) sent Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) Lái Liàng (來亮) into Wǎnlíng (宛陵).
Wǎnlíng (宛陵) County
belonged to Dānyáng (丹楊) Commandery during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
During the Jìn (晉) dynasty, it was divided to become the seat of Xuānchéng (宣城) Commandery.

formerly called Wǎnlíng (宛陵).
On the day Jiǎshēn (甲申),
Jǐng (景) sent his general Lǐ Xiánmíng (李賢明) to attack it,

Jǐng (景) also sent Zhōngjūn (中軍) Hóu Zǐjiàn (侯子鑒) into Wú Jùn (吳郡).
Zhōngjūn (中軍) refers to the Zhōngjūn Dūdū (中軍都督).
He sent Yítóng (儀同) Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙) and others with troops to encamp in Qiántáng (錢塘) in the east.

Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Shěn Jùn (沈浚) fled east to avoid disaster,

Shèng (嵊) was the son of Jì (稷).
The Governor of Dōngyángzhōu (東揚州), Línchéng Gōng Dàlián (臨城公大連),

The Wǔdàizhì (五代志) states: Kuàijī (會稽) Commandery,
during the Liáng (梁) dynasty, established Dōngyángzhōu (東揚州).
Only west of Wú Jùn (吳郡) and north of Nánlíng (南陵) were under Jǐng's (景) control.

"Those Dài (代) people who changed their surnames during Tàihé (太和) are all to revert to their old surnames."
The change of surnames

on the day Bǐngxū (丙戌),

25 Previously,
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) intended to have Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿) Liú Zhīlín (劉之遴) of Nányáng (南陽) present the imperial seals and ribbons to Línhé Wáng Zhèngdé (臨賀王正德).
Zhīlín (之遴) shaved his head, donned monastic robes, and fled.

when Zhīlín (之遴) reached Xiàkǒu (夏口),

On the *rénchén* day [of the 26th month],

Dàkuǎn as Jiānglíng Wáng;
Dàlín as Nánhǎi Wáng;
Dàlián as Nánjùn Wáng;
Dàchūn as Ānlíng Wáng;
Dàchéng as Shānyáng Wáng;

Chángshè city lacked salt,
people suffered from paralysis and swelling,
with eight or nine out of ten dying.
A strong wind rose from the northwest,
blowing water into the city,
and the city walls collapsed.
The Eastern Wèi Grand General Chéng issued an order to those in the city, saying:

if Grand General's body is injured,
all his close attendants shall be executed."
In the first year of Tàiqīng,
the Western Wèi conferred the title of Grand General upon Wáng Sīzhèng,

The Eastern Wèi built earthen mounds to attack Yǐngchuān,
but Sīzhèng captured and occupied them.
*Shuài* (帥),

"My strength is exhausted, my plans are at an end;
I can only repay the nation with my death."
Thereupon he looked up to the sky and wept bitterly,

and was about to commit suicide by slitting his throat when
Military Supervisor Luò Xùn said:
"You often told us, your subordinates:
'If you bring my head and surrender,
not only will you gain wealth and status,

The crowd restrained him,

Chéng sent Palace Censor Zhào Yànshēn to the earthen mound to present Sīzhèng with a white feather fan,
grasp his hand to express his goodwill,

Chéng dispersed and assigned all of his officers and soldiers to distant places,

According to Wèi Shōu's *Zhì*: Yǐngzhōu was originally administered from Chángshè;
after being renamed Zhèngzhōu,
its administration was moved to Yǐngyīn Chéng,
governing Xǔchāng, Yǐngchuān, and Yángzhái Commanderies.
Western Pavilion Libationer Lú Qián said:
"According to the system of the Later Qí,
the Three Mentors, Two Grandees, and Three Dukes

The Two Grandees were
the Grand Marshal and Grand General."
"Sīzhèng could not die for his integrity;

Qián
was the great-grandson of Dùshì.
Lú Dùshì
served Emperor Tàiwǔ of Wèi.
Initially,

Western Wèi established Xīzhōu.

"Xiāngchéng controls the route between the capital and Luòyáng,
truly a critical strategic location today.
If there is any disturbance,
it is easy to respond and connect.
Yǐngchuān, however, borders the enemy territory
and lacks natural mountain and river defenses.
If the enemy comes covertly,
they will arrive directly at the city walls.
It would be better to station troops at Xiāngchéng
as the seat of the Mobile Secretariat;
establish a prefecture in Yǐngchuān
and send a good general to guard it.
Then the internal and external defenses would be solidified,

Even if there were unexpected events,

When Zhòng met Tài,
he fully reported what he had heard.
Both Sīzhèng's request

Sīzhèng earnestly requested,

When Chángshè was not held,
Tài deeply regretted it.
Yóu
was the son of Xiàofēn.

his son Yóu entered the pass

When Hóu Jǐng rebelled in the south,
the account is in Volume 160, first year.
[Tài] ordered his generals to divide and guard various cities.

the Wú rebels Lù Jí and others
