and secretly wrote a letter summoning Póyáng Wáng Fàn,
instructing him to bring troops.
Jǐng intercepted the letter,
and on the *guǐchǒu* day,
strangled Zhèngdé to death.
Jǐng appointed Guō Yuánjiàn, formerly an Administrator of Qin, as Minister of Works, Mobile Secretariat of the Northern Route, and overall commander of all military affairs north of the Jiāng,
garrisoned at Xīnqín.
Qínjùn was formerly established at Liùhé.
Xīnqín is Qínjùn.
When Emperor Jiǎnwén was deposed,
Yuánjiàn rushed back from Qínjùn to admonish Jǐng.
This can be used as evidence.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Tàiqīng Jì* places this on the 28th day of the eighth month.
We follow the *Diǎnlüè* here.
He always kept him by his side.
Shàolíng Wáng Lún secretly sent someone to call him,
and Què said:
"Jǐng is fickle,
and just a single man.
I want to kill him with my own hands,
I just regret not having found the opportune moment.
You should return and report to your lord,
and do not worry about me."
Jǐng and Què were strolling at Zhōngshān,
and Jǐng drew his bow to shoot a bird.
Què then tried to shoot Jǐng,
but the bowstring broke,
and it did not fire.
Jǐng noticed and killed him.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Tàiqīng Jì* places Què's death in the ninth month.
We follow the *Diǎnlüè* here.
31 Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì married Xú Xiàosì's granddaughter,
and she bore him the heir apparent Fāngděng.
She was ugly and jealous,
and often behaved improperly,
so Yì visited her chambers only once every two or three years.
Hearing that Yì was coming,
and knowing Yì was blind in one eye,
she put on half a face of makeup to await him.
Yì was enraged and left,
which is why Fāngděng also received no favor.
When she returned to Jiānglíng from Jiànkāng,
Yì saw that her army was well-ordered and disciplined,
and only then did he praise her ability.
He went in to tell Xú,
but she did not reply,
merely shed tears and withdrew.
Yì was furious,
listed her vile deeds,
and posted them in the great hall.
Fāngděng saw this,
and grew even more fearful.
The Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, Hédōng Wáng Yù,
was valorous and won the hearts of his soldiers.
When Yì was about to campaign against Hóu Jǐng,
he sent an envoy to supervise Yù's provisions and troops.
Yù said:
"Each of us has our own military headquarters,
why should I suddenly be subordinate to others!"
The envoy returned three times,
but Yù did not comply.
Fāngděng requested to lead a punitive expedition against him,
so Yì appointed his youngest son, Ānnán Hóu Fāngjǔ, as Inspector of Xiāngzhōu,
and sent Fāngděng to escort him with twenty thousand elite soldiers.
As Fāngděng was about to depart,
he said to his close associates:
"On this journey,
I shall surely die;
if I die in the right place,
what more regret could I have!"
32 Hóu Jǐng appointed Zhào Wēifāng as Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng.
The Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, Xúnyáng Wáng Dàxīn, sent troops to resist him,
captured Wēifāng,
and imprisoned him in the provincial jail.
Wēifāng escaped back to Jiànkāng.
33 Xiāngdōng Shìzǐ Fāngděng's army reached Máxī.
According to the Commentary on the Water Classic,
the mouth of Máxī is north of Línxiāng County and south of Liúkǒu Garrison.
Fāngděng's army was defeated,
and he drowned.
Ānnán Hóu Fāngjǔ gathered the remaining troops and returned to Jiānglíng,
but Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì showed no sign of grief.
Yì's favorite concubine, Wáng Shì,
bore him a son, Fāngzhū.
When Wáng Shì died,
Yì suspected Xú was responsible,
suspecting she had poisoned her.
Xú threw herself into a well and died,
and was buried with the rites of a commoner.
Yì forbade her sons from wearing mourning clothes.
Historians say Xiāngdōng Wáng was suspicious and cold-hearted.
34 The Superintendent of Xījiāng, Chén Bàxiān, intended to raise an army to campaign against Hóu Jǐng.
Jǐng sent someone to entice the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu, Yuán Jǐngzhòng,
promising to make him their lord.
Yuán Jǐngzhòng was
Fǎsēng's son.
In the sixth year of Pǔtōng (525 CE),
father and son submitted to Liáng.
Yòu (誘)
pronounces "yǒu".
Jǐng secretly plotted against Bàxiān.
Bàxiān learned of this,
and with the Inspector of Chéngzhōu, Wáng Huáimíng, and others, assembled troops in Nánhǎi.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Cāngwú Commandery,
Liáng established Chéngzhōu.
Nánhǎi Commandery
was the seat of Guǎngzhōu.
"Yuán Jǐngzhòng allied with the rebels,
and the court sent Qǔyáng Hóu Bó as Inspector;
his army was already encamped at Cháotíng."
Lì Dàoyuán said: Thirty *lǐ* northeast of Guǎngzhōu city is Cháotái.
Formerly, Wèi Tuó built a terrace on a ridge,
facing north to pay homage to Hàn.
Its circular base was a thousand paces,
its sheer height a hundred *zhàng*,
the top three *mǔ*,
with winding corridors looping around,
twisting and turning.
On the first and fifteenth day of each month, one would ascend to prostrate oneself,
hence it was called Cháotái.
Cháo (朝)
pronounces "cháo".
All abandoned Jǐngzhòng and dispersed.
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the *Jiǎyín* day,
Jǐngzhòng hanged himself in his chambers.
Bàxiān welcomed the Inspector of Dìngzhōu, Xiāo Bó, to garrison Guǎngzhōu.
The former Inspector of Gāozhōu, Lán Yù,
was Qīn's younger brother.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Gāoliáng Commandery,
Liáng established Gāozhōu.
See Lán Qīn in volume 157, first year of Dàtóng.
Yù attacked Ōuyáng Wěi, who was supervising affairs in Héngzhōu.
Bó sent Bàxiān to rescue him,
and Bàxiān captured Yù and the others.
Kǎoyì states: Qīnyù was captured in the eighth month according to Tàiqīng Jì.
We follow Chén Shū here.
35 Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì dispatched the Grand Administrator of Jìnglíng, Wáng Sēngbiàn, and the Inspector of Xìnzhōu, Dōnghǎi Bāo Quán, to attack Xiāngzhōu,
allocating soldiers and provisions,
and setting a departure date.
Sēngbiàn, as his Jìnglíng subordinates had not all arrived,
wished to wait for the troops to gather before departing.
He and Quán went in to report to Yì,
requesting an extension of the deadline.
Shēn (申)
means "to repeat";
to repeat the date.
Yì drew his sword and said in a harsh voice:
"Are you afraid to go and defying orders,
intending to join the rebels?
Today, there is only death!"
Thereupon he struck Sēngbiàn,
wounding him in his left thigh.
Sēngbiàn fainted,
and only revived after a long time.
He was immediately sent to prison.
Quán was terrified,
and dared not speak.
Sēngbiàn's mother walked weeping to apologize,
confessing her lack of proper training.
Yì's anger subsided,
and he bestowed good medicine,
so Sēngbiàn was saved from death.
On the *Dīngmǎo* day,
Bāo Quán led the troops alone to attack Xiāngzhōu.
36 Lù Jí and others competed in violence and plunder.
The people of Wú did not support them,
so Sòng Zǐxiān rotated his army from Qiántáng to attack them.
At this time, Sòng Zǐxiān was attacking Dài Sēngtì,
encamped at Qiántáng.
On the *Rénxū* day,
Jí abandoned the city and fled to Hǎiyán.
Wújì states: Hǎiyán,
originally named Wǔyuán Township,
was made a county by Qín,
subordinate to Wú Commandery,
now subordinate to Jiāxīng Prefecture,
eighty *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
On the *Wùchén* day,
Hóu Jǐng established Wúzhōu in Wú Commandery,
appointing Ānlù Wáng Dàchūn as Inspector.
37 On the *Gēngwǔ* day,
Nánkāng Wáng Huìlǐ was concurrently appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
Kǎoyì states: Tàiqīng Jì records this as the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month.
We follow Diǎnlüè here.
38 Pōyáng Wáng Fàn (鄱陽王範) heard that Jiànkāng (建康) had not been defended.
He ordered a strict alert,
and wanted to enter [the city].
Some of his subordinates advised him, saying:
"Now the Wèi (魏) people have already taken Shòuyáng (壽陽).
If Your Highness makes a move,
the barbarian cavalry will surely spy on Héféi (合肥).
If the former rebels are not yet pacified,
and the latter city is lost,
what shall we do!
It would be better to wait for forces from all four directions to gather,
and then send a good general to lead elite troops to them.
Advancing, we would not fail in our duty to the emperor;
retreating, we could secure our foundation."
Fàn (範) then stopped.
At this time, the Eastern Wèi (東魏) Grand General Chéng (澄) sent the Inspector of Xīyǎnzhoū (西兗州), Lǐ Bómù (李伯穆), to press Héféi (合肥),
and also sent Wèi Shōu (魏收) with a letter to admonish Fàn (範).
Fàn (範) was then planning to attack Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
and relied on Eastern Wèi (東魏) for assistance.
So he led twenty thousand warriors out through Dōngguān (東關),
surrendered Hégzhōu (合州) to Bómù (伯穆),
and also sent the Counsellor Líu Língyì (劉靈議) with his two sons, Qín (勤) and Guǎng (廣), to be hostages in Eastern Wèi (東魏) to request troops.
"Counsellor" (諮議)
refers to Cānchūn Cānjūn (諮議參軍).
"Zhì" (質)
is pronounced [zhì].
He sent his heir, Sì (嗣), to guard Ānlè Zhà (安樂柵) with over a thousand men.
Ānlè Zhà (安樂柵)
was a palisade built by Fàn (範),
named after Ānlè (安樂).
However, the palace city had fallen,
and his father and elder brothers were disgraced;
this was a time for sons and younger brothers to shed blood and sleep on weapons.
Naming the palisade Ānlè (安樂)
was an inappropriate name.
"Lè" (樂)
is pronounced [luò].
Fàn's (範) provisions ran short,
and he gathered wild rice, water caltrops, and lotus roots to sustain himself.
When Qín (勤) and Guǎng (廣) arrived in Yè (鄴),
the Eastern Wèi (東魏) people ultimately did not send out troops.
Fàn (範) was at a loss, caught between advancing and retreating;
advancing, his isolated and weak army was insufficient to control Hóu Jǐng (侯景);
retreating, Héféi (合肥) had already been occupied by the Eastern Wèi (東魏) people.
"Shàng" (上)
is pronounced [shí zhǎng fān].
Cōngyáng Xiàn (樅陽縣)
belonged to Lújiāng Jùn (廬江郡) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
According to the Jìn Shū (晉書) and the Wǔdài Zhì (五代志),
Tóng'ān Jùn Tóng'ān Xiàn (同安郡同安縣)
was formerly called Cōngyáng (樅陽),
and Cōngyáng Jùn (樅陽郡) was also established there.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Cōng (樅)
is pronounced [qī róng fān].
Fàn's (範) general Péi Zhītì (裴之悌) surrendered with his troops.
Zhītì (之悌)
was Zhīgāo's (之高) younger brother.
39 The Eastern Wèi (東魏) Grand General Chéng (澄) went to Yè (鄴),
declined titles and special honors,
and also requested the establishment of a crown prince.
Chéng (澄) asked Jìyīn Wáng Huīyè (濟陰王暉業):
"What books have you been reading recently?"
Huīyè (暉業) replied:
"I often consult the biographies of Yī (伊) and Huò (霍),
but I do not read the books of Cáo (曹) and Mǎ (馬)."
This means Yī (伊) and Huò (霍) assisted young rulers,
while Cáo (曹) and Mǎ (馬) usurped the throne.
"Jì" (濟)
is pronounced [zǐ lǐ fān].
"Bǐ" (比)
is pronounced [pí zhì fān].
"Shù" (數)
is pronounced [suǒ jiǎo fān].
"Chuán" (傳)
is pronounced [zhí liàn fān].
40 In the eighth month,
on the day Jiǎshēn (甲申), which was the first day of the month,
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) sent his Central Army Commander Hóu Zǐjiàn (侯子鑒) and others to attack Wúxīng (吳興).
41 On the day Jǐhài (己亥),
Bào Quán's (鮑泉) army was stationed at Shíguǒ Sì (石椁寺), where Hédōng Wáng Yù (河東王譽) engaged them in battle but was defeated;
on the day Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
he was again defeated at Júzhōu (橘洲).
Yàn Gōnglèi Yàoyǔ (晏公類要) states: Júzhōu (橘洲)
is forty *lǐ* (里) southwest of Chángshā (長沙).
Among the four islands in the Xiāngjiāng (湘江) River, Júzhōu (橘洲) is one of them.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) says: The Yuánshuǐ (沅水) River flows eastward past Fànzhōu (汎洲) in Lóngyáng Xiàn (龍陽縣).
The island is twenty *lǐ* (里) long.
Lǐ Héng (李衡), the Administrator of Dānyáng (丹楊) for the Wú (吳) dynasty, planted citrus trees on it.
Before he died,
he instructed his sons:
"My village has a thousand 'tree slaves,'
who require no food or clothing,
and provide a thousand bolts of silk annually."
Today, there are still old stumps on the island.
I (the annotator) believe Fànzhōu (汎洲) is Gānzhōu (柑洲),
not Júzhōu (橘洲).
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) also says: The Xiāngshuǐ (湘水) River flows north past the west of Línxiāng Xiàn (臨湘縣),
and then north past the west of Nánjīn Chéng (南津城),
opposite Júzhōu (橘洲) to the west.
This must be it.
Lèiyào (類要) also refers to this.
Zhāng Shùnmín's (張舜民) Chēn Xínglù (郴行錄) says: Júzhōu (橘洲) faces Tánzhōu (潭州) city to the east.
Yù (譽) retreated and fortified Chángshā (長沙),
and the multitude
led their army to besiege it.
42 On the day Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
Eastern Wèi (東魏) established Prince Chángrén (長仁) as the Crown Prince.
Bóhǎi Wénxiāng Wáng Chéng (勃海文襄王澄) considered his younger brother, Tàiyuán Gōng Yáng (太原公洋), to be the next in age.
"Next in age" (次長)
means in terms of sibling order,
Chéng (澄) was the eldest and Yáng (洋) was the next.
"Zhǎng" (長)
is pronounced [zhú zhàng fān].
Yáng (洋) was deeply secretive and concealed himself,
not speaking his mind.
He often humbled himself and retreated,
and when speaking with Chéng (澄),
he was always compliant.
Chéng (澄) thought little of him,
often saying:
"Even this man can attain wealth and honor;
how can physiognomy books be understood!"
Yáng (洋) would acquire beautiful ornaments for his wife, Lady Lǐ (李氏) of Zhàojùn (趙郡),
and Chéng (澄) would always take them away.
If his wife was angry and unwilling to give them,
Yáng (洋) would laugh and say:
"These things can still be acquired;
what my brother desires, why be stingy and withhold it!"
"Xū" (須)
here means what one desires or seeks.
Yáng (洋) would then accept it,
without any feigned humility.
Whenever he returned to his residence after court,
he would close the gate and sit quietly.
Even when facing his wife and children,
he could remain silent all day long.
Sometimes he would strip naked and run and jump.
When his wife asked him why,
Yáng (洋) said:
"I'm just playing around idly."
"Mànxì" (漫戲)
means to play around casually.
Chéng acquired Lán Qīn's son Jīng, who was the Inspector of Xúzhōu,
and made him a kitchen slave.
Lán Qīn served the Liáng dynasty
as Inspector of Xúzhōu.
The "Kǎoyì" says that the biography of Chén Yuánkāng states
"Lán Gùchéng."
We now follow the Northern Qí Imperial Annals.
This was not permitted.
Jīng repeatedly protested on his own behalf.
Chéng flogged him,
saying:
"If you protest again,
I will kill you!"
Jīng and six of his associates plotted rebellion.
Chéng was in Yè,
residing in the Bǎitáng east of the northern city wall.
He favored Princess Lángyá.
The first mention of Princess Lángyá appears in volume 159, Datóng 11th year.
He often sent his bodyguards outside.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
Chéng, along with Regular Attendant Sànqí Chén Yuánkāng, Minister of Personnel and Palace Attendant Yáng Yīn, and Yellow Gate Attendant Cuī Jìshū, dismissed their attendants
to conspire about receiving the Wèi abdication
and appointing various officials.
Lán Jīng presented food.
Chéng pushed it away
and said to everyone:
"Last night I dreamt this slave was hacking me.
He must be killed immediately."
Jīng heard this,
placed a knife under the tray,
and falsely announced that he was presenting food.
Chéng angrily said:
"I have not yet asked for food!
Why have you come so quickly?"
Jīng brandished the knife and said:
"I have come to kill you!"
Chéng threw himself down, injuring his foot,
and went under the bed.
The rebel moved the bed
and assassinated him.
Yīn fled in a panic,
losing one boot.
Jìshū hid in the latrine.
Yuánkāng shielded Chéng with his body,
and was injured struggling for the knife with the rebel,
with his intestines exposed.
Kùzhí Wáng Hóng braved the blade to fend off the rebel.
Héxī Shèlè died fighting.
At that time, the sudden upheaval
shocked everyone inside and outside.
The Duke of Tàiyuán, Yáng, was in Shuāngtáng, east of the city.
Hearing of it,
his expression remained unchanged.
He directed and allocated forces,
entered to suppress the rebels,
chopped them up,
then calmly exited,
saying:
"The slaves have revolted,
and the Grand General has been injured.
It's not a great tragedy."
Everyone inside and outside was astonished.
Yáng had always kept a low profile.
Now, encountering this upheaval, he remained unperturbed,
so everyone was surprised and marveled at him.
Chén Yuánkāng wrote a letter with his own hand to bid farewell to his mother,
and dictated to the Aide to the Governor, Zǔ Tǐng, to write a memorial proposing suitable measures.
He died that night.
Yáng had him entombed in his residence,
falsely claiming he was on a mission,
and fictitiously removed Yuánkāng as Minister of the Central Secretariat.
He also kept secret the news of Chén Yuánkāng's death,
which also served to calm public sentiment.
Hóng
was the son of Jī.
Wáng Jī is mentioned in volume 156, Dàtōng 6th year.
The honored nobles, whose heavy troops were all in Bīngzhōu,
advised Yáng to go to Jìnyáng quickly.
Yáng agreed.
At night,
he summoned the Grand General's Commandant, Táng Yōng,
and had him allocate generals and soldiers
to guard the four directions.
Yōng completed the allocation in a moment.
"Zhī"
means to divide.
"Pèi"
means to be subordinate.
"Zhīpèi"
is like what people now call 'pǐnpèi' (ranking and allocation).
On the Guǐsì day,
Yáng subtly prompted the Lord of Eastern Wèi to issue a general amnesty for the establishment of the heir apparent.
He used the pretext of establishing the heir apparent and a general amnesty
to appease those among Lán Jīng's faction who harbored rebellious intentions.
The Lord of Eastern Wèi secretly said to his attendants:
"If the Grand General dies now,
it seems to be Heaven's will,
and authority will return to the imperial house!"
Yáng left Grand Commandant Gāo Yuè, Grand Protector Gāo Lóngzhī, Governor-General Sīmǎ Zǐrú, and Palace Attendant Yáng Yīn to guard Yè.
The rest of the honored nobles followed him.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
he entered to pay respects to the Lord of Eastern Wèi in the Zhāoyáng Palace,
accompanied by eight thousand armed guards.
Over two hundred people ascended the steps,
all rolling up their sleeves and gripping their blades,
as if facing a formidable enemy.
He ordered the official in charge to transmit his message, saying:
"Your subject has family matters
requiring him to go to Jìnyáng."
"Zhǔzhě"
refers to the official in charge of court ceremonies.
The Lord of Eastern Wèi lost color,
and watched him leave, saying:
"This man also seems incompatible with me.
I do not know on what day I will die!"
The old officials and veteran generals of Jìnyáng had always slighted Yáng.
Upon his arrival,
he convened a great assembly of civil and military officials.
His spirit and demeanor were splendid and fluent,
and his words were agile and apt.
Everyone was greatly astonished.
The astonishment of Jìnyáng's civil and military officials at Yáng
was like that of those inside and outside Yèchéng.
Yáng reformed all of them.
Gāo Lóngzhī and Sīmǎ Zǐrú disliked Minister of Revenue Cuī Xiān.
They memorialized Xiān and Cuī Jìshū's transgressions and wickedness,
and they were flogged two hundred times and exiled to the frontier.
The two had always been trusted by Chéng,
which is why Lóngzhī and others disliked them.
43 Hóu Jǐng appointed Sòng Zǐxiān as Grand Minister of Agriculture and Guō Zǐ
jiàn as Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs,
along with Commander of the Army Rèn Yuē and forty others, all as Governor-Generals.
He then issued an edict:
"From now on, Governor-Generals no longer need to additionally hold the title of general."
Under the Liáng system,
even the Three Ducal Ministers were given the title of general.
Now, even Governor-Generals are not given it.
This cannot be recorded again.
44 The King of Póyáng, Fàn, sent a message from Cóngyáng to inform the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, the King of Xúnyáng, Dàxīn.
Dàxīn sent a message inviting him.
Fàn led his troops to Jiāngzhōu.
Dàxīn settled him in Péchéng.
"One perch cannot hold two male birds"
sets the stage for Fàn and Dàxīn to become mutually suspicious.
"Chǔ"
is read as chāng lǚ fān.
45 Wúxīng's military strength was weak.
Zhāng Shèng was a scholar,
not skilled in military affairs.
"Xián"
means practiced.
Shèng sighed, saying:
"The Yuán clan has for generations upheld loyalty and integrity.
From Shú to Yǐ, Càn, and Áng, all members of the Yuán clan were known for their loyalty and integrity.
How could I not know that with Wújùn already lost,
Wúxīng's situation would be difficult to maintain for long?
But I have pledged my body to the state,
and I would rather die than betray it!"
In the ninth month,
on the Guǐchǒu day (the first day of the month),
Zǐjiàn's army reached Wúxīng.
Shèng was defeated in battle,
returned to his residence,
straightened his clothes, and sat calmly.
Zǐjiàn captured and sent him to Jiànkāng.
Hóu Jǐng admired his steadfastness
and wanted to spare his life.
Shèng said:
"I was entrusted with governing a city.
The court is in peril,
and I could not restore it.
Today, to die quickly is my good fortune."
Jǐng still wanted to spare one of his sons.
Shèng said:
"My entire family is already on the ghost register."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's book says: "Looking at their names,
they are already on the ghost register."
"Lù"
means register.
Jǐng became enraged
and killed them all.
Zhāng Shèng's entire family died for righteousness,
to wash away the disgrace of his father's regicide.
The blood sacrifice is now broken.
When Shěn Jùn reproached Hóu Jǐng,
he faced death as if returning home.
Afterward, when he raised an army with Zhāng Shèng,
how could he have expected to live?
10 Shàolíng Wáng Lún (邵陵王綸) wished to rescue Hédōng Wáng Yù (河東王譽), but his troops lacked provisions.
He then wrote a letter to Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì (湘東王繹), saying:
"Timely opportunities and geographical advantages
are not as important as human harmony.

it was renamed Níngdū [Níngdū].
The *Wǔdài Zhì* [Wǔdài Zhì] states: Qiánhuà Xiàn [Qiánhuà Xiàn] in Nánkāng [Nánkāng] was formerly called Níngdū [Níngdū].
She occupied its city.
Lady Xǐ [Xǐ] met Bàxiān [Bàxiān] at Gǎnxí [Gǎnxí].
Returning,
she said to Bàofù [Bàofù]:
"Commander Chén [Chén] is no ordinary man;
he has greatly won the hearts of the people,
and will surely be able to suppress the rebels.
You should generously assist him."
Yì [Yì], Prince of Xiāngdōng [Xiāngdōng], appointed Bàxiān [Bàxiān] as Inspector of Yùzhōu [Yùzhōu],
concurrently serving as Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng [Yùzhāng].
41st year, Xīnchǒu.
Péi Zhīhéng attacked Jītíng,
Xú Sìhuī repelled him.
42nd year, Autumn,
7th month,
Xīnhài.
Qí enthroned Shìzōng Yuán Shì as Empress Wénxiāng.
The Empress
was the daughter of Dōng Wèi Xiàojìng Dì.
They also enfeoffed Shìzōng's son Xiàowǎn as Hèjiān Wáng,
and Xiàoyú as Hénán Wáng.
Yǐmǎo.
Shàngshū Lìng Fēng Lóngzhī was appointed Lù Shàngshū Shì,
and Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Píngyáng Wáng Yān became Shàngshū Lìng.
43rd year, Xīnyǒu.
Liáng Wáng Chá entered Wèi to pay respects.
From this point, Wèi treated Chá with increasing generosity.
朝 (cháo),
read as zhí yáo fān (zháo).
44th year. Previously,
Dōng Wèi dispatched Yítóng Wǔwēi Dié Yúnluò and others.
"雲" (yún),
should be
"云" (yún).
Dié Yún
was a family name of the Rúrán.
When Rúrán Ānàhuái sought to attach himself to Wèi,
Wèi sent Dié Yún Jùrén as an envoy.
The surname Dié Yún was already ancient.
They were sent to garrison Wǎnchéng.
Liú Xù said: Huáiníng, Sùsōng, Wàngjiāng, Tàihú, and other counties
were all territory of Hàn's Wǎnxuàn County.
This city was likely the old city of Wǎnxuàn County.
皖 (wǎn),
read as hù bǎn fān.
When Rèn Yuē's army arrived,
Luò and others withdrew;
Sì then lost support,
went out to battle,
and was defeated and killed.
Yuē then seized territory up to Pénchéng.
Xúnyáng Wáng Dàxīn sent Sīmǎ Wéi Zhì to battle, who was defeated.
He still had over a thousand soldiers under his command.
All advised Dàxīn to flee and secure Jiànzhōu.
In the Later Hàn, Rǔnán Jùn had Bāoxìn County.
During the Eastern Jìn, it was relocated to Yìyáng territory.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Yìyáng Jùn Yīnchéng County,
formerly Bāoxìn,
was where Liáng established Yìchéng Jùn and Jiànzhōu.
Those under Dàxīn's command who advised him to flee and secure it
found it convenient for entering Qí.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Yīnchéng County was merged into Gùshǐ.
Wùchén.
Jiāngzhōu surrendered to Yuē.
Earlier,
Dàxīn had sent Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ Wéi Zàng to garrison Jiànchāng.
He had five thousand armored soldiers.
Hearing that Xúnyáng could not be held,
he intended to lead his troops to Jiānglíng.
Before he could depart,
he was killed by his subordinates.
Zàng
was the son of Càn.
In the third year of Tàiqīng,
Wéi Càn died in the Battle of Qīngtáng.
45th year. Yú Qìng seized territory up to Yùzhāng.
Hóu Tián, outmatched,
surrendered to him.
Qìng sent Tián to Jiànkāng.
Jǐng, seeing Tián as a kinsman,
treated him very well,
keeping his wife and children and younger brother as hostages,
and sent Tián to accompany Qìng in campaigns against the southern Lǐ-region prefectures.
Lǐnán
refers to the area south of Lake Pénglǐ.
The Kǎoyì states: The Tàiqīng Jì places this in the 11th month.
Here we follow the Diǎnlüè.
46th year. Earlier,
Huáng Fǎ from Bāshān
was strong and brave.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Línchuān Jùn Chóngrén County,
where Liáng established Bāshān Jùn.
Liú Xù said: Wú divided Línrǔ to establish Xīnjiàn County;
Liáng established Bāshān Jùn.
俱 (jù), read as jù fān.
He gathered a multitude to defend his homeland.
When Tàishǒu Hè Xǔ went down to Jiāngzhōu,
going down from Bāshān along the river to Jiāngzhōu is referred to as "down."
Fǎ garrisoned Xīngàn.
Yú Qìng dispatched troops from Yùzhāng to attack Xīngàn.
Xīngàn County,
in Hàn it belonged to Yùzhāng Jùn;
the Wǔdài Zhì places it under Lúlíng Jùn.
淦 (gàn), read as gǔ àn fān.
Chén Bàxiān sent Zhōu Wényù to advance and attack Qìng,
and Fǎ led his troops to join him.
47th year. Shàolíng Wáng Lún, hearing that Rèn Yuē was approaching,
sent Sīmǎ Jiǎng Sī'ān with five thousand elite soldiers to attack him.
Yuē's forces dispersed;
Sī'ān was unprepared,
so Yuē regrouped his troops and attacked him.
Sī'ān was defeated and fled.
48th year. Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì changed Yídū to Yízhōu.
Shěn Yuē said: Liú Bèi divided Nánjùn to establish Yídū Jùn;
Liáng established Yízhōu in Yídū Jùn;
Suí merged Yídū into Yílíng Jùn.
49th year. This month,
Nánjùn Wáng Dàlián was appointed Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
50th year. Wèi Chéngxiàng Tà, upon hearing that Qí Zhǔ had claimed emperorship,
led all his armies to attack him.
He stationed Qí Wáng Kuò in Lǒngyòu,
and summoned Qínzhōu Cìshǐ Yǔwén Dǎo as Dà Jiàngjūn and Dūdū Èrshísān Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì,
to garrison Xiányáng
and secure Guānzhōng.
51st year. Sūn Tiānyīng, a Buddhist monk from Yìzhōu, led several thousand followers in a night attack on the provincial capital.
Wǔlíng Wáng Jì fought him
and cut him down.
52nd year. Shàolíng Wáng Lún extensively repaired armor and weapons,
intending to attack Hóu Jǐng.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì resented this.
He resented Lún for thereby gaining strength,
which would be detrimental to himself.
惡 (è),
read as wū lù fān.
Jiǎwǔ.
He sent Zuǒwèi Jiàngjūn Wáng Sēngbiàn, Xìnzhōu Cìshǐ Bào Quán, and others with a fleet of ten thousand ships eastward towards Jiāng and Yǐng.
They declared their intention to resist Rèn Yuē,
and also claimed to be escorting Shàolíng Wáng back to Jiānglíng,
to be granted Xiāngzhōu.
53rd year. When Qí Zhǔ was first enthroned,
he strove diligently for good governance.
Zhào Dàodé assigned a matter to Líyáng Tàishǒu Qīnghé Fáng Chāo.
Chāo did not open the letter
and clubbed the envoy to death.
The Wèi Shōu Zhì states: During Xiàochāng,
Jí Jùn was divided to establish Líyáng Jùn,
belonging to Sīzhōu,
with its seat in Líyáng Chéng.
棓 (bàng),
read as bù xiàng fān.
使 (shǐ),
read as shū lì fān;
same below.
He ordered all governors to set up clubs to execute any envoy who requested favors.
After a long time,
Dūguān Zhōngláng
Sòng Guǐ memorialized, saying:
"中郎" (zhōngláng)
should be
"郎中" (lángzhōng).
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Dūguān Lángzhōng was in charge of illegalities and transgressions within the imperial domain.
This was the Qí system.
"If one accepts bribes through an envoy,
it still leads to great punishment.
If one breaks the law oneself,
how can the punishment be increased!"
So it was abolished.
Sīdū Gōngcáo Zhāng Lǎo submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of the Qí Code.
Sīdū Gōngcáo
was the Gōngcáo of Sīzhōu.
At that time, the capital was Yè,
so Yè was the seat of Sīzhōu.
Note that the Northern Qí rulers sometimes resided in Jìnyáng,
not always in Yè.
Further discussions were held to amend and improve it.
The Línzhǐ Gé
is mentioned in scroll 158, Wǔ Dì Dàtóng 7th year.
琡 (shú), read as chāng liù fān.
Qí Zhǔ selected and trained men from the six divisions.
Each man was expected to be worth a hundred,
guaranteed to fight to the death on the battlefield.
Between Wèi and Qí,
the imperial guard soldiers
were divided into six divisions.
任 (rèn),
means guarantee.
陳 (chén),
read as zhèn.
They were called
"Bǎibǎo Xiānbēi."
Bǎibǎo means that their bravery guarantees one person is worth a hundred.
The Gāo clan founded their dynasty with the Xiānbēi,
who were then renowned for their fighting prowess.
Therefore, all imperial guards were Xiānbēi,
just as people in the north now call brave warriors bàdūlǔ.
They were called
"Yǒngshì" (brave warriors),
to defend important border areas.
Biānyào
means vital places on the border.
Initially, nine grades of households were established.
Households were divided into three main grades: upper, middle, and lower.
Each of these grades was further subdivided into upper, middle, and lower,
making nine grades in total.
The poor were conscripted for their labor.
In the 9th month of the 54th year,
on the *dīngsì* day,
the Wèi army departed from Cháng’ān.
They left Cháng’ān and marched east to attack Qí.
Wáng Sēngbiàn’s army reached Yīngwǔzhōu.
Yīngwǔzhōu is in the Jiāngxià River.
In the past, Huáng Zǔ had Ní Héng compose the "Yīngwǔ Fù" (Ode to the Parrot) on this island,
from which it got its name.
Below the island is Huánghú Jī.
Shàolíng Wáng Lún heard of this
and sent his son, Wēizhèng Hóu Zhì, to lead troops to attack them.
Lónghǔ was defeated
and fled to Sēngbiàn.
Lún sent a letter to Sēngbiàn, scolding him:
"General, last year you killed my nephew."
This refers to killing Hédōng Wáng Yù.
Lún is Yì’s elder brother.
"I fear the world will not permit this!"
Sēngbiàn sent the letter to Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì,
and Yì ordered an advance.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Lún gathered his subordinates at Xīyuán.
The garden was located on the western side of Yǐngchéng,
hence the name Xīyuán.
There was also Dōngyuán,
on the Dōnghú lake east of the city.
Lún said, "Originally, I had no other intention;
my goal was to eliminate the rebels.
Xiāngdōng constantly speaks of vying for the emperorship with me,
and thus I am being attacked.
Today, if I wish to defend, the grain supply will be cut off.
If I wish to fight, I will be ridiculed for a thousand years.
It is not acceptable to be captured without a struggle.
I should avoid them downstream."
His brave subordinates eagerly requested to go out and fight,
but Lún refused.
He and Zhì boarded a boat from Cāngmén and headed north.
According to Yáo Sīlián's *Liáng Shū*,
Cāngmén
was the northern gate of Yǐngchéng,
bordering the river and strategically difficult.
Yì appointed Nánpíng Wáng Kè as Shàngshū Lìng and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
his heir apparent Fāngzhū as Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Wáng Sēngbiàn as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Lún encountered Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn Péi Zhīgāo on the road.
Zhīgāo's son, Jī, plundered his military equipment.
Lún, with his attendants, fled in a light boat to Wǔchāng Jiànyǐnsì.
Wǔchāng
is today's Shòuchāng Jūn.
Lún's Chángshǐ Wéi Zhì and Sīmǎ Jiāng Lǜ, among others, heard that Lún was still alive
and rushed to welcome him,
persuading the vagrants of the Seven Stockades to seek provisions and weapons.
At that time, vagrants had established seven stockades in Běijiāngzhōu to protect each other.
"Shuō" (說) is pronounced *shì ruì*.
Eight or nine thousand vagrants joined him.
He gradually gathered scattered soldiers
and garrisoned at Qíchāng.
According to Wèi Shōu's *Zhì*, Liáng Wǔdì established Běijiāngzhōu,
governing Lùchéngguān,
and administering the commanderies of Yìyáng, Qíchāng, Xīnchāng, Liáng’ān, Qíxīng, and Guāngchéng.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* states: Huángzhōu Mùlán Xiàn was called Liáng’ān Jùn during the Liáng dynasty.
There was also Yìyáng Jùn.
Later, Qí established Xiāngzhōu,
which was later renamed Běijiāngzhōu.
Thus, Qíchāng should also be within the Mùlán Xiàn boundaries.
During the Táng dynasty, Mùlán was abolished and merged into Huánggāng Xiàn.
Sòng Bái said: Wú established Qíchūn Jùn.
Jìn Huìdì renamed it Xīyáng Jùn.
Nán Qí and Běi Qí renamed Xīyáng to Qíchāng Jùn.
During the Táng dynasty, it was Qízhōu.
In Qí,
Qí appointed Lún as Liáng Wáng.
In the 55th year,
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì enfeoffed imperial son Dàkuǎn as Línchuān Wáng,
Dàchéng as Guìyáng Wáng,
and Dàfēng as Rǔnán Wáng.
On the *guǐhài* day of the 56th year,
the Wèi army reached Tóngguān.
On the *gēngwǔ* day of the 57th year,
the Qí ruler went to Jìnyáng,
ordering Crown Prince Yīn to supervise the state from Liángfēng Táng.
According to the *Běi Shǐ* and the biography of Qí Lèlíng Wáng Bǎinián: Liángfēng Táng was located in the Xuándū Yuàn of the Yè Palace.
"Jiān" (監) is pronounced *gōng xián*.
The Nánjùn Wáng's Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Zhāng Biāo and others,
when Nánjùn Wáng Dàlián was stationed in Kuàijī,
appointed Zhāng Biāo as Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Ruòyé Shān
is forty *lǐ* southeast of present-day Yuèzhōu.
He had several tens of thousands of troops.
Lù Lìnggōng and others from Wújùn persuaded the Grand Administrator Nánhǎi Wáng Dàlín to join them.
Dàlín said:
"If Biāo succeeds,
he won't need my strength;
if he fails,
he will use me to exonerate himself."
This means he will blame Dàlín to exonerate himself to Hóu Jǐng.
Rèn Yuē advanced to raid Xīyáng and Wǔchāng.
Previously,
Níngzhōu Cìshǐ Péngchéng Xú Wénshèng had recruited several tens of thousands of soldiers to suppress Hóu Jǐng.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì appointed him Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* states: Jiāngdū Jùn Liùhé Xiàn originally had Qín Jùn established.
Later, Qí established Qínzhōu.
Was it already established by Liáng?
Wénshèng encountered Yuē at Wǔchāng.
Yì appointed Lúlíng Wáng Yìng as Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Wénshèng as Chángshǐ, acting as Fǔzhōu Shì,
overseeing the various generals to resist him.
Yìng
was the son of Xù.
Lúlíng Wáng Xù
died in the first year of Liáng Wǔdì’s Tàiqīng era.
They moved their camp to Mǎzhà,
eighty *lǐ* from Xīyáng.
Xīyáng
is today’s Huángzhōu Huánggāng Xiàn,
ancient Zhūchéng.
They sent Yítóng Chìluó Zǐtōng and others to lead two hundred cavalry to attack them.
Chìluó
is a foreign compound surname.
"Jì" (騎) is pronounced *qí jì*.
They spurred their horses and fled.
At that time, Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì was also allied with Qí,
so the Qí people observed and did not help Lún.
Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ Tián Zǔlóng welcomed Lún.
Lún, fearing that Zǔlóng was favored by Yì
and might seize him,
returned to Qíchāng.
When he reached Rǔnán,
Lǐ Sù, the Rǔnán Chéngzhǔ appointed by Wèi
and Lún's former subordinate,
opened the city gates and received him.
Wèi Shōu's *Zhì* states: Yǐngzhōu had Rǔnán Jùn,
governing Shàngcài Xiàn.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* states: Jìnglíng Jùn originally established Yǐngzhōu,
which administered Hàndōng Xiàn,
formerly called Shàngcài.
Thus, Rǔnán Chéng was Hàndōng Xiàn Chéng.
Also, according to Yáo Sīlián's *Liáng Shū*: Rǔnán was governed by Anlù Chóngchéng.
Sòng Bái said: People from Jìn Rǔnán Jùn migrated to Xiàkǒu,
and thus a temporary Rǔnán Jùn, Rǔnán Xiàn was established at Tóngkǒu.
The *Jīngxiāng Jì* states: The old Rǔnán city is on the north bank of Jīnshuǐ.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Liáng Dìjì* places this in the 11th month.
We follow the *Tàiqīng Jì* here.
Péi Zhīgāo led his sons, disciples, and over a thousand troops to Xiàshǒu.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì summoned him
and appointed him Grand Administrator of Xīnxīng and Yǒngníng commanderies.
Xīnxīng Jùn was established within the Jiānglíng Xiàn boundaries.
Yǒngníng Jùn was established within the Xiāngyáng Nánzhāng Xiàn boundaries.
He was stationed at Wǔlíng.
Wǔlíng was Lǎngzhōu in the Táng dynasty,
and was changed to Dǐngzhōu in our present dynasty.
Previously,
Shàolíng Wáng Lún had appointed Héngyáng Wáng Xiàn as Qízhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Qíchāng.
Rèn Yuē attacked and captured him,
sent him to Jiànkāng,
and killed him.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Liáng Dìjì* places this in the 11th month.
We follow the *Tàiqīng Jì* here.
He was the grandson of Chàng.
Chàng
was Wǔdì’s younger brother.
On the *yǐhài* day of the 63rd year,
Hóu Jǐng was promoted to Xiāngguó,
enfeoffed with twenty commanderies,
made Hàn Wáng,
and granted special courtesies.
Yuèyáng Wáng Chá returned to Xiāngyáng.
He returned after an audience with Wèi.
It was previously written that Chá was Liáng Wáng.
Now, his old title is written again.
According to the principle of meaning and examples,
this should be corrected.
In 65, the people of Lízhōu attacked and stabbed the Inspector, Zhāng Bēn.
Bēn abandoned the city and fled.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Yìchéng Jùn,
was called Lízhōu by the Liáng dynasty,
and Lízhōu of the Táng dynasty is this place.
The Wèi dynasty designated Wǔxīng as Dōngyìzhōu,
and the Dī king, Yáng Shì, resided there.
The Liáng dynasty probably took it as Běiyìzhōu.
Further down in the following scroll,
Yáng Fǎchēn governed Píngxīng,
so the Liáng dynasty established Běiyìzhōu in Píngxīng.
Qióu,
pronounced cí qiū.
Jì Shēn reprimanded him severely,
imprisoning Fǎchēn's hostage sons Chóngyōng and Chónghǔ.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on Dīngchǒu, the first day of the lunar month,
Fǎchēn sent an envoy to pledge allegiance to Wèi.
On Jǐmǎo,
the Qí ruler arrived at Jìnyáng Gōng.
Jìnyáng Gōng
was established by Qí Xiànwǔ Wáng.
The Táng Zhì states: Jìnyáng Gōng,
is in the northwest of the Northern Capital.
The palace city wall measured 2,520 paces in circumference.
The capital city had the Fén River on its left and the Jìn River on its right,
with Qiánqiū in the middle,
measuring 4,321 paces long,
3,122 paces wide,
and 15,153 paces in circumference.
East of the Fén River was called Dōngchéng.
When the Qí ruler was about to go to Jìnyáng,
Chángbì spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Sháo commands strong troops there;
I fear he may not be to your liking,"
meaning he feared Sháo might rebel.
The Emperor did not listen.
Upon arrival,
he told Sháo Chángbì's words,
saying:
"Even with your loyalty,
people still slander you,
how much more so others!"
Chángbì was
Yǒnglè's younger brother.
Gāo Yǒnglè did not accept Gāo Áng's counsel,
causing him to lose his head.
Chángbì also slandered Duàn Sháo.
Gāo Huān and his son were wrong in their judgments.
On Yǐyǒu,
Yuán Sháo, who was a Special Grand Master, was appointed Minister of the Left of the Department of State Affairs,
and Duàn Sháo was appointed Minister of the Right.
On Yǐwèi,
Hóu Jǐng bestowed upon himself the title of Grand General of the Universe, Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs of the Six Directions,
and presented the imperial decree to the Emperor.
The Emperor exclaimed in surprise:
"Does the General truly hold the title of Universe?"
He established the imperial princes: Dàjūn as Xīyáng Wáng,
Dàwēi as Wǔníng Wáng,
Dàqiú as Jiàn'ān Wáng,
and Dàxīn as Yì'ān Wáng.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Zhì states:
Among the territories governed by the Níngmán Fǔ was Yì'ān Jùn.
Shěn Yuè's Zhì states: In the thirteenth year of Yuánjiā of Sòng Wéndì (436 CE),
Suíjiàn Jùn was established on the land of Sìhuì Xiàn in Hán Nánhǎi Jùn.
Lèliáng is
not found in historical records.
The titles of the various kings at this time
were all names of commanderies.
They must have been among the more than twenty prefectures divided during the Dàtóng period,
but their exact locations are unknown.
The Kǎoyì states: The record in Tàiqīng Jì is on the fourteenth day of the eleventh month.
We now follow the Liáng Dì Jì.
The Qí Dōngxúzhōu Inspector and Acting Imperial Secretary, Xīn Shù, was stationed at Xiàpéi.
In the eleventh month,
Hóu Jǐng requisitioned grain for Jiànkāng.
Shù led his troops across the Huái River to cut off the transport,
burning a million *shi* of their grain.
He then besieged Yángpíng,
and Jǐng's Acting Imperial Secretary, Guō Yuánjiàn, led troops to relieve it.
On Rénxū,
Shù plundered over three thousand households
and returned to Xiàpéi.
Wǔlíng Wáng Jì led all his armies from Chéngdū.
The Kǎoyì states: The Nán Shǐ says,
"On Rén'yín in the eleventh month."
However, the first day of this month was Rénzǐ,
so there was no Rén'yín.
"The people of Shǔ are brave and fierce,
easily agitated and difficult to pacify.
You, my brother, can pacify them;
I myself will eliminate the rebels."
Another separate note says:
"The lands are like those of Sūn and Liú,
each settling their own borders;
the affection is deep like that of Lǔ and Wèi,
with constant communication by letters."
"The lands are like those of Sūn and Liú"
means wishing Wú and Shǔ to each be a separate state;
"the affection is deep like that of Lǔ and Wèi"
refers to the brothers.
Héng,
pronounced hù dēng.
On Jiǎzǐ,
Nánpíng Wáng Kè, leading civil and military officials, presented a memorial proposing to appoint Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì as Chancellor,
to oversee all governmental affairs;
Yì refused.
Wèi Chancellor Tàizì constructed a bridge from Hóngnóng,
crossed the Hé River,
and reached Jiànzhōu.
On Bǐngyín,
the Qí ruler personally led his troops out to encamp at Dōngchéng.
This was the Dōngchéng of Jìnyáng.
Jiāng,
pronounced jí liàng.
He sighed:
