Gù Kuàng’s (顧況) collected works from the Táng (唐) dynasty contain a poem titled “Tí Língshān Sì” (題靈山寺詩),
with a note below: Zhànniǎo (戰鳥) is probably Zhànniǎo Qí (戰鳥圻),
which later became Língshān Sì (靈山寺).
Zǐjiàn (子鑒) was shocked and afraid,
and fled back to Huáinán (淮南).
Huáinán (淮南) is now the region of Dāngtú (當塗) in Tàipíng Zhōu (太平州).
7 Hóu Jǐng’s (侯景) Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) Xiè Dárén (謝答仁) attacked Liú Shénmào (劉神茂) at Dōngyáng (東陽).
Chéng Língxǐ (程靈洗) and Zhāng Biāo (張彪) both marshaled their troops to rescue him.
Shénmào (神茂) wanted to claim the credit for himself,
so he refused,
encamping at Xiàhuái (下淮).
Someone said to Shénmào (神茂):
“The enemy excels at open-field combat.
The ground at Xiàhuái (下淮) is flat,
open to attack from all sides.
It’s better to occupy Qīlǐ Lài (七里瀨).”
Qīlǐ Lài (七里瀨) is in Tónglú Xiàn (桐廬縣);
it is over forty li from Jiàndé (建德)
and adjoins Yánlíng Lài (嚴陵瀨).
He did not follow the advice.
Many of Shénmào’s (神茂) junior officers were northerners
and not loyal to Shénmào (神茂).
Separate generals Wáng Yè (王曄) and Lì Tōng (酈通) both held outer camps
and surrendered to Dárén (答仁).
Liú Guīyì (劉歸義) and Yǐn Sīhé (尹思合) and others abandoned the city and fled.
Shénmào (神茂) was isolated and precarious.
On the day Xīnwèi (辛未),
he also surrendered to Dárén (答仁).
Dárén (答仁) sent him to Jiànkāng (建康).
8 On the day Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) and others arrived at Wúhú (蕪湖).
Hóu Jǐng’s (侯景) defending general Zhāng Hēi (張黑) abandoned the city and fled.
When Jǐng (景) heard of this,
he was greatly alarmed.
He issued an edict pardoning the Prince of Xiāngdōng Yì (湘東王繹) and Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) of their crimes,
which everyone laughed at.
Hóu Zǐjiàn (侯子鑒) occupied the Nánzhōu (南洲) of Gūshú (姑孰) to resist the western army.
Jǐng (景) sent his partisans Shǐ Ānhé (史安和) and others with two thousand soldiers to assist him.
In the third month,
on the first day, Jǐsì (己巳),
Jǐng (景) issued an edict stating he wished to go to Gūshú (姑孰 himself.
He also sent someone to warn Zǐjiàn (子鑒), saying:
“The westerners are skilled in naval warfare.
Do not contend with them directly.
Rèn Yuē’s (任約) defeat last year
was precisely due to this.”
Last year, Jǐng (景) himself was also defeated in a naval battle against Xú Wénshèng (徐文盛) and fled,
not just Rèn Yuē (任約),
which is why he was afraid.
為 (wèi),
read as yú wěi.
“They can certainly be defeated,
but you should just establish your camp on the shore,
and draw your ships into the inlet to await them.”
Zǐjiàn (子鑒) then abandoned his boats and went ashore,
closing his camp and not coming out.
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) and others camped at Wúhú (蕪湖) for over ten days.
Jǐng’s (景) partisans were greatly pleased,
and informed Jǐng (景):
“The western army fears our strength
and is about to flee.
If we don’t attack,
we will lose them.”
Jǐng (景) then ordered Zǐjiàn (子鑒) again to prepare for a naval battle.
On the day Dīngchǒu (丁丑),
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) arrived at Gūshú (姑孰).
Zǐjiàn (子鑒) led over ten thousand infantry and cavalry across the island
and challenged them from the shore.
He also loaded a thousand 鵃䑠 (zhōuyì) boats with warriors.
Lèipiān (類篇) says: 鵃䑠 (zhōuyì)
describes long boats.
Yùpiān (玉篇) says: 鵃䑠 (zhōuyì)
are small boats.
Jíyùn (集韻): 鵃 (zhōu),
read as dīng liǎo.
䑠 (yì),
read as lǎng niǎo.
According to Wáng Sēngbiàn Zhuàn (王僧辯傳): 鵃䑠 (zhōuyì),
carried soldiers within.
Each side had eighty oars,
and the oarsmen were all Yuè (越) people.
They moved back and forth for quick attacks,
swifter than wind and lightning.
They are similar to today’s naval scouts.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Diǎnlüè (典略)
writes
“a thousand Wūquè Fǎng (烏鵲舫)”.
Now following Liáng Shū (梁書).
He left large ships moored along both banks.
Zǐjiàn’s (子鑒) troops thought the naval force was retreating
and rushed out to pursue them.
The large ships cut off their retreat,
beating drums and shouting loudly.
They engaged in battle in the middle of the river.
Zǐjiàn (子鑒) was utterly defeated,
with several thousand soldiers drowning.
Zǐjiàn (子鑒) barely escaped with his life.
He gathered his scattered troops and fled back to Jiànkāng (建康),
occupying Dōngfǔ (東府).
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) left Hǔchén Jiāngjūn (虎臣將軍) Zhuāngqiū Huìdá (莊丘慧達) to guard Gūshú (姑孰),
and led his army forward.
The Líyáng (歷陽) garrison surrendered.
When Jǐng (景) heard of Zǐjiàn’s (子鑒) defeat,
he was greatly terrified.
Tears streamed down his face,
and he pulled the quilt over himself and lay down.
After a long while, he finally got up,
sighing:
“I have mistakenly killed myself!”
On the *gēngchén* day,
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) led the various armies to Zhānggōng Zhōu (張公洲).
Zhānggōng Zhōu (張公洲)
is Càizhōu (蔡州).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Diǎnlǜe* (典略) writes
“*wùyín* (戊寅).”
We now follow the *Tàiqīng Jì* (太清紀).
On the *xīnsì* day,
they entered the Huái River (淮) with the tide,
advancing to before Chánlíng Sì (禪靈寺).
Chánlíng Sì (禪靈寺)
was built by Qí Wǔdì (齊武帝).
He ordered the rafts and seagoing junks in the Huái River (淮) to be brought,
weighted them with stones,
and blocked the mouth of the Huái River (淮);
along the Huái River (淮), they built a city,
from Shítóu (石頭) to Zhūquè Jiē (朱雀街),
over ten *lǐ* long,
with towers and battlements connecting one another.
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) asked Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先) for advice.
Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先) said:
“Previously, Liǔ Zhònglǐ (柳仲禮) with several hundred thousand troops sat across the water,
Wéi Càn (韋粲) was at Qīngxī (青溪),
but ultimately did not cross the bank.
When the rebels climbed high and looked down,
they saw everything inside and out,
thus they were able to defeat our forces.
This event is found in volume 162, Wǔdì (武帝) Tàiqīng (太清) 3rd year.
We must cross to the north bank.
If the generals cannot face the vanguard,
Bàxiān (霸先) requests to go first and set up palisades.”
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Bàxiān (霸先) built palisades at Luòxīng Shān (落星山) west of Shítóu (石頭).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Chén Shū* (陳書) says,
“built palisades horizontally along the ridge.”
We now follow the *Diǎnlǜe* (典略).
It stretched directly out to the northwest of Shítóu (石頭).
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) feared that the western road would be cut off,
so he personally led Hóu Zǐjiàn (侯子鑒) and others to also build five forts northeast of Shítóu (石頭) to block the main road.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) ordered Wáng Wěi (王偉) to guard Táichéng (臺城).
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) killed Xiāngdōng Wáng Shìzǐ Fāngzhū (湘東王世子方諸) and the former Píngdōng Jiāngjūn Dù Yòu'ān (平東將軍杜幼安).
Líu Shénmào (劉神茂) arrived in Jiànkāng (建康).
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) ordered a large crusher to be made,
first feeding in his feet,
chopping him inch by inch,
until his head.
Líu Shénmào (劉神茂) had initially guided Hóu Jǐng (侯景) to capture Shòuyáng (壽陽),
and when he crossed the river,
Líu Shénmào (劉神茂) again served as his henchman.
The disaster in the southeast
was truly caused by Shénmào (神茂);
his death came late!
The “large crusher” means
a large chopper knife,
activated like a pestle,
to make him step on it.
*Duì* (碓)
is pronounced *dū nèi* (都內).
Thus he was spared disaster.
On the *dīnghài* day,
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) advanced his army north of Zhāotí Sì (招提寺).
Zhāotí Sì (招提寺) is north of Shítóuchéng (石頭城).
Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先) said:
“We are many, the rebels are few;
we should divide their forces
to overpower the weak.
Why gather their sharpest edge
and let them fight to the death against us!”
He then ordered the various generals to deploy their troops separately.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) charged Jiāngjūn Wáng Sēngzhì's (將軍王僧志) formation.
Wáng Sēngzhì (王僧志) recoiled slightly.
Bàxiān (霸先) sent Jiāngjūn Ānlù Xú Dù (將軍安陸徐度) with two thousand archers to cut off their rear horizontally.
The power of crossbow arrows
can reach far,
cutting off their rear horizontally,
wherever the arrowheads reached,
the enemy would surely be startled and retreat.
Bàxiān (霸先), along with Wáng Lín (王琳) and Dù Kān (杜龕), attacked them with iron cavalry.
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) followed with a large army.
Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) forces were defeated and retreated,
occupying their palisade.
Kān (龕)
was Dù Àn's (杜岸) nephew.
Dù Àn (杜岸) died during the troubles between Jīng (荊) and Yōng (雍) in Tàiqīng (太清) 3rd year.
Kān (龕)
was the son of Dù Àn's (杜岸) elder brother Cén (岑).
Kān (龕)
is pronounced *kǔ hán* (苦含).
They opened the north gate and surrendered.
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) entered and occupied it.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) fought to the death against Bàxiān (霸先).
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) led over a hundred cavalry,
abandoning his spear and wielding a saber,
charging the formations left and right;
the formations did not budge.
His forces then completely collapsed.
The various armies pursued the fleeing enemy to Xīmíng Mén (西明門).
Xīmíng Mén (西明門)
was the western central gate of Jiànkāng's (建康) outer city.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) reached the palace gate,
not daring to enter the platform.
He summoned Wáng Wěi (王偉) and reproached him, saying:
“You made me emperor,
today you have misled me!”
Wáng Wěi (王偉) could not reply
and hid behind the palace gate.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) wanted to flee.
Wáng Wěi (王偉) seized the reins and admonished him, saying:
“Since ancient times, has there ever been a rebel against the Son of Heaven?
The palace guards
are still enough for one battle.
If we abandon this,
where will we go?”
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) said:
“I once defeated Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝)
(see volume 156, Wǔdì (武帝) Zhōngdàtōng (中大通) 6th year).
*Bài* (敗)
is pronounced *bǔ mài* (補邁).
See volume 152, Dàtōng (大通) 2nd year.
I crossed the river and pacified Táichéng (臺城),
making Liǔ Zhònglǐ (柳仲禮) surrender as easily as turning my hand.
See volume 162, Tàiqīng (太清) 3rd year.
*Xiáng* (降)
is pronounced *hù jiāng* (戶江).”
He then looked up at the stone gate towers
and sighed for a long time.
He put his two sons born in Jiāngdōng (江東) into a leather bag,
hung it behind his saddle,
and fled east with Fáng Shìguì (房世貴) and over a hundred cavalry,
intending to join Xiè Dárén (謝答仁) in Wú (吳).
Hóu Zǐjiàn (侯子鑒), Wáng Wěi (王偉), and Chén Qìng (陳慶) fled to Zhūfāng (朱方).
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) ordered Péi Zhīhéng (裴之橫) and Dù Kān (杜龕) to garrison Dù Mǔzhái (杜姥宅).
Dù Zé (杜崱) entered and occupied Táichéng (臺城).
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) did not restrain his soldiers,
who plundered the residents.
Men and women were naked,
from Shítóu (石頭) to the East City,
crying filled the roads.
That night,
soldiers accidentally started a fire,
burning Tàijí Diàn (太極殿) and the treasures, feather ornaments, and carriages of the East and West Halls, leaving nothing.
The historian says Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) managed his army without discipline,
losing the intent of punishing the guilty, comforting the people, and clearing the imperial precincts.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) ordered Hóu Tián (侯瑱) and others to lead five thousand elite armored troops to pursue Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
Wáng Kè (王克) and Yuán Luó (元羅) and other former officials from inside the platform welcomed Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) on the road.
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) comforted Wáng Kè (王克), saying:
“How bitter
to serve a barbarian ruler.”
Wáng Kè (王克) could not reply.
He then asked:
“Where are the imperial seals and ribbons?”
Wáng Kè (王克) pondered for a long time and said:
“Zhào Píngyuán (趙平原) took them away.”
Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) Shìzhōng Zhào Sīxián (侍中趙思賢) concurrently held the title of Píngyuán Tàishǒu (平原太守).
“The Wáng (王) family, a noble clan for a hundred generations,
fell in a single morning.”
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) welcomed the *Zǐgōng* (梓宮) of Tàizōng (太宗) to the imperial court,
and led the various officials in wailing and stamping their feet as per ritual.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Sēngbiàn and others submitted a memorial urging the emperor to ascend the throne,
and welcomed the capital to Jiànyè.
Xiāngdōng Wáng replied:
"The long whale of Huáihǎi,
though it is said to have surrendered;
the short fox of Xiāngyáng,
has not yet fully changed its ways.
The *Yǔgòng* states: 'Between the Huái and the sea is Yángzhōu.'
The long whale
refers to Hóu Jǐng.
In ancient times, when a state was attacked,
its whales and *ní* (a type of dragon) were captured for a great slaughter.
Yuèyáng Wáng Chá occupies Xiāngyáng
and is an enemy of Xiāngdōng,
hence he is called a 'short fox.'
A short fox
is a *yù*,
which shoots sand at people,
and those hit by it die.
The *Yì* says: 'The petty man changes his face.'
You may then deliberate on this."
The *Ěryǎ* states: "Spring is called Qīngyáng,
summer is called Zhūmíng,
autumn is called Báicáng,
winter is called Xuányīng;
when the four seasons are harmonious, it is called Yùzhú."
The commentary explains: "This describes a time of great peace,
when the four energies are harmonious and smooth,
leading to auspicious events.
Saying spring is Qīngyáng
means that when the energy of spring is harmonious, it is green and warm and bright.
Saying summer is Zhūmíng
means that when the energy of summer is harmonious, it is red and bright and clear.
Saying autumn is Báicáng
means that when the energy of autumn is harmonious, it is white and gathers and stores.
Saying winter is Xuányīng
means that when the energy of winter is harmonious, it is black and pure and brilliant.
Saying that when the four seasons are harmonious, it is called Yùzhú,
means that the harmonious energies of the four seasons,
warm, moist, bright, and illuminating,
are therefore called Yùzhú."
Lǐ Xún said: "The ruler's virtue is beautiful like jade and bright like a candle."
The *Pìngyì* states: "The *jūnzǐ* compares his virtue to jade."
At this time, if the ruler's virtuous radiance moves within,
then harmonious energy responds without,
and speaking comprehensively,
it is called Yùzhú.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Guō Yuánjiàn, the Administrator of Nányǎnzhōu,
Guō Zhèngmǎi, the garrison commander of Qínjùn,
Hóu Jǐng designated Guǎnglíng as Nányǎnzhōu, following the old system of the Southern Dynasties.
Guō Zǐzhòng, acting for Nánxúzhōushì,
all surrendered with their cities.
When Sēngbiàn departed from Jiānglíng,
he presented a memorial to Xiāngdōng Wáng, saying:
"After the bandits are pacified,
the successor ruler will enjoy great blessings.
I am unsure what kind of ritual should be performed?"
The King said:
"Within the six gates,
exert military might yourself."
The six gates of Táichéng were Dàsīmǎmén, Wànchūnmén, Dōnghuámén, Xīhuámén, Tàiyángmén, and Chéngmíngmén.
"As for the plan to subdue the bandits,
I take it as my responsibility.
As for the matter of Chéng Jì,
I ask that another person be appointed."
Chéng Jì assassinated Wèi Gāoguìxiāng Gōng.
Wáng Sēngbiàn wished to avoid the bad reputation of assassinating a ruler,
hence he said this.
He was to be dealt with.
When Jǐng was defeated,
Tàizōng had already died.
Yùzhāng Wáng Dòng and his two younger brothers, Qiáo and Jiū, supported each other out of a secret chamber.
They met Dù Zè on the road,
who removed their chains.
The two younger brothers said:
"Today we are finally free from a violent death!"
Dòng said:
"Reliance and concealment are hard to know;
I am still fearful!"
Jiǎ Yì's "Fú Fù" states: "Calamity leans on fortune;
fortune hides calamity."
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
they encountered Zhū Mǎichén.
He called them,
they boarded a boat and drank together.
Before they finished,
they all sank into the water.
Sēngbiàn sent Chén Bàxiān to lead troops to Guǎnglíng to accept the surrender of Guō Yuánjiàn and others,
and also sent envoys to comfort them.
Many generals privately sent others to secretly demand horses and weapons.
At this time, Hóu Zǐjiàn crossed the river to Guǎnglíng
and said to Yuánjiàn and others:
"We
are sworn enemies of Liáng.
How can we face its lord again?
It would be better to surrender to the north,
and we can return to our hometowns."
So they all surrendered to Qí.
When Bàxiān arrived at Ōuyáng,
Qí Xíngtái Xīn Shù had already occupied Guǎnglíng.
Wáng Wěi and Hóu Zǐjiàn became separated.
Huáng Gōngxǐ, the garrison commander of Zhídú, captured him
and sent him to Jiànkāng.
Sūn Shèng's *Jìn Chūnqiū* states: "Zhídú is in Fāngshān."
Wáng Ānshí's poem:
"The mountain winds around Zhídú, emptying into the Huái estuary."
Lù Yóu said: "Zhídú
was opened by the Sūn clan of Wú."
Wēn Tíngyún's poem "Passing the Mausoleum of Wú Jǐngdì":
"Vainly opened three thousand *lǐ* of Zhídú,
when did the blue canopy ever reach Luòyáng?"
According to this, Hóu Zǐjiàn and Wáng Wěi had already crossed the river,
so this is not the Zhídú of Fāngshān.
Shěn Yuē's *Zhì* states: "Xúyí Administrator's jurisdiction includes Zhídú,
where Jìn Āndì established a county today."
"You were a bandit prime minister,
unable to die for your principles,
but seek to live among the weeds?"
Wěi said:
"Rise and fall are fate.
If the Hàn emperor had followed my words earlier,
how could you, Your Excellency, be here today?"
This refers to the fall of Táichéng,
Sēngbiàn's surrender,
and Hóu Jǐng's release and return to Jìnglíng,
which led to today.
Wěi's words here
also served to shame Sēngbiàn.
He then
spat in his face.
Wěi said:
"You do not read books;
you are not worth conversing with."
Sēngbiàn
was ashamed and withdrew. Sēngbiàn ordered Xú Sìhuī, the Administrator of Luózhōu, to garrison Zhūfāng.
On the *rénchén* day,
Hóu Jǐng arrived at Jìnlíng,
gathered Tián Qiān's remaining troops.
Tián Qiān had attacked Liú Shénmào to the east,
and had remaining troops in Jìnlíng.
He then headed east to Wújùn.
11. Summer,
Fourth month,
The Qí sovereign sent the Grand Commander Pān Lè and Guō Yuánjiàn to lead 50,000 troops to attack Yángpíng,
and captured it.
12. Wáng Sēngbiàn proposed that Chén Bàxiān garrison Jīngkǒu.
*Kǎoyì* states: "Chén Jì:
'Gāozǔ returned after receiving Guō Yuánjiàn.
Sēngbiàn proposed to Gāozǔ that he garrison Jīngkǒu.'"
According to this, at that time Xú Sìhuī was the Administrator of Nánxúzhōu;
Bàxiān merely commanded troops to garrison Jīngkǒu,
and was not yet the Administrator.
13. Jǐ, Prince of Wǔlíng, Administrator of Yìzhōu and Grand Commandant,
possessed considerable military strategy.
He was in Shǔ for seventeen years,
opening up Níngzhōu and Yuèsuí to the south,
connecting to Zīlíng and Tǔyùhún to the west.
Internally, he reformed the policies of agriculture, sericulture, salt, and iron,
and externally, he facilitated trade and distant profits,
thus he was able to accumulate wealth and resources.
His weapons and armor were abundant,
and he had 8,000 horses.
Hearing that Hóu Jǐng had captured Táichéng
and that Xiāngdōng Wáng was about to suppress him,
he said to his subordinates:
"How can a literary scholar like the Seventh Official
bring order and salvation?"
Xiāngdōng was the seventh among his brothers,
hence he was called the "Seventh Official."
Jǐ considered this an auspicious sign for himself.
On the *yǐsì* day,
he ascended the imperial throne,
changed the era name to Tiānzhèng,
and enfeoffed his son Yuánzhào as Crown Prince,
Yuánzhèng as Xīyáng Wáng,
Yuánmǎn as Jìnglíng Wáng,
Yuánpǔ as Qiáo Wáng,
and Yuánsù as Yídū Wáng.
He appointed Huī, Marquis of Yǒngfēng and Administrator of Bāxī and Zǐtóng Commanderies, as Grand General of the Expedition to the West and Administrator of Yìzhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Prince of Qínjùn.
Wú established Yǒngfēng County,
belonging to Shǐ'ān Commandery.
Huī,
pronounced *xū wéi*.
He did not follow.
Sēnglüè was Sēngbiàn's younger brother;
Pēng
was Mǐan's nephew by his paternal cousin.
Xú Mǐan
was a worthy prime minister in early Liáng.
"From"
is pronounced *cái yòng*.
18. Yáng GānYùn (楊乾運) reached JiànBěi (劍北).
JiànBěi (劍北)
is north of JiànGé (劍閣).
He greatly defeated GānYùn (乾運) at BáiMǎ (白馬),
displayed the captives and severed heads under the walls of NánZhèng (南鄭),
and furthermore sent someone to insult YíFēng Hóu Xún (宜豐侯循).
Xún (循) was enraged,
led out troops to engage in battle,
and Grand Coordinator Yáng Shào (楊紹) ambushed them,
killing and wounding almost all.
Liú Fán (劉璠) returned to west of BáiMǎ (白馬).
Liú Fán (劉璠) returned from ChéngDū (成都).
According to Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) Record: In MiǎnYáng (沔陽) County, HuáYáng (華陽) Commandery, there is BáiMǎ (白馬) City.
According to the Biography of YíFēng Hóu Xún (宜豐侯循): Fán (璠) was captured at BōZhǒng (嶓冢).
BōZhǒng (嶓冢) County also belonged to HuáYáng (華陽) Commandery.
According to the Record of the Five Dynasties: Xī (西) County of HànZhōng (漢中) Commandery was formerly called BōZhǒng (嶓冢).
He was sent to ChángĀn (長安).
Grand Tutor Tài (泰) had long heard of his name
and treated him like an old friend.
At that time, NánZhèng (南鄭) had not been captured for a long time.
Wǔ (武) requested to slaughter its inhabitants,
and Tài (泰) was about to grant permission.
Fán (璠) pleaded for them to the court.
The court
refers to the Wèi (魏) court.
Cháo (朝)
is pronounced zhí yáo.
It was not permitted;
Fán (璠) wept and pleaded ceaselessly.
Tài (泰) said:
“One serving others should be like this.”
Then he acceded to his request.
19. In the fifth month,
on the GēngWǔ (庚午) day,
Minister of Works NánPíng Wáng Kè (南平王恪) and others again urged him to ascend the throne.
XiāngDōng Wáng (湘東王) still refused,
and sent Palace Attendant FēngChéng Hóu Tài (豐城侯泰) to visit the imperial mausoleum.
According to Shěn Yuē’s (沈約) Record: FēngChéng (豐城) County in YùZhāng (豫章) was established by Wú (吳),
called FùChéng (富城),
and changed its name by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝).
The KǎoYì (考異) states: The LiángShū (梁書) places this in the fourth month,
with the official title Minister of Works.
The TàiQīng Jì (太清紀) places it in this month,
with the official title Grand Tutor.
Now following the LiángShū (梁書).
On the WùYín (戊寅) day,
Hóu Jǐng’s (侯景) head first arrived at JiāngLíng (江陵).
It was displayed in the market for three days,
then boiled and lacquered,
and delivered to the imperial armory.
On the GēngChén (庚辰) day,
NánPíng Wáng Kè (南平王恪) was appointed Inspector of YángZhōu (揚州).
On the JiǎShēn (甲申) day,
Wáng SēngBiàn (王僧辯) was appointed Minister of Education and Grand General Who Guards the State,
and enfeoffed as the Duke of ChángNíng (長寧公).
The Grand General Who Guards the State
was one of the 240 ranks established by Liáng (梁),
its class being extremely high.
SēngBiàn (僧辯) had great merit,
and was certainly enfeoffed as the Duke of ChángNíng (長寧) Commandery.
ChángNíng (長寧) Commandery
was established by Emperor Ān of Jìn (晉安帝),
and belonged to JīngZhōu (荊州).
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of ChángChéng (長城) County.
This was a reward for his achievement in pacifying Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
BàXiān (霸先)
was a native of ChángChéng (長城) County.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: ChángChéng (長城) County in HúZhōu (湖州),
King Hélǘ (闔閭) of Wú (吳) sent his younger brother FūGài (夫概) to build a city there,
which was narrow and long.
It was established by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝) in the third year of TàiKāng (太康).
On the YǐYǒu (乙酉) day,

Wáng Wěi (王偉), the Director of the Department of State Affairs, Lǚ JìLüè (呂季略), the Left Minister of the Common People, Zhōu ShíZhēn (周石珍), the Minister of the Lesser Treasury, and Yán Dǎn (嚴亶), the Palace Attendant, who were appointed by Hóu Jǐng (侯景), were executed in the market.
Zhào BóChāo (趙伯超) and Fú ZhīMìng (伏知命) starved to death in prison.
Xiè DáRén (謝答仁) was not disrespectful to TàiZōng (太宗),
so he was specially pardoned.
Wáng Wěi (王偉) composed a five-hundred-character poem in prison.
A five-hundred-character poem
is what is now a fifty-rhyme poem.
Shàng (上)
is pronounced shí zhǎng.
He was about to be pardoned;
but someone who envied him
said to the King:
“The proclamation Wěi (偉) wrote the other day was excellent.”
The King asked for it and looked at it.
The proclamation read:
“Xiàng Yǔ (項羽), with his double pupils,
still suffered defeat at WūJiāng (烏江);
XiāngDōng (湘東), with one eye,
how can he be accepted by the Red County (China proper)!”
The King was greatly enraged,
nailed his tongue to a pillar,
cut open his abdomen, minced his flesh, and killed him.
20. On the BǐngXū (丙戌) day,
HúSī Zhāo (斛斯昭), Inspector of HéZhōu (合州) for Qí (齊), attacked LìYáng (歷陽)
and captured it.
21. On the DīngHài (丁亥) day,
an order was issued,
stating that
“now that Wáng Wěi (王偉) and others are dead,
all other former nobles and officials who were forced to survive,
and brave warriors and distinguished figures who concealed their brilliance to escape,
shall not be questioned.”
22. Lǔ XīDá (魯悉達), a commoner from FúFēng (扶風),
gathered his fellow villagers to protect XīnCài (新蔡).
According to the ChénShū (陳書): Lǔ XīDá (魯悉達),
a native of FúFēng (扶風),
his grandfather to XīDá (悉達) all served Qí (齊) and Liáng (梁).
According to Shěn Yuē’s (沈約) SòngZhì (宋志): The commanderies administered by JiāngZhōu (江州) included NánXīnCài (南新蔡) Commandery.
It does not mention the location of the provisional settlement,
but only states that it is over 1376 *lǐ* by water from the capital.
Based on the approximate water distance,
NánXīnCài (南新蔡) Commandery should be located within the current QíZhōu (蘄州) area.
According to the Record of the Five Dynasties: HuángMéi (黃梅) County in QíZhōu (蘄Zhōu)
was formerly called YǒngXīng (永興).
In the early KāiHuáng (開皇) era of Suí (隋),
it was renamed XīnCài (新蔡),
probably named after NánXīnCài (南新蔡) Commandery.
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: HuángMéi (黃梅) County,
Sòng (宋) divided and established XīnCài (新蔡) Commandery.
At that time, there was famine and unrest in JiāngDōng (江東),
and eight or nine tenths of the people starved to death.
The surviving commoners carried their old and young to him.
XīDá (悉達) distributed grain provisions,
saving many people,
and gathered JìnXī (晉熙) and four other commanderies,
taking possession of all their lands.
He ordered his younger brother GuǎngDá (廣達) to lead troops to follow Wáng SēngBiàn (王僧辯) in suppressing Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
When Jǐng (景) was pacified,
XīDá (悉達) was appointed Inspector of BěiJiāngZhōu (北江州).
According to Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) Record: Emperor Wǔ of Liáng (梁武帝) established BěiJiāngZhōu (北江州),
governing from LùChéng (鹿城) Pass,
and administering YìYáng (義陽), QíChāng (齊昌), XīnChāng (新昌), LiángĀn (梁安), and QíXīng (齊興) Commanderies.
According to the Record of the Five Dynasties: MùLán (木蘭) County in HuángZhōu (黃州),
Liáng (梁) established BěiJiāngZhōu (北江州).
Táng (唐) merged MùLán (木蘭) into HuángGāng (黃岡) County.
23. The Qí (齊) ruler sent his Palace Attendant Cáo WénJiǎo (曹文皎) and others to make an alliance.
XiāngDōng Wáng (湘東王) sent Palace Attendant Liǔ Huī (柳暉) and others to respond,
and also announced the pacification of Hóu Jǐng (侯景);
he also sent Gentleman-in-Waiting Wèi Yàn (魏彥) to inform Wèi (魏).
24. The Qí (齊) ruler sent Pān Lè (潘樂) and Guō YuánJiàn (郭元建) to lead troops to besiege QínJùn (秦郡).
Traveling Department Director Xīn Shù (辛術) advised:
“The imperial court maintains continuous communication with XiāngDōng Wáng (湘東王).
YángPíng (陽平) was Hóu Jǐng’s (侯景) territory,
so taking it was acceptable;
but now Wáng SēngBiàn (王僧辯) has already sent Yán ChāoDá (嚴超達) to guard QínJùn (秦郡),
how can we justly contend for it again!
Moreover, the floods are about to descend,
it is better to withdraw the army.”
He did not follow.
Chén BàXiān (陳霸先) ordered his separate general Xú Dù (徐度) to lead troops to assist QínJùn (秦郡) in firm defense.
The Qí (齊) army, numbering seventy thousand,
attacked very fiercely.
Wáng SēngBiàn (王僧辯) sent Left Guard General Dù Zè (杜崱) to relieve it,
and BàXiān (霸先) also came from ŌuYáng (歐陽) to join them;
they engaged YuánJiàn (元建) in a great battle at ShìLín (士林),
and utterly defeated them.
ShìLín (士林) is within the borders of LùHé (六合) County.
Over a thousand people were captured alive.
YuánJiàn (元建) gathered his remaining troops and fled north;
as relations were still good,
they did not pursue relentlessly.
Xīn Shù (辛術) was promoted to Minister of Personnel.
Since Wèi (魏) moved its capital to Yè (鄴),
in the important position of grand selection,
several famous individuals held it.
The selection by the Ministry of Personnel was considered a grand selection.
Xuǎn (選)
is pronounced xū juàn.
Yuán ShúDé (袁叔德) was meticulous and cautious,
but what he overlooked was trivial.
Yáng Yīn (楊愔) was refined and eloquent,
but his selection of scholars was flawed by ostentation.
Only Shù (術) valued integrity and clarity in his nature,
always selecting scholars based on their talent and capacity,
demanding substance to match reputation,
considering both new and old candidates,
always promoting those from the bureaucracy,
and not neglecting those from established families.
Compared with those before and after,
his method was the most balanced.
25 Wèi’s Dáxī Wǔ sent Shàngshū Zuǒcéng Liǔ Dàiwéi into Nánzhèng,
and persuaded Yífēng Hóu Xún, saying:
“What Your Excellency relies on is danger (i.e., natural defenses),
what you depend on is support,
and what you protect are the people.
Now the royal army has advanced deep,
the formidable defenses you rely on are not sufficient to secure you;
Báimǎ has been defeated and fled,
and the chieftains have not advanced.
This refers to Yáng Qiányùn.
Qiú,
cí qiū fān.
The long siege has closed in on all sides,
and the people under your command cannot be protected.
Moreover, your home court is in chaos and disorder,
the altars of soil and grain have no master;
for whom do you wish to be loyal?
Would it not be better to turn misfortune into fortune,
and let blessings flow to your descendants!”
Xún then requested to surrender.
Dàiwéi
was the son of Qìng.
Liǔ Qìng is seen in volume 161, Wǔdì Tàiqīng 2nd year.
[Someone] requested to attack him,
but Dàdūdū Hèlián Dá said:
“To capture a city without fighting
is the best strategy.
How can we covet their women and children,
or greedily desire their wealth and goods,
and not cherish the lives of the people!
Moreover, observing their soldiers and horses are still strong,
and the city defenses are still solid,
even if we conquer it by attack,
both sides will be harmed;
it would be like a trapped beast still fighting.”
Zuǒzhuàn, words of Wú Fūgài Wáng.
Wǔ said:
“Your words are correct.”
So he accepted Xún’s surrender,
captured twenty thousand men and women, and returned.
Thereupon, all of Jiànběi submitted to Wèi.
26 In the sixth month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
the Qí lord returned to Yè;
on the Yǐmǎo day,
he again went to Jìnyáng.
27 On the Gēngyín day,
Ānnán Hóu Fāngjǔ was established as the Crown Prince.
28 Qí sent Sànqí Chángshì Xiè Jìqīng to congratulate on the pacification of Hóu Jǐng.
29 The governor of Héngzhōu, Wáng Huáimíng, rebelled,
and the governor of Guǎngzhōu, Xiāo Bó, attacked and pacified him.
30 Qí’s government was troublesome and its taxes heavy,
so the people north of the Jiāng did not happily submit to Qí.
Their heroes repeatedly requested troops from Wáng Sēngbiàn,
but Sēngbiàn, being on good terms with Qí,
refused them all.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Zhū Shèng and other resettled people of Guǎnglíng
Resettled people:
those who were not originally from Guǎnglíng but resided there temporarily.
conspired to ambush and kill Qí’s governor Wēn Zhòngyōng,
and sent an envoy to seek aid from Chén Bàxiān,
saying they had already captured its outer city.
Bàxiān sent a messenger to inform Sēngbiàn,
Sēngbiàn said:
“The truth or falsity of human nature
is not easily fathomable.
If they have truly captured the outer city,
then urgent support is needed;
if not,
there’s no need to advance the army.”
Before the messenger returned,
Bàxiān had already crossed the Jiāng,
so Sēngbiàn ordered Wǔzhōu governor Dù Zè and others to assist him.
At that time, Shèng’s conspiracy was exposed,
so Bàxiān took advantage and advanced to besiege Guǎnglíng.
31 In the eighth month,
Huáng Zhòngbǎo, a person from Ānkāng in Wèi, rebelled,
attacked Wèixīng,
captured its prefect Liǔ Huì,
and advanced to besiege Dōngliángzhōu.
Liáng established Nánliángzhōu in Xīchéng Jùn,
Xī Wèi changed it to Dōngliángzhōu;
Xīchéng
was the seat of the ancient Wèixīng Jùn.
Wèi Shōu’s Zhì says: In Hòu Wèi, Tàiyán 5th year,
Wèixīng Jùn was separately established within Shàngluò Jùn’s boundaries,
containing Dàiyángtíng Xiàn,
belonging to Luòzhōu;
Luòzhōu
was later changed to Shāngzhōu.
Huì refused to comply and died.
Huì
was the younger brother of Qiú.
Liǔ Qiú,
elder brother of Liǔ Qìng,
is seen in volume 251, Wǔdì Dàtóng 3rd year.
32 Wǔlíng Wáng Jǐ raised an army and traveled eastward down the outer water,
appointing Yǒngfēng Hóu Huī as the governor of Yìzhōu,
to guard Chéngdū,
and made his son Yídū Wáng Yuánsù his deputy.
33 In the ninth month,
on the Jiǎxū day,
Sīkōng Nánpíng Wáng Kè passed away.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
Wáng Sēngbiàn was appointed as the governor of Yángzhōu.
34 The Qí lord sent a message to Wáng Sēngbiàn and Chén Bàxiān, saying:
“Please lift the siege of Guǎnglíng,
and we will certainly return the two cities of Guǎnglíng and Lìyáng.”
Bàxiān led his troops back to Jīngkǒu,
and over ten thousand people from north of the Jiāng who followed Bàxiān crossed the Jiāng.
Xiāngdōng Wáng appointed Bàxiān as Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and governor of Nánxúzhōu,
and summoned Bàxiān’s heir Chāng.
Bàxiān was enfeoffed as Chángchéng Xiànhóu,
Chāng was his heir.
He appointed Chāng as Sàn
qí Chángshì,
and Xū as Lǐngzhí.
Among the officials of the Liáng imperial guards were the Sīxiāng Lǐngzhí,
which meant leading the guardsmen,
hence the name of the office.
This created a foundation for Chāng and Xū to fall into Wèi.
35 When Yífēng Hóu Xún surrendered to Wèi,
Chancellor Tài promised his return to the south,
but after a long time had not yet sent him.
He casually asked Liú Fán:
“To whom among the ancients can I be compared?”
Fán replied:
“Fán has always considered you to be Tāng and Wǔ,
but what I see today
is not even as good as Huán and Wén!”
Tài said:
“How dare I compare myself to Tāng and Wǔ,
I merely hope to be like Yī and Zhōu.
How can I be not even as good as Huán and Wén!”
Fán replied:
“Qí Huán preserved three fallen states,”
Zuǒzhuàn: Sòng Sīmǎ Zǐyú said: Qí Huán preserved three fallen states to attach them to the feudal lords.
Dù Yù’s commentary says: The three fallen states were
Lǔ, Wèi, and Xíng.
Before he finished speaking,
Tài clapped his hands and said:
“I understand your intention,
you wish to provoke me.”
He then said to Xún:
“Does the King wish to go to Jīng?
What would benefit him?”
Wǔlíng Wáng Jǐ had enfeoffed Xún as Suí Jùn Wáng,
hence he was referred to as King.
Tài treated him with great courtesy and sent him away.
Kǎoyì says: Diǎnlüè states:
“In the tenth month,
on the Yǐwèi day, the first day of the month,
Tàizǔ said to Xún…”
and so on.
According to Tàiqīng Jì,
Xún arrived at Jiānglíng in this month,
and we follow this account.
Xiāngdōng Wáng was suspicious of him,
and sent envoys to observe,
who watched each other along the road;
on the evening of his arrival,
he ordered his property to be plundered,
and the next morning,
Xún reported the surrender of his horses and weapons.
The King then felt at ease,
brought him in,
they wept together,
and appointed Xún as Shìzhōng, Piàojì Jiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
36 In winter,
in the tenth month,
the Qí lord traveled from Jìnyáng to Líshí,
and built a long wall from Huánglú Lǐng
northward to Shèpíng Shù,
over four hundred *lǐ*,
establishing thirty-six garrisons.
This long wall likely started from Táng Shízhōu
and extended northward to the border of Wǔzhōu.
Lú,
pronounced lú.
“Shèpíng”
is written as
“Shèzǐ” in Qí Jì.
According to Húlǜ Jīn Zhuàn: Huánglú Lǐng is east of Wūtū Shù.
37 On the Wùshēn day,
Xiāngdōng Wáng seized the governor of Xiāngzhōu, Wáng Lín, in the palace,
and killed his deputy general Yīn Yàn.
Lín was originally a military family from Kuàijī.
His sisters all entered the royal palace,
so Lín grew up by the king's side.
Lín was fond of bravery,
and the king appointed him a general.
Lín dedicated himself to treating scholars with respect,
and whatever rewards he received
he did not bring into his home.
He commanded ten thousand men,
many of whom were bandits from Jiāng and Huái.
He followed Wáng Sēngbiàn in pacifying Hóu Jǐng,
and his achievements with Dù Kān were ranked first.
While in Jiànkāng,
he relied on royal favor and acted violently,
which Sēngbiàn could not restrain.
Sēngbiàn attributed the burning of the palace
to the soldiers' carelessly leaving fires that burned the Tàijí Diàn and the eastern and western halls.
Wishing to make Lín bear the blame,
he secretly memorialized the king
to request Lín's execution.
The king appointed Lín as the governor of Xiāngzhōu.
Lín suspected misfortune was imminent,
and so he sent his chief clerk Lù Nà to lead his troops to Xiāngzhōu,
while he himself went to Jiānglíng to offer his apologies.
He said to Nà and others:
"If I do not return,
where will you go?"
Zhī (之)
means "to go."
"I would rather die."
They wept and parted.
When he arrived in Jiānglíng,
the king had Lín arrested.
On the day of Xīnyǒu,
Prince Fānglüè was appointed Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
Also, Huáng Luóhàn, the Court Judge, was made Chief Clerk,
and was sent with Zhāng Zài, the Grand Minister of Shipping, to Bālíng
to first take control of Lín's army.
The Wǔdài Zhì says: The Grand Minister of Shipping
was initially the Administrator of the Dūshuǐ Tái in early Liáng.
In the seventh year of Tiānjiān, the name was changed.
His rank was equivalent to that of the Zhōngshū Láng,
and he was the lowest of the high ministers.
He was in charge of boats, waterways, and dikes.
Yet, he was severe and harsh with his subordinates,
and the people of Jīngzhōu detested him as an enemy.
When Luóhàn and others arrived at Lín's army,
Lù Nà and the soldiers all wept
and refused to obey the order.
They seized Luóhàn and Zài.
The king sent the eunuch Chén Mín to deliver an instruction.
Nà, facing Mín, disemboweled Zài,
pulled out his intestines and tied them to a horse's leg,
making it run in circles until
his intestines were completely out and he expired.
He then butchered him,
took out his heart,
and danced, clapping his hands towards it.
Bìanwǔ (抃舞)
means to clap hands and dance.
He spared Huáng Luóhàn because he was clear and cautious.
Nà and his generals led their troops to attack Xiāngzhōu.
At that time, there was no master in the province,
so Nà took control of it.
The dukes, ministers, and regional governors repeatedly urged the King of Xiāngdōng to ascend the throne.
In the eleventh month,
on the day of Bǐngzǐ,
Shìzǔ ascended the imperial throne in Jiānglíng,
changed the era name,
and granted a general amnesty.
The era name Tàiqīng was changed to Chéngshèng.
The Emperor did not ascend the main hall;
the dukes and ministers merely lined up.
Historians say the Emperor could not establish his rule properly from the beginning.
On the day of Dīngchǒu,
Yífēng Hóu Xún was appointed Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
On the day of Jǐmǎo,
the king's heir apparent Fāngjǔ was established as Crown Prince,
and his name was changed to Yuánliáng.
The imperial prince Fāngzhì was made Prince of Jìn'ān,
Fānglüè was made Prince of Shǐ'ān,
and Fāngděng's son Zhuāng was made Prince of Yǒngjiā.
Fāngděng had attacked Xiāngzhōu
but was defeated and died.
Xiūróng
was a title created by Emperor Wèi Wén.
Since the Jìn Dynasty,
it was ranked among the Nine Concubines.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
more than half of the provinces and commanderies defected to Wèi.
From Bālíng down to Jiànkāng,
the Yangtze River was the boundary.
The northern border of Jīngzhōu ended at Wǔníng,

zhōng shì and above, up to shàng dàfū, each doubled the amount;

The Qí ruler personally braved arrows and stones,
fought repeatedly,
and greatly defeated them,
pursuing them as far as Wòyě,
capturing their chieftain.
Shuǐjīngzhù: Yúnzhōng Jùn has Báidào Lǐng and Báidào Chuān.
帥 (shuài),
read as shuài.
騎 (qí),
pronounced qí jì.
酋 (qiú),
pronounced cí qiū.
長 (zhǎng),
pronounced zhī liǎng.
and tens of thousands of cattle and sheep.
On the day Rénshēn,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
23 In the eighth month,
on the day Xīnsì,
Wáng Lín returned to Chángshā from Zhēngchéng.
24 The Qí ruler returned to Yè.
Observing the differences between Buddhism and Daoism,
and wishing to abolish one of them,
he gathered scholars from both traditions
to debate before him.
He then ordered all Daoists to shave their heads and become Buddhist monks;
four people who refused
were killed,
and then they complied with the order.
Consequently, there were no Daoists left in the Qí territory.
The current Daoist text, Tàixiāo Lángshū Jīng, says: One who practices the Great Dao
is called a Dàoshì.
What does "shì" mean?
It means principle (lǐ) and affairs (shì).
When one's body and mind conform to principle,
following only the Dao,
and taking the following of the Dao as one's task,
therefore one is called a Dàoshì.
I observe that this explanation
is a Daoist appropriation of our Confucian classics to expound the meaning of the two characters "Dàoshì."
Although Daoism claims Lǎozǐ as its patriarch,
before the Western Hàn, they never called themselves Dàoshì.
It was only in the Eastern Hàn that figures like Zhāng Dàolíng and Yú Jí appeared,
and in fact, both it and Buddhism arose during the Eastern Hàn period.
25 Initially,
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) and Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先) together exterminated Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
(See Volume 164, Shìzǔ Chéngshèng (世祖承聖) First Year.)
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) arranged for his son Wèi (頠) to marry Bàxiān's (霸先) daughter.
It happened that Sēngbiàn (僧辯) was in mourning for his mother,
so the marriage had not yet taken place.
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) resided in Shítóu Chéng (石頭城),
and Bàxiān (霸先) was in Jīngkǒu (京口).
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) trusted him wholeheartedly.
Wèi's (頠) elder brother Yǐ (顗) repeatedly admonished him,
but he did not listen.
When Sēngbiàn (僧辯) received Zhēnyáng Hóu Yuānmíng (貞陽侯淵明),
Bàxiān (霸先) sent envoys to vehemently dispute it.
After several exchanges,
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) did not comply.
Bàxiān (霸先) secretly sighed
and said to his confidants:
"Wǔdì's (武帝) descendants are numerous,
but only Xiàoyuán (孝元) could avenge and wipe out the shame,
referring to the extermination of Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
Yet he was suddenly deposed!
I and Duke Wáng (王公) were both entrusted with the care of the orphan (emperor),
but Duke Wáng (王公) suddenly changed his plan,
externally relying on the Róngdí (戎狄),
and supporting an unworthy successor.
What is his true intention?!"
Sēngbiàn's (僧辯) establishment of Yuānmíng (淵明)
was illegitimate in name and irrational in speech.
Therefore, the cunning hero could use this as leverage.
At that time, there were reports that the Qí (齊) army was making a large-scale advance towards Shòuchūn (壽春) and would invade.
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) dispatched his record keeper Jiāng Gàn (江旰) to inform Bàxiān (霸先),
instructing him to prepare for it.
Bàxiān (霸先) consequently detained Gàn (旰) in Jīngkǒu (京口)
and raised an army to attack Sēngbiàn (僧辯).
In the ninth month,
on the day Rén Yín (壬寅),
he summoned his generals Hóu Āndū (侯安都), Zhōu Wényù (周文育), and from Ānlù (安陸), Xú Dù (徐度), and from Qiántáng (錢塘), Dù Léng (杜稜) to deliberate.
Léng (稜) considered it difficult.
Bàxiān (霸先) feared that his plan would be leaked,
so he strangled Léng (稜) with a hand towel.
(Today, when people wash,
they use a cloth to wipe their hands,
seven or eight feet long.
This is called a hand towel.)
He then imprisoned him in a separate room.
He divided his officers and soldiers,
distributed gold and silk,
and appointed his nephew, Assistant Literati Officer Tánlǎng (曇朗), to garrison Jīngkǒu (京口),
to manage the affairs of the remaining headquarters.
(Tánlǎng (曇朗) was the son of Bàxiān's (霸先) younger brother Xiūxiān (休先).)
(Tán (曇) is pronounced tú hán.)
Bàxiān (霸先) led his cavalry and infantry from Jiāngchéng Luóluò (江乘羅落) to rendezvous.
(Jiāngchéng Luóluò (江乘羅落) refers to Luóluò Qiáo (羅落橋) in Jiāngchéng Xiàn (江乘縣).
From Jiāngchéng (江乘) to Luóluò Qiáo (羅落橋)
was the main road from Jīngkǒu (京口) to Jiànkāng (建康).
Liú Yù (劉裕) marched against Huán Xuán (桓玄) by this route.)
All set out,
summoning Dù Léng (杜稜) to accompany them.
Only Āndū (安都) and the other four generals knew of his plan.
Outsiders all thought that Jiāng Gàn (江旰) was summoning troops to resist Qí (齊),
and did not find it strange.
On the day Jiǎ Chén (甲辰),
Āndū (安都) led his boats and ships towards Shítóu (石頭).
Bàxiān (霸先) held his horse back and did not advance.
Āndū (安都) was greatly alarmed,
and pursuing Bàxiān (霸先), he cursed him, saying:
"Today we are acting as rebels.
The situation is already set;
we must decide between life and death.
What do you expect by staying behind?
If we fail,
we all die.
Will delaying help us avoid decapitation?"
Bàxiān (霸先) said:
"Āndū (安都) is angry with me!"
Then he advanced.
(Bàxiān (霸先) held his horse back and hesitated
to observe Āndū's (安都) intention.
Seeing that Āndū (安都) was determined to advance,
he then moved forward.)
(Chēn (嗔) is pronounced chāng zhēn,
meaning angry.)
They abandoned their boats and landed.
Shítóu Chéng (石頭城) was connected to hills in the north,
not particularly steep.
Āndū (安都), clad in armor and bearing a long sword,
was lifted by his soldiers
and thrown inside the parapet.
The troops followed him in,
advancing to Sēngbiàn's (僧辯) bedchamber.
Bàxiān's (霸先) troops also entered through the south gate.
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) was still attending to affairs
when a report came from outside that there were soldiers.
Soon, soldiers emerged from within.
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) hurriedly fled,
meeting his son Wèi (頠).
They both exited the chamber,
leading dozens of personal guards to fight fiercely in front of the audience hall.
Overpowered,
they fled up the south gate tower,
bowing and pleading for mercy.
Bàxiān (霸先) wanted to set it on fire,
but Sēngbiàn (僧辯) and Wèi (頠) both descended and were captured.
Bàxiān (霸先) said:
"What crime have I committed that you wish to attack me with the Qí (齊) army?"
And he further said:
"Why were you completely unprepared?"
Sēngbiàn (僧辯) replied:
"I entrusted the northern gate to you.
How can you say I was unprepared?"
(Jīngkǒu (京口) was the northern gate of Jiànkāng (建康).)
Bàxiān (霸先) strangled Sēngbiàn (僧辯) and his son to death.
Afterwards, there were no Qí (齊) troops,
nor was it Bàxiān's (霸先) trickery.
The former Qīngzhōu (青州) Administrator Chéng Língxǐ (程靈洗) of Xīn'ān (新安) led his forces to rescue Sēngbiàn (僧辯),
fighting fiercely at the west gate of Shítóu (石頭),
but his army was defeated.
Bàxiān (霸先) sent envoys to persuade him,
and after a long time, he surrendered.
Bàxiān (霸先) greatly esteemed him,
appointed him Administrator of Lánlíng (蘭陵),
and had him assist in defending Jīngkǒu (京口).
On the day Yǐ Sì (乙巳),
Bàxiān (霸先) issued a proclamation to all within and without,
listing Sēngbiàn's (僧辯) crimes,
and further stating:
"The object of our military action
is only Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) and his son and brothers.
All other relatives and partisans
will not be questioned."
On the day Bǐng Wǔ (丙午),
Zhēnyáng Hóu Yuānmíng (貞陽侯淵明) abdicated, and retired to his residence.
(Kǎoyì (考異) says: The *Liáng Shū* (梁書) records:
"In the ninth month,
on the day Bǐng Wǔ (丙午),
the emperor ascended the throne.
In the tenth month,
on the day Jǐ Sì (己巳),
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed."
According to the *Cháng Lì* (長曆),
Bǐng Wǔ (丙午) was the twenty-ninth day of the ninth month;
Jǐ Sì (己巳) was the twenty-second day of the tenth month.
How could the era name and general amnesty only occur twenty-four days after the enthronement?
Perhaps on Bǐng Wǔ (丙午) he resumed his title as Prince of Liáng (梁王),
and only in the tenth month did he ascend the imperial throne.
The *Diǎn Lüè* (典略) states:
"On the day Dīng Wèi (丁未),
Zhēnyáng Hóu (貞陽侯) was deposed and sent to his residence."
Now we follow the *Chén Shū* (陳書).)
He was urged to ascend the throne.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Jǐ Yǒu (己酉),
the Prince of Jìn'ān (晉安王) ascended the imperial throne,
declared a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
The era name was changed to Shàotài (紹泰).
He appointed Zhēnyáng Hóu Yuānmíng (貞陽侯淵明) as Sītú (司徒) [Grand Minister over the Masses],
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Jiàn'ān (建安公).
He announced to Qí (齊) that:
"Sēngbiàn (僧辯) secretly plotted usurpation and rebellion,
therefore he was executed.
We still request to be your subject,
and forever your vassal state."
Qí (齊) sent Executive Assistant Sīmǎ Gōng (司馬恭) to ally with the Liáng (梁) people at Lìyáng (歷陽).
26 On the day Xīn Hài (辛亥),
the Lord of Qí (齊) went to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
27 On the day Rén Zǐ (壬子),

Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先) was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) [Director of the Imperial Secretariat], Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì (都督中外諸軍事) [Grand Marshal of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital], Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) [General of Cavalry], and Administrator of Yáng (揚) and Nán Xú (南徐) Prefectures.
On the day Guǐ Chǒu (癸丑),
Yífēng Hóu Xún (宜豐侯循) was made Tàibǎo (太保) [Grand Protector],
Jiàn'ān Gōng Yuānmíng (建安公淵明) was made Tàifù (太傅) [Grand Tutor],
Qújiāng Hóu Bó (曲江侯勃) was made Tàiwèi (太尉) [Grand Commandant],
and Wáng Lín (王琳) was made Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) [General of Cavalry] and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司) [Establishing a Bureau with the Same Privileges as the Three Excellencies].
When the Emperor first became Prince of Liáng (梁王),
all other feudal princes were promoted in office,
but Wáng Lín (王琳) alone was not mentioned. Could it be that Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) was already aware that Wáng Lín (王9) could not be controlled?
28 On the day Wù Wǔ (戊午),
the Emperor's birth mother Xià Guì (夏貴) was honored as Huáng Tàihòu (皇太后) [Empress Dowager],
Dù Kān 杜龕, relying on Wáng Sēngbiàn's 王僧辯 power,
had long been disrespectful towards Chén Bàxiān 陳霸先.
In Wúxìng 吳興,
he often used the law to punish Bàxiān's 霸先 clan,
which Bàxiān 霸先 deeply resented.
When he was about to plot against Sēngbiàn 僧辯,
he secretly sent his nephew Qiàn 蒨 back to Chángchéng 長城.
Chángchéng 長城 county
was where Bàxiān 霸先 and his clan had lived for generations.
In the third year of Tàikāng 太康 of the Jìn 晉 dynasty (282 CE),
Chángchéng 長城 county was established by dividing Wūchéng 烏程.
It belonged to Wúxìng Jùn 吳興郡,
which is modern-day Chángxìng Xiàn 長興縣 in Húzhōu 湖州.
It is seventy *lǐ* (li) northwest of Húzhōu 湖州.
Qiàn 蒨
is pronounced *qì* (qi), seventh tone.
After Sēngbiàn 僧辯 died,
Kān 龕 occupied Wúxìng 吳興 and resisted Bàxiān 霸先.
Wéi Zài 韋載, the Administrator of Yìxìng 義興, responded by offering his commandery.
*Kǎoyì* 考異 says: *Diǎnlüè* 典略 records
"Wéi Zài 韋載."
We follow the *Liáng Shū* 梁書 and *Chén Shū* 陳書 here.
We note that if *Diǎnlüè* 典略 indeed records
"Wéi Zài 韋載,"
then it would be consistent with the *Liáng Shū* 梁書 and *Chén Shū* 陳書,
making a textual variation unnecessary.
Sēngbiàn's 僧辯 younger brother
also held the city and resisted.
*Kǎoyì* 考異 says: *Nán Shǐ* 南史 states,
"Sēngzhì 僧智 fled to Rèn Yuē 任約."
We follow *Diǎnlüè* 典略 here.
Having only a few hundred soldiers,
Dù Kān 杜龕 sent his general Dù Tài 杜泰 with five thousand elite troops to attack suddenly.
The officers and soldiers looked at each other, their faces pale with fright.
Qiàn 蒨 remained calm and composed,
and his orders became clearer,
which finally settled the morale of the troops.
Tài 泰 attacked fiercely day and night,
but after several tens of days,
he failed to conquer the city and retreated.
Bàxiān 霸先 sent Zhōu Wényù 周文育 to attack Yìxìng 義興.
The soldiers from the counties subordinate to Yìxìng 義興 were all Bàxiān's 霸先 former troops,
skilled in using crossbows.
Wéi Zài 韋載 captured several tens of them,
bound them with long chains,
and ordered his trusted aides to supervise them,
making them shoot at Wényù's 文育 army.
He promised:
"Anyone who fails to hit twice in ten shots will be executed."
Therefore, each shot killed someone,
and Wényù's 文育 army gradually retreated.
Zài 載 then established a stockade outside the city, relying on the water,
and they held their ground for several tens of days.
Dù Kān 杜龕 sent his cousin Běisǒu 北叟 to lead troops to resist the battle.
Běisǒu 北叟 was defeated
and returned to Yìxìng 義興.
Bàxiān 霸先 heard that Wényù's 文育 army was at a disadvantage.
On the day of Xīnwèi 辛未,
he personally requested permission to launch an eastern expedition,
leaving Hóu Āndū 侯安都, the Inspector of Gāozhōu 高州, and Dù Léng 杜稜, the Inspector of Shízhōu 石州, to guard the imperial palace and ministries.
*Wǔdài Zhì* 五代志 states: Yǒngpíng Jùn 永平郡:
The Liáng 梁 dynasty established Shízhōu 石州,
and after the Suí 隋 dynasty, it was renamed Téngzhōu 藤州.
Sòng Bái 宋白 says: Téngzhōu 藤州
was governed from Tánjīn Xiàn 鐔津縣,
which was Měnglíng Xiàn 猛陵縣 during the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
On the day of Jiǎxū 甲戌,
the army arrived at Yìxìng 義興.
On the day of Bǐngzǐ 丙子,
they captured its water stockade.
Xú Sìhuī 徐嗣徽, the Inspector of Qiáozhōu 譙州 and Qínzhōu 秦州, had a cousin named Sìxiān 嗣先,
who was Wáng Sēngbiàn's 王僧辯 nephew.
After Sēngbiàn 僧辯 died,
Sìxiān 嗣先 fled to Sìhuī 嗣徽.
Sìhuī 嗣徽 then offered his prefecture to the Qí 齊 dynasty.
*Wǔdài Zhì* 五代志 states: Qīngliú Xiàn 清流縣 of Jiāngdū Jùn 江都郡:
The Liáng 梁 dynasty established Xīnchāng Jùn 新昌郡 and Qiáozhōu 譙州.
Also,
Liùhé Xiàn 六合縣:
Qín Jùn 秦郡 and Qínzhōu 秦州 were established.
Sìhuī 嗣徽 secretly allied with Rèn Yuē 任約, the Inspector of Nányùzhōu 南豫州,
and with five thousand elite troops, they took advantage of the weakness to attack Jiànkāng 建康.
On that day,
they attacked and occupied Shítóu 石頭.
Their cavalry reached the imperial palace gates.
Hóu Āndū 侯安都 closed the gates and hid the banners and flags,
showing weakness.
He ordered the city:
"Anyone who climbs the ramparts to spy on the rebels will be executed!"
By evening,
Sìhuī 嗣徽 and others withdrew their troops back to Shítóu 石頭.
Āndū 安都 prepared for battle during the night.
At dawn,
Sìhuī 嗣徽 and others arrived again.
Āndū 安都 led three hundred armored soldiers and opened the East and West Yèmén 掖門 gates to sally forth and fight.
The main south gate of Táichéng 臺城 was Duānmén 端門,
and its left and right gates were called the East and West Yèmén 掖門.
*Shuài* 帥
is read as *shuài* (shuai).
Sìhuī 嗣徽 and others fled back to Shítóu 石頭,
no longer daring to approach Táichéng 臺城.
Chén Bàxiān 陳霸先 sent Wéi Zài's 韋載 clan cousin, Huì 翽, carrying a letter to persuade Zài 載.
On the day of Dīngchǒu 丁丑,
Zài 載 and Dù Běisǒu 杜北叟 both surrendered.
Bàxiān 霸先 treated them generously,
making Huì 翽 supervise Yìxìng Jùn 義興郡,
and keeping Zài 載 by his side
to consult with him.
Bàxiān 霸先, armor-clad, returned to Jiànkāng 建康,
and sent Zhōu Wényù 周文育 to attack Dù Kān 杜龕
and relieve Chángchéng 長城.
General Huáng Tā 黃他 attacked Wáng Sēngzhì 王僧智 in Wújùn 吳郡 but failed.
Bàxiān 霸先 sent Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn 寧遠將軍 Péi Jì 裴忌 to assist him.
Jì 忌 selected elite soldiers from his unit, traveled lightly and at double speed,
proceeding directly from Qiántáng 錢塘 to Wújùn 吳郡.
According to records, Chén Bàxiān 陳霸先 returned from Yìxìng 義興 to Jiànkāng 建康
and sent Péi Jì 裴忌 to assist Huáng Tā 黃他 in attacking Wújùn 吳郡.
Traveling directly from Qiántáng 錢塘 to Wújùn 吳郡
is not the correct route;
Qiántáng 錢塘 must be a mistake.
*Qù* 趣
is pronounced *qù* (qu), seventh tone.
Upon arriving at the city,
they beat drums and shouted to approach it.
Sēngzhì 僧智, thinking that a large army had arrived,
fled in a light boat to Wúxìng 吳興.
Jì 忌 entered and occupied Wújùn 吳郡,
and was then made its Administrator.
In the eleventh month,
on the day of Jǐmǎo 己卯,
Qí 齊 sent five thousand troops to cross the river and occupy Gūshú 姑孰
in response to Xú Sìhuī 徐嗣徽 and Rèn Yuē 任約.
Chén Bàxiān 陳霸先 sent Xú Dù 徐度, the Inspector of Hézhōu 合州, to erect a stockade at Yěchéng 冶城.
On the day of Gēngyín 庚寅,
Qí 齊 again sent Zhái Zǐchóng 翟子崇, the Inspector of Ānzhōu 安州, Liú Shìróng 劉士榮, the Inspector of Chǔzhōu 楚州, and Liǔ Dámó 柳達摩, the Inspector of Huáizhōu 淮州.
*Wǔdài Zhì* 五代志 states: Zhōnglí Jùn 鍾離郡:
The Liáng 梁 dynasty established Běixúzhōu 北徐州,
which Qí 齊 renamed Chǔzhōu 楚州,
administering Dìngyuǎn Xiàn 定遠縣.
The Liáng 梁 dynasty established Ānzhōu 安州.
In Shānyáng Xiàn 山陽縣 of Jiāngdū Jùn 江都郡, there was Huáiyīn Jùn 淮陰郡;
the Eastern Wèi 東魏 established Huáizhōu 淮州.
Zhái 翟
is pronounced *zhái* (zhai), second tone.
Húshù 胡墅
was on the north bank of the Great River,
opposite Shítóuchéng 石頭城.
*Shù* 墅
is pronounced *shù* (shu), fourth tone.
Zài 載 said:
"If the Qí 齊 army divides its forces and first occupies the routes to the Sāwú 三吳 region
and takes over the eastern territories,
then the situation will be lost.
Now, we must quickly build a city on the former fortifications of Hóu Jǐng 侯景 in Huáinán 淮南
to facilitate transportation and supply to the east.
Huáinán 淮南
refers to south of the Qínhuái 秦淮 River.
*Shū* 輸
is pronounced *shū* (shu), first tone;
the same applies to the following *yùnshū* 運輸 (transportation).
Then
the heads of the Qí 齊 generals can be brought within ten days."
Bàxiān 霸先 followed his advice.
On the day of Guǐwèi 癸未,
he ordered Hóu Āndū 侯安都 to launch a night attack on Húshù 胡墅.
*Kǎoyì* 考異 says: *Diǎnlüè* 典略 records
"Jǐsì 己巳."
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first day of this month was Wùyín 戊寅;
there was no Jǐsì 己巳.
We follow the *Chén Shū* 陳書 here.
Rénwēi Jiāngjūn 仁威將軍 Zhōu Tiěhǔ 周鐵虎 cut off Qí 齊 transportation
and captured Zhāng Lǐngzhōu 張領州, their Inspector of Běixúzhōu 北徐州.
*Wǔdài Zhì* 五代志 states: Lángxié Jùn 琅邪郡:
Běixúzhōu 北徐州 was previously established here.
He ordered Dù Léng 杜稜 to guard it.
The Qí 齊 people erected two stockades at Cāngmén 倉門 and Shuǐnán 水南.
Cāngmén 倉門
refers to the gate of Shítóu Cāngchéng 石頭倉城 (Stone Storage City).
Shuǐnán 水南
refers to south of the Qínhuái 秦淮 River.
On the day of Rénchén 壬辰,
Xiāo Guǐ 蕭軌, the Grand Commandant of Qí 齊, led troops to garrison north of the river.
At first,
Qí Píng Qín Wáng Guī Yàn was orphaned young.
Gāozǔ ordered Qīnghé Zhāowǔ Wáng Yuè to raise him.
Guī Yàn
was a distant cousin of Gāo Huān.
Guī Yàn's father, Huī,
had an old favor owed to Huān.
Therefore, Huān pitied his orphan and commanded Yuè to raise him.
Huān's temple name was Gāozǔ.
Guī Yàn held this in his heart.
When Xiǎnzǔ ascended the throne,
Guī Yàn became Lǐngjūn Dàjiàngjūn,
and was greatly favored;
Yuè thought Guī Yàn was grateful to him,
and relied on him even more.
Yuè had repeatedly led troops and achieved merits,
gaining a formidable reputation,
but his nature was extravagant and opulent,
fond of wine and women.
He built a mansion in the south of the city.
The south of the city
was the south of Yèchéng.
Guī Yàn slandered him to the Emperor, saying:
"Qīnghé presumes to imitate the imperial palace,
constructing a Yongxiang,
only lacking the palace gate."
The Emperor consequently disliked him.
The Emperor took the singing woman Xue Shì into his harem.
Yuè had previously, through her elder sister, welcomed her to his residence.
One night, the Emperor went on an outing to Xue Shì's house.
Her elder sister begged for her father to be made Sītú.
The Emperor was greatly enraged,
hung her elder sister,
and sawed her to death.
He reprimanded Yuè for his promiscuity.
Yuè did not admit guilt.
The Emperor grew more enraged.
On the Yǐhài day,
he ordered Guī Yàn to poison Yuè.
Yuè pleaded that he was innocent.
Guī Yàn said:
"Drink it, and your family will be spared."
He drank it and died.
He was buried and posthumously honored according to the rites.
Consort Xue was favored by the Emperor.
After some time,
the Emperor suddenly recalled her affair with Yuè.
Without cause, he cut off her head,
hid it in his bosom,
and went out to East Mountain for a feast.
As the toasts began,
he suddenly took out her head
and threw it onto a platter,
dismembered her body,
and played a pipa with her thigh bone.
The entire assembly was greatly shocked.
The Emperor then picked it up,
and facing it, shed tears, saying:
"A beautiful woman is hard to find again!"
Hàn Lǐ Yánnián sang:
"In the north there is a beautiful woman,
unique in her generation and standing alone.
One glance overturns a city,
a second glance overturns a state.
How can one not know that overturning cities and overturning states,
a beautiful woman is hard to find again!"
He let down his hair, walked, and wept as he followed it.
On the Jiǎchén day,
Xú Sìhuī and others attacked Yěchéngzhà.
Chén Bàxiān led elite armored troops and sallied out from Xīmíngmén to attack them.
Sìhuī and others were greatly defeated.
He left Liǔ Dámó and others to defend the city,
and went himself to Cáishí to welcome Qí reinforcements.
Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ Yífēng Hóu Xún was appointed Tàibǎo,
and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ Qǔjiāng Hóu Bó was appointed Sīkōng,
both summoned to serve at court.
Xún accepted the Tàibǎo title but declined to enter court.
Bó was already planning to raise an army,
and thus did not accept the appointment.
Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Wáng Lín invaded Wèi.
Wèi Dàjiāngjūn Dòulú Níng resisted him.
In the Xìngshì Zhì: The Dòulú originally had the surname Mùróng.
Yān Běidì Wáng Jīng surrendered to Wèi.
Northerners called those who returned in allegiance "Dòulú,"
and thus it was bestowed as their surname.
In the twelfth month,
on the Guǐchǒu day,
Hóu Āndū launched a surprise attack on Qínjùn,
destroying Xú Sìhuī's palisade,
and capturing several hundred people.
He seized Sìhuī's belongings,
obtaining his pipa and hawk,
and sent an envoy to return them, saying:
"Yesterday I arrived at your brother's place and obtained these;
now I return them to you."
Sìhuī was greatly frightened.
On the Bǐngchén day,
Chén Bàxiān erected a floating bridge opposite Yěchéng,
crossed all his troops,
and attacked the two palisades south of the water.
These were the Cāngmén and Shuǐnán palisades.
Bàxiān commanded his troops to fight fiercely,
setting fire to the palisades.
The Qí troops were thoroughly defeated,
jostling each other for boats.
Thousands drowned.
Their shouts shook heaven and earth.
All their boats and ships were captured.
On that day,
Sìhuī and Rèn Yuē led over ten thousand Qí land and naval troops back to occupy Shítóu.
Bàxiān sent troops to Jiāngníng,
occupying strategic strongholds.
Sìhuī and others, with their land and naval forces, dared not advance.
They camped at Jiāngníng Pǔkǒu.
Bàxiān sent Hóu Āndū to lead a naval force to attack and defeat them.
Sìhuī and others escaped in single skiffs,
and all their military supplies and equipment were captured.
On the Jǐwèi day,
Bàxiān attacked Shítóu from all four sides.
There was no water in the city;
a sheng of water cost one bolt of silk.
On the Gēngshēn day,
Dámó sent an envoy to request peace with Bàxiān,
and also requested a hostage.
The request for peace while also requesting a hostage
was because he feared returning without merit and being punished,
thus wishing to use a hostage as an excuse.
Zhì
pronunciation is zhì.
The food supply was cut off,
and all court officials wished to make peace with Qí,
requesting to send Bàxiān's nephew Tánlǎng as a hostage.
Tánlǎng was then garrisoned in Jīngkǒu.
Cóng
is pronounced cái yòng fān.
Tán
is pronounced kǔ hán fān.
"Now the gentlemen in office wish to rest their shoulders on Qí.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: When Zhèng Chéng Gōng was ill,
Zǐsì requested to rest his shoulders on Jìn.
Dù Yù commented: Using a burden as a metaphor.
You say I love Tánlǎng
and do not care for the state.
Now I decisively send Tánlǎng,
abandoning him to the enemy's court.
The Qí people are untrustworthy.
They will consider us weak
and surely break the alliance.
If the Qí invaders come,
gentlemen, you must fight with all your might for me!"
Bàxiān knew that the Qí people were ashamed of their lack of success,
and would certainly send more troops to return,
so he first used this to warn the multitude,
demanding that they fight to the death.
Wèi
is pronounced yú wěi fān.
"Yǔ"
should be
"yǐ",
then the meaning of the text is clear and smooth.
[Chapter: The Yǐ shíyī Háng Běn correctly writes
"yǐ";
Tuìzhāi also noted this.]
Outside the city
refers to outside Shítóu City.
Xú Sìhuī and other southerners indulged in their southern ways,
and Liǔ Dámó and other northerners indulged in their northern ways.
Indulging in their north and south
means acting as they pleased.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
Bàxiān arrayed his troops at the southern gate of Shítóu,
sending the Qí people back north.
Xú Sìhuī and Rèn Yuē both fled to Qí.
The captured Qí horses, weapons, boats, and rice
were beyond counting.
The Qí lord executed Liǔ Dámó.
On the Rénxū day,
Qí Hézhōu Zhǎngshǐ Wūwán Yuǎn fled from Nánzhōu back to Lìyáng.
Liú Xù said: Qí and Liáng made peace,
establishing Hézhōu in Lìyáng Jùn.
The Wūwán probably descended from the Wūwán tribe of Dōnghú,
and adopted it as their surname.
Chén Sì, Magistrate of Jiāngníng,
and Cáo Lǎng, Huángmén Shìláng, occupied Gūshú and rebelled.
Bàxiān ordered Hóu Āndū and others to suppress them.
Bàxiān feared that Chén Tánlǎng might flee,
so he personally led infantry and cavalry to Jīngkǒu to welcome him.
Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ Liú Yuányǎn led his subordinates, several thousand strong, to pledge allegiance to Wáng Lín.
Wèi appointed Shìzhōng Lǐ Yuǎn as Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè.
37 Wèi's Yìzhōu Cìshǐ, Yǔwén Guì, sent Qiáo Yān’s nephew, Zǐsì, to entice Yān,
offering him the position of Dàjiàngjūn.
Yān refused,
and executed Zǐsì.
Guì was enraged
and attacked him.
Yān moved his garrison from Dōngsuìníng to Diànjiāng.
Jìn established Suìníng Commandery southeast of Dédòng County.
Wǔdài Zhì states: Suìníng Commandery's Fāngyì County,
during the Liáng dynasty, was called Xiǎoxī,
and Dōngsuìníng Commandery was established.
Diànjiāng County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Bā Commandery.
During the Liáng dynasty, it was the seat of Chǔzhōu.
During the Suí dynasty, it was Yúzhōu.
Diàn,
pronounced Dié.
38 Initially,
Jìn'ān Mín Chén Yǔ,
when Wú established Dōng'ān County,
Jìn Wǔdì renamed it Jìn'ān.
In Tàikāng three years,
Jìn'ān Commandery was established by dividing Jiàn'ān.
Wǔdài Zhì states: Jiàn'ān Commandery's Nán'ān County was formerly called Jìn'ān.
The present-day Quánzhōu is that area.
His son, Bǎoyīng, was resourceful and cunning,
and the people of the commandery feared and obeyed him.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Jìn'ān Tàishǒu, Bīnhuà Hóu Yún, ceded the commandery to Yǔ.
Yǔ was old,
but managed the commandery's affairs,
and ordered Bǎoyīng to command the troops.
At that time, the eastern region suffered from famine,
but Jìn'ān alone was prosperous.
Bǎoyīng frequently went out by sea,
raiding and plundering Lín'ān, Yǒngjiā, and Kuàijī.
Shěn Yuē Zhì states: Wú divided Yúháng to create Línshuǐ County.
Jìn Wǔdì, in Tàikāng first year, renamed it Lín'ān.
Wǔdài Zhì has no Lín'ān Commandery or Lín'ān County,
only Yúháng Commandery.
Shù,
pronounced Suǒjiǎo.
Chāo,
pronounced Chǔjiāo.
Kuài,
pronounced Gōngwài.
Because of this, he was able to become rich and powerful.
When Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Shìzǔ then appointed Yǔ as Jìn'ān Tàishǒu.
When Chén Bàxiān became regent,
Yǔ requested to pass his position to Bǎoyīng,
and Bàxiān granted it.
This laid the groundwork for the later rebellion of Chén Bǎoyīng in Mǐnzhōng.
39 In this year,
Wèi's Yǔwén Tài influenced Huái'ān Wáng Yù to submit a memorial requesting to reduce his noble rank to gōng, in accordance with ancient customs.
Thereupon, all the imperial princes were demoted to gōng.
40 Tūjué Mùgān Kèhán attacked Rórán Dèng Shúzi,
and annihilated them.
Shúzi gathered their remnants and fled to Wèi.
Mùgān crushed the Yàndá in the west,
drove the Qìdān in the east,
and annexed the Qìgǔ in the north.
Qìgǔ
is the same as Táng's Jiégǔ.
Táng Shū states: Xiájiásī,
the ancient Jiānkūn Kingdom,
is also called Jūwù,
or Jiégǔ.
Probably, Jiānkūn was corrupted into Jiégǔ,
later known as Gěgǔ,
also called Gějísī.
Qìdān,
pronounced Qīqì,
also Chī.
Qìgǔ,
pronounced Kǔjié.
Its territory stretched from Liáohǎi in the east
to Xīhǎi in the west,
spanning ten thousand li in length.
South of the desert, five to six thousand li were all subject to it.
Mùgān, relying on his strength,
requested that Dèng Shúzi and others be executed in Wèi.
Envoys continuously arrived on the road.
Tàishī Tài handed over Shúzi and over three thousand others to their envoys,
and they were all killed outside Qīngmén.
The first gate to the south of the eastern side of Cháng'ān city was called Bàchéng Mén.
The common people, seeing the gate's green color,
named it Qīngchéng Mén,
or Qīngmén.
Qín Dōnglíng Hóu Zhào Píng planted melons outside Qīngmén,
which is that very place.
Shǐ,
pronounced Shūlì.
41 Initially,
Wèi's Tàishī Tài, considering the excessive number of officials in Hàn and Wèi,
ordered Sū Chuò and Shàngshū Lìng Lú Biàn to revise the six official positions based on the Rites of Zhōu.
Tàipíng first year (bǐngzǐ, 556)
In this year, the reign title was changed to Tàipíng in the ninth month.
1 In spring,
first month,
on the Dīngchǒu day,
Wèi first established the six official positions.
Yǔwén Tài was appointed Tàishī and Dàzhǒngzǎi.
Zhùguó Lǐ Bì was appointed Tàifù and Dàsītú.
Zhào Guì was appointed Tàibǎo and Dàzōngbó.
Those above Zōngbó
held the positions of the Three Dukes concurrently with the Six Ministers.
Běishǐ, Lú Biàn Zhuàn states: One Tàishī, one Tàifù, and one Tàibǎo were established,
these are the Three Gū.
Yú Jǐn was appointed Dàsīkòu,
Hóu Mòchén Chóng was appointed Dàsīkōng.
All other officials
imitated the Rites of Zhōu.
2 On the Wùyín day,
a general amnesty was declared.
Those who had conspired with Rèn Yuē and Xú Sìhuī
were all pardoned.
On the Guǐwèi day,
Chén Bàxiān sent Cóngshì Zhōngláng Jiāng Gàn to persuade Xú Sìhuī to return south,
but Sìhuī arrested Gàn and sent him to Qí.
3 Chén Qiàn and Zhōu Wényù combined their forces to attack Dù Kān in Wúxīng.
Kān was brave but lacked strategy,
and was habitually drunk.
His general, Dù Tài, secretly communicated with Qiàn and the others.
Kān was defeated in battle against Qiàn and the others.
Tài then persuaded Kān to surrender,
and Kān agreed.
His wife, Wáng Shì, said:
Wáng Shì was Sēngbiàn’s daughter.
"Bàxiān's enmity is so deep,
how can peace be sought!"
Thereupon, she used her private wealth for rewards and recruitment,
and again attacked Qiàn and the others,
greatly defeating them.
Later, Dù Tài surrendered to Qiàn.
Kān was still drunk and unaware.
Qiàn sent men to carry him out
and executed him in front of the Xiàngwáng Temple.
Xiàng Yǔ rose in Wúxià,
hence later generations built a temple for him in Wúxīng.
Kǎoyì states: Liáng Shū:
"In Tàipíng first year,
first month, Guǐwèi day,
Dù Kān surrendered,
and an imperial edict ordered his death."
Chén Shū:
"In Shàotài first year,
twelfth month,
Dù Kān surrendered with the city;
the next year,
first month, Guǐwèi day,
Dù Kān was executed in Wúxīng.
Kān's cousin, Běisǒu, and Sīmǎ Shěn Xiàodūn were also ordered to die."
Diǎnlüè:
"In Wèi Gōngdì second year,
twelfth month,
Qiàn ordered Liú Chéng and others to attack Kān,
greatly defeating him,
whereupon Kān surrendered;
the next year,
first month, Dīnghài day,
Zhōu Tiěhǔ sent Dù Kān to sacrifice to the god of Xiàngwáng,
and ordered strongmen to pull Kān from his seat.
His cousin, Běisǒu, and Sīmǎ Shěn Xiàodūn were also ordered to die."
Now following Nán Shǐ.
Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Biāo had always been favored by Wáng Sēngbiàn,
and did not side with Bàxiān.
In the second month,
on the Gēngxū day,
Chén Qiàn and Zhōu Wényù led light troops to raid Kuàijī.
Biāo's forces were defeated
and fled into Ruòyé Shān.
Jiǎnwén Dì Dàbǎo first year,
Zhāng Biāo raised troops in Ruòyé Shān.
Yé,
pronounced Yé.
Dōngyáng Tàishǒu Liú Yì supplied provisions to Qiàn.
Bàxiān appointed Yì as Jìnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jìnzhōu was established due to Jìnyún Shān.
Wǔdài Zhì states: Chǔzhōu's Kuòcāng County has Jìnyún Shān.
Jìn,
pronounced Jìn.
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Hóu Tián had originally served Wáng Sēngbiàn,
and also held troops in Yùzhāng and Jiāngzhōu,
not siding with Bàxiān.
Bàxiān appointed Zhōu Wényù as Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and sent him to lead troops to attack Pénchéng.
On the Gēngshēn day,
he also dispatched Hóu Āndū and Zhōu Tiěhǔ to lead a naval force to erect a barricade at Liángshān,
to guard against Jiāngzhōu.
4 On the Guǐhài day,
Xú Sìhuī and Rèn Yuē attacked Cǎishí,
captured the garrison commander, Míngzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Huáijūn, and sent him to Qí.
Wǔdài Zhì states: Rìnán Commandery's Jiāogǔ County,
during the Liáng dynasty, Míngzhōu was established.
Zhāng Huáijūn probably held the title of Cìshǐ while guarding Cǎishí.
5 The lord of Hòu Liáng attacked Hóu Píng in Gōng'ān.
Píng and Chángshā Wáng Sháo led their troops back to Chángshā.
Wáng Lín sent Píng to guard Bāzhōu.
6 In the third month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
an edict was issued for the mixed use of ancient and modern coins.
7 On the day Wùxū,
Qí sent Yítóng Sānsī Xiāo Guǐ, Kùdí Fúlián, Yáo Nánzōng, Dōngfāng Lǎo, and others, who, joining forces with Rèn Yuē and Xú Sìhuī, led 100,000 troops to invade.
They came out of Zhákǒu.
Zhákǒu
is Zhá Jiāngkǒu,
located 150 lǐ southwest of modern Hézhōu Lìyáng Xiàn,
bordering Wúwéi Jūn,
which is the ancient Rúxūkǒu.
Sòng Bái said: From Lúzhōu southeast to Zhákǒu,
now called Xīnfùkǒu,
is 384 lǐ.
The opposite bank is the old Nánlíng Xiàn territory,
and across the river is Fánchāng Xiàn.
Chén Bàxiān's zhàngnèi dàngzhǔ Huáng Cóng met them with a counterattack
and defeated them.
Dàngzhǔ
refers to the commander of brave warriors who charge and break the enemy lines.
Bàxiān sent Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ Shěn Tài and others to Hóu Āndū,
to jointly hold Liángshān to resist them.
Zhōu Wényù attacked Pénhchéng,
but had not yet taken it.
He was recalled.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Dīngsì,
Bàxiān went to Liángshān to inspect and comfort the various armies.
8 On the day Yǐchǒu,
Qí Yítóng Sānsī Lóu Ruì suppressed the Lǔyáng Mán,
and defeated them.
9 Hóu Āndū launched a light cavalry raid on Qí Xíngtái Sīmǎ Gōng in Lìyáng.
Kǎoyì says: Liáng Shū states:
"On the day Rénwǔ,
Āndū raided Gōng."
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first day of this month was Yǐsì,
there was no Rénwǔ.
Tens of thousands were captured.
10 Wèi Tàishī Tái was married to Fúyì Gōngzhǔ, the younger sister of Xiàowǔ,
and she gave birth to Lüèyáng Gōng Jué.
Yáo Fūrén gave birth to Níngdū Gōng Yù.
Yù was the eldest among the sons.
Wǔdài Zhì: Xīchéng Jùn Ānkāng Xiàn
was formerly called Níngdū.
Yù,
pronounced as "yú liù."
Zhǎng,
pronounced as "zhī liǎng";
same below.
When Tái was about to establish an heir,
he said to the gōngqīng:
"I wish to establish my son by the嫡 (legitimate wife),
but I fear Dà Sīmǎ has doubts. How should I proceed?"
The crowd remained silent,
no one spoke.
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Lǐ Yuǎn said:
"To establish a son by the嫡 and not by seniority
is what the Chūnqiū Gōngyáng Zhuàn says.
What does Your Grace doubt?
If you suspect Xìn,
please allow me to behead him first."
He then drew his sword and rose.
Tái also rose,
saying:
"Why go to such an extreme!"
Xìn then also made a self-explanation to clear himself,
and Yuǎn stopped.
Thereupon,
all the gōng followed Yuǎn's suggestion.
When Yuǎn went outside,
he bowed and apologized to Xìn, saying:
"When facing a great matter, I had no choice but to act that way!"
Xìn also thanked Yuǎn, saying:
"Today, I relied on your decision in this important deliberation."
So, Jué was established as the heir apparent.
11 Tàishī Tái conducted a northern inspection tour.
12 In the fifth month,
the Qí people summoned Jiàn'ān Gōng Yuānmíng,
falsely promising to withdraw their troops.
Kǎoyì says: Diǎnlüè states:
"In the fifth month,
the Qí lord was drinking in Dōngshān,
threw his cup in a fit of rage,
summoned Wèi Shōu before him,
and dictated an imperial decree,
intending to personally lead an army westward to attack Cháng'ān,
and ordered Shàngdǎng Wáng Huàn to lead troops to attack Liáng.
Thus, Huàn invaded the south."
However, there is no mention of this matter in the imperial annals of Liáng, Chén, Běi Qí, or in Huàn's biography,
so we omit it here.
On the day Guǐwèi,
Yuānmíng died of a carbuncle on his back.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Qí troops departed from Wúhú.
On the day Gēngyín,
they entered Dānyáng Xiàn.
This Dānyáng Xiàn was an ancient county of Hàn,
not the Dānyáng Xiàn of present-day Zhènjiāng Fǔ.
According to Shěn Yuē's records,
in the third year of Tàikāng of Jìn Wǔdì,
Yúhú Xiàn was established by splitting Dānyáng Xiàn.
Yúhú
is modern Tàipíng Zhōu.
The territory of Dānyáng Xiàn should be northeast of Tàipíng Zhōu.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
they reached the old site of Mòlíng.
Shěn Yuē said: The original seat of Mòlíng was 60 lǐ from the capital.
The present-day Gùzhì Cūn is that site.
In the ninth year of Yìxī of Jìn Āndì, its seat was moved to the capital,
at Dòuchǎng.
Dòuchǎng
is like what is called a training ground today.
In the middle of Xiánhé of Jìn Chéngdì,
an edict ordered all troops, internal and external, to practice in the southern suburban field,
and it was thus named Xìchǎng,
also known as Dòuchǎng.
Dānyáng Jì says:
Qín Shǐhuáng excavated Fāngshān,
and where it was cut became a canal,
which is the present-day Huái Shuǐ.
Mǎmù
is a place for pasturing horses.
13 Qí Hànyáng Jìnghuái Wáng Qià died.
Qià
was the younger brother of the Qí lord.
14 On the day Xīnchǒu,
the Qí people built a pontoon bridge and stockades across the Huái River to cross their troops.
By night, they reached Fāngshān.
Xú Sìhuī and others arrayed their ships at Qīngdūn,
extending to Qī Jī,
to cut off Zhōu Wényù's return route.
Wényù advanced with shouts and drumbeats,
and Sìhuī and his forces could not stop him.
By dawn,
Wényù counterattacked Sìhuī.
Sìhuī's brave general Bào Pēng alone brought up the rear with a small boat.
Wényù engaged him on a single small boat,
leapt into his ship,
beheaded Pēng,
and then towed his ship back.
Sìhuī's army was greatly terrified,
and consequently left their boats in Wúhú,
marching on foot from Dānyáng.
Chén Bàxiān recalled Hóu Āndū and Xú Dù, both of whom returned.
He recalled the troops from Liángshān back to Jiànkāng
to defend against the Qí army.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
the Qí troops advanced from Fāngshān and reached Nítáng.
Nítáng is east of Táichéng.
Jiànkāng was shaken with alarm.
The emperor personally led the imperial guards out to garrison Chánglè Sì,
and all within and without the palace were put on alert.
Bàxiān resisted Sìhuī and others at Báichéng.
