how dare I refuse?"
Jǐn had always been Tài's peer.
Hù used to bow to him.
At this point,
Jǐn stood up and said:
"If you, Duke, preside over the military and state,
we, Jǐn and others, will all have someone to rely on."
Thereupon, he bowed twice.
The various dukes, constrained by Jǐn,
also bowed twice.
Thus, the collective decision was finally settled.
Hù brought order to internal and external affairs
and appeased both civil and military officials,
whereupon people's hearts settled.
33 In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnchǒu day,
Fēngchéng Hóu Tài fled to Qí.
Qí made him Yǒngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the south, Línglíng Jùn was called Yǒngzhōu.
Qí making Tài Yǒngzhōu Cìshǐ,
it is unknown where this Yǒngzhōu was located.
This is a Qí edict.
He left his general Pān Chúntuó to oversee Yǐngzhōu,
and returned to Chángshā himself.
The Wèi people returned his wife and children.
34 On the Rénzǐ day,
the Qí ruler issued an edict stating:
"At the end of the Wèi dynasty, heroes gathered their local communities,
and through connections and influence,
each established zhōujùn.
Dividing the large and combining the small,
public and private expenses became burdensome,
and the population decreased compared to former days."
Chóurì
means "former days."
"Moreover, the distant and wild regions are inclined towards transformation."
Yàohuāng
refers to the ancient "yaofu" and "huangfu" systems.
"Yao" means
to form good ties and trust, and thus submit.
"Huang" means
that their submission is distant and irregular.
Yao,
pronounced yī yáo fān.
"A settlement of a hundred households
hastily establishes a zhōu name;
a population of three families
emptily claims a jùn title."
This refers to the zhōujùn established by the Liáng dynasty at its end, located between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
"Matters have come to naught."
Thereupon, three zhōu and
one hundred fifty-three jùn were merged and abolished.
35 An edict divided four jùn of Jiāngzhōu to establish Gāozhōu.
The four jùn were probably Línchuān, Ānchéng, Yùníng, and Bāshān.
Because their land was west of the southern Jiāng,
backed by mountains and facing water,
occupying high ground and overlooking depths,
it was named Gāozhōu accordingly.
Huáng Fǎ was appointed Cìshǐ,
stationed in Bāshān.
36 In the twelfth month,
on the Rénshēn day,
Qǔjiāng Hóu Bó was made Tàibǎo.
37 On the Jiǎshēn day,
Wèi buried Āndìng Wén Gōng.
On the Dīnghài day,
the heir-apparent Jué was enfeoffed as Zhōu Gōng with the land of Qíyáng.
Qíyáng
is the land of Fúfēng.
In the past, the Zhōu dynasty arose in Qízhōu,
and thus its state was named.
Yǔwén assisted Wèi
and modeled laws and institutions after Zhōu.
Therefore, the Wèi court ministers enfeoffed him with Zhōu,
intending a transfer of power.
38 At first,
during Hóu Jǐng's Rebellion,
a Línchuān local, Zhōu Xù, raised troops within the commandery.
Línchuān,
was the land of Nánchéng County, Yùzhāng Commandery, during the Hàn dynasty.
In the Later Hàn, the northern border of Nánchéng was separated to form Línrǔ County.
In the second year of Tàipíng (257 CE) during Sūn Liàng's reign in Wú,
the eastern parts of Yùzhāng, Nánchéng and Línrǔ counties, were separated to establish Línchuān Commandery.
During the Suí and Táng dynasties, it became Fǔzhōu.
Xù's subordinate generals were all powerful clans from within the commandery,
mostly arrogant and overbearing.
Xù restrained them.
All the generals resented him,
and conspired together to kill him.
Xù's kinsman, Dí,
was foremost in bravery within the commandery.
The multitude supported him as their leader.
Dí was originally of humble origin,
and feared the people of the commandery would not submit to him.
Considering that Zhōu Fū, from the same commandery, had high and prominent family prestige,
Dí humbled himself to befriend him.
Fū also served Dí very respectfully.
Dí occupied Shàngtáng.
"Shàngtáng",
in the next scroll it is written as
"Gōngtáng".
There must be an error in one of them.
According to the "Biography of Zhōu Dí" in the *Chén Shū*,
the character "gōng"
is correct.
The court appointed Dí as the Inspector of Héngzhōu,
concurrently holding the position of Línchuān Administrator.
He merely held the position of Línchuān Administrator while concurrently serving as Inspector of Héngzhōu.
(Others) all abandoned agriculture,
and gathered together to become bandits.
Only Dí's subordinates alone engaged in agriculture and sericulture,
each having surplus stores.
His administration and decrees were strict and clear.
"Jiào"
refers to edicts.
Orders issued by prefectures and commanderies were called "jiào".
Those in want from other commanderies all relied on him for provisions.
Dí's nature was simple and unadorned,
and he did not care for formal decorum.
He was ordinarily barefoot.
Although he had soldiers and guards stationed outside,
and female entertainers inside,
he would twist ropes and split bamboo strips,
as if no one else was around.
He was slow in speech but his character was trustworthy and sincere.
All the people of Línchuān followed him.
39 The Qí dynasty built the Great Wall from Xīhé and Zǒngqín Garrison.
Notes on Discrepancies say: It was already mentioned last June that the Great Wall was built,
but the place names,
and length, were different,
so it is not known if this is one event or two separate events.
The *Běiqí Shū* and *Běi Shǐ* both record it this way.
Now both are preserved.
In total, the sections built before and after, from east to west, amounted to over three thousand *lǐ*.
On average, there was one garrison every ten *lǐ*.
At strategic points, prefectural towns and garrisons were established,
totaling twenty-five locations.
40 Yǔwén Hù of Wèi, considering that the Duke of Zhōu was young and weak,
wished to expedite his enthronement to assume his proper position in order to stabilize public sentiment.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Emperor Gōngdì of Wèi, by imperial edict, abdicated the throne to Zhōu.
Emperor Dàowǔdì of Wèi changed his reign era to Huángshǐ in the twenty-first year of Tàiyuán (396 CE) during Emperor Xiàowǔ of Jìn's reign,
and after twelve generations, until the third year of Yǒngxī (534 CE) during Emperor Xiàowǔdì's reign, moved west.
Wèi was consequently divided into Eastern and Western (Wèi).
Western Wèi then lasted for three more generations.
In total, fifteen generations,
one hundred and sixty years, and then perished.
Jìběi Gōng Dí presented the emperor's imperial seal and official ribbons.
Emperor Gōngdì went to reside at the Grand Marshal's residence.
Punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ, re-collated by Niè Chóngqí.
